Sectarianism, hostility between Catholic and Protestant communities that shapes politics, ran through Irish public life at the end of the 1840s. Orange marches were the most visible sign, and Dolly's Brae showed how quickly they could turn violent.

The Orange Order was founded in 1795 near Loughgall, County Armagh, after the Battle of the Diamond, a clash between Protestant and Catholic groups in September 1795. It aimed to defend the Protestant ascendancy (the dominant position of Protestants in Irish life) and the link with Britain.

The Order was dissolved in 1836 after a parliamentary inquiry into its spread in the army, so it lost its formal organisation. It was revived in Ulster in the 1840s, which is why Orange marches were a live issue by 1849.

On 12 July 1849 an Orange procession returning from Lord Roden's estate at Tollymore passed through Dolly's Brae, near Castlewellan, County Down. Armed Catholics, known as Ribbonmen (members of a secret agrarian and Catholic society), had gathered there.
Fighting followed and Catholics were killed, though the number is disputed because estimates vary widely. Catholic houses nearby were burned.
An inquiry criticised the Orangemen and Lord Roden, and he lost his place on the commission of the peace (the body of local magistrates).
The Party Processions Act (1850) banned party processions, such as Orange and Catholic marches, in an attempt to stop clashes like Dolly's Brae. It was repealed in 1872.
Sectarian feeling also came from Britain. A decision by the Pope in 1850 provoked a British law that Irish Catholics saw as an insult, and it drew them closer to tenant-right politics.

In September 1850 Pope Pius IX restored the Catholic hierarchy in England with territorial titles (bishops named after English places), making Wiseman archbishop of Westminster. Lord John Russell, the Whig prime minister, condemned this as papal aggression, a phrase widely used by the press and his supporters.

The Ecclesiastical Titles Act (1851) banned Catholic bishops from taking territorial titles in the United Kingdom. It was never enforced, so it achieved little except anger, and it was repealed in 1871.
Irish Catholic MPs opposed the Act, and the Catholic Defence Association was formed in 1851 to resist it. This pushed Catholic politics and tenant-right politics together.
Do not confuse this Act with the Irish Church Act of 1869. The Titles Act (1851) dealt with Catholic bishops' titles, while the 1869 Act disestablished the Church of Ireland.
A new alliance of tenant-right campaigners and Catholic MPs promised independent opposition in the 1850s. Then it collapsed when two of its leading MPs took government jobs.

The Irish Tenant League was founded in Dublin in 1850 by Charles Gavan Duffy, Frederick Lucas, a Catholic convert and editor of the Tablet, and others, with support from Presbyterian ministers in Ulster. Its Ulster backers show it was not only a Catholic movement.

It demanded fair rent, fixity of tenure (the right not to be evicted while paying rent) and free sale of the tenant's interest (the right to sell the tenancy). The label 'the three Fs' became common only later.

Archbishop John MacHale of Tuam and Fr Patrick Lavelle supported the League, but the clergy were not united, so its backing was limited. Cardinal Cullen and many bishops distrusted priests in politics.

At the 1852 general election more than 40 MPs were returned pledged to independent opposition (refusing office from any government that did not meet tenant demands). They formed the Independent Irish Party.

In December 1852 William Keogh became solicitor-general for Ireland (a law officer of the government) and John Sadleir a Lord of the Treasury in Lord Aberdeen's government. This broke the pledge of independence.
Duffy, Lucas and others denounced them as betrayers because they had broken the pledge, so the party fractured as members drifted to the Liberals.
Lucas died in 1855 and Duffy emigrated to Australia in 1855, ending the movement. Sadleir, a financier, died by suicide in 1856 after the Tipperary Bank collapsed, and Keogh became a judge.
Many nationalists lost faith in parliamentary action because the party's own MPs had sold out, which helped turn young men towards Fenianism.

Fenianism was a transatlantic revolutionary movement that aimed to end British rule by force and set up an Irish republic. It grew from the disappointments of the 1840s and 1850s, and its creed is known as physical force republicanism.

Physical force republicanism is the belief that Ireland could win independence as a republic only by armed rebellion. Fenianism (the movement of the IRB and the Fenian Brotherhood) was its main expression in this period.

The Irish Republican Brotherhood (IRB) was founded in Dublin on 17 March 1858 by James Stephens, with Thomas Clarke Luby and others, as an oath-bound secret society. The oath and secrecy were meant to protect members from informers.

In New York in the same year John O'Mahony founded the Fenian Brotherhood, which raised money and men in the United States. Its name came from the Fianna, the legendary warrior bands of Irish tradition. 'Fenians' covers both organisations.

The roots of Fenianism lay in the failed 1848 rising, bitterness left by the Famine, disillusion with parliamentary politics after the Independent Irish Party, and the experience of emigrants in exile.

The IRB was organised in circles under local leaders and reported to Stephens, who took the title of Chief Organiser of the Irish Republic. Members were mainly artisans (skilled workers), clerks, shopkeepers and farmers' sons, and the IRB tried to recruit soldiers in the British army.

The funeral of Terence Bellew MacManus, a 1848 rebel who died in California, drew a very large crowd in Dublin in November 1861 and showed Fenian strength. Cardinal Cullen refused to let his body lie in the Pro-Cathedral.
The movement's newspaper, the Irish People, began in Dublin in 1863, with Luby, John O'Leary and Charles Kickham as editors and Jeremiah O'Donovan Rossa as manager.
American Fenians included many veterans of the American Civil War (1861-65), whose military experience raised hopes that a rising in Ireland could succeed.
The government struck at the Irish organisation before it was ready. The rising Stephens had promised was delayed, his followers removed him, and when it came in 1867 it was quickly crushed.
In September 1865 the police raided the offices of the Irish People and arrested Luby, O'Leary, Rossa and Kickham. In November Stephens himself was arrested.
Stephens escaped from Richmond Prison in Dublin in November 1865 with the help of warders and fellow Fenians, and went abroad.
Habeas corpus (the right not to be held without trial) was suspended in Ireland in February 1866, allowing arrest without trial and making it easier to round up suspected Fenians.
In 1866 Stephens was in the United States, where he postponed the rising he had promised. His own followers deposed him in December 1866.
The rising took place in early March 1867 in snow and bad weather. Small risings in Dublin (Tallaght), Cork, Limerick and Tipperary were crushed within days.
Informers had compromised the plans, and the Fenians lacked arms and trained leaders, so the rising had little chance once the government knew what was coming.
Even after 1867 failed in Ireland, Fenian actions in England and Canada kept the movement in the public eye. They also showed its transatlantic reach and cost it sympathy in Britain.
On 18 September 1867 in Manchester, Fenians freed two prisoners, Thomas Kelly and Timothy Deasy, from a prison van, and a police sergeant, Charles Brett, was shot dead.

Three men, William Allen, Michael Larkin and Michael O'Brien, were hanged in Manchester on 23 November 1867 for Brett's death. They became known as the Manchester Martyrs and were mourned across Ireland, while Kelly and Deasy escaped.

On 13 December 1867 a Fenian bomb blew a hole in the wall of Clerkenwell prison in London in an attempt to free a prisoner. About a dozen people in the street nearby were killed, which turned British opinion against the Fenians.
Michael Barrett was hanged for Clerkenwell in 1868, the last public execution in England, so the affair ended a long tradition.
American Fenians raided Canada from the United States, at Ridgeway in June 1866 and again in 1870. Both raids failed to win Canadian territory, but they show the movement's international dimension.

Cardinal Cullen and most bishops condemned Fenianism as a secret society (the Church forbade oath-bound societies), and many priests denounced it from the altar. This cut Fenian support among devout Catholics.
Stephens founded and led the IRB and built the first lasting revolutionary organisation. His leadership failed at the decisive moment, when the promised rising did not come.

Born in Kilkenny in 1825, he took part in the 1848 rising at Ballingarry under William Smith O'Brien, where he was wounded, and escaped to Paris. Ballingarry gave him both his revolutionary experience and his sense that the next attempt needed better organisation.
He returned to Ireland in 1856 and travelled the country, then founded the IRB in 1858 as its Chief Organiser.
He worked with O'Mahony's Fenian Brotherhood in America, which sent money and supporters to Ireland, so the IRB had resources it could not raise at home.
He organised the Irish People in 1863 and built a network through secret circles, including recruitment in the British army.
He was arrested in November 1865 and escaped from Richmond Prison within a fortnight. In 1866 he was in the United States and failed to deliver the rising he had promised.
His own followers deposed him in December 1866, and he spent most of the rest of his life abroad, mainly in Paris. He returned to Ireland in 1891 and died in Dublin in 1901.
Contemporaries saw him as a gifted organiser and a charismatic figure, but also as autocratic (ruling without consulting others), secretive and over-promising.
Historians credit him with building the first lasting revolutionary organisation, while criticising his indecision and his failure to lead the rising he had promised.
Kickham combined Fenian leadership with literature. He was a writer and editor more than a conspirator, and he paid for his role with prison.

Born in Mullinahone, County Tipperary, in 1828, he was left almost deaf and with poor sight by a gunpowder accident in boyhood. This made him an unlikely soldier, so his contribution was in writing and ideas.
He wrote for The Nation, the Young Ireland newspaper, and joined the Fenians, becoming one of the editors of the Irish People.
Arrested in 1865, he was sentenced in 1866 to fourteen years' penal servitude (imprisonment with hard labour). He was released in 1869 on grounds of ill health.
He wrote the novel Sally Cavanagh (1869), about the eviction of a tenant family, and Knocknagow, or The Homes of Tipperary (1873), his most popular novel.
He became a prominent member of the IRB's Supreme Council (its governing body) in the 1870s and died at Blackrock, County Dublin, in 1882.
A practising Catholic, he was caught between his faith and the bishops' condemnation of the movement, and he rejected the clerical condemnation.
Contemporaries admired his courage, honesty and endurance in prison, which won respect even from people who disliked Fenianism.
Historians see him as the voice of rural, literary Fenianism, the link between nationalism and literature.
After the Fenian scare, William Gladstone's first government (1868-74) set out to remove Irish grievances. The first target was the Church of Ireland, the state church of a mostly Catholic country.
Gladstone became prime minister in December 1868 and is reported as saying "My mission is to pacify Ireland", which is his stated aim.
The Manchester executions and Clerkenwell showed that Irish discontent could threaten Britain, which made reform politically urgent.
The Irish Church Act (1869) disestablished the Church of Ireland, ending its status as the state church, with effect from 1 January 1871. The Act was passed in 1869 but took effect only then.

The Church lost most of its endowments (property and income), which passed to a commission, while serving clergy received compensation. This removed an old grievance for Catholics and Presbyterians, who had paid for a church they did not attend.
Fenian prisoners were released in stages from 1869, with a conditional pardon for most in 1871, as the amnesty movement (the campaign for their release) grew.
Gladstone's second target was the land system, in which tenants had no legal security and landlords could raise rents or evict. The Land Act went some way but stopped short of real security.
The Irish Land Act (1870) gave legal force to the Ulster custom, the tenant's right to sell his interest to an incoming tenant. Before this the custom depended on landlords' goodwill.
It gave tenants compensation for disturbance when evicted for reasons other than non-payment of rent, and compensation for improvements they had made to the holding.
Its Bright clauses, named after John Bright, offered loans to help tenants buy their holdings, but few did.

The Act did not stop evictions for non-payment, and landlords could still raise rents, so it failed to give security of tenure. A landlord could in effect evict by demanding more rent than the tenant could pay.
Isaac Butt founded the Home Government Association in 1870, the next constitutional step, as nationalists looked to self-government by peaceful means.
Judgements turn on whether Fenianism or constitutional reform did more to change Irish politics by 1870. Good answers state a view first and weigh the evidence on both sides.
Fenian achievement: it revived physical force republicanism, built a disciplined oath-bound organisation across Ireland, Britain and America, and kept the republican idea alive.

Fenian limits: it failed militarily in 1867, was heavily infiltrated by informers, split into rival groups, was condemned by the Church and had small support, so it could not threaten British rule directly.
Contemporary views: the British government saw a conspiracy; many Irish nationalists admired the martyrs; the Church saw a sinful secret society; bishops and moderate nationalists feared it.

Later views: historians argue that Fenianism, through the Manchester executions and Clerkenwell, prompted Gladstone's reforms. Its tradition lived on in the IRB, which helped organise the Easter Rising of 1916.
Liberal achievement: disestablishment ended Protestant privilege in the Church, and the Land Act gave the first legal recognition of tenants' claims.
Liberal limit: the Land Act failed to prevent eviction for non-payment, and neither measure answered demands for tenant ownership or self-government.

Overall: Fenianism or Liberal reform? Violence gave the push, but reform could not remove the grievances behind violence. Reform changed more in law, while Fenianism changed the mood and the tradition.

After Catholic Emancipation (1829) removed the main political barrier, the Church was free to expand and organise. From the 1840s Catholic practice became more disciplined and more uniform, a change the historian Emmet Larkin named the devotional revolution (in an article of 1972).
Church building expanded sharply after Emancipation, with new parish churches and cathedrals raised on money collected from the faithful, so the Church's growth was visible in every town and parish.

St Patrick's College, Maynooth (founded 1795) trained most of the clergy, and by mid-century the priests were better educated and under closer episcopal discipline, so each bishop could direct his priests far more firmly.

Religious orders and congregations (communities of nuns and brothers) grew, and they ran schools, hospitals and orphanages. Examples are the Christian Brothers (Edmund Rice began his school in Waterford in 1802), the Presentation Sisters (Nano Nagle, Cork), the Sisters of Mercy (Catherine McAuley, Dublin, 1831) and the Sisters of Charity.

Parish missions, which were short, intense series of sermons given by Redemptorists, Vincentians and Jesuits, spread new forms of piety. These included the rosary, novenas (nine days of prayer), confraternities (lay prayer societies), benediction and devotion to the Sacred Heart and the Virgin Mary.

Larkin argued that weekly Mass attendance rose from about a third of Catholics before the Famine to a large majority (around 90 per cent) by the 1870s. Treat this as his claim, because other historians give a higher pre-Famine figure and argue that the change began earlier.

Historians link the change to the Famine (1845 to about 1850), which killed and removed the poor who had been least regular in practice, so those who remained were more observant. It also left a more prosperous farmer class and strengthened clerical authority.
The debate is whether the change was imposed from above by the clergy or grew from below.

Catholic identity became tied to nationality, because the Church's building programme and schools made it the main institution of the Catholic majority, who had been poor and shut out of power under the Penal Laws.

Protestants were a minority, and they responded to Catholic revival in two ways. Some pursued evangelical revival and conversion, while others defended Protestant privilege and loyalty to the Union. The result was sectarianism, meaning hostility between religious communities that shaped politics and everyday life.
Evangelicalism was a Protestant revival stressing personal conversion, Bible reading and missionary work. It grew in the Church of Ireland and among Presbyterians and Methodists from the 1820s.

The Second Reformation was the evangelical drive of the 1820s to 1850s to convert Catholics, using Bible societies, schools and missions. The name suggests a second attempt to spread Protestantism after the sixteenth-century Reformation.
Edward Nangle's mission colony on Achill Island (1834) and the Irish Church Missions (founded 1849 by Alexander Dallas) were well-known examples of this conversion drive.

In the Famine years, Protestant soup kitchens that required conversion led Catholics to coin the term souperism, meaning buying converts with food. The bitterness lasted for generations because it seemed to exploit starving people.

The Orange Order, founded in 1795, was dissolved in 1836 and revived in the 1840s. It expressed Protestant loyalty to the Crown, the Union and Protestant ascendancy (the dominance of Protestants in Irish life).

Henry Cooke, a Presbyterian minister and Ulster evangelical, promoted an alliance of Presbyterians and Anglicans against O'Connell and Catholic nationalism. This joined two Protestant groups that had often been rivals.
A great evangelical revival swept Ulster in 1859, which shows that Protestant revival continued strongly into the 1850s.

The Church of Ireland remained the established church (the state-backed church) until the Irish Church Act of 1869 took effect on 1 January 1871, although it served only a small minority of the population.

Young Ireland, the group of nationalists around the newspaper The Nation, tried to define what the Irish nation was in terms of culture and history rather than religion. Yet while they praised the Irish past, the Irish language was in steep decline.
Young Ireland's idea of the nation was a community of shared history, culture and territory, so it could include Protestants as well as Catholics. This was meant to rise above sectarianism.
The Nation, founded in October 1842 by Thomas Davis, Charles Gavan Duffy and John Blake Dillon, used poems, ballads and history to teach this idea to ordinary readers.
Cultural nationalism in the 1840s encouraged the study of Irish history, manuscripts and antiquities (the remains and records of the past), but it did not stop the language declining.
O'Connell, though a native Irish speaker from Kerry, saw English as the language of progress, and had little interest in saving Irish.

The 1851 census, the first to record Irish speakers, found about 1.5 million, nearly a quarter of the population, reporting that they spoke it, so the language was still widely spoken despite its decline.
Irish was strongest in the west and south-west, where the Famine killed or scattered the poorest and the most Irish-speaking, so the heartland of the language lost people fastest.
The national schools, set up in 1831, taught through English, and parents saw English as the key to a job or to emigration, so many chose not to pass Irish on to their children.

Cullen was the architect of the Romanisation of the Irish Church and the leading Catholic figure of the period. Romanisation meant bringing the Irish Church into line with Rome, and he drove it as a direct participant.
Born near Ballitore, County Kildare, on 27 April 1803, he studied in Rome, was ordained there in 1829 and became rector of the Irish College in Rome in 1832.

Career: Archbishop of Armagh (appointed December 1849, installed early 1850), Apostolic Delegate (the pope's representative with special powers) in 1850, Archbishop of Dublin in 1852, first Irish cardinal in 1866; he died on 24 October 1878. He presided at the Synod of Thurles in 1850.

As a direct participant he drove the devotional revolution: ultramontane devotion (loyalty to the pope), strict clerical discipline, church building, religious orders, parish missions and Catholic schools. He opposed the Queen's Colleges and backed the Catholic University founded under Newman in 1854.

In politics he distrusted Young Ireland, the Tenant League (a farmers' organisation for tenant rights) and priests in politics, because he thought agitation threatened the Church's discipline. He also opposed the Fenians, a revolutionary movement.

In 1861 he refused to let the body of Terence Bellew MacManus, a Young Irelander who died in San Francisco, lie in the Pro-Cathedral in Dublin, which showed his hostility to revolutionary nationalism.
He favoured co-operation with the Liberals, and he supported Gladstone's Liberals. He did not oppose disestablishment of the Church of Ireland.
He shaped events but was also shaped by them. The Famine-weakened Church and Rome's backing gave him his chance, while MacHale's resistance and the failure of the Catholic University limited him.

Contemporaries differed. Supporters admired his devotion to Rome and his organisation, but nationalists and some bishops, notably MacHale, resented his authority. Historians see him as the central figure of the devotional revolution but debate whether he shaped Catholic political conservatism or reflected what the Church wanted.
A synod is a formal meeting of a Church's bishops. The Synod of Thurles was called to unify an Irish Church that had run its dioceses independently for decades and to settle the education question.

It was the first national synod of the Irish Catholic Church for about two centuries, the last having been held at Kilkenny in 1642, which is why it was seen as a landmark. Do not confuse the two synods.
Before 1850 each bishop ran his own diocese with little central direction, so clerical discipline and practice varied widely from place to place.

Rome wanted uniform practice and a clear Irish policy. Pope Pius IX also wanted the Church to resist the secular and mixed (non-denominational) education of the Queen's Colleges, the university colleges set up in 1845 at Belfast, Cork and Galway and opened in 1849.
The bishops were divided. John MacHale, Archbishop of Tuam, opposed the colleges outright, while Daniel Murray, Archbishop of Dublin (he died in 1852), was more willing to accept them.

A papal rescript (an official reply from Rome, here from Propaganda Fide) of 1847 had condemned the Queen's Colleges. The Famine had also weakened the old order and made Church leaders open to reform.
Rome made Paul Cullen Archbishop of Armagh in December 1849 and Apostolic Delegate in 1850, so that he could organise the Synod and carry out Roman policy.
The Synod met in Thurles, County Tipperary, from 22 August to 9 September 1850. Its decrees (binding rulings) aimed to give the Church one policy on education, worship and discipline.
Cullen presided as Apostolic Delegate, so the meeting carried the pope's authority, and the bishops of the four provinces attended.
The decrees condemned the Queen's Colleges as dangerous to faith and morals and forbade clergy to take posts in them, because mixed education was seen as a threat to Catholic belief.
It ordered the setting up of a Catholic University, which opened in Dublin in 1854 with John Henry Newman as rector, so that Catholics would have an acceptable alternative.
It laid down uniform liturgical practice (the form of worship) and church discipline, with the Roman rite followed everywhere.
It regulated clerical dress, behaviour and the conduct of the sacraments, and increased the bishops' authority over priests.
It discouraged priests from political agitation, notably at the altar and election meetings, so the pulpit would not be used for politics.
Opposition came from MacHale and from lay Catholics and liberal clergy, who supported the Queen's Colleges and resented Roman control.
Rome supported Cullen, and the Synod's decrees were later confirmed there.
The Synod began the Romanisation of the Irish Church and shaped Catholic life and politics for the rest of the century. Its education policy, however, met with limited success.
Ultramontanism was the belief in strong papal authority over national churches and bishops, and the Synod made it the guiding principle of Irish Catholicism.

Romanisation meant closer links with Rome, uniform liturgy and devotions in the Roman style, and a centralised Church under the bishops. It is related to, but not the same as, ultramontanism and the devotional revolution.
The Catholic University failed to attract many students and had no state-recognised degrees.
Most Catholics who wished to attend university still entered Trinity College or the Queen's Colleges, and the bishops later campaigned for a Catholic university with state support.
Cullen's authority over the bishops made him the dominant Catholic voice in public affairs for the next quarter-century, because he could speak for a united hierarchy.
Contemporaries disagreed. Protestants and some liberal Catholics saw an alien and authoritarian power, while supporters saw order and renewal.
Historians such as Emmet Larkin treat the Synod as the start of the devotional revolution, while others argue that the changes were already under way.

Aikenhead founded the Religious Sisters of Charity, an early Irish order of nuns devoted to work among the poor outside the convent. She was a participant, as founder, in the growth of Catholic social services.
Born in Cork on 19 January 1787 to a Protestant father and a Catholic mother, she became a Catholic.

Guided by Archbishop Daniel Murray of Dublin, she trained with the Bar Convent in York and founded the Religious Sisters of Charity in 1815. Do not confuse her with Catherine McAuley, who founded the Sisters of Mercy in 1831.
The Sisters visited the poor in their homes, ran schools and nursed the sick, which took nuns out of the enclosed convent and into the community.
In 1834 she opened St Vincent's Hospital in St Stephen's Green, Dublin, described as the first hospital in Ireland run by nuns, which treated the sick poor regardless of creed.
She directed the order from Stanhope Street in Dublin, the mother house, much of the time as an invalid, until her death on 22 July 1858.
As founder she was a participant in the growth of Catholic social services, not merely a witness, because she created the institutions herself.
Contemporaries admired her charity and her courage in running an institution while an invalid, for example in managing St Vincent's Hospital.
Historians see her as a pioneer of active women's religious life and Catholic nursing and as a founder of institutions that shaped Irish health care.
Carleton was the leading chronicler of the Irish peasantry before the Famine. He was a witness to the world he described rather than a political actor.
Born in 1794 at Prillisk, County Tyrone, the son of a Catholic Irish-speaking tenant farmer, he went to Dublin in about 1817 and began writing. He died in 1869.
He first wrote for the Christian Examiner, an evangelical Protestant paper, so his early stories had an anti-Catholic edge.
Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry appeared in 1830, with a second series in 1833, describing wakes, pilgrimages, faction fights and hedge schools (informal open-air schools).
Fardorougha the Miser (1839) and The Black Prophet (1847), a novel of famine, explored the life of the rural poor.
As a witness rather than a political actor, he recorded rural life without leading a movement. He received a government pension in 1848.
Contemporaries admired his realism, but some Catholic nationalists resented his early anti-Catholic writing.
Historians value him as a source on pre-Famine rural life and as a realist who showed the violence and poverty as well as the humour.
Davis shaped the cultural idea of the Irish nation. Here only his cultural role is covered;

Born in Mallow in 1814 into a Protestant family, he was educated at Trinity College Dublin and called to the bar in 1838. In 1842 he co-founded The Nation with Charles Gavan Duffy and John Blake Dillon.
His songs and ballads, including A Nation Once Again and The West's Asleep, put history and patriotism into popular verse, so that people who did not read history could still learn it.
He urged the study and teaching of Irish history and the Irish language.
He argued that the nation should unite Catholic, Protestant and Dissenter (a Protestant outside the Church of Ireland) on a shared Irish identity.
He died of scarlet fever on 16 September 1845, aged 30, so his career was very short.
Contemporaries saw him as a model of principled youth, but critics thought his ideas were idealistic.
Historians credit him with laying the cultural foundations of Irish nationalism, though his appeal to Protestants was limited.
Irish writers, musicians and antiquarians (scholars of the past) drew on Irish history and folklore. Their work showed that Irish culture could win recognition even in a poor, divided country.
Thomas Moore's Irish Melodies, published in numbers from 1808 to 1834, set Irish airs to words and were popular in Britain, Ireland and America.
James Clarence Mangan (1803–1849) wrote poems for The Nation, including Dark Rosaleen (1846), adapted from the Irish. He died of cholera in June 1849, in the Famine years.

George Petrie, painter and antiquarian, showed in an essay (of 1833, published in 1845 as The Ecclesiastical Architecture of Ireland) that the round towers were Christian in origin, and he collected traditional music in The Ancient Music of Ireland (1855).

The Ordnance Survey (the official mapping of Ireland) in the 1820s and 1830s employed scholars in its topographical department under Larcom's organisation. John O'Donovan and Eugene O'Curry recorded Irish place names and studied manuscripts, working with Petrie.
O'Donovan edited the Annals of the Four Masters (1848-51), and O'Curry became professor of Irish history and archaeology at the Catholic University (1854).
The Royal Irish Academy (1785) and the Royal Dublin Society (1731) supported scholarship.
The Famine drew writers to themes of hunger, eviction and emigration, as in Carleton's The Black Prophet.
Irish scientists made international contributions in mathematics, physics and astronomy, often in difficult conditions. This showed Irish capacity despite poverty.

William Rowan Hamilton, Royal Astronomer of Ireland at Dunsink, discovered quaternions (a kind of number used to describe rotations in three dimensions) on 16 October 1843 while walking by the Royal Canal at Broom Bridge, Dublin.

William Parsons, 3rd Earl of Rosse, built a six-foot reflecting telescope (one that gathers light with a mirror) at Birr Castle, known as the Leviathan. Completed in 1845, it was the largest in the world until 1917.
With it he saw the spiral shape of the galaxy M51, later known as the Whirlpool Galaxy, in 1845.
Nicholas Callan, a priest and professor of natural philosophy at Maynooth, built an induction coil in 1836 (a device that produces high voltage from a low-voltage current) and developed batteries.
George Boole was the first professor of mathematics at Queen's College Cork, from 1849, and published The Laws of Thought (1854), the basis of Boolean algebra, a way of handling logic.
Robert Kane, a chemist and first president of Queen's College Cork, wrote The Industrial Resources of Ireland (1844), urging the use of science for economic development.
The Queen's Colleges, the Royal Dublin Society and the Royal Irish Academy supported such work.
Judgements turn on whether the changes were imposed from above or grew from below. Examiners reward paired points that set achievements against limits and contemporary views against later ones.
Achievement of the devotional revolution: a more disciplined clergy, more churches and schools, and a strong Catholic identity, because the Church was now organised across the whole country.
Limit: the Church's authoritarian leadership split bishops, alienated liberal Catholics and Protestants, and left the Catholic University weak, so its gains were uneven.
Contemporary view: Protestants saw papal domination, while supporters saw renewal after the Famine.

Later view: historians broadly agree that the Church's changes gave Catholics a shared religious identity that later nationalism drew on. Larkin saw a revolution from the 1840s, while others argue that the change began earlier and grew from below.
Achievement of the arts and sciences: Moore, Carleton, Petrie, O'Donovan, Hamilton, Rosse and Boole won international recognition.
Limit: the Famine and emigration weakened the rural culture and the Irish language that cultural nationalists wished to save, because they removed the people who spoke and sang it.

By 1870 Irish nationalism had tried repeal, rebellion and Fenian conspiracy without success. Home Rule offered a constitutional, moderate alternative that might attract Protestants as well as Catholics.
The Act of Union (in force from 1 January 1801) abolished the Irish parliament, so Irish MPs sat at Westminster and decisions on Irish affairs were made there.
Daniel O’Connell’s Repeal campaign (the demand to undo the Union) peaked in 1843 but failed in the 1840s, and the Young Ireland rising of 1848 collapsed.

The Fenians (the IRB, the Irish Republican Brotherhood) wanted an Irish republic won by force. Their rising of 1867 was crushed, but the arrest and trial of Fenians produced a public movement in 1869 for an amnesty (a pardon) for political prisoners, and Isaac Butt took part in it.
Clan na Gael was the Irish-American Fenian organisation, so it later became an important source of money and support for Irish nationalists.

Gladstone became Prime Minister in December 1868 saying his mission was to pacify Ireland. He passed the Irish Church Act (1869), disestablishing the Church of Ireland (ending its status as the state church, from 1871), and a first Land Act in 1870.
Those reforms did not satisfy nationalists, because the 1870 Land Act gave tenants compensation for improvements and for disturbance but no secure tenure or fair rents, so tenants stayed insecure.

In the 1860s Irish MPs were mostly Liberals or Conservatives rather than members of a separate Irish party, so nobody pressed for self-government in a united way. This gap is what the Home Rule movement set out to fill.
Three ideas run through this whole topic. Knowing exactly what each means as used here stops you mixing Butt’s moderate aims with Fenian separatism.

Home Rule meant an Irish parliament for domestic affairs within the United Kingdom and empire. It was not separation, which is why it differed from the Fenian demand for a republic and could appeal to moderates and Protestants.

Democracy here means government by elected representatives answerable to voters. In this period it showed itself in the secret ballot, in a disciplined party that spoke for its voters, and in the widening of the voters’ influence.

Political agitation means organised public pressure through meetings, newspapers, petitions, elections and parliamentary tactics, rather than violence. O’Connell had used it to build a mass base, and Home Rulers hoped to do the same.

Isaac Butt, a Protestant barrister and former Conservative MP, founded the movement in Dublin in 1870. His own journey from unionism to nationalism shows why Home Rule could appeal to people who rejected the Fenians.

Butt (1813–1879) was born in Co. Donegal, the son of a Church of Ireland clergyman. He became a Dublin barrister, professor of political economy at Trinity College Dublin, and a Conservative MP in the 1850s and 1860s.

He began as a unionist opponent of O’Connell, but defending the Young Irelanders in 1848 and Fenian prisoners in the 1860s turned him towards nationalism. He also took part in the 1869 amnesty campaign.

Butt’s programme was federal: a parliament in Dublin would deal with domestic affairs, while Westminster kept control of the empire, defence and foreign policy. This kept Ireland inside the empire, which made the plan acceptable to moderates.
Butt’s method was constitutional: persuasion, parliamentary motions and public meetings, and a rejection of physical force, so he could appeal to people who would never back the Fenians.
Butt turned an idea into an organisation in three steps: an association, a by-election win and a parliamentary party. The Ballot Act helped by making it safer for voters to back him.
The Home Government Association was founded in Dublin in May 1870. Its members included Conservatives, Liberals, former Repealers and Catholic moderates, so it was a deliberately cross-party body.
Butt won the Limerick City by-election in 1871 as a Home Ruler, which showed that the new demand could win votes.
The Ballot Act (1872) introduced the secret ballot, so landlords and agents could no longer watch how tenants voted. This reduced landlord pressure on voters.
The Galway election petition of 1872 heard evidence of priests pressing voters, so clerical pressure was also a concern.
A national conference in Dublin in November 1873 replaced the Association with the Home Rule League. Its MPs were to form a distinct, independent party pledged to act together.

Remember the three similar names, because they are easily confused: the Association (1870) was the first body, and the League (1873) was the party. The Home Rule Confederation of Great Britain was a separate body that organised Irish voters in England.
The 1874 election produced the first sizeable Home Rule party, but Butt could not make it effective. His failure explains why more aggressive tactics followed.

In the 1874 general election about 60 of the 103 Irish seats were won by Home Rulers (59 or 60 by different counts). They were the first sizeable Home Rule party, though Disraeli’s Conservatives won the election and governed to 1880.

Many of those MPs were Liberals who had taken the Home Rule label for local reasons and did not vote consistently with the party. The League had no pledge or whip to bind them, which meant weak discipline and mixed loyalties.
Butt’s Home Rule motions at Westminster were heavily defeated, and neither Disraeli’s Conservatives nor the Liberals took them seriously.
Butt relied on persuasion, hoping to win English sympathy through argument, but the Commons treated Irish business as a nuisance rather than a priority.

The electorate was small (it was widened only in 1884), and the League had little money or local organisation. The movement therefore remained a body of MPs and lawyers with few roots among tenant farmers.
Younger members, including Joseph Biggar and John O’Connor Power (MP for Mayo from 1874 and an IRB member), believed politeness had failed and demanded a more aggressive policy.

Butt’s health and finances weakened his authority, as he was often in debt. William Shaw succeeded him as party leader in 1879, and Butt died on 5 May 1879, by which time leadership had passed in practice to the obstructionists.
Obstruction was the first tactic that forced the House of Commons to take Irish MPs seriously. It showed that a few determined members could use the rules of the House against the government.
Obstruction meant prolonged speeches, endless amendments and procedural objections designed to jam Commons business until the government gave way.
Joseph Biggar (1828–1890) began obstruction in 1874–75. He was a Belfast-born Presbyterian provision merchant, a member of the IRB, and MP for Cavan from 1874.
Charles Stewart Parnell was elected MP for Meath in a by-election in April 1875. He joined obstruction in earnest from 1877, and the South Africa Bill debate of 1877 is an early example.
Parnell also broke with Butt’s caution by refusing, in the Commons, to call the executions of the Manchester Martyrs (Fenians executed in November 1867) murder. This won him Fenian respect.
In August 1877 Parnell replaced Butt as president of the Home Rule Confederation of Great Britain, the body that organised Irish voters in English cities.

In January–February 1881 Irish MPs obstructed the coercion bill in a sitting of about 41 hours (31 January–2 February). The Speaker, Henry Brand, ended the debate on his own authority, and the Commons adopted the closure rule (a way to end debate) in 1882.

Both main parties condemned obstruction as an abuse of parliament, and Butt himself deplored it. It still showed that a small, disciplined group could make the House unworkable, which is why the rules were changed.
The New Departure linked three forces that had worked apart: Fenian-minded nationalists, constitutional Home Rulers and the land-reform movement. Hard times in the countryside made the link possible.
The agricultural depression from 1877 (poor harvests, falling prices and cheap American grain imports) brought a threat of evictions and a crisis in the countryside.

Michael Davitt was a Fenian sentenced in 1870 to fifteen years for arms trafficking. Released on licence in December 1877 after about seven years, he travelled to the USA in 1878 and met John Devoy of Clan na Gael.
In October 1878 Devoy telegraphed Parnell, offering Clan na Gael support if he adopted a more active programme: self-government, peasant ownership of land, and an independent parliamentary party.
Parnell never formally accepted the offer, but he moved towards it, so his public alliance with Davitt created the working partnership known as the New Departure.
The New Departure committed Fenians to co-operate with a parliamentary party. This was a break with the IRB’s refusal to accept constitutional politics.
It also tied Home Rule to the land question, so a tenant-farmer movement could supply the votes and funds for national politics.
The alliance was always uneasy. The IRB Supreme Council opposed co-operation, and Davitt favoured land nationalisation while Parnell favoured peasant proprietorship (tenants owning their farms).
Between 1879 and 1880 Parnell turned a land protest into a national organisation and then took control of the parliamentary party.

The Irishtown meeting in Co. Mayo (20 April 1879) began the protest. The Land League of Mayo followed in August 1879 and was extended into the Irish National Land League, founded in Dublin in October 1879 with Parnell as president and Davitt a leading organiser.

Parnell and John Dillon toured the United States from January to March 1880, and Parnell addressed the US House of Representatives in February. The tour gave the movement American money and publicity.
At the April 1880 general election about 60 Home Rulers were returned. Parnell was elected for Meath, Mayo and Cork City and chose Cork City, which he held until his death in 1891.

In May 1880 Parnell was elected chairman of the Irish Parliamentary Party (the Home Rule MPs), defeating William Shaw by 23 votes to 18. Shaw had been Butt’s successor in 1879, so this transferred leadership to Parnell.
Do not confuse the offices: Parnell was president of the Land League from 1879 and chairman of the party from May 1880.
Between October 1881 and May 1882 Parnell went from prison to a deal with the government. Its results show how he steered the Land War back into politics.
Gladstone’s Chief Secretary, W.E. Forster, introduced coercion in 1881, allowing detention without trial. The Land Act of August 1881 followed.

Parnell was arrested on 13 October 1881 and held in Kilmainham Gaol. From prison he and other leaders issued the No Rent Manifesto, calling on tenants to withhold rent, so the Land League was suppressed within days.
Captain William O’Shea carried messages between Parnell and the government. In April–May 1882 an arrangement was reached, nicknamed the Kilmainham treaty, and Parnell was released on 2 May 1882.

It was an unwritten understanding, not a treaty, because nothing was signed. Parnell signalled that he would help restore order and co-operate with the Liberals, and the government would deal with rent arrears.
Forster resigned in protest at the release, and the Arrears Act (August 1882) cancelled arrears for poorer tenants.

Opinion divides on it. Some read it as a sensible deal that brought land reform and steered Parnell towards parliamentary politics. Critics read it as an opportunistic retreat from the Land League’s aims.
Days after Parnell’s release, murders in Dublin threatened to destroy the understanding and to discredit him.

On 6 May 1882 Lord Frederick Cavendish, the new Chief Secretary who had arrived in Dublin that day, and Thomas Henry Burke, the Under-Secretary, were stabbed to death in Phoenix Park. Forster, the previous Chief Secretary, had resigned and was not a victim.
The killers were the Invincibles, a small IRB breakaway group (an IRB splinter), who carried out the killings.
Parnell denounced the murders and offered to resign his seat, and Gladstone refused the offer. The government nevertheless introduced the Prevention of Crimes Act (1882).
The informer James Carey gave evidence against his fellow Invincibles, and five of them were hanged in 1883.
After the Land League was suppressed, Parnell built an organisation he could control. By 1885 it had a press, pledged MPs, a parish network and steady funds.
United Ireland, founded in 1881 and edited by William O’Brien, became the party’s weekly newspaper.

The Irish National League, founded in October 1882, replaced the suppressed Land League. It put Home Rule first, with land reform and local self-government, and Parnell kept personal control of it. Do not confuse it with the Land League or with the Irish Parliamentary Party, which was the MPs.

Parish branches of the National League gave the movement an organisation in nearly every county, with priests often serving as chairs or treasurers. This gave Home Rule the local roots Butt had lacked.
By 1884–85 candidates had to take a pledge to sit, act and vote with the party. They were chosen by constituency conventions, with priests prominent, which ended the independent Home Rule MP.
Funding came from the Irish diaspora (Irish emigrants and their descendants, especially in America) and from local collections.
The Parnell Tribute of 1883, a national collection, raised about £37,000 for Parnell, although the Vatican disapproved of it.
By 1885 the result was a mass movement and a disciplined party that was likely to hold the balance of power at Westminster. The election of 1885 would test this.
Parnell’s early career shows an unlikely rebel becoming the leader of a mass movement. This part runs from his background to the eve of the 1885 election.
Parnell was born in 1846 at Avondale, Co. Wicklow, into a Protestant landowning family; he was not Catholic. His mother, Delia Stewart, was the daughter of an American naval officer.
He studied at Magdalene College, Cambridge, and was High Sheriff of Wicklow in 1874, hardly an obvious future rebel.

His main steps were: elected for Meath in 1875, obstruction with Biggar, the Confederation of Great Britain in 1877, the Land League in 1879, the party chair in 1880, Kilmainham in 1881–82, the National League in 1882 and the pledge in 1884–85.
He was a direct participant. He organised the party, led the Land League, and negotiated with Davitt, Devoy and Gladstone’s government.
He was also shaped by events, for example the agricultural depression, Fenian and American pressure, coercion, imprisonment and the Phoenix Park murders each pushed him in new directions.
His speeches urged tenants to keep a firm grip of their homesteads (Westport, June 1879) and to isolate anyone who took a farm from which a tenant had been evicted (Ennis, September 1880).
In Cork in 1885 he declared that "no man has a right to fix the boundary to the march of a nation".

Supporters admired his aloof, disciplined manner and his ability to hold Fenians and constitutionalists together. Critics, including The Times, unionists, the Vatican (over the Tribute) and some moderates in his own party, distrusted him.
F.S.L. Lyons, in Charles Stewart Parnell (1977), stresses his political skill and the fragile alliance he led. Other historians stress a pragmatic parliamentarian steering the Land War into politics.
Judgement turns on whether the movement’s success owed more to Butt’s foundation or to Parnell’s machine. A good answer gives credit and limits to each.

Butt’s achievements: he founded a national, respectable and constitutional movement and won about 60 seats in 1874. His limits were that he had no discipline, money or mass base, and won no concession.

Parnell’s achievements: he gave the party discipline (the pledge, conventions), a press, American money and a mass base through the land movement, and by 1885 held the likely balance of power. His limits were dependence on the land movement and on Fenian allies he could not fully control.
Parnell’s structure also rested on his personal control rather than a lasting system, and Home Rule had still not been won.
On land, Butt supported tenant right, but Parnell made land the engine of the national movement, because tenant votes and funds gave it a mass base.
On method, Butt tried to persuade English opinion by argument, whereas Parnell used disruption and organisation.
On social base, Butt’s was gentlemen and lawyers, whereas Parnell’s was a parish-based mass movement. Both were Protestants.
Contemporaries saw Butt as an honourable failure and Parnell as dangerous but effective, because Parnell’s tactics actually won attention.
The overall judgement is that Butt prepared the ground and Parnell built the machine, so the movement needed both.

Most Irish farmers were tenants at will or on short leases, and the law gave them little protection against eviction or rent increases. Gladstone's first big Irish reform tried to help them, but it left the central problem untouched, and that failure is why a mass land movement followed.

Land was owned by a small landlord class, mostly Protestant and often absentee (living elsewhere); most farmers rented their holdings, usually without a lease, and paid rent to the landlord or his agent.
Memory of the Great Famine (1845-50) and of the evictions that followed it made insecurity feel especially threatening, because a tenant who lost his holding had nowhere else to live.

The tenants' grievances were insecurity, rack-renting (very high rents), eviction and no payment for improvements they had made. Their three demands became known as the Three Fs: fair rent, fixity of tenure (the right to stay while paying rent) and free sale of the tenant's interest in the holding.

Ulster had the Ulster Custom, a tradition of tenant right that let an outgoing tenant sell his interest in his holding. Gladstone's Land Act of 1870 gave it legal force, though protection for tenants elsewhere was weak.
The Landlord and Tenant (Ireland) Act of 1870 offered compensation for improvements and for disturbance (eviction other than for non-payment of rent), but it did not control rents.

Landlords could therefore still raise rents beyond what tenants could pay and then evict for non-payment, which the Act did not forbid. This left tenants without real security of tenure, the main reason for the later land agitation.
The purchase clauses (the Bright clauses) offered loans to help tenants buy their holdings, but they were little used, so little land changed hands under them.
A farming crisis turned long-standing grievances into a mass movement. Michael Davitt supplied the organisation, and Charles Stewart Parnell the national leadership.
From 1877 poor harvests, falling prices and cheap American grain imports hit Irish farmers hard, and the wet summer of 1879 brought a partial potato failure, which reminded people of the Famine.
Rent arrears (unpaid rent) mounted, so evictions rose sharply: about 460 families were evicted in 1877 and more than 2,000 in 1880.

The New Departure of 1878 linked Fenians (revolutionaries in the IRB), land agitation and constitutional politics. Davitt met John Devoy of Clan na Gael, the Irish-American Fenian organisation, in the USA.
Davitt organised a meeting at Irishtown, Co. Mayo, on 20 April 1879 against a landlord's high rents, which showed that tenants could be drawn into open protest.
At Westport in June 1879 Parnell told tenants to keep a firm grip of their homesteads (the farms and houses they lived in). This was his first major public identification with the agitation.
The Land League of Mayo was founded in August 1879. The Irish National Land League followed in Dublin in October 1879, with Parnell as president and Davitt as a leading organiser.

The League's programme was to reduce rents first and then to make tenants owners of their land, known as peasant proprietorship. Davitt personally favoured land nationalisation (state ownership of the land).
Funds came from Irish America: Parnell and John Dillon toured the United States in 1880 raising money, and Land League branches multiplied across the south and west in 1880.
The League fought evictions with collective action rather than force, and the government answered with coercion (emergency laws that restrict normal rights). This struggle is known as the Land War.
The League's methods included rent strikes, in which tenants refused to pay unless rents were cut, and the shunning of anyone who profited from an eviction.
At Ennis in September 1880 Parnell urged that anyone who took a farm from which a tenant had been evicted should be shunned by the whole community, which is the policy that gave us the word boycott.
The first victim was Captain Charles Boycott, agent for Lord Erne at Lough Mask, Co. Mayo, whose workers and tradesmen left him in 1880. The word boycott entered the language.

In November 1880 about fifty Orange labourers from the north were brought in to save Boycott's harvest, guarded by about 1,000 soldiers and police. The huge protection for so few workers made the operation a national joke.
Moonlighting, the night-time maiming of cattle and attacks on property, accompanied the campaign. Parnell's opponents, unionists and many Liberals, blamed the League for this agrarian crime.

The Ladies' Land League, a separate organisation led in Dublin by Anna Parnell (Parnell's sister) from early 1881, kept the campaign going when the men were jailed and helped evicted families with huts and relief. It was dissolved in 1882.
Gladstone's Chief Secretary, W.E. Forster, secured the Protection of Person and Property Act in March 1881, allowing detention without trial, so hundreds of local leaders were jailed.
Parnell's obstruction of the coercion bill in the Commons in early 1881 contributed to the introduction of closure (a rule allowing a debate to be ended by vote).
The 1881 Act met most of the League's demands on paper. It gave tenants what the 1870 Act had withheld, though some tenants were left out at first.

The Land Law (Ireland) Act (August 1881) granted the Three Fs: fair rents set by land courts, fixity of tenure while the tenant paid the rent, and free sale of the tenant's interest. A body called the Land Commission oversaw the system.
The courts fixed fair (judicial) rents for fifteen years, and the first judicial rents cut rents by about one fifth on average, a real gain for tenants.
The landlord kept ownership but shared control of the holding with the tenant, a system known as dual ownership. This is why the Act did not end landlordism, only weakened it.
Leaseholders and tenants in arrears were excluded at first, so these groups did not benefit until the Arrears Act of 1882 dealt with arrears.
Parnell did not want the League to accept the Act without testing it, which led to a clash with Gladstone. The crisis ended with the League suppressed and a deal that helped tenants in arrears.
Parnell advised testing the Act by sending selected test cases to the land courts, in effect telling tenants to wait rather than rush in.
Gladstone denounced Parnell at Leeds on 7 October 1881, and Parnell was arrested on 13 October 1881 and held in Kilmainham.
The League replied with the No Rent Manifesto on 18 October 1881, telling tenants to pay no rent. The manifesto failed to win broad support, and the Catholic hierarchy opposed it.
The Land League was suppressed on 20 October 1881, two days after the manifesto, which ended it as an open organisation.

The Kilmainham settlement of spring 1882 was an understanding between Parnell and the government, and Parnell was released in May 1882. Do not confuse it with his imprisonment in Kilmainham in 1881-82.
The Arrears Act (August 1882) cleared arrears of rent for tenants with small valuations (rent under £30), with the state contributing. It helped those left out in 1881.
The Irish National League replaced the suppressed Land League in October 1882.
When prices fell again in 1885-86, a new campaign sought rent reductions estate by estate rather than nationally. It was a local, organised version of the earlier rent campaign.
The Plan of Campaign was launched in October 1886 in United Ireland by William O'Brien, John Dillon and Timothy Harrington, not by Parnell or Davitt.
Tenants on an estate offered a reduced rent. If the landlord refused, they paid it into a fund held by trustees, which supported evicted tenants.
It was applied on estates such as those of Lord Clanricarde in Co. Galway, the Vandeleur estate at Kilrush, Co. Clare, and Lord Massereene in Co. Louth.
Arthur Balfour, Chief Secretary from 1887, answered with the Criminal Law and Procedure (Ireland) Act of 1887, called the Crimes Act, allowing trial by magistrates without a jury for listed offences.
On 9 September 1887 police fired on a crowd at Mitchelstown, Co. Cork, killing three. Nationalists called it a massacre, and Balfour was nicknamed Bloody Balfour.
A papal rescript from the Holy Office in Rome condemned the Plan of Campaign and boycotting in April 1888, an unwelcome intervention for nationalists.
Parnell was never close to the Plan because the Liberal alliance mattered more to him. The movement was weakened by the Parnell split of 1890-91.

Conservative governments tried to defuse the land question by funding tenants' purchase of their farms. The policy is called constructive unionism, or killing Home Rule with kindness, because it hoped reform would reduce support for nationalism.

The Ashbourne Act (1885), passed by Salisbury's Conservative government (Lord Ashbourne), advanced loans of the full purchase price to tenants who bought from willing landlords, repayable by annuities (fixed yearly payments).
Arthur Balfour's Land Purchase Act (1891) extended the funds for purchase, so that more tenants could buy.
The Congested Districts Board (1891) targeted the poor, overcrowded districts of the west. It bought and divided estates and aided fisheries, crafts and farming.
Gerald Balfour's Land Act (1896), by Arthur's brother, made minor changes to the purchase terms, and little changed in practice.
Defenders of constructive unionism say it removed a major grievance by turning tenants into owners.
Critics argue that it made landlords richer, while the problem of poor western farms remained.
A negotiated settlement between landlords and tenant leaders brought mass tenant purchase. This was the peaceful end of the long conflict, and the state paid for it.

The Land Conference met in Dublin in December 1902, with landlord and tenant representatives: Lord Dunraven (chair), Captain John Shawe-Taylor, William O'Brien and John Redmond, among others. It proposed a purchase scheme with a bonus to landlords.
The Wyndham Act (1903), introduced by the Chief Secretary George Wyndham, offered tenants loans of the full price repayable over about 68 years at low interest.
Landlords received a bonus of 12 per cent of the price as an inducement to sell.
More than 200,000 tenants bought or agreed to buy within about six years. The bonus proved costly to the Treasury, so the terms were revised.

The Labourers (Ireland) Act (1906), a Liberal measure, provided for cottages for farm labourers, with tens of thousands built by 1914. The Evicted Tenants Act (1907) enabled reinstatement of tenants evicted in the Land War.
The Birrell Land Act (1909), named for the Chief Secretary Augustine Birrell, allowed compulsory purchase where landlords refused to sell and gave stronger powers to the Estates Commissioners.
By 1914 most tenants had bought, or were buying, their holdings, and landlordism was finished as a political and social force. Tenant proprietorship (tenants owning their farms) had replaced it.
Davitt was the son of an evicted Mayo tenant who became a Fenian, then the organiser of the Land League and later a voice for labour. He was both a leader of the land movement and its historian.

Born in 1846 at Straide, Co. Mayo, he was evicted with his family in 1850 and grew up in Haslingden, Lancashire. He lost his right arm in a cotton-mill accident aged 11, and educated himself while working.

He joined the IRB (the Fenian movement), was arrested for arms trafficking in 1870 and sentenced to fifteen years. He was held at Dartmoor and released on licence in December 1877, after about seven years.

Through the New Departure he linked Fenians with the land movement, organised the Irishtown meeting in April 1879 and founded the Land League of Mayo in 1879. He was the main organiser beside Parnell's national leadership.
He was re-arrested in February 1881 and held at Portland until May 1882. His prison experience produced Leaves from a Prison Diary (1885).
He argued for land nationalisation and was dismayed that the League accepted peasant proprietorship. He opposed violence against individuals, and his social radicalism set him apart from Parnell.
In 1890 he opposed Parnell's continued leadership after the O'Shea divorce, and he founded the newspaper Labour World in the same year.

He resigned his seat in 1899 in protest at the Boer War, published The Fall of Feudalism in Ireland in 1904, and died in 1906. As both participant and writer, he left the best insider account of the movement.
Contemporaries saw him as a dangerous agitator (unionists) or a hero of the tenants (nationalists). Historians now stress his social radicalism and how he joined Fenians and constitutionalists.

The land campaign changed who owned Irish land, but it was less successful in solving rural poverty and in delivering Home Rule. Judgement questions reward paired points: what was won and what was left undone.
Achievement: agitation forced the state to concede the Three Fs in 1881 and then to finance the transfer of land from landlords to tenants by 1914.
Limit: the settlement came through state funding and compromise, not land nationalisation, so labourers and small western farmers gained least.
Achievement: the Land League mobilised a mass base, which made Parnell's party a national force.
Limit: the agitation depended on Parnell's control, and violence, divisions over the Plan of Campaign and the papal condemnation weakened it.
Contemporary unionists claimed concessions were extracted by intimidation, while nationalists said that only pressure had moved Westminster.
Historians differ on whether constructive unionism worked: it removed a major grievance, but did not stop the growth of nationalism.
Davitt's social vision (land nationalisation, labour rights) was more radical than Parnell's, who favoured peasant proprietorship.
The two elections of 1885 and 1886 were fought over one question, Home Rule. To follow them you need to know what Home Rule meant, who Parnell was by 1885 and how British government worked.

Home Rule was the demand for an Irish parliament in Dublin to handle domestic affairs, while Ireland stayed inside the Union of 1800 (the Acts of Union joining Ireland to Great Britain). It is not separatism, which means full independence.
Butt's Home Rule League (1873) had made Home Rule a parliamentary movement, pursued by votes at Westminster rather than by force.

By 1885 Charles Stewart Parnell had risen fast: Land League president (1879), chairman of the Irish Parliamentary Party (1880), imprisoned in Kilmainham Gaol (October 1881 to May 1882) and founder of the Irish National League (1882), which replaced the banned Land League.

Gladstone's Liberal government (1880-85) answered the Land War (the campaign by tenant farmers against landlords) with coercion, meaning emergency laws such as the Coercion Act of 1881 and the Crimes Act of 1882. Nationalists never forgave this.
The Phoenix Park murders of 6 May 1882 (Lord Frederick Cavendish and Thomas Burke) left Liberals and nationalists with a bitter legacy, which is why co-operation between them in 1885 was surprising.

In Britain the Liberals (led by W.E. Gladstone) and the Conservatives (led by Lord Salisbury) alternated in power. A government needs a majority of seats in the Commons, and the House of Lords could still reject a bill.
Lord Hartington led the Whig wing of the Liberals, the cautious, landowning side, so he was likely to resist radical change such as Home Rule.

Ulster had a Protestant majority in the north-east, above all Belfast and east Ulster, and a Catholic nationalist majority in the south and west of the province. Unionists wanted to keep the Union; nationalists wanted Home Rule.

Two Acts rewrote the electoral map just before the 1885 election, and Parnell's organised party was the main beneficiary. This was a step towards democracy, which means government through elected representatives, though here for men only.

The Representation of the People Act 1884 (the Third Reform Act) gave the vote to male householders and lodgers in the counties on the same terms as the boroughs (towns), ending the old gap between town and country. It applied to Ireland, and women were still excluded.
In Ireland the electorate rose from about 220,000 to about 740,000, more than tripling, because the new voters were mostly small farmers and agricultural labourers (estimates vary a little).

The Redistribution of Seats Act 1885 abolished many small boroughs and made most constituencies single-member, though a few, such as Cork City and Dublin University, stayed two-member. Ireland kept its 103 seats.
Single-member rural seats favoured a party organised in every parish, and the Irish National League had branches across the country, run by local committees and often led by priests.

Candidates were chosen at constituency conventions, where the clergy were influential. From 1884 each candidate had to take the pledge, an undertaking to sit, act and vote with the Irish Party, so the party could vote as a bloc.
Voting stayed secret under the Ballot Act of 1872, so tenants could vote against their landlords without fear of eviction.
The Catholic hierarchy, led by William Walsh, Archbishop of Dublin, and Thomas Croke, Archbishop of Cashel, backed the party in return for its support on Catholic education.

Parnell's aim was to hold the balance of power, meaning a smaller party whose votes decide which larger party governs. He would bargain with both British parties and give support to whichever offered more on Home Rule.

At Cork on 21 January 1885 Parnell declared that no man had the right to fix the boundary to the march of a nation. This was a demand for Home Rule as a national claim, not a limited local parliament.

In 1884 Conservatives such as Lord Randolph Churchill joined the Irish MPs in attacking the Liberal Lord Lieutenant, Earl Spencer (Lord Lieutenant 1882-85), over the Maamtrasna murders of August 1882.
At Maamtrasna, Myles Joyce was hanged in December 1882 despite doubts about his guilt, so nationalists used the case as a symbol of the injustice of Liberal coercion.
That common cause is called the Maamtrasna alliance, and it opened the way to co-operation between Parnell and the Conservatives, though the two sides wanted different things.

On 9 June 1885 the Irish Party voted with the Conservatives on an amendment to Gladstone's budget and brought down his government. Lord Salisbury formed a minority Conservative ministry, one that could survive only while others did not combine against it.
With Salisbury in office, Parnell tested what each side would give. Home Rule emerged as the only demand that satisfied him.
Lord Carnarvon, Salisbury's Lord Lieutenant of Ireland (a Conservative), met Parnell secretly in London in August 1885. The Crimes Act was allowed to lapse, which removed coercion, a major grievance.
The Ashbourne Act (August 1885) provided state loans for tenant purchase, so that tenants could buy their land from landlords. It was part of the Conservatives' offer.

Joseph Chamberlain, a Liberal radical, proposed an elected Central Board for Ireland, discussed through Captain William O'Shea. Parnell and Gladstone's Cabinet both rejected it in 1885, which left Home Rule as the demand.
At Arklow in October 1885 Parnell set out a demand for a legislature with control of Irish domestic affairs, and he stressed that Ireland would not be satisfied with less.
Parnell's manifesto of 21 November 1885 told Irish voters in Britain to vote against Liberal candidates, because of Liberal coercion in 1881-82. This was reversed after the Hawarden Kite.
The election produced a hung Parliament, one in which no party has an overall majority, with the Irish Party holding the balance. It also split Ireland along religious and regional lines.
Polling ran from late November to mid-December 1885. The Irish Party won 85 of the 103 Irish seats, plus T.P. O'Connor at Liverpool Scotland, giving 86 MPs in all.
Outside Ulster the only seats the party did not win were the two for Dublin University. The party swept the south and west (85 = 17 in Ulster + 68 elsewhere).
In Ulster the party won 17 of 33 seats, in the Catholic-majority districts of the south and west of the province. Unionists won the rest, strongest in the east of Ulster.
In Great Britain the Liberals won about 335 seats, the Conservatives about 249 and the Irish Party 86, in a House of 670 (counts vary slightly).
Neither big party could govern without the Irish: the Irish Party plus the Conservatives could equal the Liberals, and Irish votes could decide who governed. Parnell held the balance of power.
The Irish vote in British cities, especially Liverpool, may have helped Conservative candidates in some constituencies after the manifesto, though its effect is hard to measure.

Nationalists and Liberals saw the result as a national mandate, a clear verdict that Ireland, outside Protestant Ulster, wanted Home Rule. Unionists and Conservatives replied that two Irelands had voted.
Gladstone moved to Home Rule within weeks of the election and took office again in February 1886. His move cost him part of his own party.

On 17 December 1885 newspapers published the Hawarden Kite, a leak by Gladstone's son Herbert reporting that Gladstone favoured Home Rule. Hawarden, in Flintshire, was Gladstone's home, and a kite is a trial balloon to test opinion.

Salisbury's ministry was defeated on 26 January 1886 on an amendment about allotments for labourers (Jesse Collings), with the Irish voting against it. Gladstone formed his third ministry in February 1886, with John Morley as Chief Secretary for Ireland.

Joseph Chamberlain joined the Cabinet but resigned in March 1886, along with Sir George Trevelyan, because they would not accept Home Rule, which showed the Liberals splitting. Lord Hartington declined to serve.
Historians disagree why Gladstone took up Home Rule: genuine conviction after the 1885 result, or tactical manoeuvre to keep the Liberals together, as argued by A.B. Cooke and John Vincent.
The Government of Ireland Bill was Gladstone's attempt to give Ireland self-government without breaking up the empire. It reserved to Westminster the matters that made the empire one state.
Gladstone introduced the Government of Ireland Bill on 8 April 1886. It would have set up an Irish legislature in Dublin with an executive (government) responsible to it.
The Crown, defence, foreign policy, trade and the customs remained with Westminster, so Ireland would not have been independent.
Ireland was to pay a fixed share, one fifteenth, of imperial expenditure. The Irish members would no longer sit at Westminster, which meant Ireland would have no voice in imperial decisions.
The Irish legislature was to have two orders, designed to reassure Protestants and property owners, and it was forbidden to establish or endow any religion.
A companion Land Purchase Bill would have offered loans to buy out the landlords. It was unpopular in Britain and was not proceeded with, which weakened the main bill.
Parnell accepted the bill as a basis for a settlement, because it granted an Irish legislature, though he objected to its financial terms.
The Liberal split, not the Conservatives alone, defeated the First Home Rule Bill. Both sides had set out their arguments during weeks of debate.
The bill was debated for several weeks in April-June 1886, and the second reading was defeated in the early hours of 8 June 1886 by 341 votes to 311, a majority of 30.
About 93 Liberals, led by Hartington and Chamberlain, voted with the Conservatives against the bill. They became the Liberal Unionists, a Liberal group that opposed Home Rule and kept the Union.
John Bright, the veteran radical, also opposed the bill. Chamberlain argued that it would break up the empire and treat Ulster Protestants unfairly.
Conservatives such as Lord Randolph Churchill argued that Home Rule meant separation and the loss of the Protestant minority's rights.
Gladstone's supporters argued that coercion had failed, that Ireland's verdict was clear and that Home Rule would give Ireland a settled government and reconcile it to the Crown.
In his closing speech on 7 June 1886 Gladstone said Ireland "stands at your bar, expectant, hopeful, almost suppliant", an appeal to conscience made before the vote.
After the defeat Gladstone dissolved Parliament in late June 1886 and called a general election.
The crisis of 1886 created organised unionism in Ulster and in the south. Unionists feared an Irish parliament would be a Catholic parliament.

In a letter of February 1886 Lord Randolph Churchill wrote that the Orange card was the one to play against Home Rule, meaning an appeal to Ulster Protestants (the Orange Order is their loyalist society). He spoke at the Ulster Hall, Belfast, on 22 February 1886.
The phrase Ulster will fight and Ulster will be right is associated with Churchill in 1886, and unionists used it as a slogan for decades.
The Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union, formed in 1885 by southern unionists, mainly landlords and professionals, who had property to lose, organised opposition to Home Rule.
Ulster Protestants established a Loyalist Anti-Repeal organisation in 1886 (repeal meaning undoing the Union), and the Orange Order grew sharply.
The Belfast riots began in early June 1886, with the bill's defeat in prospect, and lasted into September. About 30 or more people were killed and many injured (estimates vary).
The violence deepened sectarian division, and both sides used it as evidence. Nationalists blamed unionist mobs and the Orange Order; unionists blamed Home Rule agitation.
The voters rejected Gladstone, and the Conservatives governed for most of the next twenty years. The elections left a changed political landscape.
In July 1886 the Conservatives and Liberal Unionists won a combined majority of over 100 over the Gladstonian Liberals and the Irish Party.
Salisbury formed his second government in July 1886, which survived because it was supported by the Liberal Unionists, who entered a coalition with the Conservatives in 1895.
The Irish Party again won about 85 seats, so the nationalist case was undiminished.

Home Rule was now the policy of the Liberal Party. The Liberal-Nationalist alliance became the central fact of Irish parliamentary politics until 1914, because Home Rule now depended on Liberal votes.
Home Rule could pass only when the Liberals had a majority able to overcome the Lords, which was not achieved until the Parliament Act of 1911, because the Liberal split had weakened them.
Unionism became a lasting organised force in Ireland and Britain, and this was the origin of the Ulster question, the problem of Protestant Ulster's opposition to Home Rule.
Parnell was at the height of his power, with a disciplined party and a Liberal ally. The Pigott forgeries and the O'Shea divorce came next.
Parnell was the central figure in the case study. He made the Irish Party decisive and tied Home Rule to the Liberals.
Parnell was born in 1846 at Avondale, Co. Wicklow, a Protestant landowner and an MP from 1875, and leader of the Irish Party.
He built the party machine, using the National League, the pledge and conventions, so that the party could deliver its votes as a bloc.
He bargained with Carnarvon in 1885 and issued the manifesto against the Liberals, then supported Gladstone, showing tactical skill in keeping both British parties guessing.
In the Galway by-election of February 1886 he imposed Captain O'Shea on the party against Tim Healy's objections, which showed his control but sowed resentment.
He was a participant who led the campaigns and the bargaining, but events also shaped him: he depended on Gladstone surviving, and the Liberal split and unionist backlash limited him.

Nationalist contemporaries saw the 85 seats as a personal triumph and a national mandate. Unionists and many Conservatives saw an agitator linked to violence, a reputation The Times later attacked with forged letters.

Examiners ask about his strengths, such as discipline and the pledge, tactics with both parties, balance of power, and appeal to Fenians and constitutionalists, and skill in the Commons. His weaknesses were reliance on a British ally, secrecy about his private life, imposing O'Shea, and aloofness.
F.S.L. Lyons (1977) sees 1885-86 as Parnell's zenith; others note that his strategy depended on Gladstone surviving the Liberal split.
Documents on this case study are speeches, newspaper reports and cartoons. Each can be placed by who produced it, when and why.
Nationalists (Freeman's Journal, United Ireland) presented the 1885 result as a national verdict and the First Home Rule Bill as a just but limited settlement.
Unionists (Belfast News-Letter, the Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union) presented Home Rule as a threat to the empire, to property and to Protestants.
