Gladstone's speeches argued that Home Rule was a moral duty after the failure of coercion; his critics called it a surrender to agitators.
Liberal Unionist speeches, by Chamberlain and Hartington, argued that Irish self-government would endanger the union of the two islands.

Punch, drawn by John Tenniel and others, usually depicted Irish agitators as violent or ape-like, as in The Irish Frankenstein of 1882, and took an anti-Home Rule line. Some Irish and radical papers published pro-Home Rule cartoons.

A cartoon can be placed by its date and symbols: Gladstone as the old man with an axe, Parnell as a tempter or bully, Hibernia (Ireland personified) as a woman, John Bull (Britain personified) as a stout man.

Historians differ on why Gladstone took up Home Rule: conviction after the 1885 result, or tactics to keep the Liberals together, as argued by A.B. Cooke and John Vincent in The Governing Passion (1974).
The elections were a triumph for the Irish Party and a defeat for Home Rule. Examiners reward paired judgements.
Achievement: the Irish Party won a national mandate, forced Home Rule onto the British agenda and won over a major British party.
Limit: the party could not pass a bill without a British majority, and Gladstone's conversion split the Liberals and put the Conservatives in power.
Achievement: the bill's defeat was narrow, and the Liberal alliance gave nationalists a realistic route to Home Rule.
Limit: the elections showed that Ulster Protestants were opposed, a problem that Parnell's party never answered.
Contemporary nationalists blamed the Liberal Unionists and the House of Commons; contemporary unionists said the vote showed the Union was safe.
Later historians see 1886 as the origin of the Ulster question as well as of the Liberal-Nationalist alliance, which makes it a turning point whatever its immediate failure.

By 1886 Parnell had built a disciplined Irish Party and an alliance with Gladstone's Liberals, and the First Home Rule Bill had just been defeated in the Commons in June 1886. Over the next four years he kept his distance from agrarian violence, and his enemies tried to destroy him with forged evidence and failed.

Background: Parnell had been chairman of the Irish Parliamentary Party since 1880, and in the 1885 election the party won 85 of the 103 Irish seats. This strength is why Liberals and Conservatives alike had to take Home Rule seriously.

The Plan of Campaign (October 1886) was launched by William O’Brien, John Dillon and Timothy Harrington. Tenants offered what they thought a fair rent and, if the landlord refused it, paid it into a fund instead.

Parnell did not endorse the Plan, because he feared that evictions and violence would alarm British Liberals. His main concern was the Liberal alliance, so he spent much of 1887–89 away from Ireland and the daily running of the party.

In March 1887 The Times began a series called Parnellism and Crime. On 18 April 1887 it printed a letter, apparently signed by Parnell, that excused the Phoenix Park murders (the killing of Lord Frederick Cavendish and T.H. Burke in May 1882), so it aimed to link him to assassination.
The letter was one of several forged by Richard Pigott, a discredited Dublin journalist, who sold them to The Times.
The government set up a Special Commission of three judges in 1888, by Act of Parliament, to examine the charges against Parnell and about 65 other Irish MPs. It sat from 1888 into 1889.

Under cross-examination by Sir Charles Russell, Parnell’s counsel (lawyer), in February 1889 Pigott collapsed. He had misspelled the word hesitancy in the same way as in the forged letter, which exposed the forgery, and he fled to Madrid, where he shot himself on 1 March 1889.
Parnell was cheered by MPs in the Commons and visited Gladstone at Hawarden in December 1889. In 1890 The Times paid him £5,000 in an out-of-court settlement.

The Commission’s report (February 1890) rejected the forged letters, though it criticised the methods of the Land League (the tenant organisation of the Land War). Parnell now stood at the height of his reputation.

Parnell’s private life, hidden for years, now decided his career. The divorce case of November 1890 turned the Liberal alliance and the Catholic hierarchy (the bishops) against him and split the party.

Parnell had lived with Katharine O’Shea for years. Her husband Captain William O’Shea, a former Irish Party MP, filed for divorce in December 1889 and named Parnell as co-respondent (the man accused of adultery with the wife).
The case was heard on 15–17 November 1890. Parnell did not contest it, so a decree nisi (the first order ending the marriage) was granted.

On 25 November the Irish Party re-elected Parnell as chairman, before Gladstone’s letter to John Morley was published. The letter made Gladstone’s position plain: his leadership of the Liberals would be made almost useless if Parnell stayed.
Non-conformist Liberals threatened to desert Gladstone, and the pressure on him to break with Parnell grew.
Parnell refused to step aside, so the pressure from the Liberals turned into an open fight inside his own party and in the country.
On 29 November Parnell issued a manifesto, To the People of Ireland. It attacked the Liberals and disclosed details of private talks with Gladstone, and it deepened the bitterness.

On 3 December 1890 the Catholic bishops, with Archbishop Walsh prominent, condemned Parnell as unfit to lead. The manifesto came first, on 29 November; the bishops’ condemnation followed on 3 December.
The debate in Committee Room 15 at Westminster lasted from 1 to 6 December 1890. On 6 December about 45 MPs led by Justin McCarthy walked out, leaving a minority of about 26–28 with Parnell.

The anti-Parnellites (the majority) included Dillon, William O’Brien, McCarthy and the fierce critic Tim Healy, and were later organised as the Irish National Federation (1891). The Parnellites kept control of the Irish National League.

Parnell’s candidates lost by-elections in North Kilkenny (December 1890), North Sligo (April 1891) and Carlow (July 1891), in vicious campaigns, which showed that the country as well as the party had turned against him.
He married Katharine on 25 June 1891 and died at Brighton on 6 October 1891, aged 45. He was buried at Glasnevin, and a very large crowd attended.
This part covers the years of Parnell’s peak influence, his fall and the overall judgement. The strengths and weaknesses below are the usual basis for essays on him.

What he did: between 1886 and 1890 he combined an alliance with Gladstone with firm control over a disciplined party of about 85 MPs. He was born in 1846 and was 45 when he died, so his career ended while he was still in his prime.
He was a participant in the Pigott and O’Shea affairs. He lost control of events after the divorce, when his refusal to step aside split the movement.
Contemporary nationalists were divided: the Parnellites saw him as a leader betrayed by Liberals and bishops, while the anti-Parnellites saw a leader who put himself above the cause.
Contemporary unionists (opponents of Home Rule) saw him as a dangerous agitator, until the Pigott collapse made The Times and his accusers look foolish.
Strengths: party discipline, tactical skill, ability to unite Fenians (physical-force nationalists), land reformers and constitutionalists, and a clear command of Commons procedure.

Weaknesses: aloofness and an autocratic style, dependence on the Liberals, ambiguity about violence in the Land War, and a private life that he did not manage, which handed his enemies the means to destroy him.

Historians differ: F.S.L. Lyons in Charles Stewart Parnell (1977) stresses the tragic collision of ambition and scandal. Paul Bew in C.S. Parnell (1980) presents a conservative landlord politician whose strategy had limits.
His legacy was the idea of an independent Irish party. He also left the Parnell legend of a betrayed leader, a martyr, which later nationalists and writers, including Yeats and Joyce, drew on.
Gladstone’s last attempt at Home Rule was killed by the House of Lords, which could reject a bill passed by the Commons. The Irish Party then spent the 1890s in feud.
The Liberals returned to office after the 1892 election with a small majority that depended on the Irish MPs. Gladstone, aged 83, introduced the Second Home Rule Bill on 13 February 1893.

The Bill proposed an Irish legislature of two houses, and it kept a reduced number of Irish MPs at Westminster, to meet the objection that Ireland would otherwise be excluded from the parliament that still ruled the empire.
The Commons passed the Bill in September 1893 by 301 votes to 267, after eighty-two sittings, so the elected house backed it and only the Lords stood in the way.
The House of Lords threw it out on 8 September 1893 by 419 votes to 41, so a huge Conservative and Unionist majority in the Lords outweighed the Commons. Gladstone retired in March 1894.
Unionists had mobilised against the Bill, so Ulster resistance was already organised, notably at the Ulster Convention in Belfast in June 1892.

The Conservatives under Salisbury won the 1895 election, and Unionist governments held office for most of the next ten years. They tried to kill Home Rule with kindness, through land purchase, local government and the Congested Districts Board.
In the 1890s the Irish National Federation (Dillon and McCarthy), Healy’s followers and Redmond’s small Parnellite group fought each other, and voters became disillusioned.

The United Irish League was founded by William O’Brien at Westport, Co. Mayo, in January 1898 to revive the land agitation in the west. Do not confuse it with the Irish National League or the Irish National Federation.
The parties reunited in January 1900, and Redmond was elected chairman in February 1900.
Redmond rebuilt the party, won land reform and then used the Liberals’ dependence on his votes to put Home Rule on the statute book. The last step came at a price in Ulster.
Redmond and William O’Brien took part in the Land Conference of December 1902–January 1903, with landlord representatives, which led to the Wyndham Act (1903).

In May 1907 a national convention of the party rejected the Irish Council Bill, a limited devolution scheme introduced by Chief Secretary Augustine Birrell. It offered less than Home Rule, so the party refused it.
Two general elections in 1910 (January and December) left the Liberals short of a majority without Irish nationalist votes. The nationalist MPs numbered in the low 80s and held the balance.

The Lords rejected the People’s Budget (1909), so the Liberals, backed by Redmond’s party, passed the Parliament Act (1911). It removed the Lords’ veto, leaving only a delay of two years; it did not itself grant Home Rule.
Asquith introduced the Third Home Rule Bill in April 1912. It became law on 18 September 1914, and a Suspensory Act held it back until the end of the war, which Redmond accepted.

Under pressure from the unionist threat, in March 1914 Asquith proposed that Ulster counties could opt out for six years. Redmond, who had resisted, accepted it, a concession he had previously refused.
In June 1914 Redmond insisted that 25 of his nominees join the Irish Volunteers’ provisional committee, and the committee accepted, so he gained control of the new force.
Redmond led the reunited party for eighteen years and believed that Home Rule could be won by constitutional methods and kept by loyalty to the empire. The First World War wrecked that belief.
John Redmond (1856–1918) was born at Ballytrent, Co. Wexford, into a Catholic landed family. He was educated at Clongowes, became a barrister and was an MP from 1881.
He stayed loyal to Parnell in 1890, which is why he led the small Parnellite group after Parnell died in 1891. He sat for Waterford City from 1891 until his death in March 1918.
As a participant he reunited the party in 1900 and negotiated the Land Conference, the 1911 Parliament Act and the 1912 Bill, relying on his control of the party’s votes.
Contemporary nationalists generally admired him as the leader who delivered Home Rule. Critics such as Griffith and the IRB attacked his reliance on Liberal goodwill.
In August 1914 he offered the Volunteers for the defence of Ireland. His Woodenbridge speech, in Co. Wicklow on 20 September 1914, urged them to fight in the war, and this split the Irish Volunteers.
The great majority followed him as the National Volunteers, and about 10,000–12,000 stayed with Eoin MacNeill’s Irish Volunteers (estimates vary).
Strengths: party management, which kept the reunited party together, parliamentary skill, a genuine achievement in land and the Home Rule Act, and personal integrity.
Weaknesses: dependence on the Liberals, failure to resolve the Ulster problem, acceptance of partition in principle in 1914 and poor judgement of the new separatism.

Historians differ: Denis Gwynn’s The Life of John Redmond (1932) is sympathetic, and Dermot Meleady’s John Redmond: The National Leader (2013) presents a statesman wrecked by war. Others see a leader out of touch with the new generation.

Separatism means full independence from Britain, whereas Home Rule meant a parliament in Dublin within the United Kingdom. Arthur Griffith proposed a separatist policy of abstention and economic self-reliance as an alternative to Home Rule.
Arthur Griffith, a Dublin printer and journalist, founded the newspaper The United Irishman in 1899 with William Rooney.
Cumann na nGaedheal was founded in 1900 to unite groups promoting Irish language, industry and the national cause, so it gathered scattered separatist and cultural groups in one body.

In The Resurrection of Hungary (1904) Griffith argued that Ireland should follow Hungary, which had won its own parliament within a dual monarchy (Austria-Hungary, in 1867) after refusing to sit in the Vienna parliament. This is abstentionism: refusing to attend the imperial parliament.

At a convention in November 1905 the National Council adopted what became the Sinn Féin policy: abstain from Westminster, set up a national assembly in Dublin and protect Irish industry with tariffs (taxes on imports).
The weekly Sinn Féin followed in 1906. The Dungannon Clubs of Bulmer Hobson merged with Cumann na nGaedheal in 1907 as the Sinn Féin League, and the party was fully constituted as Sinn Féin in 1908.
In the North Leitrim by-election of February 1908 the Sinn Féin candidate C.J. Dolan, who had left the Irish Party, was beaten by roughly three to one.
Sinn Féin lost support after 1908 and the party remained small, but its ideas about abstention and self-reliance were revived in 1917.

The IRB (Irish Republican Brotherhood) was the secret Fenian organisation committed to physical force. A younger generation revived it, and the Ulster Volunteers (the unionist armed force formed in 1913) became the model for militarism, meaning armed volunteer forces used as a political instrument.
Tom Clarke, a Fenian who had served about fifteen years in prison, returned from the USA in December 1907 and opened a tobacconist’s shop in Dublin.
With Bulmer Hobson and Seán Mac Diarmada, Clarke revived the IRB and founded the paper Irish Freedom (1910).
Eoin MacNeill’s article The North Began, published in An Claidheamh Soluis on 1 November 1913, argued that the Ulster Volunteers had shown that Irishmen could arm and organise to defend their rights.
The Irish Volunteers were founded on 25 November 1913 at the Rotunda Rink in Dublin. MacNeill became chairman, and IRB men worked behind the scenes, so the separatists had a hidden influence.
Cumann na mBan, a women’s organisation to support the Volunteers, was founded in April 1914.
The Howth gun-running on 26 July 1914 landed about 900 rifles from Erskine Childers’s yacht Asgard. British soldiers then fired on a crowd at Bachelor’s Walk in Dublin, killing four.
After Redmond’s Woodenbridge speech the Volunteers split in September 1914: the majority became the National Volunteers and a minority kept the name Irish Volunteers.
The period shows constitutional nationalism at its strongest and the first serious challenge to it. Examiners reward a clear judgement backed by paired points.
Achievements of the Home Rule movement: a united parliamentary party, land reform and, by 1914, a Home Rule Act on the statute book.
Limits: Parnell’s fall wasted a decade, the Lords killed the 1893 Bill, and the Ulster question remained unsolved in 1914, so Home Rule was law but had not yet taken effect.
Sinn Féin and the IRB offered a separatist alternative, but before 1914 they were small and divided. Their growth after 1914 owed more to war and the 1916 Rising than to their own efforts.

Contemporary unionists judged Redmond a threat to the Union because Home Rule would weaken it; separatists judged him too moderate because he sought less than independence; most nationalists in 1914 supported him.
Historians now often argue that Home Rule was not doomed before 1914 and that its collapse came from the war, the Rising and the conscription crisis.
Three terms run through the story of Ulster resistance to Home Rule (a separate parliament in Dublin for Irish affairs, with Ireland still under the Crown). Each has a specific meaning in this topic.
Unionism was the movement to keep Ireland in the United Kingdom and to oppose Home Rule. Its supporters were called unionists.

Militarism, as used here, means using armed, drilled volunteer forces as a political tool, so that the threat of force stands behind a political demand. The Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), formed in 1913, is the main example.

Democracy means rule by the elected majority. Nationalists said unionist threats of force defied democracy, because they were meant to overrule a Home Rule Bill passed by the elected House of Commons.
Unionists answered that Ulster must consent to its own government, so a Dublin parliament could not rightly be imposed on it against its will.

Unionism was a coalition of Protestants of all classes in Ulster with landlords and business people elsewhere in Ireland, united by opposition to a Dublin parliament. It was never simply ‘all Protestants’.

Ulster had a slight Protestant majority (about 56 per cent in 1911), concentrated in the east. Antrim, Down, Armagh and Londonderry had Protestant majorities, while Tyrone and Fermanagh had narrow Catholic majorities.

Protestants of every class were unionist: landlords and gentry, industrialists, shopkeepers, Presbyterian tenant farmers and Protestant workers in Belfast. Shared fear of Home Rule, not shared wealth, held them together.

Southern unionists were a small minority (Protestants were about a tenth of the population outside Ulster), made up of landlords, professionals, businessmen and Church of Ireland clergy, strongest in Dublin and parts of Munster and Leinster.
Gladstone, the Liberal leader, announced his conversion to Home Rule in December 1885, and the First Home Rule Bill was defeated in the Commons in June 1886.
Most Ulster Presbyterians had supported the Liberals before 1886, so Gladstone’s conversion pushed many of them into the unionist camp.

Many Protestants had already been alarmed by Gladstone’s disestablishment of the Church of Ireland (the Irish Church Act of 1869, which ended its status as the state church) and by the Land Acts of 1870 and 1881, and they saw Home Rule as the next step.
Colonel Edward Saunderson led the Irish Unionist MPs at Westminster from 1886 until his death in 1906. Walter Long followed him, and Carson took over in February 1910.

Unionists opposed Home Rule for three linked reasons: religion, economics, and identity and empire. Two of them were fears about everyday life, namely what a Catholic majority might do and what a Dublin parliament might do to Belfast’s trade.
Religion: Protestants feared that a parliament elected by a Catholic majority would be under Catholic Church influence. The slogan was that Home Rule is Rome Rule.
The Ne Temere decree (effective 1908) required the children of mixed marriages to be brought up Catholic, and unionists cited it as later support for the fear of Catholic Church influence.

Economy: Belfast’s linen, shipbuilding (Harland and Wolff), engineering and rope-making depended on British and imperial markets and raw materials, so unionists feared tariffs and higher taxes under a Dublin parliament.

Ulster’s industrial north-east had a different economy from the agricultural south and west, so unionists argued that an Irish parliament would favour agricultural interests at the expense of industry.
The third reason was about who unionists believed they were, and it was joined by fears of life as a minority and by an argument that went beyond Ulster.
Identity and empire: Ulster Protestants saw themselves as British, were proud of the empire, and believed that Home Rule was the first step towards separation from Britain.

Protestants also feared for their position as a minority in a self-governing Ireland, and many believed nationalists would dispossess them, as they thought the Land War (the campaign against landlords) had shown.

Many Ulster unionists believed that the Land Acts and the Irish Party’s links with Fenians (members of the revolutionary movement for an Irish republic) showed that nationalists would not respect property.

Joseph Chamberlain and Lord Hartington led the Liberal Unionists, who voted against the 1886 Bill. They argued that Home Rule would threaten the integrity of the United Kingdom, not only the Ulster minority.
From 1885 unionists built organisations to match the nationalist National League. Each new body answered a particular threat, which is why the order of dates matters.
The Orange Order, founded in 1795 after the Battle of the Diamond in County Armagh, revived in the 1880s and gave Ulster unionism a mass base of lodges across the province.
The Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union was founded in Dublin in 1885 by southern unionists. The Ulster Loyalist Anti-Repeal Union followed in 1886.

In February 1886 the Conservative Lord Randolph Churchill urged unionists to “play the Orange card”, meaning to use Ulster Protestant feeling against Home Rule, and said “Ulster will fight and Ulster will be right”.
Belfast riots in summer 1886, in which several were killed, sharpened sectarian division.
The Irish Unionist Alliance was formed in 1891 to unite the Irish unionist bodies.
The Ulster Convention met in the Botanic Gardens, Belfast, on 17 June 1892, with about 12,000 delegates. It protested against the coming Second Home Rule Bill, and a Dublin convention followed.
The Second Home Rule Bill (1893) passed the Commons but was defeated in the Lords in September 1893, so unionist resistance had not yet been put to the test.
By the early 1900s unionists needed a permanent central body for Ulster, and later they drew women into the movement as well.
Lord Dunraven’s Irish Reform Association (1904) proposed limited devolution (giving Ireland some self-government short of Home Rule), which alarmed Ulster unionists.
This 1904–05 devolution scare convinced Ulster unionists that they needed their own permanent body, so the Ulster Unionist Council was founded in March 1905 (first meeting 3 March).
The Council brought together Orange lodges, constituency associations and unionist MPs, so it joined the mass base, the local organisers and the parliamentary leaders in one body.
The Ulster Women’s Unionist Council, formed in January 1911 under its president Lady Londonderry, mobilised tens of thousands of women for the unionist cause.
Carson, a Dublin-born barrister, led the unionist campaign against the Third Home Rule Bill and made the threat of armed resistance credible.

Edward Carson (born in Dublin on 9 February 1854, died 1935) was educated at Trinity College and became a leading barrister. In 1895 he cross-examined Oscar Wilde as counsel for the Marquess of Queensberry, after which Wilde lost his libel case and was prosecuted.

He was Solicitor General for Ireland and MP for Dublin University from 1892 (to 1918), and Solicitor General for England in 1900–06 (knighted 1900). In February 1910 he succeeded Walter Long as leader of the Irish Unionist parliamentary party, and he was the chief unionist campaigner from 1911 to 1914.
He was a leading participant: he spoke at the Craigavon rally, led the Ulster Day campaign on 28 September 1912 and signed the Covenant first at Belfast City Hall.
He was chairman of the Provisional Government plan of 1913, rejected Asquith’s county option in 1914 and took part in the Buckingham Palace Conference.

He made the threat of resistance credible, but James Craig’s organisation and Conservative backing gave it force. His Dublin background made him an unlikely leader of Ulster, but he spoke for all Irish unionists.
Contemporary unionists revered him as the defender of the Union. Nationalists and many Liberals thought him a man ready to defy Parliament, and Redmond denounced the threat of force.
Historians differ: some say he never intended to fight and bluffed to protect the Union; others that his threat made partition inevitable and that he left southern unionists exposed.
He resigned the Ulster Unionist leadership in February 1921 (Craig succeeded him) and became a law lord (Lord of Appeal) that year, the year Northern Ireland came into being.
After the Parliament Act of 1911 removed the Lords’ power to block Home Rule, unionists organised a campaign of mass resistance with Conservative backing.
The Parliament Act (royal assent, August 1911) meant that the Lords could delay a Bill for two years but not block it, so Home Rule could now become law within about two years.

James Craig (born 1871), a wealthy Belfast whiskey-fortune businessman and MP for East Down from 1906, became Carson’s chief organiser and planned the campaign. He later became the first Prime Minister of Northern Ireland (1921).
A huge unionist demonstration was held at Craigavon, outside Belfast, in September 1911, with Carson as speaker. Tens of thousands attended.

The Third Home Rule Bill was introduced by Asquith on 11 April 1912. An amendment to exclude Antrim, Down, Armagh and Londonderry, moved by the Liberal Thomas Agar-Robartes, was defeated in June 1912.

Andrew Bonar Law, Conservative leader since November 1911, spoke at Blenheim Palace on 27 July 1912: “I can imagine no length of resistance to which Ulster can go in which I should not be prepared to support them.” This pledged his party to back Ulster.
The unionist campaign reached its peak with the Covenant, while the Third Home Rule Bill moved slowly through Parliament.

On Ulster Day, 28 September 1912, about 237,000 men signed the Solemn League and Covenant, and Carson signed first, at Belfast City Hall. Signatories pledged to “use all means which may be found necessary to defeat the present conspiracy to set up a Home Rule Parliament in Ireland”.
About 234,000 women signed a separate declaration, so about 471,000 signed in all, which showed how wide the support was.
The Twelfth of July Orange demonstrations and Presbyterian and Church of Ireland ministers gave the campaign a religious character, with many ministers joining Covenant services.
The Commons passed the Third Home Rule Bill in January 1913 and the Lords rejected it (30 January 1913). The same happened in July 1913.
The Commons passed the Bill a third time in May 1914, so under the Parliament Act it could go for royal assent without the Lords’ consent.
In 1913 unionist leaders organised an armed force and prepared to take over the government of Ulster. This is militarism in practice, with drilled volunteers used to back a political demand.
The Ulster Volunteer Force was formed in January 1913 from earlier local drilling clubs. Its commander was Lieutenant-General Sir George Richardson, a retired Indian Army officer.
By 1914 the UVF had about 90,000 or more members, organised in battalions, with many drilling openly and wearing uniform.
On 24 September 1913 the Ulster Unionist Council announced a Provisional Government of Ulster, with Carson as chairman, to take office if Home Rule became law.
Unionists said that they were loyal to the king but not to a Dublin parliament they believed to be illegitimate.

The government did not prosecute. Redmond warned that this failure to act encouraged separatist counter-organisation, and the nationalist Irish Volunteers were founded on 25 November 1913 at the Rotunda Rink, Dublin.
In March 1914 the government tried a compromise and then discovered that it could not be sure of the army.
On 9 March 1914 Asquith proposed that any Ulster county could vote itself out of Home Rule for six years. Carson rejected this as “a sentence of death with a stay of execution for six years”.

On 20 March 1914, in the Curragh incident (County Kildare), Brigadier-General Hubert Gough and most of his cavalry officers (57 of about 70) said they would accept dismissal rather than act against Ulster.
It was not a mutiny, because no order had been refused in action. Critics used the word, but the officers only said they would accept dismissal.

The War Minister, John Seely, and the army chief, Sir John French, resigned at the end of March. The incident showed that the government could not be sure the army would enforce Home Rule in Ulster, which narrowed its options.
While the politicians argued, the UVF armed itself, and the authorities did nothing to stop it.
On the night of 24–25 April 1914 the UVF landed about 25,000 rifles and a few million rounds of ammunition, bought in Germany and organised by Major Fred Crawford.
The guns were landed mainly at Larne, and also at Bangor and Donaghadee. The ship was the Clyde Valley.
The weapons were distributed across Ulster by car overnight. Police and army did not stop it, and the government did not prosecute, so unionists had shown that they could arm without penalty.
The Larne landing prompted nationalists to organise their own gun-running at Howth (26 July 1914) and Kilcoole (1–2 August 1914).
With both sides armed, the last attempt to agree on exclusion (leaving part of Ulster outside Home Rule) was a conference called by the king.

The Buckingham Palace Conference (21–24 July 1914) was called by George V and chaired by the Speaker, James Lowther. Asquith, Lloyd George, Redmond, Dillon, Carson, Craig, Lansdowne and Bonar Law attended.
It failed over the extent of exclusion, above all Tyrone and Fermanagh, which had narrow Catholic majorities.

By mid-1914 the Amending Bill proposed six-year exclusion of counties by option. Carson insisted on permanent exclusion of Ulster (or six counties), because temporary exclusion was not enough for him.
Nationalists resisted partition and accepted at most temporary exclusion, so the gap was never closed before the war.
The Home Rule Act and the Suspensory Act received royal assent on 18 September 1914, and Home Rule was suspended for the duration of the war, leaving Ulster’s status unsettled.
Judgements on unionism compare its success in blocking Home Rule before 1914 with its failure to hold the whole of Ireland in the Union.
Achievement: unionists defeated two Home Rule Bills (the First in 1886 and the Second in 1893), built effective organisation and mobilised mass support.
Achievement: by 1914 they had forced the government to accept the principle of exclusion for Ulster, and Home Rule was suspended in 1914.
Achievement: the UVF, the Covenant and Conservative support showed that Ulster could not be coerced, and made Carson and Craig decisive in later negotiations.

Limit: unionists could not stop the Third Home Rule Bill becoming law, and southern unionists were left unprotected because exclusion concerned only Ulster. Unionism itself was divided between Ulster and the south.
Limit: the Conservative alliance meant unionism was exposed when the Conservatives themselves compromised, as they did in 1920–21.
Contemporary nationalists thought unionist arms threatened democracy and parliament, while unionists thought them a legitimate defence of rights.
A.T.Q. Stewart (The Ulster Crisis, 1967) shows how close Britain came to civil war in 1914, and Alvin Jackson stresses unionist resilience and the divisions between Ulster and southern unionists.

Suffrage means the right to vote. In Ireland the campaign for women’s suffrage began as a small, respectable effort among middle-class Protestant and Quaker women, closely linked to property rights, education and local government. It rested on feminism (the belief in women’s equal rights and public roles) and on the democratic argument that government by elected representatives was incomplete if half the adults had no say.

In 1870 Irish women had no parliamentary vote, and under common law a married woman’s property passed to her husband, so the law clearly favoured men. This is the grievance the early campaigners set out to change.

The Married Women’s Property Acts of 1870 and 1882 improved the position of married women, and the 1882 Act applied to Ireland as well as to England and Wales. Isabella Tod campaigned for these reforms.

Isabella Tod organised a suffrage society in Belfast in the early 1870s (1872 if a single year is wanted), the first in Ulster. This made Belfast the starting point of organised suffrage activity in the north.

Anna Haslam, a Quaker, and her husband Thomas Haslam founded the Dublin Women’s Suffrage Association in 1876, which later became the Irish Women’s Suffrage and Local Government Association. Anna Haslam (1829–1922) lived long enough to see women gain the vote in 1918.

The early societies used polite, constitutional methods: they petitioned MPs, held drawing-room meetings and sent speakers out. They also worked alongside the campaign for girls’ education and the campaign against the Contagious Diseases Acts.
Women also gained a role in local government, a stepping stone to the parliamentary vote.

The Local Government (Ireland) Act of 1898 let women vote in county and district council elections. They could also stand for district councils and boards of guardians (the bodies that ran poor relief), though not for county councils.

County and borough councils were only opened to women by an Act of 1911. So by 1898 women could vote locally and hold some local office, but the higher councils stayed closed to them for another thirteen years.

Several prominent Irish suffragists, such as Tod, were unionists, while others supported Home Rule (self-government for Ireland within the United Kingdom). The societies therefore stayed neutral on Home Rule for decades, because taking sides would have split their membership.

Isabella Tod was a Belfast Presbyterian reformer who campaigned for women’s education, property rights and votes, always from a unionist outlook. She is the best example of the respectable, constitutional phase of the movement.

Isabella Tod (1836–1896) was born in Edinburgh, settled in Belfast and lived there until her death. She was a Presbyterian, which set her apart from the Catholic nationalist background of Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington.
She organised the first suffrage society in Ulster, in Belfast in the early 1870s. This was the earliest sustained women’s suffrage organisation in the north.
She was a participant in the campaigns that led to the Married Women’s Property Act of 1882, which gave married women more control over their own property.
On girls’ education she helped found the Ladies’ Institute in Belfast (1867), a society for girls’ education, and worked with Margaret Byers of the Ladies’ Collegiate School (later Victoria College).
She helped win the inclusion of girls in the Intermediate Education Act (1878) and the opening of Royal University degrees to women (1882), so she shaped both school and university access for girls.
She co-founded the Belfast Women’s Temperance Association in 1874 and campaigned against the Contagious Diseases Acts, so her reform interests went well beyond the vote.
As a Liberal Unionist she opposed Home Rule in 1886 and urged women to oppose it. She helped found the Irish Women’s Liberal Unionist Association.
Contemporaries respected her as a public speaker and organiser, though her unionism limited her influence among nationalists.
Historians present her as a pioneer who created the first sustained suffrage organisation in Ulster and helped break the exclusion of women from Irish public debate.

After 1900 the suffrage groups multiplied and divided into peaceful and radical wings. They found the main obstacle at Westminster, where the Irish Party (the nationalist party led by John Redmond) refused to back votes for women.

The Irish Women’s Suffrage Federation, founded in 1911 by Louie Bennett and others, linked local societies and used peaceful methods. Its members were suffragists, meaning peaceful, constitutional campaigners for the vote.
The Irish Women’s Franchise League (founded 1908) was more radical. It argued that no Home Rule settlement was legitimate without votes for women.
A Conciliation Bill proposing a limited vote for women was defeated in the House of Commons in March 1912, with most Irish Party members voting against it.

Redmond and his leading colleague John Dillon opposed the bill because they feared a franchise bill would complicate the passage of Home Rule, the Irish Party’s main aim. Redmond also personally opposed votes for women.

The Third Home Rule Bill of 1912 was the main political issue of the day, and unionists were resisting it. Suffragists therefore demanded that women’s votes be part of any Home Rule settlement, and argued that Home Rule without them would be incomplete.

Suffragists generally split on the national question. Some, like Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington, argued that independence would be incomplete without women’s votes, while others, notably in Ulster, were unionists.

From 1908 the Franchise League brought direct action to Irish politics, and its campaign peaked in 1912–13. Its members were suffragettes: militant campaigners for the vote who used direct action such as window-breaking. The word was coined by the British press.
The League was founded in Dublin in 1908 by Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington, Margaret Cousins, her husband James Cousins and Francis Sheehy-Skeffington. Its aim was votes for women on the same terms as men.

The League published a weekly newspaper, the Irish Citizen, from May 1912. It was edited at first by Francis Sheehy-Skeffington and James Cousins, and it ran until 1920, giving the movement a voice of its own.
In June 1912 eight League members, including Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington and Margaret Cousins, were arrested for breaking windows at government buildings in Dublin, and were imprisoned.

In July 1912 Asquith, the British Prime Minister, visited Dublin. English suffragettes of the Women’s Social and Political Union (WSPU) disrupted the visit, and Mary Leigh threw a hatchet at the carriage carrying Asquith and Redmond.
Imprisoned suffragettes went on hunger strike (refusing food as a protest). The English prisoners were force-fed in Mountjoy, the Dublin prison, which provoked public protest.

Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington was jailed again in 1913 and released after a hunger strike under the Cat and Mouse Act (1913), which let the authorities free weakened hunger strikers and re-arrest them later.

Hostile crowds attacked suffragettes at public meetings. Many nationalists and trade unionists considered the militant tactics counter-productive, because they thought the tactics turned opinion against the cause.
Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington was the leading Irish militant suffragist. She tied women’s rights to nationalism and socialism, and she was critical of the movements that put women second.
Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington (1877–1946) was born in Kanturk, Co. Cork, the daughter of the nationalist MP David Sheehy. She took an MA from the Royal University in 1902.
She married the pacifist and feminist Francis Skeffington in 1903, and they each added the other’s surname, a sign of their belief in equality in marriage.

She co-founded the Irish Women’s Franchise League in 1908, was imprisoned for window-breaking in 1912 and again in 1913 (with a hunger strike), and was a contributor and later editor of the Irish Citizen.

She was a participant in the campaign, and her organisation shaped how the issue was seen in Ireland. She was also a critic of the Irish Party and later of Cumann na mBan, which she saw as subordinating women to men.
Her husband Francis was shot without trial by Captain Bowen-Colthurst in April 1916, after this topic’s dates. She campaigned for an inquiry and refused compensation.
Contemporaries admired her courage, but many nationalists thought her tactics divisive, and unionists and the Irish Party saw her as a nuisance.
Historians now see her as a key figure of Irish feminism who insisted that independence must include equality.

The suffrage cause was entangled with the national question (whether Ireland should have Home Rule or stay fully in the Union), and women in each camp chose their side. This division was one of the movement’s main weaknesses.

Unionist women in Ulster signed their own declaration against Home Rule on Ulster Day, 28 September 1912, about 234,000 of them. This gave them a public role in unionism, and suffragists such as Tod had been unionists.

Nationalist women formed Cumann na mBan in April 1914 to support the Irish Volunteers. Suffragists such as Sheehy-Skeffington objected to its auxiliary status, meaning it served the men’s organisation rather than acting on its own.

Many suffragists argued that women should not be asked to postpone their claim until Home Rule or the Union had been settled, because the vote was a democratic right whatever the constitutional outcome.
The Irish Citizen pursued both aims, and it attracted writers from different political groups, from the pacifist movement to the trade unions.
Votes for women were granted in 1918 under the Representation of the People Act, to women over thirty with a property qualification (or married to a qualified man).
This came after the First World War, and the Irish Party that had opposed the cause had by then been destroyed, in the December 1918 election.

Before 1878 secondary schools were mostly private or run by religious orders, with little state funding. The Intermediate Education Act of 1878 began state support and used examinations to decide how much each school was paid; primary education was reformed later, in 1900.
The Intermediate Education (Ireland) Act (1878) set up an Intermediate Board that held public examinations (junior, middle and senior grades) for boys and girls from 1879.
Schools were paid results fees according to how many pupils passed, a system known as payment by results. Prizes and exhibitions (money awards) rewarded top candidates.
The system financed denominational schools (schools run by a particular church) without interfering in their management, so Catholic, Protestant and convent schools all grew.

Girls’ schools used the examinations to compete with boys, because the exams were open to girls too. Alexandra College (Dublin, 1866), Victoria College (Belfast) and the Loreto and Dominican convent schools all prepared girls.
Critics said payment by results encouraged cramming (learning facts just to pass), narrowed the curriculum to examinable subjects and neglected Irish and science.

National school (primary) teachers had been paid by results since the 1870s. The Revised Programme of 1900 ended this, broadening the curriculum to include drawing, practical work, nature study and Irish as an ordinary subject within school hours.
The bilingual programme of 1904 encouraged teaching through Irish in Gaeltacht (Irish-speaking) schools.
Victoria College in Belfast, founded by Margaret Byers in 1859 as the Ladies’ Collegiate School, and Alexandra College, founded in 1866, were pioneers of girls’ secondary education.

University education was a grievance for Catholics and a barrier for women. The Royal University opened degrees to both groups, and the Act of 1908 then settled the university question with two new universities.

Trinity College Dublin was Protestant in ethos, and the Catholic hierarchy (the bishops) banned Catholics from attending it. Catholics therefore complained that no university gave them a real Catholic institution.

The Royal University of Ireland (Act 1879, charter 1880) was an examining body that awarded degrees to students of any college or none. It replaced the Queen’s University as the examining and degree-awarding body.
Degrees were opened to women by a supplemental charter in 1882, and the first women graduated in the early 1880s. Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington was among its later graduates, taking her MA in 1902.

The Irish Universities Act (1908), prepared by Chief Secretary Augustine Birrell, dissolved the Royal University and created the National University of Ireland (NUI), with constituent colleges at Dublin, Cork and Galway, and Queen’s University Belfast.
The NUI had a Catholic ethos, which made it acceptable to Catholics, with Archbishop William Walsh of Dublin as first chancellor. It was open to women on equal terms.

The Gaelic League, the organisation promoting the Irish language, campaigned for compulsory Irish for matriculation (the entrance qualification). The NUI Senate decided in 1910 to require it, applied from 1913.

Reforms opened up public life to women and widened access to education, but the parliamentary vote came late and by a different route. Judging the movement means weighing what it achieved against what it could not do.

Achievement: women gained the vote in local government elections and the right to hold local office, gained access to degrees and the professions, and built an organised movement with its own newspaper.
Limit: Irish women had no parliamentary vote before 1918, the Home Rule Bills offered them none, and militancy gained little and divided opinion.
Achievement: the Intermediate system and the 1908 Act widened access to secondary and university education, especially for girls and Catholics.
Limit: payment by results encouraged cramming and a narrow curriculum, and denominational divisions over education persisted for decades.
Contemporary Irish Party leaders saw suffrage as a distraction from Home Rule, whereas suffragists saw the vote as a democratic right.
Historians stress that the movement was divided by the national question, which weakened it, but that its organisation gave women experience used in later politics.

Ireland's Industrial Revolution was confined mainly to Belfast and the north-east. Dublin, by contrast, was a port, administrative and commercial city with little large-scale industry, so its working class had little steady work and lived in some of the worst housing in the United Kingdom.

Ireland was part of the United Kingdom, and Dublin was run by Dublin Castle (the British administration), Dublin Corporation (the city council) and the Dublin Metropolitan Police (DMP). Workers had few ways to press for change except through their own organisations.

Dublin's tenements were old Georgian town houses on the north side and in the Liberties, divided into single rooms. The 1911 census showed more than 20,000 families living one family to a room, which meant severe overcrowding.

Rooms had no running water and the whole house shared a yard toilet. Landlords collected high rents for these rooms, and some landlords sat on Dublin Corporation, so the people who could improve conditions profited from them.

Dublin had a very high death rate, among the highest of any city in the United Kingdom, with tuberculosis and infant mortality especially severe. Overcrowded and unsanitary housing helped spread disease.
Most unskilled men, such as dockers and carters, were casual labourers at the docks, in carting and in building. They were hired by the day at the stand with no security and very low pay.
Women worked in laundries, textile mills and biscuit factories and as domestic servants, again for low wages.
On 2 September 1913 two tenement houses in Church Street collapsed, killing seven people. It happened in the middle of the lockout and exposed the state of Dublin housing to the public.
A Local Government Board housing inquiry sat in 1913-14 to report on the conditions of tenement life.

A trade union is a body of workers that bargains collectively with employers over pay and conditions; its weapon is the strike (workers withdrawing their labour). Irish unions began as craft bodies for skilled workers, and from the 1880s and 1890s a new kind of union reached the unskilled.
Craft unions organised skilled trades such as printers, carpenters and engineers. Many were branches of British unions, and they had little interest in the unskilled.
The Irish Trades Union Congress was founded in 1894 so that Irish unions would have a common voice, though most unions remained British-based.

New unionism began in Britain in the 1880s; its best-known success was the London dockers' strike of 1889. It organised unskilled workers into general unions (open to any worker, not one trade) that were willing to strike.
James Connolly founded the Irish Socialist Republican Party in Dublin in 1896, because he argued that socialism and national independence were linked.

In 1907 James Larkin, then an organiser for the National Union of Dock Labourers, led a strike of Belfast dockers and carters. Catholic and Protestant workers united for a time, but riots in August 1907 left two men dead.
Larkin broke with the British union, and so founded the Irish Transport and General Workers' Union (ITGWU) in Dublin in 1909, with its headquarters at Liberty Hall.
The ITGWU won disputes in Dublin and Cork and fought a lockout (employers shutting workers out) in Wexford in 1911. Larkin also began the weekly Irish Worker in 1911 to speak for the union.
The Irish Labour Party was founded in 1912, at the Irish TUC meeting in Clonmel, so that workers would have their own voice in parliament.

Larkin was the charismatic organiser who built the ITGWU and led the Dublin workers in 1913. His career shows both the strength and the weakness of a leader who relied on inspiration and confrontation.
James Larkin was born in Liverpool to Irish parents in the 1870s (he gave 1876; other sources say 1874) and worked as a docker before becoming a union organiser. He died in 1947.

He was a participant in the events he shaped. He led the Belfast strike of 1907 as a National Union of Dock Labourers organiser, founded the ITGWU in 1909, began the Irish Worker in 1911 and was the main figure in Dublin in 1913.

His tactics, known as Larkinism, included the sympathetic strike (workers striking in support of others) and the refusal of union members to handle tainted goods, meaning goods from a firm in dispute. This spread disputes widely and gave small groups great power.
He was a powerful speaker. On 31 August 1913 he appeared in disguise on the balcony of the Imperial Hotel, Sackville Street, which Murphy owned, to address the banned meeting, and was then arrested.
He was sentenced to seven months for sedition in October 1913 but was released on 13 November 1913 after a public campaign.
He left Ireland for the United States in October 1914, which meant Connolly took over in Dublin. He was imprisoned there in 1920 and deported in 1923, and later returned to Irish politics.
Contemporaries divided. Dublin workers revered him as a champion, while employers, Murphy's Irish Independent, much of the press and the Church condemned him as a dangerous agitator.

Historians credit him with the first mass organisation of unskilled Irish workers. Some argue that his temper and intransigence (refusal to compromise) hardened the dispute in 1913 and made a settlement harder.

Connolly was the thinker of the Irish labour movement, who argued that socialism and national freedom were inseparable. Where Larkin organised the masses, Connolly supplied the ideas and, in 1914, a workers' army.

James Connolly was born in Edinburgh in 1868 to Irish parents, served in the British army and became a socialist organiser before moving to Dublin in 1896. He was executed on 12 May 1916 after the Easter Rising.
Socialism means common ownership of the means of production and an end to the class system. Connolly's version tied it to Irish national independence.
He founded the Irish Socialist Republican Party in 1896 and edited its paper, the Workers' Republic, to spread his ideas among workers.

He lived in the USA from 1903 to 1910, working with the Industrial Workers of the World, and wrote Labour in Irish History (1910). His other writings include Labour, Nationality and Religion (1910) and The Re-Conquest of Ireland (1915).
He returned in 1910, became Ulster organiser of the ITGWU and helped found the Labour Party in 1912.
During the lockout he was Larkin's lieutenant. When Larkin was jailed and then left for the USA, Connolly led the union and the Irish Citizen Army, becoming its commander in 1914.
For example, contemporaries on the left admired him, while the Church and employers distrusted his socialism. Many nationalists saw him as a distraction from the national cause until 1916.
Historians judge him the leading Irish socialist thinker. They debate whether his turn to the Rising in 1916 showed that he put nation before class.
William Martin Murphy led the employers' attempt to destroy the ITGWU before it could win recognition. His power and his principles explain why a local dispute became a city-wide lockout.

William Martin Murphy (1844-1919) was Dublin's leading capitalist. He was chairman of the Dublin United Tramways Company (DUTC), owner of the Irish Independent and leader of the Dublin Employers' Federation.
He argued that the ITGWU's sympathetic strikes and boycotts were tyranny over business and over other workers, and that employers had the right to manage without interference.
In July and August 1913 Larkin's union won concessions from several Dublin firms, so Murphy decided to challenge it before it grew stronger, on the trams and in the Independent's despatch department.
In August 1913 Murphy dismissed ITGWU members at the Independent and the DUTC; the tram strike began on 26 August.
A tram strike on the first day of Horse Show week grew into the lockout of thousands of workers. Keep the dates apart: 26 August was the strike, 31 August the baton charge, 3 September the Document.
On Tuesday 26 August 1913, the first day of Horse Show week, tram drivers and conductors left their cars, causing chaos in the city.
Murphy replaced strikers with other workers and the police protected the trams. The ITGWU responded by calling out other workers who handled tram-related goods.
On 29 August Larkin burned the police proclamation banning a meeting, and promised to speak in Sackville (now O'Connell) Street on Sunday 31 August 1913.
On 31 August the DMP baton-charged the crowd in Sackville Street, injuring hundreds, in what became known as Bloody Sunday. Two men died of baton wounds in the disturbances of that weekend.

On 3 September 1913 about 400 employers agreed to require every worker to sign the Document, a pledge to give up the ITGWU and not support it. Many locked out those who refused, so the strike became a lockout.
About 20,000 workers were out of work by autumn (estimates range up to about 25,000), with many thousands more dependants affected.
The Board of Trade's Askwith inquiry (September-October 1913), held under Sir George Askwith, condemned the Document, but the employers refused its proposals.
George Russell (AE) published an open letter to Dublin's employers in the Irish Times on 7 October 1913, attacking them for starving workers into submission.
Help from British unions kept the workers going, but the British TUC refused the sympathetic action Larkin wanted. Without it, hunger slowly decided the dispute.
British trade unions sent food. The first food ship, the SS Hare, reached Dublin on 27 September 1913, and money and supplies kept coming from British unions.
Food and relief were distributed from Liberty Hall, with soup kitchens and food parcels, so that strikers' families could survive without wages. Constance Markievicz worked in the soup kitchen.
Larkin was sentenced to seven months for sedition in October 1913 and released on 13 November after a public campaign. Connolly took over the running of the union.

The Save the Kiddies scheme of October 1913 was Dora Montefiore's plan to send strikers' children to homes in Britain. Archbishop William Walsh condemned it as a threat to the children's Catholic faith, and clergy and others stopped children leaving.
On 23 November 1913 the Irish Citizen Army was founded at Liberty Hall to protect workers from the police, and was drilled by Captain Jack White.
A special British TUC congress in December 1913 rejected sympathetic action and a boycott of Dublin goods, a heavy blow to the workers.
Hunger drove men back, so the ITGWU advised a return in January 1914. The dispute ended in January-February 1914, gradually rather than on one day.

Many men returned without signing the Document, but employers kept the right to bar ITGWU members in some firms and some workers were blacklisted or not re-employed, so the outcome favoured the employers.
The union lost the lockout but survived, and the dispute left a lasting mark on Irish labour and politics.
Many strikers returned without recognition of the union and the ITGWU lost members, but it survived and grew during the First World War, which shows that the defeat was not final.
The Irish Citizen Army, born of the lockout, took part in the 1916 Rising under Connolly.
The dispute made labour a political force in Dublin and began the alliance of labour and nationalism that Connolly favoured.

It split nationalist opinion, for example over whom to support. Griffith's Sinn Fein and the Irish Party were largely unsympathetic to the strikers, while Connolly, Yeats, AE and Constance Markievicz supported them.
The Church sympathised with the poor but condemned the tactics and the Save the Kiddies scheme, and warned against socialism.
The housing inquiry and public sympathy increased pressure for slum clearance in Dublin, so poverty, the Church Street collapse and the lockout fed into one another.

The 1913 case study is documents-based, so you must be able to place any source. Each side wrote to serve its own interest, and the sources include newspaper reports, a poem, an open letter and cartoons.
Murphy's Irish Independent, a paper owned by the chief employer, attacked Larkin as a dangerous agitator and presented the strike as an attack on trade and liberty.
The Irish Worker, Larkin's weekly, such as its attacks on Murphy, and Connolly's writings portrayed the employers as aggressors starving workers into submission.
Archbishop Walsh criticised the housing conditions but, as a churchman, warned against socialist ideas and condemned the removal of children.

Yeats's poem September 1913, published in the Irish Times on 8 September 1913, was written in the dispute over Hugh Lane's gallery, which Murphy's Independent opposed. It attacks the narrow, commercial Dublin middle class, with the line: "Romantic Ireland's dead and gone".
AE's open letter to the employers (Irish Times, 7 October 1913) is a strong middle-class voice for the workers, written by the poet George Russell, not by a trade unionist.
Cartoons in the Irish Worker and in Dublin papers show Murphy and the police as oppressors, or Larkin as a demagogue (a leader who stirs up the crowd), depending on the paper.
To place a document, identify the stage (tram strike, Bloody Sunday, the Document, the food ships, the end), the author's interest and the audience.
Judgements on 1913 compare the strength of organised labour with the cost of defeat. Use paired points so that each achievement is set against a limit.
Achievement: the ITGWU organised thousands of unskilled workers, which showed that they could be organised, kept a mass movement alive for about five months and won widespread sympathy.
Limit: it failed to defeat the employers, because it lacked British union support for sympathetic action and ended with hunger forcing a return.
Larkin's strengths were inspiration and organising ability. His weaknesses were intransigence and the extension of the dispute into a general conflict.
Murphy's strengths were unity and resources. His weaknesses were a hardness that cost him public sympathy and drew the attention of the British government.
Contemporaries disagreed because their interests differed: employers called it a defence of liberty, workers a defence of the right to organise.
Historians see 1913 as a defeat that strengthened the labour movement, and as a source of the Citizen Army and the radicalisation that fed 1916.

By the 1880s most Irish farmers worked small tenant holdings and were squeezed by prices, debt and foreign competition. The co-operative movement was an attempt to solve these problems by self-help while the land question was moving towards tenant ownership.
Most farms were small and rented from landlords. The agricultural depression of 1877-79 hit tenants hard, and land reform was by then moving towards tenant ownership of the land.
Irish farmers sold their produce badly. They suffered from poor marketing and prices were poor.
New competition came from imports, above all Danish butter, which was better made and graded.
Denmark had answered the same pressure by organising farmer-owned co-operative creameries (dairies that process milk into butter), and this became the model Irish reformers copied.
Many farmers depended on gombeen men, the local shopkeepers and moneylenders who sold goods and lent money on credit at high prices and high interest. This kept small farmers permanently in debt.

The movement was driven by one man, an unusual figure who was a landowner and a Unionist but wanted to reform Irish farming from below. His background explains both his ideas and the suspicion he met.

Horace Plunkett (1854-1932), the son of Lord Dunsany (an Anglo-Irish peer), was an Anglo-Irish landowner. He ranched in Wyoming in the 1880s and returned to Ireland convinced that farmers needed better organisation.
He was a Unionist MP for South Dublin from 1892 to 1900 (he lost the seat in 1900), though he worked with nationalists in his reform schemes.

Plunkett took the Danish model of farmer-owned co-operative creameries, where farmers pooled their milk and shared the profits. A creamery used a mechanical cream separator (a machine that separates cream from milk), giving higher quality at lower cost.
The first co-operative creamery is usually dated to 1889 at Dromcollogher, Co. Limerick. The model then spread in Munster and elsewhere.
Plunkett's supporters included Fr Tom Finlay, a Jesuit, and the poet and writer George Russell, who used the pen name AE.
The Irish Homestead, begun in 1895, was the movement's weekly paper, which spread its ideas to farmers. AE edited it from 1905, so here he matters as a co-operator and editor.
One creamery was not a movement. In 1894 Plunkett founded a central body to promote, advise and check co-operative societies across the country, and the idea spread beyond dairying.
The Irish Agricultural Organisation Society (IAOS) was founded in 1894 by Plunkett to organise, advise and inspect co-operative societies.
Its motto was "better farming, better business, better living", a short statement of its self-help philosophy: farmers improving their own lives without waiting for the state.

Co-operative creameries multiplied in the 1890s, giving small dairy farmers a market and a share of the profits. They introduced mechanical cream separators and bought milk by its fat content, which rewarded quality and raised the standard of Irish butter.
Credit societies were modelled on German Raiffeisen banks. They lent small sums to members on the guarantee of their neighbours, which reduced dependence on gombeen men.
Other societies supplied seeds and fertiliser and sold eggs and poultry. The Irish Agricultural Wholesale Society (IAWS), the movement's wholesale body, was founded in 1897.
By 1914 there were about 1,000 societies with about 100,000 members (approximate; estimates vary). They were strongest in Munster and weakest in Ulster.
Plunkett believed the state had to back self-help. In 1895 he brought nationalists and unionists together to argue for a government department for farming and industry, and in 1899 he got one.

The Recess Committee met during the parliamentary recess of 1895 (the break when Parliament was not sitting), with Plunkett as chairman. It brought together nationalists and unionists, including Thomas Sinclair, a Belfast Presbyterian unionist, and John Redmond, a nationalist.
Its report in 1896 studied the methods of Denmark, France and Germany and recommended a government department for agriculture and technical education.

The Department of Agriculture and Technical Instruction (DATI) was established in 1899. Plunkett was its vice-president (the effective head) from 1899 to 1907, and the Chief Secretary for Ireland was its president.
DATI's work included agricultural education and instructors, research, technical schools and fisheries, so the state now supported the practical improvement the co-operatives promoted.
Plunkett lost the vice-presidency in 1907 after hostility from the Irish Party, and T.W. Russell succeeded him.

Co-operation brought clear economic gains, but because Plunkett was a Unionist working across the political divide, many groups distrusted him. Understanding who suspected him, and why, is as important as knowing what the movement achieved.

Many nationalists suspected Plunkett, a unionist, of trying to turn farmers away from the land and national questions. Irish Party hostility later cost him his post in 1907, while others, like AE, saw the movement as national self-help.
Many unionists, especially Ulster farmers, were slow to join, partly through suspicion of Plunkett's dealings with nationalists. The movement was weakest in Ulster.
The Catholic clergy had often supported local creameries. Even so, a clerical and nationalist campaign contributed to Plunkett's defeat in 1900.
Four years later, Plunkett's book Ireland in the New Century (1904) criticised Catholic influence on Irish initiative, which angered the Church and caused him further problems.
Private creamery owners and shopkeepers resented the competition from co-operatives, because the societies took away their trade.
Results: the co-operatives improved the quality of Irish butter, raised farm incomes, spread the idea of self-help and trained a generation of local leaders.
The movement did not solve the problems of poor western farmers, who were helped more by the Congested Districts Board (founded in 1891).

Most of Ireland stayed farming country, but north-east Ulster shared in the Industrial Revolution. Belfast grew from a small town into Ireland's industrial capital, tied by trade to Britain and the empire.

The Industrial Revolution (the shift to factory and machine production) reached north-east Ulster, in linen and shipbuilding, far more than the rest of Ireland. Belfast's trade was tied to Britain and the empire, which supplied its markets and raw materials.
Belfast's population was only about 20,000 around 1800, so the later growth was very rapid. It was given city status in 1888.
The census figures were about 255,000 in 1891 (255,896), about 349,000 in 1901 (349,180) and about 387,000 in 1911 (386,947). In 1891 Belfast passed Dublin city to become the largest city in Ireland.
Catholic workers from the countryside moved into west Belfast, around the Falls Road. By 1911 about a quarter of the city was Catholic.
Belfast's growth rested on several industries, with linen first and shipbuilding later. Most of them sold to Britain and the empire, which is why the city's prosperity depended on that link.
Linen, spun and woven in mills, was the first great industry. Belfast was nicknamed Linenopolis and its mills employed tens of thousands of workers, mostly women and girls.
The American Civil War (1861-65) cut cotton supplies and boosted linen. Power-loom mills (machine weaving) then replaced handloom weaving in people's homes.
The Belfast Ropeworks at Connswater, founded in 1873, was among the largest ropeworks in the world. It supplied rope to shipping across the world.
Tobacco manufacture grew with Gallaher and other firms. Engineering firms such as the Sirocco Works made machinery for export.
Whiskey distilling (Dunville) was another trade, so the city's industry was varied and not tied to one product.
Shipbuilding on Queen's Island made Belfast famous. It began with a small yard, two engineers and a young apprentice who became its driving force.

Edward Harland, an English engineer, bought a small yard on Queen's Island in 1858. In 1861 he went into partnership with Gustav Wolff, a German-born engineer from Hamburg, creating Harland and Wolff.
William Pirrie was born in Quebec in 1847 to Ulster parents and joined the yard as an apprentice. He became a partner in 1874 and chairman after Harland's death in 1895.
Pirrie's success was rewarded when he was made Lord Pirrie in 1906, for example. Remember that Harland, not Pirrie, founded the yard; Pirrie led it from 1895.
Workman Clark, founded in 1880 by Frank Workman and George Clark, was the second Belfast yard. It built cargo and passenger ships, so it competed with Harland and Wolff for the shipping trade.
Harland and Wolff won its fame by building giant liners for the White Star Line. The yards also became the city's biggest employers, so Belfast's prosperity rode on the empire's shipping trade.
The firm built ships for the White Star Line, including the Olympic-class liners Olympic (launched 1910), Titanic and Britannic (launched 1914). They were the biggest ships in the world when built.
The Arrol Gantry, built over the slipways in 1908-09 by Sir William Arrol, allowed Olympic and Titanic to be built side by side.
Titanic was launched on 31 May 1911 and sank on her maiden voyage on 15 April 1912 after hitting an iceberg, with the loss of about 1,500 lives.
Harland and Wolff alone employed about 15,000 men by 1912 (approximate). The two yards together employed tens of thousands.
Industrial Belfast offered work, but conditions were hard, and jobs were divided by religion. This divide helped link the city's industry to unionism.
Mill workers, mostly women and girls, worked long hours in hot, damp rooms full of flax dust (fine fibres from the flax plant), which caused lung disease. Wages were low.
Half-timers (child workers who split their time between school and mill) also worked in the mills. Many mill women were the main earners in their families.
Shipyard work was dangerous, and casual labourers were laid off between contracts, so their income was uncertain.

Skilled jobs in the shipyards and engineering were mainly held by Protestants, helped by family and Orange Order connections (the Orange Order being a Protestant society). Catholics tended to be labourers.
Sectarian riots occurred in Belfast in 1857, 1864 and 1886. The riots of 1886, during the Home Rule crisis of that year, included attacks on Catholic workers at the shipyards.
Religious divisions at work exploded in 1912, while an earlier moment of unity had faded. Together with economic self-interest, these events tied Belfast's workers and employers to unionism.
In 1907 Larkin's Belfast dockers' strike briefly united Catholic and Protestant workers, but the unity did not last.

In July 1912, during the Home Rule crisis, Protestant workers drove Catholic workers and some Protestant labour sympathisers out of Workman Clark and Harland and Wolff. The numbers were thousands, about 2,000-3,000 by common estimates (estimates vary).
Belfast's Protestant majority opposed Home Rule (a separate Irish parliament). Many Protestant workers feared that Home Rule would bring tariffs (taxes on trade) and Catholic dominance.
Belfast's industries depended on markets in Britain and the empire, so this fear linked industrial interests to unionism.
The two largest cities in Ireland had different economies, and these shaped their politics. A good comparison links economy to attitudes towards Home Rule.
Belfast depended on export manufacturing, mainly linen and shipbuilding, linked to British and imperial markets. Dublin depended on administration, trade, brewing and distilling.
Dublin had large employers such as Guinness at St James's Gate and Jacob's biscuits, but many of its workers were casual and poorly paid.

Skilled shipyard and engineering men in Belfast earned more than Dublin's casual labourers. Belfast's workers lived in terraced streets rather than Dublin-style tenements, though poverty and disease still afflicted the mill districts.
Belfast was strongly Protestant and unionist. Dublin was nationalist, with a strong labour movement.
Belfast's industrial development depended on its link with Britain, which was a major reason for unionist opposition to Home Rule.
Belfast's Catholic minority and Protestant majority lived in separate districts, such as the Catholic Falls and the Protestant Shankill, so the city's politics were territorial as well as economic.
Both developments brought prosperity to part of Ireland, but each left problems unsolved. Examiners reward a clear judgement with named facts on both sides.
Achievement: the co-operatives raised the quality of butter and farmers' incomes, and encouraged self-help. Belfast became an industrial city of international importance.
Limit: the co-operatives hardly reached the poor west or Ulster, and drew political suspicion. Belfast's prosperity rested on cheap female labour, harsh conditions and sectarian divisions.
Contemporary nationalists were suspicious of Plunkett as a unionist, while unionists pointed to Belfast as proof of the benefits of the Union.
Historians judge the co-operative movement a success of self-help, though it is often judged less decisive than land reform in modernising Irish farming.

By the early 1880s many Irish people felt that their own language, games and customs were being pushed aside by English ones, just as politics was stirring strong national feeling. The GAA grew out of both worries.
The Famine and the heavy emigration that followed weakened rural Irish society and the Irish language, so English language and customs spread, especially in towns and schools.

Anglicisation means the replacement of Irish language, dress, games and customs by English ones. De-anglicisation is the effort to reverse this by reviving Irish language, games and customs, and the GAA was an early example.
The Gaelic Union (1880), successor to the Society for the Preservation of the Irish Language (1876), was formed to preserve Irish, so the language already had a society while games had none.

The Land War began in 1879, when Michael Davitt founded the Land League with Parnell as president to defend tenant farmers against landlords. From 1880 the Irish Party (Home Rule Party), led by Parnell, sought self-government for Ireland.

A Fenian revival was also under way. The IRB (Irish Republican Brotherhood, the Fenians) was a secret, oath-bound society that wanted an Irish republic won by force, so it looked for new organisations to join.

The Catholic Church was a powerful influence on nationalist Ireland and was generally constitutional, preferring peaceful politics to secret societies. This is why the Church and the IRB later came into conflict inside the GAA.
Irish Ireland was the later cultural-nationalist idea of building the nation on native language, games and traditions. It was developed after 1891, but the GAA is one of its roots.

Before the GAA, organised sport in Ireland followed English rules and belonged mainly to the gentry and middle class, while the native game of hurling had declined. That gap is what the GAA set out to fill.

Organised athletics followed English-style amateur rules that excluded “mechanics, artisans and labourers” (people who earned a living by manual work), so most working people and most farmers could not compete as amateurs.

Rugby, cricket and later soccer were played in schools, in garrison towns (towns with an army barracks) and among the gentry. The Irish Rugby Football Union was formed in 1879 and the Irish Football Association (soccer, Belfast-based) in 1880.
Hurling had declined since the Famine, as landlord patronage ended and rural communities shrank. It survived in parts of Galway and Munster, including Tipperary, Limerick, Cork and Clare.
Hurling was played under varying local rules, and football had no national code, so teams from different districts could not easily play one another on agreed terms.
Michael Cusack founded the Metropolitan Hurling Club in Dublin in 1882 and pushed for standard rules, which shows that the idea of a national code existed before the GAA.
Two very different men started the GAA. Cusack supplied the drive and the ideas, and Davin supplied the respect that made others join.
Michael Cusack was born at Carron, Co. Clare, in 1847 and died in 1906. He was a teacher who ran a Dublin academy preparing pupils for exams.
Cusack was forceful and quarrelsome, which made him a tireless promoter but a difficult colleague, a point that matters when he falls out with fellow officers in 1886.
Cusack’s fame outlived him in literature: he was the model for “the Citizen”, a character in James Joyce’s novel Ulysses.
Maurice Davin was born in 1842 near Carrick-on-Suir, Co. Tipperary, and died in 1927. He was a champion athlete in weight-throwing and a champion rower.
Davin was respected for his fairness, so he was the natural first president of the GAA (1884–1889). His standing gave the new body credibility with athletes and clubs.
Do not mix the two up: Cusack was the Clare-born founder, agitator and secretary, removed in 1886, while Davin was the Tipperary sportsman and president, who resigned in 1889.
In the autumn of 1884 Cusack went from writing about Irish athletics to calling a meeting, and the GAA was founded at Thurles within weeks.
In October 1884 (on 11 October) Cusack’s article “A Word About Irish Athletics” appeared in United Ireland, calling for a national body to revive native athletics.
United Ireland was Parnell’s nationalist weekly, edited by William O’Brien, so the call reached exactly the nationalist readers Cusack wanted.
Cusack and Davin then sent out invitations to a meeting at Hayes’ Hotel, Thurles, Co. Tipperary.
The meeting took place on Saturday 1 November 1884. Seven men attended, among them Cusack, Davin and John Wyse Power, a journalist.
Davin was elected president and Cusack was elected one of the secretaries.
The aims were to revive Irish games, to open athletics to all classes, and to promote physical fitness and national pride.
The full title was the Gaelic Athletic Association for the Preservation and Cultivation of National Pastimes, where “pastimes” means games and sports.
Cusack won the backing of the most powerful figures in nationalist Ireland. Their names gave the GAA respectability and publicity it could not have won alone.
Thomas Croke, Archbishop of Cashel from 1875, had supported the tenants in the Land War and was a known nationalist, so his name carried weight with farmers.
In a letter of December 1884 Croke agreed to become patron. He condemned the imitation of English games and manners and urged the revival of Irish pastimes as an act of national self-respect.
Parnell and Davitt both agreed to be patrons (1884–85), which linked the GAA to the Home Rule movement and to the land movement.
