Davitt saw the GAA as a way of drawing working people and farmers into the national movement, and as a way of reviving Irish games to break from English influence. He wrote and spoke in support.
William O’Brien, editor of United Ireland, promised the GAA regular space in the paper, which gave it free publicity.
Croke’s letter was widely printed and made the GAA respectable, and many priests became club presidents and organisers.
The GAA set rules that separated Irish sport from English sport and built a structure on the parish. These choices explain both its quick growth and some of its later quarrels.
The first rules for hurling and Gaelic football were drawn up chiefly by Davin in 1885, replacing the old local variations with national codes.
Competition was open to all classes, so the English amateur definition that excluded manual workers was rejected.
The GAA was itself amateur (players were not paid), and it set out to keep money and professionalism out of sport.
The foreign games ban stopped members from playing foreign games such as rugby, soccer, cricket and hockey. Its purpose was de-anglicisation, and the early ban concerned playing, not attending.

Members of the Royal Irish Constabulary (the police force) and the British armed forces were also barred, because they represented British rule. The first ban covers games and the second covers people.
Each club was based on a parish, with county committees and a Central Council above them, and an annual convention (the yearly delegate meeting) that was usually held in Thurles.
The parish structure matched the Catholic Church’s own organisation, which made it easy for priests to take part.
The parish club system let the GAA spread very fast, and in 1887 it launched its first All-Ireland championships.
The GAA spread first in the south and west and then to the midlands and beyond. Within a few years hundreds of clubs had affiliated (joined the Association).
Matches became local occasions, with large crowds, bands and parades of club men. The crowds also brought problems, such as drinking.
The first All-Ireland championship was held in 1887 with an open draw and no provincial stage. It was decided in 1888, so its finals were played in 1888, not 1887.
The first hurling final was played at Birr (then King’s County, now Co. Offaly) on 1 April 1888. Thurles, representing Tipperary, beat Meelick, representing Galway.
The first football final was played in April 1888. Commercials, representing Limerick, beat Young Irelands (Dundalk), representing Louth.
Cusack founded a weekly paper, The Celtic Times, in 1887 to promote Gaelic games.
The GAA’s success made it a target for the Fenians and a worry for the Church, and its own leaders fell out. These are the first of the difficulties examiners ask about.
Members of the IRB joined in large numbers, using clubs and county boards (the committees of each county) to recruit and to gain influence. Widespread local clubs gave them a ready network.
Dublin Castle (the seat of British government in Ireland) watched the GAA closely, and RIC reports described it as a front for Fenianism.
Cusack was removed as secretary in 1886 after quarrelling with fellow officers. The causes are disputed, so the safe statement is the date and the quarrels.
At the Thurles convention of 1887, IRB-linked and moderate delegates contested control of the Central Council.

Archbishop Croke and other bishops grew uneasy, and the Church was concerned about drink and discipline. Croke wrote to a GAA convention complaining of drinking at games, and in some places priests withdrew from clubs.
Davin resigned as president in 1889 amid the disputes and divisions of those years.
The IRB’s hold on the Central Council was strong by the later 1880s, and the stronger it grew, the more the Church held back.
Two blows in quick succession, an expensive overseas tour and the split in Irish nationalism, brought the association close to collapse.
In autumn 1888 about fifty hurlers and athletes, known as the American Invasion, toured the United States, with Irish-American support in cities such as New York and Boston.
The tour lost money and left debts. It also disrupted the 1888 championship, which was left unfinished and played off in 1889, and some of the athletes stayed in America.
The O’Shea divorce case (November 1890) damaged Parnell, and the Irish Party split in December 1890 (in Committee Room 15) into pro- and anti-Parnell groups.
The split divided GAA members, with the IRB generally favouring Parnell and Church-minded members opposing him. This is the same man who had been a GAA patron in 1884 but now caused division.
Parnell died on 6 October 1891, which left the association demoralised.
By 1891 membership and the number of clubs had collapsed, and a few county boards were all that remained in many areas.
The GAA recovered slowly in the 1890s, with a new generation of leaders and the support of the Gaelic revival (the renewed interest in Irish language and culture).

The main exam question on this case study asks how the GAA dealt with its difficulties to 1891. The answers are its organisation, its patrons, the appeal of the games and a willingness to change leaders.
The parish-based club system meant that local clubs could carry on even when the Central Council quarrelled.
The patronage of Croke and the clergy gave the association moral authority, and priests helped to restore order in clubs.
The appeal of hurling and football, and of local rivalry, was strong in itself and did not depend on politics.
The removal of Cusack and the departure of Davin showed an attempt to settle disputes by changing leaders rather than breaking up the body.
Links with the nationalist movement, through Parnell, Davitt and the IRB, gave the GAA energy but also exposed it to the Parnell split.
Its identity as an Irish-only, amateur body made it a symbol of de-anglicisation, which the later Irish Ireland ideas built on.
Documents on the early GAA are letters, speeches and reports. Each was written by someone with a purpose, so judging a source means asking who wrote it, when, why and for whom.
Cusack’s article of October 1884 and his invitations are founding documents, expressing the aim of opening athletics to all classes. He was the founder, so he is not neutral.
Croke’s letter of December 1884 is the best-known statement of the GAA’s national purpose, and it should be read as a clerical and nationalist appeal against English fashions.
Croke’s later complaint to a convention about drinking at games shows a churchman’s concern about discipline, and a favourable picture of crowds and bands can be set against it.
Davitt’s letters and speeches show the GAA’s links with the land movement, and Parnell’s patronage brought political prestige.
Unionist newspapers and Dublin Castle reports describe the GAA as seditious or as a cover for the IRB. They were hostile, so they may exaggerate.
Reports of conventions and county board meetings are evidence of the dispute between moderates and the IRB, though they are written by partisans (people taking a side).

Marcus de Búrca, The GAA: A History (1980), is a full institutional history. W.F. Mandle, The Gaelic Athletic Association and Irish Nationalist Politics, 1884–1924 (1987), stresses the political and IRB links, and Paul Rouse, Sport and Ireland: A History (2015), is a later study.
The GAA’s early years show both a cultural achievement and the cost of political entanglement. A good answer gives both sides and a judgement.
Achievement: it created a national mass organisation open to all classes, standardised the rules of hurling and football and built a parish network.
Limit: IRB entanglement, the quarrel with the Church, debts from the American tour and the Parnell split brought it close to collapse by 1891.
Contemporary nationalists saw it as a school for national feeling, while unionists and the authorities saw it as Fenian, and bishops saw it as useful but dangerous.
Later historians see the GAA as a central part of the cultural nationalism of the 1880s, which anticipated the Gaelic League (1893, founded by Douglas Hyde and Eoin MacNeill) and Irish Ireland.

By the 1880s many Irish people felt that politics alone had not made Ireland distinct, and that the country's own culture was fading. Below are the background events and the vocabulary that the rest of the subsection depends on.
The Great Famine (1845–52) killed about one million people and led to the emigration of about one million more. Irish as a spoken language fell sharply after the Famine.
English was the language of the state, law and commerce, and the national school system (begun in 1831) taught in English. Revivalists later set out to restore Irish.
Anglicisation means adopting English language, dress, games, names and manners. De-anglicisation is Douglas Hyde's programme to reverse this by reviving the Irish language, games, music and customs.

The Anglo-Irish were the mainly Protestant landowning and professional class with English ties, many of them unionist (supporters of the union with Britain). In this subsection the term also labels the writers of the Literary Revival, and is the label their critics used for them.

Cultural nationalism defines the nation by its language, culture and tradition rather than by parliaments and votes. The Gaelic League, the GAA and the Literary Revival were all cultural nationalist movements.
Irish Ireland is D.P. Moran's idea of a Gaelic and Catholic nation built on the Irish language, Irish industry and Irish games. It was narrower than Hyde's approach.

The Catholic Church under Paul Cullen (archbishop of Armagh from 1849 and of Dublin from 1852, with the Synod of Thurles in 1850) set about reforming Irish Catholic practice. The Catholic majority also gave nationalist politics (the Home Rule movement and Parnell) its weight.
The GAA, founded at Thurles on 1 November 1884, was the first of the cultural bodies.
Hyde's lecture of 1892 gave the cultural revival its programme: Irish people should stop imitating England and revive their own language and customs.

Douglas Hyde delivered The Necessity for De-Anglicising Ireland to the National Literary Society in Dublin on 25 November 1892. The Society had been founded in Dublin that year, with Hyde, Yeats and John O'Leary among those involved.

Hyde argued that Ireland had been anglicised in language, names, dress, music, games and ideas. The Irish, he said, were neither fully English nor fully Irish, because they had abandoned their own ways without becoming truly English.
He urged the revival of Irish and of native customs, so that Ireland could preserve what was distinctive about it rather than copy England.

The lecture was presented as non-political: its aim was cultural, and it appealed to all creeds and parties. This is why it could later support a League that welcomed Catholics, Protestants, nationalists and unionists.
Hyde pointed to the decline of Irish as a spoken language, which had fallen sharply since the Famine, and asked for it to be cultivated and used in schools.
The GAA (1884) had already shown the appeal of native games. The lecture gave a wider programme, covering language and customs, and led within a year to the founding of the Gaelic League.
The Gaelic League, founded in 1893, turned Hyde's argument into a mass movement to revive the Irish language. Its story is one of real successes, then growing political pressure.
The Gaelic League (Conradh na Gaeilge) was founded in Dublin on 31 July 1893 by Douglas Hyde, Eoin MacNeill and others, with Hyde as president.
It was officially non-political and non-sectarian, so it welcomed Catholics, Protestants, nationalists and unionists. This broad stance helped it recruit across the divisions of Irish society.
Branches ran Irish classes, so that adults could learn the language, and timirí (travelling teachers of Irish) were sent to rural areas. There were several hundred branches by the mid-1900s.

The League organised feiseanna (festivals of music, dance and language competitions), so that people could enjoy Irish culture and not only study it, and, from 1897, the annual festival called the Oireachtas.
Its weekly paper An Claidheamh Soluis began in 1899, and Patrick Pearse edited it from 1903 to 1909. This gave the League a way to spread its ideas.
Success in schools: Irish was admitted to primary schools as an ordinary subject by the Revised Programme of 1900, and a bilingual programme followed in 1904.

Success at university: the League won a campaign to make Irish compulsory for matriculation (the entrance qualification) to the National University of Ireland. The Senate decided this in 1910 and it applied from 1913.
Language processions on St Patrick's Day began in 1903, the year it became a bank holiday in Ireland. People also took Irish names and used Irish-language signs.
The League drew on a wide social range, but the same success that made it influential also pulled it into politics and exposed its limits.
The League's membership included women, teachers and the urban middle class, and its leadership was based in Dublin. This differed from the GAA, which was rural and male.
From about 1910 a growing number of IRB members (the Irish Republican Brotherhood, a secret society that wanted an independent republic) joined the League. They pushed it towards politics.

Hyde resigned as president in 1915 after the League's Ard Fheis (annual convention) in July 1915 adopted a political aim. This is later context: it shows that the League's non-political stance did not survive.
Limit: Irish did not revive as an everyday language, so the main aim was not reached, even though the League put it into schools and the university.

Limit: the Church's support was limited. Fr Michael O'Hickey, professor of Irish at Maynooth, was dismissed in 1909 by the bishops (the college trustees) after campaigning for compulsory Irish in the National University.
Hyde was the scholar who launched the language revival and gave it a non-sectarian, non-political character. He was both a founder of the movement and, in the end, a man overtaken by it.
Douglas Hyde (1860–1949) was born in Castlerea, Co. Roscommon, the son of a Church of Ireland rector. He learned Irish from the people around him in Frenchpark and studied at Trinity College Dublin.

He published collections of Gaelic songs and folktales, including Love Songs of Connacht (1893), and wrote under the pen name An Craoibhín Aoibhinn (the little branch of delight). His Irish-language play Casadh an tSúgáin was staged in 1901.
He was a participant: he gave the 1892 lecture, co-founded the League in 1893 and led it as president for twenty-two years, until 1915.
He was shaped by events: the League's politicisation after about 1910 overtook his non-political aim, and he resigned as president in 1915 when it adopted a political aim.

Contemporaries admired his scholarship and his appeal across religious lines. Irish Irelanders disliked the League's non-political, non-sectarian stance, and republicans criticised him later as the League turned political.
He later became a senator (1925) and the first President of Ireland (1938–45), and died in 1949.
Historians credit him with launching the revival and a mass interest in the language, while recognising that its later political use went beyond his intentions.
Moran gave the revival a sharper edge by defining the Irish nation as Gaelic and Catholic. His view challenged Hyde's inclusive approach.
David Patrick Moran founded the weekly newspaper The Leader in 1900 and used it to argue for an Irish Ireland.
He urged support for Irish language, industry and games, and attacked the Anglo-Irish literary movement and the Irish Party as West Britons, his term for Irish people who imitated English ways.
In his view the nation was Gaelic and Catholic, so Protestants could be accepted only if they adopted this identity.
His book The Philosophy of Irish Ireland (1905) collected his articles and set out his creed.
The Leader promoted boycotts of English goods and entertainment, to support Irish industry, and attacked music-hall and English newspapers.
Moran's influence divided the revival between Hyde's inclusive approach and a narrower Catholic and Gaelic nationalism.

A group of mainly Protestant writers in English drew on Irish myth, folklore and peasant speech to create a national literature and theatre. Unlike the League, they wrote in English, which is why Irish Irelanders distrusted them.
The National Literary Society was founded in Dublin in 1892, with Hyde and Yeats among its leaders.

The Irish Literary Theatre was founded in 1899 by W.B. Yeats, Lady Gregory and Edward Martyn. Its first production, in May 1899, was Yeats's The Countess Cathleen. In 1901 it staged Hyde's Irish-language play Casadh an tSúgáin.
Cathleen ni Houlihan, credited to Yeats with Lady Gregory's help, was first staged on 2 April 1902, with Maud Gonne (a nationalist activist) in the title role. It was a nationalist play.
The Abbey Theatre opened on 27 December 1904, funded by the English patron Annie Horniman, with Yeats, Lady Gregory and J.M. Synge as directors.
Lady Gregory (1852–1932), for example, was an Anglo-Irish landowner from Coole Park, Co. Galway. She wrote plays, collected folklore, and acted as patron and organiser of the Abbey as a director.
John Millington Synge (1871–1909) drew on the speech of the Aran Islands and the west of Ireland. His The Playboy of the Western World was first performed at the Abbey in January 1907.
Yeats, a Protestant poet and dramatist, tried to give Ireland a literature that would shape a national identity. He found that the nationalists he wrote for did not always accept him.
William Butler Yeats (1865–1939) was born in Sandymount, Dublin, on 13 June 1865, the son of the painter John Butler Yeats. He spent much of his childhood in Sligo and London, and was a Protestant.

His early poetry, such as The Wanderings of Oisin (1889), drew on Irish mythology. His friendship with the nationalist activist Maud Gonne and with John O'Leary, the old Fenian who influenced him, linked him to political circles.
He was a participant who co-founded the National Literary Society, the Irish Literary Theatre and the Abbey (as a director), and was linked to the play Cathleen ni Houlihan.
He was shaped by events, so his views changed: the Countess Cathleen and Playboy controversies and the Lane dispute pushed him towards a critique of nationalist Ireland.

September 1913, published in the Irish Times on 8 September 1913, followed the Hugh Lane dispute. It condemned the narrow Catholic middle class for lacking the generosity of earlier Irish rebels, and its refrain is: Romantic Ireland's dead and gone.

Contemporary nationalists admired his work but distrusted his Anglo-Irish background, because he was a Protestant writing in English. Moran mocked him, and Catholic critics attacked The Countess Cathleen.
He later served as a senator (1922–28), won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923, and died in 1939.
Historians such as R.F. Foster (W.B. Yeats: A Life, volume 1 in 1997 and volume 2 in 2003) see him at the centre of Irish cultural life, while critics find an elitist streak in his politics.
The revival was marked by public disputes about who defined Irish identity. Each controversy shows the clash between the Anglo-Irish and Irish Ireland visions.
The Countess Cathleen (1899) was attacked as heretical by Catholic critics. Frank Hugh O'Donnell's pamphlet Souls for Gold (1899) was a leading attack.

The Playboy riots of January 1907 followed because nationalist audiences objected to the play's picture of rural Irish people. They showed the clash between the Abbey's artistic freedom and the nationalist demand for flattering images of Irish life.

The Hugh Lane dispute began when Sir Hugh Lane offered his collection of French paintings to Dublin and Dublin Corporation hesitated over funding and a site for a gallery (1912–13). Lane withdrew the offer and lent the pictures to the National Gallery in London in 1913.

Lane died on the Lusitania on 7 May 1915. An unwitnessed codicil (an addition to his will) left the pictures to Dublin, leading to a long dispute that was only settled by a shared arrangement in 1959.
Nationalists argued that Irish culture should be Gaelic and Catholic, while the Anglo-Irish writers claimed a place for English-language literature and for Protestant traditions.
Tension between the two visions, Anglo-Irish and Irish Ireland, ran through the revival and remained after independence.
After the Famine the Catholic Church tightened its hold on Irish life. Its influence grew through worship, buildings, schools and the clergy.

Historians speak of a devotional revolution, a term coined by the historian Emmet Larkin (1972) for the post-Famine rise in Mass attendance and devotional practice under Cullen. From the 1850s there were parish missions, retreats, confraternities and devotions such as the Rosary and the Sacred Heart.
New churches and cathedrals were built across the country, which made the Church's presence visible, funded by a more prosperous farming and trading middle class.

The Church controlled most national schools through clerical managers (priests who ran the schools). It ran secondary schools through religious orders such as the Christian Brothers, Jesuits and convent teaching orders, so it shaped what young Catholics learned.

St Patrick's College, Maynooth, trained a large clergy, which held a high social position in rural communities. Priests were often involved in politics, and individual priests were active in local GAA clubs.
Sodalities and confraternities (lay associations for prayer and devotion) organised lay devotion, so ordinary parishioners, not only priests, took part in religious life.
The Pioneer Total Abstinence Association was founded in 1898 by Fr James Cullen, a Jesuit, to fight drunkenness.
From the 1880s Catholic identity and nationalist identity increasingly overlapped, and unionists reacted with fear. This was one of the main results of the Church's growing role.

The Ne Temere decree, in force from Easter 1908, declared that marriages not before a Catholic priest were invalid for Catholics and required the children of mixed marriages to be raised as Catholics. This angered Protestants.
The land reforms and expanding education produced a Catholic middle class, which provided the personnel of the nationalist movement.
The Catholic bishops generally supported Home Rule from 1885, which tied Catholic identity to nationalism. The Irish Party was largely Catholic.

Unionists reacted by presenting Home Rule as Rome Rule, their slogan. The Church's role in the Parnell split (the hierarchy condemned Parnell in December 1890 after the divorce scandal) and Ne Temere reinforced the fear.
The GAA recovered in the 1890s and the two bodies became partners and rivals. Comparing them is a favourite exam task.
The GAA was weakened by the Parnell split and the crisis of 1891 and recovered slowly through the 1890s, when clubs were reorganised and competitions resumed.
The IRB remained influential in its leadership. The GAA also banned its members from playing foreign games, a rule formalised in the early 1900s.
It bought grounds at Jones's Road in Dublin in 1908; the ground was later called Croke Park.
The GAA was mass, rural, male and sport-based. The League drew women, teachers and the urban middle class, and its work was language and education.
The GAA was politically committed from the start, whereas the League was non-political until 1915.
Both were created by cultural nationalists and shared the aim of de-anglicisation and many members. Key names differ: Michael Cusack and Maurice Davin for the GAA, Hyde and MacNeill for the League.
The revival gave Ireland a cultural identity but left argument about who belonged to it.
Achievement: the League, GAA and theatre created lasting institutions and symbols, and gave self-confidence to the nationalist movement.
Limit: the language did not revive as an everyday tongue, and the Catholic and Gaelic emphasis excluded many Protestants and unionists.
Contemporary unionists saw the revival as a disguise for separatism, whereas Irish Irelanders such as Moran saw the Literary Revival as too Anglo-Irish.
Historians differ on whether the revival caused the revolution of 1916, as Pearse and the IRB claimed, or merely provided a language for politics that had other causes.

History means three linked things: the past itself, the evidence that survives from it, and the written accounts historians build from that evidence. Keeping the three apart explains why historians can disagree and why their conclusions can change.
The past itself is gone, so no one can examine the Dublin lockout of 1913 directly; all that remains is what it left behind, such as records, newspapers, photographs and memoirs.
Evidence is whatever survives from the past: documents, objects, images, buildings and recorded memories. Only some of it survives, so every account is built on an incomplete picture.
A written history is a historian’s account, shaped by the questions asked and the evidence found, so two historians can offer different histories of the same events.

Historical knowledge is provisional, which means open to revision, because new evidence or new questions can change an account. For example, the Pigott forgeries collapsed in 1889 and showed the letters against Parnell to be false.
A source is the item itself, such as a speech by Gladstone. It becomes evidence only when a historian uses it to answer a particular question, such as why the Liberals split in 1886.

The same source can be evidence for different questions. A Gladstone speech could explain why the Liberals split, or show how he defended Home Rule; he introduced the first Home Rule Bill on 8 April 1886 and it was defeated in the Commons on 8 June 1886.
Evidence comes in many forms, and each form tends to show a different side of events. Knowing what kind of source you hold, and where such sources are stored, tells you what it can and cannot reveal.

Public records (census returns, parliamentary papers, police reports) show official policy and statistics, for example Dublin Metropolitan Police reports for 1913 or Royal Irish Constabulary reports for the GAA.

Private institutions’ records, such as union minute books, company papers or the GAA’s convention reports, show the interests of their members, so they reveal what an organisation wanted rather than what the state decided.
Letters, memoirs and eyewitness accounts give personal views, for example Davitt’s Leaves from a Prison Diary (1885) or accounts by participants in the baton charges of 31 August 1913.

Newspapers, speeches and pamphlets show how events were presented to the public at the time. Examples are the Freeman’s Journal, Belfast News-Letter, United Ireland (Parnell’s party paper), Irish Worker (Larkin’s paper) and Irish Independent (owned by William Martin Murphy).
Maps, photographs and political cartoons are visual evidence; Punch, a British cartoon magazine, is a typical source of cartoons.
Oral testimony and radio or television transcripts are usually recorded long after the events, so memory may have faded or been reshaped by what the speaker learned later.
Archives hold state records and the papers of organisations, so they are the place to look for police reports or a union’s minute books.
Libraries hold printed books, newspapers and pamphlets, while museums hold objects, banners and photographs. Each repository holds different kinds of source, so a historian often needs several.
A historian cross-examines every source with the same five questions before using it. The answers decide how far it can be trusted and what it is good evidence of.
Who made it: a nationalist MP, a unionist editor, a bishop or a trade unionist each saw events from a position that shaped what they recorded.
Why it was made: to inform, persuade, defend an interest, record an event or claim credit afterwards. A source made to persuade will select facts that help its cause.
When it was made: a report written during the election campaign of 1885 differs from a memoir written decades later, because the memoir is shaped by what the author knew afterwards.
In what circumstances: a statement made under pressure, in secret or before an inquiry may differ from a public speech, because the speaker has different things to hide or gain.
For what audience: a speech to supporters aims to rally them, while a letter to an opponent aims to persuade or warn, so the same author may say different things to each.
Historians do not simply read a source and believe it. They follow a sequence of steps that moves from a question to a tested conclusion.
1. Choose a question, because a source is only evidence for a particular question, such as why the Liberals split in 1886.
2. Locate sources that might answer it, in archives, libraries and museums.
3. Evaluate each source by asking who made it, why, when, in what circumstances and for what audience.
4. Compare the sources with each other, because one source on its own may be biased or incomplete.
5. Form an interpretation: an explanation of what happened that fits the evidence.
6. Test the interpretation against the evidence, and revise it if some of the evidence does not fit.
Corroboration means testing a source’s claims against independent evidence. A claim that unconnected sources also support is more reliable than one that stands alone.
Sources are sorted by when they were made in relation to the events. This is a different matter from whether they can be trusted.
Primary sources were produced at the time of the events, such as a speech, a letter, a newspaper report or a cartoon.
Secondary sources are later accounts based on primary ones, such as a modern book on Home Rule.
Primary does not mean reliable: a participant’s account is close to events but may be biased, while a secondary source may be more balanced but further from the facts.
A source can be both, depending on the question. A historian’s book is secondary for the period it describes but primary evidence for the thinking of the time it was written.
Documents mix statements that can be checked with judgements and with a tilt towards one side. The historian has to separate them before using a document.
A fact can be checked against other evidence, for example that Lord Frederick Cavendish and Thomas Burke were killed in Phoenix Park on 6 May 1882.

An opinion is a judgement that evidence cannot settle, for example that the Land Act of 1881 was a betrayal of the tenants. That the Act was passed in 1881 is a fact; whether it was a betrayal is opinion.
Bias is a consistent tilt in how a source presents events, shown by loaded words, selective detail and omission, for example a unionist newspaper describing a nationalist rally as a mob.
A biased source is not worthless: it is good evidence of what its author and audience believed, even when it is poor evidence of what actually happened.
Some sources go beyond bias and set out to win over a crowd. Historians answer this with the aim of objectivity.
Propaganda is material designed to persuade a mass audience, using emotion, slogans and selected facts; the unionist slogan ‘Home Rule is Rome Rule’ (1886 onwards) works this way.
Bias and propaganda are not the same: bias is a tilt in the source, while propaganda is deliberate persuasion aimed at many people.
Objectivity is the aim of fair, evidence-based judgement, although no historian is free from all assumptions, so historians test each other’s work against the evidence.
Every source has strengths and weaknesses, and accounts are revised when the balance of evidence changes.
Strengths of a source include closeness to events, first-hand knowledge, precision and corroboration by other sources.
Limitations include bias, a narrow viewpoint, gaps and later revision. Only some records survive, so a source may be missing the very evidence that would balance it.
Historians revise their accounts when new sources appear, when old ones are tested harder, or when new questions are asked, such as about women’s roles in the suffrage movement.

The Pigott forgeries show this. The Times published letters in 1887 linking Parnell to the Phoenix Park murders; the forger Richard Pigott was exposed before the Parnell Commission, and he confessed and fled in February 1889, so the letters were shown to be forged.

Question 1 on the paper is the documents-based question on the prescribed topic, and it tests skills rather than new facts. It has four parts: comprehension, comparison, criticism and contextualisation.
Question 1 is the documents-based question, and this chapter is examined only through it. Its four parts are (a) comprehension, (b) comparison, (c) criticism and (d) contextualisation.

The documents, written or visual (including cartoons and photographs), come from one of the topic’s three case studies: the elections of 1885 and 1886, the Dublin strike and lockout of 1913, or the GAA to 1891.
Part (d) carries 40 marks, the most of the four parts.
Because part (d) carries the most marks, give it the biggest share of your time, and keep parts (a) to (c) short and precise.
Parts (a) to (c) ask what a document says or shows on a stated point, which of two documents is more favourable, more critical, more effective or more useful, and why.
Classification questions ask whether a source is primary or secondary, for a reason taken from the source note, or ask you to pick out one example of fact and one of opinion.
Other questions ask how language or imagery is propaganda, whether a source is fully objective, and whether a cartoon is hostile to a group.
Part (a) asks what a document says or shows. It tests careful reading, not outside knowledge, so the answer must come from the named document alone.
1. Read the source note giving the author, date and publication, then read the document, so that you know its context before you start.
2. Underline the exact points the question asks for, and find the line that supplies each one.
3. Put each point in your own words with a detail from the document (a name, date, place or figure), because a bare paraphrase without a detail shows less careful reading.
4. Do not add outside knowledge; part (a) is marked on what the document tells you, and extra background earns nothing.
For example, for a speech on Home Rule, list each argument the speaker gives, in order, with a short reference to each.
Comparison asks how two documents are alike or different on a stated point. Every point you make needs evidence from both documents.
Choose the exact point the question names, such as attitude to Home Rule, to the strikers or to the GAA’s bans.
State what the first document says on that point, quoting or referring to a line.
State what the second says, then say whether they agree, differ or agree only in part.
A specific similarity or difference with evidence from both documents earns marks; a description of each document separately does not, because it leaves the comparing undone.
Explain the difference where you can, using the authors’ positions: a nationalist paper and a unionist paper describing the same crowd would use different words and numbers.
Compare like with like: a private letter and a public speech can differ because of audience rather than real disagreement.
Use linking words such as whereas, both and unlike to keep every sentence a comparison.
Criticism asks how far a document can be trusted or how useful it is. The answer tests provenance, purpose, viewpoint and reliability.
Provenance means the origin of the document: who produced it, when and where. A name and date alone are not an evaluation; say what they imply for trust.
Purpose is why it was produced and for whom; a speech meant to rally supporters will present facts in their favour.
Viewpoint is the author’s party, religion, class or nationality, for example a landlord, a tenant, a priest or an employer.
Reliability is whether the claims are specific and supported by other evidence, or general and unsupported. Provenance is one test of reliability, not the same thing.
Cite a line from the document for each judgement, for example an emotional phrase as evidence of bias.
Balance the answer: say what the document is good evidence for as well as what it cannot show, because a biased source can still be useful evidence of attitudes.
Usefulness questions ask how useful a document is for a stated enquiry, so measure it against that enquiry rather than in general.
Questions on fact and opinion ask you to pick out one example of each, and questions on propaganda ask how the language and imagery persuade the audience.
Visual sources are read with the same questions as written ones, with extra attention to symbols and captions.
Identify every figure and what it stands for: Hibernia or Erin for Ireland, John Bull or Britannia for Britain, or a statesman drawn from his known appearance.
Read the caption, labels and dates, because the meaning often rests on the words.
Note the exaggeration: caricature of faces, size, dress or animal imagery shows the artist’s attitude to a person or group.
Identify the message and the target audience: Punch addressed British readers, while a cartoon in a nationalist or unionist paper addressed its own supporters.
A cartoon is opinion, not record, so use it as evidence of attitudes and propaganda, not of the facts of an event.
Ask whether a cartoon is hostile to Irish people or only to a politician, and support the answer with a detail such as the way a figure is drawn.
A photograph shows what stood in front of the camera, but the choice of subject, framing, staging and caption can mislead.

For example, a photograph of Church Street, Dublin, after tenement houses collapsed on 2 September 1913, killing seven people, is good evidence of tenement conditions but does not show who was to blame.
Part (d) is a short essay on the subject of the case study, using your own knowledge. It is not a retelling of the documents.
Part (d) carries 40 marks, the largest share of the question, and it rewards dated, named, relevant points drawn from the whole chapter.
It asks about the case study’s subject, such as a leader’s strengths and weaknesses or how an organisation dealt with its difficulties.
Open with the background and context, then deal with events in order with dates, names and numbers, then outcomes and significance.
Use the documents sparingly as supporting evidence, referring to them by letter, but do not summarise them.
Cover both sides, for example the arguments of nationalists and unionists in 1885–86, employers and workers in 1913, or the Church, the IRB and the founders in the GAA.
Finish with a judgement that answers the question set, such as how far a leader succeeded or how significant an event was.
Draw on the rest of the topic for context: Home Rule and land for the elections, labour and Dublin’s poverty for 1913, and cultural revival and the Parnell split for the GAA.
Every document can be dated by the people, events and language it contains, and dating it is the first step in using it. The cues below place a document in its case study.

Elections of 1885–86: the Third Reform Act of 1884 (new rural voters) points to 1884–85; the Irish Party’s balance of power after the November–December 1885 election and the Hawarden Kite of December 1885 point to late 1885.

Elections of 1885–86, continued: Chamberlain’s resignation from the cabinet in March 1886, the Home Rule Bill and the Liberal Unionists point to March–June 1886; the Orange card (early 1886) and Belfast rioting (summer 1886) point to 1886; the July 1886 election saw the Conservatives under Salisbury returned.
Typical voices for 1885–86: Parnell and Irish Party speakers, Gladstone, Chamberlain, Hartington, Lord Randolph Churchill, Salisbury, the Freeman’s Journal, the Belfast News-Letter, and Punch.
Dublin 1913: trams and Horse Show week point to the start of the lockout on 26 August; O’Connell Street, batons and a banned meeting point to 31 August.
The Document (a pledge not to be a member of the ITGWU, demanded by about 400 employers on 3 September), the Askwith inquiry and AE’s open letter to the employers point to September–October.
The British TUC food ship points to late September; the ‘Save the Kiddies’ scheme to October; the Irish Citizen Army to November; and a return to work to early 1914.
Typical voices for 1913: Larkin, Connolly, William Martin Murphy, Archbishop Walsh, the Irish Worker, the Irish Independent, the TUC and the Dublin Metropolitan Police.
The GAA to 1891 can be dated in the same way, by its founding events, patrons, crises and voices.
The GAA to 1891: Hayes’ Hotel, Thurles, points to 1 November 1884; Archbishop Croke, Parnell and Davitt as patrons to 1884–85; Cusack’s removal as secretary to 1886; IRB influence to the early years.
The first All-Ireland championships point to 1887, the American tour to 1888, and the Parnell split and falling membership to 1890–91.

Typical voices for the GAA: Cusack, Davin, Croke, Davitt, Parnell, the nationalist press, the Royal Irish Constabulary and Dublin Castle. Once a document is dated, ask who gains from its version of events and what it leaves out.
Marks separate answers that use the evidence precisely from those that retell it or ignore it. Strong and weak answers differ in the same way for each part.
Strong comprehension answers use only the document and give precise details; weak ones add outside facts or copy whole passages.
Strong comparison answers name a point and give evidence from each document; weak ones describe the two documents one after the other.
Strong criticism answers judge provenance, purpose and viewpoint with cited lines and reach a balanced verdict; weak ones say only that the source is biased.
Strong part (d) answers combine dated detail, two or more viewpoints and a clear judgement; weak ones paraphrase the documents or offer a general essay.
A strength of the format is that it rewards close reading; a limit is that it is tied to one case study and its documents, so it rewards answers that stay close to them.
Contemporary views and later historians’ views are both useful material for part (d), for example how contemporaries saw Parnell or Larkin and how historians now judge them.

The events of 1912 to 1916 rest on a few older ideas that examiners expect you to know. Irish politics was split between those who wanted a devolved parliament, those who wanted to keep the Union, and a small group who believed only force would free Ireland.

Home Rule meant a devolved parliament in Dublin (it would handle Irish affairs) while Ireland stayed in the United Kingdom, which had been created by the Union of 1801. The First Home Rule Bill (1886) and the Second (1893) both failed.

The Irish Parliamentary Party (IPP), reunited in 1900 and led by John Redmond, was the main nationalist party. It used constitutional methods, meaning votes and debates at Westminster, to win Home Rule.
Unionists, who wanted to keep the Union, were strongest in Ulster, so they opposed Home Rule fiercely. Edward Carson and James Craig led them. Their strength there is why Home Rule split the country.

Cultural nationalism grew with the Gaelic League (founded 1893). Labour unrest followed in the 1913 Dublin Lockout, when employers locked out striking workers, and the Irish Citizen Army, a workers' defence force, was formed in 1913 (Connolly later became its leader).

The Fenians believed Ireland could be freed only by armed rebellion. Their secret, oath-bound society, the Irish Republican Brotherhood (IRB), was founded in 1858 by James Stephens, and it planned the 1916 Rising.

Physical force means armed violence used to win political aims. The Rising revived this tradition against the constitutional methods of the IPP. The Volunteers were later called the IRA, from about 1919.
After 1910 the Liberal government needed Irish votes to survive, and a new law had weakened the Lords' power to block bills. Together these made Home Rule a real prospect.
Two general elections were held in 1910, in January and December. Each left the Liberals short of a majority, so the IPP held the balance of power (its votes decided whether the government survived).
Redmond's price for supporting the Liberals was Home Rule, because that was the purpose of his party. This is why the government of Asquith, the Liberal Prime Minister, took up a Home Rule Bill.
The Parliament Act 1911 replaced the House of Lords' veto with a delay of two years. This removed the Lords' power to block a bill for good.
Under the Act, a bill passed by the Commons in three successive sessions could become law without the Lords' consent. The Lords could therefore slow the Home Rule Bill but could no longer stop it.
Asquith introduced the Third Home Rule Bill in the House of Commons on 11 April 1912.
The Bill offered Ireland a limited parliament, not independence. It then passed through the three Commons votes that the Parliament Act required.
The Bill set up an Irish parliament in Dublin made up of a Senate of 40 and a House of Commons of 164, with an executive (the ministers who run government) responsible to it.

Westminster kept control of the Crown, war and peace, the army and navy, foreign affairs and customs and excise, so Ireland would have had only limited self-government. Most taxation also remained under Westminster.
The Bill reserved the police to British control for six years. This is why Home Rule would not have given Dublin full control of law and order at the start, although the Bill never actually operated.
Ireland would send 42 MPs to Westminster instead of the 103 Irish seats of the time, which shows that Irish representation there would shrink under Home Rule.

The Commons passed the Bill in January 1913 and the Lords rejected it on 30 January. The Commons passed it again in July 1913 and the Lords rejected it on 15 July. The Lords' rejections mattered less than usual, because the Parliament Act only allowed them to delay.
The Commons passed it a third time in May 1914. Under the Parliament Act this meant it could become law without the Lords, so Home Rule seemed certain.
Unionists answered the Bill with mass protest and then armed organisation. Nationalists formed their own volunteers in reply, and by 1914 both sides had guns.
Edward Carson, a Dublin-born barrister, led Irish unionists, and James Craig organised the campaign in Ulster. His Dublin birth is a reminder that unionism was not only an Ulster belief.
On Ulster Day, 28 September 1912, about 237,000 men signed the Ulster Covenant, a pledge to resist Home Rule. About 234,000 women signed a parallel Declaration.
The Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) was formed in January 1913 to resist Home Rule by force, which meant that the unionists were now organised as an army.

In March 1914 the Curragh incident occurred, when British cavalry officers said they would rather be dismissed than act against Ulster. This showed that the army could not be relied on to coerce the unionists.
The UVF landed about 25,000 rifles at Larne, Co. Antrim, on the night of 24–25 April 1914 (some sources say 20,000). The government did not stop it.
The Irish Volunteers were founded at the Rotunda in Dublin on 25 November 1913. Eoin MacNeill was the public leader, while the IRB, notably Bulmer Hobson, helped organise them from behind the scenes.
On 26 July 1914 the Volunteers landed about 900 rifles at Howth, Co. Dublin, from Erskine Childers's yacht Asgard.
That afternoon soldiers of the King's Own Scottish Borderers fired on a crowd at Bachelor's Walk in Dublin and killed three civilians. Nationalists contrasted this with the lack of action at Larne.
By mid-1914 Home Rule was about to become law, but exclusion of Ulster was unresolved. Then the outbreak of war removed the issue from the agenda.
In March 1914 Asquith proposed county option, under which each Ulster county could vote to be excluded for six years. Carson rejected it, and Redmond reluctantly accepted it as a concession.
In June 1914 Redmond made the Irish Volunteers' committee admit 25 of his own nominees.
An Amending Bill to provide for Ulster was introduced in the House of Lords in June 1914. The Lords changed it to exclude all nine counties of Ulster, and it never became law.

The Buckingham Palace Conference, held on 21–24 July 1914, failed to agree a border for the excluded counties. The sticking point was Tyrone and Fermanagh. This is why no agreed settlement was reached before the war began.
Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914. On 18 September 1914 the Home Rule Act (formally the Government of Ireland Act 1914) received royal assent, which made it law.

A Suspensory Act, passed at the same time, delayed the operation of Home Rule until the war ended, with an undertaking that Ulster would get special treatment by an amending Act. So Home Rule was law but could not take effect.
Redmond tied the Home Rule cause to Britain's war effort. The result was a split in the Volunteers and, over time, a loss of confidence in his party.
On 3 August 1914 Redmond offered the Irish Volunteers in the House of Commons, to defend Ireland alongside the Ulster Volunteers.
At Woodenbridge, Co. Wicklow, on 20 September 1914, Redmond urged the Volunteers to join the British army and fight in the war.
The Volunteers split. About 170,000 (some sources say about 150,000) followed Redmond as the National Volunteers, while about 11,000 (some say 9,000) stayed with MacNeill as the Irish Volunteers.
About 200,000 Irishmen served in the British forces, and Irish deaths are estimated between about 30,000 and about 50,000. Conscription (compulsory service) did not apply to Ireland in 1916.

The 10th (Irish) Division fought at Suvla Bay, Gallipoli, in August 1915. The 16th (Irish) Division fought at Guillemont and Ginchy on the Somme in September 1916, and the nationalist MP Tom Kettle was killed at Ginchy.
The 36th (Ulster) Division, drawn largely from the UVF, attacked at Thiepval on 1 July 1916, the first day of the Somme, and suffered over 5,000 casualties in two days.
Farmers gained from high food prices and Belfast shipbuilding and engineering boomed. Prices rose faster than wages in the towns, which meant that poor townspeople suffered, especially in Dublin.

Redmond's party lost ground because it had delivered only a suspended Home Rule Act. Separatists, who wanted a republic, grew angrier as the war dragged on, and the IRB saw the war as its opportunity.
The Rising was planned by a secret group inside the IRB, which treated Britain's war as the chance to strike. German help was promised but badly co-ordinated.
The IRB set up a Military Council in 1915. It had seven members: Patrick Pearse, Joseph Plunkett, Éamonn Ceannt, Tom Clarke, Seán MacDiarmada, James Connolly and Thomas MacDonagh.
Connolly, who led the Irish Citizen Army and had been planning a rising of his own, was co-opted (brought in) in January 1916, so the plans of the IRB and the Citizen Army were joined.

The funeral of the Fenian Jeremiah O'Donovan Rossa on 1 August 1915 was organised as a show of strength. Pearse's graveside oration gave him a platform and ended with the line 'Ireland unfree shall never be at peace'.
Roger Casement went to Germany in autumn 1914 to seek arms and an Irish Brigade made up of Irish prisoners of war. Very few prisoners joined, so the brigade was a failure.
The Castle Document, a forgery circulated in Dublin on 19 April 1916, claimed that the British planned to arrest the Volunteer leaders. It persuaded MacNeill to accept the plan for a rising.

A German ship, the Aud, disguised as a Norwegian ship, carried about 20,000 rifles for Tralee Bay, Co. Kerry. The Royal Navy intercepted it on Good Friday, 21 April 1916, and its captain scuttled it in Cork Harbour on 22 April, so the arms were lost.
Casement came ashore from a German submarine at Banna Strand, Co. Kerry, on 21 April and was arrested. That night three Volunteers drowned at Ballykissane pier on their way to meet him.
MacNeill reversed when he learned of the loss of the Aud and issued a countermand (an order cancelling the Rising), published in the Sunday Independent on Easter Sunday, 23 April.
The Military Council put the Rising back to noon on Easter Monday, 24 April, so only part of the Volunteers turned out, because many had obeyed the countermand.

About 1,200 Volunteers and Citizen Army members turned out on the first day, took over strong points in Dublin and proclaimed a republic. They were outgunned and outnumbered, and the fighting was mostly in Dublin.

On Monday 24 April the rebels seized the General Post Office (GPO) in O'Connell Street as their headquarters. Pearse was President of the Provisional Government and Commandant-General, and Connolly commanded the Dublin forces.

Pearse read the Proclamation of the Irish Republic outside the GPO. It was addressed to 'Irishmen and Irishwomen' and guaranteed religious and civil liberty and equal rights and opportunities. It was signed by the seven members of the Military Council.

The main garrisons were the GPO (Pearse, Connolly), Boland's Mill (de Valera), the South Dublin Union (Ceannt, with W.T. Cosgrave serving there) and Jacob's biscuit factory (MacDonagh). Others were St Stephen's Green and the College of Surgeons (Michael Mallin and Countess Markievicz) and the Four Courts (Edward Daly).
The rebels did not take Dublin Castle, Trinity College or the docks, which stayed in British hands, so the British kept their centre of government.

Women took part too, including those of the Citizen Army and Cumann na mBan (the women's republican organisation), and Markievicz served as an officer. Elizabeth O'Farrell carried the surrender order.

Martial law (rule by the army) was proclaimed on 25 April, and Sir John Maxwell took command on 28 April. At Mount Street Bridge on 26 April a few Volunteers inflicted heavy casualties on the Sherwood Foresters.
The gunboat Helga shelled Liberty Hall, and artillery and fire wrecked much of O'Connell Street.
Outside Dublin, Thomas Ashe's Volunteers fought at Ashbourne, Co. Meath, on 28 April, Enniscorthy was held for several days, and Liam Mellows led a rising in Galway.
Fire and shelling forced the rebels out of their headquarters within a week. The surrender ended the fighting but left a heavy toll, especially among civilians.
The GPO was evacuated on Friday 28 April after fire, and the garrison retreated to Moore Street, where The O'Rahilly was killed. The fire made the building impossible to hold.
Pearse surrendered to Brigadier-General Lowe on Saturday 29 April. The other garrisons surrendered on 30 April.
About 485 people were killed: about 260 civilians, about 140 British soldiers and police, and about 80 rebels. Thousands were wounded.
These figures are research estimates, which is why they are given as 'about'. The large number of civilian dead is one reason later historians judged the Rising harshly.
The Rising was at first unpopular in Dublin. The speed and manner of the executions, together with mass arrests, turned opinion towards the rebels.
As rebel prisoners were marched away, some Dubliners jeered them, and the IPP and most newspapers condemned the Rising. This shows how little public support the rebels had at first.
About 3,500 people were arrested and about 1,800 were interned (held without trial) in Britain, many at Frongoch camp in north Wales.

Ninety men were sentenced to death by courts-martial (military trials), and 15 were shot between 3 and 12 May 1916: 14 at Kilmainham Gaol and Thomas Kent at Cork. The other 75 sentences were commuted (reduced), including those of de Valera and Markievicz.

The dates were: 3 May Pearse, Clarke and MacDonagh; 4 May Plunkett, Daly, Michael O'Hanrahan and Willie Pearse; 5 May John MacBride; 8 May Ceannt, Mallin, Seán Heuston and Con Colbert; 9 May Kent; and 12 May Connolly and MacDiarmada.

Joseph Plunkett married Grace Gifford the night before his execution. Connolly, wounded in the fighting, was shot seated in a chair. The slow drip of executions over nine days turned sympathy towards the dead men.

Maxwell was the military commander. Bishop O'Dwyer of Limerick refused to discipline priests and criticised the executions. Augustine Birrell resigned as Chief Secretary on 3 May, and Asquith visited Dublin in May.
Lloyd George's talks in June and July 1916 offered Home Rule at once with temporary exclusion of six counties. They failed when Unionist ministers demanded permanent exclusion.

Casement was tried for treason and hanged at Pentonville Prison on 3 August 1916. The British circulated extracts from his diaries to damage his reputation. The Frongoch prisoners were released at Christmas 1916, and a general amnesty followed in June 1917.
Pearse was the chief ideologue of the Rising (the man whose ideas drove it) and its leading public figure. He is judged both as an educator and cultural figure and as an advocate of armed sacrifice.
Pearse was born in Dublin on 10 November 1879 to an English father and an Irish mother. He joined the Gaelic League in 1896 and qualified as a barrister, though he hardly practised.
He edited the League's paper An Claidheamh Soluis from 1903 and founded St Enda's, a bilingual school, in 1908. His essay The Murder Machine (1912) attacked the state education system.

He joined the IRB in 1913 and became Director of Military Organisation of the Irish Volunteers. In 1915 he joined the Military Council, so the educator became a revolutionary who saw the war as an opportunity.
In his graveside oration for O'Donovan Rossa on 1 August 1915 he said 'Ireland unfree shall never be at peace'. This speech remains his best-known statement of separatist nationalism.

His 1915 writings praised war as cleansing and sanctifying. Critics later called this 'blood sacrifice', the idea that a willing sacrifice of life would renew the nation, but Pearse did not use the phrase as a slogan himself.

In 1916 he was President of the Provisional Government and Commandant-General at the GPO, read the Proclamation and ordered the surrender on 29 April. He was executed at Kilmainham Gaol on 3 May 1916, aged 36, and his brother Willie was shot on 4 May.
Contemporaries were divided: Redmond's supporters and many Dubliners condemned him in April 1916, while by autumn he was honoured as a martyr.

Historians differ. Ruth Dudley Edwards (Patrick Pearse: The Triumph of Failure, 1977) treated him as a gifted but troubled figure, Conor Cruise O'Brien criticised the cult of sacrifice, and Joost Augusteijn (2010) stressed his development as an educator and a revolutionary.
Markievicz was a participant in the Rising and its most prominent female combatant.

Constance Gore-Booth was born in London in 1868 and brought up at Lissadell, Co. Sligo. She studied art at the Slade School in London and in Paris, and in 1900 married the Polish count Casimir Markievicz.
She joined Inghinidhe na hÉireann (a women's nationalist society) and Sinn Féin in 1908. In 1909 she helped Bulmer Hobson found Fianna Éireann, a republican youth organisation.
She joined the Irish Citizen Army and in the 1913 Lockout ran the soup kitchen at Liberty Hall, which fed families of locked-out workers.
In the Rising she was second-in-command to Michael Mallin at St Stephen's Green and the College of Surgeons, and she surrendered with the garrison.
At her court-martial on 4 May 1916 she was sentenced to death. Maxwell commuted it to penal servitude for life, citing her sex, and she was held in Aylesbury Prison until the amnesty of June 1917.
Contemporaries admired her courage but also mocked her aristocratic background.
Later historians stress her place as an early woman in revolutionary politics and her commitment to labour and women's causes. She died in 1927.
Judgements of the Rising depend on whether it is measured by its military result, by the aims of the Proclamation, or by its political effects.

Military failure: the rebels held no major target outside their garrisons, were contained within a week, and had few arms. Political success: the executions, internment and the Proclamation's republican claim gave the survivors a moral authority the Parliamentary Party could not match.

Contemporary view: unionists and Redmond's party called it a German-backed rebellion, and the British called it the 'Sinn Féin rebellion', a misnomer since Sinn Féin did not organise it. The Catholic press, which at first condemned it, shifted after the executions.

Later view: revisionist historians stressed its small support, secret planning and the fact that civilians were the largest group of dead. Other historians stressed the effect of the British reaction in changing opinion.

Yeats's poem Easter, 1916 has the line 'All changed, changed utterly: A terrible beauty is born'. This sums up the sense that Irish politics had changed, though historians still ask how far Ireland really was changed.
Home Rule was overtaken by events: the Act was suspended and never came into force, and partition came instead through the Government of Ireland Act of 1920.

The Rising set up a debate over legitimacy (whether the rebels had the right to speak for the nation) that shaped later republican claims. Its fiftieth anniversary in 1966 and centenary in 2016 became public occasions.
The second Sinn Féin grew out of the 1916 Rising and the collapse of the older nationalist politics. A few pieces of background explain why Irish opinion moved so fast after 1916.
The Rising began on Easter Monday, 24 April 1916, and its leaders were executed in May 1916. The executions turned opinion towards the rebels.

The British called the Rising the 'Sinn Féin rebellion', and survivors and the public took up the name, so 'Sinn Féin' became a label for the Rising and everyone who supported it, even though the party had played little part.

Before 1916 the Irish Parliamentary Party (IPP), led by John Redmond, dominated nationalist politics and sought Home Rule (self-government within the United Kingdom) by constitutional means. It lost ground after 1916.

The Irish Volunteers (founded 1913) and the secret Irish Republican Brotherhood (IRB) were the physical-force organisations behind the Rising, and the Volunteers later became the IRA. This is why the IRA later drew on the same men.

Britain governed Ireland from Dublin Castle through the Lord Lieutenant (the Viceroy, the crown's representative), the Royal Irish Constabulary (RIC, an armed police force) and the Dublin Metropolitan Police (DMP). This is why attacks on the police and the Castle were attacks on British rule itself.
World War I ended with the Armistice on 11 November 1918. Britain's desperate need for soldiers in the last year of the war is what caused the conscription crisis of 1918.
Four ideas run through this period, and examiners expect you to use them precisely. Each one is a demand Sinn Féin made or a method it used.
A republic is a state with no monarch as head of state. Sinn Féin demanded one from 1917 and the Dáil declared one in 1919.

Sovereignty is supreme authority over a state's own affairs, with no other power able to override it. The Dáil claimed sovereignty over Ireland in the Declaration of Independence, which is why it set up its own government and courts.
Abstention means refusing to attend. Sinn Féin MPs refused to take their seats at Westminster, the British parliament, and sat in their own assembly, the Dáil, instead.

The IRB (Irish Republican Brotherhood) was a secret society. The IRA (Irish Republican Army) was the Volunteers' fighting force, owing allegiance to the Dáil, so it claimed to be the army of an elected government.

Sinn Féin was a small party before 1916. In 1917 a run of by-elections (elections held to fill a single vacant seat) showed that separatists, who wanted a complete break with Britain, could beat the IPP.

Arthur Griffith founded the first Sinn Féin in 1905. It stood for economic self-reliance, abstention from Westminster and a dual monarchy of Britain and Ireland on the Austro-Hungarian model, which is very different from the republic the party wanted by 1917.

Count Plunkett, father of the executed Joseph Plunkett, won the North Roscommon by-election in February 1917 as an independent separatist and then abstained from Westminster. His win showed that the rebels' cause had public support.
Joseph McGuinness, a prisoner in Lewes, won South Longford in May 1917 by 37 votes, helped by the slogan 'Put him in to get him out'. This showed that a prisoner could be a successful candidate.
De Valera won East Clare in July 1917 by a large majority, and W.T. Cosgrave won Kilkenny City in August 1917, so the successes were repeated in different parts of the country.
Together the four results showed that separatists could win seats from the IPP and that voters would back men who were in jail or had fought in 1916.
A martyr and a new constitution turned a set of election victories into a movement. The Ard Fheis (the party's annual conference) of October 1917 gave it a leader and a united aim.

Thomas Ashe, one of the 1916 leaders, died on 25 September 1917 after being forcibly fed during a hunger strike in Mountjoy prison. His funeral drew huge crowds and became a rallying point for the movement.
Michael Collins spoke at the graveside, which marked his rise among the republicans.

At the Sinn Féin Ard Fheis of 25-26 October 1917 de Valera was elected president, with Griffith standing aside. De Valera also became president of the Volunteers that month, so political and military leadership was joined in one man.

The new constitution was a compromise: the aim was an independent Irish republic, and once that was achieved the people could choose their own form of government. This allowed republicans and Griffith's followers, who wanted a monarchy, to stay in one party.

Sinn Féin now drew in ex-Volunteers, the IRB, Gaelic Leaguers (supporters of the Irish-language revival) and many younger priests, and its clubs spread through the country. The IPP, by contrast, seemed discredited.
Conscription (compulsory military service) united nearly all Irish nationalist opinion against the government and gave Sinn Féin credit for leading the resistance.
The German spring offensive began in March 1918 and Britain was desperately short of men, so the Military Service Act of 18 April 1918 allowed conscription in Ireland.

An all-party anti-conscription conference met at the Mansion House in Dublin on 18 April, with Dillon, de Valera, Griffith, William O'Brien, Tim Healy and Labour representatives. The Catholic bishops, meeting at Maynooth, backed resistance, which gave it moral weight.
A national pledge to resist conscription was signed at church doors on 21 April, and on 23 April a one-day general strike closed most of the country outside Belfast.

The government never applied conscription, but it replaced the Viceroy with Lord French in May 1918. It also arrested about 70 Sinn Féin leaders on the claim of a 'German Plot' (a supposed plot with Germany), citing the landing of Joseph Dowling from a German submarine as its pretext.
De Valera, Griffith, Count Plunkett and Markievicz were among those held in Britain, while Collins and Harry Boland avoided arrest.
The arrests removed the older leaders and strengthened the radicals. Sinn Féin won by-elections in the summer, and Redmond's party, weakened by Redmond's death on 6 March 1918, lost ground.
The first election after the end of the war was fought on a franchise (the right to vote) that roughly tripled the electorate, and it transformed the Irish party system.
The Representation of the People Act 1918 gave the vote to all men over 21 and women over 30, and the Irish electorate rose from about 700,000 to about 1.9 million.
The election was held on 14 December 1918 and counted on 28 December. Sinn Féin won 73 of Ireland's 105 seats, the Unionists won 26 and the Irish Parliamentary Party won only six.
Sinn Féin took about 47 per cent of the votes, and 25 of its seats were won without a contest (uncontested, because no rival stood).
The IPP was almost wiped out, but Joe Devlin held a Belfast seat.
Unionists won most of the seats in the north-east, so Belfast and Ulster supplied the evidence for partition.
Constance Markievicz won St Patrick's, Dublin, while in Holloway prison, and became the first woman elected to the House of Commons. She did not take her seat, in line with the policy of abstention.

De Valera was elected for East Clare and East Mayo, and many successful Sinn Féin candidates were in prison. This meant the Sinn Féin benches in the Dáil would be thin, so few could attend its first meeting.

Sinn Féin had promised to abstain and set up an Irish assembly, so the result gave it a mandate for that. It showed a vote for a republic and against the IPP, but with only about 47 per cent of votes, not every voter backed Sinn Féin.
Sinn Féin kept its election promise to set up its own parliament instead of going to Westminster. The Dáil (the Irish assembly) then began to behave like a government.
The First Dáil met at the Mansion House, Dublin, on 21 January 1919, but only 27 of the elected deputies attended because many were in jail.

It adopted three documents: a Declaration of Independence, a Message to the Free Nations of the World and the Democratic Programme. The Programme put the nation's claim to its resources and the right of every citizen to a living above private property.
De Valera escaped from Lincoln Gaol on 3 February 1919 with help from Collins and Boland, and was elected Príomh Aire (head of the Dáil ministry) on 1 April 1919.
The ministry included Griffith (Home Affairs), Collins (Finance), Cathal Brugha (Defence), Count Plunkett (Foreign Affairs) and Markievicz (Labour).
Remember that the First Dáil and the shooting at Soloheadbeg both took place on 21 January 1919, but they were separate events.
A counter-state is a rival government that takes over the work of the official one. Between 1919 and 1921 the Dáil built one alongside Dublin Castle, which is what made its claim to sovereignty real.

The Dáil Loan (the National Loan), organised by Collins from 1919, raised over £350,000 in Ireland and more than 5 million dollars in the United States. These are two distinct sums, so do not add them up or confuse them.
Sinn Féin won most of the councils in the 1920 local elections, and local authorities then pledged loyalty to the Dáil, which gave the Dáil a base of local power.
The Dáil set up arbitration courts in 1919, which developed into Dáil courts from mid-1920, and republican police replaced the RIC in many areas.
The British banned the Dáil in September 1919, and in 1920 many of the republican ministers worked in hiding.
From August 1920 the Volunteers swore an oath of allegiance to the Dáil, which tied the army to the elected government. The name IRA was in general use during the war.
The IRA waged a guerrilla war (small-scale surprise attacks rather than open battles) on the RIC and the army. A few thousand active men tied down many times their number.

The first shots came at Soloheadbeg, Co. Tipperary, on 21 January 1919, when Seán Treacy, Dan Breen and others killed two RIC constables guarding gelignite (an explosive). The Dáil had not ordered the attack. It is often seen as the start of the war.

The RIC withdrew from many isolated barracks in 1919-20, because they were hard to defend, and the IRA burned the empty buildings and attacked others. The IRA burned the empty buildings and attacked others.
Active service units, known as flying columns, ambushed patrols and barracks and then dispersed into the countryside. Tom Barry's West Cork column was the best known.
Collins understood that in a war against a much larger force, information mattered more than numbers. Three deaths in 1920 also moved opinion against the British.
Collins was Director of Intelligence and used moles (informers inside the enemy's own offices) in Dublin Castle and the police, such as Ned Broy, a Dublin Castle clerk, to get information.
His Squad, formed in 1919, killed detectives of the DMP's G Division, the political branch of the Dublin police, and other agents.
Tomás Mac Curtain, Lord Mayor of Cork, was murdered by police in March 1920, and Terence MacSwiney, his successor, died on hunger strike in Brixton prison on 25 October 1920.

Kevin Barry, an 18-year-old medical student, was hanged on 1 November 1920 for his part in an ambush that killed three soldiers. His death, like the deaths of MacSwiney and Mac Curtain, affected opinion.
The war reached its most violent point in the winter of 1920-21. Then in May 1921 the IRA suffered a heavy loss.
On Bloody Sunday, 21 November 1920, the Squad killed 14 men, mostly British officers and intelligence agents, in Dublin.
That afternoon Auxiliaries and RIC opened fire on the crowd at a football match at Croke Park, killing 14 civilians, including a player, Michael Hogan.

At Kilmichael, Co. Cork, on 28 November 1920, Tom Barry's column killed 17 Auxiliaries and lost three men. This was the same week as Croke Park, but it was an IRA ambush of Auxiliaries, not a British killing of civilians.
In May 1921 the IRA burned the Custom House in Dublin but lost five men killed and about 80 captured, a heavy blow to the Dublin Brigade.
About 2,000 people were killed in the war, including soldiers, police, IRA men and civilians, though estimates vary.
Britain reinforced the police and the army, but its harsher methods turned opinion against it instead of beating the IRA.

The Black and Tans were ex-soldiers recruited as temporary RIC constables. Because of a shortage of police uniforms they wore a mix of khaki and dark green, which gave them their nickname; they began arriving in March 1920 and about 10,000 served.

The Auxiliary Division of the RIC (ADRIC), about 2,000 ex-officers, was formed in July 1920. Unlike the Tans, it operated in companies with considerable independence. This is why they were a separate force from the Tans.

The Restoration of Order in Ireland Act (August 1920) allowed courts-martial (military trials) for civilians, and martial law (rule by the army) was declared in several southern counties from December 1920.

Reprisals (revenge attacks on civilians) included the sacking of Balbriggan in September 1920 and the burning of Cork city centre on the night of 11-12 December 1920, after an IRA ambush at Dillon's Cross. Auxiliaries and Black and Tans were blamed.
The Labour Party, the press and many Church leaders in Britain criticised the reprisals, and the Liberal and Labour leaders called for talks. International opinion also turned against them.
By mid-1921 politics, not just fighting, was pushing both sides towards talks. The Truce followed within weeks of the first formal invitation.
The Government of Ireland Act of 1920 set up a Northern parliament (and a Southern one). The elections of May 1921 confirmed Sinn Féin's hold on the south and unionist control in the north-east.
In June 1921 George V opened the Northern parliament and called for reconciliation, and Lloyd George, the British prime minister, invited de Valera to talks on 24 June.
The Truce (a halt to the fighting) began on 11 July 1921.

Britain went to the negotiating table for several reasons. Reprisals damaged its reputation, the IRA could not be crushed without a much larger force, dominion premiers (leaders of self-governing countries of the Empire) and American opinion urged a settlement, and the cost of the war was rising.
De Valera spent June 1919 to December 1920 in the United States raising money and seeking recognition for the republic.
Collins was the organiser of the IRA's intelligence war and of the republican finances. He was a participant in the Rising and the war and then a negotiator of the Treaty.
Collins (1890-1922) was born near Clonakilty, Co. Cork. He worked in London in the post office and then in a financial firm from 1906 to 1916, and joined the IRB there.
He fought in the GPO in 1916 as aide to Joseph Plunkett and was interned at Frongoch, where he built a network of future activists.
After his release he rose in the Volunteers, the IRB and Sinn Féin. He organised the National Aid funds (support for the families of those killed or jailed) and spoke at Ashe's funeral.
He was Minister for Finance from April 1919, organised the Dáil Loan, and as Director of Intelligence ran the Squad and the spy network. This is why money, as well as guns, was central to his role.
He escaped capture throughout the war and was the most wanted man in Ireland. This made him a symbol of the IRA's survival.
After the Truce he went on to negotiate the Treaty, so he was both a soldier and a negotiator.
Contemporaries: republicans admired him as the man who won the war, while British officials regarded him as a ruthless organiser of killing. Churchill and others came to respect him in London.
Historians: Tim Pat Coogan (1990) portrayed a hero of the revolution, while Peter Hart (2005) gave a more critical account of the killings in which he was involved.
De Valera held the movement together as the leader of Sinn Féin and the Dáil before the Treaty talks. This part covers only the years 1917-1921.
De Valera (1882-1975) was born in New York and raised in Bruree, Co. Limerick. He was a maths teacher who joined the Volunteers in 1913.
He commanded the garrison at Boland's Mill in 1916, and his death sentence was commuted, partly because he was born in America, and most of the other leaders were shot.
He was released in June 1917 under the amnesty, won East Clare in July, and became president of Sinn Féin and of the Volunteers in October 1917.
He was arrested in the German Plot in May 1918, escaped from Lincoln on 3 February 1919, and was elected head of the Dáil as Príomh Aire in April 1919.
He was in America from June 1919 to December 1920, where his disputes with the Irish-American leaders John Devoy and Judge Cohalan limited his success.
After his return he took the lead in the talks with Lloyd George in the summer of 1921.
Contemporaries: supporters saw him as the leader who held the movement together, while critics said he was rigid and out of touch with the IRA's campaign.
Historians: Tim Pat Coogan (1993) and Diarmaid Ferriter (Judging Dev, 2007) debate whether he was a pragmatist (willing to compromise) or an ideologue (bound by principle).
This part covers Markievicz after her release in 1917, as a Sinn Féin politician and Dáil minister. Prison and hiding shaped much of her career in these years.
After her release in June 1917 under the amnesty she joined Sinn Féin and the Volunteers' public campaign, and she was elected to the executive.
She was arrested in the German Plot of May 1918 and held in Holloway, where she was elected in December 1918, and she was released in March 1919.
She was Minister for Labour in the Dáil ministry from April 1919 to January 1922, the only woman in the cabinet and one of the first women in Europe to hold cabinet rank.
In September 1920 she was arrested again and sentenced to two years' hard labour; she was released in July 1921, after the Truce.
Her work as minister was limited because she was in jail or on the run for much of the time.
She later opposed the Treaty in the Dáil vote in January 1922.
Contemporaries admired her bravery but some Sinn Féin colleagues distrusted her socialism and her flamboyance.
Historians now emphasise her importance as a pioneer of women's participation in revolutionary politics.
