Judgements depend on whether the 1918 election, the Dáil and the IRA are credited with winning the settlement or blamed for its costs. Examiners reward answers that weigh both sides.
Achievement: the 1918 result gave Sinn Féin a democratic mandate, and the counter-state showed that Irish people could run their own affairs.
Achievement: the IRA campaign made Ireland costly and hard to govern and, with Dáil publicity abroad, brought Britain to talks.
Limit: the IRA never controlled much territory, and it was small, short of arms and under strain by mid-1921.

Limit: the election was won on about 47 per cent of the votes, with many seats uncontested. It was a vote for a republic or against the IPP, not an approval of every IRA act, and many voters wanted an end to Home Rule rather than war.
Limit: the war also involved violence and the intimidation of informers.
Contemporary view: nationalists saw a legitimate government defending itself, while the British government at first treated the IRA as a criminal conspiracy before changing course.
Later view: historians debate how far the war was supported by the majority and how far it involved intimidation of informers and loyalists, as in Peter Hart's work on Cork.
The dual strategy of Dáil and IRA left the movement with two sources of authority, which left it open to the split over the Treaty in 1922.

Partition (the division of Ireland into Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland) came about because unionists would not accept Home Rule (self-government for Ireland within the United Kingdom), British governments failed to find an all-Ireland settlement, and the 1918 vote showed a divided island.

Unionist resistance came first: the Ulster Covenant (signed 28 September 1912) and the Ulster Volunteer Force, or UVF (an armed unionist militia formed in January 1913), showed that Home Rule for all Ireland could be imposed only by force.

Exclusion debates followed, all assuming that some Ulster counties would be left out of Home Rule. These were the county option (Asquith's proposal of March 1914, letting Ulster counties opt out for six years), the failed Buckingham Palace Conference (July 1914) and Lloyd George's 1916 proposals.

The 1916 plan collapsed over whether exclusion would be permanent or temporary: nationalists were told it would be temporary, while unionists were told it would be permanent. Unionist and Conservative members of the cabinet, including Lansdowne and Long, then insisted on permanence.
The First World War and the 1916 Rising changed nationalist politics, and the Irish Convention of 1917–18 failed to produce agreement. Sinn Féin, the rising republican party, boycotted it.
The 1918 general election (December) confirmed the divide, because Sinn Féin won 73 seats, the Irish Parliamentary Party 6, and unionists 26, mostly in the north-east.

The six counties were chosen, not all nine of Ulster. Only Antrim, Down, Armagh and Londonderry had unionist majorities, Tyrone and Fermanagh had narrow nationalist majorities, and Donegal, Cavan and Monaghan were left out. Six counties gave a safer unionist majority than nine would have.

Northern Ireland had about 1.25 million people (1926 census), of whom about two-thirds were Protestant and about one-third Catholic. This one-third minority is why the new state's treatment of Catholics mattered so much later.

British policy made partition the practical answer. Lloyd George's coalition, with a large Conservative element, was unwilling to coerce Ulster, so the Government of Ireland Act of 1920 gave the unionists the offer of their own parliament.

The Act of 1920 created two Home Rule parliaments, but only the northern one worked. The Treaty then let Northern Ireland stay out of the Free State, and the Boundary Commission failed to move the border.

The Government of Ireland Act (royal assent December 1920) set up a parliament for the six counties of Northern Ireland and one for the 26 counties of Southern Ireland. A Council of Ireland was meant to link the two, but it never worked.
In the Northern election of 24 May 1921 the Unionists won 40 of 52 seats. Sinn Féin and the Nationalists won six each but refused to take part, an abstention (staying away from the parliament).
Craig became Prime Minister on 7 June 1921, and George V opened the Northern parliament in Belfast on 22 June 1921, which gave the new state royal approval.

Southern Ireland's parliament never worked, because Sinn Féin won 124 of 128 seats in the same election (the other four went to Dublin University unionists) and treated it as an election to the Dáil, the republican assembly.

Under the Treaty (the 1921 agreement creating the Irish Free State) Northern Ireland could opt out of the Free State. It did so on 7 December 1922, the day after the Free State came into being on 6 December.

The Treaty also provided for a Boundary Commission (set up 1924) to review the border. Richard Feetham, a South African judge, was chair, with Eoin MacNeill for the Free State and J.R. Fisher for Northern Ireland, appointed by Britain because Craig refused to nominate.

The commission's expected report was leaked to the Morning Post in November 1925, and MacNeill resigned. On 3 December 1925 the three governments (British, Free State and Northern Ireland) agreed in the Tripartite Agreement that the border would stay as it was.

The Tripartite Agreement also released the Free State from its share of the imperial (UK) debt and abolished the powers of the Council of Ireland. So the border was fixed, and the Council had no further role.
The new state was born amid sectarian rioting and an IRA campaign. The government answered with a Protestant-recruited police force and exceptional powers that stayed in place long after the crisis.
Expulsions of Catholic workers, and of some Protestant labour supporters, from the Belfast shipyards began in July 1920 amid IRA violence and unionist anger. Thousands of people were affected.
Riots in Derry in June 1920 and in Belfast through 1920–22 killed about 500 people, most of them Catholics, and drove many families from their homes.
The Dáil organised a boycott of Belfast goods in 1920. It hurt Catholic workers and shopkeepers in Belfast more than it hurt unionist business.
The Ulster Special Constabulary, formed in late 1920, had full-time A Specials, part-time B Specials and reserve C Specials. It was recruited almost entirely from Protestants.
The Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) replaced the older Royal Irish Constabulary (RIC) in June 1922. A third of its places were notionally reserved for Catholics, but Catholics never filled them.
The Craig–Collins pacts of January and March 1922 failed. After the IRA offensive on the border in May 1922 the government interned republicans (imprisoned them without trial).

The Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Act of April 1922 allowed internment, curfews, the banning of meetings and organisations, and arrest without warrant. It was renewed each year and made permanent in 1933.
Some of the interned men were held on the prison ship Argenta in 1922.
The Ulster Unionist Party governed without interruption from 1921. It also changed the electoral rules in ways that kept it in power, while nationalists took little part in the system.

Nationalists abstained from Stormont (the Northern Ireland parliament, named after its later building) at first. The Nationalist Party under Joe Devlin took its seats in 1925, but Sinn Féin remained abstentionist.

In 1922 Tyrone and Fermanagh county councils, which refused to recognise the Belfast government, were dissolved and replaced by commissioners (officials appointed by the government), as were other nationalist-controlled councils.
The Local Government Act of 1922 abolished proportional representation, or PR (a voting system that gives parties seats in proportion to their votes), in local elections, and boundaries were redrawn.
PR for Stormont elections was abolished in 1929 and replaced by single-member constituencies (one winner per area). This helped the Unionists and hurt Labour and independents.

Derry Corporation stayed under unionist control from 1923 to 1969 although Catholics were a majority of the city's population. This is the best-known case of gerrymandering, drawing electoral boundaries to favour one side.
The Unionist Party won every Stormont election from 1921 to 1969 by large margins. A bloc vote on the border issue kept Protestant workers within the party.

Stormont Parliament Buildings, on the outskirts of Belfast, were opened by the Prince of Wales in 1932. Before then the parliament had sat in the Presbyterian Assembly's College in Belfast, so the new building was a symbol of the permanence of the state.

Discrimination means unequal treatment of Catholics in jobs, housing, policing and local government. Nationalists said that the state practised it, while unionists denied it and argued that Catholics refused to take part in the state.
Catholics were about a third of the population but held a small share of senior posts, for example in the civil service, the judiciary and local government.

The shipyards and heavy industry employed few Catholics. Protestant workers' networks and the Orange Order (a Protestant fraternal society) helped to secure jobs for their own members, which kept the pattern in place.
Local councils controlled by unionists allocated public housing, so nationalists argued that houses went to Protestant families first.
In speeches in the 1930s (in 1933 and 1934) Basil Brooke urged unionists not to employ Catholics. His remarks are widely quoted as evidence of the attitudes of leading unionists.

On 24 April 1934 Craig told the Stormont parliament, in reply to claims that the South was a Catholic state, that he boasted of “a Protestant Parliament and a Protestant State”. It is the best-known statement of the attitudes of the unionist government.

Historians disagree. Michael Farrell, in The Orange State (1976), sees systematic discrimination, while others accept discrimination in some fields but stress that it was uneven and not centrally planned.

Unionists defended the system by pointing to nationalist non-participation. Abstention in the early years and the Catholic Church's separate schools left the minority with a limited voice in the state.

Northern Ireland began with high-value industries that depended on export markets. The post-war slump and then the Depression hit them hard, so poverty and unemployment shaped the state's first two decades.
Shipbuilding at Harland and Wolff and linen were the two main industries. Both fell back after the post-war boom ended in 1920–21, because they depended on export markets.
Unemployment was about 20 per cent for much of the 1920s and above 25 per cent in the early 1930s, among the highest in the United Kingdom.
Agriculture remained important because small farms could still sell goods, such as cattle and eggs, to Britain.

The government followed a policy of ‘step by step’ with Britain, keeping welfare benefits such as pensions and unemployment pay in line with British levels. This was financed by the Imperial Contribution (Northern Ireland's payment towards UK-wide costs).
Housing in the slums of Belfast was poor and overcrowded because the government built little until the late 1930s.

In October 1932 unemployed Catholic and Protestant workers joined together in the Outdoor Relief strike and riots in Belfast against the harsh relief rules (the payments to the unemployed). Police shot dead two people, and relief rates were increased.
Partition broke up an economy that had been built on all-Ireland trade, and it weakened both parts. It also left a lasting political issue in the border.
Customs controls on the border from 1923 interrupted the flow of goods and cattle. The Economic War (1932–38) between the Free State and Britain then made smuggling common.
Belfast's linen, shipbuilding and engineering had sold to a UK and world market, so they lost the southern market they had counted on.
The South lost most of the island's large-scale industry, which was in the north-east, so it was left with an economy dependent on agriculture.
Railways were also split by the border. The Great Northern Railway, for example, crossed it.
Society divided as well. Catholics in the North were cut off from the southern state's institutions, while the Southern Protestant minority declined and had a smaller place in public life.
Politically the border became the main theme of Northern nationalism and of southern foreign policy. Articles 2 and 3 of the 1937 Constitution claimed the whole island.
Craig organised unionist resistance to Home Rule and became the first Prime Minister of Northern Ireland. He is judged both as the builder of a stable state and as the leader of a sectarian one.
Craig (1871–1940) was born in Belfast, the son of a wealthy whiskey distiller, and worked as a stockbroker. He served in the Boer War and became MP for East Down in 1906.

Before partition he organised the UVF and the Larne gun-running of April 1914 with Carson (the unionist leader). From 1916 to 1921 he held junior ministerial posts in the British government, the last as Parliamentary and Financial Secretary to the Admiralty (1920–21).

He succeeded Carson as Unionist leader in February 1921 and became Prime Minister of Northern Ireland in June 1921, serving until his death on 24 November 1940. He was made Viscount Craigavon in 1927.
He met Collins in January and March 1922 (the pacts) and negotiated with Lloyd George, but insisted that the border was settled. He also refused to nominate a member to the Boundary Commission.

His government created the RUC and the Special Powers Act and abolished PR, and he told Stormont in 1934 that it was a Protestant parliament and state. Critics therefore see him as a sectarian figure. His government also kept welfare in line with Britain's step by step.
Events shaped him: the violence of 1920–22, the Boundary Commission and the Depression all shaped him. His defenders say he held the state together against IRA violence and economic crisis.
Contemporaries: unionists revered him as the founder of their state, while nationalists considered him responsible for their exclusion and for sectarian rule.

Historians: Patrick Buckland's biography James Craig (1980) portrays a cautious, conservative leader who made no attempt to win Catholic consent. Others likewise criticise the lack of any attempt to win minority consent.
Bates was the minister who ran the machinery of control for more than 20 years. His name is tied to the security system and the electoral changes.

Richard Dawson Bates (1876–1949) was a Belfast solicitor. He was secretary of the Ulster Unionist Council (the governing body of the unionist movement) from 1906 to 1921 and helped to organise the UVF.
He was Minister of Home Affairs from 1921 to 1943, which made him responsible for the RUC, the Special Constabulary, the Special Powers Act, local government and elections.
He introduced the Special Powers Act and the Local Government Act of 1922, which abolished PR for local elections, and he was the minister responsible for the 1929 change for Stormont elections.
He used his powers to ban republican parades and organisations, to arrest and intern suspects and to censor some publications.
Events shaped him: the security crisis of 1921–22 created the powers that he then used for over twenty years. He left office in 1943 in ill health.
Contemporaries: nationalists blamed his department for the system of control, and many unionists praised his efficiency.

Historians: Patrick Buckland, in The Factory of Grievances: Devolved Government in Northern Ireland, 1921–39 (1979), describes how his department's decisions, even if cautious, left a legacy of grievances.
Judgements depend on whether the state is measured by survival and stability or by its treatment of the minority. Good answers set paired points against each other and reach a verdict.
Achievement: it survived the violence of 1920–22 and the Depression, and secured the position of Northern Ireland within the United Kingdom.
Achievement: through its step-by-step parity policy it maintained British standards in education, health and welfare.
Limit: it relied on emergency powers, a largely Protestant police and manipulated electoral rules, so the minority never accepted the state.
Limit: a one-party government with a permanent majority did not develop real opposition, and its economic and housing policy was timid.
Contemporary view: unionists regarded the state as a bulwark against a Catholic all-Ireland state, while nationalists saw a Protestant state.
Later view: historians disagree on how far the system was planned discrimination, but accept that its legacy shaped the Troubles.

The War of Independence (1919–21) ended in a Truce, but a truce only stops the fighting. Months of talk and letters were needed before a formal conference could meet, and the central question was already clear: the Crown, meaning the British monarchy and Ireland's link to it.

The First Dáil (the Irish assembly set up by Sinn Féin) had declared a republic in January 1919, and the IRA owed its loyalty to the Dáil. This is why anything short of a republic was bound to be controversial.

Partition was already in place: the Government of Ireland Act 1920 had created Northern Ireland, with its own parliament and a unionist government under James Craig, and the talks had to deal with this existing border, which is why Ulster became one of the hardest issues.
George V called for reconciliation in his Belfast speech on 22 June 1921, and Lloyd George then invited de Valera to talks in a letter of 24 June. The Truce came into force at noon on 11 July 1921.
De Valera met Lloyd George in London four times in July 1921 (14, 15, 18 and 21 July), and neither side could shift the other on principle, so the talks produced no agreement.

The British proposals, handed over on 20 July, offered dominion status (self-government within the Empire, like Canada) with restrictions: British control of defence and the ports, free trade, and no change to the position of the six counties, which republicans saw as too restrictive for independence.

In August 1921 Ireland's government rejected the offer. De Valera's counter-proposal was ‘external association’: Ireland would be a separate state linked to the British Commonwealth, with the Crown recognised only as head of the association, not as ruler of Ireland.
After the offer was refused, both sides kept talking by letter. Each also had practical reasons to want a settlement, which is why the conference finally met.

Through the late summer Lloyd George insisted that Ireland accept the Crown and remain within the Empire, while de Valera insisted on the right of self-determination, that is, the Irish people's right to choose their own government.

Lloyd George's invitation of 29 September proposed a conference to see how the association of Ireland with the Empire might be reconciled with Irish national aspirations. The Irish accepted, and the conference opened at 10 Downing Street on 11 October 1921.

Britain wanted a settlement because the war was costing money and reputation, the dominion prime ministers urged compromise, and reconquest would have needed a very large army and martial law over the whole island.
The Irish side wanted a settlement because the IRA was short of arms and ammunition, and because civilians in the war zones were paying a heavy cost.
Who went to London, and with what powers, shaped the outcome and the argument about it afterwards. De Valera chose to stay in Dublin, and the delegates carried two different sets of authority.
The Irish delegation was agreed in September 1921: Arthur Griffith (chairman), Michael Collins, Robert Barton, George Gavan Duffy and Éamonn Duggan.
Erskine Childers was the delegation's secretary, with Diarmuid O'Hegarty, John Chartres and others as assistant secretaries.
The delegation lived at 22 Hans Place in Knightsbridge, while Collins stayed separately at 15 Cadogan Gardens. Keep the two addresses apart: it matters when placing a document.
De Valera stayed in Dublin, saying that as head of state he should be held in reserve and that he had to keep republican opinion on side. Cathal Brugha and Austin Stack also stayed at home.

Critics, including Collins, argued that this was a mistake, because the man with most authority and most experience of Lloyd George was absent, and he later disowned the result, which is why the criticism was so sharp.
The delegates' credentials described them as plenipotentiaries, which meant they had full power to negotiate and sign a treaty without further approval.

Their written instructions were different: they were to submit the draft treaty to Dublin before signing and await a reply. How binding this was is still disputed, and it is the heart of the plenipotentiary issue, because full powers and a duty to refer back pulled in opposite directions.

The British team was Lloyd George (Prime Minister), Austen Chamberlain (Lord Privy Seal), Lord Birkenhead (Lord Chancellor), Winston Churchill (Colonial Secretary), Sir Laming Worthington-Evans (War Secretary), Sir Hamar Greenwood (Chief Secretary for Ireland) and Gordon Hewart (Attorney General).
Lionel Curtis and the cabinet secretary Tom Jones acted as advisers and go-betweens, carrying messages between the two sides.

The conference began with full meetings of both sides but soon moved into small private groups, where Griffith and Collins argued with the British over four problems: the Crown, Ulster, defence and finance.

The plenary sessions (full meetings of both delegations) came early in the conference and produced no agreement. After that small sub-conferences met, with Griffith and Collins facing Lloyd George, Chamberlain and Birkenhead, so most of the bargaining was done privately, away from the full delegations.

The Crown and the oath: the British demanded an oath of allegiance (a promise of loyalty) to the Crown and membership of the Commonwealth, and the Irish tried to substitute external association and an oath to the constitution.
Ulster: the Irish argued that Ireland was one nation and that the six counties should not be allowed to opt out, because partition would divide the nation. Lloyd George said he could not coerce them.
The Boundary Commission idea came from the British side. Griffith and Collins took it as a way of removing large nationalist areas from the North, reducing it so much that it could not survive.
Defence: Britain insisted on naval facilities in Irish ports and coastal defence, which the Irish saw as a limit on their sovereignty (supreme power over their own affairs).
Trade and finance: the British wanted free trade between the two islands and a share of the British public debt, for example, while the Irish claimed offsetting counter-claims for overtaxation.

Craig and the Northern government refused to join the talks and refused to accept any all-Ireland arrangement, and Lloyd George, who had difficulty with the unionists, tried to extract concessions from Craig on the basis of a united Ireland within the Empire.
The delegates travelled to Dublin to consult the cabinet in November and December, so the process was not entirely independent of de Valera and the cabinet.
Throughout, Tom Jones and Lionel Curtis passed messages between Lloyd George and Griffith, and Collins formed a good relationship with Birkenhead.
The final week was a negotiation under deadline pressure. The decision to sign without sending the final text back to Dublin is the central controversy of the whole case study.

On 2 December Griffith privately assured Lloyd George that he would not let the conference break on Ulster, provided a Boundary Commission was set up. Lloyd George later treated this as a commitment, and republicans saw it as a concession made without the cabinet's knowledge.

On 3 December the delegates went to Dublin and met the cabinet. There was no agreement on the oath wording, and the delegates returned to London having been instructed not to accept the oath as drafted. So the delegates did consult Dublin, but not on a final text.

On 4 and 5 December the British pressed for signature. On 5 December Lloyd George said that refusal meant war, that he wanted a signature that night, and that his couriers were ready to carry letters to Craig either way.
Barton later recalled that Lloyd George warned of ‘immediate and terrible war’. Whether the threat was a bluff is still disputed.
The delegates returned to Hans Place, where Collins and Griffith argued that the alternative to signing was war. Barton, who had at first refused, gave way because he accepted that refusal meant war.

The Treaty (officially the Articles of Agreement for a Treaty between Great Britain and Ireland) was signed at 10 Downing Street at about 2.10 am on 6 December 1921 by all five Irish delegates, with the British team.
Collins afterwards wrote, in a letter of December 1921, that he had signed his own death warrant.
De Valera was not told in advance. He learned of the signing on 6 December and was angry that the delegation had not sent the final text to Dublin.
The Treaty created the Irish Free State as a self-governing dominion in the Empire. It kept the Crown, an oath, British naval bases and partition, qualified by a Boundary Commission.

Article 1: the Irish Free State was to have the same constitutional status as Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Newfoundland. This is dominion status, which falls short of a republic because the Crown remained, so republicans objected to it.

The Crown was represented in Ireland by a Governor-General, and the Free State's ministers were to be responsible to the Irish parliament, following Canadian practice, so real power rested with elected ministers and not the Crown.

The oath: members of the Free State parliament had to swear allegiance to the Constitution of the Free State and to be faithful to the King, ‘in virtue of the common citizenship of Ireland with Great Britain’.

Defence: Britain would defend the coasts and kept the use of the treaty ports (the naval harbours) of Berehaven, Queenstown (Cobh) and Lough Swilly, and of Belfast Lough, with the right to use other Irish ports in time of war.
The Free State army was to be limited in proportion to population.
Finance: the Free State was to bear a share of the British public debt, subject to counter-claims, so Irish claims such as those for overtaxation could reduce the final sum.

Ulster: Northern Ireland could opt out of the Free State within one month of the Treaty's ratification, and a Boundary Commission would then settle the border ‘in accordance with the wishes of the inhabitants, so far as may be compatible with economic and geographical conditions’.
A Provisional Government would take over from the British administration until the Free State was established.
The Treaty had to be approved by the Dáil and by the British Parliament, and it was also to be ratified by a meeting of the House of Parliament of Southern Ireland.
The Treaty still needed the Dáil's approval, and the debate that followed split the cabinet, the army and families, and led towards the Civil War.
On 8 December 1921 the cabinet divided four to three in favour of the Treaty. De Valera, Brugha and Stack were against.
De Valera issued a statement to the press saying that he could not recommend the Treaty to the Dáil.

The Dáil debated in private from 14 to 17 December. De Valera put forward his own alternative text, Document No. 2, based on external association. It was never presented to the British, so it was never a Treaty draft.
The public debate began on 19 December, was adjourned for Christmas and resumed in January 1922. Speakers included Griffith, Collins, Brugha, Mary MacSwiney and Childers.
Collins described the Treaty as giving ‘the freedom to achieve freedom’, a stepping stone to full independence, which is why he defended it, while Brugha attacked Collins's reputation.
Opponents argued that the oath and the Crown betrayed the republic proclaimed in 1916 and declared in 1919. Supporters argued that the people did not want more war.
All six women deputies voted against the Treaty.
The vote decided the Treaty's fate, and the changes of government that followed put pro-Treaty leaders in power in Dublin and in the new Provisional Government.
The Dáil approved the Treaty on 7 January 1922 by 64 votes to 57. Do not confuse this with the cabinet vote of four to three.
De Valera resigned as President on 9 January and lost a vote to be re-elected, and Griffith was elected President of Dáil Éireann on 10 January.
A Provisional Government under Collins was set up on 14 January and took over from the British administration when Dublin Castle was handed over on 16 January.
Griffith was chairman of the delegation and its senior negotiator. After the Treaty he led the pro-Treaty side in the Dáil until his early death.

Griffith (born 1871) was a Dublin printer and journalist who founded Sinn Féin in 1905. He advocated a dual monarchy, on the Hungarian model (two kingdoms sharing one king), and economic self-reliance.
He was arrested after the Rising, although he had not taken part in it, and in 1917 he stood aside for de Valera as Sinn Féin president.
He was acting head of the Dáil during de Valera's American tour in 1919–20 and was Minister for Foreign Affairs in 1921.

In London he led the negotiations on the Crown and Ulster, and he was prepared to accept dominion status within the Empire with the Boundary Commission. His letter of assurance of 2 December committed him on Ulster.
He was a shy, scholarly man, in poor health after months in prison, so the strain of the negotiations told heavily on him.
After his election as President of Dáil Éireann in January 1922 he led the pro-Treaty side until his death from a cerebral haemorrhage on 12 August 1922.
Contemporaries: supporters of the Treaty praised his courage and integrity, which is a judgement rather than a fact, while republicans condemned him as having abandoned the republic.
Historians stress his role in creating the political movement that won independence, through Sinn Féin, and his realism in 1921.
Collins was reluctant to go to London, but his reputation as the man who had beaten the British gave the delegation influence and made it hard for the Dáil to reject the result.
Collins was Minister for Finance, president of the IRB (the Irish Republican Brotherhood, a secret republican organisation) and director of intelligence in the War of Independence.
He warned the cabinet that he would be a poor negotiator. He believed that his name was needed for the military side but that the politicians should lead, which explains why he went reluctantly.
In London he handled the military and financial issues and built relationships with Birkenhead and Churchill.
He accepted the Boundary Commission clause in the expectation that Tyrone, Fermanagh and parts of Armagh and Down would be transferred, and he believed Northern Ireland could not survive after that.
He argued on the night of 5 December that the IRA could not win another round and that the Treaty gave the means to build up the army and the state.
He saw the Treaty as giving ‘the freedom to achieve freedom’, so he signed it as a first step and not as the end.
He became chairman of the Provisional Government on 14 January 1922.
Contemporaries: anti-Treaty republicans accused him of using his IRB position to override the cabinet, while his supporters said he was honest about the Treaty's limits.
Historians: Tim Pat Coogan sees him as a pragmatic realist, while Peter Hart draws attention to his ruthlessness.

De Valera was President of Dáil Éireann, and his title was changed to President of the Republic in August 1921. He set the strategy and then rejected the outcome, and historians still argue about whether his decision to stay at home was shrewd or a mistake.
His talks with Lloyd George in July 1921 showed that the British would not allow an Irish republic, yet he remained committed to external association.
He chose the delegation and wrote its instructions, but did not join it. His reasons were to keep a power in reserve and to avoid committing the head of state.
He sent messages to London advising the delegates to hold out on the Crown and oath, and kept in touch with cabinet colleagues in Dublin.

After the signing he opposed the Treaty on the grounds that the delegates had signed without the cabinet's approval of the final text. He resigned as President on 9 January 1922 after the Treaty vote.
His Document No. 2 would have accepted the Crown as head of an association with the Commonwealth, with an oath to the constitution only. The Dáil did not adopt it.
Contemporaries: supporters of the Treaty said that he had set a trap for Collins and Griffith, and republicans said that he was upholding the Republic.

Historians: the Earl of Longford's Peace by Ordeal (1935) defended the delegates, while later writers such as Joseph Lee and Diarmaid Ferriter see him as a politician who used ambiguity to hold the movement together.
Judgements depend on whether the Treaty is measured against the republic of 1916 and 1919 or against the realistic alternatives of December 1921. Weigh each claim against the other side's.
Achievement: Britain withdrew its army and administration from 26 counties, and the Free State got its own parliament, police, army and civil service.
Limit: the Treaty kept the Crown, the oath, British bases and partition, which republicans said betrayed the declared republic.
Pro-Treaty view: it gave the freedom to achieve freedom, and a refusal would have meant war in 1922 with the IRA short of arms.
Anti-Treaty view: the delegates were bullied into signing, and the Dáil had no right to give away the republic.
Public opinion: most newspapers, the Catholic bishops, farmers and business supported the Treaty, and pro-Treaty candidates won a clear majority in the June 1922 election.
Unionists saw the Treaty as removing the threat to the North, but the Boundary Commission disappointed nationalists in 1925.
Later view: historians debate whether the delegates were out-manoeuvred, whether the ultimatum was a bluff, and whether de Valera's absence made a bad outcome more likely or was a shrewd move.
The Civil War grew out of a quarrel over the Anglo-Irish Treaty. To follow the fighting you need to know what the Treaty gave, what it withheld, and why two sides formed around it.

The Treaty, signed on 6 December 1921, gave Ireland dominion status (self-government within the Commonwealth, as Canada had), an oath to the Crown, British retention of three ports, and partition, because Northern Ireland could opt out and a Boundary Commission would fix the border.

The Dáil (the Irish parliament) approved the Treaty by 64 votes to 57 on 7 January 1922. De Valera resigned as President of the Dáil on 9 January, and Griffith was elected in his place on 10 January 1922.
The War of Independence (1919-21) had ended in a truce in July 1921. The IRA had fought it as the army of the Dáil, so when the Dáil split, the army's loyalty was also in question.
Pro-Treaty leaders argued that dominion status gave the 'freedom to achieve freedom': a self-governing state that could win more independence step by step.
A republic, the form of state the anti-Treaty side demanded, means a state with no king and no Crown. Anti-Treaty supporters therefore rejected the oath and the Crown as a betrayal of that aim.
The argument was mainly over the oath and the Crown, that is, republic against dominion status, and not mainly over partition.
After the Dáil vote, Ireland had two rival governments and two armies in the making. The split in the IRA turned a political quarrel into a military one.
The Provisional Government took office in January 1922 with Collins as chairman, and took over Dublin Castle from the British on 16 January. Collins was also Minister for Finance.
Griffith led the Dáil government, so for five months two authorities existed side by side, each claiming to speak for the Irish people.
A new National Army was recruited from early 1922 under Mulcahy, who was Minister for Defence and chief of staff. Mulcahy, not Collins, ran the army as it was built up.

Anti-Treaty IRA officers held a convention on 26 March 1922 and rejected the authority of the Dáil. Rory O'Connor and Liam Lynch were their leaders, and Lynch became chief of staff of the anti-Treaty IRA.
British troops handed over barracks from January 1922, and both pro- and anti-Treaty forces took them over, which led to local clashes.

On 14 April 1922 the anti-Treaty IRA under Rory O'Connor occupied the Four Courts in Dublin and held it as a headquarters. This occupation was a challenge to the government, but it was not the start of the fighting.
In the weeks before the election, both sides tried to avoid war, but a series of events in June pushed the government into attacking the Four Courts.
The Collins-de Valera pact of 20 May 1922 proposed a joint Sinn Féin panel of pro- and anti-Treaty candidates. Collins repudiated it in mid-June, just before the poll.
In the general election of 16 June 1922 pro-Treaty candidates won 58 seats and anti-Treaty candidates 36. Labour won 17, and the remainder went to Farmers and independents.
The draft Constitution was published on the morning of the poll, so voters could see the form the new state would take. The Dáil did not meet until September 1922.
On 22 June 1922 two IRA men, Reginald Dunne and Joseph O'Sullivan, shot Sir Henry Wilson, a unionist MP and security adviser to the Northern government, in London.
The British government pressed Collins to act against the Four Courts garrison.
On 26 June 1922 the Four Courts garrison kidnapped J.J. ‘Ginger’ O'Connell, a National Army general. This was a further trigger for the attack that followed.
The fighting began when the National Army attacked the Four Courts. With the better weapons, it then retook the towns, and the anti-Treaty side changed its tactics.

On 28 June 1922 the National Army began shelling the Four Courts with British field guns (18-pounders). The garrison surrendered on 30 June after an explosion in the Public Record Office destroyed many records.
Fighting in Dublin ended in early July. Cathal Brugha was fatally wounded on 5 July and died on 7 July 1922.
The National Army held the larger forces and better arms, and it relied on British guns and supplies, which the anti-Treaty IRA could not match.
It took Limerick and Waterford in July, and landed at Fenit, Co. Kerry, on 2 August and at Passage West, Cork, on 8 August 1922.
By the end of August the anti-Treaty side had lost the main towns, so it turned to guerrilla warfare: ambushes and the destruction of roads, bridges and railways.
Within ten days the pro-Treaty side lost both of its leaders. The government that was left was led by new men with a harder line.
Arthur Griffith died of a cerebral haemorrhage on 12 August 1922.
Michael Collins was killed in an ambush at Béal na Bláth, Co. Cork, on 22 August 1922. By then he was commander-in-chief of the National Army, a post he took only in July, after the war began.
Mulcahy became commander-in-chief, and Cosgrave became head of the government as chairman of the Provisional Government. In December he became President of the Executive Council.
Cosgrave and Mulcahy took charge after Collins's death.
As the guerrilla war dragged on, the government decided to use the law and the firing squad to break it. These executions were the most bitter memory of the war.
The Army Emergency Powers Resolution of 27 September 1922 set up military courts and made possession of arms punishable by death. It took effect from 15 October, after an amnesty.
The first four executions took place on 17 November 1922. Erskine Childers was shot on 24 November for possessing a small pistol.
On 8 December 1922 Rory O'Connor, Liam Mellows, Joe McKelvey and Dick Barrett were executed in reprisal for the killing of the TD Seán Hales the day before.
In total the Free State executed about 80 anti-Treaty prisoners. The figures given are between 77 and 81 depending on the source, so the safe way to give it is ‘about 80’.
The executions, along with the emergency law, were the main complaint of the government's critics, who described them as repression.
By 1923 the war was a grim guerrilla struggle. Atrocities by the National Army hardened opinion, but the anti-Treaty leadership was running out of men and places to fight from.

At Ballyseedy, Co. Kerry, on 7 March 1923, prisoners were tied to a mine, which National Army soldiers then detonated. Eight died and one, Stephen Fuller, survived. There were other Kerry killings the same week, and they shocked many on the pro-Treaty side as well.
Liam Lynch, the anti-Treaty chief of staff, was mortally wounded in the Knockmealdown Mountains on 10 April 1923. He died that day or the next, and 10 April is the date to use.
Frank Aiken became chief of staff, and a ceasefire began on 30 April 1923.
On 24 May 1923 Aiken ordered the anti-Treaty side to dump arms, with a message from de Valera supporting the order.
The war ended in defeat for the anti-Treaty side because it lacked the support, the weapons and the territory to win. The costs were high and are still debated.
The anti-Treaty side lacked public support, as shown by the June 1922 election, in which pro-Treaty candidates won 58 seats and anti-Treaty candidates 36.
The Church condemned the anti-Treaty campaign, which weakened its moral claim in a deeply Catholic country.
Its arms were weaker than those of the National Army, which used British guns and supplies. It also lost the towns by the end of August 1922, leaving it with only guerrilla tactics.

Physical force (the tradition of armed struggle) was used by the anti-Treaty IRA against the Free State. The state met it with its own force and emergency law, which is why the army, the military courts and the executions were so central to the war.
The number of dead has no agreed figure. Estimates range from about 1,500 to about 4,000 or more, so give the range and not a single total.
Thousands were imprisoned, about 12,000 by the end of the war, and roads, bridges and railways had been destroyed.
With the war won, the government set out to build a stable state. Cumann na nGaedheal, the pro-Treaty party, set up the institutions with an emphasis on continuity, law and order.
Cumann na nGaedheal was founded in April 1923 (use 1923) and led by Cosgrave. It governed from 1922/23 until 1932.

The Constitution of the Irish Free State came into force on 6 December 1922, which formally established the Free State, the new self-governing state. The Executive Council is the Free State's cabinet.
The Oireachtas (parliament) was made up of the Dáil, the Seanad and the King. Elections used proportional representation by the single transferable vote (PR-STV), so smaller parties could win seats.
The Executive Council was responsible to the Dáil, which means the government could stay in office only while it had the Dáil's support.
The Governor-General was the King's representative. Members swore an oath of fidelity to the Free State and faithfulness to the King, which was the symbol the anti-Treaty side most disliked.
Tim Healy was Governor-General from 1922 to 1928, and James McNeill held the post from 1928 to 1932.
The Referendum and Initiative provisions, which gave voters a way to challenge or propose laws, were removed in 1928.
A new state needs a police force, courts and administrators it can trust. The government chose to build these in a way that kept as much order and continuity as it could.
The Civic Guard was founded in 1922 by the Provisional Government and renamed the Garda Síochána by the Garda Síochána Act 1923. It was unarmed.
Eoin O'Duffy was Commissioner from September 1922. The Dublin Metropolitan Police merged into the Garda in 1925, so there was one national police force.
The Courts of Justice Act 1924 set up the District Court, Circuit Court, High Court and Supreme Court, replacing both the British-era courts and the Dáil courts.
The civil service and local-government system were largely inherited from British rule, which gave the new state continuity and efficiency.
The Ministers and Secretaries Act 1924 set out the government departments.
The government also won recognition abroad and tackled land and power. These were practical achievements that gave the state credibility.
The Free State joined the League of Nations in September 1923 and opened a legation (a small embassy) in Washington in 1924, which showed that it was accepted as a state in its own right.
The Land Act 1923, brought in by the Minister for Agriculture Patrick Hogan, completed the transfer of land to tenants by compulsory purchase of untenanted land.

The Shannon Scheme was approved in 1925 under the Minister for Industry and Commerce, Patrick McGilligan, and was built by Siemens-Schuckert of Germany. It harnessed the river Shannon to produce electricity.
The Electricity Supply Board (ESB) was created in 1927, and the Ardnacrusha power station opened in 1929, which gave the state a national electricity supply.
The first serious test after the war came from inside the army. It showed whether elected ministers or armed officers would decide the state's policy.
The Army Mutiny of March 1924 was led by Liam Tobin and Charles Dalton, former IRA and IRB officers who had been Collins's intelligence men.
They objected to demobilisation (the reduction of the army after the war) and to ex-British army officers in the National Army, whom they distrusted.
Mulcahy resigned as Minister for Defence and the Army Council resigned. Kevin O'Higgins took charge of reorganising the army.
The result was that the army was firmly under civilian control.
The Treaty had promised a Boundary Commission, and nationalists hoped it would move the border in their favour. In 1925 those hopes collapsed and the government faced a political crisis.
The Morning Post published the expected findings of the Boundary Commission on 7 November 1925.
Eoin MacNeill, the Free State's member, resigned from the Commission on 20 November, which deepened the crisis.
The Tripartite Agreement of 3 December 1925, between Britain, the Free State and Northern Ireland, left the border unchanged and freed the Free State of its share of the British public debt.
The Boundary Commission, set up under the Treaty in 1924-25, was ended by the Tripartite Agreement.
The government's main answer to armed opposition was emergency law, and its leading figure was Kevin O'Higgins. His murder in 1927 brought the state to a turning point.
Kevin O'Higgins (born 1892) was Vice-President of the Executive Council and Minister for Justice (and External Affairs).
The Public Safety (Emergency Powers) Act 1923 gave the government special powers against armed opposition.
O'Higgins was shot dead on 10 July 1927 at Booterstown, on his way to Mass, by three anti-Treaty IRA men acting without the authority of the IRA leadership.

After the murder the government introduced the Public Safety Act 1927 and the Electoral Amendment Act 1927, which required candidates to swear to take the oath if elected or be disqualified from standing.

The Constitution (Amendment No. 17) Act 1931 added Article 2A, which allowed military tribunals, and Saor Éire and the IRA were declared unlawful in October 1931. This was the last of the emergency measures of this period.
The anti-Treaty side could not win by force, so its main political leader changed course. Constitutional republicanism, led by de Valera, replaced armed resistance.
De Valera left Sinn Féin in March 1926 after its Ard Fheis (annual conference) refused to drop abstention, the policy of not taking seats in the Dáil.
Fianna Fáil was founded on 16 May 1926 at the La Scala Theatre, Dublin. De Valera called the oath ‘an empty political formula’, so it could be sworn in order to enter the Dáil.
In the June 1927 election Cumann na nGaedheal won 47 seats and Fianna Fáil 44. In the September 1927 election Cumann na nGaedheal won 62 and Fianna Fáil 57.

Fianna Fáil TDs signed the oath book and entered the Dáil on 12 August 1927, under the threat of the Electoral Amendment Act. If they had refused, they would have been disqualified, so they had to choose between entering the Dáil and leaving politics.
By entering the Dáil, the main opposition accepted the Free State's parliamentary system, which gave the state legitimacy.
The real test of democracy came when the government that won the war lost an election. In 1932 power passed peacefully to the other side of the Civil War.
The world Depression from 1929 and falling farm prices hurt the Free State. Cumann na nGaedheal's cuts and balanced budgets lost it support.
Fianna Fáil promised protective tariffs, an end to the land annuity payments to Britain and the removal of the oath.
In the February 1932 general election Fianna Fáil won 72 seats, Cumann na nGaedheal 57 and Labour 7.
De Valera was elected President of the Executive Council on 9 March 1932 with Labour support.
Cosgrave's government handed over power peacefully, and the army and police accepted the change. This was the first democratic transfer of power in the new state, just nine years after a civil war.
The war ended in 1923, but its effects lasted much longer. It shaped the party system and left memories that many people preferred not to discuss.

The two sides became the two main parties. Fine Gael was formed in 1933 from Cumann na nGaedheal, the Centre Party and the Blueshirts, with Eoin O'Duffy as first leader. Fianna Fáil came from the anti-Treaty side.
In the August 1923 election Cumann na nGaedheal won 63 seats and the republicans (Sinn Féin) 44. The republicans abstained, so they did not take their seats.
De Valera was arrested at Ennis on 15 August 1923 and released on 16 July 1924.
Thousands of republican prisoners were held. A hunger strike from October to November 1923 ended without success, and two prisoners died.

Both sides committed atrocities, and families and communities were divided, because neighbours and relatives had fought on opposite sides, and this made the war a subject of silence in Irish public life.
Cosgrave led the pro-Treaty side from 1922 to 1932 and built the state's institutions. He is judged as a cautious administrator who secured democracy but did little about the Depression.
William Thomas Cosgrave was born in Dublin on 6 June 1880, the son of a publican in James's Street. He was a Sinn Féin member of Dublin Corporation from 1909.
In 1916 he was in the South Dublin Union garrison. His death sentence was commuted to penal servitude.
He won the Kilkenny City by-election in August 1917 and was Minister for Local Government in the Dáil ministry from April 1919.
He became head of the government in August 1922, as chairman of the Provisional Government, and was President of the Executive Council from 6 December 1922 to 9 March 1932.

As a participant, he led the government through the Civil War executions, the Mutiny, the Boundary Commission crisis, the assassination of O'Higgins and the 1932 handover. The war and the killings of Hales and O'Higgins pushed him toward harsher measures.
His cautious style suited a state that needed stability, but it was less suited to the Depression.

Contemporaries: supporters admired his honesty and defence of law and stability, but critics called him conservative and authoritarian, described his government as ‘the Treaty government’, and attacked the executions, the emergency laws and economic conservatism.

Historians: Tom Garvin (1922: The Birth of Irish Democracy, 1996) praises him for defending democracy against militarism, while John M. Regan (The Irish Counter-Revolution, 1921-1936, 1999) calls the government a conservative, elitist counter-revolution. Michael Laffan (Judging W.T. Cosgrave, 2014) gives a balanced assessment.
Judgements depend on whether the test is survival and legitimacy or social and economic performance. Examiners reward paired points: achievements against limits, and contemporary against later views.
Achievement: the state survived civil war, mutiny and assassination, and had working institutions by 1927, such as the Garda, the courts and the civil service.
Achievement: the army was brought under civil control after the Mutiny of 1924, which meant the state's policy would be decided by elected ministers.
Achievement: the Shannon Scheme and the ESB gave the state a modern electricity system.
Achievement: the peaceful transfer of power in 1932, accepted by the army and police, showed that democratic institutions had become accepted.
Limit: the government used military courts, executions and public safety laws that opponents described as repression.

Limit: its economic conservatism, based on low spending and balanced budgets, did little for the Depression's hardship, and the Boundary Commission outcome of 1925 showed that hopes of the Treaty on the north were unrealistic. The Treaty symbols, the oath and the Governor-General, were also left in place.
Contemporary view: supporters saw the government as the defender of law and stability, while opponents called it ‘the Treaty government’.
Later view: historians disagree over whether it was a successful counter to militarism (Garvin) or a conservative counter-revolution (Regan).

The Treaty of December 1921 left the Free State short of full sovereignty (complete independent authority over its own affairs). The Cosgrave governments accepted it but used the Commonwealth to widen the Free State's independence step by step, by agreement with Britain.

The Treaty, signed on 6 December 1921, gave the Free State dominion status: a self-governing place in the British Commonwealth, but still tied to the Crown. The Civil War followed between those who accepted it and those who rejected it.

The Treaty's symbols of British authority were the oath of allegiance (a promise of loyalty to the Crown), the Governor-General (the King's representative in Ireland), the Crown itself and British use of three Treaty ports: Berehaven (Bantry Bay), Spike Island (Cork Harbour, Cobh) and Lough Swilly.
The Free State joined the League of Nations in 1923 and registered the Treaty there in 1924, treating it as an international agreement rather than an internal British matter. Britain objected.

The Boundary Commission crisis (the dispute over the border with Northern Ireland) ended with the Tripartite Agreement of December 1925, which released the Free State from its share of the imperial debt, so the border question was set aside.

The Imperial Conference of 1926 produced the Balfour Declaration, which described Britain and the dominions as autonomous communities, equal in status and freely associated. Kevin O'Higgins took a leading part for the Free State.

The Statute of Westminster (December 1931) gave the dominions legislative independence by removing the British Parliament's power to override dominion laws. It was the legal foundation for what de Valera did next.
Cosgrave's government held that independence should come by agreement with Britain, so it left the oath, the Governor-General and the Treaty ports in place.
The Free State also kept paying the land annuities (the repayments tenant farmers owed for land bought under the Land Acts) to the British Exchequer, under arrangements of the 1920s.
De Valera had led the anti-Treaty side in the Civil War, and Fianna Fáil's pledge was to remove the oath and the Treaty's symbols. First he had to win power and then secure it.
De Valera left Sinn Féin and founded Fianna Fáil in 1926, so that the anti-Treaty republican cause could be pursued through elections. The party entered the Dáil in 1927.
Cumann na nGaedheal, led by W.T. Cosgrave, had governed from 1922 until 1932, which is why Fianna Fáil's victory in 1932 marked a real change of direction.
In the election of February 1932 Fianna Fáil won 72 seats, short of a majority, and governed with the support of Labour.

De Valera became President of the Executive Council (the head of government, the title used until 1937) on 9 March 1932. He was also Minister for External Affairs, so he personally ran relations with Britain.
He then called a snap election in January 1933. Fianna Fáil won 77 seats, an overall majority, so it no longer depended on Labour and could pass the Treaty-dismantling laws that followed.

De Valera removed the Treaty's symbols one at a time by legislation, relying on the Statute of Westminster and his own Dáil majority. Learn these steps in date order, because each one builds on the last.

In autumn 1932 he removed James McNeill as Governor-General after a public dispute with the government. In November 1932 he appointed Domhnall Ua Buachalla, a Fianna Fáil figure and former TD, and gave him only a minimal role, so the office lost its importance.

The Constitution (Removal of Oath) Act, May 1933, ended the oath of fidelity to the King for members of the Oireachtas (the Irish parliament). This is a different thing from the Treaty's oath of allegiance (the oath to the Free State and the King).
The Constitution (Amendment No. 22) Act 1933 ended appeals to the Privy Council, the British body that had been the final court of appeal for Irish cases, so Irish courts now had the last word.
The Seanad (the Senate, the upper house) was abolished in 1936.
Edward VIII abdicated in December 1936, which gave de Valera his chance. On 11 December the Constitution (Amendment No. 27) Act removed the Crown and the Governor-General from the Constitution.

On 12 December 1936 the Executive Authority (External Relations) Act brought back a limited role for the King: he acted for the state only in appointing diplomats and signing international agreements.

Britain took no military action and did not accept that the Free State had left the Commonwealth. The Statute of Westminster supported de Valera's constitutional argument, and Britain did not want a confrontation.

De Valera's decision to stop paying the land annuities (the repayments tenant farmers owed for land bought under the Land Acts) became a trade conflict between the two states. It was only ended by the agreements of 1938.
The annuities amounted to about £3 million a year. De Valera withheld them from mid-1932, arguing that they were owed to the Irish state, not to Britain.
Britain held that the arrangements of the 1920s bound Ireland to pay. The two sides read those arrangements differently, and this disagreement was the cause of the war.
From July 1932 Britain imposed special duties (extra import taxes) on Irish cattle, beef, butter and other exports, which hit the Irish farmers who depended on the British market.

The Free State responded with duties on British goods such as coal, cement and iron and steel products, and began a policy of self-sufficiency, meaning producing more of what the country needed rather than importing it.
The Coal–Cattle Pact of 1935 exchanged Irish cattle for British coal and slightly reduced the damage, but it did not end the dispute.
Fianna Fáil argued that the conflict was the price of sovereignty, so in rural constituencies it kept its voters. Cosgrave's party attacked the policy as damaging.
The first years of Fianna Fáil rule brought a challenge from the right. It strengthened the government's hand and led to the creation of a new opposition party.
The Army Comrades Association (ACA) was founded in February 1932 by pro-Treaty ex-officers to protect Cumann na nGaedheal meetings from disruption by the IRA.

In February 1933 de Valera dismissed Eoin O'Duffy as Garda Commissioner (head of the police). O'Duffy took over the ACA in July 1933, when it adopted a blue shirt and a stiff-armed salute, which is why its members became known as the Blueshirts.

The movement was renamed the National Guard in July 1933. A march on Dublin planned for August 1933 was banned, and the National Guard itself was banned in August 1933, though the movement continued under other names.
In September 1933 Cumann na nGaedheal, the National Centre Party and the Blueshirts merged as Fine Gael, with O'Duffy as its first leader. He resigned in 1934, and Cosgrave was leader by 1935.
Vice-Admiral Henry Somerville, a retired naval officer, was killed by the IRA in March 1936. De Valera banned the IRA in June 1936, which removed the Blueshirt and IRA challenge to the state.
O'Duffy later led an Irish Brigade of about 700 men to fight for Franco in Spain in 1936–37.

The new constitution replaced the Free State Constitution of 1922 and gave the state a more Irish and Catholic character. It also avoided the word republic (a state with no monarch as head), which only came into use in 1948–49.
De Valera drafted it himself, with John Hearne (legal adviser in the Department of External Affairs) and Maurice Moynihan (Secretary to the Government). Catholic clerical advice was also taken.

It was approved in a plebiscite (a referendum on the Constitution, a vote of the whole electorate) on 1 July 1937, held on the same day as a general election, by about 56 per cent to 44 per cent. It came into force on 29 December 1937.

Article 4 named the state Éire, or in the English language, Ireland. Article 5 declared that Ireland was a sovereign, independent, democratic state, so it claimed full independent authority but did not call itself a republic.
The head of state was a President elected for seven years, and the head of government was the Taoiseach, the new title replacing President of the Executive Council.

Three articles show the constitution's character most clearly, and each drew criticism. They claimed the whole island, defined the family in a conservative way and recognised the Catholic Church's special position.

Articles 2 and 3 claimed the whole island of Ireland as the national territory, while limiting the exercise of the state's laws to 26 counties until reunification. This was a claim on Northern Ireland without any power there.
Article 41 recognised the family as the foundation of society, spoke of the woman's life within the home, and the Constitution barred divorce.

Article 44 recognised the special position of the Catholic Church as guardian of the faith of the great majority. It also named the Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, Methodist and other churches and the Jewish congregations. The clause was removed in 1972.
Unionists, women's groups and some nationalists criticised the document.
Douglas Hyde was inaugurated as the first President on 25 June 1938.
Three agreements signed in London on 25 April 1938 settled the main disputes between the two governments. They also removed the Treaty's last military restriction, the British hold on the ports.
The defence agreement handed over the Treaty ports at Berehaven, Spike Island (Cobh) and Lough Swilly to Ireland, and the handover took place in July 1938.

The financial agreement settled all annuities and other financial claims for a single payment of £10 million, far less than Britain had claimed. This ended the annuities dispute that had caused the Economic War.
The trade agreement ended the special duties on both sides, which brought the Economic War to a close.

Neville Chamberlain, the British Prime Minister, agreed partly to improve relations as war approached, so Britain preferred a friendlier Ireland to a quarrel over the ports. Winston Churchill opposed giving up the ports.
De Valera raised partition in the talks and linked it to the ports, but Britain would not move on the border.
Controlling its own harbours made it possible for Ireland to remain neutral in 1939.
The inter-party government formally ended the External Relations Act and left the Commonwealth. Britain responded by guaranteeing Northern Ireland's position.

Fianna Fáil lost its majority in the general election of 4 February 1948. John A. Costello of Fine Gael became Taoiseach on 18 February 1948 at the head of an inter-party government (Fine Gael, Labour, Clann na Poblachta, Clann na Talmhan and others).

Seán MacBride, leader of Clann na Poblachta, was Minister for External Affairs. He wanted to repeal the External Relations Act, which he regarded as an anomaly because it still gave the King a role in Irish diplomacy.
Costello announced the decision in Ottawa in September 1948. The causes of the announcement are disputed.
The Republic of Ireland Act was passed in December 1948 and came into force on Easter Monday, 18 April 1949. It repealed the External Relations Act and ended the state's link with the Commonwealth.
The British Ireland Act 1949 recognised that Ireland was no longer a member of the Commonwealth, but said Irish citizens would not be treated as foreigners.
It also declared that Northern Ireland would remain in the United Kingdom unless the Parliament of Northern Ireland consented to change, which strengthened the unionist position.
The southern parties united in an anti-partition campaign in 1949, but it achieved little.
Independence had largely been achieved by 1938, so 1949 was the formal break with the Crown and the Commonwealth, not the moment Ireland became independent.

De Valera dominated the 1930s and 1940s and shaped the state's constitution, relations with Britain and neutrality. He led Fianna Fáil in government from 1932 to 1948, again in 1951–54 and 1957–59, was President of Ireland from 1959 to 1973, and died in 1975. Judgements about him are divided.

Between 1932 and 1948 he removed the oath, the Governor-General and the Privy Council appeal, passed the 1936 Acts, drafted the 1937 constitution, secured the ports in 1938, banned the IRA in 1936 and kept Ireland neutral in the Second World War.

Events shaped him as well. The Statute of Westminster gave him room to act, the abdication gave him his chance in 1936, the Blueshirts strengthened his hand against opponents, and the approach of war helped persuade Britain to give up the ports.
He was a direct participant: as his own Minister for External Affairs he negotiated personally with Britain, and he drafted the 1937 constitution himself with Hearne and Moynihan.
He did not end partition, and the Economic War cost the farming economy dearly.
The social and economic record was weak, with high emigration and unemployment, a conservative Catholic constitution and wartime censorship.

Contemporaries: supporters, especially small farmers and workers, saw him as the man who finished the work of independence. Opponents in Cumann na nGaedheal and the Blueshirts called him a dictator, or said he damaged the economy for the sake of symbols.

Historians: J.J. Lee (Ireland 1912–1985, 1989) credits him with consolidating democracy and with strong political skills, while criticising the economy. Deirdre McMahon (Republicans and Imperialists, 1984) examined his diplomacy with Britain.
Tim Pat Coogan (De Valera: Long Fellow, Long Shadow, 1993) is critical, while Diarmaid Ferriter (Judging Dev, 2007) is balanced, stressing both his stubbornness and his pragmatism.
Both leaders increased Irish independence, but by different methods and at different costs. Weigh them in pairs: what each achieved, and what each left undone.
Cosgrave's strengths: he secured the Free State's international recognition, used the Commonwealth to widen independence, and avoided economic conflict with Britain.
Cosgrave's limits: he left the oath, the Governor-General and the ports in place, and the Boundary Commission failed.

De Valera's strengths: he removed the symbols of the Treaty, settled the ports and the annuities, and created a constitution that Britain accepted in practice. His ports settlement also made neutrality possible.
De Valera's limits: the Economic War, the failure to end partition, and the fact that his changes relied on the groundwork Cosgrave laid at the Imperial Conferences (Balfour and Westminster).
Contemporary view: Fianna Fáil supporters said de Valera achieved real sovereignty, while Fine Gael said he damaged the economy for the sake of symbols.
Later view: the Republic of 1949 is often judged mainly a formal act, because de Valera had already made independence real. Neither leader ended partition.
Irish economic policy between 1922 and 1945 swung between two opposite approaches to trade. Four terms describe that swing, and every later block uses them.

Free trade means few or no tariffs (taxes on imported goods), so goods cross borders cheaply. It suited an economy that earned its living selling farm produce to Britain, because the Free State wanted Britain's market kept open and its own food and goods cheap.

Protectionism means shielding home industry from foreign competition, using tariffs, quotas (limits on the quantity of a good that may be imported) and licences. Its aims were self-sufficiency, meaning the country supplies its own needs, and jobs for Irish workers.
A semi-state body is a state-owned company run commercially, like a business. Examples are the Electricity Supply Board (ESB), the Irish Sugar Company and Aer Lingus.
Land annuities were the repayments farmers made to the state for the holdings they had bought under the Land Acts, so they were repayments for land purchase, not rent.
The Economic War (1932-38) was the trade war between the Free State and Britain over the annuities, and it hit cattle farmers hardest.

The two main parties were Cumann na nGaedheal, in government from 1922 to 1932 under W.T. Cosgrave, and Fianna Fáil, in government from 1932 under de Valera. Cumann na nGaedheal favoured free trade; Fianna Fáil moved to protection.

The Irish Free State came into being on 6 December 1922 with a small, mainly agricultural economy tied to Britain. Partition (1920-22) had separated the industrial North-East from the rest of Ireland, so the new state had less industry to build on.
Agriculture was the main employer, and more than 90 per cent of exports, mainly cattle, butter, bacon and eggs, went to Britain. This made the economy very dependent on a single customer.

Partition left the Belfast shipyards (Harland and Wolff), the linen mills and most heavy engineering in Northern Ireland, so the Free State had little industry beyond Dublin brewing (Guinness), biscuits (Jacob's), food processing, and the Ford factory at Cork.

The Free State set up its own customs barrier on the border in April 1923. This interrupted trade in cattle and manufactured goods and created a smuggling economy, because goods taxed on one side were cheaper on the other.

The Currency Act of 1927 created the Saorstát pound at parity with sterling (equal in value), so the Irish pound stayed tied to the British pound and Irish monetary policy, the control of money and interest rates, followed Britain's.

The Free State had a population of under three million, and a small home market limited the scope for industrial growth, because few customers meant a factory could not sell enough to cover its costs.

The civil service, taxation and financial institutions were largely inherited from British rule. The Department of Finance, the ministry that controls government spending, took over the cautious approach of the British Treasury, which affected policy for decades.

The Cumann na nGaedheal governments believed that the farm sector could carry the economy and that low taxes and free trade were the best policy. They aimed at quality exports, low taxes and balanced budgets (spending no more than the state collects).

Patrick Hogan, Minister for Agriculture from 1922 to 1932, concentrated on quality exports of beef, butter and bacon to Britain, because a good reputation kept Irish produce selling in its main market.

The Dairy Produce Act and the Creamery Act of 1924 and the Live Stock Breeding Act of 1925 improved standards. The Agricultural Credit Corporation, founded in 1927, lent to farmers, and the government also promoted co-operative creameries.

Ernest Blythe, Minister for Finance from 1923, kept taxes and spending low. His 1924 budget cut the old age pension from 10 shillings to 9 shillings a week, a clear sign of the policy of fiscal conservatism (cautious public finances).
Public-sector pay was also cut, and the government made balanced budgets a priority, so little money was left for new schemes.

A Tariff Commission was set up under the Tariff Commission Act of 1926 to examine applications for protection, but it recommended tariffs on only a limited number of goods, so the government stayed essentially committed to free trade.

The Shannon Scheme, a hydroelectric power station at Ardnacrusha, was approved in 1925 and opened in 1929. It was the chief exception to the policy of low state spending, and it was justified as providing cheap power for industry. The ESB was set up in 1927 to run it.
Critics said that the policy favoured large farmers and left cities, labourers and small farmers with little help, because the state spent so little on anyone outside the export trade.
McElligott was a civil servant, not a politician, but as Secretary of the Department of Finance he was one of the most influential figures in economic policy for a quarter of a century.

James J. McElligott (1893-1974) joined the Department of Finance in 1923, as an Assistant Secretary, and was Secretary of the Department from 1927 to 1953. A Secretary is the senior civil servant, serving whichever party holds power.
He later served as Governor of the Central Bank, from 1953 to 1960.

He worked with Blythe under Cumann na nGaedheal and then with Fianna Fáil's Finance Minister Seán MacEntee in the 1930s, advising ministers on the budget, spending and taxation, and controlling other departments' spending.
His approach was financial orthodoxy: balanced budgets, low taxes, limited state borrowing and strict control of spending by other departments.

He was sceptical of high-spending social programmes and of industrial protection as practised by Seán Lemass, Minister for Industry and Commerce. Finance regularly opposed the cost of new schemes through the 1930s, so he shaped events as well as serving ministers.
Contemporaries in other departments, especially Industry and Commerce, saw Finance as a brake on development.

Historians such as Ronan Fanning, in The Irish Department of Finance 1922-58 (1978), argue that Finance's caution shaped policy for decades and held back growth until the reappraisal of the late 1950s.

The Wall Street Crash and the Depression cut the prices of farm exports and closed foreign markets just as Britain began to move away from free trade. The Free State felt the slump through falling farm prices and closed emigration routes, not through bank failures.
The Wall Street Crash of October 1929, the collapse of share prices in the United States, began a worldwide slump, and farm prices fell sharply.
The Free State's farmers lost income because they sold the same produce for less. Emigration to the United States dropped as the American economy shut its doors.
In September 1931 Britain left the gold standard (the system tying a currency to gold), but the Free State kept its currency tied to sterling, so its money moved with Britain's.
Britain moved away from free trade in 1931-32 and turned to protection of its own market, which showed the weakness of Irish dependence on a single market.
Unemployment rose in the towns, and the Cumann na nGaedheal government cut spending and did not bring in tariffs on a large scale, so the policy offered little relief.
The crisis helped Fianna Fáil, which promised protection and self-sufficiency, win the election of February 1932 and take office on 9 March 1932.
Irish farm prices fell steeply in the early 1930s, and the cost of the annuities (the repayments farmers made for their land) became harder to bear.

Fianna Fáil, with Seán Lemass as Minister for Industry and Commerce from 1932, abandoned free trade. Its aims were self-sufficiency and industrial jobs, and it tried to build industry behind tariff walls.
Tariffs and quotas were imposed on a wide range of imports, from clothing and shoes to household goods, so that Irish firms could sell to the home market without foreign competition.
The Control of Manufactures Acts of 1932 and 1934 (two Acts) required that majority ownership of manufacturing firms in the Free State be Irish, so that profits and control stayed in the country.
The Industrial Credit Company, set up in 1933, provided capital to new Irish firms.

Semi-state bodies were state-owned companies run commercially. The Irish Sugar Company (1933) ran the beet industry and the sugar factories; the Turf Development Board (1934) and Aer Lingus (1936) were further examples.
Wheat and beet growing were encouraged by subsidy and rose sharply.
By 1939 industrial employment had risen, but many of the new firms were small, inefficient and depended on the home market, so they could not export.
Critics said protection raised prices and did not lead to exports; supporters said it created jobs which free trade would never have provided.
The policy of self-sufficiency was reinforced after 1939 by the Emergency (the Second World War), when imports were cut off.

The trade war with Britain over the land annuities hit the largest group of farmers hardest. Britain imposed special duties on Irish cattle, beef and butter from July 1932, and the Free State put duties on British goods such as coal and cement.
The annuities were about 3 million pounds a year. British duties on cattle, beef and butter from 1932 cut the price of cattle and made many exports uneconomic.
Cattle exports to Britain, the single largest item, fell sharply, and cattle farmers across the country saw their incomes drop, because Britain was their main buyer.
The government paid bounties (payments to exporters) and subsidised wheat and beet to make up for lost income, financed by higher taxes.
The Coal-Cattle Pact of 1935 was a partial truce: Britain took more Irish cattle, and Ireland took British coal.
Dairy farmers and small farmers were affected by the fall in prices, so the cost of the trade war fell on the whole rural economy.

The Anglo-Irish agreement of April 1938 ended the Economic War, settling the annuity dispute for a lump sum of 10 million pounds, but cattle exports did not return to their former level before the war.
Fianna Fáil spent more than its predecessor on housing and welfare, but resources were limited and poverty remained widespread.
The Housing Acts of 1932 and 1936 raised state subsidies, and local authorities built many new houses, helped by slum clearance (pulling down unfit housing) in Dublin.
The Unemployment Assistance Act of 1933 gave relief to those who had run out of insurance benefit.
The Widows' and Orphans' Pensions Act of 1935 introduced a contributory pension scheme, meaning that workers paid in to qualify.
Tenements in Dublin remained overcrowded, and the tuberculosis death rate was high, which shows how much poverty continued despite the new housing.
Emigration fell in the early 1930s as the Depression closed American and British job markets, then rose again in the late 1930s and during the Second World War.
Emigrants' remittances (money sent home) were an important source of income for families in the west, so their reduction in the Depression hurt small farmers.
The marriage bar required women teachers and civil servants to resign on marriage. It was introduced in the 1920s-30s, and it kept married women out of these public posts.
Neither free trade nor protection produced rapid growth. Judgements depend on whether the aim is stability, self-sufficiency or living standards.
