Cumann na nGaedheal's achievement: financial stability, a sound currency, an efficient farm export trade and the Shannon Scheme.
Cumann na nGaedheal's limit: dependence on the British market and low spending left little help for the poor when the Depression came.
Fianna Fáil's achievement: new industries and jobs, a larger state role through semi-state companies and more housing and welfare.
Fianna Fáil's limit: the Economic War, a small and protected market, continued emigration and low living standards.
Why success was hard: a small home market, few natural resources, dependence on Britain, the Depression and then the Second World War.
Contemporary view: supporters of protection held that it was necessary for independence; critics held that it hurt consumers and farmers.

Later view: historians such as Mary Daly (Industrial Development and Irish National Identity, 1922-1939, 1992) and Joe Lee (Ireland 1912-1985, 1989) say that protection created jobs but not an efficient industry, while the Finance Department's caution restricted investment.

When war broke out in Europe in 1939, Ireland chose to stay out of it. The government called the war years the Emergency, and neutrality (staying out of a war while remaining a sovereign state) came to be seen as proof that Ireland was truly independent.
Fianna Fáil, led by Éamon de Valera, had been in government since March 1932, and de Valera was also Minister for External Affairs, so he personally steered Irish foreign policy as war approached.

Britain declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939, and Northern Ireland, as part of the United Kingdom, was at war from that date. Partition (the division of Ireland) therefore left the island split between a belligerent and a neutral state.
The Dáil passed its emergency resolution on 2 September 1939, a day before Britain declared war, and the policy of neutrality followed from it. Do not give 3 September as the date of the resolution.
The Emergency was the official name for the war years in the South. The name let the government avoid the word war, in keeping with a policy of staying out of it.
Neutrality was formal but benevolent in practice: it leaned towards Britain and the Allies, yet it was never formally broken. Ireland was not pro-German, and it was never a member of the Allies.
No single cause explains the decision. Several reasons reinforced each other, and the strongest answers rank them or link them rather than just listing them.

Sovereignty was the central reason: a state that followed Britain into war would look like a dominion (a self-governing state still tied to Britain) in practice, whereas staying out showed that Irish governments made their own decisions.

Partition was a second reason. Ireland could not ally with Britain while Britain held Northern Ireland, because joining Britain's war would have meant fighting beside the power that kept the island divided.

The Treaty ports (Cobh, Berehaven and Lough Swilly, naval bases Britain had kept) were handed back in July 1938 after the Anglo-Irish agreements of April 1938. Neutrality was therefore possible, since Britain no longer held bases on Irish soil. Churchill had opposed their return.
The Defence Forces were small and poorly equipped, and bombing of Irish cities was feared, so a state with weak defences had good reason to avoid becoming a target.

Civil War divisions were still felt, and the IRA (declared illegal in June 1936) was hostile to the government. Joining a British war might have split the country again, so neutrality helped keep national unity.

Most of the public supported neutrality, and the main parties, Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael and Labour, all accepted it. James Dillon of Fine Gael was the dissenter: in 1941 he argued for abandoning neutrality and joining the Allies.

Once neutrality was declared, the government took wide powers over the economy and over public opinion. Control of information was meant to protect neutrality, and it also pressed the public to follow the official line.

The Emergency Powers Act was passed on 3 September 1939 and let ministers make orders with the force of law, without a new act of parliament each time. It covered prices, supplies, movement and censorship, and its powers continued through the war years.
Frank Aiken, Minister for the Co-ordination of Defensive Measures, ran censorship, so one minister controlled what the public could read and hear about the war.
Press censorship forbade reports on troop movements, ship sinkings, weather and criticism of neutrality. Reports that might help a belligerent (a country at war) or upset one were kept out of print.
Weather forecasts were banned from the radio and the press because they might help the belligerents, for example by guiding aircraft or ships.
Letters and telegrams were opened and censored. The Censorship of Publications Board, set up under the Censorship of Publications Act of 1929, continued to ban books during the war.
Radio Éireann (the state radio station) avoided comment that might offend any belligerent, and war news was heavily controlled.

This is conformity: state control of information that pressed the public to follow the official line. It limited press freedom and public debate, and criticism of neutrality in particular could not be published.

A neutral state still had to be ready to defend itself. The government greatly expanded the army and created volunteer reserves, while quietly preparing for the possibility that neutrality would fail.
The army was greatly expanded during the Emergency, with Reserve forces added. This was a response to the weakness of the Defence Forces and the fear of invasion or bombing.

The Local Defence Force (LDF) was founded in June 1940, after the fall of France, as a volunteer army reserve, and tens of thousands joined. The fall of France made a German invasion of Ireland seem much more likely.
The Local Security Force was a different body: it worked with the Gardaí in civil defence (protecting the civilian population). Do not confuse it with the LDF, which was a volunteer army reserve.

The government made secret contingency plans (plans for a situation that might arise) for co-operation with Britain if Germany invaded. This shows that neutrality did not mean Ireland was indifferent to who won.

The government saw the IRA as a threat to neutrality and to the state, because its campaign in Britain and its raids at home could draw in a belligerent. It dealt firmly with the organisation, and this firm treatment is part of the story of state control in the war years.
The IRA had been banned in 1936, and the Offences Against the State Act of June 1939 reinforced the law against it by giving the government powers to act against the organisation.
The IRA's S-Plan bombing campaign in Britain began in January 1939. The Coventry bomb of August 1939 killed five people.

On 23 December 1939 the IRA raided the Magazine Fort in the Phoenix Park, Dublin, and removed the army's reserve ammunition. The government recovered most of it, but the raid showed how serious the threat was.

The Offences Against the State (Amendment) Act of 1940 introduced internment without trial (holding people without charge or court), and hundreds of IRA men were held at the Curragh. Do not confuse it with the 1939 Act, which gave powers against the IRA but not internment.
Several IRA men were executed during the war for the killing of Gardaí, and others died on hunger strike in 1940, including Tony D'Arcy and Seán McNeela.

Shipping losses and British restrictions meant shortages of coal, petrol, tea and wheat. The government stepped in to control production and distribution, so that scarce goods were shared out rather than left to the market.

Seán Lemass was Minister for Supplies from 1939 to 1945. His Department of Supplies controlled imports, prices and rationing (limiting how much of a scarce item each person could buy), so it was the main instrument of wartime economic control.
Tea, sugar, butter, flour, bread and fuel were rationed. Petrol was restricted so tightly that private motoring almost stopped.
Compulsory tillage orders required farmers to plough more land. The wheat acreage and harvest rose, though wartime bread became darker and coarser.
Coal imports collapsed, so turf (cut and dried peat) was used as a substitute. Production grew, huge turf stacks were built in the Phoenix Park and elsewhere, and trains and homes burned turf.
Gas supplies were limited to certain hours, and inspectors, known as glimmer men, checked on households that used gas outside the permitted times.
The state had to find ships to carry the goods it needed and had to hold down wages as prices rose. The burden fell unevenly: farmers did well, while wage earners and industry suffered.
Irish Shipping Ltd was set up in 1941 to buy and run ships, since British shipping was unavailable. Its ships sailed unescorted under the Irish flag.
Irish merchant seamen died when ships were sunk by submarines and aircraft despite their neutral markings. Neutrality did not protect them at sea.
The Wages Standstill Order of 1941 froze most wages while prices rose, so real incomes (what wages can actually buy) fell. The Trade Union Act of 1941 was aimed at the unions.
Exports of cattle to Britain continued, and farmers gained from guaranteed prices for produce. Industry, however, suffered from lack of raw materials.
Neutrality brought repeated pressure from Britain. The pressure continued through the battle of the Atlantic, the struggle over shipping routes in the Atlantic.

In June 1940, after the fall of France, Malcolm MacDonald visited Dublin and brought de Valera an offer: if Ireland joined the Allies, Britain would make a declaration in principle for a united Ireland.
De Valera declined in early July 1940. He doubted that Britain could deliver unity, and he distrusted the offer.
Churchill, who had opposed the return of the ports in 1938, publicly complained about the loss of the bases in the battle of the Atlantic. No seizure took place.
The Irish government complained when Britain restricted supplies of coal, wheat and shipping to Ireland, since these restrictions hit the economy hard.
Once the United States joined the war, American pressure was added to British pressure. It ended in a formal request in 1944 which de Valera refused.
David Gray, the American Minister in Dublin (the US representative in Ireland), was strongly critical of neutrality.
The United States entered the war in December 1941 and pressed the government to give up neutrality.

On 21 February 1944 the United States, with Britain, presented the American Note, asking the government to remove the German and Japanese diplomats before the D-Day landings. This is distinct from the 1940 offer: it was American, it came in 1944, and it concerned Axis diplomats.
De Valera refused. Britain restricted travel to and from Ireland from February 1944.
Neutrality was formal, but in practice it leaned towards Britain and the Allies. The help given was real, though it was kept quiet so that Ireland could still claim to be neutral.

Irish military intelligence (G2, army intelligence) co-operated with British intelligence, and the Garda watched German agents. Hermann Görtz, a German agent who parachuted into Ireland in 1940, was arrested in 1941 and interned.

Allied aircraft were allowed to fly over Donegal to the Atlantic, a route known as the Donegal air corridor, and Allied airmen who crashed in Ireland were quietly released, while Germans were interned in the Curragh.

A weather report of 3 June 1944 from Blacksod Point lighthouse, Co. Mayo, contributed to the decision to put D-Day back from 5 to 6 June 1944. This was a small but important contribution to the Allied invasion.
Tens of thousands of people from the Free State served in the British forces (estimates vary). Deserters from the Irish army who joined them were barred from state employment in 1945.
Neutrality did not keep Irish towns safe from German aircraft. Bombs fell on the South in 1940 and 1941, although the Irish government still sent help north when Belfast was bombed.
German aircraft bombed the creamery at Campile, Co. Wexford, on 26 August 1940, and three people were killed. Other places were also bombed.
On the night of 31 May 1941 German bombers dropped bombs on the North Strand in Dublin, killing about 30 people (counts range from 28 to 34) and destroying or damaging many houses.
The government protested to Germany, and Germany said it was an error. West Germany paid compensation after the war.

Fire brigades from Dublin and other towns went north to help Belfast in April 1941, with the approval of de Valera. The Belfast blitz was the bombing of Northern Ireland, and the North Strand raid, in contrast, was a German error in a neutral state.
De Valera's insistence on diplomatic correctness (following proper diplomatic form) to the end brought a public attack from Churchill.
On 2 May 1945, after Hitler's death was announced, de Valera called on the German minister, Eduard Hempel, to express condolences.

He had made a similar call on Gray, the American Minister, after Roosevelt's death in April 1945. He defended the visit to Hempel as diplomatic protocol that a neutral state had followed throughout the war.
Many Irish and Allied commentators criticised the visit to Hempel.
In his victory broadcast of 13 May 1945 Churchill attacked Irish neutrality and referred to the ports.
De Valera replied on Radio Éireann on 16 May 1945. He argued that Churchill had shown how a great power might justify interfering with the rights of a small state, and that Ireland had stood alone.
The broadcast was widely praised in Ireland and strengthened de Valera's reputation, though it did not improve relations with Britain.

The war closed many routes abroad and imposed austerity at home, but the British labour market opened up. Those who stayed faced hardship, and the first steps in social policy came late in the period.
Tens of thousands of workers went to Britain during the war to work in factories and construction, and sent money home (remittances), which helped families who stayed in Ireland.
The Irish economy suffered from shortages, and unemployment remained high for those who stayed, which is why emigration to British war work attracted so many.
Prices rose faster than wages, so the poor in Dublin and other towns suffered most.
The government used its emergency powers to maintain control of the press and labour, and there was little organised protest.
The Children's Allowances Act of 1944 and the creation of a separate Department of Health in 1947 were the first steps in post-war social policy.
Many Irish women and men served in the British forces, and the Irish government gave them little recognition after the war.
Judgements depend on whether the priority is sovereignty and survival or the moral and economic costs. Strong answers argue that neutrality kept independence, but at a heavy cost.
Achievement: the state avoided invasion and bombing on the scale of Belfast and kept its independence, so neutrality delivered the sovereignty it was meant to protect.
Achievement: neutrality was popular and strengthened national unity after the Civil War.
Limit: shortages, wage controls and censorship reduced living standards and freedom of expression.
Limit: the policy isolated Ireland from the Allies and left it without a voice at the end of the war.
Contemporary view: supporters called it a principled defence of independence, while critics said it was selfish, as Churchill suggested.

Later view: historians such as J. J. Lee (Ireland 1912-1985) and Brian Girvin (The Emergency, 2006) stress the practical advantages of neutrality and its pro-Allied bias, but also question the moral cost. Robert Fisk (In Time of War, 1983) was critical.
Northern Ireland was part of the United Kingdom, so it went to war with Britain, while the South stayed neutral. That contrast shaped how unionists and nationalists in the North each saw the war.

Under the Government of Ireland Act (1920), Northern Ireland was a self-governing part of the United Kingdom with a Unionist government at Stormont since 1921, a Protestant majority and a Catholic nationalist minority. This is the background to every wartime division.

The United Kingdom declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939, so Northern Ireland was at war from that day. Unionists contrasted its loyalty with the South's neutrality (the South's policy of the 'Emergency', staying out of the war).

Ulster Unionism, the political tradition defending Northern Ireland's place in the United Kingdom, presented the war effort as proof of the region's British loyalty. This strengthened the unionist case against a united Ireland, because the South had stayed out.

Nationalists in the North (those who wanted a united Ireland) were divided. Many Catholics volunteered for the forces, while others resented unionist rule and would not back a war effort run by a government they felt excluded them.
Conscription (compulsory military service) was introduced in Britain in 1939 but not applied to Northern Ireland. This meant that enlistment from the North, Catholic and Protestant, was voluntary.

In May 1941 the British government announced, then abandoned, a plan to extend conscription to Northern Ireland. Nationalists, the Catholic bishops (for example Cardinal MacRory of Armagh) and the Dublin government protested, although unionist ministers had favoured extension.

The IRA (the Irish Republican Army, a group that used force against partition) was active in Belfast. Tom Williams, an IRA member aged 19, was hanged at Crumlin Road Gaol on 2 September 1942 for killing a policeman during an IRA operation in April 1942.
The execution of Tom Williams deepened nationalist resentment.
Northern Ireland changed prime minister in the middle of the war. The change came from a death, then from a loss of confidence in the man who replaced him.
James Craig (Lord Craigavon), the long-serving Prime Minister, died on 24 November 1940. John Miller Andrews succeeded him as Prime Minister in late November 1940.
Andrews was criticised for an elderly cabinet and for a slow response to the Blitz (the German bombing of British cities). This made his government look unfit to lead a region at war.

Andrews resigned in April 1943 after a revolt by younger ministers and backbenchers over his leadership. Criticism over preparation for air attack was one strand in the discontent that ended his premiership, not the only cause.
Basil Brooke became Prime Minister in April 1943 and led the government until 1963. Do not confuse the three leaders: Craig (died November 1940), Andrews (1940 to 1943) and Brooke (1943 to 1963).
Brooke was an energetic unionist. He had been Minister of Agriculture (1933 to 1941) and then Minister of Commerce and Production, so he was well placed to push war production and farming.
The war brought full employment to a region that had suffered mass unemployment since the 1920s. Belfast's heavy industries were exactly what a country at war needed.
In the 1930s the Depression hit Northern Ireland's export industries, shipbuilding and linen, and left heavy unemployment. War orders reversed this.
Harland and Wolff, on Queen's Island in Belfast, built warships and merchant ships and repaired many vessels for the Admiralty (the British navy's governing department).
Short Brothers (Short and Harland) built Stirling bombers and other aircraft in Belfast, which made the aircraft factory a vital war industry.
Engineering firms made munitions and other war equipment. The rope works and linen mills made parachutes, tents, uniforms and rope, so even a traditional peacetime industry was turned to war needs.
Farmers were ordered to plough more land under compulsory tillage orders, which raised the acreage under crops. Northern Ireland became an important food supplier to Britain.
Unemployment fell sharply as war contracts came in, women entered factories in large numbers, and wages rose.
Industrial unrest still occurred over pay and conditions in the shipyards and engineering works, despite full employment.
The Northern Ireland government worked closely with Whitehall (the British government's ministries in London), including the Ministry of Aircraft Production and the Admiralty.
Belfast's industries made it a natural target, yet the government and city were badly prepared for air attack. This mismatch explains the scale of the damage in 1941.
Germany's conquest of France in 1940 brought Belfast within range of German bombers, and the Blitz on British cities began in 1940.
Belfast was an obvious target because of the shipyard, the aircraft factory, the docks and the engineering works, all producing for the war effort.
The Northern government assumed that Belfast was out of range of German airfields. This assumption of safety is the main reason preparations were weak.
Before April 1941 the city had few public air-raid shelters, and many working-class houses had no shelter at all, so people had nowhere safe to go when the bombers came.
Anti-aircraft defences were small: the city had only a handful of heavy guns, and no night-fighter squadrons were based in Northern Ireland in April 1941.
A German reconnaissance flight photographed Belfast in late 1940 and showed that the city was within reach, but the government did not accelerate preparations.
Fire services were small and under-equipped, so the authorities depended on outside help once the fires began.
Overcrowded slum housing near the docks and mills increased the risk of casualties and fire, because bombs and flames spread quickly through tightly packed terraces.
Three raids in spring 1941 devastated Belfast. Keep them apart by date and scale: a small raid in early April, the Easter Tuesday raid, and the May incendiary attack.
The raid of 7-8 April 1941 was smaller and aimed at the shipyard. About a dozen people were killed.
The main raid was on the night of 15-16 April 1941, Easter Tuesday (15 April), when about 180 German bombers attacked the city.
About 900 people were killed on Easter Tuesday, and the working-class districts of north and east Belfast were worst hit. It was the deadliest night of the Blitz outside London.
The raid of 4-5 May 1941 was an incendiary attack (using bombs that start fires) on the shipyard, the aircraft factory and the docks. About 150 people were killed.
In all the Blitz killed about 1,000 people and damaged more than half of the city's houses. Do not give a larger total.
Tens of thousands of people were left homeless.
The raids overwhelmed the city's ability to cope. People fled, help came across the border from a neutral state, and the authorities struggled to deal with the dead.
After the raids, tens of thousands of people left the city each night to sleep in the countryside. They were known as ditchers.
On the night of 15-16 April, fire brigades from Dublin, Dun Laoghaire, Dundalk and Drogheda crossed the border to help, with de Valera's authorisation.
This help was significant because it came from a neutral state: the South was not at war, yet it sent firefighters into the United Kingdom to save a city in the North.
Public buildings served as temporary mortuaries, among them the Falls Road baths, because the city mortuaries were overwhelmed by the number of dead.

The raids showed up the city's poverty and the weakness of its public services. The treatment of the evacuees (people moved out of danger) and the criticism of the government were the political consequences.

Children and mothers were evacuated to country areas, and many people took refuge in barns and church halls. Churches, schools and halls in towns near Belfast took in refugees, and the authorities opened emergency rest centres.
Host families in rural areas were shocked by the poor health, clothing and hygiene of some evacuees from the slums, because they had not met such poverty before.
The condition of the children became a theme in debates on housing and public health, as it had in Britain in 1939.
Many evacuees drifted back to Belfast within weeks, and housing remained scarce for years.
The Unionist government was criticised for its slow response and its poor preparation. This was one strand in the discontent that ended Andrews's premiership in 1943.
From 1942 Northern Ireland became a staging area for the Allied build-up (the gathering of troops and supplies for the invasion of Europe). The American presence changed daily life.
The first American troops landed at Dufferin Quay, Belfast, on 26 January 1942.
By 1944 there were over 100,000 American servicemen in Northern Ireland, in camps, airfields and ports.
They brought money, goods unavailable in rationed Britain and a new popular culture, including dances and cinema, so their presence was felt widely in everyday life.
US units were segregated, with Black American soldiers serving in separate units from white soldiers.

Northern Ireland's ports and airfields supported the Atlantic convoy escort (the protection of merchant ships crossing the Atlantic) and the preparation for D-Day, the Allied invasion of France in 1944.
The war raised expectations that the state should provide better housing, health and employment. Northern Ireland followed Britain in welfare reform, but its political structure stayed the same.
The destruction of housing made housing an urgent political issue after the war.

The Beveridge Report of 1942, a British plan for a post-war welfare state, shaped discussion of better health, housing and employment. Northern Ireland followed British welfare legislation under the policy of parity.
In February 1943 Jack Beattie, a Labour candidate, won the Belfast West by-election at Westminster, a sign of working-class discontent with the Unionist government.
Labour support rose, but the Unionist Party kept power at Stormont.

The Education Act (Northern Ireland) 1947 and the Health Services Act (Northern Ireland) 1948 came out of the wartime reform climate, which is how the war led to the origins of the welfare state in the North.
Sectarian divisions remained, and the Unionist government made no changes to the electoral system or policing.
The war changed Belfast's economy and housing but not its religious division. This comparison is the core of the most common essay question.
Unemployment, high in 1939, was low in 1945 because of war contracts.
Large areas of housing had been destroyed or damaged, and many families lived in temporary housing.
Industries such as shipbuilding and aircraft were running at full capacity, but depended on wartime orders, so their future was uncertain once the orders stopped.
The Unionist Party was still in control, though challenged by Labour and criticised for the failures of civil defence.
The links with Britain were stronger, because of wartime co-operation and the promise of welfare reform.
Catholic and Protestant communities remained separate, and the border and the division from the South were more entrenched.
Judgements depend on whether economic and social change or political continuity is stressed. Good answers weigh both and reach a conclusion.
Achievement: war production ended mass unemployment and brought full employment and better wages for many workers.
Achievement: the war strengthened Northern Ireland's place in the United Kingdom and prepared it to take part in the post-war welfare state.
Limit: the Blitz exposed poor preparation and housing, and the government had to answer for it.
Limit: the Unionist Party's control and the exclusion of the Catholic minority were unchanged, and sectarian division and the border were entrenched.
Contemporary view: unionists praised Northern Ireland's contribution to the war, while nationalists were critical of both the war role and the unionist government.
Overall: the war brought economic and social change but political continuity. Brian Barton is the main historian of the subject.

Both parts of Ireland were brand new in the early 1920s, and each government used language, religion, schools and culture to build or defend a sense of who its people were. The South promoted a Gaelic and Catholic identity, the North a Protestant and British one.
Northern Ireland was created in 1920-21 under the Government of Ireland Act 1920, and the Free State came into being in December 1922, so both states had to decide what kind of society they wanted.

In the South the cultural programme came from the Gaelic revival before 1914, led by the Gaelic League (which promoted the Irish language) and the GAA (the Gaelic Athletic Association, which promoted Irish games). The Church was the dominant institution, and after 1922 the Protestant minority was small.
In the North the state was run by Unionists, who wanted to keep the link with Britain, and Catholics were about a third of the population, so they were a large minority and not a tiny one.

Conformity means pressure to follow the accepted values, here Catholic and Gaelic ones, enforced through law, schools and public opinion. This is why those who did not fit, such as Protestants or writers, could feel left out.

Censorship is state control of what may be shown or read, carried out by film and publications censors who had the power to ban. Discrimination is unequal treatment of one group; in the North it was aimed at Catholics, including in school funding and control.

The Free State made reviving Irish (which had become a minority language) a central aim of cultural policy. It used schools and the civil service to spread it, and tied knowing Irish to getting a job.

Irish became a compulsory subject in national schools (primary schools) in 1922, and infant classes were taught wholly through Irish. This was a change in national schools only; second-level requirements came later.

A pass in Irish became necessary for State examinations at second level and for entry to the civil service and the Garda, so that knowing the language was tied to careers. No exact year is given for these rules, which belong to the 1920s and 1930s.
Ernest Blythe, Minister for Finance from 1923 to 1932, was a leading advocate of Irish, and the civil service was required to learn it.
The Gaeltacht Commission (the Gaeltacht is the Irish-speaking districts) was set up in 1925 and reported in 1926. It defined those districts and recommended economic and educational support for them.
An Gúm was founded in 1926 to publish books in Irish, including translations of foreign works, so that schools had texts and readers in the language.

Taibhdhearc na Gaillimhe, an Irish-language theatre, opened in Galway in 1928. Preparatory colleges trained teachers who could teach through Irish, because the policy depended on teachers able to do so.
The 1937 constitution recognised Irish as the first official language, with English as the second.
The policy raised the number of people who could say they knew Irish, but few used it in daily life. Judging it means weighing the census figures against what happened in everyday speech.

Census returns showed that about 18 per cent of people said they could speak Irish in 1926, rising to nearly a quarter by 1936. The rise came mainly through schooling, so it measured what pupils had learned and not what they spoke at home.
The Gaeltacht, the real Irish-speaking districts, continued to shrink because of emigration and poverty, so the policy failed to protect the places where Irish was a living language.
Many parents and teachers resented the compulsion, and some pupils learned little, which weakened support for the policy.
Irish remained a symbol of national identity, so the state kept it as a school subject even where it failed as a spoken language.
In the Free State the Church ran most schools and the state accepted its role. The state paid for education but left control largely to the clergy.

National schools were managed by clergy of the local denomination, and the state paid teachers' salaries and set the curriculum, so the Church controlled the running of schools while the state supplied the money.
The School Attendance Act of 1926 made school attendance compulsory for children from 6 to 14.
Secondary schools were mostly fee-paying and run by religious orders, so few working-class children reached them and access for the poor was limited.
The Vocational Education Act of 1930 set up vocational education committees to provide technical education, a route outside the fee-paying secondary schools.
The Church influenced the content of teaching, and the 1937 constitution recognised the family and the Church's role.
John Charles McQuaid, Archbishop of Dublin from 1940, was an influential voice on social and educational issues.
Laws in the Free State reflected Catholic teaching on morality, and critics saw the result as an enforced conformity. Each law below can be dated and linked to that ethos.
The Censorship of Films Act of 1923 set up a film censor who could cut or ban films, so what people saw at the cinema was controlled from the start of the state.

In 1925 the Dáil changed its standing orders (its own rules) so that private bills for divorce could no longer be introduced. W.B. Yeats made a famous speech in the Seanad defending the Protestant minority, who did not share the Catholic view of divorce.
The Censorship of Publications Act of 1929 set up a board with the power to ban books and periodicals considered indecent or immoral.
Writers were banned, among them Samuel Beckett (More Pricks Than Kicks, 1934) and, later, Kate O'Brien and Seán Ó Faoláin. A banned writer is good evidence of censorship.
The Public Dance Halls Act of 1935 required dance halls to be licensed, after clerical concern about dances.
The Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1935 banned the sale and import of contraceptives, in line with Catholic teaching.
Article 41 of the 1937 constitution, on the family, banned divorce, and Article 44 recognised the special position of the Catholic Church (it also named other churches and Jewish congregations).

The Protestant population of the Free State fell in the 1920s and 1930s, partly through emigration, the Ne Temere rule (the Church rule on the religion of children of mixed marriages) and the violence of the revolution and Civil War. No figure is given.

The state promoted a national culture through games, theatre, radio and the collection of folklore, while the GAA enforced a cultural boundary. Behind all of this lay the ideal of a Gaelic and Catholic Ireland.
The Tailteann Games were held in Dublin in 1924, 1928 and 1932, a festival of sport and the arts modelled on the ancient Irish games and open to people of Irish descent abroad.

The Abbey Theatre received a state subsidy from 1925, regarded as the first state subsidy for a national theatre in the English-speaking world. The Gate Theatre was founded in 1928 by Hilton Edwards and Micheál Mac Liammóir to stage international plays.
The state radio station 2RN began broadcasting from Dublin on 1 January 1926, a high-power transmitter at Athlone opened in 1932, and the station was renamed Radio Éireann in 1938.

The Irish Folklore Commission was established in 1935 under Séamus Ó Duilearga to record traditional stories and customs. In the Schools' Collection of 1937-38, primary pupils collected local folklore.
The GAA's Rule 27, in the rulebook from 1905, banned members from playing foreign games such as soccer, rugby, hockey and cricket, and was later extended to attending them. It was repealed in 1971.
In 1938 the GAA removed Douglas Hyde, President of Ireland, as its patron after he attended an international soccer match in Dublin. Hyde had founded the Gaelic League in 1893.

Culture was linked to nationalism by the idea of a Gaelic and Catholic Ireland, which excluded many Protestants and urban people, because it measured Irishness by language, religion and rural tradition.
Education was contested between the Unionist government, which wanted a non-denominational state system, and the churches. The outcome was a school system split by religion.
The Lynn Committee was appointed in 1921 to review education under the first Minister of Education, Lord Londonderry, and reported in 1922-23.

The Education Act (Northern Ireland) 1923, known as the Londonderry Act, created education committees run by local authorities, with public elementary schools to be non-denominational, that is, free of church control.

Protestant churches and the Orange Order objected to the lack of religious instruction, so the Act was amended in 1925 to allow Bible instruction, and the Orange Order and clergy gained places on school committees.
The Catholic Church refused to transfer its schools to state control and kept them as voluntary schools, outside the state system, with only partial public funding.

The 1930 Amendment Act gave committees of transferred schools four representatives of the transferors (the churches that handed over their schools) and two of the local authority, which Catholics saw as favouring Protestant interests.
The result was a divided school system, which remained a source of segregation and a grievance for Catholics, an example of discrimination.
In the North the unionist and nationalist communities expressed separate identities in a state that favoured the first. This was the Northern counterpart of the Southern Gaelic and Catholic ideal.
Orange Order parades on 12 July and loyalist bands were central to unionist culture and enjoyed official protection.
The Protestant ethos of the state was symbolised by the flag, the Union Jack, and by the royal visits and ceremonies at Stormont.
Nationalists supported the GAA, Irish-language classes and Catholic schools, but the Irish language received little state support.
Under the Special Powers Act (1922) the authorities could ban processions and emblems, and nationalist parades were more likely to be banned, so the law fell unevenly on the two communities.

James Craig (Lord Craigavon), the prime minister, said in 1934 that it was "a Protestant Parliament and a Protestant State". This was matched in the South by the Catholic emphasis of the 1937 constitution.

Hone was a leading modernist painter who turned to stained glass and became the best-known Irish stained-glass artist of her time. Her career shows how art could express an independent Ireland's identity.
Evie Hone (1894-1955) was born in Dublin and studied art in London and later in Paris under André Lhote and Albert Gleizes.
With Mainie Jellett she was one of the first Irish painters to work in a cubist style, which breaks a subject into geometric shapes.
From the 1930s she worked in stained glass with An Túr Gloine (the Tower of Glass), the Dublin studio founded by Sarah Purser in 1903 to revive Irish stained glass.
She converted to Catholicism in 1937, and much of her work was for churches, so church patronage shaped her career.
My Four Green Fields, a window symbolising the four provinces, was made for the Irish pavilion at the 1939 New York World's Fair.
The Crucifixion east window of Eton College Chapel was commissioned in 1949 to replace glass destroyed by a bomb in 1940, and was installed in 1952.
Contemporaries praised her work as modern Irish art of international standing.
Later writers on Irish art place her in the effort to give independent Ireland a modern cultural identity.
Cultural policy gave each state a distinct identity, but it also narrowed the range of what was acceptable. Each state promoted the identity of its own majority community.
Achievement: institutions such as An Gúm, the Folklore Commission, the Abbey and Radio Éireann preserved and promoted Irish culture, giving the new state a distinct identity.
Limit: compulsory Irish did not make it the daily language of most people, and the Gaeltacht continued to decline.
Achievement: arts and crafts, including the work of Hone, flourished with state and church patronage.
Limit: censorship and moral legislation restricted writers and individual choice, and minorities felt excluded, which produced conformity.
In the North the divided education system and separate cultural traditions deepened the communal division, in contrast with the South, where the state and the majority shared one cultural ideal.
Contemporary view: supporters saw cultural policy as defending Irish identity; critics, including writers such as Ó Faoláin, saw a narrow and conformist vision.
Later view: historians stress the tension between revival and restriction, and the influence of the Church.

The Eucharistic Congress was an international Catholic gathering held in Dublin in 1932. Its date was chosen to tie Catholicism to Irish identity, and it came ten years after independence, in a country where the Church was very strong.

An International Eucharistic Congress is a gathering of Catholics from many countries to honour the Eucharist, the sacrament in which Catholics believe bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ. The first was held in 1881, and each is held in a different city.

Dublin's was the 31st Congress. 1932 was chosen because it was the 1,500th anniversary of the traditional date of St Patrick's arrival in Ireland in 432, which linked the event to Irish Catholic identity.

The invitation and the early planning were made while Cosgrave's government (Cumann na nGaedheal, in office 1922-32) was in power, so the Congress was planned under Cosgrave. The Church and the state treated it as a national occasion.
Archbishop Edward Byrne of Dublin headed the organising effort, and the Pope sent a legate (a personal representative), Cardinal Lorenzo Lauri.
The Free State was ten years old in 1932, after the Treaty and the Civil War, so the Congress was an opportunity for the new state to show itself to the world.

The Catholic Church had a strong position in Irish life because the vast majority of the population was Catholic and the Church ran most schools and many hospitals. This is why a religious event could become a national one.
The Congress was planned under Cosgrave but held under de Valera, whose Fianna Fáil party took office three months before it opened. Both governments backed it, and the preparations were large.
Fianna Fáil won the February 1932 election and de Valera became President of the Executive Council (head of government) on 9 March 1932, three months before the Congress.
De Valera was known for his personal piety, so he took a leading part and his government gave the planning full support. He did not issue the invitation, which had come from Cosgrave's government.
Dublin was prepared with altars, decorations, flags and illuminations, and the streets of poorer districts (the slums) were decorated too, so that the whole city took part.
A large altar was built in the Phoenix Park for the final Mass, and the arrangements for transport, accommodation and crowd control were extensive because very large crowds were expected.

A radio station at Athlone was brought into use in 1932, so that the ceremonies and the Pope's message could reach listeners around the country. A loudspeaker system let the huge crowds hear the services.
Visitors came from the United States, Britain and Europe, and thousands of pilgrims came from Northern Ireland.
A national committee raised money by public subscription (donations from the public), and parishes organised local groups for the processions.
Thousands of volunteers acted as stewards, and special first-aid and catering services were arranged for the Phoenix Park.

The Congress showed close co-operation between the Catholic hierarchy (the bishops) and the new Fianna Fáil government. It also exposed the unresolved question of the Crown's representative in the Free State.
Cardinal Lauri arrived at Dún Laoghaire on 21 June 1932, the day before the Congress opened. De Valera and Archbishop Byrne welcomed him, and he was escorted through crowds to Dublin.

The Governor-General, James McNeill, who represented the Crown in the Free State, was not invited to the legate's reception at Dublin Castle. The Crown and the oath were live issues for the new government, so this was a deliberate snub.
The affair was part of the conflict that ended in McNeill's dismissal on 1 November 1932, after the government advised the King to remove him.
De Valera used the occasion to present his government as both Catholic and independent of the Crown. In this way the dispute showed sovereignty, the state's independent standing, being asserted.
The Congress also gave de Valera's new government a chance to show that it could work with the Church.
Five days of Masses, processions and services culminated in an open-air Mass in the Phoenix Park and a procession to O'Connell Bridge. Remember the dates, since examiners reward dated detail.

The Congress ran from 22 to 26 June 1932 and opened at the Pro-Cathedral in Dublin, with Masses and services in city churches, including a procession of the Blessed Sacrament (the consecrated bread of the Eucharist).
On 25 June a children's Mass was held in the Phoenix Park, attended by about 100,000 children.

On Sunday 26 June the closing Mass was celebrated at the altar in the Phoenix Park before a crowd often estimated at about a million. This may be exaggerated, but it is described as about a quarter of the population of the state.
John McCormack, the famous Irish tenor, sang César Franck's Panis Angelicus at a Mass of the Congress.
A message from Pope Pius XI was broadcast live by radio from the Vatican to the crowd, so the Pope could address the people of Ireland without being present.
After the Mass a procession went from the park to O'Connell Bridge, where Cardinal Lauri gave the closing benediction (a final blessing) to a very large crowd, up to several hundred thousand people.
Cardinal Lauri addressed the crowds and presided as the Pope's representative throughout the Congress.
The size of the event tested the state's administration and brought international attention. Its success helped present the Free State as a stable and devout country.
Special trains, buses and sailings brought crowds from all over Ireland and abroad, and the Garda and the Army managed the crowds.
Loudspeakers allowed huge crowds to hear the ceremonies, and radio carried the broadcast to the country, so people who could not be in the Phoenix Park could still take part.
Foreign newspapers reported the event, and it gave the Free State international publicity as a devout, stable Catholic country.
The Congress passed off without major disorder, which was a strong demonstration of public order only ten years after the Civil War.
The event was a success for de Valera, whose prestige grew at home and abroad.
Archbishop Byrne and the organising committee had to coordinate bishops from around the world, and papal flags and Irish flags were flown together.
The state radio service, which grew from the Athlone station brought into use for the Congress, was named Radio Éireann in 1938.

In the North the Congress was seen very differently. It highlighted the religious divide on the island, since unionists (who wanted Northern Ireland to remain in the United Kingdom) saw it as a threat.
Catholic pilgrims travelling by train and bus to and from Dublin were attacked in Northern Ireland, and trains were stoned at places such as Portadown, Lisburn and Belfast.
Police made baton charges at some stations to protect pilgrims.
Unionists saw the Congress as proof that the Free State was a Catholic state, which reinforced their support for partition (the division of the island) because they feared Rome rule.
Protestant newspapers and Orange leaders criticised the scale of Catholic display, and the attacks on pilgrims added to sectarian tension.
For Northern nationalists, the Congress was a source of pride and reinforced their sense of belonging to an Irish Catholic nation.

The Congress is usually assessed through four themes: Church-state relations, Catholic identity, Ireland's image and standing abroad, and unionist perceptions. Naming each and giving evidence earns credit, whereas narrative alone does not.

Church and state: it showed the alliance between the hierarchy and the political leadership, the same alignment that is seen in the tone of the 1937 constitution and in social legislation. The Congress passed no laws and did not cause the constitution.

Catholic identity: it presented Ireland as a Catholic nation, in line with the Gaelic and Catholic ideal of the 1930s. This is an example of conformity, the pressure to share the dominant Catholic values, as censorship laws of the period were too.
International image: it presented the Free State as stable, devout and independent, and made de Valera well known abroad.
Sovereignty: the Governor-General dispute showed the government's desire to downgrade the Crown's representative and assert the state's independent standing.
Unionist view: it confirmed fears of a state dominated by the Catholic Church.
Contemporary view: the Catholic press and most of the public regarded it as a great national triumph.
Later view: historians describe it as the high point of the Church's public influence, and a sign of the conformity that marked the 1930s. Some stress it as a political success for de Valera.
De Valera's critics in Cumann na nGaedheal noted that the Congress had been planned by Cosgrave's government but that Fianna Fáil gained the credit.
The Congress was a great public success, but its effect was largely symbolic. Examiners reward judgements set out as paired points.
Achievement: it showed the state could organise a major international event soon after the Civil War.
Achievement: it united people across party lines at a time of political change.
Limit: it did not change any laws or institutions, so its influence was cultural and political rather than legal.
Limit: it deepened the distrust between North and South, and Catholic and Protestant, on the island.
Contemporary view: a triumph for the Church and the nation.
Later view: a moment when church, state and nation appeared identical, which later generations judged more critically.

Emigration was already an established part of Irish life before the potato blight struck in 1845. What changed over time was who left and where they went, and that pattern is the background to the Famine exodus.
Ulster Presbyterians (Scots-Irish) were the first large group of Irish emigrants to North America, sailing to the American colonies through the 18th century.
After 1815 the flow widened, and about one million people left Ireland between 1815 and 1845. Estimates vary, so say 'about one million'.
Pre-Famine emigrants were often Protestant small farmers, weavers and tradesmen from Ulster and the midlands. They could pay their own fares and had some capital to start again abroad.
From the 1830s Catholic emigrants from the south and west made up a growing share. They were poorer and less skilled than the earlier emigrants, so the typical emigrant was changing.
Canada (British North America) was the cheapest crossing of the Atlantic, so many emigrants landed there and then moved on into the United States.
Britain received the poorest emigrants, because the crossing to Liverpool or Glasgow cost only a few shillings.
The 1841 census counted about 420,000 Irish-born people in Britain, concentrated in Liverpool, Glasgow, Manchester and London.

Not all emigration was permanent. Many Irish people worked abroad for a season or settled into the poorest jobs and districts of British and North American towns, driven out by hardship at home and drawn by work abroad.

Seasonal migration meant going abroad for part of the year and then returning. Tens of thousands of labourers from Mayo, Donegal, Galway and other western counties crossed each summer to English and Scottish harvests and brought home cash for the rent.
In Britain Irish labourers worked as navvies (labourers digging canals and railways), as dockers, as building labourers and in textile mills.
Irish districts grew in the poorest parts of British cities, such as Little Ireland in Manchester and St Giles in London.
In North America Irish men dug canals such as the Erie Canal in New York State (opened 1825) and built roads and early railways, while Irish women went into domestic service.

Push factors (conditions that drove people out) were the subdivision of holdings into tiny plots, a population that had risen to about 8.2 million by the 1841 census, dependence on the potato, the decline of domestic linen and wool spinning, and evictions for rent arrears.
Pull factors (attractions abroad) were higher wages and demand for labour in industrial Britain and North America, cheap land in Canada, and letters from earlier emigrants describing work abroad.
Timber ships carried Canadian timber to Britain and Ireland and returned westwards nearly empty, so they took emigrants cheaply as ballast (weight to steady the empty ship).

Repeated failures of the potato, the food of the poorest, turned a steady flow of emigrants into a mass exodus. Ireland was then part of the United Kingdom, and most of its rural poor held tiny plots from landlords.
Potato blight, caused by the water mould Phytophthora infestans, destroyed about a third of the crop in 1845 and almost all of it in 1846.
The 1847 crop was largely free of blight but very small because little seed had been planted, and blight returned in 1848. The year 1847 is remembered as Black 47 for its deaths and fever.
About one million people died of starvation and famine-related disease between 1845 and 1851 (estimates vary). Note that the death toll is dated 1845–1851, while the emigration decade runs to 1855.
Between 1.5 and 2 million people emigrated between 1845 and 1855 (estimates vary), the great majority to the United States, with several hundred thousand to British North America and Britain.
Deaths and emigration together cut Ireland's population from about 8.2 million in 1841 to about 6.5 million in 1851.

Famine emigrants were mostly Catholic, poor and unskilled, and many were Irish-speaking. They came heavily from the west and south-west, and many travelled as whole families rather than as single young adults.
Emigration was panic flight rather than planned movement. In 1847 about 300,000 destitute Irish people landed at Liverpool alone, and many stayed there.
By 1851 about 730,000 Irish-born people lived in Britain, and about a fifth of Liverpool's population was Irish-born.
Government relief did little to keep people on the land, and some of it pushed them off. These policies are part of the explanation for why so many chose, or were forced, to leave.
Public works were the main relief in 1846. The pay was low and late, and heavy labour weakened the starving people it was meant to help.
The Temporary Relief Act of 1847 replaced the public works with soup kitchens, which fed about 3 million people a day at their peak in the summer of 1847 before closing that autumn.

The Poor Law Extension Act of June 1847 made the Poor Law unions (local districts running the workhouses) pay for relief. Its Gregory clause (quarter-acre clause) denied relief to anyone holding more than a quarter acre unless they gave up the land.
The Gregory clause meant a starving smallholder had to surrender the family holding to get food.
Rising poor rates (local taxes that paid for relief) gave landlords a reason to clear smallholders, and evictions rose sharply between 1847 and 1852.
The Encumbered Estates Act of 1849 allowed bankrupt estates to be sold, and many new owners cleared tenants to consolidate farms into larger units.
Some landlords and the state paid for people to leave. Assisted emigration means passages paid by landlords, unions or governments, and it was the clearest case of tenants being pushed out.
Landlords paid passages because shipping tenants abroad was cheaper than paying rates to support them in the workhouse.

Major Denis Mahon of Strokestown, Co. Roscommon, sent about 1,490 tenants (the usual figure) via Liverpool to Quebec in 1847. Many died on the voyage or soon after, and Mahon was shot dead on 2 November 1847.
Lord Palmerston assisted tenants from his Sligo estate to Canada in 1847, and there were reports of their poor condition on arrival.
Lord Lansdowne assisted tenants from Kenmare, Co. Kerry, in the early 1850s. The number was several thousand.
The Earl Grey scheme (1848–1850) sent about 4,000 orphan girls from Irish workhouses to Australia as domestic servants. Do not confuse it with landlord-assisted emigration to Canada.
Assisted emigration paid for only a small minority of those who left, so most Famine emigrants paid their own way or had it paid by relatives.
Most Famine emigrants were not helped by landlords. They were helped by their own families abroad, through two linked practices that the syllabus names as key concepts.
Pre-paid passages were tickets bought from shipping agents by relatives already abroad and posted home, so people with no money could still leave.
Much Famine emigration was funded this way rather than by landlords or the state, because assisted emigration paid for only a small minority of those who left.
Chain-emigration meant the first member of a family to settle abroad sent money and tickets for the next, who in turn paid for others. In this way whole families and parishes moved in stages.
Pre-paid passages were the tickets themselves, while chain-emigration was the stage-by-stage pattern they produced along family networks. Sending one ticket once is not chain-emigration.
Emigrants from the same district tended to settle in the same streets and parishes abroad, where kin found them lodgings and work.
Letters home described wages, prices and fares and were read aloud in villages, which spread information about where to go and how to get there.
Where a poor emigrant went depended on the cost of the fare, and what the voyage was like depended on what that fare could buy.
Most transatlantic emigrants first crossed to Liverpool, which had the most frequent sailings. Others sailed direct from Cork harbour, Dublin, Limerick, Sligo, Derry, Galway and smaller ports.
Fares to Quebec were cheaper than to New York, so the poorest emigrants went to British North America.
The US Passenger Act of 1847 limited the number of passengers per ship and so raised fares on the US route, which diverted more of the poorest emigrants to Canada.
Steerage passengers (those in the cheapest accommodation) were crammed into the lower decks of sailing ships for a voyage of six weeks or more, with poor ventilation, little water and poor food.
Typhus (ship fever), spread by lice, and dysentery killed thousands at sea. Ships with high death rates became known as coffin ships.
Ports of arrival included New York, Boston, Philadelphia, Quebec and Saint John (New Brunswick), where fever sheds and quarantine stations were set up.

Grosse Isle (Grosse Île) was the quarantine station for the port of Quebec and the first North American landfall for tens of thousands of Famine emigrants. A quarantine station holds arriving ships and passengers apart so that disease cannot spread inland.
Grosse Isle is an island in the St Lawrence River, the great river that carries ships to Quebec, about 48 km downstream from Quebec City.
The quarantine station was opened in 1832 to stop cholera reaching Quebec from emigrant ships.
Every ship bound for Quebec had to stop there. A medical officer inspected the passengers, and the sick were landed at the hospital while the healthy were held in sheds or on board.
Dr George Mellis Douglas had been medical superintendent of the station since 1836.
The station was built for the normal flow of a season, so it was unprepared for the numbers and the fever of 1847.
In 1847 the station was overwhelmed by fever ships. The events show what happened when mass emigration met an unprepared system.
The first ship of the season, the Syria, arrived in mid-May 1847 with fever on board, and the hospital was full within days.
By 31 May 1847 about 40 ships carrying about 12,500 passengers lay at anchor off the island (some sources say about 13,000), in a queue stretching down the river.
Ships waited days or weeks for inspection, and the sick and dead lay in the holds alongside the healthy, so fever spread among people who had been well.
Tents and new sheds were put up, but sick and dying people lay on the ground and on the beaches. Healthy passengers were crowded into sheds, where many caught typhus.
Dr Douglas warned the authorities in advance and asked for more help, and his reports are a major source on the season. Several doctors on the island caught typhus and some died.
Catholic priests, many of them French-Canadian, and Anglican clergy took turns on the island. Several caught typhus and some died.
More than 5,000 people were buried on the island in 1847, most of them Irish. Some estimates of the deaths there are higher.
Passengers passed as healthy carried typhus up the river, and about 6,000 Irish died in the fever sheds at Montreal in 1847. Montreal's mayor John Mills died of typhus while helping the sick.

The suffering at Grosse Isle was matched by generosity, and the island's story gains meaning when set beside other ports. This is the material that lifts an account of 1847 into an argument about significance.
Hundreds of children orphaned at Grosse Isle and in the fever sheds were adopted by French-Canadian families, many of whom let them keep their Irish surnames. This shows the generosity of Quebec.
Partridge Island, the quarantine station at Saint John, New Brunswick, had a similar fever crisis in 1847.

New York received far more Famine emigrants than Quebec, but the poorest and sickest were more often diverted to Canada by the dearer US fares. The Castle Garden emigrant landing depot opened there in 1855.
Grosse Isle shows the human cost of unregulated mass emigration, and the failure of governments on both sides of the Atlantic to prepare.
Most Famine emigrants went to the United States and Britain, not Quebec, so Grosse Isle shows one part of the story rather than the typical journey.
The dead of 1847 were remembered on the island itself, and what was said there became part of a wider argument over who was to blame for the Famine.
The Ancient Order of Hibernians erected a large Celtic cross on the island's highest point, unveiled on 15 August 1909, with inscriptions in Irish, English and French.
The Irish text of the cross blames British rule for the Famine more bluntly than the English text does, so the memorial speaks differently to different readers.
The quarantine station closed in 1937 and the island became a Canadian national historic site. Since the 1990s it has been Grosse Île and the Irish Memorial National Historic Site.
John Mitchel and later nationalists used Grosse Isle as evidence that British policy, not only the blight, killed the Irish poor.
Others stressed landlord clearances and the limits of colonial resources, which means the island is used to support more than one interpretation.
Judging Famine emigration means weighing what it achieved against what it cost, and how people at the time saw it against how historians see it now.
Relief versus loss: emigration saved many from starvation, but it emptied poor districts and began long-term population decline.
Choice versus force: pre-paid tickets show families making their own decisions, while clearances and assisted schemes such as Mahon's show tenants being pushed out.
Contemporary view: officials, landlords and many economists welcomed emigration as a cure for overpopulation, while John Mitchel and the Young Irelanders saw it as expulsion.
Later view: Kerby Miller (Emigrants and Exiles, 1985) argued that emigrants saw themselves as exiles banished by England.
Revisionist historians of the 1950s to 1970s played down British blame, while Cormac Ó Gráda and Christine Kinealy, since the 1990s, stress failures of relief policy as well as the blight.
Grosse Isle has become a leading memorial to the Famine, but most Famine emigrants went to the United States and Britain, so it must be set against that wider pattern.
The Famine (1845–1852) broke the old pattern of Irish life, and after it emigration did not stop. It became a settled part of Irish rural life, with a steady outflow in good years and bad.
About 4 million people left Ireland in the six decades after the Famine (estimates vary), so the population of the whole island fell from about 6.5 million in 1851 to about 4.4 million in 1911.
The United States took about four out of five emigrants; Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand took most of the rest.
The number of Irish-born people in the United States peaked at about 1.87 million in the census of 1890, the highest total ever recorded there.
Emigrants were mostly young and single, aged roughly 15 to 30, so the country lost people in the years when they would have worked and raised families.
Ireland was unusual in Europe in sending about as many women as men; in some decades women outnumbered men.
Emigration was heaviest from the west and south-west (Connacht and Munster), and the poorest counties of the west sent the highest proportion of their people.
Emigrants were pushed out by how rural Ireland worked after the Famine. Several changes together left young people with few chances at home.

After the Famine farms were no longer subdivided. Under impartible inheritance (the whole holding passes to one heir) one son inherited the farm and one daughter received a dowry (a sum of money paid to a husband's family on marriage), so the other children had to emigrate or stay unmarried.
Late marriage was another cause, and it left many young adults without prospects at home.
The shift from tillage (growing crops, which needs many workers) to cattle grazing (which needs few) reduced the work available on the land.
There was little industry outside the north-east (Belfast and the Lagan valley), so young people from the rest of the country had no factory jobs to turn to.
Agricultural depression from 1879 and evictions around 1880 to 1882 (families put out of their holdings for not paying rent) caused a fresh surge, especially from the west.
The Land War, which began in 1879, was partly a response to the insecurity that fed this emigration.
Leaving became a normal stage of life, and both the crossing and the farewell changed in this period.

The American wake was a farewell gathering with music, dancing, food and drink as well as tears, held on the night before an emigrant left. It was treated like a wake (a gathering for the dead) because most emigrants never came back.
Steamships replaced sail from the 1860s, cutting the Atlantic crossing from about six weeks to about two weeks (or less) by the 1870s, which made the voyage far safer.
Liners called at Queenstown (Cobh) and at Moville near Derry to pick up emigrants travelling steerage (the cheapest, most crowded accommodation).

In New York emigrants landed at Castle Garden from 1855 to 1890 and at Ellis Island from 1892. Traditionally the first person processed at Ellis Island, on 1 January 1892, was Annie Moore from Cork, though recent research has questioned details of her identity.

Colonial governments in Australia and New Zealand paid or subsidised passages to attract settlers, so Irish emigration there was largely assisted. Passages to America were mostly paid privately, often with money sent by relatives.
Cheap passages and pre-paid tickets (tickets bought abroad and sent home) were already used before 1855, so the system the later emigrants used was well established.
Where emigrants settled and what work they did depended on their destination, their sex and the skills they brought. Most started at the bottom and many worked their way up.

In the USA the Irish settled overwhelmingly in cities such as New York, Boston, Philadelphia and Chicago, and in the mill and mining towns of New England and Pennsylvania, where unskilled work was plentiful.
Irish men mostly began as unskilled labourers on docks, railways, canals and building sites and in mines and factories. Many later moved up into skilled trades, police forces and fire departments.
Irish women dominated domestic service in American cities, because the job gave board, lodging and wages that could be saved and sent home.
Irish Americans moved into city politics through the Democratic Party, and the second generation (the American-born children of emigrants) began to enter teaching, clerical work and the professions.
In Britain the Irish settled in Liverpool, Glasgow, London, Manchester and the industrial towns of Lancashire and west-central Scotland, working on the docks, in building, in mills and in mines.
Irish nurses, teachers and domestic servants were prominent among women emigrants to Britain, and Irish harvest labourers continued to cross seasonally, returning home when the work ended.

In Australia Irish-born people and their descendants made up roughly a quarter of the European population (estimates vary), settling as farmers, labourers and gold-miners in New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland.
Many Protestants who went to Canada settled in Ontario, and some Irish emigrants went to New Zealand and Argentina.
Emigrants did not cut their ties with home. Money and letters flowed back, and the same flow brought more people out.
Emigrants' remittances were money and pre-paid tickets sent home by emigrants, and in total they were large.
Much of the money came from servant girls and labourers, who sent home a large share of their wages.
Remittances paid for the passages of younger brothers and sisters, so one emigrant could bring out a whole family over a few years.
Remittances also paid rent, shop debts and dowries and helped families keep their holdings, which made emigration a support for the rural economy as well as a drain on it.
The American letter, often containing dollars, was a regular event in western households, and it kept relatives informed of jobs and wages abroad.

Chain-emigration (emigration in stages along family and parish networks) meant that new arrivals stayed with kin, found work through them and settled in the same parishes, so emigrant communities reproduced the networks of home.
Letters collected by historians such as David Fitzpatrick (Oceans of Consolation, 1994, on emigrant letters from Australia) show how strongly emigrants kept family ties.

After 1920 the United States began to limit immigration by law. Ireland was partitioned and the Free State was set up in 1922; its economy was weak and mostly agricultural, so the quotas changed where emigrants went rather than whether they left.
The Emergency Quota Act of 1921 limited immigrants of each nationality to 3 per cent of that nationality's foreign-born population in the 1910 US census.

The Immigration Act of 1924 (Johnson-Reed Act) set quotas at 2 per cent of each foreign-born group in the 1890 census, a base chosen to favour north-western Europeans over southern and eastern Europeans.
The Irish Free State received a quota of 28,567 a year under the 1924 Act, cut to 17,853 from 1929 when the national-origins formula took effect. Northern Ireland was counted under the British quota.
The quotas redirected rather than ended emigration: emigration to the USA fell sharply from the 1920s, and Britain became the main destination.

Britain was easy to enter, jobs were close, the journey was short and the fare was low, and many Irish people already had family and friends there. This is why the Irish moved to Britain in large numbers in the 1930s.
The Great Depression after 1929 cut American demand for labour and reduced Irish emigration to the USA still further, and some emigrants returned.
The Free State governments did not try to restrict emigration, which they treated as an economic problem they could not quickly solve.
The Second World War and the years after it brought new rules about who could travel, and made Britain even more open to the Irish while the USA grew harder to enter.

During the Emergency (the Irish name for the Second World War, 1939 to 1945) Irish people needed travel permits and identity documents to go to Britain, and both governments controlled who could travel.

Britain recruited Irish workers for war factories, building and farm work, so over 100,000 people from the Irish state worked in Britain during the war (estimates vary); tens of thousands more joined the British forces.
The Ireland Act of 1949 confirmed that Irish citizens in the United Kingdom were not treated as aliens and could live, work and vote there.
The Common Travel Area allowed free movement between the two islands, which kept the journey simple for Irish workers.
Irish people were also exempted from the controls of the Commonwealth Immigrants Act of 1962, so they stayed free to enter when other newcomers were restricted.

The US Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 (Hart-Celler Act) abolished the national-origins quotas from 1968 and gave priority to family ties and skills, which made it harder for Irish people without American relatives to enter.
After the war Britain was rebuilding and needed workers, and the Irish were the nearest and easiest supply.
Post-war reconstruction created huge demand for labour in Britain, so Irish men worked as navvies (labourers who built roads, canals and railways) on roads, building sites and power stations.
Irish women trained as nurses in the new National Health Service, founded in 1948, or worked in factories and offices.
The Irish in Britain clustered in London (Kilburn, Camden Town, Cricklewood), Birmingham, Coventry, Luton, Manchester and Liverpool.
In the 1950s emigration reached a level that alarmed the state. The government investigated its causes, and a change of economic policy later eased the problem.
The government set up the Commission on Emigration and Other Population Problems in 1948, and it reported in 1954.

The Commission found that emigration was caused mainly by economic factors such as low incomes, unemployment and small farms, but also by the attractions of better living standards and social life abroad.
It accepted that emigration could not be ended quickly and urged economic development and better rural conditions rather than any ban on leaving.
Emigration peaked in the 1950s: about 400,000 people left the state between 1951 and 1961 (net, meaning departures minus returns), most of them for Britain.
The 1961 census recorded about 2.8 million people, the lowest population in the history of the state.
The Vanishing Irish (1953), a collection of essays edited by the American priest John A. O'Brien, warned that the Irish nation was dying out through emigration and late marriage.

Economic Development (1958), drawn up by T.K. Whitaker, and the First Programme for Economic Expansion (1958), pursued by Seán Lemass as Taoiseach from 1959, brought growth, so emigration fell in the 1960s, though it did not end.
Life for young emigrants in Britain was hard at first. Churches and community groups helped them cope.
Many young emigrants arrived in Britain with no training and lived in lodging houses or navvy camps, where hard drinking and long hours were common.
Navvy work was often arranged through subcontractors who paid cash in hand, leaving workers without insurance or job security.
Notices reading 'No Irish' are widely remembered from lodging-house windows in the 1950s and 1960s, though historians disagree about how common they were.
Catholic chaplaincies, the Legion of Mary and Irish centres in London and other cities helped new arrivals find lodgings and work.
Irish dance halls such as the Galtymore in Cricklewood and the Gresham on the Holloway Road became centres of emigrant social life, where people met others from home.
Assimilation means adopting the language, customs and identity of the new country. The Irish assimilated quickly in the USA and more partially in Britain.

Assimilation in the USA was helped by the English language, the Democratic Party, the Catholic parish and its schools, and the size of the Irish community; by 1914 the second generation increasingly thought of itself as American.
In Britain the Irish were also English-speaking but remained a visible Catholic working-class minority, and Catholic schools and parishes helped to keep a distinct identity.
Irish-born people could return home easily, so many saw their stay in Britain as temporary, which slowed assimilation.
Enda Delaney (The Irish in Post-War Britain, 2007) argued that Irish emigrants to Britain kept strong ties with home while integrating into British working life.
Irish-speaking emigrants from the Gaeltacht (the Irish-speaking districts) tended to lose the language within a generation abroad.
Domhnall (Dónall) Mac Amhlaigh (1926–1989) was an Irish-language writer whose diary of navvy life is the best-known first-hand account of 1950s emigration to Britain.
Born in Galway in 1926 and raised in Co. Kilkenny, he wrote in Irish.
Facing poor prospects at home he went to England in 1951 and worked as a labourer (a navvy) on building sites and roads, based in Northampton.
His diary of 1951 to 1957, Dialann Deoraí (An Exile's Diary), was published in 1960; Valentin Iremonger translated it as An Irish Navvy: The Diary of an Exile (1964).
It describes the work, the lodgings, the pubs and dance halls, homesickness, the company of other Irish navvies and the mixture of welcome and prejudice the Irish met in England.
He was a participant, not an observer, because he lived the life he described and wrote it down as it happened.
He also wrote novels and short stories in Irish, including Schnitzer Ó Sé (1974), and journalism; he died in 1989.
Contemporaries in Ireland valued the diary as a frank picture of a life that official Ireland preferred not to discuss.

Historians now treat it as a key source on the Irish in post-war Britain. As one author's account (a single man, an Irish speaker, a navvy, in the 1950s) it cannot stand for every emigrant's experience.
Historians weigh emigration as both a loss and a relief, and as both a choice and a necessity. These paired judgements help to frame an answer.
Safety valve versus drain: emigration relieved rural poverty and unemployment and brought in remittances, but it took the young and kept the population falling until 1961.
Opportunity versus exile: many emigrants gained better wages and lives, while others, as Mac Amhlaigh shows, felt themselves exiles doing the hardest work.
US restriction redirected rather than stopped emigration, because Britain's open door absorbed the flow after the 1930s.

Assimilation: it was fast in the USA, helped by language, the Democratic Party and the parish, but only partial in Britain, where the Irish stayed a visible Catholic working-class minority with easy return.
Contemporary view: churchmen and politicians spoke of the vanishing Irish and blamed modern attractions as well as poverty, while the Commission of 1954 placed the cause in economic weakness.

Later view: Kerby Miller (Emigrants and Exiles, 1985) stressed exile and banishment, while historians such as Enda Delaney see emigration to Britain as a choice by individuals within family strategies, not simply as forced exile.

Famine-era emigrants were mostly poor, Catholic and unskilled, and they settled in the cities of the north-east USA and industrial Britain, where host communities saw them at close quarters. Hostility rested on religion, poverty and competition for work, and it was reinforced by stereotypes that were widely printed. This is discrimination: unfair treatment of a group in jobs, housing, politics or public life.
