John McCormack, a tenor born in Athlone in 1884, became famous in America and Britain and recorded Irish ballads. He died in 1945.
McCormack's concerts made Irish songs part of mainstream concert repertoire, and he was a leading figure in Irish-American cultural life.
Céilí bands (groups playing traditional Irish dance music for dancers) performed in Irish halls and clubs in America and Britain. They are not the same thing as the later folk revival.
Parish halls, clubs and dance halls kept Irish-American song and dance alive, and they gave emigrant communities a shared cultural life.
The Clancy Brothers, from Carrick-on-Suir, Co. Tipperary, and Tommy Makem, from Co. Armagh, became popular in America after appearing on the Ed Sullivan Show in 1961.

The folk revival (popular interest in traditional and ballad music in the late 1950s and 1960s) brought Irish songs to a young audience in America and Britain. It was led by the Clancy Brothers and, from 1962, the Dubliners, and it changed how Irish music was seen abroad.

The Irish state promoted tourism to attract visitors, including descendants of emigrants who wanted to see the places their families had left. Each development has its own date, and examiners expect them.
Bord Fáilte, the Irish Tourist Board, was set up in 1952 under the Tourist Traffic Act to promote tourism and develop tourist facilities.
An Tóstal, a national festival of Irish culture and heritage, was launched in 1953 to draw visitors. It was a festival, whereas Bord Fáilte was a permanent body, so they are not the same thing.
Shannon Airport opened in 1945 as a transatlantic stop for aircraft, which brought American travellers through Ireland.
Shannon opened the world's first duty-free shop in 1947, which made it a point of contact between Irish life and travellers from America.
Aer Lingus began flights between Dublin, Shannon and New York in 1958, which made it easier for Irish Americans to visit.
Heritage tourism (travel to places of historical and cultural interest) grew in the 1950s and 1960s.
Roots tourism, the visiting of ancestral places by people of Irish descent, linked the Irish state's promotion of tourism with the emigrant communities abroad.
Tourism was valued as an export industry that brought in dollars and sterling, so it fitted the drive for economic growth of the late 1950s.
Films about Ireland reached Irish audiences too, and Ireland had little film production of its own, so foreign productions and state censorship shaped the images on Irish screens.
Robert Flaherty's documentary Man of Aran (1934), by an American director, presented a romantic picture of life on the Aran Islands that many islanders did not recognise.
Carol Reed's film Odd Man Out (1947), set in Belfast and starring James Mason, showed the Irish revolutionary underworld to international audiences.
The Censorship of Films Act of 1923 gave the Irish state power to ban films, and the film censor (the official who judged films) removed or refused films on moral grounds.
Ardmore Studios opened at Bray, Co. Wicklow, in 1958 as the main film studio in Ireland.
Foreign productions, including Hollywood films, were shot in Ireland in the 1950s, and they brought Irish scenery and Irish actors to the screen.
Irish cinema-goers saw mostly Hollywood and British films, so the American image of Ireland reached Irish audiences as well as Americans.
John F. Kennedy's election and his visit in 1963 changed how Irish Americans and the Irish public saw one another. Examiners want both sides, the USA and Ireland.
Kennedy's great-grandfather Patrick Kennedy left Dunganstown, Co. Wexford, in 1849. His mother, Rose, was a Fitzgerald, and her family was also of Irish descent.

Kennedy was elected in November 1960, becoming the first Catholic president of the United States. Many Irish Americans saw this as acceptance of Irish Catholics in public life, because Al Smith, a Catholic, had lost the 1928 election.
Kennedy visited Ireland from 26 to 29 June 1963, going to Dublin, Wexford (including Dunganstown), Cork, Galway and Limerick.
On 28 June 1963 he addressed the Oireachtas, the Irish parliament, in Dublin.
The visit drew large crowds and intense press coverage in Ireland, and it was widely celebrated as a moment of Irish pride.

Kennedy's image in Ireland combined ancestry with success in American politics, so it encouraged Irish people to think of their emigrant relatives as part of a shared story. For Irish America it confirmed that Irish Americans had arrived in American public life.
His assassination on 22 November 1963 was widely mourned in Ireland.
Historians argue that the visit fitted the self-confidence of Seán Lemass's government as the economy opened to the world, rather than causing it.
John F. Kennedy the president is a different person from his father Joe Kennedy, the ambassador, and from his great-grandfather Patrick Kennedy, who left in 1849.
Judging these images means weighing what they achieved against what they left out, and how people at the time saw them against how historians see them now.
Achievement: Hollywood films, music and tourism made Ireland widely known abroad, so they attracted visitors, brought in dollars and sterling and strengthened ties with emigrant descendants.
Limit: the images were often sentimental, rural and stereotyped, and they left out industrial and urban Ireland.
Contemporary view: tourism bodies and many audiences welcomed the images, while some critics objected that they stereotyped Irish people as comic or drunken.
Later view: historians see an Ireland made for export, and they debate how far the Kennedy visit changed Irish self-image or only celebrated it.
Film versus music: films fixed a rural, comic image, while the folk revival gave Irish culture a younger and more confident voice abroad.
Northern Ireland was born of partition in 1920-21 and held two rival loyalties. The events of 1949 then fixed its place in the United Kingdom in law.

The Government of Ireland Act 1920 created Northern Ireland from six counties, with its own devolved parliament (a parliament with powers over local affairs) that opened in 1921, later housed at Stormont in Belfast. The other twenty-six counties got a separate settlement.

The population was split into mostly Protestant unionists, who were loyal to the Union with Britain and to the Crown, and mostly Catholic nationalists, who wanted a united Ireland. Catholics were about a third of the population (35 per cent in the 1961 census).
The Republic of Ireland Act 1948 took effect on 18 April 1949, ending Ireland's membership of the Commonwealth and formally declaring the twenty-six counties a republic.
Westminster responded with the Ireland Act 1949, which declared that Northern Ireland would not cease to be part of the United Kingdom without the consent of the Northern Ireland parliament.

This consent guarantee gave unionists a legal safeguard against a united Ireland imposed without their agreement, so the border question seemed settled for as long as unionists held a majority at Stormont.

The Unionist Party never lost power at Stormont, and the rules for local elections helped it hold councils even where Catholics were numerous. This is the political system that Brookeborough inherited and left alone.
The Unionist Party governed continuously from 1921 to 1972 and held a majority at every Stormont election, so nationalists formed a permanent opposition with no chance of forming a government.

The Stormont general election of 10 February 1949 was fought on the border question after the declaration of the Republic, and is called the border election. Nationalists ran an anti-partition campaign and the Unionist Party won 37 of the 52 seats.

Proportional representation (a voting system that gives parties seats in line with their share of votes) was abolished for local elections in 1922. The first-past-the-post system that replaced it helped unionists win control of councils in mixed areas.

The local franchise (the right to vote) was limited to ratepayers and their spouses, and company directors had extra votes, known as the business vote. Reforms from 1969 removed this system, so many poorer people had no local vote.

The Flags and Emblems (Display) Act (Northern Ireland) 1954 let the police remove a flag if its display was likely to cause a breach of the peace. It applied to any flag, but in practice the target was the Irish tricolour, which nationalists resented.
Basil Brooke led the Unionist government for twenty years and put stability and loyalty to the Crown first. He saw no reason to change a system that kept his party in power.

Basil Brooke was Prime Minister of Northern Ireland from 1943. He was created Viscount Brookeborough in 1952, so he is only correctly called Brookeborough from then. He came from County Fermanagh and died in 1973.
His government resisted reform of local government and the franchise, because the existing system kept unionists in power and he saw no need to change it.

As Minister of Agriculture in the 1930s he urged loyalists to employ Protestants rather than Catholics, in speeches of 1933 and 1934 as reported. Nationalists cited these for decades as proof of sectarian attitudes at the top of the Unionist Party.
Brooke retired in March 1963 at the age of 74 and was succeeded as Prime Minister by Terence O'Neill.
Unionist rule rested on emergency law and a police system that nationalists did not trust. Meanwhile the opposition was too divided and too reluctant to take part to challenge the government.

The Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Act (Northern Ireland) 1922 stayed in force. It allowed internment (detention without trial) and the banning of organisations, which nationalists saw as a weapon aimed at them.
The Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) was the regular police force, and Catholics made up only a small minority of its ranks.
The Ulster Special Constabulary, including the part-time B Specials, was kept as an armed reserve alongside the RUC. It was almost wholly Protestant, with almost no Catholics in the Specials.

The Nationalist Party abstained from Stormont for long periods (refused to take its seats) and accepted the role of official opposition only in 1965. This meant there was little effective challenge to the government in the 1950s.

In the 1940s, after the Second World War, Britain built a welfare state, a system in which the government pays for health care, education, housing and benefits. Northern Ireland followed it on a basis of parity, meaning its services matched Britain's.

The reforms followed the Beveridge Report (1942), which set out a plan to tackle want and ill health, and the laws passed by the Labour government of 1945-51, with the main legislation coming in 1945 to 1948.
National Insurance, unemployment benefit and pensions were run on a UK-wide basis, so benefits in Northern Ireland matched those in Britain.
The principle of parity meant Stormont was expected to follow British social policy, which limited its freedom to set different rules.
The National Health Service began in Northern Ireland on 5 July 1948, the same day as in England, Scotland and Wales.
The Social Services Agreement of 1949 formalised parity. Britain's subsidy covered what Northern Ireland's own taxes could not, so the cost was met largely by the British Treasury.
The Catholic minority benefited from the same services as Protestants, but this did not remove discrimination in the allocation of houses and jobs.
Stormont copied Britain's school reforms, which opened secondary schooling to every child. The system still kept the two communities apart and selected pupils at eleven.
The Education Act (Northern Ireland) 1947 provided free secondary education for all pupils, so children from poorer families could stay in school beyond primary level.
It set up a tripartite (three-part) system of grammar, technical and secondary intermediate schools.
Pupils transferred at about age eleven after the eleven-plus, an examination that decided who went to a grammar school, the route to university.

Voluntary schools, mostly Catholic, kept their own management and received a state capital grant (money towards building costs only) of 65 per cent. Controlled schools were run by the education authorities.
State awards helped more Catholic students reach Queen's University Belfast from the 1950s.
Free secondary education gave Catholic children access to a wider range of qualifications, so by the 1960s a new educated Catholic middle class was emerging.
Education stayed segregated by religion, so Protestant and Catholic children grew up in separate schools.
State housing was a major gain, but who controlled allocation mattered as much as how many houses were built. The Housing Trust and the local councils behaved differently.
The Northern Ireland Housing Trust was set up in 1945 and built houses and estates in towns and cities across the province.
The Trust allocated its houses on a points system (applicants were awarded points) and was regarded as fair.
Most council houses, however, were allocated by local councils, and many unionist-controlled councils allocated houses in ways that favoured Protestant families. Not all housing was discriminatory.
Control of housing mattered because control of housing gave councils power over where families lived, so allocation tied housing to political power.
Catholic and Protestant families were increasingly housed in separate estates, which later made segregated housing a feature of Belfast and Derry.
Gerrymandering was the standard example of how electoral rules could be used to keep one group in control. Derry shows it most clearly.
Gerrymandering means drawing electoral boundaries so that one group's voters are concentrated in a few wards and the other group wins more seats than its share of the vote justifies.
Londonderry Corporation was controlled by unionists even though Catholics were a majority of the city's population.
The ward boundaries were redrawn in 1936 to concentrate Catholic voters in one ward, so they could win only a few seats however many Catholics there were.
Control of the council mattered because councils allocated houses and were major employers, so gerrymandering fed the housing and jobs grievances.
Northern Ireland's economy depended on old industries that declined from the 1950s. The new industry that replaced some of them was not spread evenly.
Harland and Wolff, Belfast's main shipyard, had built the Titanic, completed in 1912, but its workforce shrank in the post-war decades as shipbuilding declined.
Linen manufacturing, once a major employer, declined as cheaper foreign competition and synthetic fibres spread.
Unemployment stayed well above the UK average, and emigration drained the province of young people, so the economy lagged behind Britain throughout the Brookeborough years.
The Stormont government offered grants and incentives to attract new industry, including man-made fibre plants and aircraft production at Short Brothers.
Most new investment went to the Belfast area and towns east of the River Bann, so the largely Catholic west, including Derry, had fewer jobs.
Agriculture remained a large employer, and the farming economy was supported by British agricultural subsidies.
Discrimination means unequal treatment of Catholics, and it was the main grievance of the minority. Historians and contemporaries disagreed about how far it went.
Catholics made up about a third of the population but were under-represented in the RUC, in senior civil service posts and in local-council posts.
Some large private employers, especially in Belfast's shipyards and engineering works, employed very few Catholics.
Local councils in unionist hands were also major employers, and nationalists complained that they hired few Catholics for senior posts.
Nationalists argued that Stormont treated the minority as second-class citizens and that discrimination in housing, jobs and local voting was systematic.
Unionists argued that discrimination was exaggerated and that Catholics had equal access to state services and to the vote.
Unionist governments saw the Specials and the RUC as essential defences against republican violence, not as sectarian forces, which is why they rejected criticism of the security forces.
Sectarianism is hostility and discrimination between Protestants and Catholics, tied to political allegiance. It shaped where people lived, worked and went to school.
Religious segregation in schools, housing and workplaces meant that most people had little regular contact with the other community.
The Orange Order (Protestant) and the Ancient Order of Hibernians (Catholic) were the main fraternal bodies, each with a political dimension.
Mixed marriages were uncommon, and religious differences were a factor in many social and personal decisions.
Sectarian prejudice was strongest in working-class areas where jobs and houses were scarce and rival communities lived side by side.
Parades and the display of flags marked out territory, so symbols of identity were also symbols of division.
The Belfast riots of 1920 to 1922, which killed hundreds, were background memory of violence that both sides carried into the 1950s.
The IRA's Border Campaign, called Operation Harvest, was an attempt to end partition by force. It failed to win popular support and ended in defeat.
The IRA launched the campaign in December 1956 with attacks on RUC barracks, customs posts and border installations. Its aim was to end partition by force.
On 1 January 1957 the IRA raided Brookeborough RUC barracks. Seán South and Feargal O'Hanlon were killed and became republican martyrs, and South was commemorated in a ballad.
Internment without trial was introduced in the North in 1957, and the Republic also interned IRA men that year, so the IRA was hit on both sides of the border.
The campaign attracted little support from the nationalist community, which is why it failed, and its members were largely rounded up under internment north and south.
The IRA Army Council called off the campaign in February 1962, after which the movement was weak for several years.
The failure led some republicans to rethink their strategy, and a faction turned towards left-wing politics and social campaigns in the 1960s.
Brookeborough's record can be judged by what his government delivered and what it left untouched. Contemporaries and later historians weigh these differently.
Achievement: the welfare reforms in health, education and housing raised living standards for citizens of both communities across Northern Ireland.
Achievement: Stormont kept political stability through the 1950s, with no sustained challenge to the Union, and the IRA border campaign was defeated.
Failure: discrimination in housing, jobs and local voting, and gerrymandering, were left untouched, and this grievance was later taken up by the civil rights movement.
Failure: the economy stayed weak, with unemployment and emigration, and new industry was poorly distributed between east and west. There was no outreach to Catholics.
Contemporary view: unionists praised Brooke's stability and loyalty to the Crown, and saw his government as the guardian of the Union.
Contemporary view: nationalists condemned the Special Powers Act and discrimination as proof that the state was sectarian.
Later view: historians stress that the welfare gains were real, but that without power sharing or reform the grievances stayed alive and fed the civil rights movement of the 1960s.

To understand why a civil rights movement appeared in the 1960s, you need to know how Northern Ireland was run and what Catholics complained about. The background and key ideas used throughout the topic come first.

Northern Ireland was created by the Government of Ireland Act (1920) and came into operation in 1921. The Ulster Unionist Party governed at Stormont (the Northern Ireland parliament) continuously from 1921 to 1972, so the state was Protestant and unionist in character.

Catholics were about one third of the population (about 35 per cent in the 1961 census) and were mostly nationalists, who wanted a united Ireland. This meant they were a permanent minority who could never win a majority at Stormont.

In local elections only ratepayers (householders) and their spouses could vote, and companies had extra votes. In Westminster elections all adults could vote. This is why 'one man, one vote' (every adult having one vote) was a demand about local elections only.

Gerrymandering means drawing electoral boundaries to give one group an advantage. In Derry nationalists were a clear majority of the population, but unionists controlled Londonderry Corporation (the city council) because of the way the ward boundaries were drawn.

Unionist-controlled councils allocated council houses and many local jobs, so Catholics complained of discrimination in housing and employment. They also resented the Special Powers Act (1922, giving the government sweeping emergency powers), the B Specials (the part-time Ulster Special Constabulary) and the RUC (the police).

Brookeborough was Prime Minister from 1943 to 1963 and left these grievances in place, so they were waiting for O'Neill. The welfare state had also produced a more educated Catholic middle class, less willing to accept them.

Civil rights means equal treatment of Catholics in voting, housing and jobs, sought by peaceful protest and by appeals to British opinion. Tolerance is willingness to accept other beliefs and identities; intolerance is refusing to.
The unionist and nationalist divide, and Paisley's opposition to reform, are the examples of intolerance used in this topic, because each side often refused to accept the other's identity.
Terence O'Neill came to power in 1963 believing that Northern Ireland's future lay in a modern, prosperous economy. His programme combined economic planning with gestures towards Catholics.

Terence O'Neill succeeded Lord Brookeborough as Prime Minister in March 1963, having been Minister of Finance from 1956. His time at Finance gave him the experience of economic planning that shaped his premiership.

The Matthew Report (the Belfast Regional Survey and Plan, 1963, by Sir Robert Matthew) was a plan for regional development around Belfast. It proposed a new city, and Craigavon in County Armagh (Lurgan and Portadown) was planned from these proposals, with government acceptance in 1964.

The Wilson Plan (Economic Development in Northern Ireland, 1965, by Professor Thomas Wilson) was about economic development generally, not about the new city. Together the two reports shaped planning, so it is wrong to credit Craigavon to the Wilson Plan alone.

Government-backed projects such as Craigavon and the new university at Coleraine were part of a wider plan to show that Northern Ireland could be modern and prosperous. Coleraine's choice as the site angered Derry, which had wanted the university.

O'Neill made symbolic visits to Catholic schools and hospitals. This was a famous gesture of goodwill towards a community that had been shut out of public life, and unionist hardliners resented it as a concession to nationalists, because it suggested that the government might treat them as equal citizens.

O'Neill went beyond economics and tried to improve relations with Catholics and with the Republic of Ireland. This policy is known as bridge-building, and its high point was the exchange of visits with the Taoiseach in 1965.

Bridge-building was O'Neill's name for his policy of improving relations with Catholics in Northern Ireland and with the government of the Republic. He hoped that prosperity and goodwill would reduce the tension between the two communities.

On 14 January 1965 the Taoiseach, Seán Lemass, visited Stormont. This meeting is often described as the first between the heads of the two governments since partition, though earlier contacts existed in the early 1920s, so the phrase should not be given as flat fact.
O'Neill returned the visit to Dublin on 9 February 1965. He had not told most of his cabinet in advance, which shows that he expected opposition within his own government.

Nationalists responded in February 1965 when the Nationalist Party, led by Eddie McAteer, became the official opposition at Stormont for the first time. This was a sign that some nationalists were prepared to work within the state, which shows that some nationalists were prepared to work within the state.

Catholics welcomed the gestures but judged that real change in housing, jobs and voting was too slow. Visits and speeches had not altered the council allocation of houses or the local franchise, so hopes were raised without being met.
O'Neill's reforms split his own side. Hardline unionists saw the Lemass meeting as the first step towards a united Ireland, and they began to organise against him.

Ian Paisley, a Protestant minister, was by the mid-1960s the leading Protestant critic of O'Neill's policies. He and other hardliners opposed the Lemass meeting, arguing that it undermined the Union (the link with Britain) and Protestant identity.

The 'O'Neill must go' campaign, led by Paisley and others from 1966, sought the Prime Minister's removal from office. Its rallies showed O'Neill that a section of the unionist community would not accept his policy of bridge-building, because it showed that part of the unionist community would not accept bridge-building.

In 1966 Paisley set up the Ulster Constitution Defence Committee and the Ulster Protestant Volunteers. He was jailed for three months in 1966 after a June protest at the Presbyterian General Assembly in Belfast, when he refused to be bound over (to promise to keep the peace).

William Craig, Minister of Home Affairs from 1966, was a hardline figure in the cabinet who banned the Derry march of 5 October 1968. O'Neill dismissed him on 11 December 1968 after he clashed with O'Neill over policy.

Unionist MPs in the Stormont parliament and in the party organisation argued that O'Neill was giving away too much to nationalists. Opposition therefore came from inside the Unionist Party, not just from street protest.

The Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), a loyalist paramilitary group, murdered three people in May and June 1966: John Scullion, Peter Ward (a Catholic barman) and Matilda Gould. Its leader Gusty Spence was convicted of the murder of Ward and jailed for life. This was the violent edge of loyalism.

O'Neill was therefore squeezed between reformers, who thought he was too slow, and hardliners, who thought he was going too fast. His position weakened as unionist opposition grew and as violence on both sides increased in 1968 and 1969.

O'Neill was the reforming Prime Minister whose policies helped to create the conditions for the civil rights movement, and whose authority collapsed under its pressure. Examiners want a verdict on him, not a biography.

He was born in London on 10 September 1914 into a landed family whose seat was Shane's Castle, County Antrim, and he was educated at Eton. He entered Stormont in 1946, was Minister of Finance from 1956 to 1963 and became Prime Minister in 1963.

As Prime Minister he made modernisation and reconciliation the centre of his programme, because he believed prosperity would ease sectarian tension. He drew on the Matthew and Wilson reports and tried to build contact with Dublin through the Lemass meetings of 1965.
In 1968 and 1969 he came under pressure from London, from the civil rights movement and from within his own party, so he conceded reforms step by step.
He announced the five-point package on 22 November 1968 and appealed for moderation in the 'Ulster stands at the crossroads' broadcast on 9 December 1968.
As Prime Minister he was a participant who decided policy and spoke for the government; later he wrote and gave interviews about the crisis as a witness.

He resigned on 28 April 1969 after a crisis in his party, a poor showing in the February election and a series of bomb attacks on water and electricity installations. He was made a life peer in 1970 as Baron O'Neill of the Maine, and died in 1990.
Contemporaries were divided. Hardline unionists accused him of betraying the Union, nationalists welcomed the gestures but judged them too slow, and British opinion backed him.

Historians generally judge him a modernising planner and a sincere but limited reformer, who reformed on his own terms and from above. Some argue that he did not regard Catholic grievances as primarily political, citing his reported 1969 opinion that Catholics given jobs and houses would live like Protestants.
Historians also note that his authority was constrained by his own party, which is why they debate whether he was a failure or a reformer who was undermined.

Dr Conn McCluskey and his wife Patricia gathered evidence of discrimination against Catholics through the Campaign for Social Justice. Their moderate, documentary campaign made discrimination a public issue before the mass movement began.

Conn McCluskey was a Dungannon doctor and Patricia was his wife. In 1963 Patricia and others set up the Dungannon Homeless Citizens League, which campaigned about the allocation of council houses in the town.

The league grew into the Campaign for Social Justice in Northern Ireland, founded in January 1964 in Dungannon, County Tyrone. It gathered evidence on discrimination in housing, jobs and local government in Tyrone, Fermanagh and Derry, and published it in pamphlets such as 'Northern Ireland: the Plain Truth'.

The McCluskeys were participants who led the campaign. They sent their findings to MPs at Westminster, and the lobbying helped to lead to the formation of the Campaign for Democracy in Ulster at Westminster in 1965, made up of Labour MPs and others such as Paul Rose.

They shaped events by providing evidence and a model of constitutional protest, and they were ahead of NICRA (the Civil Rights Association). Their method was documentary and moderate, appealing to British opinion through facts rather than street protest, because it gave the movement a model to follow.

Some unionists dismissed the campaign as a front for republicans, a charge the McCluskeys rejected; they described their aim as equal treatment of citizens. Nationalists and sympathetic British MPs welcomed the evidence.

Historians credit the Campaign for Social Justice with turning discrimination into a public issue before the Civil Rights Association was formed, so its work provided the evidence on which the later movement drew.

By the mid-1960s several developments came together to make a mass civil rights movement possible. The Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association (NICRA) was founded in 1967 to campaign for equal rights for Catholics on the British model.

The movement emerged now for several reasons. There was a generation of educated Catholics produced by the welfare state, the American civil rights movement of the 1960s offered an example of peaceful protest, and a Labour government under Harold Wilson came to power in Britain in 1964.

O'Neill's gestures had also raised Catholic hopes without delivering change, and the McCluskeys' evidence gave campaigners facts to use. In short, expectations had risen faster than reform, because new hopes had been created without matching reforms.

NICRA was founded in Belfast on 29 January 1967. It drew together the Campaign for Social Justice, nationalists, republicans, socialists, trade unionists, Communists, Labour supporters and some liberal Protestants.

Its demands were one man, one vote in local elections, an end to gerrymandering, fair allocation of council houses on a points system and laws against discrimination by public bodies. It also demanded the repeal of the Special Powers Act and the disbanding of the B Specials.

Westminster elections already used one man, one vote, so the demand applied to local elections, where the franchise was restricted to ratepayers and their spouses and companies had a vote. This is why it was the central and most contested demand.
The movement used peaceful marches and sit-ins to draw attention to discrimination, and it sought British support for reform, so peaceful pressure was the movement's chosen method.
In 1968 the movement moved from complaint to action. A series of dated protests, easily confused with one another, shows how it grew and how the authorities and loyalists reacted.

On 20 June 1968 at Caledon, County Tyrone, Austin Currie, a Nationalist MP at Stormont, squatted in a council house that had been allocated to a single 19-year-old Protestant secretary. He was evicted by the RUC, and the incident drew attention to housing allocation.

NICRA's first march, from Coalisland to Dungannon on 24 August 1968, was followed by marches in Derry, Newry and Belfast. It showed that the movement could draw a crowd and keep the protest peaceful, so it proved that the movement could draw a crowd and keep order.

The authorities banned or obstructed many marches, which led to confrontations with the police and loyalist counter-demonstrators. Bans turned peaceful protest into a test of whether the state would allow it.

On 30 November 1968 a NICRA march in Armagh was blocked by Paisley's followers and others. This shows how counter-demonstrations were used to stop marches, and it was a confrontation between supporters of Paisley and the movement.
The banned civil rights march in Derry was broken up by the police. Television pictures of the violence turned the movement into an international story.
Derry was a flashpoint because it had a Catholic majority but unionist control of Londonderry Corporation through gerrymandering. Housing and jobs were also scarce, and many Catholics felt neglected.

The march of 5 October 1968 was organised by NICRA and was banned by the Minister of Home Affairs, William Craig. Marchers who defied the ban were confronted by RUC officers, who used batons on the crowd in Duke Street.
Gerry Fitt, MP for Belfast West at Westminster, was among those struck. Film shot by RTÉ and others was seen widely and shocked opinion in Britain and Ireland.

The event is seen as the start of the civil rights crisis of 1968 and 1969, because it moved the movement from marches to confrontation. Riots followed in Derry, and British and international attention increased, because the violence showed that the demand for change was being met by force.
Nationalists in Derry saw the police action as proof of discrimination, while unionists blamed the civil rights organisers for provoking disorder.
The Derry Citizens' Action Committee was formed in October 1968, with John Hume as vice-chairman, to keep protests peaceful. At the same time, students were radicalised by what they saw.
After Derry, the British government pressed O'Neill to act. His response was a package of reforms that went some way towards the civil rights demands but left the central one untouched.
British pressure was direct. Harold Wilson, the British Prime Minister, met O'Neill, Craig and Faulkner in London on 4 November 1968.
The five-point package of 22 November 1968 promised a points system for allocating council houses, so that need rather than religion would decide who got a house.

It promised an ombudsman, a Parliamentary Commissioner, to investigate complaints against government departments, and it promised that Londonderry Corporation would be replaced by a development commission.
It promised that the Special Powers Act would be withdrawn when the situation allowed, and that the company vote in local elections would be ended.
One man, one vote in local elections was not in the package, which was the main demand of the movement. The parliamentary party accepted it only in April 1969.

On 9 December 1968 O'Neill made his 'Ulster stands at the crossroads' television broadcast, appealing for moderation. Many moderates backed him and hardliners were angry; Craig was dismissed two days later, on 11 December.
Some young activists thought NICRA's methods were too cautious. People's Democracy, a student group, marched across Northern Ireland, and the attack on its march made the crisis worse.

People's Democracy was formed on 9 October 1968 at Queen's University Belfast, after the Derry march, by students including Bernadette Devlin and Michael Farrell. Its aim was to press for civil rights and for one man, one vote, because some students thought NICRA too cautious.

The march from Belfast to Derry began on 1 January 1969, with about 40 people at the start. The aim was to protest against discrimination and to press for one man, one vote, in the manner of American civil rights marches.
On 4 January 1969 the marchers were ambushed at Burntollet Bridge, near Derry, by loyalists, among whom were off-duty B Specials. The RUC failed to protect the march.

On the night of 4-5 January RUC men went through the Catholic Bogside, and residents set up barricades. 'Free Derry' became the name for the area, after the slogan painted on a gable end in January 1969.

The effect was a loss of Catholic confidence in the RUC, because marchers and supporters accused it of failing to protect the march. The movement became more confrontational, and in early 1969 NICRA and People's Democracy briefly split over tactics.
Through the spring of 1969 O'Neill lost control of his party. A divided election, a wave of bombs and the demand for one man, one vote ended his premiership.

The Stormont general election on 24 February 1969 left the Unionist Party divided between pro-O'Neill and anti-O'Neill candidates, and its overall result was disappointing for O'Neill, which showed that his party was split down the middle.
O'Neill held his own seat at Bannside against Paisley by a majority of 1,414 votes. A narrow win against a hardline challenger showed how far his support among unionists had fallen.

Bombs at water and electricity installations, including the Silent Valley reservoir in the Mournes, began on 30 March 1969. They were first blamed on the IRA but were later shown to be the work of loyalists in the UVF, who hoped to discredit O'Neill, and they undermined his position.
The Mid Ulster by-election on 17 April 1969 returned Bernadette Devlin as a unity candidate. Do not confuse it with the general election of 24 February.
In April 1969 the cabinet debated one man, one vote, and the Unionist parliamentary party accepted it in local elections. This split the party further, because hardliners saw it as surrender.
O'Neill resigned on 28 April 1969. James Chichester-Clark became Prime Minister by 17 votes to 16 over Brian Faulkner, a one-vote margin. The crisis led on to the Troubles;
Devlin was a student leader and civil rights activist who, in 1969, became the youngest woman elected to Westminster at the time. She carried the movement's demands into the British parliament.

Bernadette Devlin was born on 23 April 1947 in Cookstown, County Tyrone, and studied psychology at Queen's University Belfast, where she became a leading student activist, so she was a student leader before she was an MP.
She was a participant in People's Democracy, formed in October 1968, and in the Belfast to Derry march of January 1969. She became a prominent speaker in the civil rights campaign.
She was elected MP for Mid Ulster at the by-election of 17 April 1969, aged twenty-one, as a unity candidate. She was the youngest woman elected to Westminster up to then.

She shaped events by carrying civil rights to Westminster, and was in turn shaped by the movement that made her a public figure. She wrote a memoir, The Price of My Soul, published in 1969, which presented the struggle from her own perspective.
Contemporary nationalists and supporters saw her as a symbol of youth and defiance, while unionists regarded her as a dangerous agitator.
Historians tend to view her as a key figure who brought the civil rights movement into Westminster politics.

She was convicted of incitement to riot after the Battle of the Bogside in August 1969 and served a sentence in 1970. On 31 January 1972, after Bloody Sunday, she struck the Home Secretary Reginald Maudling in the House of Commons.
She lost her Westminster seat in February 1974, and in January 1981 she and her husband were seriously wounded by loyalist gunmen at their home.
Paisley's opposition to O'Neill made him the most visible unionist critic of reform before 1969. His career is covered here to 1969 only.

Ian Paisley was born in 1926 in Armagh and was a minister who founded the Free Presbyterian Church of Ulster in 1951. Its doctrine was strict, anti-Catholic and anti-ecumenical (opposed to friendly contact between Churches). Do not confuse it with the Presbyterian Church in Ireland.

Before 1969 he was a public campaigner who organised rallies and protests against O'Neill's policies. He founded the Protestant Telegraph in 1966, set up the Ulster Constitution Defence Committee and the Ulster Protestant Volunteers, and was jailed for three months in 1966.

He opposed the Lemass meeting, arguing that the Prime Minister was undermining the Union and Protestant identity, and he led the 'O'Neill must go' campaign. His followers helped to block the NICRA march in Armagh on 30 November 1968.
He was a participant in his own campaign and, through his followers, in the Armagh blocking and the Bannside contest of February 1969, where O'Neill held the seat against him by a majority of 1,414.

He shaped events by mobilising grassroots Protestant opinion and restricting O'Neill's room to reform; his stand grew with each concession, which is why the more he conceded, the harder the hardliners pushed.

Contemporaries saw him as the voice of hardline unionism: many unionists regarded him as a defender of the Union and Protestant identity, moderates found him an embarrassment, and nationalists saw him as a bigot.

Historians argue that his campaign against O'Neill helped to pull unionist politics towards the harder line of the 1970s. In April 1970 he won the Bannside seat at Stormont at a by-election after O'Neill's departure.
Judging this period means weighing what reform achieved against what it failed to do, and separating aims from results. The points below are paired to help you build a balanced argument.

O'Neill's successes: he modernised the economy through planning and Craigavon, built bridges to Catholics and Dublin, and conceded much of the civil rights programme, including a points system for housing, an ombudsman and, by April 1969, one man, one vote in local elections.

O'Neill's limits: his reforms came late, after the Derry march of October 1968 and British pressure, and he did not tackle discrimination until forced. They were too slow for Catholics and the movement but too fast for his party, so he lost control.

The movement's successes: it put discrimination on the British political agenda, brought the question of Northern Ireland's government into the open and secured reforms such as the points system, the ombudsman and one man, one vote.

The movement's limits: it provoked a loyalist reaction, bans and violence, and some of its leaders were divided, as in the split between NICRA and People's Democracy. Many leaders judged the reforms concessions forced by protest.
Contemporary views: nationalists welcomed the gains but argued that discrimination had not ended. Unionists were divided, with hardliners blaming the movement for provoking violence.

Later views: Michael Farrell stresses systematic discrimination by the unionist state, Marc Mulholland sees a reformer constrained by his party, and Thomas Hennessey examines the O'Neill years and the build-up to violence.
Overall, reform from above met resistance from below and a unionist backlash, and his resignation in April 1969 showed the limits of reform from above. The crisis led to the Troubles.

To see why the choice of a university site caused a row, you first need to know how Northern Ireland was governed and what Derry's position in it was. Derry had a college but not a university, and its nationalist majority saw the choice of site as a test of fair treatment.

Northern Ireland was governed by a Unionist (mainly Protestant) government at Stormont, the seat of its parliament. Catholics and nationalists (who wanted a united Ireland) were a large minority, and Derry (Londonderry) had a Catholic nationalist majority.

Derry's local council, Londonderry Corporation, was controlled by unionists despite that majority, because ward boundaries were redrawn in 1936 in their favour. This meant the city's own representatives could not influence decisions about it.

Derry, the second largest city in Northern Ireland, suffered high unemployment and more emigration than the Belfast area. Its traditional industry of shirt-making employed mainly women, so male unemployment was especially high.

Magee College in Derry was founded in 1865 by the Presbyterian Church and taught degrees of Trinity College Dublin, so it was a college rather than a university. Before 1968 the only university in Northern Ireland was Queen's University Belfast.

The Robbins Report of 1963 recommended a large expansion of higher education across the United Kingdom. Robbins and the Lockwood Committee (appointed the same year) belong to the same wave of expansion, which made a second Northern Ireland university a live question.

Terence O'Neill became Prime Minister in 1963. His government's modernisation programme included expanding higher education, building new towns and economic planning, so the new university was part of a wider plan.

Derry nationalists argued that their city, with its existing college and decades of neglect, deserved the university, and many Derry unionists agreed. The site was therefore a test of whether Stormont treated the west of the province fairly.
Only one new university was planned, so choosing one town meant that no other town could host it. This is why the contest between towns was bound to leave a loser.
The Lockwood Committee was set up to advise on the site, and in response a campaign in Derry, backed across the community, pressed for the city to be chosen.
The Lockwood Committee, chaired by Sir John Lockwood, was appointed in 1963 to advise on higher education in Northern Ireland, including the second university and where to place it.
The committee took evidence from the Derry campaign and from other towns, such as Coleraine, that were competing for the university.
The University for Derry Committee was formed to campaign for the city. John Hume, then a young teacher, was its chair, and it ran in 1964-65.

The campaign drew support from across the community: nationalists, some unionists and business people in Derry. This cross-community base made it harder for the government to dismiss it as purely nationalist.
The campaign argued that Derry had the population, the existing Magee College buildings and the need for jobs, and that the west deserved fair treatment.
Campaigners used meetings, pamphlets and slogans to put the case that Derry had been overlooked. This is propaganda in the sense of material used to shape opinion, not necessarily to deceive.
The Lockwood report chose Coleraine over Derry, Derry protested, and the government accepted the choice. Each step fed the belief in Derry that the decision was unfair.

The Lockwood report of February 1965 recommended Coleraine, in County Londonderry, rather than Derry. Coleraine is about 30 miles from Derry and much smaller. Do not confuse County Londonderry with the city.
Derry supporters answered with a motorcade (a convoy of vehicles) to Stormont in February 1965 to protest against the report.
Derry supporters alleged that 'faceless men', unseen people rather than an open process, had really decided the matter. No proof was offered, so this was an allegation and not an established fact.
The government accepted the report and won the Stormont debate and vote by its majority. Nationalist members and some Derry unionists opposed the decision.
The government's case for Coleraine was that it offered a central site, good access and room for expansion, as a planned new university town. It said Derry's case had been fully considered.
The campaign continued after the vote, and the grievance lasted for years. In Derry the decision was widely seen as a sign that Stormont would not give the city equal treatment in public investment.

Hume was the chair of the University for Derry campaign. The campaign made him a public figure, was an early step in his career and shaped the constitutional, cross-community approach that marked his later politics.

Who he was: John Hume was born in Derry in 1937, was educated in Derry and at St Patrick's College, Maynooth, and worked as a teacher. About 1960 he helped found a credit union (a community savings and loan society) in Derry.

What he did: he chaired the University for Derry Committee in 1964-65, organised across the community, and led public meetings and the protest. He was a leader of the campaign, a participant and not an observer.
Shaped by events: the defeat taught him that protest needed organisation and cross-community support, and the campaign made him a public figure in Derry.
Contemporaries: supporters saw him as a moderate and effective campaigner who could organise across the community. Some unionists saw him as a nationalist agitator.
Historians: they see the campaign as the start of his career and of his constitutional, cross-community approach to politics.
Pointer only: his later roles include the Derry Citizens' Action Committee in 1968, Stormont MP for Foyle in 1969, founder of the SDLP in 1970 and MP for Foyle from 1983.
Putting the dates in order matters because essays on this controversy are rewarded for facts in sequence. The result was that Coleraine got the university and Derry did not.
1963: the Robbins Report, the Benson Report and the Matthew Report all appear (three separate reports), and the Lockwood Committee is appointed.
1963 to 1965: the Lockwood Committee investigates sites and takes evidence, while the University for Derry Committee campaigns for Derry.
February 1965: the Lockwood report recommends Coleraine, and Derry supporters travel to Stormont by motorcade to protest.
1965: the Stormont government accepts the report and wins the vote by its majority.
1965 to 1968: planning and building of the new university at Coleraine proceed while the Derry campaign continues.
1968: the New University of Ulster opens at Coleraine, so Derry is left without a new university.
Magee College remained in Derry. In 1984 the New University of Ulster merged with Ulster Polytechnic to form the University of Ulster, and Magee later became a campus of that university.
Both sides used the controversy to argue about fairness, and the decision became a symbol of regional and religious inequality. Two key concepts apply here: discrimination and propaganda.
Discrimination means unequal treatment because of religion or background. Here it is the claim that the location decision favoured the unionist east over the nationalist west.
Derry campaigners used posters, pamphlets, public meetings and the motorcade to present their case, and their message was that Derry had been overlooked.
The government and its supporters presented Coleraine as a sound academic and economic choice, and rejected charges of sectarian motives. This too was propaganda: material shaping opinion.

The 'west of the Bann' grievance (the River Bann runs through the north of the province) held that new industry, investment and public bodies were placed east of it, leaving Derry and the west with fewer jobs.
Critics linked the decision to other public investment decisions, such as Craigavon, designated in 1965, so it seemed one of a pattern rather than a single choice.

The controversy therefore fed a wider belief that discrimination was built into government decisions, not only into local councils. Nationalists argued they had no fair share of public investment, a view the civil rights movement later made central.
The university decision was one of several decisions of the mid-1960s that Derry nationalists saw as favouring the east, so examiners expect you to name at least two others.
The Benson Report of 1963 (by Sir Henry Benson) recommended closing unprofitable railway lines. The Derry Road line from Portadown through Omagh to Derry closed in 1965.
The closure ended the line through Omagh to Portadown and weakened the city's links with the south-west and the Dublin direction, which nationalists argued reinforced Derry's isolation.
The Matthew Report of 1963 (by Sir Robert Matthew) was a regional plan for growth around Belfast and proposed a new city between Lurgan and Portadown.

Craigavon, the new city between Lurgan and Portadown in County Armagh, was designated in 1965. It was seen in Derry as drawing investment east. It is named after Lord Craigavon, the first Prime Minister.
Derry's economic decline, with high unemployment, emigration and few new industries, made each decision against the west feel worse.
Unionist control of Londonderry Corporation meant Derry's own representatives could not influence these decisions.
Housing in Derry was overcrowded, which added to the sense that the city's needs were ignored.
The controversy mattered beyond one university because it gave Derry a concrete example of unfair treatment and gave Hume his first campaign.
For Derry, the decision confirmed a sense of neglect and gave nationalists a clear example of the discrimination grievance, which fed the civil rights movement in Derry.
For Hume, chairing a broad campaign gave him experience of organising across the community and a public reputation.
For the civil rights movement, the controversy showed that public investment could be a political issue, and it added to housing and voting grievances.
Unionists regarded the decision as a rational choice of site and an example of the government's modernising programme.
Historians view the decision as one of several episodes that deepened nationalist distrust of Stormont in the mid-1960s.
Judging this controversy means weighing both sides' cases, strengths against limits, and contemporary views against later ones.
Strength of the nationalist case: Derry was larger, had Magee College's existing buildings and had high unemployment, which gave a strong economic argument.
Strength of the government's case: Coleraine offered a central site and room to grow, and a formal committee, the Lockwood Committee, had made the recommendation.
Limit of the nationalist case: the 'faceless men' allegation came with no proof of a plot, so it could not show that the decision was made on sectarian grounds.
Limit of the government's case: Coleraine was a small town, and the wider pattern of investment in the east weakened the claim that spending was spread evenly.
Contemporary view: Derry nationalists saw discrimination, while unionists saw a planning decision.
Later view: historians tend to see the controversy as a symbol of wider inequality rather than proof of a single plot.
Both sides agreed that Derry deserved higher education, so the dispute was about the site and not the principle.

By 1969 Northern Ireland had been governed for almost fifty years by one party, and many Catholics felt shut out of the state. Knowing what had built up before August 1969 explains why the violence broke out so quickly once it started.

The Government of Ireland Act 1920 set up the Northern Ireland parliament (Stormont), and the Unionist Party governed from 1921 to 1972. Westminster kept sovereignty but in practice rarely interfered in Northern Ireland's internal affairs.

The Ireland Act 1949 guaranteed that Northern Ireland would stay in the United Kingdom unless its parliament (later its people) consented, which is why unionists treated any talk of change as a threat to the border.
Catholics complained of discrimination in housing, jobs and local voting. The Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association (NICRA), founded in 1967, campaigned on these grievances through marches.

A NICRA march in Derry on 5 October 1968 and the attack on a People's Democracy march at Burntollet in January 1969 deepened tension, and the Prime Minister, Terence O'Neill, resigned on 28 April 1969. Such marches mattered because they brought the grievances onto the streets.

The RUC (Royal Ulster Constabulary) was the regular police, armed and mostly Protestant. The B Specials (the Ulster Special Constabulary) were a part-time reserve, almost entirely Protestant, and Catholics distrusted both.
The IRA's border campaign of 1956-62 had failed, and Stormont had used internment (detention without trial) against it in the 1950s, so the IRA was weak and divided in 1969.
Four terms run through this period, and each is used in a specific way in this topic. Defining them first makes the events easier to follow.

Terrorism means violence against civilians and the state for political aims. In this topic it applies to both republican and loyalist paramilitaries, and examiners reward answers that name both sides.

Sectarianism means hostility between Protestants and Catholics based on religious identity and political allegiance, so an attack on a Catholic or Protestant as such, not as a soldier or politician, is sectarian.
Internment means detaining suspects without trial, so people could be held on suspicion alone. It was introduced in August 1971 and applied almost entirely to Catholics.
Direct Rule means that Northern Ireland was governed directly from Westminster, through a Secretary of State, instead of by the Stormont parliament. It began on 30 March 1972.
The Apprentice Boys' parade in Derry in August 1969 led to street fighting, and British troops were sent in to restore order. The crisis then forced London to take a hand in policing and reform.
On 12 August 1969 the parade of the Apprentice Boys of Derry passed close to the Bogside (a Catholic area of Derry), and stone-throwing and clashes with the RUC began.
The Battle of the Bogside lasted from 12 to 14 August 1969. Residents put up barricades, which created the 'Free Derry' area.

British troops were deployed in Derry on 14 August 1969 and in Belfast shortly afterwards, on 15 August. This was the start of the army's long involvement in internal security. The UK Prime Minister was Harold Wilson (Labour).
Rioting in Belfast on 14 and 15 August 1969 saw Catholic streets such as Bombay Street in the Lower Falls burned and several people killed, most of them Catholics.

Thousands of families, most of them Catholic, fled their homes in Belfast, and refugee centres were set up in the Republic and in Catholic parishes. August 1969 is also often treated as the start of the Troubles in their most violent form.

The Downing Street Declaration of 19 August 1969, issued by Wilson and Chichester-Clark, restated that Northern Ireland would not cease to be part of the United Kingdom without the consent of its people, and promised reforms.

The Hunt Report, published on 10 October 1969 by a committee led by Lord Hunt, recommended a reformed, unarmed RUC under a police authority, so that the police would no longer look like a partisan armed force. It also said the B Specials should be replaced.

The B Specials (Ulster Special Constabulary) were stood down in April 1970. The Ulster Defence Regiment, a part-time regiment of the British army formed in 1970, took over their local security duties.
Chichester-Clark's two years as Prime Minister saw reform under pressure from London and a rising tide of violence. He could satisfy neither unionist hardliners nor nationalists.
James Chichester-Clark became Prime Minister on 1 May 1969, defeating Brian Faulkner in the party vote by 17 votes to 16, a very narrow margin that left Faulkner as his rival.
He presided over the Battle of the Bogside and the disbanding of the B Specials, and London pressed him to carry out the reforms of the Hunt Report.

His government announced a points system for housing allocation, which made the awarding of council houses fairer, the creation of a Housing Executive (established in 1971) and reform of local government.
Unionist hardliners saw these steps as surrender, while nationalists said they came too late, so the reforms won him little credit from either side.
He resigned on 20 March 1971 after London would not give him the security measures he wanted.
Brian Faulkner succeeded him as Prime Minister on 23 March 1971, so the man he had narrowly beaten in 1969 took over because security policy had failed.

August 1969 convinced many Catholics that the IRA had failed to protect them, and the movement split. At the same time new political parties appeared, offering constitutional alternatives to violence.
The IRA split in December 1969 into the Provisional IRA, whose chief of staff was Seán Mac Stíofáin, and the Official IRA, led by Cathal Goulding.

The split followed the failure to defend Catholic areas in August 1969, which discredited the old leadership, and a dispute over abstentionism (refusing to take seats in parliaments) and the political, socialist direction.
The Provisionals argued that the IRA must defend Catholic areas and that British forces should be driven out, in pursuit of a united Ireland. This position gained support after August 1969.
Provisional Sinn Féin was set up in January 1970 to match the new military wing, so the Provisionals had a political party as well as an army.
The Falls curfew of 3 to 5 July 1970 saw troops search houses for weapons in the Lower Falls, and four civilians were killed. The operation alienated Catholics from the army.
The Alliance Party was founded in April 1970 as a cross-community party, and it later chose Oliver Napier as leader.

The Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) was founded on 21 August 1970 by nationalist politicians including Gerry Fitt (leader), John Hume, Austin Currie and Paddy Devlin. It stood for constitutional nationalism, seeking change by political means.
The SDLP withdrew from Stormont in July 1971 after the army shot dead two men in Derry, Séamus Cusack and Desmond Beattie.
The Official IRA, which stressed a left-wing political strategy, declared a ceasefire in May 1972, which left the Provisionals as the main republican force.

Loyalist paramilitary groups grew in response to the republican campaign and to the fear that the Union was under threat. They attacked Catholic civilians and republicans, which fed the cycle of reprisal.

The Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) was revived in 1966 and killed three people that year. In the early years of the Troubles it carried out attacks on Catholic targets. It was a small, secretive killer group.

The Ulster Defence Association (UDA), a loose umbrella of loyalist vigilante groups, was formed in 1971 and grew rapidly in working-class Protestant areas. It was a legal organisation until 1992, which marks it out from the UVF.
The bombing of McGurk's Bar in Belfast on 4 December 1971 killed 15 Catholic civilians. The police first blamed the IRA, but the Police Ombudsman's report of 2011 found that the UVF was responsible.
Loyalist groups claimed that their violence defended the Union and Protestant areas, but most of their victims were Catholic civilians, which is why their violence is called sectarian.
William Craig founded the Ulster Vanguard movement in 1972, which held large rallies against the loss of Stormont's powers.
Faulkner was the Prime Minister who introduced internment and then saw his government collapse under the pressure of violence and British policy. His career is followed here only up to March 1972.

Brian Faulkner, born in 1921, was a Unionist businessman and politician. He was Minister of Home Affairs in 1959-63 and Minister of Commerce in 1963-69, and he resigned from O'Neill's cabinet in 1969.
He lost the party vote to Chichester-Clark by 17 to 16 in 1969, but became Prime Minister on 23 March 1971, winning the party vote against William Craig.
He asked London to authorise internment, which began on 9 August 1971 under the UK Prime Minister, Edward Heath. Faulkner defended it as necessary to stop the IRA, but it hardened Catholic opinion.

In June 1971 he offered the opposition committee chairmanships at Stormont. The SDLP did not take up the offer and withdrew from Stormont in July 1971 after the Derry shootings, so his attempt to draw nationalists in failed.

He talked with Heath about control of security and insisted that Stormont should keep its powers over policing and order. He and his ministers resigned on 24 March 1972 because he refused London's demand to transfer security powers.
He was shaped by events: the violence, the SDLP withdrawal, Bloody Sunday and London's demand for security powers ended his government.
Contemporary unionists praised his firmness on security, while nationalists saw internment as a deliberate attack on the Catholic community.

He was a participant who wrote of events from the inside in his memoirs, published in 1978 after his death in 1977. Historians generally see him as a pragmatic, able, reforming politician whose attempts at reform were swamped by violence he could not contain.
Internment was introduced on 9 August 1971 to break the IRA, but it was applied almost entirely to republicans, and the violence that followed killed civilians.

Internment, the detention of suspects without trial, began on 9 August 1971 in Operation Demetrius, which arrested about 340 people in its first sweep. The intelligence used was poor, so many of those arrested had no paramilitary links.
Those arrested were almost entirely Catholic, and no loyalist was interned until 1973. This is why nationalists saw internment as proof of bias.
Interrogation methods known as the five techniques, which included hooding and sleep deprivation, were used on fourteen internees, known as the Hooded Men.
The Compton and Parker inquiries examined the methods, and in 1978 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the techniques were inhuman and degrading treatment, but not torture.

At Ballymurphy in west Belfast, eleven civilians died during army operations of 9 to 11 August 1971, including a priest, Father Hugh Mullan. A coroner's inquest in 2021 found that those killed were innocent.
Internment increased recruitment to the Provisional IRA. Separately, 1971 was the first year in which Troubles deaths passed 100.

A civil rights march in Derry against internment ended with British paratroopers killing thirteen civilians, an event that deepened the conflict. Many nationalists lost confidence in the army and the state.
The NICRA march of 30 January 1972 in Derry protested against internment and was banned by the authorities.

Soldiers of the 1st Battalion, Parachute Regiment, entered the Bogside and fired on marchers and bystanders, killing thirteen people on the day, so a banned but peaceful protest became a massacre in nationalist eyes.
A fourteenth man who was wounded died some months later, and most of the dead were shot while unarmed or while fleeing.
The Widgery Report of 19 April 1972, by the Lord Chief Justice, largely accepted the army's account, and nationalists widely rejected it as a whitewash.
The Saville Inquiry, reporting on 15 June 2010, found that soldiers of 1 PARA caused the deaths and injuries and that no casualty had posed a threat of causing death or serious injury.
In his statement to the Commons that day, the Prime Minister, David Cameron, called the killings 'unjustified and unjustifiable' and apologised.

The killings led to the burning of the British embassy in Dublin on 2 February 1972, and they increased recruitment to the Provisional IRA, because nationalist confidence in the army and the state broke down.

Stormont was suspended and government was taken over by Westminster after Faulkner's government refused to hand security powers to London. This was the end of the Unionist government that had ruled since 1921.
London, under Edward Heath, demanded that control of security be transferred to Westminster. Faulkner's government refused.
Faulkner and his ministers resigned on 24 March 1972 in protest, and Westminster suspended the Stormont parliament from 30 March.
The Northern Ireland (Temporary Provisions) Act 1972 introduced Direct Rule from 30 March 1972, placing the province under a Secretary of State.

William Whitelaw was the first Secretary of State for Northern Ireland and governed with civil servants, two ministers of state and the army. The Stormont parliament was formally abolished in 1973 by the Northern Ireland Constitution Act.
Whitelaw granted special category status to paramilitary prisoners in June 1972. He met leaders of the Provisional IRA in London on 7 July 1972 during a short ceasefire, but the talks failed.
Unionists reacted with anger because they felt abandoned, and Craig's Vanguard held large rallies against the loss of Stormont's powers, while nationalists welcomed the end of Stormont.

Direct Rule was meant to be temporary, but apart from the executive of 1 January to 28 May 1974 it continued until the 1990s, because the parties could not agree a power-sharing settlement acceptable to both communities.

Direct Rule lasted because unionists would not accept an assembly with nationalist participation, nationalists would not accept a return to majority rule, and London wished to avoid a return to the old system.
The IRA bombings of 21 July 1972 killed nine people in Belfast, and ten days later the army's Operation Motorman broke the IRA's no-go areas. Violence in 1972 reached its peak.
On 21 July 1972, the Provisional IRA set off about twenty bombs in Belfast in the space of about an hour and a half, a day that became known as Bloody Friday.
Nine people died in the bombings and about 130 were injured, and the attacks shocked public opinion in Britain and Northern Ireland.

Operation Motorman, launched on 31 July 1972 with about 12,000 soldiers, moved into the no-go areas (districts the army and police could not enter) in Belfast and Derry, including the Creggan and the Bogside.
The operation cleared the barricades and restored government control, so areas that the IRA had controlled came back under the state.
The IRA's campaign continued after Motorman, which is why 1972 was the deadliest year of the Troubles, with nearly 500 deaths.
The Troubles had long-term causes, short-term triggers and factors that kept them going. A good answer separates these and judges which mattered most.
Discrimination in housing, jobs and local voting gave the civil rights movement a sustained base of grievance, and unionist fear of change made reform hard.
The state's security forces, the B Specials and the RUC, were seen by Catholics as partisan, which turned protest into a security issue.
British misjudgement also played a part, because London had long left Northern Ireland's affairs alone and it misjudged the situation.
The Provisional IRA gave the Catholic community a military organisation, and its campaign drew the British army into the conflict.
Loyalist paramilitaries defended Protestant areas and attacked Catholic civilians, which increased the cycle of reprisal.
The army and internment alienated Catholics, and internment and Bloody Sunday hardened attitudes on both sides and made political compromise harder.
Stormont's inability to share power with nationalists meant there was no political institution capable of containing the violence.
The decline of Stormont had many causes: civil rights protest, the failure to reform fast enough, the IRA campaign, and the British government's decision to take over security.
Direct Rule can be judged as an achievement or a failure, and contemporaries judged it differently from later historians. Examiners reward paired points on both sides.
Achievement: the end of Stormont removed an institution that nationalists had rejected since 1921, and it opened the way for later settlements.
Failure: the Stormont government could not contain the violence, and its reliance on internment alienated the Catholic community.
Contemporary view: unionists saw the suspension of Stormont as a betrayal by Westminster, while nationalists welcomed it as the end of an unfair system, and were relieved.
Contemporary view: the British government saw Direct Rule as a temporary arrangement, but it proved to be a long-term one.
Later view: historians argue that the 1972 settlement was forced by violence, and that the Unionist government's decline was a product of its own policies as well as republican action.
Sunningdale only makes sense against the collapse of the old system of government in Northern Ireland. By 1973 Britain was looking for a new settlement that both communities could accept.

Stormont was Northern Ireland's devolved parliament (it handled local affairs while Westminster kept overall control), and the Unionist Party had dominated it since 1921. Nationalists felt excluded because of discrimination and gerrymandering (drawing electoral boundaries to favour one side).
Violence escalated from 1969. Internment (imprisonment without trial) began on 9 August 1971, and Bloody Sunday followed on 30 January 1972, so confidence in the old system collapsed.
As a result Stormont was suspended and Direct Rule from London began in March 1972, with William Whitelaw as the first Secretary of State for Northern Ireland.
Direct Rule meant a Secretary of State answerable to Westminster ran Northern Ireland, so the British aim was to replace it with a devolved government acceptable to both communities.

The SDLP (Social Democratic and Labour Party, the main nationalist party, founded in August 1970 by Gerry Fitt, John Hume and others) and the Alliance Party (a cross-community party, also founded in 1970) were the new parties of moderate opinion.
Unionism was split between supporters of reform and power sharing and opponents of both, so any new settlement had to win over a divided majority community.
Power sharing was the central idea of the 1973 settlement. It was an answer to the old Stormont system, in which one community held all the power.
Power sharing means unionists and nationalists both holding executive office (seats in the government), so that neither community can rule alone.

The executive was the government of Northern Ireland, the Assembly was its parliament, and the Council of Ireland was a separate all-Ireland body. Keep the three distinct, because answers often confuse them.
Unionists were split between supporters and opponents of reform and power sharing.
The first step in the 1973 plan was a vote on Northern Ireland's constitutional position. It was meant to reassure unionists, but it settled less than it appeared to.
The border poll was held on 8 March 1973. It asked voters whether Northern Ireland should remain part of the United Kingdom or join a united Ireland.
Nationalists boycotted it, so the result was never going to measure their view.
About 98.9 per cent of the votes cast were to stay in the United Kingdom, but turnout was only about 59 per cent because of the boycott.
The poll therefore confirmed that a majority of those who voted wanted the Union, but it did not settle the question for nationalists, since the boycott left their view unrecorded.
With the poll held, Britain set out its plan for a new devolved government. It combined power sharing inside Northern Ireland with a link to the Republic.

The White Paper (a government policy document) of March 1973, Northern Ireland Constitutional Proposals, proposed an Assembly elected by proportional representation, so that minority parties would win seats in line with their votes.
It also proposed an executive in which unionists and nationalists shared power, meaning that power sharing would be built into the government itself.

The White Paper proposed a Council of Ireland linking Belfast and Dublin as an Irish dimension (a recognised role for the Republic). Many unionists regarded this as a first step towards a united Ireland.
The Northern Ireland Constitution Act of July 1973 abolished the old Stormont parliament, so that the new Assembly could replace it.
Under the Act the Secretary of State kept responsibility for security, so the new executive would not control the police or army.
The Assembly election tested whether power sharing had enough support. It showed how badly unionism had split.

The Assembly election was held on 28 June 1973 and used the single transferable vote (a form of proportional representation in which voters rank candidates and surplus votes transfer), which gave small parties a fair chance of seats.
The Assembly had 78 members. The SDLP won 19 seats and the Alliance Party won 8.
Unionists were divided between Faulkner's supporters in the Ulster Unionist Party, who accepted power sharing, and unionists who opposed it.

The opponents of power sharing included unionists inside the Ulster Unionist Party itself, Ian Paisley's Democratic Unionists and William Craig's Vanguard. Unionist seat totals are disputed, so none are given here.
This split mattered because the new system depended on unionist consent, and the party that was meant to deliver it was fighting itself.
After the election the parties that accepted power sharing negotiated an executive. Its make-up shows how power sharing worked in practice.
Agreement to form an executive was reached in November 1973, so it could take office on 1 January 1974.
Brian Faulkner (Unionist) was Chief Executive, and Gerry Fitt (SDLP) was Deputy Chief Executive.
John Hume (SDLP) was Minister of Commerce, and Oliver Napier (Alliance) was in charge of legal affairs.
Austin Currie (SDLP) held Housing, and Paddy Devlin (SDLP) held Health and Social Services.
The voting membership was 11: six pro-agreement Unionists, four SDLP and one Alliance. This put unionists and nationalists in government together for the first time.
Faulkner led this executive, but his own party was split, so the party's ruling body would soon turn against it.
The executive was agreed inside Northern Ireland, but the Irish dimension needed the two governments. They met with the Northern Ireland parties at Sunningdale to settle it.
The conference was held at Sunningdale Park in Berkshire, England, from 6 to 9 December 1973.
The British Prime Minister Edward Heath and the Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Liam Cosgrave attended, along with the three parties that backed power sharing.
The Northern Ireland parties present were Faulkner's Unionists, the SDLP (Fitt, Hume and others) and the Alliance Party (Napier).
The agreement was announced on 9 December 1973, and the British government said it was committed to implementing it.
Heath was Prime Minister at Sunningdale, while Harold Wilson was Prime Minister during the strike. This is a common confusion in dated answers.
The agreement dealt with three linked questions: how Dublin and Belfast would co-operate, what the status of Northern Ireland was, and how law and order would be policed.
The agreement set up a Council of Ireland with a council of ministers, seven members from each side, to give the Irish dimension a formal body.
The Council also had a consultative assembly (an advisory body without law-making power) of 60 members, 30 from the Dáil (the Irish parliament) and 30 from the Northern Ireland Assembly.
On status, the Irish government accepted that Northern Ireland's status would not change without the consent of a majority of its people. This is the consent guarantee.
The British government declared that it would support a united Ireland if that majority wished it, so consent worked in both directions.
A Law Enforcement Commission was set up to examine how to deal with fugitive offenders (people who fled across the border) and a possible all-Ireland court.
