Both governments also promised policing acceptable to both communities, because nationalists distrusted the police.
Unionists did not accept the safeguards as enough. Two issues in particular fed the fear that the Republic had not really given up its claim to the North.
Unionists saw the Council of Ireland as an Irish dimension that could grow into a united Ireland by stages.
Articles 2 and 3 of the Irish constitution were not changed at Sunningdale.
Kevin Boland, a former Fianna Fáil minister, took a court case in the Republic in early 1974 challenging the declaration on Northern Ireland's status.
The Irish government's defence was that the declaration did not alter the constitutional claim to the North.
Unionists used that defence to say the Republic had not given up its claim, which damaged Faulkner's position because he had presented Sunningdale as safe for the Union.

The executive took office with its own party turning against it. Faulkner lost the leadership of his party within days, and the government's practical work was overshadowed by the row over the Council of Ireland.
The Ulster Unionist Council (the party's ruling body) voted by 427 to 374 on 4 January 1974 to reject the Council of Ireland.
Faulkner resigned as party leader on 7 January 1974, and Harry West replaced him as leader of the Ulster Unionist Party.
Faulkner later formed the Unionist Party of Northern Ireland in 1974.
The executive's work on housing, health and education was overshadowed by the argument over the Council of Ireland, which Faulkner tried to postpone.
The executive lasted only about five months, from 1 January to 28 May 1974.
Unionists opposed to Sunningdale organised themselves, and the Westminster election gave them a powerful argument that the people of Northern Ireland did not back the agreement.
The United Ulster Unionist Council (UUUC) was formed in January 1974 by unionists opposed to Sunningdale: Paisley's supporters, Vanguard (Craig) and anti-Faulkner Unionists (West).
Paisley's role in the UUUC was as a leader of the opposition to Sunningdale, which is why his supporters were central to it.
In the Westminster general election of 28 February 1974 the UUUC won 11 of the 12 Northern Ireland seats. Gerry Fitt held Belfast West for the SDLP.
No party won a majority in Britain, and Harold Wilson formed a Labour government in March 1974, with Merlyn Rees as Secretary of State. Rees followed William Whitelaw, who held the post in 1972-73.
Unionist opponents of the agreement argued that it was imposed on the majority, and they used this claim to justify the strike.
The strike was the event that finally broke the executive. It showed that a determined protest by loyalist workers could stop Northern Ireland running.
The Assembly voted by 44 to 28 on 14 May 1974 to support the Sunningdale policy, and the strike began the next day, 15 May 1974.

The Ulster Workers' Council (UWC) led the strike. Its chairman was Harry Murray, and it was supported by loyalist paramilitaries, the UDA and UVF. Glenn Barr and Andy Tyrie were also associated with the strike as other leaders.
The strike drew on workers in power generation and essential industries, and it was enforced by roadblocks and intimidation.
Power output was cut, fuel became short and services were paralysed, which meant the executive could not govern.
The Dublin and Monaghan bombings of 17 May 1974, two days after the strike began, killed 33 people in the Republic.
London did not defend the executive. Its failure to confront the strikers, and a broadcast that angered unionists, left Faulkner with nothing to bargain with.
Merlyn Rees refused to negotiate with the UWC, and the army did not take on the strikers directly, so the executive could not restore services.

Wilson made a televised broadcast on 25 May 1974 accusing the strikers and their backers of 'sponging' on Westminster and British democracy. It became known as the 'spongers' broadcast and angered unionists.
Faulkner proposed delaying the later stages of the Council of Ireland.
The SDLP and Alliance rejected the delay proposal, so Faulkner resigned as Chief Executive on 28 May 1974, which ended the executive.
The executive had lasted from 1 January to 28 May 1974, about five months.
The collapse had several causes. In an essay, rank them rather than listing them, with the Council of Ireland, the strike and British weakness at the top.
Unionists rejected the Council of Ireland as a step towards a united Ireland, which many believed was the aim of the nationalists in the executive.
The power-sharing arrangements were not supported by a majority of unionists, and the Unionist Party's own members split over the agreement.
The UWC strike showed that a determined protest by loyalist workers could paralyse Northern Ireland's economy and government.
The British government's reluctance to use force against the strikers signalled to unionists that London would not defend the executive.
The Boland case allowed unionists to say the Republic had not given up its claim to the North, so it damaged Faulkner's standing among unionists.
Republican violence continued during the executive's term, and this made moderate unionists more fearful about security and nationalist intentions.
The Labour government of 1974 was weaker in its commitment than Heath's government at Sunningdale, which left the executive with less backing.
The executive had no mechanism to build consent among the unionist community, which was essential to any settlement that depended on majority support.
Faulkner accepted power sharing at Sunningdale and paid the political price. His record shows both courage and a misreading of unionist opinion.
Faulkner was a Unionist politician, and a former Prime Minister of Northern Ireland whose earlier career belongs to the previous notes.
He was Chief Executive of the power-sharing executive from January 1974 and was the main unionist negotiator at Sunningdale, taking part directly in the talks with the British and Irish governments.

He defended the agreement to his party but was defeated, since the Ulster Unionist Council rejected the Council of Ireland by 427 to 374 on 4 January 1974. He resigned as party leader on 7 January 1974.
He resigned as Chief Executive on 28 May 1974 after SDLP and Alliance rejected his proposal to delay the Council of Ireland, and he never returned to office.
Contemporaries were divided: loyalist opponents denounced him as a traitor, while nationalists and the British government saw a leader who had taken a risk for peace.
Historians credit him with courage and realism, but argue that he misjudged the depth of unionist opposition and lacked sustained British support.
He later formed the Unionist Party of Northern Ireland, which failed to attract wide support, and his Memoirs of a Statesman were published in 1978.
He died on 3 March 1977 after a fall from his horse while hunting, and he had been made Baron Faulkner of Downpatrick in 1977.
Hume was a key architect of the power-sharing executive, and he argued that cross-community government was the only realistic path to peace.
Hume was born in Derry in 1937 and was a co-founder of the SDLP in 1970.
He was a leading SDLP negotiator at Sunningdale and served as Minister of Commerce in the executive from January 1974.
He argued for power sharing and an Irish dimension, and believed that a Council of Ireland would give nationalists a stake in the settlement.
He defended the executive in the strike of May 1974, and its collapse confirmed his belief in an agreed, cross-community settlement.
Contemporaries saw him as a capable nationalist negotiator, although republicans, who rejected any settlement within Northern Ireland, attacked him.
Seamus Mallon, his SDLP colleague, later called the Belfast (Good Friday) Agreement of 1998 'Sunningdale for slow learners', and historians often link the two settlements.
Sunningdale failed, but its ideas did not disappear. Later attempts to find a settlement kept returning to power sharing, consent and an Irish dimension.
The Constitutional Convention, elected on 1 May 1975, tried to restore devolved government but ended in March 1976 without agreement.
After the failure Westminster relied on Direct Rule, with Northern Ireland run from London.
The Anglo-Irish Agreement, signed on 15 November 1985, gave the Irish government a formal role, but it did not restore power sharing.
The Downing Street Declaration of 15 December 1993 was a further attempt to find a settlement.
Seamus Mallon's remark that the Belfast (Good Friday) Agreement of 1998 was 'Sunningdale for slow learners' reflects the link historians draw between 1973 and 1998.
Sunningdale became the reference point for later debate on whether any settlement could be imposed without majority unionist consent.
Historians judge Sunningdale as both a first and a failure. Weigh the achievements against the limits, and the contemporary views against later ones.
Achievement: Sunningdale produced the first power-sharing executive in Northern Ireland, with unionists and nationalists in government together.
Achievement: the agreement set out principles, consent and an Irish dimension, that later settlements built on.
Failure: the executive lasted only about five months, from 1 January to 28 May 1974, and it could not survive a general strike.
Failure: the agreement lacked the consent of the majority of unionists, and the Council of Ireland was rejected as a threat to the Union.
Contemporary view: the British and Irish governments and the SDLP regarded Sunningdale as a sound basis for peace.
Contemporary view: the UUUC and the Ulster Workers' Council regarded it as a betrayal of the Union and a surrender to republicans.
Later view: historians judge Sunningdale a failure, because it showed both that a settlement was possible and that it was difficult when it needed unionist consent.
Later view: the collapse showed that no executive could survive without the support of a majority of unionists, a lesson applied in later talks.

After the power-sharing executive fell in 1974, Northern Ireland went back to being governed directly from London. This is the background to everything in this subsection, because no local government existed to solve the conflict.

Direct Rule (government of Northern Ireland straight from Westminster) was first imposed in March 1972, when the Stormont parliament was suspended. The power-sharing executive took office on 1 January 1974 and fell on 28 May 1974, so Direct Rule returned.

Under Direct Rule a Secretary of State and the Northern Ireland Office governed, which meant that decisions were made by British ministers rather than by elected local politicians, so local politicians had no real power.

The Secretaries of State were Merlyn Rees (1974 to 1976), Roy Mason (1976 to 1979), Humphrey Atkins (1979 to 1981), Jim Prior (1981 to 1984), Douglas Hurd (1984 to 1985), Tom King (1985 to 1989), Peter Brooke (1989 to 1992) and Patrick Mayhew (1992 to 1997).

Power sharing (unionists and nationalists sharing government) was the aim of most British and Irish policy after 1974, but it was not restored by 1993, so Direct Rule remained the basis of British policy throughout.
The Troubles began in 1969, and the Provisional IRA, loyalist paramilitaries and the British army were already in conflict when Direct Rule returned in 1974.

Terrorism, as used in this topic, means violence against civilians and the state for political ends. It is used here of the IRA and loyalist paramilitaries, and the British response was a mixture of security measures and politics.

The consent principle, that Northern Ireland's status would not change without the consent of a majority of its people, was already stated in 1973. It is the thread that runs through every step to 1993.
While London governed, it tried one more devolved solution and then changed its security policy. In 1976 these changes shifted who fought the conflict and how prisoners were treated.
The Constitutional Convention was elected on 1 May 1975 to find a devolved settlement (one where Northern Ireland has its own local government). The unionist coalition (UUUC) held a majority in it.

The unionist majority recommended a return to majority rule, which meant government by the largest community. Westminster rejected this because it lacked cross-community support, and the Convention was dissolved in March 1976.

Ulsterisation was the policy, under Roy Mason from 1976, of giving the RUC (the police) and the Ulster Defence Regiment, or UDR (a locally recruited army regiment), the lead in security in place of the British army. The aim was to reduce the army's role.
Criminalisation was the policy of treating paramilitary offenders as ordinary criminals, not as political prisoners, so that violence would lose any political status.
Special category status, which had given paramilitary prisoners some of the privileges of political prisoners, was ended on 1 March 1976 for prisoners convicted of offences from that date.
Diplock courts, in which a judge sits without a jury for scheduled (terrorist-related) offences, had been introduced in 1973. They were part of the same approach.
In August 1976 a shocking accident turned ordinary people on to the streets in protest at the violence. The Peace People became the best-known peace movement of the Troubles, though it did not last.
On 10 August 1976 three children were killed in Belfast when a car, driven by an IRA volunteer who had been shot dead by soldiers, crashed into them. This tragedy was the cause of the movement.

Betty Williams, a witness to the crash, and Mairead Corrigan, the children's aunt, founded the Peace People in August 1976 and led the first peace march. The journalist Ciaran McKeown was a third founder.

The movement was one of ordinary people who held large peace rallies in Belfast and across Northern Ireland. It appealed to both communities and called for an end to paramilitary violence on both sides.
Williams and Corrigan were awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for 1976. The award was announced in 1977, so the prize should not be dated 1977.
Contemporaries praised the movement, but some republicans and loyalists dismissed it as naive. Its support faded after 1977 as the violence continued.

When special category status ended, republican prisoners fought back with protests inside the Maze prison. The protests escalated step by step to the hunger strikes of 1980 and 1981, in which the government and the prisoners each refused to give way.

The H-Blocks were the H-shaped cell blocks of the Maze prison, also called Long Kesh. Republican prisoners there wanted political status, meaning treatment as prisoners of war or political prisoners rather than as ordinary criminals.
The blanket protest began in 1976, when prisoners refused to wear prison uniform and wore only blankets. In 1978 it escalated into the dirty protest.
The first hunger strike (a refusal to eat) began in October 1980 and ended on 18 December 1980.

The second hunger strike began on 1 March 1981 under Bobby Sands, to demand the restoration of political status. He was elected MP for Fermanagh and South Tyrone in April 1981 while on hunger strike, which gave the protest wide publicity.
Sands died on 5 May 1981 after 66 days. Nine further hunger strikers died between May and August 1981, including Francis Hughes, Patsy O'Hara and Kieran Doherty, making ten deaths in all.
Margaret Thatcher declared that 'crime is crime is crime; it is not political', so her government refused to concede political status.
The hunger strike ended on 3 October 1981 without formal political status. Concessions were made afterwards, including on clothing and remission (shortened sentences).
The hunger strikes changed republican tactics. The publicity and sympathy they created showed that republicans could win votes, so Sinn Féin began to contest elections alongside the IRA campaign.

The strikes brought wide sympathy and recruits to republicans, and they hardened attitudes on both sides. They were also a propaganda success (propaganda means messages used to shape opinion), because each death drew attention to the republican case.
In June 1981 two prisoners, including Kieran Doherty, were elected to the Dáil (the Irish parliament), which showed that there was a republican vote to be won.
Owen Carron, Sands's election agent, won the Fermanagh and South Tyrone by-election in August 1981 as an Anti H-Block candidate, so Sands's seat stayed in republican hands.

Sinn Féin adopted an electoral strategy in 1981, summed up in the phrase 'the Armalite and the ballot box', used by Danny Morrison at the party's Ard Fheis (annual conference) in October 1981. It meant seeking votes while the armed campaign went on.
In the October 1982 Northern Ireland Assembly election Sinn Féin won five seats. Gerry Adams was among those elected, but the members abstained, which means they refused to take part.

In June 1983 Gerry Adams won the West Belfast seat at Westminster, which Gerry Fitt had held since 1966. Sinn Féin members refused to take their seats there, so they abstained from Westminster as well.
The strategy was a deliberate move to build political support. Critics regarded it as a cover for continued IRA violence.
Adams was the Sinn Féin leader who turned the party into an electoral force, and he became the main republican voice in dealings with the British and Irish governments.
Gerry Adams was born in 1948 in Belfast and grew up in a republican family in West Belfast.
He was interned (imprisoned without trial) in the early 1970s. In July 1972 he was released to take part in the secret talks between the Provisional IRA and William Whitelaw in London.
He was elected president of Sinn Féin in November 1983, a post he held until 2018, and he led the party's move into electoral politics.
He took part in talks with the SDLP's John Hume in 1988 and again from 1991 to 1993, so he helped to shape the search for a settlement.

In October 1988 the Home Secretary, Douglas Hurd, banned the broadcast of the voices of Sinn Féin spokespeople, including Adams, as a propaganda move. Broadcasters used actors' voices, and the ban ended in 1994.
He was shaped by events too. He was shot and wounded by loyalist gunmen in Belfast in March 1984, lost his Westminster seat to Joe Hendron of the SDLP in 1992, and regained it in 1997.

Contemporaries disagreed about him. Supporters regarded him as the political face of the republican movement, while critics, including unionists and many nationalists, regarded him as the political wing of the IRA.

Supporters credit him with leading republicans from armed struggle towards negotiation. Critics, including unionists, argued that he used Sinn Féin's electoral strategy to complement the IRA campaign, so that republicans kept both.
Adams has always denied membership of the IRA, though others have alleged it.

In 1983 the Dublin government tried to agree a common nationalist view of the future. Its report offered Britain three options, and Margaret Thatcher's blunt rejection of them in 1984 showed how far Britain was willing to go.
The New Ireland Forum was set up in 1983 by the Dublin government, under the Taoiseach Garret FitzGerald. It included Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael, Labour and the SDLP, while Sinn Féin was excluded.
The unionist parties declined to take part, which meant that its report reflected the views of nationalist parties and the Dublin government only, so unionists could reject it.

The Forum's report, published on 2 May 1984, set out three options, such as a unitary Irish state, a federal or confederal state, and joint authority by Britain and Ireland. It said that the unitary state was the preferred option.
At a press conference on 19 November 1984, Margaret Thatcher rejected all three options, saying 'Out, out, out'.
Her rejection marked the limits of British willingness to change Northern Ireland's constitutional position in the mid-1980s, though within a year she signed an agreement giving Dublin a role.
In October 1984 the IRA bombed the Conservative Party conference in Brighton. The attack showed the danger of the IRA campaign.
On 12 October 1984 the IRA bombed the Grand Hotel in Brighton, where the Conservative Party conference was being held.
Five people were killed in the bombing, and Margaret Thatcher escaped. The IRA said it would try again.
Patrick Magee was later convicted of planting the bomb.
Thatcher was the British Prime Minister who led the government through the hunger strikes and signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement, a shift in British policy.
Margaret Thatcher was Prime Minister from May 1979 to November 1990, and she made security and the defeat of terrorism central to her policy in Northern Ireland.

Her years in office were shaped by violence. On 27 August 1979 the IRA killed Lord Mountbatten at Mullaghmore, Co. Sligo, and on the same day the Warrenpoint ambush killed eighteen soldiers. Later came the hunger strikes and the Brighton bombing.
She refused to grant political status to the hunger strikers, saying 'crime is crime is crime', and her government held firm during the 1981 protest.

She rejected the three options of the New Ireland Forum in November 1984, saying 'Out, out, out', yet in November 1985 she signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement with the Taoiseach Garret FitzGerald at Hillsborough Castle.
She was personally involved in the negotiations with FitzGerald in 1984 and 1985, and she signed the Agreement despite strong opposition from unionists.

Contemporary unionists regarded her as having betrayed the Union, while nationalists and Dublin welcomed the Agreement as a sign of British recognition of an Irish interest. Republicans regarded her as intransigent over the hunger strikes.

Historians differ on her motives. Some stress the hope of improved security cooperation with Dublin, others the aim of undercutting Sinn Féin's growth after 1981, and others her relations with Dublin and Washington. The Agreement did not end the violence.

The Agreement gave the Irish government a formal consultative role in Northern Ireland. It was the biggest British policy shift since Sunningdale (the 1973 power-sharing agreement), and it survived fierce opposition.
It was signed on 15 November 1985 at Hillsborough Castle by Margaret Thatcher and Garret FitzGerald.

Thatcher's motives included improving cross-border security and winning back nationalist support from Sinn Féin, which was growing after 1981. The Irish government wanted to protect the SDLP, and the Forum had also shown that Dublin wanted a role.

It set up an Intergovernmental Conference of ministers, with a permanent joint secretariat at Maryfield near Belfast. Through it the Irish government could put forward views on Northern Ireland, though its role was consultative only.

Article 1 affirmed that there would be no change in the status of Northern Ireland without the consent of a majority of its people. This was the consent principle, and it reassured unionists in theory.

Unionists responded with the slogan 'Ulster says No', a large rally at Belfast City Hall on 23 November 1985 and a day of action in March 1986. Fifteen unionist MPs resigned their Westminster seats in January 1986, forcing by-elections, but the Agreement remained in force.

Republicans rejected the Agreement because it left British jurisdiction in place, and Fianna Fáil under Charles Haughey opposed it in the Dáil. The SDLP welcomed it as a limited but real step towards Irish involvement.
It was the biggest British policy shift since Sunningdale, and it survived despite the unionist campaign.
Molyneaux led the Ulster Unionist Party through the period of the Anglo-Irish Agreement and was the main voice of mainstream unionist opposition.
James Molyneaux was born in 1920 and was MP for South Antrim from 1970 and for Lagan Valley from 1983. He became leader of the Ulster Unionist Party in 1979 and led it until 1995.
He led mainstream unionist opposition to the Anglo-Irish Agreement, and he worked with Ian Paisley, the confrontational leader of the DUP, on the 'Ulster says No' campaign.

He took part in the unionist campaign of 1985 and 1986, which included the 'Ulster says No' rally at Belfast City Hall on 23 November 1985 and the resignation of fifteen unionist MPs from Westminster in January 1986.
He favoured the integration of Northern Ireland into the United Kingdom's system of government rather than devolution (a separate local parliament).
He cultivated good relations with Conservative ministers in the 1990s, and John Major's government at times relied on Ulster Unionist votes at Westminster, which gave him influence.
Contemporaries valued his caution and his commitment to the Union, although some unionists felt he was too passive in opposing the Agreement.
Historians regard him as a steady, quiet leader of mainstream unionism who opposed the Agreement without the confrontational style of Paisley. His strategy of opposition did not stop the Agreement.
Hume led the SDLP from 1979 and became the leading constitutional nationalist voice. His dialogue with Sinn Féin reshaped the search for peace.
John Hume became leader of the SDLP in 1979 and was elected to the European Parliament the same year.
He supported the Anglo-Irish Agreement, arguing that it gave nationalists a role in Northern Ireland's government.

He described the conflict as a problem of three relationships: within Northern Ireland, between North and South and between Ireland and Britain. This is why he believed that no solution could come from one relationship alone.
He began the dialogue with Gerry Adams in 1988 and argued that the IRA campaign must end if nationalists were to achieve their goals by dialogue.
He took part in the Brooke–Mayhew talks of 1991 and 1992, such as the attempt to set up a new devolved settlement.
Contemporaries regarded him as a moderate and effective nationalist leader, while unionists criticised him for talking to Sinn Féin.

Historians credit him with shaping the nationalist case for a peace process based on consent and dialogue, because his work with Adams and with the Irish government influenced the Downing Street Declaration.
By 1988 the governments and republicans were fighting a battle over opinion as well as a military one. At the same time, the leaders of constitutional nationalism and republicanism began to talk.
In October 1988 the Home Secretary, Douglas Hurd, banned the broadcast of the voices of Sinn Féin spokespeople and others. Broadcasters used actors' voices, and the ban ended in 1994.
The ban was a propaganda measure by the government, intended to deny republicans a public platform, so it shaped opinion against them.
The Hume–Adams dialogue began in 1988, when the SDLP leader and the Sinn Féin president held talks that were publicly acknowledged.
The talks were controversial, with unionists and some nationalists objecting to contact between the SDLP and Sinn Féin while the IRA campaign continued.
The dialogue resumed in 1991 and produced joint statements in 1993. Historians regard it as an important precursor to the peace process, though it did not end the IRA campaign in this period.
The Enniskillen bombing of 1987 became one of the best-known atrocities of the Troubles. It increased pressure for peace and damaged the IRA's standing.
On 8 November 1987, Remembrance Sunday, an IRA bomb exploded at the war memorial in Enniskillen, County Fermanagh, killing eleven people.
The victims were mostly elderly civilians who had gathered for the ceremony. A twelfth person, Ronnie Hill, died in 2000 after a long coma.
The IRA said it had intended to attack soldiers, but it admitted that the bombing was an error, and the attack was widely condemned.
Gordon Wilson, whose daughter Marie was killed, said in a BBC interview 'I bear no ill will', and he called for an end to violence.
The bombing was condemned in Britain, in Ireland and in the United States, and it damaged the IRA's standing.
After the Agreement, the British government tried to bring the constitutional parties together again. Peter Brooke started the process, and Patrick Mayhew continued it, but no settlement followed.

Peter Brooke, as Secretary of State, said in November 1990 that Britain had no selfish strategic or economic interest in Northern Ireland. This signalled that Britain would not stand in the way of an agreed outcome.

The Brooke initiative of 1991 and the Mayhew talks of 1992 brought the parties together in multi-party talks, such as the British government and the constitutional parties, so they were a different format from Hume–Adams.
The talks did not produce agreement, so no devolved government was restored.
After the failed talks and continued violence, the British and Irish prime ministers issued a joint statement of principles. It set out the principles on which later peace efforts were built.
The Downing Street Declaration was issued on 15 December 1993 by Prime Minister John Major and Taoiseach Albert Reynolds.

It said that the Irish people as a whole had the right to self-determination, which could be exercised by agreement between North and South. It also said that a united Ireland would require the consent of a majority in Northern Ireland.

It said that the British government had no selfish strategic or economic interest in Northern Ireland and would legislate for a united Ireland if a majority wished it. It invited republicans to renounce violence and join talks.
The Irish government committed itself to set up a Forum for Peace and Reconciliation, and to examine Articles 2 and 3 of its constitution (the articles that claimed the whole island).

Nationalists and the Dublin government welcomed it, while unionists denounced it as a sign that Britain was moving towards a united Ireland. Sinn Féin and the IRA considered it, and the IRA ceasefire came in 1994, which falls outside this subsection.
To judge these steps, weigh what each achieved against what it failed to do. The Agreement and the Declaration are the two main steps, and examiners reward answers that compare them.
Achievement: the Anglo-Irish Agreement gave the Irish government a formal consultative role in Northern Ireland's affairs, a larger role than Sunningdale had given it.
Achievement: the Downing Street Declaration set out principles of consent and self-determination that became the basis for later agreements.
Limit: between 1974 and 1993 no devolved government was restored, and Direct Rule remained the basis of British policy.
Limit: the Hume–Adams dialogue and the Brooke and Mayhew talks did not end the IRA campaign. Violence continued throughout the period, as Brighton and Enniskillen show.
Contemporary view: nationalists and the Irish government regarded the Anglo-Irish Agreement and the Declaration as steps towards justice and peace.
Contemporary view: unionists regarded the Agreement as an infringement of their constitutional rights and denounced the Declaration as a sign that Britain was moving towards a united Ireland.
Later view: historians regard the period as one in which the framework for peace was built gradually, through dialogue, agreements and the acceptance of consent as a principle.

Three ideas run through the whole story of violence in the Troubles, and they rest on the divide between Northern Ireland's two communities. Knowing the terms makes it easier to judge each attack and each response.

Northern Ireland had two main communities: unionists or loyalists, mostly Protestant, who wanted to stay in the United Kingdom, and nationalists or republicans, mostly Catholic, who wanted a united Ireland. Loyalists are unionists who accept violence, and republicans seek a united Ireland.

Terrorism means violence against civilians and the state for political aims. Both republican and loyalist groups used it, which is why bombings and shootings are judged as political acts and not only as crimes.

Sectarianism means hostility and violence between Protestants and Catholics, based on religious identity and political allegiance. It explains why so many victims were ordinary civilians killed only because of their community.

Propaganda means murals, publications, broadcasts and statements used to win opinion, and also the broadcast bans that tried to deny paramilitaries a voice. Each side needed public support, so the fight for opinion ran alongside the fighting.
The Troubles began in 1968 to 1969, and the British army was deployed in August 1969. Direct Rule, meaning government of Northern Ireland straight from London, came in March 1972.

The Provisional IRA was the biggest republican paramilitary group and the one that killed the most people in the Troubles. It came out of a split in the older IRA and set itself the aim of ending British rule by force.

The IRA split in December 1969 into the Provisional IRA, led by Seán Mac Stíofáin, and the Official IRA, led by Cathal Goulding. The Provisionals rejected the Officials' policy and took up armed defence of Catholic areas, and then a campaign against British rule.

The Provisionals' aims were to end British rule in Northern Ireland and to bring about a united Ireland through a campaign of armed attacks, because they believed only force would make Britain withdraw.

Their targets were British soldiers, members of the RUC (the Royal Ulster Constabulary, Northern Ireland's police) and the UDR (the Ulster Defence Regiment, a locally recruited army regiment), and also civilians.
Their methods were bombings, shootings and car bombs.
The Provisional IRA was responsible for the largest number of killings in the Troubles, followed by the loyalists of the UDA and UVF, so it dominates any account of who caused the deaths.

The Provisional IRA's campaign in Northern Ireland hit soldiers, police, civilians and, in some attacks, Protestant communities. Several of the worst attacks also caused public revulsion, which damaged republican claims to be defending their community.
Bloody Friday, 21 July 1972, saw more than twenty bombs go off in Belfast in about an hour and a half, killing nine people.
On 27 August 1979 Lord Mountbatten was killed with three others, one of them a fourteen-year-old grandson, by a bomb on his boat at Mullaghmore, County Sligo.
On the same day eighteen British soldiers were killed in two bombs at Warrenpoint, County Down. Mullaghmore and Warrenpoint were separate attacks, so keep them apart in an answer.

The Enniskillen bombing, 8 November 1987, killed eleven people at a Remembrance Day ceremony. Gordon Wilson, whose daughter Marie died, publicly forgave the bombers, and this made the attack even more shocking.

Attacks on Protestants included the La Mon House Hotel firebomb near Belfast in February 1978, which killed twelve people, and Teebane, County Tyrone, in January 1992, where eight Protestant workmen were killed.

At Kingsmill, South Armagh, in January 1976, ten Protestant workmen were shot dead. The killings were attributed to republicans, were claimed under a cover name, and followed the killing of Catholics by loyalists.

The Shankill Road fish shop bomb of 23 October 1993 killed ten people, including one of the two bombers. The target was thought to be a loyalist meeting upstairs, but the dead were people in the shop.

From 1974 the IRA took its campaign to England, bombing pubs, London parks, a department store and a party conference. These attacks aimed to put pressure on the British public and government, and two of them led to wrongful convictions.
The Guildford pub bombings of 5 October 1974 killed five people. The Guildford Four, convicted of them, were freed in 1989 when their convictions were overturned.

The Birmingham pub bombings of 21 November 1974 killed 21 people. The IRA never formally claimed them, and the Birmingham Six, convicted of them, were freed in 1991 when their convictions were quashed.
The IRA bombed Hyde Park and Regent's Park in London on 20 July 1982, killing eleven soldiers and bandsmen, who were chosen as military targets in public places.
A bomb at Harrods in December 1983 killed six people, and it showed that civilian shoppers in central London could be caught up in the campaign.
The Brighton bombing of 12 October 1984 killed five people. It was aimed at the Conservative government at its party conference, and Margaret Thatcher survived.
The Warrington bombing of 20 March 1993 killed two boys, Johnathan Ball, aged 3, and Tim Parry, aged 12, and injured many more. Warrington was an IRA bomb, not a loyalist one.
The Provisional IRA was not the only republican group, and it needed weapons and money to keep going. Arms from abroad and funds from the United States kept the campaign supplied.
The Irish National Liberation Army (INLA) was a republican splinter group of the mid-1970s, separate from both the Provisional and Official IRA.
The INLA killed 17 people in the Droppin' Well bar bombing at Ballykelly, County Londonderry, in December 1982. 11 of the dead were soldiers.
A cargo of arms from Libya on the ship Eksund was seized by French customs in November 1987, which showed how the IRA was supplied for its campaign from abroad.
NORAID, an Irish-American fundraising committee formed in 1970, gave republicans funds and publicity in the United States.

Loyalist paramilitaries rose to defend the Union and to oppose a united Ireland and power sharing, meaning the sharing of government between unionists and nationalists. In practice most of their victims were Catholic civilians.
The Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) was revived in 1966 and carried out attacks in the early years of the Troubles, including bombings and shootings.
The Ulster Defence Association (UDA) was formed in 1971 as an umbrella for local loyalist groups. The Ulster Freedom Fighters (UFF), formed in 1973, was the UDA's cover name for killings.
Their aims were to defend the Union with Britain, and to oppose a united Ireland and power sharing.
Loyalist paramilitaries claimed to be defending the Union, but most of their victims were Catholic civilians with no paramilitary links. This is why their violence is described as sectarian.
UVF and UDA gunmen attacked Catholic bars and homes in Belfast during the 1970s, and Catholic workers on the roads, because any Catholic could be chosen as a target.

Loyalist attacks hit Catholic civilians in bars, in a Dublin street and on a country road. They became more frequent again in the early 1990s, when loyalists answered republican attacks with attacks on Catholic crowds.

The bombing of McGurk's Bar in Belfast on 4 December 1971 killed 15 Catholic civilians, so the attack was sectarian. Police first blamed the IRA, but the Police Ombudsman reported in 2011 that the UVF was responsible.
On 17 May 1974 car bombs in Dublin and Monaghan killed 33 people and an unborn child. This was the largest loss of life in a single day of the Troubles, and the attack was attributed to the UVF.
The Miami Showband killings of 31 July 1975 saw UVF men kill three members of a popular band at a fake army checkpoint in County Down.
On 5 February 1992 the UFF killed five Catholics at Sean Graham's bookmakers on the Ormeau Road, Belfast. Loyalist killing rose sharply in the early 1990s.

The Greysteel massacre of 30 October 1993 saw the UFF kill eight people at the Rising Sun bar, at a Halloween dance. It came a week after the Shankill bomb, and was the UFF's response to it, not an IRA reprisal.

Some loyalist groups carried out sectarian murders of Catholics that were marked by torture and brutality, and the Shankill Butchers were the most notorious. Their crimes shocked people in both communities.
The Shankill Butchers were a UVF gang from the Shankill Road in west Belfast, who abducted Catholics at night and killed them between 1975 and 1977.
Many victims were killed with knives and hatchets, which led to widespread revulsion in both communities because the killings were so cruel.
The gang was led by Lenny Murphy, and eleven members were convicted in 1979 of a series of murders, receiving many life sentences.
The gang's activities showed how sectarian violence could develop outside the formal paramilitary chains of command, and Murphy himself was shot dead in 1982.
Counting the dead shows how widely responsibility for killing was spread. It also shows that most of the violence came from paramilitaries and not the state.
About 3,500 people were killed between 1969 and 2001, about 3,000 of them by 1993. About half of the dead were civilians.
Republican paramilitaries were responsible for about 60 per cent of the deaths, loyalist paramilitaries for about 30 per cent and the security forces for about 10 per cent.
The worst year was 1972, with nearly 500 deaths, and the number of deaths fell sharply in the 1980s.
Loyalist killing rose sharply in the early 1990s, with many attacks on Catholics, so loyalist groups became a larger share of the violence late in the period.
The army and RUC fought the IRA with searches, arrests and surveillance, and with some armed ambushes. Several incidents led to allegations that the security forces had used lethal force unlawfully.

The British army and RUC carried out searches, arrests and surveillance operations that disrupted IRA units, but the IRA continued to recruit and attack, so security pressure alone did not end the campaign.
Republicans argued that the army's arrests and searches in Catholic areas increased recruitment to the IRA, because they alienated people who might otherwise have stayed out of the conflict.
At Loughgall, County Armagh, on 8 May 1987, the SAS (the army's special forces) killed eight IRA men attacking an RUC station. A civilian who happened to drive by was also killed.
The Gibraltar shootings of 6 March 1988 saw the SAS kill three unarmed IRA members, Mairéad Farrell, Daniel McCann and Seán Savage, and they raised questions about the use of lethal force.

Loughgall and Gibraltar fed an allegation of a 'shoot to kill' policy, meaning that suspects were killed instead of arrested. It was an allegation, and the incidents are not proof of an official policy.
The Stalker inquiry, from 1984, and the Sampson inquiry followed RUC shootings of unarmed men in 1982, and they added to the 'shoot to kill' controversy.

Both republicans and loyalists used murals, publications and political statements to shape public opinion. The British and Irish governments responded by trying to deny the paramilitaries publicity on air.

Republican murals celebrated IRA volunteers, so they became a central feature of the political landscape, and loyalist murals in Protestant areas celebrated the UVF and UDA and presented their violence as a defence of loyal communities.
Republicans used publications such as An Phoblacht to present their case, and their propaganda stressed the British occupation.
Irish-American support for republicans provided funds and publicity for the republican campaign, so the cause was heard beyond Ireland.

In October 1988 the British government banned the broadcast of the voices of spokesmen for eleven organisations, including Sinn Féin, the IRA and loyalist groups. Broadcasters used actors' voices, and the ban was lifted in 1994.
The British ban was intended to deny publicity to terrorist groups, but critics said it restricted freedom of expression, and the use of actors showed how easy it was to get round.

In the Republic, Section 31 of the Broadcasting Authority Act 1960 was used through ministerial orders that barred broadcast interviews with the IRA and later Sinn Féin. It was allowed to lapse in 1994, the same year as the British ban.

The Republic's government (the Taoiseach is its prime minister) answered the violence of August 1969 with words, aid and a border presence. The Arms Crisis of 1970 then split the governing party, Fianna Fáil, and Bloody Sunday brought an angry public reaction.

On 13 August 1969 the Taoiseach Jack Lynch broadcast that the government 'can no longer stand by' while Catholics were attacked in Belfast and Derry, and he asked for a United Nations peacekeeping force.
The Irish army set up field hospitals near the border. Refugees from Belfast and Derry were housed in army camps such as Gormanston, County Meath.

In May 1970 Lynch dismissed Charles Haughey and Neil Blaney on 6 May, after allegations that money for relief was being used to import arms for Northern nationalists. This was the Arms Crisis, and it divided Fianna Fáil.
At the Arms Trial in autumn 1970, Haughey, Captain James Kelly, John Kelly and Albert Luykx were tried for conspiracy to import arms. They were acquitted in October 1970.
After Bloody Sunday, 30 January 1972, when 13 were killed in Derry, the Irish government declared a day of mourning and recalled its ambassador from London for consultations.
The British embassy in Merrion Square, Dublin, was burned on 2 February 1972 during a demonstration, as anger over Bloody Sunday boiled over.

As the Northern conflict spread south, the Republic tightened its laws against the IRA. The coalition of Liam Cosgrave also backed the Sunningdale settlement, to show Dublin's support for cross-border cooperation.
The IRA was declared an unlawful organisation in 1936, and the Offences against the State Act 1939 created the Special Criminal Court, which has no jury and three judges.
The Special Criminal Court was revived in 1972 to try paramilitary offences.

The Offences against the State (Amendment) Act 1972 was passed in December 1972, after loyalist car bombs in Dublin. It allowed a chief superintendent's statement that he believed a person to be an IRA member to be accepted as evidence.

Cosgrave's Fine Gael and Labour coalition, in power from 1973 to 1977, signed the Sunningdale Agreement in December 1973, which included a Council of Ireland. Garda (Irish police) cooperation with the RUC increased.
The Criminal Law (Jurisdiction) Act 1976 allowed certain offences committed in Northern Ireland to be tried in the Republic, so suspects who fled south could still face a court.
The IRA killed the British ambassador, Christopher Ewart-Biggs, in July 1976, and the Emergency Powers Act 1976 followed, giving the state stronger powers in response.
President Cearbhall Ó Dálaigh referred the Emergency Powers bill to the Supreme Court. He resigned in October 1976 after a government minister criticised him.
In the 1980s the Republic's governments worked with Britain on a political settlement while extradition, the handing over of wanted people to another state, stayed a source of tension.
Charles Haughey, Taoiseach in 1979 to 1981, 1982 and 1987 to 1992, held a summit with Margaret Thatcher in Dublin in December 1980 to study 'the totality of relationships' between the two islands.

Garret FitzGerald, Taoiseach in 1981 to 1982 and 1982 to 1987, pursued the New Ireland Forum of 1983 to 1984. He signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement with Thatcher at Hillsborough on 15 November 1985, which set up an Intergovernmental Conference.
Unionists complained that the Republic gained too much influence through the Intergovernmental Conference. The Agreement also put cross-border security cooperation on a formal footing.
Fianna Fáil under Haughey voted against the Agreement in 1985, but kept it in place when it returned to power in 1987.

Extradition was a recurring dispute between Dublin and London. The Extradition (European Convention on the Suppression of Terrorism) Act 1987 was passed in December 1987, after the Enniskillen bombing.
Judging terrorism means weighing what it did against what it set out to achieve. The best answers state a view, pairing impact with failure and contemporary opinion with later judgement.
Impact: terrorism killed large numbers of civilians and security force members, and it made political compromise harder by hardening attitudes on all sides.
Impact: republican and loyalist campaigns shaped British and Irish policy, because security measures and political initiatives were both shaped by the need to contain violence.

Failure: neither the IRA nor the loyalist groups achieved their stated aims, a united Ireland or the defence of the Union, and the main IRA and loyalist ceasefires came in 1994, after the period covered here.
Failure: terrorism deepened sectarian divisions, and its victims in both communities created lasting grievances.
Contemporary view: the British and Irish governments condemned terrorism and sought to isolate paramilitaries from political influence.
Contemporary view: republicans argued that the IRA was defending the Catholic community and fighting an occupying power, while loyalists claimed to defend the Union.
Later view: historians point out that most of the killing was done by paramilitary groups, not the state, and that the long campaign persuaded many in each group that violence could not win.

Later view: the Republic's responses leaned on security measures, such as the Special Criminal Court and extradition, while its political aims were pursued through Sunningdale and the Anglo-Irish Agreement.

The Troubles (the conflict in Northern Ireland that began in 1969 and continued into the 1990s and beyond) caused thousands of deaths and injuries. Here the focus is the human cost and where it fell, not the causes or events.
Between 1969 and 1993 the Troubles caused about 3,000 deaths. The total for the whole conflict to about 2001 is about 3,500 or more, and figures vary by source, so always say "about".
1972 was the deadliest year of the Troubles, with nearly 500 deaths.
About half of the dead were civilians. Members of the security forces (the army and police), republican paramilitaries and loyalist paramilitaries also died in large numbers.
Tens of thousands of people were injured, and the harm was psychological as well as physical, because survivors and the bereaved lived with trauma.

The violence was concentrated in Belfast, especially north and west Belfast, in Derry and in the border counties. Working-class districts such as Ardoyne, the Falls and the Shankill in Belfast, and the Bogside in Derry, suffered most.
Most deaths took place in Northern Ireland, though bombings in Britain and the Republic also caused deaths, including the Dublin and Monaghan bombings of 1974 in the Republic.
Violence made Northern Ireland look like a risky place to do business or take a holiday. Investment and tourism fell, and the cost of insurance and security rose for businesses across the province.

Foreign investors were reluctant to open or expand factories in Northern Ireland because of the risk of bombing, disruption and bad publicity, so jobs that might have replaced declining industries never arrived.
Tourism fell sharply because visitors avoided the province. This hurt hotels, shops and the wider local economy that depended on visitors' spending.
Bomb attacks damaged city-centre trade. From 1972 a security zone with barriers and gates surrounded central Belfast, popularly called the ring of steel, and the checks discouraged shoppers.

Businesses faced high insurance premiums to cover bomb damage and had to spend on security. Some companies closed or moved their operations to Britain or the Republic, which put further pressure on local jobs.
Security measures, such as checkpoints and searches, increased the time and cost of moving goods and people.
The government paid compensation for criminal damage under official schemes, which added to public spending.

Before 1969 the economy depended heavily on shipbuilding, linen and engineering, and in the 1960s new industries, including man-made fibres, were promoted to modernise it. Manufacturing then kept shrinking while public-sector and security jobs grew, so the province became more dependent on the British state.
Manufacturing employment continued to decline, so many workers lost their jobs, with shipbuilding, linen, engineering and man-made fibres all shedding jobs through the 1970s and 1980s.
This decline began before 1969 and had international causes, including wider recession, so the Troubles worsened it rather than caused it alone.
Harland and Wolff, the Belfast shipyard, was taken into public ownership in 1975 because the government wished to protect jobs.
Public-sector employment (jobs paid for by government, such as health, education and local administration) grew as a share of the workforce.

The security sector also provided many jobs: the Ulster Defence Regiment (formed 1970 and merged into the Royal Irish Regiment in 1992), the RUC (the police), the prison service, the army and private security.
British subvention, the public money transferred from the Treasury (the British finance ministry) to cover the gap, kept public services and living standards above what local output could pay for.

Because the public sector was so large, Northern Ireland's economy was exposed to any change in British government spending. Subvention is not the same as British security spending, though the two are related.
The De Lorean factory at Dunmurry, south-west Belfast, was a government-backed attempt to bring in investment and jobs. It collapsed in 1982 and cost the taxpayer heavily.
The DeLorean Motor Company built a factory at Dunmurry to make a stainless-steel sports car. Production began in 1981, funded by British government grants and loans of tens of millions of pounds.

The factory was intended to create about 2,000 jobs in an area of high unemployment. The site lay between Catholic and Protestant housing estates, in the hope of drawing both communities into work, though the workforce was never as mixed as hoped.
The car sold poorly, so the company went into receivership (was taken over by an administrator because it could not pay its debts) in February 1982.
John De Lorean, the man behind the company, was arrested in the USA in October 1982 on a drug-trafficking charge and was acquitted in August 1984. His case is separate from the company's failure.
The collapse left the British government with heavy losses. It showed both the government's willingness to subsidise investment and the difficulty of attracting investors to Northern Ireland.

Unemployment stayed well above the UK average, and it fell unequally: Catholics were out of work far more often than Protestants. Governments responded with fair employment law, and campaigners abroad with the MacBride Principles.
Unemployment in Northern Ireland was above the UK average through the 1970s and 1980s.

Catholic unemployment was consistently higher than Protestant unemployment, roughly twice as high. Causes include discrimination, location in the west of the province, and the sectors where Catholics worked.

The Fair Employment (Northern Ireland) Act 1976 set up a Fair Employment Agency to investigate discrimination in employment. It could not compel employers to monitor their workforces, so its power was limited.
The Fair Employment (Northern Ireland) Act 1989 replaced the Agency with a Fair Employment Commission, required employers to monitor their workforce by religion, and brought stronger enforcement.
The MacBride Principles of 1984, named after Sean MacBride, were a code of fair employment for US firms operating in Northern Ireland, promoted by Irish-American campaigners.
West Belfast and Derry suffered the highest deprivation (poor housing, income and opportunity), with families who had lost jobs and had few alternative sources of income.
Historians link unemployed young men, especially young Catholic men in the 1980s, to recruitment to paramilitaries. This is a link they raise, not a proven single cause.

Catholic complaints about housing allocation had been central to the civil rights movement before 1969. The Housing Executive was set up to answer them, but violence pushed communities apart faster than policy could bring them together.
The Northern Ireland Housing Executive was established in 1971 to take over public housing from the local councils and the Northern Ireland Housing Trust.
It allocated houses by a points system based on need, so that religion no longer decided who got a house, to end the discrimination that the civil rights movement had criticised.

Intimidation (threats and violence meant to force people out) drove families from mixed areas into areas where their own community was the majority. Tens of thousands of people moved home in Belfast between 1969 and 1973.

Peace walls (also called peace lines) are barriers between Protestant and Catholic streets. They were first built in Belfast in 1969, grew in number in the 1970s and 1980s, and were later built in Derry and elsewhere.
Peace walls were built to protect people, but they also reinforced the segregation that intimidation had created.
Segregation made communities more distinct, so it made it harder for people from different backgrounds to meet.
Segregation cut across the Executive's allocation policy in practice, because families moved from mixed areas into segregated estates.
Schools remained largely divided by religion throughout the Troubles. A small, parent-led integrated movement began in the 1970s, and the state gave it legal support in 1989.
Most children went to either Catholic maintained schools or mainly Protestant controlled schools, so the school system mirrored the religious divisions of the province.
The Catholic Church controlled its schools and defended its right to do so, so Catholic voluntary schools kept state support, and the system stayed divided.
Teacher training was also separate: Catholic teachers trained mainly at St Mary's College and Protestants at Stranmillis College, both in Belfast.
The integrated education movement began when parents in both communities formed All Children Together in 1974 to campaign for mixed schools.
Lagan College, opened in Belfast in September 1981 with 28 pupils, was the first integrated secondary school in Northern Ireland.
The Education Reform (Northern Ireland) Order of 1989 gave statutory (legal) support to integrated schools. It placed a duty on the Department of Education to encourage and facilitate them.
Integrated schools were few by 1993 and at first depended on parents and charitable funding, so most children remained in separate schools.
The health service had to treat the wounded of a violent conflict, and the strain of living through it left lasting psychological harm.
The Royal Victoria Hospital on the Falls Road in Belfast developed world-leading expertise in treating gunshot wounds and blast injuries, and its surgeons' experience was used elsewhere.
Because the casualties were so many, hospitals and ambulance crews had to treat large numbers of injured civilians and members of the security forces, which placed heavy demands on staff.
Ambulance crews and hospital staff faced danger when responding to bomb incidents.
Mental health problems, such as stress and trauma, were widespread among people who had lived through bombings, shootings, bereavement and displacement.
Security measures and fear of attack affected access to health care, through delays and restrictions on movement.

In 1973 health and personal social services were reorganised into four Health and Social Services Boards (Eastern, Northern, Southern and Western). This was an administrative reform, not a result of the Troubles.
Beyond the headline events, the Troubles changed ordinary routines. Security measures and community division shaped how people shopped, travelled and grew up, especially in Belfast and Derry.
Because of the threat of bombs, security checkpoints, searches and vehicle checks were a feature of daily life in Belfast and Derry, and they changed the routines of shopping and travel.
Town centres were sealed or controlled after bombings, with security gates, so shoppers had to pass through checks to enter them.
Car bombs prompted security checks and car-park controls in city-centre shopping areas.
In divided towns and estates, some people avoided areas where the other community lived, which limited social contact.
Children grew up, for example, with soldiers and barriers around them and with memories of violence in their local areas.
Examiners reward a judgement on how serious the impact was. Weigh the costs against the reforms, and compare how people at the time and historians since have seen it.
Cost: investment, tourism and manufacturing were damaged, and the economy came to rely on public money and the security sector.
Cost: segregation in housing and schooling deepened the social divisions between the communities.
Achievement: the Housing Executive, the Fair Employment Acts and integrated schools were real reforms towards equal treatment in housing, jobs and education.
Limit: the Catholic-Protestant gap in unemployment and deprivation persisted, which means reforms were incomplete, and integrated schools were few.
Contemporary view: unionists pointed to public investment and the British subvention as proof that the state supported the province.
Contemporary view: nationalists argued that discrimination and deprivation were rooted in state policy and that the Troubles had made them worse.
Later view: historians stress that the Troubles were both a cause and a consequence of inequality, and that the costs fell on both communities, most heavily on working-class areas.
The impact was uneven: some areas, and middle-class suburbs, were largely untouched.

In Northern Ireland, which was created in 1921, religion was never only about belief. It marked which community a person belonged to, and so which political future they wanted. This is why the Troubles, the conflict that began in 1968-69, cannot be understood without it.

Unionists, who wanted Northern Ireland to remain in the United Kingdom, were mostly Protestant, and nationalists, who wanted a united Ireland, were mostly Catholic. Religion and political allegiance therefore overlapped, though the boundary was never absolute.

Catholics made up about a third of the population, about 35 per cent in the 1961 census, and Protestants were the majority. The Presbyterian Church in Ireland was the largest Protestant church, with the Church of Ireland and the Methodist Church also significant.

Unionist identity combined Protestantism, loyalty to the British Crown and attachment to the Union with Great Britain. Historical memory reinforced it: Protestants looked back to the Reformation, which split Christianity into Catholic and Protestant churches, and to the Boyne of 1690 and the Derry events of 1688-89.

Nationalist identity combined Catholicism, Irish cultural heritage and support for a united Ireland. Many nationalists were not practising Catholics, so the overlap was one of identity and community, not of personal belief.

Cultural identity means a sense of belonging through shared religion, language, history and customs, and in Northern Ireland it was tied to political allegiance. Cultural traditions are the distinct heritage, customs and practices of the unionist and nationalist communities.

Separate schooling, separate social life and marriage patterns kept the communities apart, so many people had little regular contact across the divide. Denominational identity was passed on through baptism and schooling, which reinforced the divisions across generations.

Sectarianism, meaning hostility between the Catholic and Protestant communities, grew in this setting. Bigotry is obstinate intolerance of people with different beliefs or identities, and tolerance is the opposite: accepting that others hold different beliefs and identities.
The Orange Order was the largest Protestant fraternal organisation. Its parades became both a focus of unionist identity and a cause of conflict.

The Order was founded in 1795 after the Battle of the Diamond, near Loughgall in County Armagh, a clash between Protestant and Catholic groups. Its origins were therefore in rivalry between the two communities.

Its central public ritual is the parade on 12 July, the Twelfth, which marks the Battle of the Boyne of 1690. The Twelfth is a public holiday in Northern Ireland, so the tradition is part of the calendar of the whole province.
Bands and banners are part of the parades, and bonfires are lit on the eleventh night, 11 July. These displays gave Protestant tradition a strong public presence in local communities.
Membership was open to Protestants only, and the Order was organised in local lodges (branches) in communities across the province. This is why it reinforced the separation of the communities.

The Order was closely linked to the Ulster Unionist Party, because Orange delegates sat on the Ulster Unionist Council, the party's governing body. Many unionist politicians were also members, so religion and politics were joined at the top.
Parades through or near Catholic areas were a source of tension. Marches were often restricted or rerouted to avoid confrontation.
The Black Preceptory and the Apprentice Boys of Derry are related Protestant institutions with their own parades.
Catholic and nationalist identity rested on the Church, Gaelic sport and the Irish language. Together they gave nationalists institutions of their own, parallel to the Protestant ones.
The Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA) was founded in 1884 and promoted Gaelic games as an expression of Irish identity. It is not the same body as the Gaelic League.

The GAA's Rule 21 banned members of the RUC (the Northern Ireland police) and the British army from membership, and it was removed in 2001. It was a grievance for unionists and a symbol of separateness for nationalists.
The Ancient Order of Hibernians was a Catholic fraternal body that paralleled the Orange Order in its social and political role.
The Irish language had a small but active community in Northern Ireland. In 1971 an Irish-medium primary school (one teaching through Irish) opened at Shaw's Road in Belfast.

Catholic churches and schools were central to community life in nationalist areas, and the Catholic Church was a major provider of education. Church, parish halls and GAA clubs were the main centres of social life, so the community lived largely within its own institutions.

Nationalists felt that the Stormont state, the government of Northern Ireland, did not respect Irish identity. One example is the Flags and Emblems (Display) Act of 1954, which restricted the display of the Irish tricolour.

Ecumenism is dialogue and cooperation between Christian churches. It gained momentum in the 1960s from a change within the Catholic Church and from local initiatives in Northern Ireland, and it became more urgent once the Troubles began.

The Second Vatican Council, held from 1962 to 1965, was a gathering of Catholic bishops that encouraged dialogue between the Catholic Church and other Christian churches. This opened the way for contact that had been rare before.

The Corrymeela Community was founded in 1965 at Ballycastle, County Antrim, as a centre for reconciliation. Its founder was Ray Davey, a Presbyterian minister who had been chaplain at Queen's University Belfast.

The Irish School of Ecumenics was founded in 1970 in Dublin by the Jesuit priest Michael Hurley to promote reconciliation and interchurch dialogue. Do not confuse it with Corrymeela, which was Presbyterian-led, in Ballycastle, and five years earlier.
In 1973 the leaders of the Catholic Church and the main Protestant churches held their first formal meeting, at Ballymascanlon, County Louth. It was an official meeting of church leaders.

In December 1974 a group of Protestant clergy met IRA leaders at Feakle, County Clare, and the IRA declared a ceasefire over Christmas into early 1975. Unlike Ballymascanlon this was unofficial, a clergy initiative to end violence.
Pope John Paul II appealed for an end to violence at Drogheda on 29 September 1979, begging the men of violence 'On my knees I beg you' to turn away from violence. He did not visit Northern Ireland.
Ecumenism was supported by moderate church leaders, but it met hostility from hardline Protestant and Catholic traditions.
Ecumenism built contacts between churches, but it ran into opposition inside both communities and into the violence of the Troubles. Its limits explain why it did not change the political division.
Hardline Protestant opposition was led by Ian Paisley and the Free Presbyterian Church. They portrayed ecumenism as a betrayal of the Protestant faith and the Reformation.
In June 1966 Paisley led a march against the Presbyterian General Assembly in Belfast, and he was jailed for three months. This shows how hostile the hardline reaction to church contacts could be.

Catholic and Protestant clergy and lay people who joined joint initiatives were sometimes criticised or denounced by their own congregations or hierarchies (church authorities), so taking part could carry a cost.
Mixed marriage and joint worship faced disapproval in both communities. This limited the practical impact of ecumenism, because the closest personal contacts were the ones discouraged.
The Catholic Church's mixed-marriage rules, the Ne Temere decree of 1908, required the children to be raised as Catholics. They caused resentment among Protestants until they were relaxed in 1970.
Violence and sectarian killing undermined trust between the churches, and clergy were themselves targets of attacks, which made cooperation harder to sustain.
Ecumenism succeeded in building contacts and dialogue, but it did not change the political division between unionists and nationalists. This is why it is usually judged a limited success.

Paisley was a preacher, a protest leader and a politician, and his religion drove his politics. His opposition to ecumenism and to the Catholic Church shaped the hardline unionist position of the 1970s and 1980s.
Ian Paisley was born in Armagh in 1926. He founded the Free Presbyterian Church in 1951 and was its moderator (leader), and he combined his ministry with a political career.
He won the Bannside seat at Stormont in April 1970 and the North Antrim seat at Westminster in June 1970. He founded the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) in 1971 and led it until 2008.

He opposed ecumenism and any dialogue with the Catholic Church, and he attacked the Papacy and the Catholic Church in public speeches. In June 1966 he led a march against the Presbyterian General Assembly.

He was elected to the European Parliament in 1979, topping the poll in Northern Ireland. In October 1988 he interrupted Pope John Paul II there, in Strasbourg, calling him the Antichrist, and was removed from the chamber.

As a participant he was the leader and preacher at the centre of events, and he opposed Sunningdale and the Anglo-Irish Agreement. His religious beliefs drove these political stands, and events in turn gave him a platform.
Contemporaries saw him as a powerful and divisive figure, admired by his supporters and condemned by his opponents for his rhetoric (his forceful, inflammatory style of speaking).

The sociologist Steve Bruce, in God Save Ulster! (1986), argued that evangelical Protestant belief was central to Paisley's politics. Historians note that his religious politics made ecumenism more difficult.
Seamus Heaney was the leading poet of the Troubles. Writing from inside the Catholic community, he explored violence, identity and the inheritance of the past.

Heaney was born on 13 April 1939 at Mossbawn, near Castledawson in County Derry, the eldest of nine children of a Catholic farming family. He was educated at St Columb's College, Derry, and Queen's University Belfast.
His early collections were Death of a Naturalist (1966), Door into the Dark (1969) and Wintering Out (1972). Do not confuse these with North, which came in 1975.

North (1975) drew on P. V. Glob's The Bog People and on Iron Age bog bodies, preserved bodies found in peat, such as the victim in 'Punishment'. The bog body became a symbol of ritual killing, a way to reflect on violence in Northern Ireland.

He moved to Glanmore, County Wicklow, in the Republic in 1972, which is a different place from Mossbawn. He later taught at Harvard, was Oxford Professor of Poetry from 1989 to 1994, and won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1995.
Field Work (1979) and Station Island (1984) continued his engagement with violence, memory and the Catholic tradition. He was a director of Field Day, though not a founder.
Ciaran Carson criticised North in a 1975 review for mythologising violence and making it seem inevitable. Others praised the poems as a major contribution to literature.
In 'An Open Letter' (1983), a Field Day pamphlet, he objected to being included in a British poetry anthology, writing 'My passport's green'. This shows his sense of Irish identity.
Historians see his work as a key cultural response to the Troubles, giving expression to grief, guilt and the search for an identity beyond sectarianism.
Writers, playwrights, musicians and artists responded to the Troubles in many forms. The Field Day Theatre Company was a leading cultural initiative.

Field Day was founded in 1980 in Derry by the playwright Brian Friel and the actor Stephen Rea. Its directors included Seamus Heaney, Seamus Deane, Tom Paulin and David Hammond, and from 1983 it also published pamphlets.

Friel's play Translations was Field Day's first production, at the Guildhall in Derry in September 1980. Set in Donegal in the 1830s, it deals with the Ordnance Survey's English renaming of Irish placenames and the loss of the Irish language.
Other poets from Northern Ireland, including Derek Mahon, Michael Longley and John Montague, explored identity, landscape and violence in their work.

Novels, plays and songs also dealt with life in the Troubles: Bernard MacLaverty's Cal (1983), Brian Moore's Lies of Silence (1990), Frank McGuinness's Observe the Sons of Ulster Marching Towards the Somme (1985) and Stiff Little Fingers' 'Alternative Ulster' (1978).
Film and television were further outlets through which writers and filmmakers responded to the conflict.

Murals in Catholic and Protestant areas of Belfast and Derry became popular forms of political expression. An example is the gable end at Free Derry Corner in the Bogside, painted in 1969, which reads 'You are now entering Free Derry'.
Cultural production in both communities reflected a desire to express identity, but it also reinforced the sense of separate traditions, which is the other side of the achievement.
Edna Longley, a critic, argued that Field Day's emphasis on a shared Irish culture neglected the unionist tradition.

The Cultural Traditions Group was set up in 1988 to promote mutual understanding of the different cultural traditions in Northern Ireland. It was a small cultural-relations body, not a political settlement.
The Group was set up in 1988 by the government's Central Community Relations Unit. It later came within the Community Relations Council, which was formed in 1990.
Its aims were to recognise both the unionist and the nationalist traditions and to encourage the sharing of culture across the community divide, so that each side would understand the other better.
Its work centred on cultural events, education and shared activity across the community.
The Education Reform (Northern Ireland) Order of 1989 made Education for Mutual Understanding and Cultural Heritage cross-curricular themes in schools, meaning they ran through several subjects.

Critics on both sides questioned whether equal recognition of traditions could replace political agreement on the constitutional question, that is, whether Northern Ireland should stay in the United Kingdom or join a united Ireland.

Judgement questions reward weighing what ecumenism and culture achieved against what they could not do. Both opened dialogue and gave expression to the conflict, but neither changed the political divide.
Strength: ecumenism built dialogue between churches and clergy, through Corrymeela, Ballymascanlon and Feakle, which gave some moderates a voice during the Troubles.
Limit: hardline religious opposition, led by Paisley, together with violence, restricted ecumenism and made dialogue politically costly.
Strength: Heaney's poetry and the Field Day movement gave a language to the violence and to the search for identity.
Limit: cultural initiatives did not change the political divisions between the communities. Some critics also argued that they reached mainly educated and middle-class audiences.
Contemporary view: unionists saw religious and cultural traditions as central to their British identity and resisted anything that appeared to dilute them.
Contemporary view: nationalists saw their culture and religion as the basis of a distinct Irish identity, which they wanted recognised within a united Ireland.
Later view: historians argue that cultural responses to the Troubles were genuine and productive, but that they were not sufficient on their own to resolve the political conflict.
The Apprentice Boys exist to remember one event, the siege of Derry in 1688-89, and that event only makes sense against the planting of the city and the struggle between two kings.

Derry, formally called Londonderry, is a walled city on the River Foyle. It was planted (settled with colonists) by London companies in the early 1600s as a Protestant settlement, which is why it carries the 'London' name.
Nationalists tend to say Derry and unionists often say Londonderry, so the name itself shows the divide. This case study uses Derry.
The city walls were built between 1613 and 1619 and were never breached, so they gave Derry its distinctive fortified character and later became the focus of the parades.

In 1688 the Catholic King James II was deposed in the Glorious Revolution, and the Protestant William of Orange took the throne in 1689. James then tried to win back his thrones by fighting from Ireland, which produced the Williamite-Jacobite war (Jacobite means supporter of James).

The siege of Derry was part of that war. The Battle of the Boyne on 1 July 1690 followed it, and the Apprentice Boys must not be confused with the Orange Order, a separate loyal order that marks the Boyne on 12 July.
The siege began with an act of defiance by young Protestants and was shaped by a quarrel over whether Derry should resist James II at all. Both episodes became central to later Protestant memory.

In December 1688 thirteen apprentice boys shut Derry's gates against a regiment loyal to James II. This 'Shutting of the Gates' is the event the apprentices' name comes from, and the thirteen became the organisation's symbol.
Robert Lundy, the governor, was a Protestant who believed resistance was hopeless and favoured negotiating with James. The defenders distrusted him, and he left Derry in April 1689.

Lundy's name has become a byword for treachery in unionist tradition, and an effigy (a model figure) of him is burned each December as a long-standing tradition. George Walker is the opposite figure: a defence leader remembered as a siege hero.
The siege proper began in April 1689 and lasted 105 days. George Walker and Henry Baker led the defence, and Baker died of fever during the siege.
Conditions inside the walls were terrible because the city was cut off. There was severe famine and disease, and the garrison ate horses, dogs and other animals to survive.
The siege ended when a supply ship broke the blockade of the river, and several objects from the siege became lasting symbols that the Apprentice Boys still use.
On 28 July 1689 the ships Mountjoy and Phoenix broke the boom (a barrier floated across the river to block ships) across the River Foyle, bringing food to the starving garrison.
The Jacobite army then withdrew. Sources vary on the exact day, so the safe way to date the lifting of the siege is late July to early August 1689.
