Garret FitzGerald built on the Forum to reach the main achievement of Anglo-Irish diplomacy in this period, the agreement signed at Hillsborough. It gave Dublin a formal consultative role in Northern Ireland affairs without granting it authority.
The New Ireland Forum opened in Dublin Castle on 30 May 1983 and reported on 2 May 1984. It brought together Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael, Labour and the SDLP.
Its report offered three options: a unitary state (the preferred option), a federal or confederal state, and joint authority (shared British and Irish rule).
Thatcher publicly rejected all three at a press conference on 19 November 1984 ('out, out, out'). Even so, the Forum had strengthened the SDLP and shown that nationalists had a common position.
Negotiations between officials followed, and FitzGerald and Thatcher signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement at Hillsborough Castle, Co. Down, on 15 November 1985.

Both governments affirmed the consent principle: the status of Northern Ireland would change only with the consent of a majority there. The Intergovernmental Conference was co-chaired by the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland and the Irish Minister for Foreign Affairs, with a secretariat at Maryfield, near Belfast.
The Irish government could put forward views on Northern Ireland affairs through the Conference, but it could not exercise authority, so this was a consultative role and not joint authority.
Unionists protested strongly. A huge rally at Belfast City Hall in November 1985 was followed by the resignation of fifteen unionist MPs in January 1986 to force by-elections.

Fianna Fáil under Haughey opposed the agreement. Desmond O'Malley had been expelled from Fianna Fáil in February 1985 over a vote on family planning law. He and Mary Harney founded the Progressive Democrats in December 1985, in opposition to Haughey's leadership.
The agreement drew on motives from both governments, and nationalists and unionists drew opposite conclusions from it. These contrasting reactions are what examiners ask you to name.
Thatcher accepted the agreement partly for security reasons, because she wanted closer cooperation with Dublin against the IRA.
She also hoped that a role for Dublin would strengthen the SDLP, the nationalist party that rejected violence, against Sinn Féin.
Contemporary nationalists saw the agreement as recognition of their rights and of Dublin's concern for them.
Contemporary unionists saw it as a betrayal and a threat to the union, because it was made without their consent, which is why they protested and later boycotted the Conference.

By 1989 relations were far closer than in 1949, although the basic dispute over Northern Ireland remained unresolved. The agreement had survived and changed how the two governments dealt with each other.
The Intergovernmental Conference met regularly and cooperation on security and cross-border matters had grown, although unionists continued to boycott it.

Friction continued over extradition (handing suspects to the other state), over alleged miscarriages of justice affecting Irish people in British courts, and over the British army's conduct in Northern Ireland.
The IRA's campaign continued, and the North remained divided and violent.
Haughey had opposed the agreement in 1985, but he left it in place when Fianna Fáil formed a coalition with the Progressive Democrats in July 1989, after the general election of June 1989.
Joint EEC membership, the growth of North-South contacts and the habit of regular meetings meant that relations were closer than in 1949, even though the fundamental dispute remained.

Examiners reward a judgement on how far Anglo-Irish relations improved. The evidence falls into paired points: what was achieved against what was not, and how contemporaries judged events against how historians judge them now.
Achievement: from the hostility of the Ireland Act in 1949, Ireland moved to regular contact with London and a formal consultative role in 1985.
Limit: Sunningdale collapsed within months, the 1985 agreement did not end the violence, and the two governments kept different aims.
Contemporary view: nationalists saw the Anglo-Irish Agreement as recognition of their rights.
Contemporary view: unionists saw it as betrayal, a threat to the union made without their consent.
Later view: historians see the agreement as a foundation for the Downing Street Declaration of December 1993 and the Good Friday Agreement of 10 April 1998, although its immediate effect was limited.

To see why Ireland's entry to international bodies was slow and then fast, you need three pieces of background: its record in the League of Nations, its neutrality, and the Cold War split of the world into two camps.

Ireland was a member of the League of Nations (the interwar association of states) from 1923 to 1946, and was neutral in the Second World War (1939-45), which Irish people called 'the Emergency'. This is why it was not a stranger to international bodies in 1946.
That wartime neutrality shaped how other states saw Ireland in 1946, which is why it became an obstacle when Ireland first asked to join the United Nations.

The Cold War was the rivalry between the United States-led West and the Soviet bloc. NATO, the Western military alliance, was founded in April 1949. This is why the Soviet Union and the West treated each new UN member as a point scored.

The UN Security Council has five permanent members (the United States, Soviet Union, Britain, France and China), and each holds a veto, meaning one of them can block a decision on its own. This power decided Ireland's first application.
Ireland declined to join NATO in 1949, giving partition (the division of the island) as its reason, and kept to a policy of military neutrality: belonging to no military bloc.
In the 1950s Britain was Ireland's main market for exports, so any British decision about Europe would force an Irish one. This mattered once the EEC appeared.

Ireland wanted to join the UN as soon as it was founded, but the Cold War kept it out for nearly a decade. It was outside the UN until 1955, even though it had been in the League of Nations and other European bodies.

Ireland applied for UN membership in 1946, but the Soviet Union used its veto in the Security Council, citing Ireland's neutrality in the Second World War and the lack of diplomatic relations between the two states.

The deadlock over new members lasted until 1955, when a package deal in the General Assembly (the UN's body of all member states) allowed sixteen states to be admitted together, so neither side had to approve a state it disliked on its own.

Ireland was admitted on 14 December 1955, alongside states as varied as Italy, Spain, Austria, Hungary and Jordan. It was a package, so Ireland came in with states from both sides of the Cold War, such as Italy and Hungary.
Ireland was neutral in the Cold War sense of belonging to no military bloc, but it was a Western, Christian democracy and generally sympathetic to the West on issues of communism.
Membership gave a small state a voice on world affairs, recognition, and a means of showing independence of Britain.
Do not confuse the vetoes: the Soviet Union vetoed Ireland in 1946 in the Security Council, whereas de Gaulle later vetoed Britain's EEC entry, a different veto in a different body.
Frank Aiken, Minister for External Affairs from 1951 to 1954 and from 1957 to 1969, used the UN to pursue a policy not tied to the Western powers. His line was independent, but it was not pro-Soviet.

Aiken was a veteran of the War of Independence and Civil War who had been in de Valera's governments since 1932, and he led the Irish delegation to the General Assembly nearly every year. This is why he had the standing to set policy independently of the Western powers.

From 1957 Ireland would not support the American-led move to block debate on the seat of the People's Republic of China, a position that irritated Washington because it broke with the usual Western line.
In 1959 Ireland and Malaya sponsored a resolution at the UN criticising the suppression of human rights in Tibet, which shows the independent line was not simply pro-communist.
Aiken took an anti-colonial line on some issues, reflecting a small, formerly colonised state's sympathy with peoples seeking independence.
His main contribution was the effort to stop the spread of nuclear weapons (non-proliferation): Irish resolutions were introduced from 1958.
Resolution 1665 of 4 December 1961 called on all states to agree not to transfer or acquire nuclear weapons. It led to negotiations on the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.
The treaty opened for signature on 1 July 1968, and Ireland was the first state to sign it.
Critics said the Irish line was naive or inconsistent with Ireland's position in the West; supporters said it showed that a small state could influence world opinion.
Peacekeeping means soldiers sent by the UN to separate fighting sides and hold a peace, rather than to fight a war. Irish soldiers served in it from 1958, and the Congo was the first major test.

Irish officers served as UN observers in Lebanon from 1958. This was a different, earlier mission from the later force of 1978. It was a small observer mission, so it is not the same as the larger force that came later.

The Belgian Congo became independent on 30 June 1960 and descended into disorder, with Katanga province declaring secession in July 1960. The UN sent a force, ONUC, and Irish troops joined it in July 1960.
On 8 November 1960 an Irish patrol was ambushed at Niemba in Katanga and nine soldiers were killed, the first big loss of Irish life in UN service.

In September 1961, 155 men of A Company, 35th Battalion, under Commandant Pat Quinlan, were besieged at Jadotville by Katangese forces and foreign mercenaries. After about five days, with ammunition and water short, they surrendered, and were released after some weeks.

About 6,000 Irish soldiers served in the Congo until 1964, and twenty-six lost their lives. The loss of twenty-six lives was heavy for a small army, which is why it counts in judgements on the cost of peacekeeping.

Irish troops joined the UN force in Cyprus (UNFICYP) from 1964, to keep apart the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities. The two communities were in conflict, so a neutral force was needed between them.
From 1978 an Irish battalion served with the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), set up after Israel's invasion of southern Lebanon.
Peacekeeping linked Ireland's identity as a neutral state to practical service, and it gave the Defence Forces an important role and good reputation abroad.
Peacekeeping needed a legal basis at home, and it fitted Ireland's neutrality: a neutral state could serve the UN without joining a military alliance.
Ireland refused to join NATO in 1949, with partition as the stated reason, and kept to a policy of military neutrality in the Cold War.
The Defence (Amendment) Act 1960 allowed the government to send Irish contingents abroad on service under the United Nations, which provided the legal basis for the Congo mission.

Peacekeeping allowed a neutral state to take part in world affairs without joining an alliance, and it became a source of national pride. For example, Irish soldiers could serve in the Congo without any alliance commitment.
Opponents of EEC entry raised in 1972 the question of whether membership would affect neutrality, and the government replied that membership did not require Ireland to join a military alliance.
Frederick Boland was a diplomat rather than a minister, and in 1960 his career brought a small, new member state a high honour at the UN.
Frederick Boland, formerly Secretary of the Department of External Affairs (the senior civil servant) and ambassador in London, was Ireland's permanent representative at the UN from 1956.

He was elected President of the fifteenth session of the General Assembly, which began in September 1960, an honour for a state that had joined only five years earlier. This is why the election is read as a sign of the respect Ireland had won.

The session was dominated by the crisis in the Congo and by Cold War tension, and in October 1960 Boland broke his gavel while trying to restore order during a heated exchange involving the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev.

Boland's election showed the respect Ireland had gained, and the session brought more African states into the UN as colonies became independent. Many colonies were becoming independent, so the Assembly was changing in make-up.
Ireland also served on the Security Council in 1962, the first of several terms.

The European Economic Community (EEC) was a common market, and Irish policy-makers soon saw that staying outside it carried risks. A common market is a group of states that trade freely without tariffs among themselves, apply a common tariff to outsiders, and allow free movement of goods, workers and capital.

The Treaty of Rome in 1957 created the EEC. Its six founding states were France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, with a customs union and a common external tariff (one set of import taxes on goods from outside).

Britain was Ireland's main market, so when it considered joining, Irish ministers feared that British entry would leave Ireland outside a market where its farm exports would face barriers. After 1958 Ireland had also turned from protection to freer trade.

Ireland formally applied on 31 July 1961 under Taoiseach Seán Lemass, and the Dáil, the main parties and farmers' groups supported the application. The support of the Dáil, parties and farmers' groups meant the application had wide backing at home.
Supporters hoped to gain access to a large market for beef and dairy goods and to attract investment, and Lemass argued that membership would help to modernise Irish industry.

French president Charles de Gaulle vetoed British entry on 14 January 1963, which stopped negotiations, although the Irish application remained on the table. A veto by one member was enough, which means one man could halt Britain's entry and Ireland's with it.

To prepare, the government set up bodies to improve industrial competitiveness and signed the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement with Britain in 1965. This was to make Irish firms competitive, because they would face open competition inside the EEC.

After the first veto, Ireland tried again, and only a change of French leadership opened the way to entry. The steps run from veto to summit to treaty to referendum to membership, and they are easy to muddle.

Ireland, Britain, Denmark and Norway applied again in 1967, but de Gaulle vetoed British entry a second time in November 1967. Ireland was again tied to Britain's fate, which is why de Gaulle's veto stopped all of them.

After de Gaulle resigned in 1969, the Hague summit of December 1969 agreed to enlarge the community, and negotiations opened in Luxembourg in 1970. His resignation removed the main obstacle, so enlargement could go ahead.

Patrick Hillery, Minister for External Affairs from 1969 to 1973, led the Irish negotiating team; Ireland won a five-year transitional period for industry (time to adjust before facing full competition) and agreed terms on farm prices.
The transition was so that Irish industry could adjust gradually rather than face full competition at once.
The Treaty of Accession was signed in Brussels on 22 January 1972.

The government held a referendum on 10 May 1972 (the Third Amendment) to amend the Constitution to allow membership; about 83 per cent of those who voted were in favour, on a turnout of about 71 per cent.
A referendum was needed because the Constitution had to be changed before Ireland could join.
Ireland, Britain and Denmark became members on 1 January 1973, with Jack Lynch as Taoiseach; Norway's voters had rejected membership in September 1972.
Hillery became Ireland's first member of the European Commission in 1973.
Ireland's bid to join the EEC rested on economic and political hopes, and it met organised opposition. The size of the final yes vote shows which side persuaded the public.

Economic motives: the failure of protection (shielding home industry with tariffs), the need for markets for beef and dairy goods beyond Britain, and the hope of attracting industry looking for access to a large market. This is why joining looked like the answer to the problems of a protected economy.

Political motives: membership would end the dependence on the British market and give a small state a seat among the major European powers. Relying on one customer left Ireland exposed, so a wider market meant more independence.

The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), which would pay guaranteed prices to farmers, was the strongest attraction for farmers and the Irish Farmers' Association, which supported entry. Guaranteed prices meant farmers could plan with confidence.
Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael and farmers' and employers' organisations supported entry and campaigned for a yes vote.

Opponents, grouped in the Common Market Defence Campaign, argued that entry would cost sovereignty (the state's freedom to make its own laws) and neutrality, force small firms and farms out of business, and give control of the economy to foreign companies.
For example, they feared small firms could not compete with larger European companies.
Labour opposed entry in 1972, as did Sinn Féin and some trade unionists.
Raymond Crotty, an economist, was a prominent critic of the EEC.
The size of the yes vote in 1972 showed how strongly the public linked membership to economic hopes.
In the 1980s a new European treaty raised the question of how far Ireland could hand over power without asking the people. A court case then forced a second EEC referendum, in 1987.

The Single European Act, signed in February 1986, aimed to complete the single market (free movement of goods, services, people and capital) by the end of 1992 and extended qualified majority voting, where a decision passes without every state agreeing, to more decisions.
This is why it was seen as a step beyond a simple trading arrangement.
It also gave a legal basis to European political cooperation, the effort of member states to coordinate foreign policy. Ireland ratified it in 1987, after the Crotty case.

Raymond Crotty, an economist and critic of the EEC, challenged the government's plan to ratify the Act. He lost in the High Court but won in the Supreme Court. He argued that ratifying would give away Irish freedom of action, so the courts were asked to decide.

On 9 April 1987 the Supreme Court ruled that the provisions on political cooperation limited the state's freedom to conduct its foreign policy, so ratification required an amendment to the Constitution.

The Tenth Amendment, approved by referendum on 26 May 1987 by about 70 per cent to 30 per cent, on a low turnout of about 44 per cent, allowed ratification. The amendment was needed because the Supreme Court had ruled the Constitution blocked ratification.
The Crotty judgment established that major transfers of power to the EEC and the EU would require a referendum in Ireland.
Both organisations ended Ireland's isolation, but they did so in different ways. A strong answer sets them side by side and reaches a clear judgement.

The UN gave Ireland international recognition, a platform for independent policies on China, Tibet and nuclear weapons, and a respected peacekeeping role. It also shaped Irish identity and foreign policy.

The EEC had greater practical effect: it gave farmers guaranteed prices and access to a large market, brought regional and social funds, attracted foreign investment and reduced Ireland's dependence on Britain.
Contemporary view: supporters of the UN saw it as the best guarantee of Irish independence and neutrality, because it let a small state act without joining a bloc.
Contemporary view: supporters of the EEC saw it as the only way to modernise the economy and end dependence on Britain, since the home market and protection had failed.
Later view: historians generally judge that EEC membership had the deeper impact on Irish society and economy.
Later view: the UN involvement shaped Ireland's self-image and foreign policy and has remained an important part of its identity.

By 1973 Ireland had already spent fifteen years moving away from protection, and it still depended heavily on the British market. Those two facts explain both why entry was sought and why its effects were mixed.

Before 1958 Ireland was protectionist (it shielded home industry with tariffs, taxes on imports) and its economy was stagnant. The First Programme for Economic Expansion, 1958 to 1963, and Seán Lemass's policies began to move it towards free trade.

The Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement of 1965 cut tariffs on trade with Britain, so protected Irish industries already faced competition before 1973. This is why entry deepened an existing trend rather than starting it.
Ireland depended heavily on the British market for exports, above all farm produce.
Ireland's application of 1961 fell when de Gaulle vetoed British entry in 1963, and he vetoed it again in 1967. Ireland and Britain were finally admitted together.
The 1972 referendum approved entry, with about 83 per cent voting yes, under a Fianna Fáil government led by Jack Lynch.
The economic problems of the 1970s and 1980s (oil price shocks, inflation, unemployment, debt and emigration) are the setting in which the gains and costs of membership have to be judged.

The European Economic Community (EEC) was built as a common market, meaning its members traded with one another as if they were a single economy. Several technical terms recur through this topic, so each is defined here as it is used.
A common market means free trade among its members, a common external tariff (one shared tax on goods from outside), and free movement of goods, workers and capital across member borders.

The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) was the EEC's system of farm support. Intervention meant the EEC buying surplus produce into storage at a guaranteed price, so that market prices could not fall below a floor.
A quota is a limit on how much a farmer or fishing state may produce or land. A derogation is a temporary exemption from a general rule, such as the one Ireland won on fishing limits.

A total allowable catch (TAC) is the whole limit set for a fish species. Relative stability is the rule that divides a TAC into national quotas according to each state's past catches. Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM) is the Irish state fisheries board.
The European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) gave money to poorer regions. A directive is an EEC instruction that member states must turn into their own national law.

On 1 January 1973 Ireland joined the EEC, together with Britain and Denmark, which raised the Community from six members to nine. Membership changed how Ireland traded, who made its laws and where its money came from.

Tariffs on industrial trade with other members were phased out over a transition period ending in 1977, and farm prices were brought into line in stages over about five years. Ireland also adopted the common external tariff on goods from outside the Community.

EEC law took precedence over Irish law in the areas covered by the treaties. The Third Amendment to the Constitution, approved by referendum in May 1972, made this possible by allowing the state to join and giving EEC law effect in Ireland.

Irish ministers sat on the Council of Ministers, Irish members sat in the European Parliament, and Patrick Hillery was the first Irish member of the Commission, serving from 1973 to 1976. The other main institution was the European Court of Justice.
Ireland held the presidency of the Council of Ministers for the first time from January to June 1975, which gave a small state a turn at chairing the Community's business.
Membership reduced dependence on Britain. Britain took well over half of Irish exports in the early 1970s and only about a third by the late 1980s, because trade with the continent grew.

Net payments from the EEC budget to Ireland (what it received minus what it paid in) amounted to several per cent of national income by the 1980s. This helped to pay for farm support, training and infrastructure.
Ireland joined the European Monetary System in March 1979, a scheme to keep member currencies stable against one another. Britain stayed out, so the Irish pound broke its link with sterling.

Farming was the sector with most to gain from entry, because the CAP promised farmers prices that Irish producers had never been guaranteed. The gains were large, but they were not shared equally and they brought a new problem of surplus.
The CAP guaranteed minimum prices for products such as beef, milk and cereals, and bought surplus produce into intervention stores. Farmers therefore knew they could sell at a fixed floor price.
Irish farm prices were raised towards EEC levels during the transition. Farm incomes rose sharply in the early years of membership, especially for beef and dairy farmers.
Land values rose, and farmers invested in machinery, buildings and drainage, helped by grants, because higher guaranteed prices made the investment worth making.

The benefits were uneven. Larger and more productive farms in the east and south gained most, while small farms on poor land in the west gained less, because they had less produce to sell at the higher prices.
Guaranteed prices encouraged overproduction, because farmers produced more whatever the demand. In 1984 the EEC introduced milk quotas, limiting output on Irish dairy farms.
The number of people working on the land continued to fall, and agriculture's share of employment and output declined, even though farm incomes had risen.
Alongside farm support, the EEC redistributed money to poorer places and people. Ireland was one of the poorer members, so it received a large share compared with its size.
The European Regional Development Fund was created in 1975, and Ireland, as one of the poorer members, was a leading beneficiary relative to its size.
The European Social Fund paid for training and employment schemes for young and unemployed people. It helped to pay for the training schemes of AnCO, the state training authority.
The funds were spent on roads, water and sewerage schemes, telecommunications and industrial estates, mainly under the direction of the Irish government.

A reform of the structural funds (the regional and social funds together) in 1988, linked to the Single European Act of 1987, roughly doubled the money available. Ireland's programme ran from 1989 to 1993.
Membership opened the EEC market to anyone who produced inside Ireland, but it also stripped away the tariffs that had sheltered older Irish firms. New industry grew while old industry shrank.

American and other foreign firms set up factories in Ireland to sell into the EEC, drawn by Industrial Development Authority (IDA) grants, a young English-speaking workforce, low taxes and access to the EEC market.
From 1981 manufacturing profits were taxed at 10 per cent, which made Ireland even more attractive to firms looking for a low-tax base.

Electronics, pharmaceuticals, chemicals and engineering became leading sectors. Digital, for example, opened a plant in Galway in 1971, before entry, which shows the kind of foreign investment the IDA attracted.
Protected Irish industries such as clothing, textiles and footwear lost their tariff protection, and many firms closed with heavy job losses, because they could not compete with cheaper imports.
Employment in traditional manufacturing fell. The rise in unemployment of the late 1970s and 1980s showed that membership did not by itself solve the economy's weaknesses.
Irish exports became more diversified, and manufactured goods became the larger share of exports, overtaking farm produce in value.
Membership changed Irish law and outlook as well as incomes. Some changes were required by EEC directives, while others coincided with entry.

The equal pay directive of 1975 and the equal treatment (employment) directive of 1976 required changes in Irish law. They reinforced the Anti-Discrimination (Pay) Act 1974 and the Employment Equality Act 1977.

The marriage bar (the rule forcing women to resign from the civil service on marrying) was lifted in 1973, the year of entry. It followed the Commission on the Status of Women rather than an EEC directive.
A directive on equal treatment in social welfare, adopted in 1978, forced Ireland to change payments to married women in the 1980s.
Irish citizens gained the right to live and work in other member states, which eased emigration, and young people had more contact with continental Europe, so attitudes became more outward-looking.
Irish judges were obliged to apply EEC law, and the European Court of Justice became a route for individuals to challenge Irish law.
Critics argued that membership cost Ireland some of its independence. The debate over sovereignty returned in the Crotty case and in the later referendums on European treaties.

Irish fishing was small and under-developed, but it was important to coastal communities and became a sensitive issue in the accession negotiations. Knowing its state before entry explains why the terms mattered and why they were disputed.
Irish waters were rich in fish, but the industry was small. Most boats were old, small and inshore, and the fleet lacked the range to fish far from land.
Fishing employed only a few thousand full-time fishermen, concentrated in coastal counties, and many combined it with farming.
Irish consumers ate little fish outside Fridays, so the home market was small and the industry exported little.
Foreign trawlers fished close to the Irish coast under historic rights (long-established claims to fish there), because the exclusive Irish limit was narrow.
Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM), the state fisheries board, was created in 1952 to develop the industry through grants and loans for boats, training and marketing.
In the 1960s and early 1970s BIM helped to build a more modern fleet, including larger boats able to catch herring, whitefish and shellfish.
Fish made up a tiny share of Irish exports and national output before 1973, which is why governments treated the fishing terms as less important than the farming terms.

Fishing rules went through three stages: an equal-access principle in 1970, a temporary Irish exemption in 1973 and the Common Fisheries Policy of 1983, which was to be reviewed after ten years. Keeping the dates and terms straight is the key to this case study.
In 1970 the EEC agreed the principle of equal access for all members' fleets to Community waters, just as the applicant states opened negotiations.

Irish negotiators argued that fishing mattered to poor coastal communities. Ireland obtained a derogation: an exclusive six-mile zone for Irish boats, and a 12-mile zone in parts of the coast, for ten years to the end of 1982.

Other members could fish beyond those limits, and Irish boats gained access to British and Danish waters. Critics said the government gave away too much in order to secure the farming terms, and that fishing was treated as expendable.

In 1976, at The Hague, member states agreed to extend fishing limits to 200 nautical miles from 1 January 1977 and gave Ireland (and Britain) preferential treatment, known as the Hague preferences. This is not the 1969 Hague summit of EEC leaders.
Negotiating a new common policy took until January 1983, when member states agreed on the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP), which replaced the temporary derogation that ended at the close of 1982.

The CFP set annual total allowable catches (TACs) for the main species, shared out as national quotas on the principle of relative stability, meaning shares based on past catches, with some preference for Ireland.
It reserved a 12-mile coastal belt for local fishermen, and the arrangements were to be reviewed after ten years.
Irish fishermen and ministers complained that Ireland's quotas were small compared with the value of the fish in its waters.
Grants turned a small inshore industry into a more modern one centred on a few ports, while foreign fleets and quota disputes kept the industry in the news.
With EEC and state grants, BIM financed new and larger vessels, and the Irish fleet grew in the late 1970s and 1980s.

Killybegs, Co. Donegal, developed into Ireland's leading fishing port, with a fleet of larger trawlers and pelagic boats (which catch fish such as herring that swim near the surface), processing factories and a growing service industry.
Castletownbere, Co. Cork, became a major whitefish port, with boats landing fish for sale and export.
Other ports, namely Dunmore East (Co. Waterford), Howth (Co. Dublin), Rossaveal (Co. Galway) and Kilmore Quay (Co. Wexford), also received investment in piers and harbours.
Foreign fleets fished in Irish waters, and the Irish Naval Service did fishery protection, inspecting and arresting vessels that broke the rules.
Spain and Portugal joined the EEC on 1 January 1986, after which Spanish vessels had a legal but limited route to Irish waters. Before then Spain was not a member.
Disputes over illegal fishing, over the size of quotas and over the shares given to other states recurred through the 1980s.
Judging the EEC's impact on fishing means weighing real investment against real grievances. The two sides in the argument were the fishermen and the government, each with a case.
Benefits: investment in harbours, boats and processing plants created jobs in some coastal towns, and the 200-mile limit gave Ireland a large area of sea to manage.
Fish processing and exports to continental markets expanded through the 1980s, which widened the market for an industry that had once sold little abroad.
Costs: quotas limited what Irish boats could land, small inshore fishermen often lost out to larger vessels and fewer ports, and young people left declining harbours.
Fishermen's organisations claimed that Ireland received a small share of the fish caught in its own waters, and argued that the government treated fisheries as secondary to farming.
The government's side was that it had obtained the best terms it could, the 12-mile zone and the Hague preferences, and that fishing mattered little beside farming.
Supporters of EEC membership pointed to the new money for the industry. Opponents of entry, such as the Common Market Defence Campaign (1972), warned mainly of lost sovereignty in general.
The fishing industry remained a source of grievance, and its history became a standard example in debates on the costs of membership.
Examiners reward a clear judgement backed by paired points, so weigh what membership achieved against what it failed to do, and say who gained and who lost.
Achievements: secure and better-priced markets for farmers, large transfers from Europe, foreign investment in new industries, equality legislation and a wider international outlook.
Limits: protected firms closed, unemployment rose in the 1980s, small farms and the west benefited least, and the fishing industry gained less than farming.
Contemporary view: supporters said membership was the only way to modernise an economy that relied on protection and emigration; opponents said it threatened sovereignty and traditional industries.

Later view: historians generally accept that membership underpinned the transformation of the economy and society, while stressing that the full benefits came later, from the 1990s, and that farmers and fishermen did not all gain equally.

To follow how the status of women and Irish society changed between 1949 and 1989, you need to know how conservative the starting point was. Law, work and family life were all shaped by religion and by a stagnant economy.
Ireland in 1949 was a conservative, Catholic and mainly rural society, and the Catholic Church shaped the law and public attitudes on sex, marriage and the family.
The 1937 Constitution gave the family and the home a central place for women, so the law tended to treat a woman's main role as that of wife and mother.

The stagnant economy of the 1950s drove mass emigration. The turn to economic expansion from 1958, and Ireland's entry to the EEC (the European Economic Community, forerunner of the European Union) in 1973, then changed both the economy and the pressure for reform.

Contraception was banned: a law of 1935 forbade its sale and import, and the Church opposed artificial contraception, so the ban had strong moral backing, a position Pope Paul VI reaffirmed in his encyclical (a formal papal letter) of 1968.

Three key concepts run through the topic. Discrimination is unequal treatment on grounds such as sex or marital status. Liberalisation is the relaxing of legal or social restrictions, for example on contraception, censorship or homosexuality.
Equality of opportunity means the same access to education, jobs and promotion regardless of sex.
For about a century Ireland's population had been falling or static. From the 1960s it began to grow, and the census figures are useful evidence of how the economy and emigration changed.
The census recorded 2,960,593 people in 1951 and 2,818,341 in 1961, a fall of about 140,000, and the cause was emigration, because many more people left than were born to replace them.
The population rose to about 2.88 million in 1966 and about 2.98 million in 1971, as net emigration (people leaving minus people arriving) fell and the birth rate remained high.
It then grew rapidly, to about 3.44 million in 1981 and about 3.54 million in 1986, the highest figure for about a century.
Births peaked at about 74,000 in 1980, and the population was young, with a large proportion under 25, which kept the birth rate high.
Growth slowed after 1986 because heavy emigration returned, and the 1991 census recorded a small fall to about 3.53 million.
Emigration is the key to the population story, because the economy decided whether young people stayed or left. It moved through four phases, each with a different cause.
1950s: net emigration was about 400,000, and most emigrants were young people going to Britain for work, because the stagnant economy offered them few jobs at home.
1960s: economic expansion cut net emigration sharply, to about 80,000 for 1961 to 1966, because more jobs were available in Ireland.

1970s: the flow reversed and there was net inward migration of about 100,000 over the decade. Many of the arrivals were Irish emigrants returning home as Britain suffered recession and Ireland joined the EEC in 1973.
1980s: emigration returned, with around 200,000 net emigrants over the decade, as unemployment rose above 15 per cent in the mid-1980s.
The 1980s emigrants were often well educated, and they went to Britain, the United States, Australia and continental Europe, so Ireland lost skilled people as well as labour.
Emigration was a continuing feature of Irish society, and it shaped family life, because families were split across countries. It also caused rural depopulation and affected attitudes to politics.
As people left farms and small villages for towns, the shape of Irish society changed. Marriage and family patterns changed with it.
The urban population passed half the total around 1971 (about 52 per cent), and more than a quarter of the people lived in the Dublin area by 1981.
New suburbs and towns such as Tallaght, Clondalkin and Blanchardstown absorbed people moving from the countryside, while small farms and rural villages lost population.
Marriage rates rose in the 1960s and 1970s, and people married at a younger age than in the 1950s, when late marriage and non-marriage were common.
Large families were the norm in the 1960s, but the fertility rate (the average number of children per woman) fell steadily afterwards, to close to replacement level by the late 1980s.
Falling family size was linked to more use of contraception, which was illegal to sell until the late 1970s, and to women's rising education and employment.
Before the 1970s, the law and employers openly treated married women as less entitled to work. The Commission on the Status of Women turned complaints about this into a programme for reform.
The marriage bar was the rule requiring women in the civil service and other public posts to resign when they married, so a woman had to choose between marriage and a career.
The bar was removed for primary teachers in 1958 and for the civil service in 1973. Banks and other employers kept their own bars on married women.
Women were also paid less than men for similar work, which was a form of discrimination on grounds of sex.
The Commission on the Status of Women was set up by the Lynch government in 1970, after pressure from women's organisations, and it was chaired by Thekla Beere.
Its interim report in 1971 recommended equal pay, and its final report in December 1972 made 49 recommendations on equal pay, employment, education, family law and social welfare.
The report provided a programme for reform, so campaigners could point to official backing, and many of its recommendations were implemented during the 1970s and 1980s.
From 1970 a new generation of women campaigned in public rather than quietly lobbying. Their most famous action put contraception on the national agenda.
The Irish Women's Liberation Movement was formed in 1970 by journalists and activists including Mary Kenny, Nell McCafferty, June Levine and Nuala Fennell.
Its manifesto Chains or Change (1971) demanded equal pay, equal education, contraception and legal changes for unmarried mothers and deserted wives.

On 22 May 1971 dozens of members travelled by train from Dublin to Belfast, bought contraceptives that were illegal to import into the Republic and returned openly to Connolly Station in Dublin, challenging customs officers to stop them.
The action attracted large media coverage, which made contraception a public issue. It was a protest, not a court case, and it did not change the law itself.
Later groups provided services that the state did not: Women's Aid, founded in 1974 to help victims of domestic violence, and the Well Woman Centre, opened in 1977.
Women's organisations also used the trade unions and the Council for the Status of Women to lobby ministers.

The law on contraception was the most controversial issue in the status of women in the 1970s. It was legalised in stages, not by one event: a court ruling in 1973, an Act in 1979 and an amendment in 1985.
Mary McGee, a mother of four who was medically advised against another pregnancy, took a case against the State after customs seized contraceptive jelly sent to her from abroad.

In McGee v Attorney General, decided in December 1973, the Supreme Court found by four to one that the ban on importing contraceptives for her was unconstitutional, because it infringed the right to marital privacy.
McGee was about importing contraceptives for a married woman, so it did not legalise sale, which stayed restricted.
In 1974 the Fine Gael-Labour government introduced a bill to regulate contraceptives, but it was defeated when Taoiseach Liam Cosgrave voted against his own government's bill.

The Health (Family Planning) Act 1979, brought in by Charles Haughey as Minister for Health, allowed contraceptives to be sold on prescription to people with a bona fide (genuine) need for family planning. Haughey called it "an Irish solution to an Irish problem".
The Act was in operation in 1980, and a 1985 amendment allowed sale to people over 18 without prescription.
The Catholic Church officially opposed artificial contraception, a position reaffirmed by Pope Paul VI in 1968, but surveys suggested that many Irish married Catholics ignored the rule.
Campaigning, the Commission's report and EEC membership together pushed the state to make sex discrimination unlawful. Each Act tackled a different area of women's lives.
The Anti-Discrimination (Pay) Act 1974 required equal pay for men and women doing the same or similar work, taking effect from the end of 1975, in line with EEC requirements.
The Employment Equality Act 1977 made it unlawful to discriminate on grounds of sex or marital status in recruitment, training and promotion.

The Employment Equality Agency was set up under the 1977 Act to promote equality, investigate, research and advise the government. It did not decide individual complaints itself, and its powers were limited.
The Juries Act 1976 ended the exclusion of women from jury service, so women could now take part in trials as jurors.
The Family Home Protection Act 1976 stopped a husband selling the family home without his wife's consent, which protected wives who owned no property in their own name.
The Maternity Protection of Employees Act 1981 gave women the right to maternity leave and to return to their jobs, so having a baby no longer meant losing a post.
Social welfare was reformed in the 1980s to give married women equal treatment, under pressure from EEC law.
Legal equality did not quickly produce equal representation. Women stayed a small minority in politics, though a few broke through to ministerial office, and more women went out to work.
Women remained a small minority in the Dáil (the lower house of parliament): six sat after the 1977 election, and the number reached 14 by 1987.
Eileen Desmond of Labour, for example, became Minister for Health and Social Welfare in 1981, the first woman in a cabinet since Constance Markievicz.
Gemma Hussey of Fine Gael was Minister for Education from 1982 to 1987, and Nuala Fennell was a Minister of State for women's affairs from 1982.
More women entered the workforce, particularly married women, whose participation rate rose from about 5 per cent in 1961 to about 17 per cent in 1981.
Mary Robinson, a senator from 1969, was the most prominent woman in public life outside government, because she pressed reform from the Seanad and the courts.
Meehan was a trade unionist and campaigner who became the first head of the Employment Equality Agency. Her work was to make the new laws operate in practice.

Sylvia Meehan was born in Dublin in 1929, worked as a teacher, and was vice-president of the Association of Secondary Teachers, Ireland and chairperson of the women's committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions.
She was appointed in 1977 as the first chairperson of the new Employment Equality Agency, a post she held until 1992.

She was a participant in the enforcement of the equal pay and equal treatment laws, leading the agency as they were implemented and supervising research, investigations and advice on discrimination at work.
The agency's research into the position of girls and women in education, pay, maternity leave and childcare helped to shape later legislation.
Contemporaries regarded her as an effective and determined advocate, though employers and some politicians resisted the agency's findings.
Historians see her as a key figure in turning the 1970s equality laws into practice, though they stress that the agency's powers were limited.
Robinson was a lawyer and senator who used the courts and the Oireachtas (the Irish parliament) to challenge discriminatory law. Here her career is taken only to 1989.

Mary Robinson was born in Ballina, Co. Mayo, in 1944, graduated from Trinity College Dublin, was called to the bar in 1967, studied at Harvard and became Reid Professor of Law at Trinity at the age of 25.

She was elected to the Seanad (the upper house) for the University of Dublin in 1969 and served until 1989, as an independent. She campaigned there for women to serve on juries, a change enacted in the Juries Act 1976.
In the early 1970s she introduced private members' bills (bills brought by an individual member, not the government) to liberalise the law on contraception, which the Seanad refused to debate.
She later sought reform of the law on homosexuality. Neither the contraception bills nor this reform became law at the time.

As a barrister she took cases on behalf of individuals against the State, including a tax case brought by a married couple, which the Supreme Court decided in their favour in 1980, and the Airey case on legal aid, heard by the European Court in 1979.

She also took the case of the campaigner David Norris against the law criminalising homosexual acts. The Supreme Court upheld the law in 1983, the European Court of Human Rights found against Ireland in 1988, and the law changed in 1993.
She joined the Labour Party in 1976 and left it in 1985 in protest at the Anglo-Irish Agreement, and she was a Dublin city councillor from 1979 to 1983.
Contemporaries saw her as a liberal reformer and an able lawyer, attacked by conservatives and the church for her views but respected for her persistence.
Historians credit her with creating a legal and political basis for reform that prepared the way for the 1990s and her election as President in 1990.
Examiners reward a judgement that change was real but uneven. Pair what was achieved with what was not, and show how contemporaries and historians differed.
Achievements: the marriage bar ended, equal pay and employment equality were legislated, contraception became legally available and women gained new organisations, rights and visibility.
Limits: women remained scarce in politics and senior jobs, pay gaps persisted, divorce and abortion remained prohibited and the church kept its influence.
Contemporary view: conservatives argued that the reforms threatened the family and Catholic values, whereas reformers saw the changes as too little and too slow.

Later view: historians see the period as the beginning of social liberalisation, driven by economic change, EEC law and campaigning, but argue that change was uneven and that Ireland remained more conservative than many European states in the 1980s.

To judge how much changed between 1949 and 1989, you need to know what the starting point was: a state built around the Irish language and the Catholic Church, and cut off from much of the outside world.

The 1937 Constitution (Article 8) made Irish the national language and first official language, with English recognised as a second official language. State policy was to revive Irish through schools, the civil service and the Gaeltacht, the mainly western and south-western districts where Irish was still spoken daily.
The Catholic Church shaped schools, health and social policy, giving the state a strongly Catholic ethos, and Mass attendance was very high.
The Mother and Child dispute of 1951, in which the bishops opposed Noel Browne's health scheme and the government dropped it, showed the church at the peak of its influence over policy.

Ireland in the 1950s was isolated and suffered heavy emigration, which drained rural areas and the Gaeltacht. From 1958 and through the 1960s, economic expansion, urbanisation and rising living standards opened the country to outside influences, which is why old certainties came under pressure.
Irish was the first official language of the state, but it was losing ground as a community language, and by the 1960s public attitudes were turning against compulsion.

Official policy rested on compulsion. Irish was a compulsory school subject, a pass in Irish was required for the Leaving Certificate (the final secondary school exam) and Irish was needed for entry to the civil service.

Gael Linn, founded in 1953, tried to promote the language positively through popular means, including records, the Amharc Éireann newsreel from 1956 and the feature film Mise Éire in 1959, a documentary on the years before 1916.
The Gaeltacht was in decline in the 1950s because of emigration, so the state set up Gaeltarra Éireann in 1957 to encourage industry in Irish-speaking areas and give people a reason to stay.

The Commission on the Restoration of the Irish Language reported in 1963, and a government White Paper of 1965 accepted the aim of restoration but proposed a more flexible approach, showing that policy was softening.

The Language Freedom Movement, founded in 1966, campaigned against compulsory Irish, arguing that compulsion turned pupils against the language, and it provoked counter-campaigns from defenders of the language.

In 1973 the Fine Gael-Labour government, with Richard Burke as Minister for Education, ended the rule that students must pass Irish to gain the Leaving Certificate. The requirement for civil service entry was also relaxed later.
Do not overstate the 1973 change. Only the compulsory pass at the Leaving Certificate ended, and Irish itself stayed a compulsory school subject.
From the late 1960s, Irish speakers themselves pressed for services in their own language, and the state responded by creating new broadcasting and development bodies.

The Gaeltacht Civil Rights Movement, formed in 1969, demanded better services and Irish-language radio because the state offered none. In 1970 it ran a pirate station (an unlicensed broadcaster), Saor Raidió Chonamara.

Raidió na Gaeltachta began broadcasting from Connemara on Easter Sunday, 2 April 1972, giving Irish speakers a regular, official service in their own language, so they no longer needed pirate broadcasts. Do not confuse it with the pirate Saor Raidió Chonamara of 1970.
Bord na Gaeilge was set up in 1975 to coordinate efforts to promote Irish.
Údarás na Gaeltachta, created in 1980, took over responsibility for the economic and social development of the Gaeltacht. It later absorbed the work of Gaeltarra Éireann, set up in 1957.

The Irish language retained its symbolic status, but the number of everyday speakers continued to decline outside the Gaeltacht, which itself was shrinking. Compulsion had also left many pupils indifferent.
Ó hEithir was a writer, journalist and broadcaster whose work in Irish and English brought the culture of the Gaeltacht and the Irish language to a modern audience.
Breandán Ó hEithir was born in 1930 on Inis Mór, one of the Aran Islands, and died in 1990.
He was a journalist and a broadcaster with RTÉ, reporting on current affairs, culture and sport in Irish and English, and he wrote for newspapers, including a regular column.
His novel Lig Sinn i gCathú (1976), a satirical novel about the life of a Galway student, was widely read in Irish, and he translated it himself as Lead Us into Temptation in 1978.
His Over the Bar (1984) was a personal account of the GAA, and The Begrudger's Guide to Irish Politics (1986) was a witty account of political life, written in English.

He was a participant in the cultural change of the period rather than a leader of a movement. He presented Irish as a living medium for modern subjects, not as a duty, which fitted the move away from compulsion.
Contemporaries valued him as a bridge between the Gaeltacht and the English-speaking world and as a rare Irish-language writer with a wide readership.
Later critics regard him as one of the most accomplished bilingual writers and broadcasters of his generation.
Alongside the debate about the language, traditional music enjoyed a revival that made Irish culture feel modern and attractive rather than a duty.
Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann was founded in Mullingar in 1951, and the fleadh cheoil (music festival and competition) held from 1952 helped to spread traditional music and dance.

Seán Ó Riada composed the score for Mise Éire (1959). From 1961 his group Ceoltóirí Chualann played traditional music in a concert style, which brought it to a wider audience. Do not confuse the group with Comhaltas.

Ó Riada's Ceol an Aifrinn (1968), the Mass in Irish set to sean-nós-style music (the old unaccompanied singing style) for the church at Cúil Aodha, linked the music revival to the changes brought by Vatican II.
The Chieftains were formed in 1962, and the Clancy Brothers, The Dubliners and later Planxty made Irish ballads and traditional music popular at home and abroad.
The revival gave Irish culture a modern commercial and international dimension, and it reduced the old divide between a rural traditional culture and urban popular culture.
The Second Vatican Council, the worldwide meeting of Catholic bishops in Rome, changed Catholic worship and the church's relationship with other Christians and the modern world.
Pope John XXIII opened the council on 11 October 1962 and it closed on 8 December 1965 under Paul VI. Irish bishops, including McQuaid, attended.
The council allowed the Mass to be said in the vernacular (the everyday language) instead of Latin, so people could follow it. The first Masses in English in Ireland were celebrated in 1965.
Priests now faced the congregation, laypeople could be readers and distribute communion, and parish councils and lay organisations were encouraged, giving ordinary Catholics a bigger role.

The council promoted ecumenism, closer relations and dialogue between Christian churches. The Catholic ban on Catholics attending Trinity College Dublin was lifted in 1970, and the first formal inter-church talks with the main Protestant churches in Ireland were held at Ballymascanlon, Co. Louth, in 1973.
It declared in 1965 that religious freedom was a right, which weakened the claim that the Catholic Church should have a special position in law.
Many Irish Catholics welcomed the changes, but others, mostly older, felt unsettled by the loss of Latin and old devotions, because these had been part of their lifelong habits of worship.
Vatican II also encouraged people to think for themselves on moral questions and to follow their conscience, which contributed to a questioning of church authority.

McQuaid, Archbishop of Dublin from 1940 to 1972, was the most powerful churchman in Ireland, and he was cautious about the changes brought by the council. His reaction shows the gap between the council's openness and his conservative style.

McQuaid was born in 1895 in Cootehill, Co. Cavan. He was a participant in church-state relations, with direct access to ministers, and his influence had peaked in the Mother and Child dispute of 1951, when the bishops opposed a state health scheme.
He attended Vatican II and on returning reassured Dubliners that the council would not disturb their faith, a message of reassurance in tune with his conservative outlook.
He implemented liturgical reforms in Dublin, but slowly. He was wary of ecumenism, which he regarded as risky for Catholic doctrine, and of lay initiatives outside the control of the clergy.
His reach showed in the McGahern case: John McGahern's novel The Dark was banned in 1965, and McGahern lost his teaching post at a Dublin primary school after pressure involving the Archbishop.

He was also involved in education, social work and the building of new churches and schools in the Dublin suburbs, and the Catholic Social Service Conference, set up in 1941, was one of his charitable bodies.
He retired in January 1972, at the end of more than thirty years as archbishop, and died in 1973. He was succeeded by Dermot Ryan.
Contemporaries admired his efficiency and devotion to the church, but critics complained of his authoritarian style and his readiness to intervene in politics and in people's lives.
Historians, notably John Cooney in his biography John Charles McQuaid: Ruler of Catholic Ireland (1999), portray him as a ruler whose style came to seem out of date.
Other historians stress his building of schools and welfare services. They argue that the decline of church power came from social change as much as from his policies, so he cannot be blamed alone.

Secularisation is the decline of religion's influence over public life, institutions and personal behaviour. The evidence for it in Ireland points both ways, which is why historians treat the period as a slow shift rather than a sudden break.
A survey in 1973 and 1974 found about nine in ten Catholics attending Mass weekly, so practice remained high even as other signs of change appeared.

Pope Paul VI's encyclical (a formal papal letter) Humanae Vitae in 1968 reaffirmed the ban on artificial contraception, and many Irish married Catholics found it difficult to accept. It was a papal decision after the council, not a Vatican II reform.

Vocations to the priesthood and religious life began to fall from the late 1960s, and fewer young people entered seminaries and convents, which shows that commitment was weakening even while Mass attendance stayed high.
Pope John Paul II visited Ireland from 29 September to 1 October 1979, and a Mass in the Phoenix Park drew over a million people, but the visit did not halt the long-term shift.
Secularisation advanced through the 1970s and 1980s, helped by education, television, emigration and contact with Europe, which exposed people to other ways of life.
Pluralism, acceptance that a society contains different beliefs and traditions, none privileged by the state, was at the centre of the 1983 referendum on abortion and the 1986 referendum on divorce.

The results showed that traditional views remained strong: the Eighth Amendment on abortion was carried in September 1983 by about two-thirds, and the divorce proposal was rejected in June 1986 by about two-thirds.

Censorship is the official banning or restriction of books, films and other material judged indecent, obscene or otherwise unacceptable. The system built in the 1920s and 1940s was relaxed in the 1960s as attitudes changed.

The Censorship of Publications Act 1929 set up a board that could ban books for being indecent or obscene, and the Act of 1946 added an appeals board. Thousands of books were banned, including works by leading Irish writers.
John McGahern's novel The Dark was banned in 1965, and he lost his teaching post after pressure involving the Archbishop of Dublin. The case became a symbol of the censorship of the time.
The Censorship of Publications Act 1967, introduced by the Minister for Justice, Brian Lenihan, provided that a ban lasts twelve years unless renewed, so many thousands of titles were released.
Film censorship became more liberal during the 1960s and 1970s, as television and cinema showed material from abroad.
Contraceptives and publications about them were covered by separate laws until the Health (Family Planning) Act 1979, so the 1967 relaxation did not change that area.
Broadcasting was controlled in a different way, through the powers of the minister over RTÉ, rather than by the publications board.
From the 1960s, better transport, telephones, newspapers, radio, television and computers ended the isolation of the 1950s.
Car ownership rose sharply between 1960 and 1980, and better roads, bus services and air travel reduced rural isolation by making it easier to travel and to meet outsiders.
Telephone services, once poor and slow to expand, were improved, and in 1984 Bord Telecom Éireann was set up to run them as a separate state company.
Television reached most households in the 1960s and early 1970s, and RTÉ 2 started in 1978, bringing more programmes and choice. British channels could be received in much of the east and north.
The Irish Times under the editor Douglas Gageby, from 1963, became a forum for new ideas, and magazines such as Magill, founded in 1977, expanded political journalism.
Pirate radio stations grew in the 1970s and 1980s, challenging RTÉ's monopoly (its sole right to broadcast), and the Radio and Television Act 1988 licensed independent local radio.
Computers were adopted in business and government from the 1970s, and American firms such as Digital opened plants in Ireland, laying the base for the electronics industry.
These changes exposed people to a wider range of ideas and lifestyles, and helped to break down the isolation on which traditional authority had rested.
Judging this period means weighing real change against its limits, and comparing how people at the time saw it with how historians see it now.

Achievements: the Irish language gained broadcasting and institutions, traditional music was revived and reached a world audience, the church accepted liturgical reform and ecumenism, and censorship was relaxed.
Limits: the language continued to decline as a community language, the compulsion debates left many pupils indifferent, and the church's leadership, especially under McQuaid, was slow to adapt.
Contemporary view: traditionalists feared that television and liberal reform threatened Irish identity and Catholic values, while reformers regarded the changes as overdue.
Later view: historians regard the period as the start of the shift to a more secular and pluralist society, with the church retaining strong influence on law and public life well into the 1980s.

Irish television began late, after a long debate about whether and how the state should run it. It arrived in a country with an established state radio service, a Church that shaped public morals and a government keen to modernise.

Radio had been run by the state since 2RN opened in Dublin in 1926; it later became Radio Éireann and in the 1950s it was part of the Department of Posts and Telegraphs, so the minister in charge of post and telegraphs also oversaw broadcasting.

Before 1961 some viewers in the east, the north and along the coast could pick up BBC and Ulster Television signals from Britain and Northern Ireland (Ulster Television began in 1959), and this showed that Irish demand for television was growing.

Seán Lemass was Taoiseach (prime minister) from 1959 to 1966, and his government stressed economic modernisation and opening Ireland to outside influences, which made a national television service attractive; Jack Lynch succeeded him in November 1966.

The Catholic Church, led in Dublin by Archbishop John Charles McQuaid (Archbishop from 1940 to 1972), had great influence on morals, and the state censored books and films, meaning officially banned material it judged harmful. Television would test these limits.
The government decided that television should be a national service under public control. The law that set it up also decided who would run it and what the broadcaster owed the state.

The Broadcasting Authority Act 1960 set up an Authority to run radio and the new television service; the government appointed its members, which gave ministers a strong influence over who ran broadcasting. The Authority became known as Radio Telefís Éireann (RTÉ).
The service was financed by licence fees (paid by households that owned a set) and by advertising, so RTÉ needed both public approval and commercial income.
The Authority was a statutory body, meaning one created and governed by law, not a government department, and the Act required it to be impartial in news and current affairs.
Telefís Éireann began broadcasting on 31 December 1961, and President Éamon de Valera spoke at the opening and warned that television had a great power for good and for ill.
Transmitters were built so that television reached most of the country within a few years, and by the early 1970s most households had a set, which is why its influence grew so fast.

Take care with names: Telefís Éireann was the television service launched in 1961, while RTÉ was the name of the Authority running both radio and television, and Radio Éireann was the older radio service.
RTÉ was meant to be independent, yet the state kept strong powers over it. This tension between public service and government influence runs through the whole case study.

Section 31 of the Act let the Minister for Posts and Telegraphs direct the Authority to refrain from broadcasting a specified matter, so ministers could ban a topic. This is censorship in the sense used here: official restriction of broadcasts.
In practice the Act's duty of impartiality in news and current affairs sat alongside ministerial power, so how far RTÉ was independent was a constant source of conflict.

Seán Lemass saw television as a means of national development and public information, and he called RTÉ "an instrument of public policy". By this he meant that it should support the government's national goals, not that it should be a mouthpiece for the government.
The opposing view, held by many in RTÉ, was that a broadcaster serves the public only if it is free to criticise the government, because a station that cannot criticise cannot hold power to account.
The clash between these two views shaped the history of RTÉ in the 1960s and led to the crisis of 1971 and 1972.
Television filled the schedule with a mix of foreign programmes and Irish ones. The Irish programmes mattered most, because they showed Irish people to themselves.
Much early output was imported from Britain and the United States, including westerns, comedies and films, so imported programmes gave Irish viewers a view of life elsewhere.
Home-produced programmes covered news, sport, current affairs, drama, light entertainment and Irish-language material.
Gaelic games and other sport drew large audiences.
The Riordans, a drama about a farming family that began in 1965, was a hit with viewers, especially in rural Ireland, because it dealt with real issues of farming life and change.
Telefís Scoile, which began in 1964, broadcast programmes for secondary schools, bringing television into the classroom.
Irish-language programmes and news bulletins in Irish were part of the service from the start, though they took a small share of airtime and often had a small audience.
RTÉ also raised standards for Irish drama and music, and helped writers, actors and musicians to reach a national audience.

The Late Late Show became the best-known programme on Irish television and a forum for national debate. It began modestly, but its willingness to discuss sensitive subjects made it a symbol of change.
The programme was first broadcast on Friday 6 July 1962 as a live summer filler, a programme meant only to fill the schedule, and it became a fixture.
It was a live talk show with guests, music and audience participation, and Gay Byrne presented it from 1962 until 1999, bringing an open-minded, humorous but probing style.

The show discussed subjects that were rarely talked of in public, including sex, marriage, contraception, unmarried mothers and the church, which is why it came to be seen as a force for liberalisation (the relaxation of controls on what could be discussed or done in public life).

In 1966 a quiz item for married couples led to the episode known as the Bishop and the Nightie: when Gay Byrne asked a wife, Eileen Fox, what she had worn on her honeymoon night, she said she had worn no nightdress, and the remark caused uproar.
Bishop Thomas Ryan of Clonfert condemned the programme, and other clergy and some viewers complained, while many viewers defended Byrne and the show, so the public split.
The incident showed that television could provoke public argument about morality and the limits of church authority, and it brought the Late Late Show to national attention.
Serious current affairs programmes put RTÉ on a collision course with ministers. The government had the means to pressure the broadcaster, and it used them.

Seven Days, a current affairs series launched in 1966, used young producers and reporters to investigate housing, poverty, emigration and other social issues. It began in autumn 1966, shortly before Lemass left office, but most of its run fell under Lynch.
Ministers resented programmes that criticised policy, and they complained to the RTÉ Authority, which was under pressure to restrain current affairs.
A Seven Days programme on illegal moneylending in 1969 led to a government-ordered inquiry and a row over RTÉ's independence, after which current affairs was reorganised.
From 1969 the Troubles made coverage of Northern Ireland a major source of conflict between RTÉ and the government, which feared that broadcasts would encourage violence.
The government held financial and legal power over the broadcaster, since it appointed the Authority and could change the law, so RTÉ could resist pressure only so far.
Once most homes had a set, television began to change everyday life and public attitudes. The effects were felt in the countryside, in the Church's influence and in how politicians won votes.
Television altered how evenings were spent, since people stayed at home to watch rather than go to dances or visit neighbours, and it reduced the isolation of rural communities.
It brought national and international news and sport into every home, so people in the countryside had access to the same culture and entertainment as city people.

Programmes on social issues exposed viewers to arguments about contraception, divorce and the church that censorship had kept out of print. This contributed to secularisation, the decline of religion's influence on public life and personal behaviour.

Church leaders such as McQuaid were concerned about the effects of television on faith and morals, but the church also used television to broadcast Mass, the Angelus (a traditional prayer) and religious programmes.
Politicians had to learn to use the medium: party leaders appeared on television to speak directly to voters, and campaigns began to focus on television appearances and image.
Viewers' reactions varied: many welcomed the new window on the world, while others, including some clergy and traditionalists, saw it as a threat to Irish values.
Coverage of the Northern conflict led to the first serious use of the government's powers over broadcasting. Two separate events, a year apart, showed how limited RTÉ's independence was.

1. On 1 October 1971 the Minister for Posts and Telegraphs, Gerry Collins, issued the first order under Section 31, directing RTÉ not to broadcast material that could promote the aims of organisations advocating violence.
RTÉ journalists protested that the order restricted reporting of the Troubles and argued that the public had a right to hear different views.
2. On 19 November 1972 the radio programme This Week broadcast an interview by Kevin O'Kelly with Seán Mac Stíofáin, chief of staff of the Provisional IRA, who was arrested the same day.
3. The government regarded the broadcast as a breach of the Section 31 order, and in late November 1972 Collins dismissed the whole RTÉ Authority and appointed a new one.
4. O'Kelly was later prosecuted and jailed for refusing to identify Mac Stíofáin's voice in court.
The sacking caused protests by journalists and in the Oireachtas (the Irish parliament), and it raised the question of whether a state broadcaster could report freely.
The order was renewed and widened in 1976 under Conor Cruise O'Brien, then Minister for Posts and Telegraphs, and it was not renewed in 1994.
Byrne was the presenter of The Late Late Show and the best-known broadcaster in Ireland for decades. He is both a participant in the change of the 1960s and a figure that historians use to judge it.
Gay Byrne was born in Dublin in 1934, worked in Britain in the 1950s and then returned to Irish radio and television, becoming a presenter on Telefís Éireann in its first years.
He presented The Late Late Show from 1962 to 1999 and a radio programme from the early 1970s, which gave him a wide audience in every part of the country.

He was a participant in the change of the 1960s: his questions to guests and audience on sex, marriage and religion set the agenda for debate, and he hosted the 1966 episode and handled the controversy.
He generally avoided taking sides, presenting himself as a neutral host, yet his willingness to air subjects that the church or the government preferred to avoid had a liberalising effect.
Contemporaries were divided: many welcomed him as a modern voice, while others, including some clergy and traditionalists, attacked his programme as a danger to morals.

Historians regard him as a major influence on how Irish people talked about sexuality, the church and social issues, while noting that he was also shaped by changes already under way, so television reflected change as well as causing it. He died in 2019.
People disagreed about what RTÉ was for. Each group judged it by its own interests, and historians now weigh these views against one another.
The government and Lemass: RTÉ should help to modernise the country, explain official policy and support national aims, and ministers expected a degree of cooperation from its Authority.
RTÉ journalists and producers: a national broadcaster should be free to investigate and criticise, and many saw ministerial pressure as censorship.

The Catholic Church: television was a powerful influence on the young that needed to be watched, and bishops and priests objected to some programmes, though the church also valued the airtime given to religion.

Language activists: Irish-language output was too small a share of the schedule, and imported English-language programmes, mostly from Britain and the United States, risked weakening the language further.
Rural viewers: programmes such as The Riordans showed their own lives, while others thought the city-based producers misrepresented the countryside.
Politicians outside government: opposition parties complained of bias in favour of the government, and some felt that the Authority was too ready to give way to ministers.
Robert Savage, in A Loss of Innocence? Television and Irish Society, 1960-72 (2010), argues that television reflected changes already under way and also accelerated them.

John Horgan, in Broadcasting and Public Life: RTÉ News and Current Affairs, 1926-1997 (2004), shows that the relationship between the state and the broadcaster was complicated rather than simply one of control.
The best way to judge RTÉ is to take the three verbs in turn and set the achievements against the limits. Examiners reward a clear judgement backed by named programmes and events with dates.
Entertained: it brought sport, drama, light entertainment and music to a national audience, and many programmes, such as The Riordans (1965) and The Late Late Show (1962), were hugely popular.

Challenged: current affairs and chat shows questioned authority and exposed issues that were taboo, such as contraception, poverty and the Northern conflict, as in Seven Days and the 1966 Late Late Show episode.

Changed: viewers had a wider view of the world, attitudes to church and state became more questioning, and the habit of national debate grew, which marks a move towards liberalisation and secularisation.

Limits: the government held strong powers, and Section 31 (1971) and the dismissal of the Authority (1972) showed that independence was fragile, while Irish-language programmes struggled for audiences.
Contemporary view: viewers welcomed the entertainment and new voices, while the church and government saw risks in the programmes.

Later view: historians argue that television both entertained and challenged, and that it sped up changes in attitudes to religion, sexuality and authority, while acknowledging that television was one cause among several.
Other causes of change mattered too: education, emigration, EEC entry and the economy all helped to alter attitudes, so television should not be given all the credit.

To understand the settlement of 1815 you need to know what it was reacting to. Napoleon had spread revolutionary ideas across Europe, and the victors wanted to undo his work and make sure it could not happen again.

The French Revolution and Napoleon spread liberal ideas (written constitutions, elected parliaments) and national ideas (that a people sharing a language and history should form a state), which unsettled the rulers who had fought him.

Napoleon dissolved the Holy Roman Empire in 1806 and set up the Confederation of the Rhine the same year, so Germany was reorganised before 1815 and the old order could not simply be switched back on.
