Napoleon was beaten at the Battle of Leipzig (the Battle of the Nations) in October 1813. The first Treaty of Paris (30 May 1814) left France roughly its 1792 frontiers.

Napoleon escaped from Elba in March 1815 (the Hundred Days) and was finally beaten at Waterloo on 18 June 1815. The second Treaty of Paris (20 November 1815) then reduced France to roughly its 1790 frontiers, imposed an indemnity of 700 million francs and left an allied army of occupation.
The great powers of 1815 were Austria, Britain, Prussia and Russia, with defeated France soon readmitted to their company.

The Habsburg (Austrian) Empire was a dynastic, multinational state ruled by one family. Its peoples included Germans, Hungarians (Magyars), Czechs, Slovaks, Poles, Croats, Serbs, Slovenes, Romanians and Italians, so nationalism threatened to break it apart.
Four ideas run through the whole period. Metternich's system makes sense only as conservatism and autocracy defending themselves against liberalism and nationalism.

Liberalism means constitutions, elected parliaments, civil liberties such as a free press and free speech, and limits on rulers. It was supported mainly by the educated middle class and students, which is why universities became centres of trouble.

Nationalism means that a people sharing a language, culture and history should have its own state. For Germans and Italians it meant unity; for Greeks, Belgians and Poles it meant independence from foreign rule.

Autocracy means rule by one person with unlimited power and no constitution or elected body. In practice Austria, Russia and Prussia were autocracies, so liberal demands for constitutions challenged them directly.

Conservatism was Metternich's own belief that monarchy, aristocracy, the Church, tradition and hierarchy are the basis of order. He therefore saw liberals and nationalists as threats to society itself, not just to his government.
The powers that defeated Napoleon met at Vienna to redraw the map of Europe. They wanted to contain France, restore the old order and prevent another bid for European domination.
The Congress met from autumn 1814, as the delegations gathered between September and November 1814, and its Final Act was signed on 9 June 1815, nine days before Waterloo (18 June 1815).

The leading delegates were Metternich for Austria, Castlereagh for Britain (Wellington replaced him in early 1815), Tsar Alexander I for Russia, Hardenberg for Prussia and Talleyrand for defeated France. The first four are the Big Four, with Talleyrand as the fifth delegate.
Metternich was Austrian foreign minister (from 1809) at the Congress and hosted it at Vienna, so he dominated the talks. He became state chancellor only in 1821.

The aims were to contain France, restore legitimate rulers, create a balance of power, reward the victors and prevent revolution. The last aim explains why the powers ignored the demands of liberals and nationalists.

Two principles guided the settlement. Legitimacy meant putting back the rulers Napoleon had removed, and the balance of power meant that no single state should be strong enough to dominate Europe again.

Legitimacy: rulers deposed by Napoleon were restored. Louis XVIII returned in France (1814), Ferdinand VII in Spain (1814) and Ferdinand IV (later Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies) in Naples (1815). The Pope regained the Papal States.

Balance of power: a ring of buffer states was built around France so that it could not expand again. This ring included the Kingdom of the Netherlands, enlarged with Belgium (the former Austrian Netherlands), and Piedmont-Sardinia, strengthened by gaining Genoa.
Prussia was placed on the Rhine so it could guard against France, and Switzerland's neutrality was guaranteed in 1815, completing the barrier against France.
Britain, represented by Castlereagh, favoured a moderate peace that did not humiliate France, because a resentful France would be a lasting danger to the balance.
The victors were rewarded with territory, mostly in the places that would block France or balance each other. The gains of Austria, Prussia and Russia shaped central Europe for decades.
Austria gave up the Austrian Netherlands but gained Lombardy-Venetia in northern Italy, and also the Tyrol, Salzburg and the Illyrian provinces and Dalmatia on the Adriatic coast.
Habsburg relatives ruled Tuscany and Modena, and Parma went to Marie-Louise (Napoleon's Habsburg wife), so Austria dominated the Italian peninsula either directly or through relatives.

Prussia gained the Rhineland, Westphalia, about two-fifths of Saxony and Swedish Pomerania. Holding the Rhineland made Prussia the guardian of the Rhine frontier against France, the 'watch on the Rhine'.
Russia gained most of the Duchy of Warsaw as the Kingdom of Poland (Congress Poland), with the Tsar as its king.
Britain kept colonies and bases taken during the wars: Malta, the Cape Colony, Heligoland and a protectorate over the Ionian Islands. These gave its navy bases and secured sea routes.
Italy shows the settlement's priorities clearly. Old rulers and Austrian power mattered more to the diplomats than the wishes of the peoples being governed.

Italy after 1815 was divided into separate states, not a nation. Austria dominated it through Lombardy-Venetia and its Habsburg relatives, the Papal States were restored to the Pope, and Piedmont was strengthened by Genoa as a barrier against France.
Nationalist and liberal hopes awakened by the French Revolution and Napoleon were ignored. Germans, Italians, Poles and Belgians were placed under rulers chosen by the great powers.
Judgement of the settlement: it kept the peace among the great powers, but it ignored liberal and national feeling, so it stored up trouble that later broke out in 1820, 1830 and 1848.
Napoleon had destroyed the old German structure, and the Congress had to put something in its place. It chose a loose league of rulers, not a nation-state, which suited Austria.

The Federal Act (June 1815, signed on 8 June) replaced the Holy Roman Empire, dissolved in 1806, with a German Confederation (Bund) of 39 sovereign states. Counts vary slightly with later changes, but 39 is the figure to use.

Its only institution was a Diet (Bundestag) at Frankfurt, made up of delegates sent by the member governments, with Austria presiding. There was no elected national parliament, so ordinary Germans had no voice in it.

Important decisions needed large majorities or unanimity, and the member states kept their own rulers and armies. This meant the Bund could act only when Austria and Prussia agreed (Austro-Prussian dualism).
Its main purpose was the security of its members against France and against revolution, not German unity, which is why it gave Germans no national institutions.
Article 13 of the Federal Act promised each state a constitution with assemblies of estates. Saxe-Weimar (1816), Bavaria (1818), Baden (1818) and Württemberg (1819) granted constitutions.
Austria granted none, and Prussia's king, who had promised a constitution in 1815, did not grant one. This angered liberals, who felt the promise of Article 13 had been broken.
Austria and Prussia were the two dominant members, and their rivalry shaped German politics until 1866.
After the settlement the powers wanted a way to defend it. Two alliances were signed in 1815, and they are easily confused because they had very different purposes.
The Holy Alliance (26 September 1815) was proposed by Alexander I and signed by Russia, Austria and Prussia. It pledged rulers to govern by Christian principles, and Britain refused to join.

Castlereagh called the Holy Alliance 'a piece of sublime mysticism and nonsense' and Metternich called it 'a loud-sounding nothing'. Yet Metternich used it to bind the eastern monarchies together, so it came to stand for the eastern autocracies.

The Quadruple Alliance (20 November 1815, the same day as the second Treaty of Paris) was the working treaty. Britain, Austria, Prussia and Russia bound themselves to uphold the settlement, keep France in check and meet periodically.
Those periodic meetings gave birth to the Congress System, the series of congresses of 1818–1822 at which the great powers managed crises together.
The congresses began as cooperation among the victors, but they turned into a tool for crushing revolutions. Britain would not follow that path, and the split ended the system.
Aix-la-Chapelle (1818) ended the allied occupation of France and admitted France to the Concert of Europe, making the Quadruple Alliance a Quintuple Alliance.

Troppau (1820): Austria, Prussia and Russia signed the Troppau Protocol, claiming the right to intervene against revolutions that threatened other states. Britain refused, and France did not sign. Castlereagh's State Paper of May 1820 rejected general intervention.

Laibach (1821) applied the Troppau principle: Austria was authorised to restore Ferdinand in Naples, and Austrian troops crushed the Neapolitan revolution in 1821, and also the Piedmontese rising of the same year.
Verona (1822): the eastern powers approved French intervention in Spain. France invaded in 1823 and restored Ferdinand VII as an absolute ruler. Wellington represented Britain at Verona and withdrew.
Castlereagh died (suicide) in August 1822, and George Canning became British foreign secretary. Canning broke with the system and recognised the Latin American republics in the 1820s.
After Britain's withdrawal, what remained was an alliance of the three eastern autocracies (Austria, Prussia and Russia).

Metternich's aim was to preserve the 1815 settlement and the multinational Habsburg Empire, which liberalism and nationalism threatened to break apart. At home that meant autocracy backed by watchfulness.
His aims were to preserve the 1815 settlement and the Habsburg Empire, to resist liberalism and nationalism, and to keep Austria's leadership in Germany and Italy.

Austria was an autocracy under Emperor Francis I (ruled to 1835) and then Ferdinand I (1835–1848), who was mentally unfit. There was no constitution or parliament, and power rested with the emperor, his ministers, the army and the bureaucracy.
Under Ferdinand I government was carried on by a State Conference in which Metternich's rival, Count Kolowrat, was powerful, so Metternich was not in sole control at home.
Inside Austria, police, informers, the opening of letters and strict censorship of books, newspapers and the theatre watched and silenced critics, so liberal ideas could spread only in secret.
Metternich needed a reason to extend his methods from Austria to the whole of Germany. The murder of a conservative writer in 1819 gave him one.

In March 1819 the conservative dramatist August von Kotzebue was murdered by Karl Sand, a Burschenschaft (student fraternity) member. Metternich used the murder to argue that radical students were a danger to every German government.
Ministers met at Carlsbad in August 1819 and the Diet adopted the Decrees in September 1819. Friedrich von Gentz helped Metternich draft them.
The Decrees banned the Burschenschaften, put each university under a government curator (supervisor), and allowed liberal professors and students to be dismissed or expelled.
They also imposed censorship on newspapers and shorter publications (under 20 printed sheets), so that new liberal ideas could not easily be printed.
A Central Investigating Commission at Mainz was set up under the Decrees to hunt down revolutionary conspiracies across the German states.
The Hambach Festival of May 1832 alarmed the princes. The Diet responded by tightening the controls of 1819 even further.

The Six Articles (28 June 1832), passed by the Diet after the Hambach Festival, reasserted the princes' authority: state parliaments could not withhold taxes to force concessions, and the Diet could intervene in states where order broke down.

Further measures in July 1832 (the Ten Articles) banned political associations, public meetings and the display of political colours, and tightened press controls. Banning colours was meant to stop displays such as the black, red and gold flags shown at Hambach.
Metternich could not hold Austria's position by Austrian strength alone. He relied on the congresses to justify intervention, and on two other powers to make it work.

Abroad, Metternich used the congresses and the alliance with Russia and Prussia to justify intervention, and Austrian troops crushed risings in Naples and Piedmont (1821) and in Modena, Parma and the Papal Legations (1831).
The system relied on Prussia's cooperation inside the Bund and on Russia's support in Europe, so it was weakened when either went its own way.

Seen together, so that the two sides explain each other, the system had an international side (the Congress System and intervention) and an internal side (censorship, police, the Carlsbad Decrees and the Bund).

The first challenges to the settlement came from liberal and nationalist students and from army-led revolts in the south of Europe. Metternich could crush all of them, but they showed that the old order was not secure.

The first Burschenschaft was founded at Jena in June 1815. These student fraternities spread liberal nationalism, and adopted black, red and gold, linked to the Lützow Free Corps of the war of liberation and later the German national colours.

The Wartburg Festival (18 October 1817) gathered about 500 students to mark 300 years since Luther's Reformation (1517) and the fourth anniversary of Leipzig. The students called for German unity, and conservative books were burned.

The revolutions of 1820–21 broke out in Spain (January 1820, an army rising that restored the 1812 constitution), Portugal (1820), Naples (July 1820) and Piedmont (March 1821). Kings were forced to grant constitutions.
These revolutions were suppressed. Austrian troops restored absolutism in Naples and Piedmont in 1821, and French troops did so in Spain in 1823.

The Greek revolt against the Ottoman Empire was different from the revolutions in southern Europe, because the great powers themselves ended up helping the rebels. This went directly against Metternich's wishes.
The Greek rising began in 1821. Lord Byron died at Missolonghi in April 1824, and his death boosted philhellenism (enthusiasm for the Greek cause) across Europe.
Britain, France and Russia intervened on the rebels' side, for example when their fleets destroyed the Turkish-Egyptian fleet at the Battle of Navarino on 20 October 1827.
The London Protocol (February 1830) recognised Greek independence, and the Convention of London (1832) made Greece a monarchy under Otto of Bavaria.
Metternich had opposed this support for rebels against a legitimate ruler. The case showed that the powers could no longer be held to a common line against revolution.
The year 1830 was a larger blow than anything in the 1820s, because revolution succeeded in the west and rocked the settlement's borders. Only the eastern risings were crushed.

The July Revolution in France (July 1830, the 'Three Glorious Days') overthrew Charles X after his July Ordinances. Louis-Philippe, Duke of Orléans, became 'King of the French'. Charles X was the last king of the senior Bourbon line.

Revolt broke out in Brussels in August 1830, separating Belgium from the Netherlands and breaching the 1815 settlement, which had joined them. The London Conference (1830–31) recognised Belgian independence, and Leopold of Saxe-Coburg became Leopold I in July 1831.
The Treaty of London (1839) guaranteed Belgian neutrality, so the great powers accepted the change.
The November Uprising (November 1830) in Russian Poland was crushed in 1831, and Nicholas I replaced the Polish constitution with the Organic Statute in 1832.
Risings in Modena, Parma and the Papal Legations in February 1831 were put down by Austrian troops, so Metternich's armies were again the means of repression in Italy.
The unrest of 1830 reached Germany too. Some princes gave way, and in 1832 a mass festival made the demand for unity and liberty public.
Several states gained constitutions after the 1830 unrest: Saxony and Hesse-Kassel (1831), Brunswick (1832) and Hanover (1833).

In 1837 the new king of Hanover cancelled the constitution, and seven Göttingen professors who protested, among them the Grimm brothers, were dismissed (the Göttingen Seven). This showed the limits of liberal gains.
The Hambach Festival (27 May 1832) took place at Hambach Castle in the Bavarian Palatinate and brought about 20,000–30,000 people together under black, red and gold flags.
The crowds demanded German unity, a free press and popular sovereignty (the idea that power comes from the people, not the ruler). This was what prompted the Six Articles and the July 1832 measures.
While Metternich policed ideas, Prussia was quietly uniting Germany's economy. This gave it an advantage that Austria could not match.
Prussia's Customs Law of May 1818 abolished internal duties across its scattered territories and set a low external tariff.
Neighbouring states joined Prussia's system. The treaties were agreed in 1833, and the Zollverein (German Customs Union) came into force on 1 January 1834 with 18 states. Baden joined in 1835.
Members traded freely with each other behind a common external tariff and shared the customs revenue in proportion to population.

Austria stayed outside, because its protected industries and separate tariff system could not fit a low-tariff union. Austria was never a member, and Metternich feared the union was building Prussian influence.
Leadership of the Zollverein gave Prussia economic leadership of Germany and accustomed the smaller states to looking to Berlin rather than Vienna.
The system survived the shocks of 1830, but the revolution of 1848 brought it down within days. Economic distress in the 1840s had left many people ready to revolt.
News of the February 1848 revolution in Paris, together with the economic distress of the 1840s, sparked demonstrations in German and Austrian cities.
On 13 March 1848 students and workers demonstrated in Vienna and troops fired on the crowd. The court made Metternich resign that evening, and he fled, reaching England.
His fall removed the main defender of the 1815 settlement, and revolution spread across the Habsburg lands and the German states.
Prince Clemens von Metternich, a Rhineland aristocrat, guided Habsburg foreign policy from 1809 to 1848 and gave his name to the conservative order of 1815–1848.

Born in Koblenz on 15 May 1773, he studied at Strasbourg and Mainz and married Eleonore von Kaunitz (1795), granddaughter of the former chancellor Kaunitz. French revolutionary armies took his family's Rhineland estates, which shaped his lifelong hatred of revolution.

He was ambassador to Saxony (Dresden, 1801), Prussia (Berlin, 1803) and France (Paris, 1806), and arranged the marriage of Marie-Louise to Napoleon (1810). He was Austrian foreign minister from October 1809, was made a prince in 1813 and became state chancellor in 1821.
He was a direct participant: he hosted and dominated the Congress of Vienna, led the congresses, drafted the Carlsbad Decrees and the 1832 measures, and sent Austrian troops into Italy.

He believed that liberalism and nationalism would destroy the multinational Habsburg Empire, so he defended monarchy, legitimacy and the balance of power. He denied that there was a Metternich system, seeing his policy as the defence of the natural order.
His policy was shaped by events he could not control: Greek independence, the 1830 revolutions and the Zollverein all showed the limits of his power, and 1848 ended his career.
In 1847 he dismissed Italy as 'a geographical expression', meaning it was not a nation.
After exile in England (1848) and Brussels he returned to Vienna in 1851 and died there on 11 June 1859. His memoirs (papers edited by his son Richard) were published from 1880.
Contemporaries: conservative rulers, including the Tsar, praised him as the guardian of peace, while liberals and nationalists saw him as the symbol of reaction, censorship and police rule.

Historians: Heinrich von Srbik (1925) and Henry Kissinger (A World Restored, 1957) praised him for the stable peace he built. Paul Schroeder (1962) was critical, calling his policy mere repression,. German nationalist historians such as Treitschke saw him as the enemy of German unity, and Alan Sked (2008) defended him.

A strong answer states a clear judgement at the start and then weighs success against limits with dates. A useful split is short term against long term, and international peace against domestic repression.
Success: the great powers fought no general war among themselves between 1815 and the Crimean War (1853–56).
Limit: the peace owed much to exhaustion after the long wars and to Britain's naval power, not only to Metternich.
Success: revolutions in Italy (1821, 1831) and liberal movements in Germany (1819, 1832) were crushed, the Habsburg Empire survived intact until 1848, and Austria kept the presidency of the Bund.
Limit: the Congress System broke up in the 1820s because Britain withdrew, and Greek and Belgian independence changed the 1815 map.
Limit: Prussia's Zollverein built a German economic unit without Austria, laying a foundation for Prussian leadership.
Limit: it was repression without reform, with no Austrian constitution and the nationalities unsatisfied, so the causes of unrest remained.
Overall: the system delayed liberal and national change for over thirty years but did not remove its causes, and it collapsed within days of the Vienna rising of March 1848.

Contemporary against later views: conservatives saw a guardian of peace and liberals a symbol of reaction, while later historians divide between Srbik, Kissinger and Sked in his defence and Schroeder against him.
In 1848 revolutions broke out in one capital after another within a few weeks. Germany was one part of a Europe-wide wave, so it helps to know the pattern before looking at the German case.
The first rising came in Palermo in January 1848. Then Paris rose on 22-24 February, when King Louis-Philippe fell and the Second Republic was declared; this news was the spark for the rest.

The risings then came fast: Vienna on 13 March, Budapest on 15 March, Venice on 17 March, and Berlin and Milan on 18 March (Milan's Five Days of street fighting ran 18-22 March). Prague's rising came later, in June.

The common causes were the crop failures and economic depression of 1846-47, which made ordinary people desperate, and middle-class liberal demands for constitutions (written limits on a ruler's power).

Nationalism (the wish of a people with a shared language and culture to form its own state) drove Germans, Italians, Hungarians and Czechs alike, so each rising had a national as well as a liberal side.
The example of Paris spread so quickly because newspapers, railways and the telegraph carried the news within days, which encouraged crowds elsewhere to press their own rulers.
Britain and Russia escaped revolution in 1848. By 1849 nearly every rising had been defeated by the old monarchies and their armies, a pattern the German case follows.
To understand 1848 in Germany you need to know what the revolutionaries wanted to change. Germany was not one country but a loose league of states.

The German Confederation, set up in 1815, was a loose league of German states (39 at its foundation) with a Diet, its assembly of state delegates, at Frankfurt under Austrian presidency. Austria and Prussia were the two great powers inside it.

Metternich's system of repression, meaning censorship, police spies and the Carlsbad Decrees of 1819, had kept liberal and national movements down. His fall in March 1848 removed the system's chief defender.
The Zollverein (customs union) of 1834 had already linked most German states economically under Prussia, with Austria outside it, so many Germans were used to thinking of a Germany without Austria.

The German revolution grew out of economic distress, liberal frustration with the system of 1815 and the wish for a united German nation. Each cause affected a different group, and news from Paris in February 1848 acted as the trigger.
Potato blight from 1845 and poor grain harvests in 1846 and 1847 sharply raised food prices, so the poor went hungry and hunger riots broke out in many areas.

A commercial and industrial depression in 1847 brought bankruptcies and unemployment. It hit artisans (skilled craftsmen) already threatened by factory competition; the Silesian weavers' rising of 1844 had shown the desperation of hand workers.
Liberals, mostly educated middle-class men, wanted constitutions, freedom of the press and assembly, trial by jury and a German national parliament.
Nationalists wanted a German nation state, but disagreed whether it should include the German lands of the Habsburg Empire, the territories ruled by Austria's emperor.
Peasants in the south and west wanted an end to the remaining feudal dues and services owed to landlords, which were a burden left over from the old order.
Liberal opposition had grown in the southern state parliaments and in Prussia's United Diet of 1847, which refused to vote a loan for a railway without constitutional concessions from the king.
The trigger was the news of the February revolution in Paris, which showed that a monarch could be overthrown and encouraged all these groups to act at once.
Within weeks of the Paris revolution, rulers across the German states gave way to crowds rather than risk being overthrown. The pattern was protest, then concession.
A mass meeting at Mannheim in Baden on 27 February 1848 demanded a free press, trial by jury, citizens' militias and a German parliament, and these March demands spread across the states.
Rulers appointed liberal March ministries, promised constitutions and lifted censorship in Baden, Württemberg, Hesse, Saxony and Hanover, because they feared a revolution like the one in Paris.
In Bavaria, Ludwig I, already discredited by his affair with the dancer Lola Montez, abdicated in March 1848.
In Berlin, troops fired on a crowd on 18 March, and a night of barricade fighting left about 200 to 300 civilians dead (sources differ).
On 19 March Frederick William IV withdrew the troops from Berlin and was forced to bare his head before the bodies of the dead in the palace courtyard, a public sign of surrender.
On 21 March he rode through Berlin wearing the black, red and gold colours of German nationalism and declared that Prussia would merge into Germany.

He appointed a liberal ministry under the Rhineland businessmen Camphausen and Hansemann and called a Prussian National Assembly, elected in May 1848. Do not confuse it with the all-German assembly at Frankfurt.
Peasant risings in the south-west in March forced governments to begin abolishing feudal dues.
The liberals who now held influence needed a way to create a German parliament. They began with an informal meeting, which also showed the split between moderates and radicals.
The Vorparlament (pre-parliament), a self-appointed gathering of liberal politicians, met at Frankfurt from 31 March to 3 April 1848. It was not the Frankfurt National Assembly, which came later.

It rejected the radicals' call for a republic and arranged elections to a national assembly by broad manhood suffrage (the vote for adult men), although each state set its own rules and some excluded servants and men on poor relief.
Disappointed radicals in Baden, led by Friedrich Hecker and Gustav Struve, launched a republican rising in April 1848, which federal troops defeated at Kandern on 20 April.
The elected assembly met in May 1848 and was meant to write a constitution for all Germany. Its membership explains both its quality and its weakness.
The Frankfurt National Assembly opened on 18 May 1848 in the Paulskirche (St Paul's Church) in Frankfurt.

About 800 men sat at some point, including substitutes, because membership changed over time. Most were lawyers, judges, civil servants, teachers and professors, so it was nicknamed the professors' parliament.
Craftsmen were few, and there were almost no peasants or workers among the deputies, which means the poor were barely represented and had little reason to defend the Assembly.
The Assembly elected Heinrich von Gagern, a moderate liberal from Hesse-Darmstadt, as its president, which shows that moderates led it.
Deputies formed clubs named after their meeting places, the forerunners of German political parties, broadly a right, a liberal centre and a democratic left.

On 29 June 1848 it chose Archduke John of Austria as Reichsverweser (imperial regent) at the head of a Provisional Central Power. This government had no army, civil service or tax revenue of its own, so it relied on the state governments.
The Assembly had to decide what rights Germans should have and which territory the new Germany should cover. The first was settled, but the second divided it.
The Basic Rights of the German People, passed in December 1848, guaranteed equality before the law, freedom of the press, speech, religion, assembly and movement, and trial by jury.
They abolished the nobility as a privileged estate, landlords' private courts and feudal dues, and abolished the death penalty except under martial law.
Grossdeutsch (Greater German) meant a Germany including the German-speaking Habsburg lands. Catholics, Austrians and many southerners favoured it.
Kleindeutsch (Lesser German) meant a Germany united under Prussia without Austria. Gagern and most Protestant northern liberals favoured it.

The Grossdeutsch plan failed because Prince Felix Schwarzenberg, Austria's chief minister from November 1848, insisted, finally in March 1849, that the whole multinational Habsburg Empire must enter any German state or none of it would.

The Assembly also voted in 1848 to include part of the Prussian province of Posen, where Poles were the majority, and Czech leaders refused to send deputies to Frankfurt. Liberal nationalism could deny other nations' rights.
A quarrel over two border duchies tested the Assembly's power and exposed that it could not enforce its will.

The duchies of Schleswig and Holstein were ruled by the King of Denmark. Holstein, wholly German, belonged to the German Confederation, while Schleswig, with a mixed Danish and German population, did not.
When the new Danish king, Frederick VII, moved to incorporate Schleswig into Denmark in March 1848, the German population rose and set up a provisional government at Kiel.
Prussian troops under General Wrangel invaded on the Confederation's behalf, which the Assembly hailed as a national war.
Under pressure from Britain and Russia, Prussia signed the Malmö armistice in August 1848 without consulting Frankfurt.
The Assembly first rejected the armistice and then, having no army of its own, accepted it on 16 September 1848, which showed its dependence on Prussia.

Radicals rioted in Frankfurt on 18 September and murdered two conservative deputies, Prince Felix Lichnowsky and General Hans von Auerswald. The Assembly had to be saved by Prussian and Austrian troops.
Fighting resumed in 1849, but Prussia made peace with Denmark in 1850, the duchies' army was defeated at Idstedt in July 1850, and the London Protocol of 1852 confirmed the Danish king's rule.
By late 1848 the old governments had regained control of their capitals through force, while the liberals at Frankfurt were still debating.
In June 1848 the Austrian general Windischgrätz bombarded Prague and crushed the Czech rising, and in July Radetzky defeated Piedmont at Custoza.
A radical rising in Vienna in October 1848 was crushed when Windischgrätz and the Croatian commander Jelačić retook the city on 31 October.

Robert Blum, a radical Frankfurt deputy from Saxony, was shot in Vienna on 9 November 1848, despite his immunity as a member of the Assembly, which showed how little the Assembly's protection was worth.
Schwarzenberg became Austrian chief minister in November, and on 2 December 1848 the 18-year-old Franz Joseph replaced Emperor Ferdinand.
In Berlin, Frederick William IV appointed a conservative ministry under Count Brandenburg, and General Wrangel's troops entered the city on 10 November 1848 without resistance.
On 5 December 1848 the king dissolved the Prussian National Assembly and imposed a constitution of his own, which kept royal control of the army and ministers.

In May 1849 Prussia brought in the three-class franchise, which divided voters into three classes by the taxes they paid. Each class chose a third of the electors, so a small wealthy minority had a vastly greater say than the poor majority.
With Austria and Prussia recovering, the Assembly finished its constitution and offered the crown to Prussia's king. His answer decided the revolution's fate.

The Frankfurt constitution, completed on 27-28 March 1849, created a federal German Empire with a hereditary emperor, a lower house elected by manhood suffrage and an upper house representing the states.
On 28 March 1849 the Assembly elected Frederick William IV Emperor of the Germans by 290 votes, with 248 deputies abstaining.

Frederick William gave an evasive answer to the Assembly's delegation on 3 April and formally refused the crown on 28 April 1849. He would not accept a crown from an elected assembly rather than from his fellow princes, and he feared Austria's reaction.
In private he described it as a crown from the gutter, tainted by revolution.
Austria rejected the constitution and recalled its deputies in April 1849, because a German empire without Austria threatened its position.
Twenty-eight smaller states accepted the constitution by mid-April, but Prussia, Bavaria, Saxony and Hanover rejected it, so it never came into force.
After the crown was refused, radicals tried to force the princes to accept the constitution, and Prussian troops put them down.
In May 1849 radicals rose in Saxony, the Palatinate and Baden to force the princes to accept the constitution. Richard Wagner and Mikhail Bakunin took part in the Dresden rising.

Prussian troops crushed the Dresden rising in May and the Baden and Palatinate risings by July 1849, when the fortress of Rastatt surrendered. The Baden campaign was commanded by Prince William of Prussia, the later William I.
Some rebels were executed and many imprisoned, and thousands fled, so the radical movement lost many of its leaders.
The moderates left Frankfurt, and about 100 radical deputies moved to Stuttgart as a rump parliament (a small remnant of the Assembly) until Württemberg troops dispersed them on 18 June 1849.
Thousands of revolutionaries emigrated, many to the United States, where these Forty-Eighters included Friedrich Hecker and Carl Schurz.
Prussia then tried to gain the unity the Assembly had failed to win, but Austria was strong enough to stop it.

The Erfurt Union plan, drawn up by Joseph von Radowitz in 1849-50, aimed at a Kleindeutsch union under Prussia by agreement of the princes, and an Erfurt Parliament met in March-April 1850. It is not the Zollverein of 1834.
Austria, backed by Russia, threatened war, and by the Punctation of Olmütz (29 November 1850) Prussia abandoned the union. Prussians remembered it as the humiliation of Olmütz, a defeat for Prussia.
The old Confederation and its Diet were restored in 1851 under Austrian presidency, and the Diet repealed the Basic Rights that year.
Otto von Bismarck was Prussia's delegate at the Diet in Frankfurt from 1851, so he saw Austrian power at close quarters.
The revolution failed for several linked reasons. The strongest answers weigh them: the Assembly lacked force while the rulers kept theirs, and the other causes follow from that.
The Frankfurt Assembly had no army, money or administration, so it depended on the very governments it was trying to limit. The Malmö armistice and the September riots showed this.
The rulers kept control of their armies and bureaucracies, which stayed loyal and were used to retake Prague, Vienna and Berlin once the shock of March had passed.
Liberals were divided from radicals and workers: middle-class deputies feared a social revolution and a republic more than they feared the princes.
Peasants lost interest once governments abolished most feudal dues in 1848, as Austria did in September 1848, so they stopped supporting the revolution.
Months of debate on the Basic Rights and the Grossdeutsch-Kleindeutsch question gave Austria and Prussia time to recover.
National rivalries with Danes, Poles and Czechs split the revolutionaries and gave the Habsburg army willing allies, such as Jelačić's Croats.
Austria recovered and Russia backed the old order; Russia also crushed Hungary in 1849.
The refusal of the crown by Frederick William IV left the constitution without the one state strong enough to enforce it.
Judging 1848 means weighing what it achieved against what it failed to do, and comparing how people saw it then and later.
Failure: no united Germany was created, the Basic Rights were repealed by the restored Diet in 1851, and the old Confederation returned.
Achievement: feudal dues and remaining serfdom were abolished, so peasants gained a lasting benefit, and Prussia kept a constitution and parliament after 1850, however limited.

Failure: liberals were discredited as impractical, and many concluded that unity would come only through Prussian power, not speeches and majority votes, a lesson Bismarck confirmed in his 'blood and iron' speech of 1862.
Achievement: the Assembly was Germany's first national parliament, created political parties and provided a model for the Weimar constitution of 1919 and the Basic Law of 1949.

Contemporary views: conservatives celebrated the restoration of order, while radicals and exiles, including Marx and Engels, blamed the cowardice of the liberal middle class. Marx edited the Neue Rheinische Zeitung in Cologne in 1848-49.
Later views: A. J. P. Taylor wrote in 1945 that 'German history reached its turning-point and failed to turn', linked to the Sonderweg idea of a German special path away from liberal democracy.
More recent historians stress the revolution's lasting gains in political culture and participation.

To follow how the German lands reached empire in 1871, you need the starting point: a loose league of states, two rival great powers and a lesson learned from failure in 1848–50. Every later block builds on this.

The German Confederation, set up in 1815 at the Congress of Vienna, was a loose league of sovereign states with a Diet (an assembly of state delegates) at Frankfurt, presided over by Austria. Austria and Prussia were the two great powers in it, so their rivalry decided its future.

In 1849 Frederick William IV of Prussia refused the imperial crown offered by the Frankfurt Parliament (the elected assembly of 1848–49 that tried to unite Germany). Nationalists drew the lesson that unity would need Prussian power, not parliamentary votes.
The point to carry forward is that votes had failed and Prussian power was the alternative.

At the Punctation of Olmütz (November 1850) Prussia abandoned its Erfurt Union plan (a Prussian-led union of German states) under Austrian and Russian pressure. This humiliated Prussia; the Confederation and Diet were restored in 1851, and Bismarck became Prussia's delegate at the Diet that year.

The choice facing Germans was Kleindeutsch (a smaller Germany without Austria, under Prussia) or Grossdeutsch (a larger Germany including Austria). The events of 1866 settled the question in favour of Kleindeutsch.

After the failure of 1848, the balance between Prussia and Austria within the German Confederation turned on economic power and on the ability of each state to manage its own affairs. Prussia grew stronger and Austria weaker, which is why Prussia could later challenge it.

The Zollverein (the German customs union, in force from 1834 under Prussian leadership) included almost all German states except Austria by the 1850s; Hanover joined in 1854. It gave Prussia control of a large common market.
Tariff revenue was shared among Zollverein members, so the members were tied to Prussia economically.

The Ruhr (Rhineland-Westphalia) and Silesia, both Prussian, provided coal and iron. Rapid railway building from the 1840s linked the Prussian industrial regions to Berlin and to the Rhineland, so goods and, later, troops could move quickly.

Alfred Krupp's cast-steel works at Essen in the Ruhr, expanded rapidly from the 1850s, produced railway materials and steel guns. It symbolised Prussia's industrial power because it supplied both the railways and the army.

Prussia's 1862 commercial treaty with France, made for the Zollverein, lowered tariffs and set a low-tariff course. The other Zollverein states had accepted it by 1865, a course that Austria's protectionist system (high tariffs to shield its own industry) could not match.
Austria's finances were weak and its government remained centralised and conservative, with the Habsburg monarchy heavily in debt. This left it less able to modernise or to pay for a large army.
Austria's defeat in 1859 by France and Piedmont, at the battles of Magenta and Solferino, cost it Lombardy and exposed its military weakness.
Austria had alienated Russia by its hostile neutrality towards Russia in the Crimean War (1853–56), so it lacked a friend when Prussia challenged it.

Austria's attempt to reform the Confederation, the Frankfurt Princes' Congress (Fürstentag) of August 1863 called by Emperor Franz Joseph, collapsed because William I stayed away on Bismarck's advice. Without Prussia the plan could not work.
Prussia's military strength was not automatic: it came from an army reform that provoked a fierce clash with the liberals in parliament. That clash is the setting in which Bismarck came to power.
William, the brother of Frederick William IV (who was incapacitated from 1857), became regent in 1858 and King William I in January 1861.
Roon's army reform kept three-year service, enlarged the regular army and reduced the role of the Landwehr (the citizen reserve militia). Liberals in the Landtag (the Prussian parliament) opposed it.
Albrecht von Roon, War Minister from 1859, organised the army, while Helmuth von Moltke, chief of the general staff from 1857, handled planning and command. Do not swap their roles.

The German Progressive Party (Fortschrittspartei) was founded in 1861. The liberal majority in the Prussian lower house refused to vote the army budget in 1862, so king and parliament were deadlocked.
The constitutional crisis deepened until William I considered abdicating and drew up an abdication document in September 1862.
In September 1862 William I appointed Otto von Bismarck Minister-President and Foreign Minister of Prussia to break the deadlock.
Bismarck had to govern without the parliament's consent to the budget. He justified this with a legal argument and set out his view of how Germany would be united.

On 30 September 1862, in a speech to the Budget Committee of the Landtag, Bismarck said the great questions of the day would be decided not by speeches and majority decisions, the mistake of 1848 and 1849, but by "blood and iron".
By this he meant that force, not parliamentary debate, would settle German unity.
In the same speech he argued that Germany looked not to Prussia's liberalism but to its power. This told the liberals that he would use the army, not their ideas, to unite Germany.

Bismarck used the gap theory (Lückentheorie): the constitution did not say what happened if king and parliament disagreed, so the king's government could carry on. On this reasoning his government declared it was entitled to go on collecting taxes.
Taxes were collected and the army reform was carried out without an approved budget from 1862 to 1866. The conflict lasted until the Indemnity Bill of 1866.
The first of Bismarck's three wars showed his method: act with Austria against a weaker opponent, then use the settlement to prepare the quarrel with Austria itself.

Schleswig and Holstein (with Lauenburg) were ruled by the Danish king. Holstein was German-speaking and in the Confederation, while Schleswig was mixed Danish and German and outside it, and Germans wanted links with Germany.

Christian IX became King of Denmark in November 1863 and signed the November Constitution (1863), binding Schleswig to Denmark. This broke Danish undertakings of 1851–52 that were confirmed by the London Protocol of 1852, which also settled the Danish succession, and it provoked the German states.
Bismarck chose to act with Austria rather than alone so that the issue stayed a matter for the two great powers, not for the Diet or the liberals. It also kept a later quarrel with Austria available.
Prussia and Austria invaded Denmark jointly in February 1864. Prussia stormed Düppel (Dybbøl) in April 1864 and captured the island of Als in June 1864.
By the Treaty of Vienna (October 1864) Denmark ceded Schleswig, Holstein and Lauenburg to Prussia and Austria jointly. Their future was left to be settled between the two victors.

By the Convention of Gastein (August 1865) Austria administered Holstein and Prussia Schleswig, and Prussia bought Austria's rights in Lauenburg. This divided administration only, so it was a ready-made source of dispute and set up the conflict of 1866.
Bismarck did not fight Austria until he had made sure it had no friends. Three separate diplomatic steps prepared the ground for war in 1866.

The Alvensleben Convention (February 1863) promised Prussian help to Russia against the Polish rising of 1863. Russian goodwill followed, which mattered because Austria had already lost Russian friendship in the Crimean War.
Bismarck met Napoleon III at Biarritz in October 1865, and Napoleon III remained neutral in the coming war. This freed Prussia from the risk of French intervention.
In April 1866 Prussia made an alliance with Italy that promised Venetia to Italy if Prussia won. Italy would attack Austria on a second front, so Austria faced war on two fronts.
In June 1866 Prussia declared the Gastein arrangements at an end and occupied Holstein. The Diet voted to mobilise against Prussia.

Most German states sided with Austria, including Bavaria, Saxony, Hanover, Württemberg and Hesse-Kassel. Prussia went to war against much of the Confederation, but its military and diplomatic advantages were greater.
The war was over in about seven weeks. Prussia's military superiority, not just its diplomacy, decided it, and Bismarck then chose a moderate peace to leave Austria a possible future friend.

Prussia won because of the Dreyse breech-loading needle-gun, which could be fired lying down and was faster than Austrian muzzle-loaders, and because of Moltke's planning. Moltke used railways to move armies quickly into Bohemia.

The battle of Königgrätz (also called Sadowa) in Bohemia, fought on 3 July 1866, was the decisive Prussian victory over the Austrian army under Benedek. The war lasted about seven weeks, which is why it is called the Seven Weeks' War.
Italy was beaten by Austria at Custoza (on land) and Lissa (at sea) in 1866 but still gained Venetia, thanks to Prussia's victory.

After Königgrätz, Bismarck persuaded William I and the generals to halt at the Nikolsburg preliminaries (July 1866), with no march on Vienna and no Austrian territory taken. His aim was to keep Austria as a future friend.

The Treaty of Prague (August 1866) dissolved the German Confederation and Austria accepted exclusion from German affairs. Venetia was ceded, via France, to Italy, and the Habsburg lands lay outside any German state.
Prussia annexed Hanover, Hesse-Kassel, Nassau, Frankfurt and Schleswig-Holstein in 1866.
In August 1866 Bavaria, Württemberg and Baden signed secret offensive-defensive alliances with Prussia (each promising to fight alongside it if attacked), which tied the southern states to Prussia.
Victory in 1866 changed how Prussian liberals saw Bismarck. The question of the years without a budget had to be settled, and it divided them.

The Indemnity Bill, passed by the Prussian Landtag in September 1866, asked the Landtag to approve retrospectively the years of government without an approved budget. It gave Bismarck's rule a legal cover after the event.
The Bill split the liberals into those who gave way and those who stayed in opposition.

The National Liberal Party was founded in 1867 by liberals who backed Bismarck's national policy, so many liberals accepted his leadership in return for national unification. The remaining Progressives stayed in opposition.
Prussia now had a framework to organise the north and to draw in the south. The Confederation was a step towards the Empire, built on Prussian dominance.
The North German Confederation was formed in 1867 by Prussia and the states north of the River Main, under Prussian leadership.

Its constitution, in force from 1 July 1867, made the King of Prussia president of the Confederation, with control of foreign policy and the armed forces. Bismarck was Federal Chancellor, so Prussia's king and minister ran the new union.

The Reichstag (the Confederation's parliament) was elected by universal manhood suffrage (every adult man could vote). The Bundesrat was made up of delegates of the state governments, and Prussia dominated it.

A Customs Parliament (Zollparlament) first met in 1868 with deputies from the southern states as well as the north. Southern voters returned many anti-Prussian (Catholic and particularist, meaning favouring each state's separate independence) deputies, so the south was not yet won.
France resented Prussia's rise, and Bismarck used a dispute over the Spanish throne to turn that resentment into a war in which France appeared the aggressor.

French resentment of Prussia's victory in 1866 was summed up as revenge for Sadowa. In the Luxembourg crisis of 1867 Napoleon III tried to buy Luxembourg from the King of the Netherlands; Prussian opposition stopped it, and the London Conference of 1867 made Luxembourg neutral.

In 1870 Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, from a Catholic branch of the Prussian royal family, accepted the Spanish crown, vacant since the 1868 revolution. This alarmed France, which feared encirclement by Hohenzollern rulers on two sides.
The withdrawal of Leopold's candidature was announced on 12 July 1870 after French pressure. France then demanded a guarantee that it would never be renewed.
On 13 July 1870 at Bad Ems the French ambassador Benedetti asked William I for that guarantee. William refused politely and had a report of the meeting telegraphed to Bismarck.
Bismarck shortened the report and released it to the press that evening. In its shortened form the Ems telegram made the exchange read as an insult to France.

France declared war on 19 July 1870 and appeared the aggressor. Bavaria, Württemberg and Baden joined Prussia under their treaties, while Austria, Italy and Britain stayed neutral and Russia was friendly to Prussia.
In July 1870 Bismarck published in The Times Benedetti's earlier draft treaty on French designs on Belgium, which turned British opinion against France. France was left with no ally.
Prussia's armies, with the southern states' troops beside them, won quickly. The war ended French resistance and removed Napoleon III.
Wörth and Spicheren (6 August 1870) were the first big French defeats. At Gravelotte–St Privat (18 August 1870) Prussia shut Bazaine's army in Metz.
Napoleon III had led the army to the front. At the battle of Sedan on 1 September 1870 the French were defeated, and Napoleon III and his army surrendered on 2 September 1870.

The Second Empire fell on 4 September 1870 when the Third Republic was proclaimed in Paris. Gambetta and the Government of National Defence carried on the war, and Gambetta left Paris by balloon to organise resistance in the provinces.
Bazaine surrendered Metz in October 1870. The siege of Paris lasted from September 1870 to January 1871, and the city capitulated in January 1871 and an armistice was signed on 28 January 1871.
Prussia won because of railways, superior artillery and Moltke's planning, together with the southern states' troops and France's isolation.
Victory over France let Bismarck complete unification. He brought the southern states in by treaty and staged the proclamation in the palace of the defeated enemy.
In November 1870 treaties brought Baden, Hesse-Darmstadt (south of the Main), Württemberg and Bavaria into the union. Bavaria kept special rights: its own army in peacetime, post and railways.

In late 1870 King Ludwig II of Bavaria sent the Kaiserbrief, a letter drafted by Bismarck, asking William I to accept the title of emperor. This made the offer come from a southern prince, not from Prussia.

The German Empire was proclaimed on 18 January 1871 in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles, with William I as German Emperor (Deutscher Kaiser). The date was the anniversary of the crowning of the first King in Prussia in 1701.
William was proclaimed at Versailles, in France, not in Berlin, and the title was German Emperor, not Emperor of Germany.

The Treaty of Frankfurt (10 May 1871) ended the war. It transferred Alsace (except Belfort) and north-eastern Lorraine, including Metz, to Germany and required France to pay an indemnity of five billion francs, with German occupation until it was paid.
The Empire's constitution gave Germany a parliament but kept real power with the emperor and Prussia.
The imperial constitution of April 1871 was based on the 1867 constitution. It created a federal state of 25 member states plus the Reichsland of Alsace-Lorraine.
The King of Prussia was always German Emperor, so Prussian royal power and imperial power were joined in one person. The emperor controlled the army and foreign policy.

The Reichstag was elected by manhood suffrage, but the Chancellor was appointed by and answerable to the emperor alone, not to the Reichstag. This meant the elected house could not remove the head of government.
The Bundesrat, made up of the states' governments, gave Prussia 17 of 58 votes, and 14 votes could block a constitutional change. Prussia alone could therefore veto any amendment.

Prussia, with about two-thirds of the Empire's territory and about three-fifths of its population, kept its own three-class franchise, a voting system weighted towards the wealthy. This kept the dominant state conservative.
Bismarck was a Prussian conservative and Junker landowner who used war and diplomacy to create the German Empire. This part covers his role in unification.

Bismarck was born on 1 April 1815 at Schönhausen, in the Prussian province of Saxony, into a Junker (Prussian landowning noble) family. He sat in the United Diet of 1847 as an ultra-conservative and in the Prussian lower house from 1849.

He was Prussian delegate at the restored German Diet in Frankfurt from 1851 to 1859, which taught him to regard Austria as Prussia's rival. He was then ambassador at St Petersburg (1859–62) and at Paris (1862) before becoming Minister-President in September 1862.

As Minister-President he gave the "blood and iron" speech and used the gap theory to collect taxes and carry through the army reform without an approved budget. These steps gave him the means to build a strong army.

He was a participant who directed each stage of unification: the Danish War (1864), the Gastein settlement (1865), the alliance with Italy (1866), the war with Austria and the Treaty of Prague (1866), the North German Confederation (1867) and the Ems telegram (1870).
He became Chancellor of the North German Confederation in 1867 and Imperial Chancellor in 1871, holding office until 1890, and he was made a prince (Fürst) in 1871.

Contemporaries were divided: conservatives admired his success, while many liberals saw an authoritarian who had broken the constitution. Most liberals were won over by 1866–71, as the National Liberal Party shows.

Historians disagree. The Prussian school (for example Heinrich von Sybel and Heinrich von Treitschke) saw a master plan, and A. J. P. Taylor, in Bismarck: The Man and the Statesman (1955), portrayed an opportunist who improvised.

Lothar Gall's biography Bismarck: The White Revolutionary (German 1980) argued that he used revolutionary means, nationalism, manhood suffrage and war, to preserve the conservative order. The phrase had been used of Bismarck before Gall.
Bismarck's aim was a Germany united under Prussian leadership. His methods were flexible, and historians argue about whether he followed a plan or seized chances.

Realpolitik, a term coined by Ludwig von Rochau in Principles of Realpolitik (1853), meant pursuing state interests through power and diplomacy rather than through principles or ideology. It was Rochau who coined it, not Bismarck.

Bismarck used liberal demands for national unity to win support for his policies, while keeping the army and the monarchy under royal control. In other words, he used liberal nationalism for Prussian ends.

He isolated each enemy before war: Russian goodwill after the Alvensleben Convention of 1863, Napoleon III's neutrality after Biarritz in 1865 and the alliance with Italy in 1866 against Austria, and France's lack of an ally in 1870.
He fought short wars with limited aims and avoided humiliating Austria in 1866, which made it easier for Austria to become a partner later.

He exploited chances as they arose: the Danish succession crisis, the Gastein arrangement, the Hohenzollern candidature and the Ems telegram, which created a public crisis that drew the southern states into the war.

The debate is whether he had a long-term plan to unite Germany under Prussia or exploited opportunities with a general aim of Prussian power. The Prussian school saw a plan, while Taylor saw an improviser.
The usual balanced verdict is a clear aim with flexible methods.
Italy and Germany were unified in the same years, so examiners ask you to compare them. Both had a strong kingdom leading the way, but their paths and results differed.

Italy was unified between 1859 and 1871, with the Kingdom of Italy proclaimed in March 1861. Venetia was added in 1866 and Rome in September 1870, after the French garrison withdrew for the war with Prussia, and Rome became the capital from 1871.
Both unifications were led by a strong kingdom, Piedmont or Prussia, which combined war with diplomacy and treated Austria as the common enemy.
Italy won Venetia from Prussia's victory in 1866 even though Austria beat it at Custoza and Lissa. Rome was blocked until the French garrison left in 1870.
Piedmont needed French armies against Austria in 1859, whereas Prussia needed only foreign neutrality, so Prussia's military strength was far greater.
Italy's unity came partly from below, through Garibaldi's volunteers and plebiscites (votes by the people), while Germany's came from above, through the Prussian army and the princes.
Germany emerged far stronger economically and militarily than Italy.

Italy left Italian-speaking Trentino and Trieste in Austria, so unity was unfinished. Germany placed Danes in north Schleswig, Poles in Prussia's eastern provinces and Alsatians inside the Empire, and left out the Austrian Germans.
The Empire was a real achievement but a limited one, and contemporaries and later historians judged it differently.
Achievement: unity, the aim of the liberals of 1848, was achieved by 1871 through Bismarck's wars and diplomacy.
Limit: unity came from above, by Prussian arms and the princes, not by a parliament, so it was not the liberal unity of 1848.
Limit: it was Kleindeutsch, leaving Austria, with its millions of Germans, outside the Empire. The Empire contained national minorities, Poles, Danes and, after 1871, Alsatians.

Limit: the Empire was a Prussian-dominated semi-autocracy (a system in which the ruler keeps most real power). The Reichstag, elected by manhood suffrage, had no control over the Chancellor and less power than the liberals had hoped.

Contemporary views: liberal supporters of unification saw the Empire as a national triumph (nationalism, the belief that a people sharing a language and culture should form one state, had been satisfied).
Later views: critics argued that the Empire was a Prussian-led autocracy built on militarism.
Italian unity was driven by two ideas and fought over by three programmes. Knowing these terms makes the whole story of 1815-1871 easier to follow.
Nationalism is the belief that people who share a language, culture and history should form one state. In Italy it meant expelling Austria and uniting the separate states into one country.

Liberalism means constitutional government, an elected parliament and civil liberties. In Italy it was represented by Piedmont's constitution, the Statuto, and by Cavour, so liberal ideas and nationalist ideas often worked together.
The Risorgimento (Italian for 'resurgence') is the name for the movement for Italian unity and independence, 1815-1870.
Nationalists disagreed about what kind of Italy they wanted. Mazzini wanted a unitary republic, so one state with no kings and the people as sovereign.
The neo-Guelphs wanted a federation of Italian states under the Pope. Their name recalls the medieval Guelphs, the papal party.

The moderates, and later Cavour, wanted a constitutional monarchy led by Piedmont. This is the programme that finally won, which is why the split between these three matters for exam answers on success and failure.

Napoleon had redrawn the map of Italy, but the Congress of Vienna (the 1815 peace settlement) restored the old rulers and made Austria the dominant power. Italy was a patchwork of states, most under Austrian influence, with the Pope ruling the centre.

Napoleon had created a Kingdom of Italy in the north (1805) with himself as king, and his brother Joseph and then Murat ruled Naples. He brought the Code Napoleon, a single centralised administration and the idea of a united Italy, which restored rulers could not entirely undo.

The Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia, ruled by the House of Savoy, was the only major state ruled by a native Italian dynasty. It was enlarged in 1815 by Genoa, the former republic, which made it the largest independent state in the north-west.

Austria directly ruled Lombardy and Venetia in the north. Tuscany and Modena had Habsburg rulers, and Parma went to Marie-Louise, Napoleon's Habsburg widow, until 1847, so family ties tied the duchies to Vienna.

The Papal States covered central Italy from Rome to Bologna. The Pope was an absolute monarch (a ruler with unlimited power) as well as head of the Church, with the clergy running the administration, so Italian unity threatened his state.
The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, ruled by the Bourbons from Naples, covered the south and Sicily. Its kings were Ferdinand I (to 1825), Ferdinand II (1830-59) and Francis II (1859-61).

Austria also had military means. Its fortresses of the Quadrilateral (Mantua, Peschiera, Verona and Legnago) guarded the north, and Field Marshal Radetzky commanded its army in Italy, which Austria used to put down revolts.

The Austrian Empire was multinational, so Italian nationalism threatened it directly. Metternich, its chief minister, said 'Italy is a geographical expression' (1847), meaning he saw a map region and not a nation.

Italy was also divided in society. The economy was mainly agricultural, communications were poor, people felt loyal to their region and spoke dialects, illiteracy was widespread and the south was poor.
Opposition to the restored rulers began in secret societies. Their risings in 1820-21 and 1831 all failed, and the reasons for those failures shaped what came next.

The Carbonari were a secret society that spread liberal and nationalist ideas among army officers, students and professional men in the 1820s. Being secret kept them safe from the police but also kept them small.

The Carbonari took part in the rising in Naples (July 1820) and the rising in Piedmont (March 1821). Both were crushed by Austrian troops in 1821, after the Congress of Laibach, and the leaders were imprisoned or exiled.

In February 1831 risings broke out in Modena, Parma and the Papal Legations (the northern provinces of the Papal States). They were crushed with Austrian help, and Ciro Menotti, leader of the Modena rising, was executed in 1831.
Louis-Napoleon, later Napoleon III, took part in the 1831 rising in the Papal States as a young man. This helps explain why he later posed as a friend of Italian nationalism.
The early risings failed for several reasons: they were run by small secret groups, had no mass support, had local rather than national aims, had no foreign help and faced Austrian military power.
The lesson Mazzini drew was that Italy needed a national movement with popular support, and this is why he founded Young Italy.

Mazzini was the most influential theorist and organiser of Italian nationalism before 1848. His ideal of a republican, unified Italy shaped the movement even though his methods failed and he was left disappointed in 1861.
Mazzini was born in Genoa on 22 June 1805, took a law degree (1827) and joined the Carbonari in 1827. He was arrested in November 1830, imprisoned at Savona and went into exile early in 1831.
In 1831 he founded Young Italy at Marseille. It was a secret society for young men under 40 who swore an oath to work for an independent, united republic, and it spread through branches across Italy.

His ideas were a unitary republic with the people as sovereign, and the motto 'God and the People' (Dio e Popolo). He wanted unity through education and popular insurrection (rising), not through kings or foreign help.
His book The Duties of Man (published in full 1860) put duty to the nation above individual rights, so citizens were asked to serve Italy before themselves.

His risings all failed for lack of popular support: the Piedmont army plot (1833, about a dozen executed), the invasion of Savoy (February 1834), the Bandiera brothers in Calabria (1844), Milan (February 1853) and Pisacane's expedition at Sapri (1857, Pisacane killed).

He founded Young Europe at Bern (April 1834) to link revolutionary movements. He lived in exile in Switzerland, France and, from January 1837, London, which stayed his main base for the rest of his life, where he ran his network of exiles.

In 1848 he returned to Italy. In 1849 he was one of the three triumvirs (joint rulers) of the Roman Republic, with Garibaldi commanding its defence. After 1849 his reputation suffered as risings failed and moderates turned to Piedmont.
His supporters, among them Francesco Crispi and Rosolino Pilo, helped prepare the Sicilian rising of April 1860 and pressed Garibaldi to lead an expedition.
Mazzini's later life shows the gap between the idea he gave Italy and the state that was built. Contemporaries and historians judge him differently from how he judged himself.
Mazzini was a participant, not a witness: he planned risings and sent agents into Italy, and his writings inspired followers, including Garibaldi.

Contemporaries were divided. Radicals and republicans admired him, Cavour and the monarchists distrusted him, Austria and the Pope saw a dangerous conspirator, and to many moderates his risings wasted lives.
He rejected the monarchical Italy of 1861 as a betrayal, because he had wanted a republic built by the people.

In August 1870 he was arrested on arrival at Palermo while trying to start a republican rising in Sicily, and was imprisoned at Gaeta. He was released in the amnesty after Rome was taken (October 1870).
He died at Pisa on 10 March 1872.

Historians now see him as the prophet and ideologue (thinker who supplies the ideas) of the Risorgimento, who kept the idea of unity alive and inspired a generation. His methods failed and his republic was not achieved.
Not every nationalist wanted revolution or a republic. In the 1840s two writers offered peaceful alternatives, and a new Pope seemed to prove that reform could work.
Vincenzo Gioberti, in On the Moral and Civil Primacy of the Italians (1843), proposed a federation of Italian states under the Pope. His followers were called neo-Guelphs.
Cesare Balbo, in The Hopes of Italy (1844), argued for reform and independence led by Piedmont's monarchy, not revolution. Massimo d'Azeglio, a Piedmontese moderate, was Prime Minister 1849-52.
Pius IX was elected Pope in June 1846. An amnesty for political prisoners (1846), a civic guard and some press freedom raised hopes of a liberal Pope who might lead Italy.
This explains the early 1848 mood: many moderates expected reform from rulers and the Pope. When Pius IX turned against the national cause the neo-Guelph programme collapsed.
In 1848 revolution spread across Italy and, for the first time, a state went to war with Austria. Austria won in 1848-49, but the failure showed which road unity would have to take.

The causes were economic distress, hopes raised by Pius IX and news of the February revolution in Paris. The first rising was at Palermo on 12 January 1848, and rulers granted constitutions: Naples, Tuscany, Piedmont (the Statuto, 4 March 1848) and the Papal States.
The Five Days of Milan (18-22 March 1848) forced Radetzky to withdraw to the Quadrilateral fortresses. Venice rose under Daniele Manin, who proclaimed the Republic of San Marco on 22 March 1848.

Charles Albert of Piedmont declared war on Austria on 23 March 1848, the First War of Independence, with the slogan 'Italia farà da sé' ('Italy will do it by herself'). He was defeated at Custoza on 24-25 July 1848, and an armistice followed in August.
Pius IX refused war against Catholic Austria in his Allocution of 29 April 1848. After the murder of his minister Pellegrino Rossi (15 November 1848) he fled to Gaeta, in the Kingdom of Naples.
The Roman Republic was proclaimed on 9 February 1849. Mazzini, Aurelio Saffi and Carlo Armellini governed as triumvirs from March, and Garibaldi commanded the defence.

Charles Albert was defeated at Novara on 23 March 1849 and abdicated that night; he died in exile in Portugal in 1849. His son Victor Emmanuel II made peace with Austria (Treaty of Milan, August 1849).

French troops under General Oudinot, sent by Louis-Napoleon, then President of France, took Rome at the start of July 1849 after a siege, restored the Pope and kept a garrison there. Garibaldi retreated with about 4,000 men, and his wife Anita died on the retreat (August 1849).
Venice held out until August 1849 (22-24 August), then surrendered after siege, cholera and bombardment.
The failure of 1848-49 matters because it fixed the lessons that later nationalists acted on. It pushed moderates away from Mazzini's way and towards Piedmont.
Austria's army was the main reason for defeat, because Radetzky's forces came back from the Quadrilateral and won at Custoza and Novara.
Nationalists were divided between republicans and monarchists, and between different states, which means there was no single leader or plan.
The Pope's withdrawal from the war (April 1848) broke the neo-Guelph hope because it showed a Pope would not fight Catholic Austria, and no foreign ally helped Italy.
The lesson was that Italy could not do it alone, as Charles Albert had claimed, so foreign help was needed.
Piedmont kept its constitution and its flag after 1849, so it became the hope of moderates and the leader of the national cause.

After 1849 Piedmont was the one Italian state that kept its constitution, and under Cavour it became the most advanced state in Italy. Cavour then used the Crimean War to turn Piedmont into a player in European diplomacy.

The Statuto Albertino (1848) was kept after 1849, which is why liberals trusted Piedmont. It gave a king, a nominated senate and an elected chamber with a narrow property franchise, and Piedmont kept the Italian tricolour. It was the only constitutional state in Italy after 1849, a refuge for exiles.
The Siccardi Laws (1850), named after the justice minister Giuseppe Siccardi, abolished separate church courts and the right of asylum in churches. This caused conflict with the Papacy.

Count Camillo Benso di Cavour, born in Turin in 1810, was a landowner and journalist who founded the newspaper Il Risorgimento (1847). He was minister of agriculture and commerce (1850), then of finance (1851), and admired Britain's economy and parliament.
He became Prime Minister on 4 November 1852 through the connubio ('marriage'), an alliance with Urbano Rattazzi's centre-left.

He modernised Piedmont with free trade treaties with Britain, France and other states, railway building, banking and credit, agricultural improvement and a reformed army. Its railway network became the largest of any Italian state by 1859, making Piedmont the most advanced Italian state.

Piedmont joined the Crimean War (Britain and France against Russia, 1853-56) in January 1855. About 15,000 troops under Alfonso La Marmora fought at the Chernaya (August 1855), which won Piedmont a seat at the Congress of Paris (February-April 1856).

At Paris Cavour raised the Italian question and the problem of Austria's presence in Italy before the Great Powers. Austria's unfriendly neutrality in the war had cost it Russia's friendship, so Austria was more isolated.
Cavour knew Piedmont could not beat Austria alone, as 1848-49 had shown. He turned to Napoleon III, who wanted to undo the 1815 settlement.

The Italian National Society (1857) was founded by Daniele Manin, Giorgio Pallavicino and Giuseppe La Farina. Garibaldi joined as vice-president. It backed unity under Victor Emmanuel and Piedmont instead of Mazzini's republic, and former republicans such as Manin and Garibaldi supported it.
Napoleon III, Emperor of the French from 1852, wanted to undo the 1815 settlement and posed as a friend of nationalities. He also needed Catholic support at home, so he protected the Pope.
Felice Orsini's bombs in Paris (14 January 1858) aimed at Napoleon III. Orsini was executed after writing to the Emperor urging him to free Italy, which pushed Napoleon III towards action.

At Plombieres (20-21 July 1858) Cavour and Napoleon III secretly agreed that France would fight Austria if Austria appeared the aggressor. Piedmont would get a kingdom of Upper Italy, and France would get Savoy and, less firmly, Nice.

Princess Clotilde, Victor Emmanuel's daughter, was to marry Prince Napoleon (Jerome), Napoleon III's cousin. The marriage, which sealed the alliance, took place in January 1859, and a formal Franco-Piedmontese treaty that month included Savoy and Nice.
The price was the cession of Nice and Savoy to France, which angered nationalists, above all Garibaldi, because he was born in Nice.
Cavour's plan worked at first: France fought beside Piedmont and Austria lost Lombardy. Napoleon III then stopped the war short of the goal, and central Italy took matters into its own hands.

Piedmont mobilised, and Austria issued an ultimatum on 23 April 1859 and began war on 29 April, so Austria appeared the aggressor as the Plombieres deal required. France joined Piedmont, and Garibaldi led volunteers called the Cacciatori delle Alpi ('Alpine Hunters').
The allies won at Magenta (4 June 1859) and at Solferino (with San Martino, 24 June 1859). Napoleon III and Victor Emmanuel II entered Milan after Magenta.
Napoleon III stopped the war because of heavy losses, Prussian mobilisation on the Rhine, Catholic anger in France and fear of a too-strong Piedmont.
He agreed the Villafranca armistice with Franz Joseph on 11 July 1859 without Cavour, who resigned. Lombardy went to Piedmont but Venetia stayed Austrian.
The Treaty of Zurich (10 November 1859) confirmed this: Lombardy was ceded through France to Piedmont.

In central Italy the rulers of Tuscany, Modena and Parma fled and the Romagna rose against the Pope. Cavour returned as Prime Minister in January 1860, and plebiscites on 11-12 March 1860 in Tuscany and Emilia (Modena, Parma, the Romagna) voted to join Piedmont.
The Treaty of Turin (24 March 1860) ceded Nice and Savoy to France in return for Napoleon III's acceptance, and plebiscites in Nice and Savoy followed in April 1860.

In 1860 an adventure that Cavour neither stopped nor openly backed turned the unification of the north into the unification of most of Italy. Garibaldi supplied the military daring that diplomacy could not.

Garibaldi was born in Nice on 4 July 1807 and was a Mazzinian, condemned to death in his absence after the 1834 plot. He spent about 1836-48 in South America, in Brazil and Uruguay, where his Italian Legion wore red shirts, and he defended the Roman Republic in 1849.
After a rising in Sicily the Thousand (about 1,000 men) sailed from Quarto near Genoa on the night of 5-6 May 1860. Cavour neither stopped them nor openly backed them.

They landed at Marsala on 11 May 1860. Garibaldi proclaimed himself dictator in Victor Emmanuel's name at Salemi, won at Calatafimi (15 May) and took Palermo at the end of May, with fighting from 27 May. He then won at Milazzo in July.
Garibaldi crossed to Calabria in August, and entered Naples on 7 September 1860 as Francis II withdrew to Gaeta. The battle of the Volturno followed on 1-2 October 1860.

Cavour feared a march on Rome and French or Austrian intervention, so he sent the Piedmontese army through the Papal Marches and Umbria, avoiding Rome itself, and it defeated the papal army at Castelfidardo (18 September 1860).

At Teano (26 October 1860) Garibaldi handed his conquests to Victor Emmanuel II and went to his island home of Caprera. Plebiscites approved annexation in Naples and Sicily (21 October) and the Marches and Umbria (November).

The first Italian parliament in Turin proclaimed the Kingdom of Italy on 17 March 1861, with Victor Emmanuel II as king (to 1878) and Turin as capital. Cavour died on 6 June 1861, aged 50, and his successors struggled to resolve the southern question.

Garibaldi's slogan was 'Rome or death' (Roma o morte). Italian troops stopped him at Aspromonte on 29 August 1862, where he was wounded. French and papal troops defeated him at Mentana on 3 November 1867.

Two areas remained outside the new kingdom: Venetia under Austria and Rome under the Pope. Venetia came in 1866 because Prussia defeated Austria, and Rome in 1870 after the French garrison left and Italian troops entered the city.
The September Convention (15 September 1864) had France promise to withdraw from Rome, and Italy moved its capital to Florence in 1865.

Italy allied with Prussia on 8 April 1866. Italy lost on land at Custoza (24 June 1866) and at sea at Lissa (20 July 1866), but Prussia beat Austria at Koniggratz (Sadowa) on 3 July 1866 and this forced Austria to give up Venetia.
Venetia was handed through Napoleon III to Italy by the Treaty of Vienna (3 October 1866), and a plebiscite in October 1866 approved it.
French troops left Rome in August 1870 on the outbreak of the Franco-Prussian War, so the Pope lost his protector.
After Sedan (1-2 September 1870), the capture of Rome followed: Italian troops entered through a breach at the Porta Pia on 20 September 1870, and a plebiscite on 2 October 1870 approved annexation.

Rome became the capital in 1871 (July), the third capital after Turin and then Florence. The Law of Guarantees (13 May 1871) offered the Pope privileges, but Pius IX rejected it and called himself a prisoner of the Vatican.
Pius IX had declared papal infallibility at the Vatican Council in July 1870, so his hostility to the new state was strong, and this kept many Catholics apart from it.
A good answer pairs each obstacle with the way it was removed. Early attempts met all the obstacles with none of the answers, while after 1852 the answers arrived together.
