Obstacle: Austria's military power and its hold on Lombardy-Venetia and the Quadrilateral until 1866. The war of 1859 with France removed Austria from Lombardy only, and the Prussian victory in 1866 that gave Italy Venetia ended the obstacle.
Obstacle: the Papacy and its French protectors until 1870. It was overcome when the French garrison left Rome in August 1870 because of the Franco-Prussian War.

Obstacle: regionalism, local loyalties, no common spoken language, illiteracy and peasant indifference. It was overcome in part by plebiscites and by the enthusiasm of 1860, though the problem remained after 1861.

Obstacle: divisions among nationalists (republicans against monarchists, unitary against federal) and reliance on small conspiracies. It was overcome when the National Society brought many former republicans behind Piedmont, ending the 1848 divisions.
Success factor: Piedmont was a strong leading state, constitutional, modernised and with a regular army, so there was now a real centre for the movement.

Success factor: Cavour's diplomacy (the Crimean War, Paris 1856, Plombieres) isolated Austria and won French help. Foreign help also came from France in 1859, Prussia in 1866 and 1870, Britain's goodwill and Austria's isolation after the Crimean War.
Success factor: Garibaldi's volunteers and popular enthusiasm in 1860 moved faster than a regular army could, for example through Sicily and Naples in a few months.

The roles compared: Mazzini gave the idea and inspiration, Cavour the diplomacy and the Piedmontese state, Garibaldi the military daring and Victor Emmanuel II the monarchy all could accept. A textbook summary of this is the soul, the brain and the sword.
The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861, but it started with serious weaknesses. Ordinary Level questions often ask about these problems and not only about how unification happened.
The franchise was narrow: only about 2 per cent of the population could vote in 1861, so the state rested on a tiny political class.
'Piedmontisation' meant that Piedmont's constitution, laws, officials and taxes were extended to the whole kingdom. It was a centralised state, not a federation.

The south gained little for peasants. The army fought brigandage in the south for several years after 1861 (roughly 1861-65), and the Pica Law (1863) allowed military courts. This is the southern question.
About three-quarters of Italians were illiterate at the 1861 census. Estimates of how many spoke standard Italian range from about 2.5 to about 10 per cent.
The Pope's hostility kept many Catholics apart from the new state, as Pius IX rejected the Law of Guarantees.
Examiners reward paired judgements: what was achieved against what was left unfinished, and how far each leader's vision won. Name a historian to add weight.
Achievement: by 1871 the peninsula was united under one constitutional monarchy with Rome as its capital, and Austria had been expelled.
Limit: unity came largely through French and Prussian victories and Piedmontese expansion, not a popular national rising, and the state was narrow, centralised and poorly integrated.
Achievement for Mazzini: the idea of a united Italy, which he had kept alive, won. Limit: his republican, popular Italy did not, and he was left disappointed.
Limit: the new kingdom stayed mostly agricultural and the south poor. What was extended was Piedmont's constitution, laws and administration, not a modern economy.
Denis Mack Smith (Cavour and Garibaldi 1860, 1954) saw Cavour and Garibaldi as rivals as well as partners, and thought Cavour's aims in 1860 were limited.
Antonio Gramsci (Prison Notebooks, written 1929-35) called the Risorgimento a 'passive revolution' led by moderates that left the peasants out.

Lucy Riall (Garibaldi: Invention of a Hero, 2007) argued that the Garibaldi legend was deliberately created through print and images. Older nationalist and liberal histories saw a heroic, almost inevitable rise of the nation.

Compared with Germany, Italy was also led by one strong kingdom using war and diplomacy, but it relied more on foreign help, ended weaker and less united, and was a constitutional monarchy rather than a Prussian-dominated empire.

In 1815 the Ottoman Empire still ruled south-eastern Europe, but its grip was weakening. The Eastern Question asked what would happen to Ottoman lands as its power declined, and which Great Power would gain from it; this question drives the whole story of Balkan nationalism.

The Ottoman Empire, ruled by the Sultan from Constantinople, was a Muslim state governing a largely Orthodox Christian population in the Balkans, including Greece, Serbia and the Danubian principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia.

The Sultan ruled Balkan Christians through local officials and the millet system, in which each religious community ran its own religious and civil affairs, so the Orthodox were led by the Ecumenical Patriarch in Constantinople.
The millet system gave religious communities legal autonomy but no political rights, and non-Muslims paid a poll tax (an extra tax on each person), which fed resentment of Ottoman rule.

Ottoman power was declining: central control was weak and local governors and the Janissaries (the Sultan's elite troops) often acted independently. Sultan Mahmud II (reigned 1808–39) tried to reform and destroyed the Janissary corps in 1826.

Russia claimed to protect Orthodox Christians because they shared its religion, sought passage through the Straits (the Bosporus and Dardanelles), and gained influence over Moldavia and Wallachia after its wars with the Ottomans; until 1821 these were ruled by Greek (Phanariot) princes appointed by the Sultan.

Austria feared Russian expansion into the Balkans and nationalism among its own Slavs, so it wanted the Ottoman Empire kept intact as a barrier. Britain wanted to protect its route to India, which ran through the eastern Mediterranean and the Straits, and to keep Russia out of the Mediterranean.

France had interests in the Levant (the eastern Mediterranean coast) and acted as protector of Catholics in the Holy Places. Because each Power wanted a different outcome, every Ottoman crisis became a Great Power quarrel.

Balkan Christians had lived under Ottoman rule for centuries without rebelling together. In the early nineteenth century several forces gave them a sense of national identity and the hope that revolt could succeed.
Religion and language gave a shared identity: the Orthodox Church and Greek or Serbian speech marked Christians as a people distinct from their Muslim rulers.
Ottoman misrule, such as the abuse of Serbs by the Janissary garrison, gave people a grievance that made revolt seem worth the risk.
Merchants and the diaspora (communities living abroad) supplied money, education and contacts. The Philiki Etaireia, for example, was founded by Greek merchants.
The example of the French Revolution showed that a people could claim rights and a nation, which encouraged educated Greeks and Serbs to think in national terms.
Nationalists hoped for Russian help because Russia was Orthodox and often at war with the Ottomans, although Russia in practice helped only when it suited its own interests.
Nationalism, as used here, means the belief that a people sharing religion, language and history should govern itself in its own state.
Serbia's path to autonomy was two risings, then a slow negotiated autonomy that depended on Russian pressure on the Sultan.

The First Serbian Uprising began in February 1804 under Karadjordje (Đorđe Petrović, 'Black George'). It was aimed against the dahije, Janissary chiefs who had seized power in the pashalik (province) of Belgrade and terrorised the Serbs.

The rising was crushed in 1813 because Russia made peace with the Ottomans in 1812 (the Treaty of Bucharest) before Napoleon's invasion, so the Serbs lost their ally. The Ottomans reconquered Serbia and Karadjordje fled across the Danube to Austrian territory.

The Second Serbian Uprising came in 1815 under Miloš Obrenović, who combined limited fighting with negotiation with the Ottoman government. This worked better than all-out war against a stronger enemy.
Russian–Ottoman agreements then bound the Sultan to grant Serbian autonomy: the Akkerman Convention (October 1826) and the Treaty of Adrianople (September 1829), which also ended a Russo-Ottoman war.
A decree (hatt-i sharif) of the Sultan in 1830 recognised Serbia as an autonomous principality with Miloš as hereditary prince, and Serbia's territory was enlarged in 1833.

Autonomy had limits. Serbia stayed under Ottoman suzerainty (the Sultan remained overlord), paid an annual tribute that was the price of its autonomy, and Ottoman garrisons stayed in Belgrade and other fortresses.
Autonomy did not bring calm. Two families, the Obrenovićs and the Karadjordjevićs, fought for the throne, and Serbia's rulers were still checked by the Ottomans and the Great Powers.
Miloš ruled autocratically and rivals were removed. Karadjordje returned to Serbia in 1817 and was murdered, on Miloš's orders according to most accounts.
The liberal Sretenje Constitution of February 1835 limited Miloš's power but was suspended within weeks under pressure from Russia, Austria and the Ottomans, who disliked a liberal Serbia.

An Ottoman statute of 1838 gave power to a council of notables to limit the prince, and Miloš abdicated in 1839. His son Milan died within weeks, and his other son Mihailo ruled 1839–42 before being overthrown.
Alexander Karadjordjević, son of Karadjordje, was prince 1842–58. Miloš was restored in 1858 and died in 1860, and Mihailo's second reign (1860–68) followed.
In 1867 the Ottoman garrisons left the fortresses, a real gain in Serbian control; Mihailo was assassinated in 1868. Full independence came only in 1878, recognised at the Congress of Berlin.
In 1844 Ilija Garašanin, a Serbian minister, drew up the secret Načertanije, a plan for a larger South Slav state under Serbian leadership, which shows Serbian nationalism growing more ambitious.
Serbia's example of autonomy under a local prince influenced other Balkan nationalists, who saw that pressure plus Great Power support could win self-government.
The Greek revolt began as a secret plot by Greek merchants. It failed in the north but caught fire in the Peloponnese, the southern peninsula of Greece, and soon declared itself a nation.

The Philiki Etaireia (Friendly Society) was a secret society founded in Odessa in 1814 by Greek merchants. It planned an armed rising against the Ottomans, recruited among merchants and intellectuals, and hoped for Russian support.

Alexander Ypsilantis, a Greek officer in the Russian army, crossed into Moldavia in March 1821 to launch a rising in the Danubian principalities. Tsar Alexander I disowned him, so he received no Russian help.

The Ottomans defeated Ypsilantis at Dragashani in June 1821, so the rising in the principalities failed. Name only Alexander, not his brother Demetrios, who fought in the Peloponnese, so that the two are not confused.
The rising in the Peloponnese began in March 1821 (25 March is celebrated as Greek Independence Day) and spread to central Greece and the islands.

Atrocities occurred on both sides, for example at Tripolitsa. When the Greeks took Tripolitsa, the Ottoman centre in the Peloponnese, in September 1821 they massacred its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants.
The Ottomans took reprisals: Patriarch Gregory V was hanged in Constantinople on Easter Sunday in April 1821, and in 1822 the Chios massacre killed or enslaved many thousands of Greeks.
The First National Assembly at Epidaurus declared independence in January 1822 and adopted a provisional constitution, so the rebels now claimed to be a state and not just rebels.
Civil wars among the Greek leaders in 1823–25 weakened the rising and left it open to counter-attack.

Atrocities such as Chios turned European opinion towards the Greeks, even though Europe's conservative governments disliked rebellion. This public sympathy made it harder for the Powers to leave the Greeks to the Sultan.

Philhellenism, European enthusiasm for Greek independence, drew on classical education (Greece as the home of ancient culture), Christian sympathy for fellow Christians, and romanticism. It brought volunteers and money to the Greek cause.
The English poet Lord Byron arrived in Greece in 1823 and joined the cause. He died of fever at Missolonghi on 19 April 1824, which made him a symbol of the cause across Europe.
Eugène Delacroix's paintings, The Massacre at Chios (1824) and Greece on the Ruins of Missolonghi (1826), gave the Greek cause a lasting image and kept public sympathy alive.
Metternich, the Austrian chancellor, opposed the Greeks because he saw them as rebels against a legitimate ruler. At the Congress of Verona in 1822 the Greek delegates were not received.
The Egyptian ruler (pasha) Muhammad Ali sent his son Ibrahim Pasha, who landed in the Peloponnese in 1825 and brought a new wave of destruction that reduced much of the region.
Missolonghi fell to the Ottomans in April 1826 after a long siege, and the Greek cause was close to defeat. The fall strengthened European sympathy instead of ending it.
With the Greeks near defeat, Britain, France and Russia stepped in. Their intervention, not the rebels' own strength, decided the outcome, as the fleet action at Navarino shows.

Nicholas I became Tsar in December 1825 and was ready to act for the Greeks, because Russia wished to protect Orthodox Christians. The St Petersburg Protocol (April 1826, Britain and Russia, after Wellington's mission) began a joint approach.
The Treaty of London (July 1827), signed by Britain, France and Russia, aimed to impose an armistice on the Ottomans and Egypt and to secure Greek autonomy. Navarino was fought as a result.

The battle of Navarino took place on 20 October 1827. British, French and Russian squadrons under the British admiral Codrington destroyed the Ottoman–Egyptian fleet in Navarino Bay, in the south-west Peloponnese.
Navarino made Greek independence possible. Ibrahim's forces could no longer be supplied by sea, and a French expeditionary force landed in the Peloponnese in 1828 and Ibrahim's army withdrew.
In the Russo-Turkish War (1828–29) Russia fought the Sultan, and in the Treaty of Adrianople (September 1829) the Sultan accepted the Powers' settlement on Greece.
The Treaty of Adrianople also gave Russia the mouths of the Danube and confirmed its influence over Moldavia and Wallachia, so Russia gained as well as the Greeks.

Independence was won on paper in 1830, but Greece was a small state whose rulers were chosen by the Great Powers. Its first governor was killed, its first king was a foreign teenager, and many Greeks lived outside its borders.
Ioannis Kapodistrias, a former joint foreign minister of Russia (to 1822), was elected governor of Greece in 1827 and arrived in January 1828. He was the first governor of independent Greece.
Kapodistrias was assassinated at Nafplio in October 1831 by members of the Mavromichalis family, whose leader he had imprisoned.

The London Protocol of 3 February 1830 made Greece an independent state under the guarantee (protection) of Britain, France and Russia. This differs from the 1852 protocol of the same name on the Danish succession.
By the Convention of London in May 1832, Otto, the teenage son of King Ludwig I of Bavaria, was chosen as king. He arrived at Nafplio in 1833, so both 1832 (chosen) and 1833 (arrived) are correct.
The 1832 frontier ran from the Gulf of Arta to the Gulf of Volos, which left most Greeks outside the kingdom.
Otto's rule used Bavarian regents and officials and was autocratic. The capital moved from Nafplio to Athens in 1834, and the Bavarian regency ended in 1835.

A revolt in Athens on 3 September 1843 forced Otto to grant a constitution, adopted in 1844. In the same year Ioannis Kolettis voiced the Megali Idea ('Great Idea'), the aim of uniting all Greeks in one state, which stayed the goal of Greek nationalism.
Otto was deposed in October 1862 and the Powers chose Prince William of Denmark as King George I in 1863. Britain ceded the Ionian Islands to Greece in 1864.
The Eastern Question exploded into a Great Power war in the 1850s. Its settlement guaranteed the Ottoman Empire but also made possible the union of Moldavia and Wallachia.

The war grew from a dispute over the Holy Places between Catholic monks (backed by France) and Orthodox monks (backed by Russia). In 1853 Prince Menshikov's mission to Constantinople demanded a Russian protectorate over the Sultan's Orthodox subjects.

Russia occupied Moldavia and Wallachia in July 1853, the Ottomans declared war in October 1853, and the Russian navy destroyed an Ottoman squadron at Sinope in November 1853. Britain and France declared war on Russia in March 1854.

Russia withdrew from the principalities in 1854 because of Austrian pressure. The Crimean War (1853–56) is named for the Crimea, where the siege of Sevastopol lasted 1854–55 and the city fell in September 1855; Nicholas I died in March 1855 during the war.
The Treaty of Paris (March 1856) guaranteed the integrity of the Ottoman Empire, neutralised the Black Sea (no warships or naval arsenals), and made Russia cede southern Bessarabia to Moldavia.

It also placed Moldavia and Wallachia under the collective guarantee of the Powers, ending Russia's protectorate. The Hatt-i Humayun (February 1856), a decree the Powers had pressed for, promised equality to non-Muslim subjects.
The Black Sea clauses removed Russian naval power from the region for a time, so Russia was weakened, and the Russian defeat became the trigger for emancipation of the serfs.
Alexandru Ioan Cuza was elected prince of Moldavia in January 1859 and of Wallachia in February 1859. The union as Romania was recognised by the Sultan in December 1861 and proclaimed in 1862.
Cuza was deposed in 1866 and replaced by Carol of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen. Romania stayed under Ottoman suzerainty until its independence was recognised in 1878.

Balkan nationalism threatened the peace of Europe because every rising on Ottoman land invited the Great Powers to intervene. Yet the Powers usually co-operated to contain these crises, so the threat was real but limited.
Threat: each rising invited Great Power intervention and rivalry, mainly Russia against Austria and Britain, which turned the Balkans into a focus of tension.
Threat: the Greek revolt split the Congress System, because Britain and Russia acted apart from Metternich, who wanted to uphold legitimate rulers.

Threat: the Russo-Ottoman wars (1828–29 and 1853) and the Crimean War, the only war between Great Powers in 1815–1854, began over the Eastern Question. Balkan crises in the 1850s and 1860s kept the Powers in tension.

Limit of the threat: the Powers usually acted together to contain crises, as in the Treaty of London (1827), the London Protocol (1830) and the Treaty of Paris (1856). They imposed small, guaranteed states with foreign kings.

Limit of the achievement: by 1871 only a small Greece was independent, Serbia and Romania were autonomous but tributary, and most Balkan Christians (Bulgarians, most Greeks, Bosnians) still lived under Ottoman rule.
The Eastern Question stayed open, and the Ottoman Empire later got the nickname the sick man of Europe, a phrase attributed to no one here.
Russia was the great autocracy of the East. Its Tsar held unlimited power, and the early hopes of reform under Alexander I faded without touching serfdom.

Autocracy means rule by one person with unlimited authority. In Russia the Tsar had no constitution or national parliament to limit him, the nobility served the state, and the Orthodox Church supported the throne.
Alexander I (reigned 1801–25) showed early reforming promise but took little action on serfdom. Mikhail Speransky drafted reform plans in 1809 but was dismissed in 1812.
His Law on Free Cultivators (1803) let landlords free serfs, with land, by agreement. Very few landlords used it, so serfdom stayed in place.

He granted a constitution to the Kingdom of Poland in 1815 and helped found the Holy Alliance (September 1815), and after 1815 he was involved in the Congress System. He became more reactionary after 1820.
The first open challenge to the Tsar came from inside the elite. Young officers influenced by western ideas rose when the succession was unclear, and its failure shaped the reign that followed.

The Decembrists were secret societies of young officers and nobles, influenced by western ideas after the wars of 1812–15. The Northern Society met in St Petersburg and the Southern Society, in the Ukraine, was led by Pavel Pestel.
Alexander I died in November 1825. His brother Constantine had renounced the throne, so Nicholas succeeded, and this confusion over the succession gave the plotters their chance.
On 14 December 1825 the Decembrists rose in Senate Square in St Petersburg demanding a constitution and the end of serfdom.

Nicholas I crushed the revolt by artillery the same day, so it was over within hours. Five leaders, including Pavel Pestel and Kondraty Ryleev, were hanged in July 1826, and more than a hundred were exiled to Siberia.
The revolt shaped Nicholas's rule, which was built on repression and strong censorship.
Nicholas I answered the Decembrists with a system of control and strengthened the autocracy. He tried some administrative reform but would not tackle private serfdom.
Nicholas I (reigned 1825–55) founded the Third Section of His Majesty's Own Chancellery in 1826, a political police force to monitor opponents of the regime.
In 1833 Sergei Uvarov, the Minister of Education, proclaimed the doctrine of Orthodoxy, Autocracy and Nationality (Official Nationality) to define Russian identity and bind subjects to the throne.
The autocracy kept rigid control of the press, universities and education, and censorship was tight under Nicholas I.
Speransky's codification of the laws appeared as the Complete Collection of the Laws (1830) and the Digest of Laws (1832–33).
Pavel Kiselev, Minister of State Domains from 1837, reformed the administration of the state peasants (peasants on state land) in 1837–41, but Nicholas did not tackle private serfdom.
Nicholas was the 'gendarme of Europe': he crushed the Polish rising of 1830–31, abolished the 1815 Polish constitution, and helped Austria crush the Hungarians in 1849.
In 1849 the Petrashevsky circle was arrested and Fyodor Dostoevsky was sentenced to death, reprieved at the place of execution and sent to Siberia, which shows how far repression went.
Serfdom was the foundation of Russian society and the economy. It had already vanished from western Europe, so Russia stood out as backward.
Serfs were peasants bound to the land and to the authority of a noble owner. Landlords controlled their labour, movement and marriage, punished them, and could sell or mortgage them.
Serfs were subject to corporal punishment and the lord's courts, and could be sent into the army for long service. The estate system kept their lives under their owners' control.
In the late 1850s there were about 22–23 million privately owned serfs, about a third of the empire's population. State peasants were roughly as numerous, so most Russians were unfree.
Serfdom had gone from western Europe by then (in France from 1789; Prussia began abolishing it in 1807), so Russia's system looked old-fashioned.
Serfs paid their owners with labour or money, and the system damaged the economy. Landlords had little reason to improve estates, and the serfs had none either.
Barshchina was labour dues, when serfs worked on the lord's land, usually about three days a week. It was most common in the fertile black-earth region of the south.
Obrok was quitrent, a payment in money or produce, and was more common in the less fertile north and centre. Household serfs (dvorovye) worked as domestic servants.

Serfdom held back agricultural productivity: landlords had little incentive to invest and serfs had little interest in improving land they did not own. Strip farming and the commune added to the problem.
It created little demand for manufactures, since peasants had little money to spend, and tied labour to the land, so a free workforce could not grow.
Possessional serfs, and peasants tied to their villages by passports, worked in Urals ironworks and other factories, which limited the growth of a free labour force.
By 1859 about two-thirds of privately owned serfs were mortgaged by their owners to state credit institutions, so many noble estates were deeply in debt.
Serf unrest brought many local disturbances under Nicholas I, and landlords feared a Pugachev-style revolt (the great rising of 1773–75).
By the 1850s there were moral, economic and military arguments against serfdom. The Crimean War made the case impossible to ignore, because it exposed an army and economy held back by the system.
Moral argument: literature such as Ivan Turgenev's A Sportsman's Sketches (1852) showed the cruelty of serf life to educated readers, which turned opinion against the system.
Economic argument: free labour would be more productive than forced labour, and noble estates were heavily mortgaged.
Military argument: the Crimean defeat showed a backward army and economy, and a serf army could not have a large trained reserve.
Serfdom was debated in secret committees under Nicholas I, but the government took no decisive action before the Crimean War exposed the weaknesses of the system.
Fear of revolt added urgency, since serf unrest was growing and landlords remembered Pugachev.
Alexander II acted after the Crimean defeat and chose to free the serfs from above, on terms the nobles could accept. The edict gave legal freedom, but at a price for the peasants.

Alexander II (reigned 1855–81) made emancipation a priority because of Russia's defeat in the Crimean War, which had shown the empire's backwardness. The fall of Sevastopol in September 1855 forced Russia to accept peace in 1856.
In a speech to the Moscow nobility in March 1856 he said, in paraphrase, that it was better to abolish serfdom from 'above' than to wait until it began to abolish itself from 'below'.
Preparation began with provincial noble committees from 1857, and the Editing Commissions of 1859, set up under Yakov Rostovtsev with Nikolai Milyutin a leading member, drafted the terms.
The Manifesto and Statutes were issued on 19 February 1861 (3 March in the western calendar). This was one event and not two.
The edict freed about 22–23 million privately owned serfs from personal bondage, with rights to marry, move, own property, trade and go to court.

Peasants received allotments of land, for example, but landlords kept much of the land and often the best of it. In the black-earth provinces peasants often lost a large part of land they had worked (the otrezki, 'cut-offs').
Household serfs were freed without land, so they had freedom but no way of earning a living from the land.
Freedom was not free. Peasants had to pay for their land over decades, through a village commune that also controlled them, and until then they still owed their old lords.
Until redemption (buying out the land) was agreed, peasants were temporarily obligated to their former lords, paying dues in labour or obrok for the land they used.
There was a two-year transition before the statutes took full effect. Redemption became compulsory for all remaining temporarily obligated peasants from 1883.

Redemption payments worked as a loan: the state advanced about three-quarters to four-fifths of the land's price to landlords in bonds, and peasants repaid the state over 49 years at 6 per cent interest, paying the remaining part to the landlord directly.
Many historians judge the land prices too high, so peasants paid more than the land was worth and were left poor and indebted for decades.
The mir (also called the obshchina, the village commune) received the land, redistributed strips in many areas, and was collectively responsible for taxes and redemption payments.
Peasants needed the mir's permission to leave, so it kept them tied to the village and to strip farming.
Redemption payments were halved for 1906 and abolished from 1 January 1907, after the 1905 revolution.
Emancipation changed the legal position of the peasants but left them poor, and it left the Tsar's power untouched. Other reforms followed because a freed society needed new institutions.

For peasants: personal freedom and civil rights, but land hunger, debt and poverty. Troops fired on peasants at Bezdna (Kazan province) in April 1861, who believed the real emancipation was being hidden from them.
For the economy: slow agricultural improvement, because the mir kept strip farming and tied peasants to villages, but also a gradual move to wage labour and, later, a labour supply for industry.
Landlords' debts were often deducted from their compensation, and many nobles sold land in later decades.

Emancipation came from above and kept the Tsar's power intact, with no national parliament. Radical and revolutionary opposition grew in the 1860s and 1870s, and Alexander II was assassinated on 1 March 1881.
The zemstva (elected district and provincial councils) were set up in 1864, and the judicial reform of 1864 brought jury trial, independent judges and public trials.
Town dumas (town councils) followed in 1870, and a military reform under Dmitry Milyutin in 1874 shortened service.
Both halves of this subsection show change that came from above or from outside, with real gains and real limits. Examiners reward paired judgements and a clear verdict.

Achievement: Serbia became autonomous (1830), Greece independent (1830–32) and Romania united (1859–62), the first national states carved from the Ottoman Empire. Greece was the first state to win full independence.

Limit: success depended on Great Power intervention and rivalry, not on the nationalists' own strength, and the new states were small with imposed rulers. Most Balkan Christians were still under Ottoman rule in 1871.
Stability: a real threat in Navarino, the 1828–29 war and the Crimean War, against containment by Great Power co-operation in London (1827 and 1830) and Paris (1856).
Achievement: emancipation ended personal bondage for about a third of the population, peacefully and from above, and opened the way to further reforms.
Limit: land loss, redemption debt, the mir and continuing poverty, with the autocracy unchanged.
Views: contemporaries were disappointed because peasants expected all the land free, whereas later historians see a major but flawed reform.
Overall: Balkan nationalism created new states but fed Great Power rivalry, while emancipation was a major reform that left the peasants with real grievances.
Every French regime after 1815 had to live with the memory of the Revolution of 1789 and of Napoleon I. This inheritance explains why no government was ever fully accepted by the whole country.

The Revolution of 1789 put forward liberty, equality and the sovereignty of the people (the idea that power belongs to the nation, not to a king). The First Republic followed in 1792, and Louis XVI was executed in January 1793.
It left France divided between those who accepted the Revolution and those, the nobles and much of the Church, who rejected it, so every later regime was contested from the start.

Napoleon I was crowned Emperor in December 1804. He left behind the Code Napoléon (the Civil Code of 1804), a centralised administration run by prefects (officials appointed by the government to run each department) and the Concordat of 1801, an agreement with the Church.
After his final defeat at Waterloo on 18 June 1815 and exile to St Helena, where he died in 1821, a Napoleonic legend of glory and order grew up, which his nephew later used to win support.

The Vienna settlement restored the Bourbons under the principle of legitimacy (the idea that the rightful old dynasties should be returned to their thrones). It left France a defeated power under Allied occupation until 1818 (the Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle ended it), so the Bourbons were later identified with foreign bayonets.
France was highly centralised and Paris dominated it, so a rising in Paris could overthrow a government. This pattern repeats in 1830, 1848 and 1870.

The population was about 30 million in 1815 and about 35 million by 1848. Most people were peasants, many owning small farms gained since the Revolution, and they were socially conservative, which often put the provinces at odds with radical Paris.
Four ideas and five political camps run through the whole period. Knowing exactly what each word meant in France stops the regimes from blurring together.

Liberalism means constitutional government, an elected parliament, civil liberties such as a free press, and limits on the ruler. In France it meant the Charter, then the July Monarchy, with a vote restricted to property owners.
Democracy means rule by the people through representatives elected by all adult men in this period. In France it meant universal male suffrage (the vote for all men), which came in 1848.

Autocracy means rule by one person whose power is not limited by a parliament or constitution. The early Second Empire was authoritarian with autocratic features, though it rested on plebiscites and kept an elected but weak legislature.

Ultras were extreme royalists who wanted the old order back. Legitimists supported the senior Bourbon line, and Orleanists supported Louis-Philippe, who came from the Orléans branch of the royal family.

Bonapartists wanted the Bonaparte family restored, and republicans wanted a republic. The rivalry of all five groups is a main cause of instability, because each regime was hated by at least two camps.
A plebiscite is a yes/no vote of all voters on a single question. Bonapartism combined strong personal rule with universal male suffrage and plebiscites, promising order and prosperity.
Liberalism is not democracy. The July Monarchy was liberal but not democratic, while the Second Empire was democratic in its franchise but not liberal until the 1860s.
After Napoleon's first abdication the Bourbon monarchy was restored, but it accepted a constitution. The compromise was fragile because the franchise was tiny and 1815 brought violent revenge.

Louis XVIII, brother of the executed Louis XVI, returned to France in April-May 1814. Napoleon's Hundred Days (his return to Paris in March 1815) interrupted his rule, and after Waterloo the second restoration followed in July 1815. Louis XVIII died in 1824.

He issued the Charter (Charte constitutionnelle) on 4 June 1814. It was a constitution granted by the king, not won from him, and it set up two chambers: a Chamber of Peers appointed by the king and an elected Chamber of Deputies.

Under the Charter the king alone proposed laws and appointed ministers, so real power stayed with the crown. Civil equality and some liberties were guaranteed, and Catholicism was the state religion with other faiths tolerated.

The Charter kept many Napoleonic institutions, including the Napoleonic Code and the Concordat, and it accepted the sale of Church and noble lands during the Revolution. This reassured the many families who had gained from the Revolution.

The franchise was very narrow. Men aged 30 or over paying 300 francs a year in direct taxes could vote, and candidates had to be 40 or over and pay 1,000 francs, so the electorate was only about 90,000-100,000 wealthy property owners in a country of about 30 million.

In 1815 royalist mobs carried out the White Terror, killing Bonapartists, Protestants and former revolutionaries, mainly in the south. The government followed with an official purge, and Marshal Ney was tried and shot in December 1815.

Within a few years the Ultras, the extreme royalists who wanted to undo the Revolution, gained the upper hand. Under Charles X the monarchy came to look like a return to the old regime, which pushed moderates into opposition.

The Duc de Berry, nephew of Louis XVIII and heir in the next generation, was murdered on 13 February 1820. The Ultras, led by the Comte d'Artois (the future Charles X), used the murder to press for a harder line.

The Law of the Double Vote (1820) let the richest quarter of voters vote twice, which strengthened the wealthy landowners who backed the Ultras, and censorship was tightened. Villèle was chief minister from 1822 to 1828, so the Ultras ran the government.
Charles X was king from 1824 to 1830 and was crowned at Reims in 1825 with the old ceremony of the monarchy. This signalled a return to the old regime and to Church power.

In 1825 he passed a law on sacrilege (a crime of profaning Church objects or rites) and paid compensation to the émigrés (nobles who fled the Revolution) for their lost lands. It was often called the émigrés' billion, about one billion francs.

In 1827 he disbanded the Paris National Guard (the citizen militia of Paris, a force of the middle class). Together with the laws of 1825, this convinced many that he aimed to restore the authority of the Church and the nobility.
From 1827 the government steadily lost the support of the electorate. Charles X chose confrontation over compromise, and this chain of events led to the ordinances that brought him down.

The elections of November 1827 went against the government and Villèle resigned in January 1828. The anti-Villèle majority joined liberals and discontented royalists, so it was a coalition against the Ultras and not a purely liberal victory.
Martignac's moderate ministry (1828-29) was brief, because Charles X would not work with it or give it real support.
In August 1829 Charles X appointed Prince Jules de Polignac, a leading Ultra whose ministry lacked support in the Chamber. This was a deliberate challenge to the elected deputies.

In March 1830 the Address of the 221 deputies told the king that the ministry lacked the Chamber's confidence. The king dissolved the Chamber, but the elections of June-July 1830 increased the opposition.

Algiers was captured on 5 July 1830, the start of the French conquest of Algeria, and his one lasting success. It came too late to save Charles X, because the election result had already gone against him.

Faced with a hostile Chamber, Charles X chose to break the Charter instead of accepting defeat. Paris rose within days, which is the clearest example of a trigger (the Ordinances) acting on deeper causes.

On 25 July 1830 (published 26 July) Charles X issued the July Ordinances. They suspended freedom of the press, dissolved the newly elected Chamber, changed the electoral law to cut the electorate, and called new elections.
A group of journalists led by Adolphe Thiers of Le National published a protest.
Paris rose on 27-29 July 1830, the Three Glorious Days (Les Trois Glorieuses). Barricades went up across the city, and the king's troops could not hold it.
Charles X abdicated on 2 August 1830 and went into exile in Britain, the end of the Bourbon senior line's rule.
Louis-Philippe, Duke of Orléans, was made Lieutenant-General of the kingdom on 31 July and King of the French on 9 August 1830, with the help of liberal deputies, Thiers and Lafayette.

The Restoration fell because it was identified with the nobles, the Church and foreign bayonets (the Allied armies that had restored it). Charles X had broken the Charter, the narrow franchise left most men outside politics, and Paris rose.
The new regime accepted the Revolution's symbols but kept power in the hands of the wealthy middle class (the bourgeoisie). It was liberal but not democratic, a distinction that explains why it fell.

Louis-Philippe was called King of the French, not of France, to show his throne rested on the nation and not on divine right. The tricolour (the Revolution's red, white and blue flag) was restored. He came from the Orléans branch, not the senior Bourbon line.
The Charter was revised in 1830. Catholicism became only the religion of the majority of the French and no longer the state religion, and censorship was abolished.
Under the revised Charter both chambers could propose laws and the king lost the power to issue ordinances suspending laws, so the July Ordinances could not be repeated.
It was called a bourgeois monarchy or the citizen king's regime because it served the wealthy middle class. It followed the juste milieu (middle way) between the old Ultras and the republicans.

The 1831 electoral law cut the voting qualification from 300 to 200 francs, so more men could vote. The electorate rose from about 100,000 to about 170,000 in 1831 and to about 240,000-250,000 by 1846-48, still under 1 per cent of the population.
The regime disappointed everyone outside the narrow circle of voters. From the start it faced risings and plots from every camp, and met them with repression.
The Lyon silk workers (canuts) rose in November 1831 and April 1834. Their risings were put down by force, so workers learned that they had no voice under a property franchise.
Republicans rose in Paris in June 1832 and again in April 1834. The April 1834 rising included the massacre in the rue Transnonain in Paris, which hardened republican hatred of the regime.

Legitimists, supporters of the senior Bourbon line, rose in 1832 under the Duchesse de Berry. Bonapartists plotted too, for example Louis-Napoleon's attempts at Strasbourg (1836) and Boulogne (1840) both failed.

Fieschi's attempt to assassinate the king on 28 July 1835 led to the September Laws of 1835, which restricted the press. The regime responded to danger by cutting freedoms, which fed the republican opposition.
In the 1840s the July Monarchy became rigid. Its dominant minister refused all reform, and its cautious foreign policy bored a country that remembered Napoleonic glory.

François Guizot was the leading minister from October 1840 and head of the government in name from 1847. He refused any widening of the vote and opposed lowering the tax qualification, so only the wealthy kept political power.
His advice to those who wanted the vote is remembered as enrich yourselves, by work and saving. It summed up a regime that told the middle class to prosper instead of asking for political rights.
Guizot governed by patronage (giving jobs and favours to win loyalty) and a docile chamber. Bribery scandals involving former ministers in 1847 damaged the regime's reputation.
The regime had a cautious, peaceful foreign policy that was seen as weak. In a speech of 1839 Alphonse de Lamartine said France is bored (La France s'ennuie).
In December 1840 Napoleon I's remains were brought back from St Helena and placed in Les Invalides. The ceremony fed the Napoleonic legend, so a memory of glory was alive for his nephew to use.
A harsh economic downturn hit a regime that already refused reform. The opposition found a way to campaign, and the government's response set off the revolution.

The potato disease of 1845-46 and the bad harvest of 1846 caused high food prices. Industrial and financial depression in 1847 added unemployment, so the poor suffered at the same time as the regime's reputation fell.
From July 1847 the opposition ran a banquet campaign for electoral reform. Public dinners were used to demand reform, so the campaign put pressure on the government.
The Paris banquet set for 22 February 1848 was banned, and the ban led directly to the crowds that brought down the July Monarchy.
The July Monarchy fell because of its narrow base and its refusal to reform. The economic crisis, the loss of the National Guard's loyalty and a Paris rising finished it.
In three days of fighting the July Monarchy collapsed. A republic was declared at once, and Paris's example set off revolutions elsewhere in Europe.

The February Days ran from 22 to 24 February 1848, with crowds and barricades in Paris. Guizot was dismissed on 23 February, and that evening troops fired on a crowd on the Boulevard des Capucines, killing dozens, whose bodies were paraded through Paris.

The National Guard sided with reform, so the king lost the force he relied on. Louis-Philippe abdicated on 24 February in favour of his grandson, the Count of Paris, and fled to England, where he died in 1850.

A republic was proclaimed at the Hôtel de Ville on 24 February 1848. The Provisional Government included Lamartine (foreign affairs), Alexandre Ledru-Rollin (interior), the socialist Louis Blanc and the worker Albert.
The revolution in Paris set off risings in other parts of Europe in 1848.
The Provisional Government tried to satisfy both middle-class republicans and workers. Its measures were bold but they split the country between Paris and the provinces.
Universal male suffrage for men aged 21 or over came by the decree of 5 March 1848. It raised the electorate from about 250,000 to about 9 million.

Other reforms included the abolition of slavery in the colonies in April 1848 (under Victor Schoelcher), the cutting of the working day to ten hours in Paris (decree of 2 March 1848) and the abolition of the death penalty for political offences.
The government recognised a right to work and set up the Luxembourg Commission on labour, chaired by Louis Blanc, to consider workers' conditions.
National Workshops (Ateliers nationaux) were set up by the decree of 26 February 1848 to give work to the unemployed. Numbers passed 100,000 in Paris by June 1848, so the cost grew very fast.
Pay was low and much of the work was unproductive earth-moving, so the workshops became a heavy cost to the government and a target for conservative hostility.
The 45-centime tax, a 45 per cent surcharge on direct taxes in March 1848, fell mainly on peasants. It angered them against the Paris government, so the provinces turned against Paris.
The Constituent Assembly was elected on 23 April 1848 with high turnout. It had a moderate republican and conservative majority, and socialists did badly. A crowd invaded the Assembly on 15 May 1848.
The conservative Assembly turned on the workshops, and the workers of Paris answered with a rising. Its defeat shaped everything that followed.
The closure of the National Workshops was announced on 21 June 1848, with young members told to join the army or go to the provinces. Workers resisted, so the closure sparked the June Days.
The June Days (23-26 June 1848) were an insurrection in Paris. General Louis-Eugène Cavaignac was given full powers and crushed it with troops.
Archbishop Affre of Paris was shot on the barricades on 25 June while trying to make peace. Thousands were killed, thousands arrested and several thousand transported to Algeria.
The June Days alienated workers from the republic, because it was a republican government that had shot them.
Property owners and peasants became afraid of the reds (radical and socialist republicans). France moved to the right, and this fear gave Louis-Napoleon his chance.
The Republic's constitution made one man the head of the state, chosen by all men. That gave a well-known name an overwhelming advantage.
The constitution of 4 November 1848 set up a president elected by universal male suffrage for four years, not immediately re-eligible, and a single-chamber Legislative Assembly of 750.
Because both the president and the Assembly were elected by the people, each could claim to speak for the nation, which set up a conflict between them.
His name was already known: Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte, nephew of Napoleon I, had been elected to the Assembly in by-elections in June and September 1848.
On 10 December 1848 he was elected president with about 5.4 million votes, about 74 per cent. Cavaignac won about 1.4 million, Ledru-Rollin about 370,000 and Lamartine under 20,000.
He won because of his famous name, peasant votes, conservative backing and a vague programme, while the other candidates had been discredited.
For three years the president worked with a conservative Assembly, but their aims drifted apart. The Assembly's conservative laws gave him the issue he needed.
In July 1849 French troops under General Oudinot took Rome, crushed the Roman Republic and restored the rule of Pius IX, which won Catholic support for Louis-Napoleon.
In May 1849 the Party of Order (monarchists and conservatives) won a clear majority, about 450 of 750 seats. The democratic-socialists, the Montagne, won a substantial minority.
Ledru-Rollin's protest rising in Paris on 13 June 1849 failed and he fled to exile in London.
The Falloux Law of 15 March 1850 gave the Catholic Church a large role in education. It showed that the Party of Order put Church influence first, such as in schooling.

The electoral law of 31 May 1850 required three years' residence, removing about 3 million voters, mostly workers. Louis-Napoleon later posed as the defender of universal suffrage against the Assembly.
In July 1851 a majority of the Assembly voted to let him stand again, but fell short of the three-quarters the constitution required, so the revision failed.
Blocked by the constitution, Louis-Napoleon seized power by force and then asked the voters to approve it. Each step was endorsed by a plebiscite.
On 2 December 1851 Louis-Napoléon carried out a coup d'état. The date was the anniversary of Napoleon I's coronation (1804) and of Austerlitz (1805).

Charles de Morny, his half-brother, was Minister of the Interior. Deputies were arrested, including Thiers and Cavaignac, the Assembly was dissolved, and universal male suffrage was restored to win popular support.
Resistance came with barricades in Paris on 3-4 December, where the deputy Baudin was killed and troops fired on crowds on the boulevards, and with risings in parts of the centre and south.
About 26,000-27,000 people were arrested and thousands were transported to Algeria or French Guiana, so resistance was broken.

A plebiscite on 20-21 December 1851 approved the coup by about 7.4 million yes to about 640,000 no. The constitution of 14 January 1852 gave a ten-year presidency, a Senate, a Council of State and a weak elected Corps législatif.

In his Bordeaux speech on 9 October 1852 he said the Empire means peace (L'Empire, c'est la paix). A plebiscite on 21-22 November 1852 approved the Empire by about 7.8 million yes to about 250,000 no.
The Second Empire was proclaimed on 2 December 1852. Louis-Napoléon took the name Napoleon III, with the title Emperor of the French.

Napoleon III was a participant in the political events of 1848 to 1870 and the central figure of the regime. Contemporaries and historians disagree about whether he was a modernising leader or an autocrat who led France into disaster.

Born in Paris on 20 April 1808, Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte was the son of Louis Bonaparte, King of Holland, and Hortense de Beauharnais, and the nephew of Napoleon I. After 1815 he grew up in exile, mostly at Arenenberg in Switzerland.

He took part in the 1831 rising in the Papal States. His coups at Strasbourg (October 1836) and Boulogne (August 1840) failed, so he was jailed at Ham for about six years, where he wrote The Extinction of Pauperism (1844). He escaped in May 1846, lived in London.

After Napoleon I's son died in 1832 he headed the Bonaparte claim. His ideas were order with universal male suffrage, economic modernisation, concern for the poor, national glory and support for nationalities against the 1815 settlement.

As president he won the election of December 1848 by appealing to peasants and the memory of his uncle, and conservatives backed him expecting to use him. The fear of the reds after June 1848 gave him his chance, so events shaped him as well as him shaping events.
He made the coup of 1851 and the Empire of 1852 and personally directed policy at home and abroad until 1870, so the regime was tied to one man.

Ill health and war with Prussia ended his reign. He surrendered at Sedan on 2 September 1870, was held at Wilhelmshöhe near Kassel, then went into exile at Chislehurst, Kent, where he died on 9 January 1873.

Contemporaries were divided. Peasants, businessmen and Catholics (until 1859) supported him, while republicans and liberals saw a usurper, as in Hugo's Napoleon the Little and Marx's Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte (1852), where history repeats itself first as tragedy, then as farce. Foreign powers distrusted his ambitions.

The older view was of a dictator and adventurer whose regime ended in disaster. Revisionists Theodore Zeldin (The Political System of Napoleon III, 1958) and Roger Price stress modernisation, social concern and liberal reforms, though his foreign policy after 1860 failed, so he was more effective at home than abroad.

In its early years the Second Empire kept the form of universal male suffrage but gave voters little real power. It rested on the emperor, the prefects (the government's local officials) and plebiscites.

Ministers were answerable only to the emperor, so parliament could not control them. The Senate was appointed for life, the Council of State drafted laws, and the Corps législatif was elected by universal male suffrage but could only vote on laws put to it.

Official candidates backed by the prefects dominated elections, and plebiscites were the link between the emperor and the people. This was why the regime was democratic in its franchise but not in practice.
The press decree of February 1852 required newspapers to get government authorisation, and two official warnings could lead to suspension. Opponents were exiled.
After Felice Orsini's bomb attack of 14 January 1858 the Law of General Security (February 1858) allowed arrest and deportation without trial.
Opposition in the Corps législatif was weak because it was only a handful of republican deputies, the Five, including Émile Ollivier.
The regime justified itself by prosperity and prestige. State-encouraged investment and a showpiece capital were meant to win the loyalty that votes alone could not.

The Crédit Mobilier, founded in 1852 by the Pereire brothers (Émile and Isaac), financed railways, industry and urban development. The Crédit Foncier was also founded in 1852, the Crédit Lyonnais in 1863 and the Société Générale in 1864.

Railways grew from about 3,000-3,500 km in 1851 to about 17,000-18,000 km by 1870. This was the basis of the boom, together with Saint-Simonian ideas (a belief in state-led investment in industry and railways).

The Paris Exhibitions (Expositions Universelles) of 1855 and 1867 showed France's economy and prestige. The Suez Canal, built by Ferdinand de Lesseps, opened in November 1869 with Empress Eugénie present.
The rebuilding of Paris under Haussmann (Prefect of the Seine, 1853-70) was part of domestic policy, aimed at prestige, health, traffic and control of riots.
Social policy included encouragement of mutual aid societies, the right to strike (1864) and Victor Duruy's expansion of primary schooling as Minister of Public Instruction (1863-69).
Napoleon III married Eugénie de Montijo, a Spanish noblewoman, in January 1853, and the Prince Imperial was born in March 1856. An heir meant that the dynasty seemed secure.
From 1860 Napoleon III loosened his grip. The aim was to secure the dynasty by broadening its support, but each concession gave the opposition more room.
He liberalised because Catholics were angry at his Italian policy, manufacturers were angry at free trade, and he wanted to secure the dynasty and broaden support.
The Cobden-Chevalier Treaty of 23 January 1860 lowered tariffs with Britain, which was good for consumers and modernisation but resented by protected industries.

The decree of 24 November 1860 allowed debate on the Address and the publication of debates. Interpellation (the right to question ministers) came in 1867, so ministers had to answer to deputies, and laws of 1868 eased press controls and allowed public meetings.
The right to strike was legalised in 1864 (proposed by Ollivier), but unions were still illegal. Trade unions were tolerated from 1868 but not legalised until 1884.

Opposition grew. Republicans gained in the 1863 and 1869 elections, Thiers was elected in 1863, and Léon Gambetta's Belleville programme of 1869 was radical and republican. Morny, the regime's skilled manager of the Chamber, had died in 1865.
Ollivier's ministry took office on 2 January 1870. A plebiscite on 8 May 1870 approved the liberal Empire by about 7.3 million yes to about 1.5 million no, just months before its collapse.
Napoleon III wanted to undo the humiliation of 1815 and win glory while claiming the Empire means peace. His early successes made the regime look strong.
His aims were to undo the humiliation of 1815, win prestige and glory, support nationalities and gain territory, while claiming the Empire means peace.
France and Britain declared war on Russia in March 1854 in the Crimean War (1854-56), so France fought as Britain's ally. Sebastopol fell in September 1855 after the French took the Malakoff.
The Congress of Paris (February-March 1856, Treaty of Paris on 30 March 1856) was held in Paris and showed France's restored standing.
In Italy he met Cavour at Plombières in July 1858. The war of 1859 brought the victories of Magenta (4 June) and Solferino (24 June), then the sudden armistice of Villafranca on 11 July 1859.
By the Treaty of Turin in March 1860 Nice and Savoy went to France, confirmed by plebiscites in April 1860.
The 1859 war angered French Catholics, and the French garrison kept in Rome until August 1870 angered Italian nationalists.
Overseas, the Empire expanded, but where Napoleon III tried to do more his policy ended in failure. Mexico was the costliest.

Algeria was completed, and expansion in Senegal was led by Governor Louis Faidherbe. Saigon was taken in 1859, Cochinchina (southern Vietnam) was ceded in 1862, and a protectorate was set up over Cambodia in 1863.
In Poland the rising against Russia began in January 1863. France showed sympathy but took no action, so it annoyed Russia and won nothing.
In Mexico a joint intervention with Britain and Spain over Mexican debts began from late 1861. Britain and Spain withdrew in 1862, but France stayed, so it was left alone in Mexico.
The French were defeated at Puebla on 5 May 1862 but took Mexico City in 1863. Archduke Maximilian of Austria (Franz Joseph's brother) accepted the crown in 1864.
Benito Juárez led the Mexican republicans. After the American Civil War ended in 1865 the USA pressed for withdrawal, and French troops left in 1866-67.
Maximilian was shot at Querétaro on 19 June 1867. It was a costly humiliation, so the regime's prestige suffered.
After 1865 Napoleon III misjudged Prussia. The quick Prussian victory of 1866 changed the balance of power, and in 1870 France went to war isolated and unprepared.

At Biarritz in October 1865 he met Bismarck, and France stayed neutral in 1866. The quick Prussian victory at Königgrätz (Sadowa) on 3 July 1866 changed the balance of power, and the government lost prestige. French demands for compensation failed.
The Luxembourg crisis of 1867 was settled at the London conference, which neutralised Luxembourg. Marshal Niel's army law of 1868 was weakened by the Corps législatif, so army reform came to little.
The Hohenzollern candidature (Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen offered the Spanish throne) was withdrawn on 12 July 1870, but France demanded guarantees.
The Ems telegram of 13 July 1870 was edited by Bismarck and published. France declared war on 19 July 1870, isolated and unprepared.
Marshal Bazaine's army was shut up in Metz from August 1870, so it could not help elsewhere, and it surrendered on 27 October 1870.
At Sedan, the battle of 1 September 1870 and the surrender on 2 September ended in the capture of Marshal MacMahon's army and the emperor.
The judgement on foreign policy is successes to 1860 (Crimea, Italy, Nice and Savoy), then failures (Poland, Mexico, 1866 and 1870) that destroyed the regime.

Victor Hugo, born in Besançon on 26 February 1802, son of a general under Napoleon, was a leading Romantic writer, but here we deal with his political role as a deputy and an opponent of Napoleon III. He was a royalist in the 1820s, writing royalist odes and receiving a royal pension, and Louis-Philippe made him a peer of France in 1845.

He was elected to the Constituent Assembly in a by-election in June 1848 and to the Legislative Assembly in May 1849. At first close to the conservatives, he defended press freedom and education, and his sons' newspaper L'Événement (founded 1848) backed Louis-Napoleon for president.

From 1849 to 1851 he moved to the democratic left. He made his speech on destitution in July 1849, spoke against the Falloux Law in January 1850 and opposed the law of 31 May 1850, because it took the vote from about 3 million men.
In the revision debate of July 1851 he attacked Louis-Napoleon's ambition, mocking the idea that Napoleon the Great must be followed by Napoleon the Little. This is the origin of the nickname.

He tried to organise resistance to the coup of December 1851 and fled to Brussels on 11 December 1851. Banished, he lived on Jersey (1852-55, until expelled) and then on Guernsey (1855-70), at Hauteville House.
His weapons from exile were Napoléon le Petit (1852) and the satirical poems Les Châtiments (1853), smuggled into France. He also published Les Misérables (1862) while in exile.

He refused the amnesty for exiles of August 1859 and stayed in exile as a symbol of republican resistance. A line from Les Châtiments ran: And if only one remains, I shall be that one (Et s'il n'en reste qu'un, je serai celui-là).

He returned to Paris on 5 September 1870, the day after the Third Republic was proclaimed, and stayed in Paris during the siege. He was elected to the National Assembly in February 1871 and resigned in March 1871.

In spring 1871 he was in Brussels, handling the affairs of his son Charles, who died in March. He condemned both the Commune's killing of hostages and the government's reprisals, offered refuge to Communards, was expelled from Belgium in May 1871 and later campaigned for their amnesty.
Contemporaries and historians have judged Hugo differently, but both agree that his exile gave the republican cause a voice.
Republicans admired him as the conscience of resistance because he stayed in exile, while opponents mocked him for his changes of side from royalism to republicanism.

He became a senator in 1876. His state funeral followed his death on 22 May 1885: he lay in state under the Arc de Triomphe and was buried in the Panthéon, and the crowds are often put at about two million.
Historians see a sincere if changeable defender of liberty, democracy and the poor. His exile gave the republican cause a voice.
Napoleon III's surrender ended the Empire at once. A republic was declared and the war went on, but defeat made peace unavoidable.
After Sedan the Empire collapsed. On 4 September 1870 the republic was proclaimed at the Hôtel de Ville in Paris by Gambetta, Jules Favre and Jules Ferry, in an almost bloodless revolution.
A Government of National Defence was set up under General Louis-Jules Trochu to continue the war, and Empress Eugénie fled to England.
The siege of Paris began on 19 September 1870. Gambetta left Paris by balloon on 7 October 1870 for Tours to raise armies in the provinces, and Parisians ate horses, rats and zoo animals.
German bombardment of Paris came in January 1871, so hunger and shelling forced the armistice of 28 January 1871.

The National Assembly was elected on 8 February 1871 and about 400 of its roughly 650 members were monarchists, a peace-seeking majority elected mainly by the countryside. Thiers became chief of the executive power, and the Assembly sat at Bordeaux and then at Versailles, not Paris.
The Treaty of Frankfurt (10 May 1871) gave Alsace and much of Lorraine to Germany, with an indemnity of 5 billion francs and German occupation until it was paid.
Paris did not accept the peace or the monarchist Assembly. The result was a second civil conflict, this time between Paris and the government of the republic.
Paris rose because of the humiliation of defeat and of the German victory parade of 1 March 1871, the end of the moratorium on rents and debts and the end of National Guard pay.
A monarchist Assembly at Versailles and the radical and socialist traditions of Paris made conflict likely.

The Commune lasted from 18 March to 28 May 1871. It began when troops sent to take the National Guard's cannon on Montmartre failed, Generals Lecomte and Clément-Thomas were killed by the crowd, and Thiers withdrew the government to Versailles.
The Commune was elected on 26 March 1871 and was a mix of Jacobins, Blanquists and socialists. Louise Michel was a leading Communard.
Its measures included the separation of Church and State, the end of night work in bakeries, the red flag and the pulling down of the Vendôme Column on 16 May 1871.

In the Bloody Week (21-28 May 1871) government troops under MacMahon retook Paris. Communards shot Archbishop Georges Darboy as a hostage on 24 May, and the Tuileries Palace and Hôtel de Ville were burned.
The last fighting was at Père Lachaise cemetery. Estimates of the dead range from several thousand to about 20,000. About 40,000 were arrested and thousands transported to New Caledonia.
The Commune left a lasting mark on French politics. It shaped how both left and right saw the republic.
Socialists made a martyr myth of the Commune because thousands had been killed, and Marx wrote The Civil War in France (1871) as a critic of the repression.
The right was left with a lasting fear of revolution, so it backed order, and the workers' movement was crushed for years.
The republic survived because it had crushed the Commune and the monarchists were divided. Thiers became president in August 1871 and MacMahon in 1873.
Constitutional laws of 1875 confirmed the Third Republic with a parliamentary system and a president, beyond this period. An amnesty for Communards followed in 1880.
Napoleon III is best judged by pairing his achievements with their limits, at home and abroad.
At home he brought order, prosperity, modernisation, a rebuilt Paris and, from 1860, liberal reforms, which won him real support.
Against this, the regime depended on repression, a rubber-stamp legislature and the personal authority of one man.
Abroad he achieved Crimea, Italy, Nice and Savoy and colonies.
Against this came Mexico, Poland, 1866 and the disaster of 1870. Overall he was more successful at home than abroad.
Five regimes in fifty-seven years show that France lacked agreement about who should govern and how. Several causes combined, and the strongest answers rank them.

Five regimes between 1814 and 1871 (the Bourbon Restoration, the July Monarchy, the Second Republic, the Second Empire and the Third Republic) reflected the lack of agreement about the basis of government.
The divided legacy of 1789 and rival dynasties and groups meant that no regime could win everyone, because each camp rejected the others.
The Bourbon and July regimes were limited by narrow franchises, and the exclusion of most men made opposition likely.
Paris was powerful and its crowd could topple governments, as in 1830 and 1848, and economic crises such as 1846-47 made this worse.
Rulers would not compromise, for example Charles X, who broke the Charter, and Guizot, who refused to extend the vote.

The Second Republic showed that universal male suffrage could bring a president who would destroy the republic. It deepened the divide between the urban poor and the conservative countryside, and the constitution pitted president against assembly.

Regimes ended in revolution (1830, 1848), coup (1851) or military defeat (1870). The town-country split (Paris radical, the provinces conservative) appears in April 1848, December 1848 and February 1871.

Beneath the changes the centralised state, the Code, the prefects and the Concordat survived every regime. Overall, each regime lacked a broad consensus and rested on personal rulers rather than a settled system. Thiers said in 1850 that the republic was the government that divides us least.
Between 1815 and 1871 Europe was changing from a world of farmers and craft workers to one of factories and towns. Britain led the way, so it helps to know what the change was and why it began there.

Industrialisation, often called the 'Industrial Revolution', was the shift from hand production at home or in small workshops (the domestic system, where families worked for merchants in their own houses) to machine production in factories powered first by water and then by steam.
The British industrial revolution began in the later eighteenth century in cotton textiles, coal and iron, which is why Britain is described as the first industrial nation.
Britain industrialised first because it had coal and iron ore close together, capital (money to invest) from trade and farming, and overseas and colonial markets to sell to.
It also had a large merchant fleet and navy, rivers, canals and ports for moving goods, and political stability, so investors could trust that their factories would not be seized or wrecked by war.
Britain's population roughly doubled between 1801 and 1851 (the first census was in 1801). This gave industry both workers to hire and customers to buy its goods.
A growing population was fed because farming had improved, which is why changes in agriculture and industry belong together in this topic.
Before 1815 most Europeans lived on the land and worked in farming. Western Europe was ahead of central and eastern Europe in both farming and industry, so change was uneven across the continent.
Britain's farming was transformed from the eighteenth century onwards. The first big change was in how land was held, because farmers could not improve land that was shared and scattered.

Enclosure replaced open fields and common land with compact, hedged farms. In the open-field system villagers farmed scattered strips and shared common land, which made it hard for anyone to try new methods.
Most enclosure was done by private Acts of Parliament. There were thousands of them, and most were passed between 1750 and 1850.
The General Enclosure Acts of 1801 and 1845 simplified the procedure, so landowners no longer needed a separate Act for every village.
The result was larger, more efficient farms and higher output, because owners could drain land, choose crops and breed animals without interference from neighbours.
The cost fell on the poor. Cottagers and labourers (people with a cottage and a few rights on the common but little or no land) lost their common rights and their access to land.
Without land of their own, many became wage labourers, moved to the towns or emigrated, which fed the growth of the industrial towns.
Enclosed farms could be run more intelligently. New crop rotations and better breeding allowed farmers to feed more people and more animals from the same land.

The Norfolk four-course rotation grew wheat, turnips, barley and clover in turn. It ended the fallow year (a year when land was left unplanted to recover), so every field produced something every year.
Turnips and clover fed livestock through the winter, so farmers could keep more animals and did not have to slaughter many in autumn. More animals also meant more manure to fertilise the fields.
The rotation was popularised in the eighteenth century, and Charles 'Turnip' Townshend is associated with it.
As background from before 1815, Jethro Tull's seed drill (early 1700s) sowed seed in rows at a regular depth, reducing the waste of scattering seed by hand.
Also as background, Robert Bakewell in Leicestershire used selective breeding (choosing the best animals as parents) to improve sheep and cattle, breeding them for meat.
From the 1840s science and machines began to raise yields and cut the labour needed on farms. This helped output, but it also left farm workers more insecure.
Guano (dried seabird droppings, rich in nutrients) was imported from Peru as fertiliser from the 1840s, so farmers could restore soil without leaving it fallow.
John Bennet Lawes patented superphosphate fertiliser in 1842 and founded the Rothamsted experiments in Hertfordshire, which tested crops and fertilisers scientifically.
Justus von Liebig's book on chemistry applied to agriculture (1840) showed that plants take nutrients from the soil, and field drainage of wet land also raised yields from the 1840s.
The threshing machine, which separates grain from straw, reduced the need for hand labour at harvest. Reapers followed, such as the American McCormick reaper shown at the Great Exhibition in 1851.
Steam power came onto farms later in the period, so machines could do work once done by hand.
Anger over threshing machines, which took away winter work, fed the Swing Riots of 1830 in southern and eastern England, when farm labourers broke the machines.
Life for agricultural workers was harsh: low wages, insecure seasonal work, the loss of common rights and poor cottages. Exams ask about both farm and factory workers.
Grain was Britain's most important crop, and landowners wanted its price kept high. The Corn Laws were their protection.
The Corn Law of 1815 banned imports of foreign wheat until the home price was high. This protected British grain growers by keeping out cheap foreign grain.
The same law kept bread dear for townspeople and factory workers, which is why it became a target of free-trade critics.
The Corn Laws were repealed in 1846.
Farming on the continent changed more slowly than in Britain, and the pattern of landholding depended on what each state had done to the old system of lords and peasants.
In France the Revolution of 1789 abolished feudal dues (payments peasants owed to their lords). By 1815 peasants owned much of the land in small farms.
French farms stayed small and methods were slow to change. Many peasants stayed on the land, which slowed migration into industry.
In Prussia the Stein–Hardenberg reforms began with the October Edict of 1807 (Stein), which abolished hereditary serfdom (peasants bound to the land and owing service to a lord), in effect from 1810.
Hardenberg's Regulation Edict of 1811 let peasants become owners of their land, but only by surrendering part of it, often a third to a half, to the lord. This is why the nobility kept large estates.
The Junker estates (the big estates of the Prussian landowning nobility) of the east grew large and were modernised. They produced grain for export and for the growing cities.
New crops spread on the continent: the potato became the staple (main everyday food) of the poor, and sugar beet was grown in France and the German lands.
The poor depended on a few crops, so when those failed the result was hunger across much of Europe. The crisis also pushed people to leave.

The potato blight (a disease that rots the crop) struck from 1845, and grain harvests were poor in 1846 and 1847. Food prices rose and there was hunger and food riots across western and central Europe.
In Britain the 1840s are often called the 'Hungry Forties'.
The hunger came together with a commercial and industrial depression in 1847, which helped create the conditions for the revolutions of 1848.
Emigration from the German lands to the United States grew strongly in the late 1840s and 1850s, as rural people and artisans (skilled craft workers) sought land and work abroad.
Ireland also lost many people. In the Famine of 1845–49 about a million died and about a million emigrated.

Three industries led the first industrial revolution: coal, iron and cotton textiles, with the factory and steam power at the centre. Steam and cotton show how invention changed where and how people worked.
James Watt improved the steam engine, patenting a separate condenser in 1769 and adding rotary motion (turning a wheel) from the 1780s. His partner was Matthew Boulton of Birmingham.
Steam was used to pump water out of coal mines and to drive machinery in factories. Because engines did not need a river, factories no longer had to be built beside fast water.
Richard Arkwright's water frame (1769) and Samuel Crompton's spinning mule (1779) mechanised spinning, the making of thread from fibre.
Edmund Cartwright's power loom (1785) spread weaving into factories as well. Hand-loom weavers, who worked at home, declined as a result.
Raw cotton for the Lancashire mills was imported in large quantities, mostly from the southern United States.
Britain became the leading exporter of cotton goods, which is why Lancashire was the centre of the industry.
Machines, rails and bridges all needed iron, and later steel. Britain's lead in metals showed in 1851, when it put its industry on show.

Abraham Darby's coke smelting at Coalbrookdale in Shropshire (1709) used coke (coal heated to remove impurities) to smelt iron. It was background to the growth of the iron industry, which produced iron on a larger scale.
Iron was used for rails, bridges and machines, which is why iron and coal grew together with railways and factories.
Henry Bessemer's converter (1856) made steel cheaply. Steel is stronger than iron, and cheap steel was the basis of later heavy industry.
The Great Exhibition of 1851 was held in the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park, London. It showed Britain as the 'workshop of the world', a nickname for the leading industrial nation.
Railways combined iron, coal and steam. They changed how goods and people moved and created demand for more industry.
The Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in 1825, so steam locomotives were already in use before the Liverpool line.
The Stephensons' Rocket (built by George and Robert Stephenson) won the Rainhill Trials in 1829, showing that steam locomotives could haul trains effectively.
The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened on 15 September 1830. It was the first inter-city railway worked by steam locomotives, with timetabled passenger trains.
A railway boom, known as 'railway mania', followed in Britain in the mid-1840s, and the rail network expanded rapidly.
Railways made transport of goods and people cheaper and faster, and they created national markets instead of local ones.
They created demand for coal, iron and engineering, and they gave work in construction, so railways pulled other industries along.
Britain's lead did not mean the rest of Europe followed at once. Obstacles delayed continental industry, but Belgium overcame them first.

The continent was slower because of the French wars, poorer transport, internal tariffs (taxes on goods crossing borders) and many separate states in the German lands, less accessible coal and smaller markets.
A peasantry that stayed on the land also meant fewer workers moved into factories.
Continental states copied British machines and hired British engineers to catch up.
Belgium was the first country on the continent to industrialise, with coal in Hainaut and Liège. It had the advantage of coal, which powered engines and furnaces.
John Cockerill, who was English-born, set up ironworks and engineering works at Seraing, near Liège, in 1817.
The Brussels–Mechelen railway, opened on 5 May 1835, was Belgium's first railway, steam-worked and the first stage of a state-built network.

Continental industry relied more on investment banks and on state help, through railways and tariffs, than British industry did. In Britain firms grew largely from their own profits and private capital.
France industrialised more slowly than Britain or Belgium. Its growth was mixed, with some regions advanced and a large rural population behind.
Textile industry developed in Alsace (Mulhouse) and Normandy (Rouen), such as cotton spinning and weaving.
The Schneider brothers took over the ironworks at Le Creusot in 1836, for example, building up iron and engineering in central France.
