The Saint-Étienne–Andrézieux line of 1827 carried coal and was horse-drawn at first.
The Railway Law of 11 June 1842 set out a national network in which the state provided the land and track bed while private companies laid the track and ran the lines.
Growth was faster in the 1850s and 1860s under the Second Empire.
The German lands industrialised late but fast. Removing barriers between states and building on rich coalfields let them catch up.
The Zollverein (customs union) of 1834 removed internal tariffs between member states, so trade and investment grew across the German lands.
The first German railway ran from Nuremberg to Fürth in Bavaria and opened on 7 December 1835.
The Ruhr and Silesian coalfields grew rapidly, which gave cheap fuel for iron and steel.
Alfred Krupp's works at Essen expanded from the 1850s, and the steel industry of the Ruhr was built on coal and iron from the region.
Friedrich List argued in The National System of Political Economy (1841) for railways and protective tariffs for young German industry.
By 1871 Germany was becoming the leading industrial power on the continent.
The factory changed how people lived their working lives. Instead of working at home at their own pace, workers had to obey the machine and the clock.
The factory system concentrated workers under supervision, working fixed hours to the pace of the machines for wages, with fines and discipline for lateness or mistakes.
Hand workers such as handloom weavers declined because machines produced cloth more cheaply.
Hours were long, often 12 to 14 a day in cotton mills, so workers had little time or energy outside work.
Children and women made up a large share of the textile workforce, and children could start work at an early age because they were cheap to employ.
Unfenced machinery caused accidents and injuries, and little or no compensation was paid to injured workers.
Poor ventilation, dust and heat made mills unhealthy, so lung disease and exhaustion were common.
In the mines, children and women worked underground in dangerous conditions, such as hauling coal in the dark.
Workers resisted the machines, reformers gathered evidence, and Parliament passed laws. Each law covered a particular group and place, so you need to know which is which.
The Luddites (1811–16, in the Midlands and the North of England) broke machines, which showed the hostility of hand workers who feared losing their living.
The Sadler Committee of 1832 (led by Michael Sadler MP) gathered evidence of the abuse of child workers. Lord Ashley, later 7th Earl of Shaftesbury, campaigned for factory reform.
The Factory Act of 1833 barred children under nine from textile mills (silk mills excepted), and limited children of 9–13 to nine hours and young persons of 13–18 to twelve hours a day.
The 1833 Act also required two hours' schooling a day for child workers, and four inspectors were appointed to enforce it.
The Mines Act of 1842 banned women and girls, and boys under ten, from working underground.
The Ten Hours Act of 1847 limited women and young persons in textile mills to ten hours a day. A Factory Act of 1844 came in between.
Many British thinkers and governments believed the state should leave the economy alone. This belief explains both why change was so fast and why the response to its harms was slow.
Laissez-faire is the belief that the state should leave the economy, prices, wages and trade to the free market.

Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations (1776) argued that free trade and competition produce prosperity. Thomas Malthus (Essay on the Principle of Population, 1798) and David Ricardo (Principles of Political Economy, 1817) were later economists in this tradition.
In practice laissez-faire meant free trade, shown by the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846.

The Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834 gave relief to the able-bodied poor normally only inside a workhouse, where conditions were made worse than those of the poorest independent labourer. This was the principle of 'less eligibility'.
The limits: the state did intervene in child and female labour (the Factory Acts and Mines Act) and in public health, but not in men's wages or hours.
The continent was more interventionist: Prussia and France promoted railways, tariffs and banks. List argued that young German industry needed protection.
Industry and farming change drew people into towns. Cities grew faster than anyone could house them, which is the root of the slum and disease problems of the industrial towns.
Manchester, nicknamed 'Cottonopolis', grew from about 75,000 people in 1801 to about 300,000 in 1851.
Liverpool, Leeds, Birmingham and Glasgow also grew quickly, because they were centres of trade and industry that offered work.
Migration from the countryside had push causes (enclosure, mechanisation, rural poverty and the 1840s crisis) and pull causes (factory work and wages).
Irish migrants came to British cities in large numbers, especially in the 1840s, because the Famine drove them from home.
Paris grew mainly by migration from the provinces, from about 550,000 in 1801 to about a million by the mid-1840s, with overcrowding in the old centre.

In the Ruhr, Essen, Bochum and Dortmund grew fast in the 1850s and 1860s, drawing workers from rural Prussia. Mass Polish-speaking migration came later, mainly after 1871, so it falls outside this period.
The 1851 census showed that, for the first time, more than half the population of England and Wales lived in towns.
Towns had grown far faster than their housing and water. The result was disease, as the poor lived in places with no drains.

Slums had back-to-back houses (built in rows sharing walls, with no back door or through air), cellar dwellings, overcrowding, no drains, shared privies, polluted water and smoke. Death rates were high, especially among infants.
Little Ireland in Manchester was an Irish slum by the River Medlock, described by Engels.
Friedrich Engels, in The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845, published in German), described Manchester, a witness account that influenced the debate on reform.
Cholera, a disease spread by dirty water, struck Britain in 1831–32, 1848–49 and 1853–54, and Paris in 1832 and 1849. Thousands died in each epidemic. Typhus and tuberculosis also killed.
Inquiry came first and law followed, but reform was slow because many believed the state should not interfere.
Edwin Chadwick's Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population of Great Britain (1842) linked dirt and poor drainage to disease and early death.
The Public Health Act of 1848 created a General Board of Health (Chadwick a member) and local boards of health.
It was largely permissive, meaning towns were not forced to act. Local boards were compulsory only where the death rate was very high.
In 1854 the London physician John Snow traced the Broad Street (Soho) cholera outbreak to a contaminated pump, showing that cholera spread through water.
After the 'Great Stink' of summer 1858, Joseph Bazalgette built London's main drainage system (sewers) from 1859.
The Peabody Trust (1862), founded by the American banker George Peabody, built model dwellings for London's poor.
The Public Health Act of 1875 made sanitary provision compulsory for local authorities, after the period.
As economies and states changed, governments wanted schooled populations. Prussia led, and France followed with a law of its own.
States expanded schooling to produce disciplined, literate workers and soldiers, and loyal citizens and subjects. Churches also had religious and moral aims.
Fear of disorder pushed states too, because schools taught obedience, and later came the need for voters who could read.

Prussia had compulsory schooling from the eighteenth century, confirmed by Frederick the Great's General School Regulations of 1763. The state supervised village schools and teachers, and teacher-training seminaries followed in the nineteenth century.
Prussia was seen as Europe's model because it had among the highest literacy rates.
The Guizot Law of 28 June 1833 (François Guizot, Minister of Public Instruction) required each commune (the smallest local government unit) to maintain a primary school, in practice for boys.
It also required each department to have a teacher-training college (école normale). Schooling was not free or compulsory for all, with free places for the poor only.
Victor Duruy's law of 1867 required communes of 500 or more inhabitants to provide a girls' school.
Britain left schooling to churches for a long time, and the state slowly came in with money, inspection and, in 1870, its own schools.
Schools were run by voluntary religious societies: the Anglican National Society (1811) and the Nonconformist British and Foreign School Society (1814).
They used the monitorial system of Andrew Bell and Joseph Lancaster, in which older pupils (monitors) taught younger ones, so one teacher could manage a large class cheaply.
The first government grant for education came in 1833: £20,000, given to the two societies.

The Committee of the Privy Council on Education (1839) was set up to supervise a larger grant, raised to £30,000, with James Kay (later Kay-Shuttleworth) as secretary. School inspectors began in 1839.
The Newcastle Commission, appointed in 1858 and reporting in 1861, found many children were poorly taught.
Robert Lowe's Revised Code of 1862 introduced 'payment by results', so grants depended on pupils' results in reading, writing and arithmetic.

The Elementary Education Act of 1870, introduced by W. E. Forster, set up elected school boards to build board schools where voluntary schools were insufficient. Fees were still charged and boards could make attendance compulsory locally; national compulsion came in 1880.
Schooling raised literacy, the ability to read and write, and literacy changed politics.

Historians measure literacy by the ability to sign the marriage register. It was highest in Prussia, Scandinavia and Scotland, lower in England and France, and much lower in southern and eastern Europe.
Literacy was higher in Protestant northern Europe and lower in the south and east, so the gap was wide across the continent.
More people could read newspapers, books and pamphlets, and a cheap popular press grew.
Political ideas, nationalism and mass politics spread, because ideas could now reach the middle and working classes in print.
Examiners reward judgement. Weigh what the period gained against what it cost, and note that change was uneven.
Gains: rising output and national wealth, and more food from improved farming.
Costs: loss of land and common rights, child labour and dangerous work, slums and epidemics, and the 1840s hunger.
Gains: railways and cheaper goods, and by the end of the period reform of factories, public health and education.
Costs: government response was slow and uneven because of laissez-faire, so harm continued even after reform began.

Uneven change: Britain went first and furthest and Belgium early, France was slower with its peasant farms, and the German lands grew rapidly after 1850. Eastern and southern Europe were largely agricultural in 1871.
Contemporary views: critics at the time such as Engels, Chadwick and the factory reformers saw misery. Supporters saw progress, as at the Great Exhibition.
Later views: historians still debate whether workers' living standards rose or fell in the early decades (the 'standard of living debate'), with broad agreement that they rose after about 1850.
Verdict: real gains in wealth and education came at a heavy social cost.
Industrialisation created a new class of factory workers who had little power over their lives. Every movement in this subsection was an attempt to answer that problem, in one of three ways.

Industrialisation created a large factory working class, crowded into fast-growing towns, with long hours, low pay, child labour and slum housing, and with no vote. This is why unions, socialists and Chartists all appeared when they did.

Britain before 1832 was ruled by a Parliament chosen by a small, mostly propertied electorate. "Rotten boroughs" (tiny electorates controlled by a patron, Old Sarum being the best-known example) had MPs, while Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds and Sheffield had none.
The first kind of response was practical self-help, such as trade unions (associations of workers who join together to bargain with employers) and co-operatives (businesses owned by their members).
The second kind was new theories about how society should be organised: socialism, communism and anarchism.
The third kind was political campaigning, either for the vote from below (Chartism) or for reform from above, carried out by governments (Peel). Essays often compare these three kinds.

Workers' first attempts to organise were met with fear and repression. A trade union is an association of workers who combine to bargain over wages and conditions, and in this period the law treated that as a danger to the state.
The Combination Acts of 1799 and 1800 (Pitt's government) banned workers from combining to raise wages or change conditions, out of fear of revolution after 1789.
The Acts were repealed in 1824 after a campaign by Francis Place, a radical tailor, and Joseph Hume MP. A wave of strikes followed repeal. This shows that repeal released pent-up grievances.
Because of the strikes, the Act of 1825 let unions meet and bargain over wages and hours but made "molestation", obstruction and intimidation offences, which restricted strike action.

In 1834 six Dorset farm labourers, the Tolpuddle Martyrs, were led by George Loveless, a Methodist preacher. They were sentenced to seven years' transportation (forced exile to Australia) for swearing a secret oath, which the law treated as unlawful.
A large London protest march in April 1834 and a public campaign followed, and the six were pardoned in 1836. This shows that public opinion could force the government to back down.
The Grand National Consolidated Trades Union (GNCTU), founded early in 1834, tried to unite all trades in one union. Robert Owen was its leading figure, though he did not found it.
The GNCTU collapsed later in 1834, because of lockouts (employers shutting workers out), the Tolpuddle case, disputes and lack of funds.
After the failure of one big union for everyone, skilled workers built smaller, more cautious unions that lasted. These New Model unions set the pattern for the rest of the century.
The Amalgamated Society of Engineers (1851) took skilled men only, charged a high subscription of a shilling a week and employed full-time officials, which made it stable.
Its central fund paid benefits for sickness, unemployment, accident and funerals, and it was cautious about strikes.

The carpenters copied the model in the Amalgamated Society of Carpenters and Joiners (1860, Robert Applegarth). The London leaders of these new amalgamated unions in the 1860s were known as "the Junta". This shows the ASE model was thought a success, so others copied it.
Unions were mainly for skilled craftsmen, who could afford the subscriptions. Unskilled workers stayed largely unorganised until later in the century.
The Trades Union Congress first met in Manchester in 1868. This gave unions a national voice, so they could lobby Parliament together.

The Trade Union Act of 1871 made unions legal and protected their funds, but the Criminal Law Amendment Act of the same year restricted picketing (standing outside a workplace to persuade others to join a strike).
Examiners reward answers on Europe that go beyond Britain. On the continent the law was generally harsher towards unions, and workers' political parties appeared in the German lands.
In France the Le Chapelier Law of 1791 banned combinations of workers, so French unions began under a legal ban lasting well into the nineteenth century.
Napoleon III granted the right to strike in 1864 and tolerated unions from 1868. Full legalisation came only in 1884, after this period.
In the German lands Ferdinand Lassalle founded the General German Workers' Association at Leipzig in 1863, an early political party for workers.
August Bebel and Wilhelm Liebknecht founded the Social Democratic Workers' Party at Eisenach in 1869, a separate party from Lassalle's.
Socialism was an idea before it was a mass movement. Early reformers wanted to replace competition with co-operation, and the word was in use well before Marx wrote.

Socialism means common or public ownership of the means of production (land, factories, mines) so that wealth is shared. The word came into use in Britain and France in the late 1820s and 1830s, used by Owen's followers and by Saint-Simon's.

Henri de Saint-Simon (1760 to 1825) wanted the whole of society organised by scientists, bankers and industrialists for the good of the poorest and most numerous class. His followers, the Saint-Simonians, were active in the 1830s.

Charles Fourier (1772 to 1837) planned co-operative communities called phalanxes, of about 1,600 people living in a building called a phalanstère and sharing work they found attractive. This is why he, not Saint-Simon, is the model-community planner.

Robert Owen, manager of New Lanark from 1800, set up New Harmony in Indiana in 1825, which failed within a few years. He is counted among the utopian socialists, those who relied on model communities.

Louis Blanc's The Organisation of Labour (1839) urged state-funded "social workshops" run by workers, and "the right to work". He sat in the Provisional Government in February 1848. This is why his ideas lay behind the 1848 demand for the right to work.
Pierre-Joseph Proudhon's What is Property? (1840) declared "Property is theft!" He was the first writer to call himself an anarchist, and he influenced Bakunin.
By 1847 socialist ideas had reached German exile workers in London. Their League turned to Marx and Engels, who also gave the earlier socialists the label "utopian".
The Communist League was formed in London in 1847, growing out of the League of the Just, a society of German exile workers.
At its congress late in 1847 the League commissioned Marx and Engels to write its programme, the Communist Manifesto. This is why the Manifesto is tied to this League.

"Utopian" and "scientific" socialism are terms Engels used in his pamphlet Socialism: Utopian and Scientific (1880). Marx and Engels called the early socialists utopian because they relied on model communities and appeals to the rich, and called their own theory scientific socialism.
Karl Marx was the most influential theorist of socialism. He was an exile and a writer rather than a leader of crowds, and his followers became a mass movement only after his death.
Marx was born on 5 May 1818 in Trier, in the Prussian Rhineland. His father, a lawyer, had converted from Judaism to Protestant Christianity.

He studied law and then philosophy at Bonn and Berlin and took a doctorate at Jena in 1841. He was influenced by Hegel's dialectic (the idea that change comes through the conflict of opposites), which later shaped his view of history.

He edited the Rheinische Zeitung in Cologne in 1842. The government suppressed it in 1843, so he moved to Paris (1843 to 1845), where he met Engels in 1844. He was expelled from Paris in 1845 and lived in Brussels from 1845 to 1848.

Friedrich Engels (1820 to 1895) was the son of a textile manufacturer from Barmen and worked in the family firm in Manchester, where he wrote The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845). He co-wrote the Manifesto and supported Marx financially for decades.

In 1848 and 1849 Marx was a participant in the revolutions. He returned to Germany and edited the Neue Rheinische Zeitung in Cologne from June 1848 to May 1849, and was expelled from Prussian territory in May 1849.
Marx spent his last decades in London, little known at first and then notorious. Judgements of him have changed as his ideas spread and the predictions were tested.
His other writings include The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte (1852), on Louis-Napoleon's coup, and The Civil War in France (1871), defending the Paris Commune.

He settled in London in August 1849 and lived there until his death on 14 March 1883, first in Soho and later in north London, often in poverty. Three of his children died young. He studied in the British Museum reading room and is buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Contemporaries knew little of him in the 1850s and 1860s. Prussian police agents watched the London exiles, and the Cologne Communist Trial of 1852 convicted members of the Communist League. This is why the public did not fear him until later.

After he defended the Paris Commune in 1871, the press called him a leader of the Commune's supporters, and he became famous and feared. He was also quarrelsome with rivals such as Bakunin and Lassalle.

Historians judge him the most influential socialist thinker, because his ideas shaped later socialist parties and twentieth-century communist states. His analysis of class and economics also influenced history, sociology and economics.
His prediction that revolution would come first in the most advanced industrial countries was not fulfilled, and workers' living standards rose.
Marx's importance rests on a theory that explained history by class struggle and promised that capitalism would be overthrown. Each of his main works and organisations belongs to a different date.

The Communist Manifesto (published in London in German in February 1848, written with Engels for the Communist League) opens "A spectre is haunting Europe – the spectre of communism" and declares "The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles."

It divides society into the bourgeoisie (the owners of factories and capital) and the proletariat (wage workers), and argues that capitalism would produce its own gravediggers. It ends with the call "Working men of all countries, unite!"
The Manifesto did not cause the 1848 revolutions. It appeared just before them and had little immediate influence on them. This is why historians do not treat it as a cause of 1848.

Historical materialism holds that the economic base, meaning who owns the means of production, shapes the political and ideological superstructure of law, religion and ideas. Marx wrote that religion is "the opium of the people" (1844).
Marx saw history in stages: ancient slavery, feudalism, capitalism, then socialism or communism. Each stage is ended by class struggle, so capitalism would fall to a proletarian revolution.
After the revolution would come a workers' state, his "dictatorship of the proletariat" (a phrase from 1850), and then a classless communist society in which the state would wither away.

Das Kapital, volume 1 (Hamburg, 1867), set out the theory of surplus value: workers produce more value than they are paid in wages, and the capitalist keeps the difference as profit, which Marx called the unpaid part of labour. Engels edited volumes 2 (1885) and 3 (1894) from Marx's manuscripts.

The International Workingmen's Association, the First International, was founded at St Martin's Hall, London, on 28 September 1864. Marx wrote its Inaugural Address and its rules and led its General Council. It linked British trade unionists with French and German socialists. This is why it brought different national movements together.
Higher essays set Marx beside other thinkers of the age. The comparison works best when you say what each thought drives change and how their ideas were received.
Marx and Metternich held opposite views of society. Marx saw conflict between classes and believed change was inevitable, while Metternich wanted order and hierarchy and aimed to prevent change.
Marx and Darwin both offered a theory of change through struggle over long periods of time. Marx's struggle was between classes, which he expected to end in revolution.
Bakunin was a Russian revolutionary and the most famous anarchist of the period, a man of action who spent years in prison. His rivalry with Marx split the First International.

Mikhail Bakunin was born on 30 May 1814 on the Premukhino estate, Tver province, into a Russian noble family. He served as an artillery officer but resigned his commission in 1835, studied philosophy in Moscow and Berlin (1840), and became a revolutionary only in the 1840s.
In 1848 and 1849 he was a participant in the revolutions: he attended the Slav Congress in Prague in June 1848 and joined the Dresden rising of May 1849.

He was sentenced to death in Saxony (1850) and again in Austria (1851), and each sentence was commuted. He was handed over to Russia in 1851. Each sentence was commuted, so he survived to continue his career.

He was held in the Peter and Paul Fortress in St Petersburg and then in Schlüsselburg, and was exiled to Siberia in 1857. In 1861 he escaped by way of Japan and the United States, reaching London at the end of that year.
In 1873 he wrote Statism and Anarchy. He died on 1 July 1876 in Bern, Switzerland.
Contemporary governments saw him as a dangerous conspirator, while some radicals admired him as a heroic rebel and champion of the oppressed. This is why he was watched and imprisoned.

Historians see him as the founder of the anarchist movement, though a poor organiser and less influential than Marx on mass labour parties. His anarchist influence was strongest in Spain, Italy and the Jura region of Switzerland, where the Jura Federation was based.

Bakunin and Marx both wanted to end capitalism but disagreed about what should replace it. Their quarrel broke the International, the first organisation to bring socialists of different countries together.

Bakunin's anarchism meant the abolition of the state, organised religion and all coercive authority, so that people would live without rulers. He wrote in 1842: "The passion for destruction is a creative passion."
He expected revolution to come from spontaneous risings of peasants and the poor as well as workers, not only an industrial proletariat. He favoured secret revolutionary societies.
Bakunin joined the First International in 1868. He argued that Marx's workers' state would become a new tyranny of a ruling minority, while Marx wanted workers' parties to win political power.

At the Hague Congress in September 1872 Bakunin and his ally James Guillaume were expelled. The General Council moved to New York, and the International faded and was dissolved in 1876, at Philadelphia.
The most common Higher pairing on this subsection is two or three of Marx, Bakunin and O'Connor. Each comparison below is a pair of contrasting points, which you can turn into a judgement.
On the state, Marx wanted workers to win power and use a workers' state, while Bakunin wanted no state at all.
On who would make revolution, Marx looked to organised industrial workers, while Bakunin looked to all the oppressed, including peasants.
On method, Marx stressed theory and patient organisation, while Bakunin stressed spontaneous insurrection.
In their lives, Marx was a London theorist, while Bakunin was a participant on the barricades.
On aims, O'Connor sought the vote and land within the British state, while Marx sought revolution and the end of capitalism.
On method, O'Connor used mass agitation, while Marx used theory and an international organisation.
Both O'Connor and Marx failed to achieve their aims in 1848, but both had longer-term influence.

Democracy means government by the people through elected representatives chosen by all, here all adult men. The franchise (the right to vote) widened slowly in Britain and faster in some continental states, usually granted from above.

The Reform Act of 1832, passed by Earl Grey's Whig government after a long crisis, gave the borough vote to men who owned or occupied property worth £10 a year. In the counties the vote went to forty-shilling freeholders plus some leaseholders and tenants.
It took both MPs from 56 boroughs and one from 30 others, and gave seats to industrial towns such as Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds and Sheffield.

Even so, only about one adult man in five in England and Wales could vote, and almost no workers, so the Act disappointed the working class. Estimates vary, so give no exact figure. This is why working men turned to Chartism.

The Second Reform Act of 1867 (Derby and Disraeli) gave the vote to many urban working men, and the Ballot Act of 1872 introduced the secret ballot. Almost all men over 21 (and some women over 30) got the vote in the Representation of the People Act of 1918.

In France the Provisional Government decreed universal male suffrage in March 1848, raising the electorate from fewer than 250,000 to about nine million. Louis-Napoleon kept it and used plebiscites (direct votes on his proposals).

The North German Confederation of 1867 elected its Reichstag by universal male suffrage, for men over 25 and by secret ballot. The German Empire kept this in 1871, and Bismarck hoped conservative rural voters would outvote the liberals.

Not every campaign of the period was a working-class one. The Anti-Corn Law League was a middle-class pressure group that showed how organised public opinion could change policy, and it won where Chartism lost.
The League was founded in Manchester in 1838 by Richard Cobden and John Bright, to end the Corn Laws (duties on imported grain that kept bread dear).
It used lecturers, pamphlets, a national fund and mass meetings, a model of how a pressure group could organise opinion. This is why it could reach many voters.
It succeeded in 1846 when the Corn Laws were repealed, whereas the working-class Chartists failed, partly because much middle-class support went to the League.
Chartism was the first national working-class political movement in Britain. It grew from hardship and from the feeling that the political system had shut workers out.
Chartism grew from disappointment with the 1832 Act, which gave workers no vote, and anger at the Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834 and its workhouses.

Other causes were the trade depression from 1837 to the early 1840s, which brought unemployment (the 1840s are called the "Hungry Forties"), the decline of handloom weavers, and the failure of trade unionism after 1834.

The London Working Men's Association was formed in 1836 by William Lovett, a cabinet-maker, with Henry Hetherington also a founder. The People's Charter, published in May 1838, was drafted by Lovett with help from Francis Place.

The six points were universal male suffrage, the secret ballot, annual parliaments, equal electoral districts, abolition of the property qualification for MPs (so poor men could stand), and payment of MPs.
The first National Convention met in London in February 1839 and later moved to Birmingham.

The National Charter Association, founded in Manchester in July 1840, was in effect the first working-class political party, with local branches and paid-up members. This is why it counts as a party, not just a campaign.
The Northern Star, O'Connor's newspaper, was the movement's voice and reached a wide readership.
Chartists tried petitions first and then stronger action, and each campaign was beaten. The three petitions and the three famous events are easily confused, so learn them with their dates.

The first petition (1839) had about 1.3 million signatures and was rejected in July 1839. The second (1842) had over three million, the largest genuine total; Thomas Duncombe MP presented it and it was rejected in May 1842.

The 1848 petition claimed about 5.7 million signatures, but a Commons committee counted under two million, including false names such as "Victoria Rex" and "the Duke of Wellington". Each petition was rejected by the Commons.

At Newport, Monmouthshire, on 4 November 1839, John Frost, a former mayor of Newport, led armed men into the town with Zephaniah Williams and William Jones. Soldiers fired from the Westgate Hotel and about twenty Chartists were killed.
Frost and two others were sentenced to death, but the sentences were commuted to transportation for life to Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania). So the government spared them, but removed them from Britain.
The Plug Plot strikes of August 1842 spread through Lancashire, Yorkshire, the Potteries and the Midlands. Strikers pulled the plugs from factory boilers to stop work, and mass arrests followed.

On 10 April 1848 a mass meeting on Kennington Common, south London, was to march the petition to Parliament. The government banned the procession, enrolled tens of thousands of special constables, and the Duke of Wellington organised the military defence of London.
O'Connor persuaded the crowd to disperse, and the petition went to Parliament in cabs. The forged signatures then brought ridicule on the movement.
The Land Plan was a scheme to take workers out of the factories and back on the land. It was also a way to win the vote, because land ownership carried a vote in the counties.

The Chartist Co-operative Land Company of 1845 (later the National Land Company) sold shares to members and bought estates. Members then drew lots for smallholdings. This meant workers could escape the factories and, because of the county vote, gain political rights.
Estates included O'Connorville at Heronsgate, Hertfordshire, and Charterville at Minster Lovell, Oxfordshire. The plan also aimed to give smallholders the county vote.
A select committee of 1848 found it legally and financially unsound, and an Act of Parliament wound it up in 1851.
Chartism was divided about methods and faced a determined government. It rose in bad times and faded in good ones, which was fatal to a movement that depended on hardship.

Moral force Chartists such as William Lovett relied on education and persuasion. Physical force Chartists such as George Julian Harney (and James Bronterre O'Brien at times) were ready to threaten or use force.
O'Connor's speeches threatened force while he avoided armed risings. The division in methods weakened the movement.

Government repression (arrests, troops, and the new railways and telegraph, which moved forces quickly) wore the movement down, and Parliament refused to listen. This is why physical force never had a chance of succeeding.
Chartism had little middle-class support, which went to the Anti-Corn Law League. It rose in slumps and faded in good times, and the prosperity of the 1850s ended it.
The 1848 fiasco at Kennington damaged it. Ernest Jones led the later Chartists in the 1850s, and the last Chartist convention met in 1858.
Its achievement was to be the first national working-class political movement, which is why historians value it despite its failure.

Five of the six points later became law: the property qualification was abolished in 1858, the secret ballot came in 1872, payment of MPs in 1911 and manhood suffrage in 1918, and districts became more equal. Only annual parliaments never came.
O'Connor was the most prominent Chartist leader of the 1840s and the owner of the movement's newspaper. His energy gave Chartism a national voice but his quarrels divided it.

Feargus O'Connor was born in Co. Cork in 1796 (some older sources give 1794). He came from a Protestant landed family with a radical tradition, being the nephew of the United Irishman Arthur O'Connor, and was called to the Irish bar.

He was elected MP for Co. Cork in December 1832 as a Repealer allied with Daniel O'Connell, and was unseated on petition in 1835 because he lacked the property qualification. He quarrelled with O'Connell and moved into English radical politics.

He founded the Northern Star in Leeds in November 1837. It was the most widely read radical newspaper in Britain, often read aloud in pubs and workplaces, and sold about 50,000 copies a week at its peak in 1839 (estimates vary). It moved to London in 1844.

He was a participant in the Chartist campaigns of 1839, 1842 and 1848, toured the industrial North as a speaker and dominated the National Charter Association. He was sentenced to 18 months for seditious libel in 1840, held in York Castle and released in August 1841.

The Land Plan was his scheme, reflecting his belief in returning workers to the land. In 1847 he was elected MP for Nottingham, the only Chartist elected to Parliament, and in 1848 he presented the petition to the Commons.

After Kennington his authority waned. He had a breakdown in 1852, was confined in an asylum in Chiswick, and died on 30 August 1855. He was buried at Kensal Green, London, with a very large funeral procession.
O'Connor divided opinion in his own day and divides historians still. The verdict depends on whether you blame him for Chartism's failure or credit him with holding it together.

Contemporaries were split. To many workers he was a hero, "the Lion of Freedom", a Chartist song and popular name for him, but to Lovett, the moral-force men, middle-class reformers and the government he was a vain, reckless demagogue.
Older accounts, such as Mark Hovell's The Chartist Movement (1918), drew on Lovett's account and blamed him for Chartism's failure.
Dorothy Thompson (The Chartists, 1984) and James Epstein (The Lion of Freedom, 1982) see a gifted speaker and organiser who held a national movement together and spoke for the rank and file.

Robert Peel was a reforming statesman who worked from inside government, and Norman Gash rates him one of the greatest statesmen of the century. He was a Conservative who believed in reforming real abuses so as to preserve the established order.
Peel was born on 5 February 1788 near Bury, Lancashire, the son of Sir Robert Peel, 1st Baronet, a cotton manufacturer and MP. He went to Harrow and Christ Church, Oxford, and became an MP in 1809.

He was Chief Secretary for Ireland from 1812 to 1818, setting up the Peace Preservation Force in 1814 and earning O'Connell's nickname "Orange Peel". He chaired the 1819 currency committee, after which Britain returned to gold.

As Home Secretary (1822 to 1827 and 1828 to 1830) he reformed the criminal law, abolishing the death penalty for many offences, and the Gaols Act of 1823 reformed prisons. This shows he was a reformer in law before he became Prime Minister.

The Metropolitan Police Act of 1829 created a professional, uniformed, unarmed force for London, with headquarters at Scotland Yard. Its first commissioners were Charles Rowan and Richard Mayne, and its first patrols began in September 1829.

Its officers wore blue uniforms and top hats and carried truncheons, not firearms, and were nicknamed "Peelers" and "Bobbies". The City of London kept its own force. The Metropolitan Police became a model for forces across Britain, though Peel did not found a national police force.

In 1829 Peel and the Duke of Wellington conceded Catholic emancipation after O'Connell won the Clare by-election in 1828, to avoid conflict in Ireland. It angered many Tories, and Peel resigned his Oxford University seat over it.

The Tamworth Manifesto of December 1834, an address to his constituents at Tamworth, accepted the Reform Act as "a final and irrevocable settlement" and promised careful reform of real abuses while preserving established institutions. It is seen as the founding statement of the Conservative Party.
He was Prime Minister from December 1834 to April 1835 and again from August 1841 to June 1846.
As Prime Minister Peel tried to make the state efficient and trade free, while keeping private property and the existing social order. His budgets and Acts of 1842 to 1844 are the core of his record.
Laissez-faire is the belief that the state should leave trade, prices, wages and hours to the free market. Peel's free trade applied it, while the Factory Acts showed its limits.

He reintroduced income tax in 1842, at 7d in the pound on incomes over £150, for three years at first and then renewed. It let him cut or abolish duties on hundreds of imports in the budgets of 1842 and 1845, and trade and revenue grew.
The Bank Charter Act of 1844 gradually concentrated the issue of banknotes in the Bank of England, so that note issue beyond £14 million had to be backed by gold.
Other banks' note issues were frozen and phased out. This was to keep banknotes trustworthy, so confidence in the currency was protected.
The Mines Act of 1842, Lord Ashley's measure, forbade women, girls and boys under ten to work underground.
The Factory Act of 1844 set the minimum age at 8, limited children aged 8 to 13 to six and a half hours a day and women and young persons to twelve hours, and required machinery to be fenced.
The Railway Regulation Act of 1844 (Gladstone, at the Board of Trade) required at least one train a day each way at a penny a mile, the cheap "parliamentary trains".
Peel opposed the Ten Hours Bill, which passed in 1847 under Russell's government after his fall.
Repealing the Corn Laws was Peel's greatest act and the end of his career as Conservative leader. It brought lower food prices but split his party.

Peel was influenced by free-trade arguments and by the Anti-Corn Law League, whose leaders Cobden and Bright had campaigned for repeal. The urgent cause was the potato blight in Ireland from 1845, and Peel bought American maize for Ireland.

The Corn Importation Act received royal assent in June 1846. It passed with Whig votes, while about two-thirds of Conservative MPs voted against, and duties were reduced to a nominal one shilling a quarter by 1849, not ended overnight.
Peel was defeated on an Irish Coercion Bill on 25 June 1846 and resigned in June 1846, on the same night that the Corn Laws were repealed.

The Conservatives split into protectionists, led by Lord Derby (then Lord Stanley) and Benjamin Disraeli, and Peelites, including William Gladstone, who joined the Liberals by 1859. The Conservatives were long out of majority power.
Peel died after being thrown from his horse on Constitution Hill, London, on 29 June 1850, and died on 2 July.
Contemporaries differed. Disraeli and the protectionists called him a traitor to his party, while the middle class and many workers praised cheap bread and sound finance.
Historians such as Norman Gash (Mr Secretary Peel, 1961, and Sir Robert Peel, 1972) rate him one of the greatest statesmen of the century, an administrator who put the national interest above party.
Critics note that he twice split his party (1829, 1846), so his career left divisions, and that he resisted a wider franchise and the Ten Hours Act.
This is the most frequent Higher question on the subsection. Owen tried to change society from outside Parliament, Peel from inside government, and the best answers weigh evidence on both sides.

Both were sons of the textile industry: Owen (born 1771 in Newtown, Wales, died 1858) a self-made Welsh mill manager, and Peel the son of a cotton millionaire. This shows that industrial wealth produced reformers of different kinds.
In method, Owen worked by example, model communities, education and co-operation outside Parliament, while Peel reformed the state from within through legislation and administration.
In aims, Owen wanted to replace competition with co-operation and common ownership. Peel wanted to preserve property, Church and Crown by making the state efficient and trade free.

There was a link: Owen's campaign helped bring about the Cotton Mills and Factories Act of 1819, introduced by Sir Robert Peel the elder. It banned children under nine from cotton mills and limited hours for those under sixteen, but had no inspectors and was poorly enforced.
Peel's changes (police, tax, free trade, the Bank Act, Factory and Mines Acts) affected the whole country and lasted, and much of the middle class accepted his policies as sound.

Owen's New Lanark worked but was rarely copied, and most of the political establishment rejected his ideas. New Harmony and the GNCTU failed, but his ideas inspired the co-operative movement (the Rochdale Equitable Pioneers' Society, 1844) and factory reform.
Most answers judge Peel the more effective in practice and Owen the more original. This is why the verdict usually favours Peel on effect and Owen on originality.
Judge the responses by what they achieved at the time and what they achieved later. The paired points below give the evidence for an achievement-against-limits answer.

Trade unions: they were legal after 1824, recognised in 1871, and the New Model unions after 1851 gave skilled workers stable organisation. But Tolpuddle showed repression, the GNCTU collapsed and the unskilled were excluded.

Socialism: it produced a new and lasting body of ideas and an international organisation in 1864. But support was tiny before 1871, the movement was divided between Marx and Bakunin, and no revolution came.
Chartism: it was a mass movement that kept democracy on the agenda, and most of its points were achieved later. But every petition failed, its leaders were divided, and it was gone by the late 1850s.

Mass politics: manhood suffrage came in France in 1848 and in the North German Confederation in 1867, while Britain moved slowly in 1832 and 1867. The vote was widened more often from above than won from below.
Peel: he made lasting reforms from above in the police, finance, free trade and factory law. But he did not extend the vote, and he left a divided party.

Overall, the responses included unions, socialist theory and Chartist agitation, yet the main political gains came from state reform led by Peel, while working-class movements won their goals only much later.

Owen's experiment only makes sense against the background of the early factory system, which grew out of industrialisation (the shift from hand work at home to machine production in factories). New Lanark stood out because almost every other mill owner worked in the opposite way.
Early cotton mills were water-powered spinning mills, where workers put in very long hours, children did much of the work, and discipline relied on fines and beatings.

Water-powered mills had to stand where there was falling water, far from towns, so owners had to build housing and bring in workers. This is why a mill and a village went together, and why many rural mills took pauper apprentices (workhouse children bound to the mill owner).
The dominant view was laissez-faire (the belief that the state should not interfere in the economy), so most employers and politicians thought the state should not regulate wages or hours.
Because of laissez-faire, Owen's ideas and his call for a factory law were unusual.

Robert Owen was a Welsh-born manager who learned the cotton trade in Manchester before taking charge of a much larger mill complex in Scotland. His early life gave him both the skills and the ideas he later used at New Lanark.
Robert Owen was born in 1771 at Newtown, Montgomeryshire, Wales. He left school at about ten and worked for drapers (cloth merchants) in Stamford, London and Manchester.

By about twenty, in the early 1790s, he was managing a large cotton-spinning mill in Manchester owned by Peter Drinkwater. Later in the 1790s he became a partner in the Chorlton Twist Company, Manchester.
His Manchester years showed him how mill workers and their families lived, which shaped his belief that people are formed by their surroundings.

His central idea was that character is formed for the individual, not by the individual, through circumstances and education. This is why every reform at New Lanark aimed at changing the environment, because he thought changing the environment would change the people.
The environmentalist ideas of Enlightenment thinkers, who held that character is formed by surroundings, shaped his outlook.
In 1799 he married Caroline Dale, daughter of David Dale, the Glasgow merchant who owned the New Lanark mills, which gave him a family connection to Dale and to the mills.
In the same year, 1799, Owen and his Manchester partners bought New Lanark from Dale. Owen took over as manager on 1 January 1800, aged 28.
New Lanark was already a very large mill community when Owen arrived. Knowing who built it, and how its workers were housed, shows what Owen inherited and what he changed.

New Lanark stands on the River Clyde near Lanark, Scotland. It was founded in the mid-1780s (building began in 1785) by David Dale, at first with Richard Arkwright, the cotton pioneer, who soon withdrew.
The mills used water power from the Falls of Clyde, which was the reason Dale chose the site, and the cotton-spinning works were among the largest in Britain.

David Dale was a Glasgow merchant and banker and was thought a comparatively humane employer. He housed the pauper children in dormitories, fed them and provided evening schooling, but the children still worked long days.
In 1800 about 2,000 people lived at New Lanark, including about 500 pauper children from the poorhouses of Edinburgh and Glasgow.
Do not mix up the three men: Dale was the founder and Owen's father-in-law, Arkwright was an early partner and inventor of the water frame, and Owen was manager from 1800 and then part-owner.
When Owen arrived he found a hard-working but troubled community. Much of this picture comes from Owen's own writings, so it is his account and not neutral evidence.
The mill day was about thirteen hours including meal breaks, and children as young as about six worked in the mills and then attended evening classes, when they were tired.
By Owen's account, the village houses were dirty and overcrowded, the streets were filthy and sanitation (drains, waste removal and clean water) was poor.
Owen described the workforce as marked by drunkenness, theft and disorder, and the people distrusted a manager from outside.
Owen said that discipline relied on fines and physical punishment, and he set out to replace it.
He saw these conditions as the result of environment rather than of individual wickedness, so he set out to change the environment in order to change character.
Owen later argued that the conditions at New Lanark reflected the wider failings of the factory system rather than the particular fault of its managers.
Owen believed that humane treatment would pay for itself, so his first reforms changed the terms of work in the mill. Each one targeted a way the old system harmed workers, especially children.

Owen stopped taking pauper apprentices, which ended the supply of workhouse children, and raised the minimum working age, so that by 1816 no child under ten worked in the mills. Younger children went to school instead, and the change was gradual.
He cut the working day, so that by 1816 it was under eleven hours of actual work (about ten and a half hours), and he argued that output did not fall.
During an American embargo on cotton exports the mills stood idle. Owen paid wages to the idle workers for about four months, which won their trust and loyalty.
He used profits to pay for schools and welfare, which he treated as a sound investment in the workforce, because he expected better-treated workers to produce better work.
Owen did not want to run the mill by fines and blows, so he looked for a way to encourage good conduct through reward and example. His best-known device was the silent monitor.
Physical punishment ended at New Lanark, and Owen replaced it with a system of reward and example.
The silent monitor was a four-sided block of wood hung beside each worker. Each side was a colour: black (bad conduct), blue (indifferent), yellow (good) and white (excellent).
The superintendent turned the block each day to show the previous day's conduct, and conduct was also recorded in books of character.
Owen used it so that behaviour was recorded without shouting or beating. Pride in a good colour and shame at a bad one were the motives, so that workers wanted to improve.
Owen believed that a worker's home and daily life shaped character as much as the mill did, so he reformed the village as well as the work.
Owen improved and repaired the village housing, had the streets cleaned and rubbish collected, and encouraged households to keep their homes clean and to live in an orderly way.
The village store sold good-quality goods at little more than cost. It made a small profit, which helped to pay for the schools.
The sale of spirits was controlled, which was meant to reduce the drunkenness Owen had found.
A sick fund, to which workers contributed part of their wages, gave help in illness, so a sick worker was not left without support.
Owen thought education was the strongest way to form character, so he made schooling the heart of New Lanark. The schools were housed in a new building, the Institute for the Formation of Character.

The Institute for the Formation of Character opened on 1 January 1816. By day it housed the infant school and children's classes, and in the evening it was used for classes, lectures, music and dancing for older children and adults.

The infant school (1816) took children from about one, as soon as they could walk, to six. It was often described as the first infant school in Britain, and its teacher was James Buchanan, who later ran an infant school in London.

In the infant school children were taught by kindness, through play, songs, dancing, pictures, maps and natural objects rather than books and rote learning (learning by repetition), and there was no punishment.
A day school took children of about six to ten, and evening classes for older children and young workers taught reading, writing, arithmetic, singing, dancing and geography.

Owen kept religious teaching out as far as he could, because he disliked organised religion. His partners, including the Quaker William Allen, opposed this and objected to the dancing and music, and the clergy also criticised it.
The infant school attracted visitors from abroad.
Owen's schemes cost money, so they needed backers who would accept them. His partnerships show how far his reforms were supported, and why they were also limited.
The mills stayed profitable under Owen, so he used it as proof that humane treatment and profit could go together.
His earlier partners objected to spending profits on schools, and the dispute ended with the mills sold at auction in 1813.

The new partnership of 1813 included the philosopher Jeremy Bentham and the Quaker William Allen. They agreed to take a fixed 5 per cent return on their capital, with the rest of the profit going to benefit the community.
Allen and other partners objected to the dancing, drill and lack of religious teaching in the schools, and to Owen's attacks on religion.
In the 1820s the partners imposed changes, which helped to push Owen out.
Owen did not keep his ideas to New Lanark. He wrote about them and pressed Parliament to pass a law, which put him ahead of most employers.

A New View of Society, or Essays on the Formation of the Human Character, was four essays published in 1813-14. In it Owen argued that character is formed by circumstances and that society could improve its people by improving conditions and education.

The state had already begun to act. The Health and Morals of Apprentices Act of 1802, promoted by Sir Robert Peel the elder (a cotton manufacturer and father of the Prime Minister), limited the hours of pauper apprentices.
From 1815 Owen campaigned for a factory law, and in 1816 he gave evidence to a select committee (a group of MPs investigating a subject) chaired by the elder Peel.
The Cotton Mills and Factories Act of 1819 allowed no children under nine in cotton mills and limited children aged nine to sixteen to twelve hours a day.
The Act was weaker than Owen wanted. It was enforced by local magistrates with no inspectors, so it was poorly enforced.
Owen's ambitions grew from one mill village to a plan for self-supporting villages of co-operation. In 1817 he also made a public move that cost him much support.

In 1817 Owen presented a plan for villages of co-operation (self-supporting co-operative communities for the unemployed poor) to a committee for the relief of the manufacturing poor in London. In 1820 he set out a similar plan in a Report to the County of Lanark.
William Cobbett, a radical who saw such villages as a way of controlling the poor, mocked them as "parallelograms of paupers".
In August 1817, at a public meeting in London, Owen denounced all organised religions. This lost him much support among the respectable and powerful.
Owen next tried to build a fully co-operative community. His absence and these experiments ended his direct involvement at New Lanark.
Owen went to the United States in 1824. In 1825 he bought Harmony, Indiana, from the Rappites (a German religious community) and founded New Harmony, a co-operative experiment.
Quarrels among the members and poor organisation brought New Harmony to a breakdown within about two years, and Owen left in 1827.
Other Owenite communities in Britain also failed: Orbiston, near Motherwell, Scotland (1825-27), and Queenwood, Hampshire (1839-45).
Owen gave up his interest in New Lanark in 1828-29. The mills carried on under others and spun cotton until 1968, and New Lanark remained a reference point for later social reformers.
Owen's ideas moved from mill reform to a wider vision of society based on co-operation. Socialism, as Owen used it, meant common ownership and co-operation instead of competition.
The National Equitable Labour Exchange, set up in London in 1832, exchanged goods for labour notes (paper money based on hours of work). It collapsed in 1834.
The Grand National Consolidated Trades Union of 1834 aimed at one great union of all workers and a co-operative society. Owen was its inspiration and best-known figure rather than its formal leader.
The union collapsed later in 1834 after employers' lock-outs (refusing to let workers in) and the Tolpuddle case. Owen's journal of 1834 was called The New Moral World.

Owen's ideas inspired co-operative societies. The Rochdale Pioneers in Lancashire opened a co-operative store in 1844, which began the lasting consumer co-operative movement, although Owen did not found it.
Owen's followers, the Owenites, were among the first in Britain to be called socialists, in the late 1820s and 1830s.
Marx and Engels later called Owen a utopian socialist, meaning that he hoped to change society by example and persuasion rather than class struggle. Owen died at Newtown in 1858.
Few owners copied New Lanark, even though it was profitable and famous. Examiners want several distinct reasons, so each one is worth learning.
Other owners thought welfare too costly in a competitive industry, and believed that their profits depended on low wages and long hours.
Laissez-faire beliefs also told owners and politicians not to interfere with how a business treated its workers.
New Lanark's success depended on Owen's personal control and on unusual partners, which few owners were willing to accept.
Urban steam-powered mills did not need to house their workers, because workers lived in the town, so they had no reason to build villages.
Because Owen attacked religion and promoted socialism, he discredited his example, and his larger schemes, New Harmony and the Labour Exchange, failed.

Some ideas were partly copied. Later employers built model villages, such as Saltaire in Yorkshire (Titus Salt's village, whose mill opened in 1853), but these were paternalist (the owner in charge) rather than co-operative, and infant schools spread.
Opinion of Owen was divided in his own lifetime and has stayed divided among historians. Both sides need evidence.
Admirers: thousands of visitors came to New Lanark in the late 1810s and 1820s, including reformers, churchmen and royalty such as the future Tsar Nicholas I of Russia.

Critics: employers who thought him a dangerous dreamer, churchmen and his own partners offended by his views on religion, and radicals such as Cobbett who saw his villages as a way of controlling the poor.
Later views: historians see him as a pioneer of industrial welfare, infant education, factory reform and co-operation, often called the father of British socialism and of the co-operative movement.
But he can also be seen as paternalist, because New Lanark depended on supervision and control (the silent monitor, house inspections) by one man.
New Lanark became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001.
Judging Owen means setting what New Lanark achieved against what limited it, and then asking how far his wider influence reached.
Achievement: New Lanark combined shorter hours, no young child labour, schools and a decent village with profit.
Limit: it was one village, it depended on Owen, and his partners curbed it.
Achievement of his wider influence: he helped bring about the 1819 Act, the infant school movement and co-operation.
Limit of his wider influence: the 1819 Act was weak, and New Harmony, the Labour Exchange and the GNCTU failed.
Contemporary view: friends saw a benevolent experiment, while critics saw a paternalist whose religious views were dangerous.
Later view: historians see a pioneer of industrial welfare, though one whose methods of control were paternalistic.
Compared with Robert Peel the Prime Minister, who changed national law, Owen worked by example outside government, so his influence stayed local.
A good verdict weighs both sides: a local success and a pioneer of ideas, but not a model that changed the system.

In the nineteenth century cities grew far faster than their streets, housing and services, and governments began to see that growth could no longer be left to chance. Several pressures pushed rulers towards planning.

Overcrowding: industrialisation and migration from the countryside brought millions into cities, so existing streets, housing, water supplies and drainage could not cope. People crowded into the old centres to be near work, in tall, decaying houses.
Disease: with no proper drainage and polluted water, epidemics spread, and municipal authorities were slow to provide clean water and sewers. Cholera struck Paris in 1832 and 1849.

Most people blamed cholera on foul air, called miasma (bad air thought to rise from dirt and stagnant water). Clearing slums, letting in light and air, and carrying sewage away therefore seemed the cure, even before germ theory.
Fire: timber-framed, crowded housing in the older districts made fire a constant danger, and wider streets allowed fire engines to reach the buildings.
Traffic: narrow, winding medieval streets could not carry growing traffic or link the new railway stations, and they were dangerous for pedestrians and for the carriages of the wealthy.

Revolution and order: the Paris crowd overthrew governments in July 1830 and February 1848, and the June Days of 1848 were fought behind barricades. Barricades went up quickly in narrow streets, whereas wide streets let troops move.
Prestige and the economy: grand streets, public buildings and open spaces displayed the power of the state, and public works gave employment and drew investment.
To judge what Haussmann achieved, you need to know what he inherited: a medieval city of about one million people, crowded, unhealthy and socially divided.
Paris had about one million people around 1850, mostly crowded into the old centre, so the pressure on housing and services was intense.
The Île de la Cité (the island in the Seine at the heart of the city) and the area around Les Halles (the central food markets) were a maze of narrow, dark streets with poor drainage and old houses.
The Hôtel-Dieu, the main hospital on the Île de la Cité, was overcrowded and its wards were in poor conditions, which shows how badly the old centre served its people.
Water was drawn largely from the polluted Seine and the Ourcq canal, many homes had no piped water, and sewage ran into the Seine, so the city's drinking water was contaminated by its own waste.
Social geography: richer districts lay to the west, and poorer districts to the east and in the centre.

Earlier attempts: Rambuteau, Prefect of the Seine (the official in charge of Paris) from 1833 to 1848 under Louis-Philippe, cut one new street, the Rue Rambuteau, and began improvements, but on a small scale.
Earlier revolutions had been fought in these narrow streets, which reinforced the case for broad avenues.
The rebuilding of Paris was the project of Napoleon III, who needed the capital to show off his regime. Here are his aims and where his ideas came from.

Background: Louis-Napoleon took power by the coup of 2 December 1851 and the Second Empire was proclaimed in December 1852. As an authoritarian ruler who needed prestige, prosperity and order, he could override local opposition to the works.
Health: he wanted light, air, clean water and drainage for the city, in line with the belief that foul air caused disease.
Traffic and order: he wanted links between the railway stations and room for troops, so fewer barricades could be built. Employment was a further aim, through public works.
Prestige: he wanted Paris to be the showcase of the Empire, and it hosted the Universal Exhibitions of 1855 and 1867.
London was a model: during his exile there (1846-48) Louis-Napoleon admired its parks and squares, which later shaped the parks of Paris.
He gave Haussmann a map with the new streets he wanted marked in colour. Haussmann then worked out the details and greatly extended the plan, so it was not the Emperor's design alone.
Napoleon III needed a forceful administrator to carry out his ideas. He found one in Georges-Eugène Haussmann, and the law gave him powers to match.

Haussmann was born in Paris in 1809 into a Protestant family of Alsatian origin. He was a career prefect in the provinces, last at Bordeaux (the Gironde), and the Interior Minister Persigny chose him as a forceful administrator.
He was appointed Prefect of the Seine (the official in charge of Paris and its department) on 22 June 1853 and served until January 1870, working directly with the Emperor.
He was made a senator in 1857. He called himself Baron Haussmann, but Napoleon III never formally created him a baron.
The expropriation law of 1841 (compulsory purchase of property for public works) was widened by a decree of 1852. The city could buy whole plots beside a new street, so whole blocks could be cleared.

Methods were centralised: control lay with the Prefect and the Emperor, and the Prefecture of the Seine had large budgets and a large team of engineers and architects, including Belgrand and Alphand. Much of the money was borrowed outside parliamentary control.
Building regulations fixed the heights and facades of buildings along the new streets, so the city's look could be controlled.

The grands travaux (great works) were the programme of demolition and rebuilding that Haussmann directed from 1853, carried out in stages. Its core was a network of new straight avenues cut through the old city.

The grande croisée (great crossing) was an east-west axis, the Rue de Rivoli, extended eastwards in the 1850s, crossed by a north-south axis of the Boulevard de Strasbourg (begun 1852), the Boulevard de Sébastopol (opened 1858) and then the Boulevard Saint-Michel on the Left Bank.
This crossing linked the Seine to the railway stations to the north, so it solved a traffic problem as well as clearing the old centre.

The Boulevard Saint-Germain on the Left Bank and the Avenue de l'Opéra were completed in the 1870s, under the Third Republic. The Avenue de l'Impératrice (now Avenue Foch) was laid out in 1854 as the route to the Bois de Boulogne.
Twelve avenues radiate from the Place de l'Étoile, which became a great star-shaped junction. The Avenue de l'Opéra was designed to frame the view of the new Opéra.

The design: long straight streets with vistas ending on a monument, lined with trees, pavements, gas lamps, benches and kiosks, and with uniform cream stone apartment facades of controlled height (the Haussmann building).
The Île de la Cité was largely cleared of housing and rebuilt with public buildings, including the rebuilt Hôtel-Dieu, the law courts and police headquarters.

The boulevards served several purposes: traffic and access to the stations, light and air, and a military argument, since troops and artillery could move along wide straight streets and barricades were harder to hold.
Haussmann himself stressed health and traffic over the military motive, which is worth remembering when judging his aims.
Wide streets alone would not cure disease, so the engineer Eugène Belgrand, in charge of water and sewers, rebuilt the city's water system underground.

Belgrand built aqueducts (channels carrying water over long distances) bringing spring water from the Dhuis valley, completed in 1865, and the Vanne valley, completed in 1874 after the Empire had fallen. The water went to covered reservoirs in the city, which kept it clean.
A double system supplied drinking water and non-drinking water: Seine water was kept for street cleaning and fountains, so the clean spring water was reserved for drinking.
Sewers: a large underground sewer network of tunnels, big enough to walk through, carried waste water away from the centre and out of the city downstream. It became a sight for visitors.
Effects: cleaner streets and water and better sanitation, which cut the disease that the polluted Seine had spread.
There were limits: many houses were not yet connected, and household sewage was not fully carried away until later in the century.
Parallel work in London: Bazalgette's main drainage there was begun in 1859, so the two capitals were doing similar sanitary engineering in the same years.
The rebuilt city also gave Parisians green space, partly on the London model. Jean-Charles Alphand, the engineer in charge of the parks and promenades, designed much of their planting and layout.
The Bois de Boulogne (west) was given to the city by the state in 1852 and laid out as an English-style park with lakes and paths. The Longchamp racecourse opened there in 1857.
The Bois de Vincennes (east) was laid out in the 1860s as a counterpart for the working-class eastern districts, so that east and west each had a large park.
The Buttes-Chaumont (north-east) was a former quarry and rubbish dump turned into a park with a lake, cliffs and a temple on a rocky island. It opened in 1867, the Exhibition year.
Smaller parks and squares: the Parc Monceau was redesigned, the Parc Montsouris was begun in the south, and many small neighbourhood squares gave residents green space close to home.
Alongside streets and parks, the works added public buildings that displayed the Empire and met practical needs.
The Opéra: Charles Garnier won the design competition in 1861, building began in 1862, and it opened in 1875, after the fall of the Empire. It stands as a symbol of Second Empire display.
Les Halles, the central food market, was rebuilt as iron-and-glass pavilions by Victor Baltard from the 1850s, the first iron pavilions dating from 1854. The pavilions were demolished in 1971.
Railway stations: the Gare du Nord was rebuilt in the 1860s (architect Jacques Hittorff), and the new boulevards linked the stations to the centre and to each other.
Street furniture and fountains: Gabriel Davioud designed kiosks, lamps and benches, and the Saint-Michel fountain (1860). These gave the new streets a uniform appearance.
Other buildings included churches, town halls for the arrondissements (the districts of Paris), schools, barracks and the new Hôtel-Dieu.
By the late 1850s Paris had spilled beyond its old customs wall. Annexing the suburbs let Haussmann plan the whole urban area.

On 1 January 1860, under a law of 1859, the communes (local districts) between the old customs wall and the fortifications were annexed to the city, and the number of arrondissements rose from twelve to twenty.
The annexed communes included both working-class districts (Belleville, Montmartre) and richer ones such as Passy, a well-off western district.
The city grew to about 1.7 million people at the 1861 census, and to about 1.8 million by the late 1860s.
Why: to plan the whole urban area, to extend the boulevards and services outward, and to bring the growing suburbs under the city's control and taxes.
The works were enormously expensive. The way Haussmann paid for them made him vulnerable once the Empire began to liberalise.

Financing came from state subsidies, city revenue (mainly the octroi, a tax on goods entering the city), loans, and the hope that rising property values would pay for the works, which Haussmann called productive expenditure.

Hidden borrowing: the Caisse des travaux de Paris (1858) and advance payments to contractors, the bons de délégation, let Haussmann borrow without the approval of the Legislative Body. The city's debt grew greatly in the 1860s.
Court decisions in the late 1850s and 1860s made the city pay more compensation to expropriated owners, which raised costs and helped speculators.

Jules Ferry, a republican journalist, attacked the cost and irregular borrowing in articles of 1867-68, collected as Les Comptes fantastiques d'Haussmann (1868; his pamphlet), a pun on Les Contes fantastiques d'Hoffmann.
The fall: the Empire was turning liberal and the opposition was strong in Paris after the 1869 elections, so Émile Ollivier's new ministry, formed in January 1870, dismissed Haussmann that month.

Afterwards the Third Republic finished many projects, such as the Avenue de l'Opéra and the Boulevard Saint-Germain. Haussmann published his Mémoires (three volumes, 1890-93) defending his work, and died in 1891.
He accepted the label artiste démolisseur (demolition artist) for himself.
The rebuilding changed who could live where in Paris. Its benefits went mainly to the wealthy, while its costs fell on the poor.
Displacement: demolition destroyed many cheap central houses, so working-class families were pushed out to the east, the north and the annexed suburbs, often further from their work.
Rents rose in the rebuilt centre, and the new apartment blocks suited the middle classes.
The east-west divide sharpened: a wealthy west, with the Bois de Boulogne, and a working-class east, with districts such as Belleville and Ménilmontant.
Speculation: property developers and financiers made fortunes from rising land values. Émile Zola's novel La Curée (serialised 1871, book 1872) portrayed this speculation.
Employment: the works employed large numbers of building workers, many of them migrants from the provinces, though much work was seasonal.

Political effect: displaced workers in the east became a base for radical and republican politics in Belleville (Gambetta's Belleville programme, 1869). The Paris Commune of March-May 1871 showed barricades were still possible, though the army retook the city in the Bloody Week of May 1871.
Critics attacked Haussmann's Paris from several directions: cost, loss of the old city, and social exclusion. Defenders replied that it brought health, jobs and beauty.

Victor Hugo had campaigned long before Haussmann against the destruction of old buildings, in his 'War on the demolishers' (written 1825, published again 1832), and in Notre-Dame de Paris (1831), which celebrated medieval Paris.

Hugo was in exile from December 1851 to September 1870, opposing Napoleon III, so he was abroad for the whole period of the works. He did not write a specific attack on them; his writing stood for the old Paris that Haussmann destroyed.
Writers mourned the old Paris: Charles Baudelaire's poem 'Le Cygne' (The Swan), published 1860 and in Les Fleurs du mal from the 1861 edition, and the journal of Edmond and Jules de Goncourt.
Political critics: republicans and liberals such as Jules Ferry and Adolphe Thiers attacked the cost, the debt and the lack of control by elected bodies.

Other criticisms: the uniform facades and straight lines were monotonous, historic buildings and neighbourhoods were destroyed, the poor were excluded from the new city, and the boulevards were seen as built for troops.
Defenders: Haussmann and the Emperor pointed to health, traffic, beauty, jobs and prestige, and visitors to the 1867 Exhibition admired the new city.
Paris was the most dramatic case, but other cities also tackled growth, and comparing them shows what was distinctive about Haussmann's method.

Vienna: Emperor Franz Joseph's decree of December 1857 ordered the old city walls demolished and replaced by the Ringstrasse, a broad ring boulevard lined with public buildings (parliament, town hall, university, opera, museums) and apartment blocks. It opened in 1865 and was mostly finished later.
Plots along the Ringstrasse were sold to private builders, whose purchases paid for much of it.
Barcelona: Ildefons Cerdà's plan of 1859 for extending the city, the Eixample, set out a regular grid of blocks with cut-off corners, so it expanded outward rather than cutting through the old town.

Brussels: the River Senne was covered over and central boulevards built (1867-71) under the burgomaster Jules Anspach, partly on the Paris model. In Berlin James Hobrecht drew up a plan for the city's expansion in 1862.

British sanitary reform: The sanitary reform movement of the 1840s, led by Edwin Chadwick and others, produced his sanitary report (1842) and the Public Health Act (1848), which pressed for drainage and public health.
London's Great Stink of summer 1858 led Joseph Bazalgette of the Metropolitan Board of Works to build main sewers from 1859, with the Victoria Embankment (1870) along the Thames.

Contrast: Paris was planned from above by an authoritarian state with power over property, whereas British cities relied mainly on local authorities and permissive laws, improving drains and water more than street plans.
Haussmann's work outlived the Empire and has been judged very differently since.
Haussmannisation became a term for large-scale clearance and boulevard planning, and it was copied in French cities and abroad.
Admirers see the creator of modern Paris and a pioneer of modern city planning and public health.
Critics see a destroyer of old Paris and a planner who served the regime, the wealthy and speculators and pushed the poor to the edges.
Lasting features: most of central Paris's street plan, apartment blocks, parks and sewers still date from his works, though Baltard's Les Halles pavilions were demolished in the early 1970s.

A good judgement of Haussmann weighs each aim against the evidence, then sets the costs against the achievements. The verdict is largely successful in physical and sanitary terms, less so socially and financially.

Success on health: water, sewers, light and air largely achieved, because Belgrand's aqueducts and sewers cleaned the city. Failure: it was not complete by 1870, since many houses were still unconnected.
Success on traffic and stations: the boulevards linked the Seine and the railway stations, so movement was transformed.
Order: barricades were harder to build but not prevented, as the Commune of 1871 showed, so this aim was only partly achieved.
Success on beauty and prestige: the parks, the Opéra, the uniform facades and the 1867 Exhibition made Paris a model. Jobs: many were created, but much work was seasonal.
Failure on social grounds: displacement, higher rents and the east-west divide, because rising property values meant rents and speculation as well as benefits.
Failure on cost: the destruction of historic Paris, and huge debt and irregular finance that brought his dismissal in 1870, plus speculation.
Contemporary vs later views: Ferry, Hugo's defence of old Paris and Baudelaire criticised it, but visitors in 1867 admired it, and later admirers see a pioneer of modern planning.
Comparison with Hugo, Darwin or Napoleon III: Haussmann's achievement was practical and physical, and it was lasting in the street plan and sewers.
