Romanticism was a cultural movement that put feeling, imagination, nature, the individual and the national past above reason and classical rules. It grew up as a reaction against the Enlightenment, and it gave nationalists their raw material.

The Enlightenment of the eighteenth century valued reason, order, universal rules and classical models in art. Romantic writers and artists rejected this rational order in favour of feeling, imagination and the national past.

The German thinker Johann Gottfried Herder (1744-1803) wrote in the late eighteenth century that each people has its own spirit, expressed in its language, folk songs and customs. This idea of a national spirit was later called the Volksgeist, and nationalists took it up.
Folklore collection and the revival of medieval legends were central to cultural nationalism, since they claimed to reveal the true character of a people, one older than any government or frontier.
Victor Hugo's preface to his play Cromwell (1827) served as a manifesto for Romantic drama, in other words a public statement of what the new drama should be, free of classical rules.

Romanticism was an artistic movement, not a political programme, so Romantics could be conservative or revolutionary. The early Hugo was a royalist, whereas Richard Wagner took part in a rising in 1849.

Nationalism is the belief that a people sharing language, culture and history forms a nation that should rule itself. Cultural nationalism uses music, art, literature, history and language to express and build that sense of nationhood, often before any political state exists.

The Vienna settlement of 1815 drew frontiers by dynasty and the balance of power, not by nationality. Italians, Germans, Poles, Czechs and Hungarians were therefore divided or ruled by others, which is why culture mattered so much to peoples without a state.

Cultural nationalism was strongest where a nation lacked its own state, as among Italians, Germans, Poles, Czechs, Hungarians and Finns. With no government of their own to express nationhood, they used songs, stories, paintings and language instead.
Cultural nationalism fed political nationalism: once people felt they shared a past, a language and symbols, it was a short step to demanding a state to match, as later happened in Italy and Germany.
Artists and composers often worked with patrons and publishers in national capitals, and their audiences helped to shape national identity by sharing the same songs, stories and images.
Nationalists treated language as the main mark of nationality, so scholars and writers who collected, wrote and standardised a language were building a nation as well as a literature.

Music could speak for a nation without words, so it escaped censors and reached people who could not read. Three composers show how folk rhythms and opera plots became symbols of Poland, Hungary and Italy.

Frederic Chopin (1810-1849) wrote mazurkas and polonaises, which are Polish dance forms. He left Warsaw in 1830, and the Polish November Rising of 1830-31 was crushed by Russia, so he settled in Paris in 1831.

Because Chopin lived in exile in Paris, his music became a voice of Polish national feeling. Robert Schumann wrote that Chopin's works were 'cannons buried in flowers', meaning that patriotic force was hidden inside delicate music.

Franz Liszt (1811-1886), born in the Kingdom of Hungary, wrote the Hungarian Rhapsodies, most of them about 1846-53. They used what he took to be Hungarian folk music, much of it in fact Romani, and presented Hungary to European audiences.

Giuseppe Verdi (1813-1901) staged Nabucco in Milan (La Scala) in 1842. Its chorus of Hebrew slaves, 'Va, pensiero', came to be heard as patriotic by Italians who felt themselves oppressed, though the patriotic reading grew later rather than at the premiere.

Around 1859 the cry 'Viva VERDI' was a coded political slogan, because the letters stood for Vittorio Emanuele Re d'Italia, the king the nationalists wanted. It let crowds shout for unification under the eyes of the authorities.
Verdi's standing as a patriotic figure was confirmed when he was elected a deputy to the first Italian parliament in 1861.
German, Czech and Russian composers drew on national myth, folk song and history to create national opera. Some of their best-known works came only after 1871, so dates matter.
Richard Wagner (1813-1883) used German myth and legend in his operas, such as Tannhauser (1845) and Lohengrin (1850), so that audiences met a shared German legendary past on stage.

Wagner's Ring cycle is based on the Nibelungenlied (a medieval German epic) and Norse sagas. It was first performed complete at Bayreuth in 1876, after the period 1815-1871, so it should not be presented as an achievement within it.
Wagner took part in the Dresden rising of May 1849 and fled to Switzerland, which shows that Romantic artists could be revolutionary as well as nationalist.

Bedrich Smetana (1824-1884) wrote the Czech national opera The Bartered Bride, first performed in Prague in 1866. It used Czech folk music, so Czech audiences heard their own culture on the opera stage.
Smetana's cycle of symphonic poems Ma vlast (1874-79), which includes Vltava, drew on Czech landscape and history, but it also came after 1871.
Mikhail Glinka's A Life for the Tsar (1836) is seen as the start of Russian national opera.
Painters gave nations visible symbols. A single image such as a flag, a landscape or a scene from the past could make a shared identity feel real to people who could not read a pamphlet.

Eugene Delacroix (1798-1863) painted Liberty Leading the People in 1830, after the July Revolution. It shows Liberty carrying the tricolour (the French flag) and leading Parisians of different classes over a barricade, so it became a symbol of liberty and of the French nation.
The painting was shown at the Paris Salon in 1831 and bought by the French state, which shows how far a revolutionary image had become part of the official picture of France.
Delacroix's Massacre at Chios (1824) showed sympathy for the Greek cause, a cultural response to the Greek revolt rather than an account of it.
Caspar David Friedrich (1774-1840) painted landscapes such as Wanderer above the Sea of Fog (about 1818). They expressed the Romantic feeling for nature, which was linked to German national feeling.
Romantic history painting showed scenes from the national past, which gave citizens a shared image of their history.
Writers could make a nation's past and language famous across Europe. These authors worked in different countries, often in exile, and each gave their people a shared story.
Jacob (1785-1863) and Wilhelm (1786-1859) Grimm published Children's and Household Tales in 1812 and 1815, which presented German folklore as the voice of the German people.
Jacob Grimm's German Grammar (first volume 1819) and the German Dictionary, begun by the brothers in 1838, treated the language itself as the nation's inheritance.

Alessandro Manzoni (1785-1873) published The Betrothed (I promessi sposi) in 1827. It is set in Lombardy under Spanish rule in the seventeenth century, which readers took as a comment on Austrian rule in their own day.
Manzoni revised the novel in 1840-42 into the educated Italian of Florence (Tuscan), and it became a model for standard Italian.

Adam Mickiewicz (1798-1855) wrote Pan Tadeusz, the Polish national epic, in exile. Published in Paris in 1834 and set in Lithuania in 1811-12, it celebrated the Polish national past at a time when Poland had no state.
Alexander Pushkin (1799-1837), author of Eugene Onegin (complete edition 1833), created the modern Russian literary language, and his works became a central part of Russian national culture.
Sandor Petofi's 'National Song', recited in Pest on 15 March 1848, shows literature acting directly in revolution.
A nation of people who speak many dialects is hard to imagine as one community. Standard languages, taught in schools and fixed in books, turned dialects into national languages.

Grammars, dictionaries and schools turned dialects into national languages and built a single community of readers, which helped create a sense of one national community. Italian and Czech are examples.
Josef Jungmann's Czech-German dictionary, produced in the 1830s, gave Czech the vocabulary of a literary language at a time when German dominated educated life in the Czech lands.
Elias Lonnrot's Kalevala (1835, enlarged 1849) was a Finnish epic put together from folk poetry. It gave Finns a national story in their own language.
Manzoni's revised Betrothed (1840-42) set Florentine Italian as a model, so a single written Italian could be learnt by readers from different regions.
Hugo's literary work made him the leader of French Romanticism and one of the most celebrated writers of the century. Here the focus is on what he wrote and how people judged it.
Victor Hugo was born on 26 February 1802 at Besancon, the son of a general under Napoleon. He became a poet, dramatist and novelist and the leader of French Romanticism.

His early works include Odes (1822), Les Orientales (1829), with poems for the Greek cause, the preface to Cromwell (1827) and the play Hernani, first performed at the Comedie-Francaise in February 1830.
Hernani provoked a riot, 'the battle of Hernani', between Romantic supporters and classical critics, and it marked the victory of Romanticism in French theatre.

His novel Notre-Dame de Paris (1831) revived interest in the Gothic past of Paris, so it helped the campaign to preserve and restore medieval buildings. He was elected to the Academie francaise in 1841 and made a peer of France in 1845.

In exile he lived on Jersey (1852-55) and then on Guernsey (1855-70) at Hauteville House. There he wrote Les Contemplations (1856), partly mourning his daughter Leopoldine, who drowned in 1843, and The Toilers of the Sea (1866), set on Guernsey.

Les Misérables (1862), written largely on Guernsey, follows the convict Jean Valjean from 1815 to the Paris rising of June 1832. It deals with poverty, injustice, the law and redemption, and it was a huge success across Europe.

As a writer Hugo shaped taste and national memory, so he was an active participant in cultural life, and his social novels gave a voice to the poor. Romantics hailed him as their leader, while classical critics attacked him for breaking the rules of form and taste.

Some critics found Les Misérables sentimental, but readers made it a best-seller. Historians now rank him among the greatest French writers, a national figure whose literary and political engagement went together, and his state funeral in 1885 and burial in the Panthéon show his standing.

The French Revolution had attacked the Catholic Church, but after 1815 the Church recovered. Its revival split between conservatives, liberal Catholics and lay charity workers, who each responded to the changes of the age.

The Revolution seized Church lands and persecuted the clergy, and Napoleon's Concordat (agreement with the Pope, 1801) restored the Church under state control. The Church was therefore linked with monarchy and order, and republicans and liberals were often anticlerical (hostile to the Church's power).

The Catholic revival after 1815 was favoured by the restored Bourbons (1814/15-1830), who stood for 'throne and altar'. New and returning religious orders appeared, and the Church was strong among women, peasants and some regions, but weak among urban workers and much of the middle class.

Liberal Catholicism was led by Felicite de Lamennais, Henri Lacordaire and Charles de Montalembert. Their newspaper L'Avenir (1830, motto 'God and liberty') demanded freedom of the Church from the state, and freedom of the press, education and association.

Pope Gregory XVI condemned these ideas in the encyclical (papal letter) Mirari vos in 1832. Lamennais left the Church in 1834 after his Words of a Believer, whereas Lacordaire and Montalembert submitted and stayed.

Frederic Ozanam (1813-1853), a Catholic student and later a Sorbonne professor, co-founded the Society of St Vincent de Paul in Paris in 1833 with fellow students. It was a lay Catholic charity that visited the poor and the sick in their homes.

The Society spread through France and abroad. It was a Catholic answer to urban poverty and to the charge that the Church ignored the poor. It was named after the seventeenth-century saint, not founded by him.
From 1850 the French Church gained schools and mass devotion, but its close ties to conservatism and to Pius IX pushed liberals, republicans and many workers away from it.

The Falloux Law (March 1850, named after the education minister Alfred de Falloux) gave freedom to open mainly Catholic secondary schools and put clergy on education councils. It greatly expanded Church schooling and was part of the conservative reaction after 1848.

Napoleon III supported the Church until 1859, and French troops protected the Pope in Rome from 1849 to 1870 (withdrawn briefly 1866-67). Italian unification, which threatened the Pope's rule in Rome, strained this relationship.
Popular piety grew too. After Bernadette Soubirous's visions at Lourdes in 1858, mass pilgrimage developed, helped by railways, which could carry large crowds to the shrine.

Ultramontanism means looking to the Pope in Rome for authority. Under Pius IX (1846-78) it grew: he defined the Immaculate Conception (Mary's freedom from sin) as doctrine in 1854 and issued the Syllabus of Errors in 1864, condemning liberalism and progress.

This deepened the split between the Church and liberals, republicans and workers. Anticlericalism and the de-Christianisation of the urban working class followed, and Ernest Renan's Life of Jesus (1863) is an example of the challenge from scholarship.

Britain had one established Church but many denominations. Industrial growth created crowded towns where the parish system and old charity broke down, and the churches competed and cooperated in responding.
The Church of England was the established (state) Church. Nonconformists such as Methodists, Baptists and Congregationalists stood outside it, and Catholics were a minority, many of them Irish.
Industrialisation and rapid town growth produced crowded towns where the parish system and old charity broke down. This is the social change the churches had to meet.

Methodism, from John Wesley (1703-1791), grew rapidly among industrial workers and miners. Its chapels, preaching, self-improvement and discipline suited working people, and it was also a training ground for trade-union and Chartist speakers.

The Oxford Movement began with John Keble's Assize Sermon in Oxford on 14 July 1833. Its Tracts for the Times (1833-41) gave its followers the name Tractarians, and it revived Catholic worship and ritual within the Church of England.
John Henry Newman became a Catholic in 1845. Later Anglo-Catholic priests worked in slum parishes.

Catholics gained the Catholic Emancipation Act in 1829. Irish immigration to the industrial cities followed, and the Catholic hierarchy was restored in England and Wales in 1850 under Cardinal Wiseman.
Many British Christians tried to answer poverty, ignorance and drink directly. They set up schools, societies and missions, often run by churches and charities rather than by the state.

Christian Socialism, from 1848, was led by F. D. Maurice, Charles Kingsley and J. M. Ludlow. They sought to apply Christian principles to the problems of industrial society and set up co-operative workshops.
The Working Men's College opened in London in 1854, and Kingsley's novel Alton Locke (1850) drew attention to the conditions of workers.

Sunday schools, begun in the late eighteenth century (Robert Raikes), and the ragged schools (the Ragged School Union, 1844) taught poor children. Along with church day schools they were run mainly by churches and charities, because the churches had a central role in schooling before state education.

Temperance societies campaigned against drunkenness, which was seen as a cause of poverty and family breakdown among the working class. The Preston teetotal pledge of 1832 (Joseph Livesey) helped to launch the cause, and many societies were chapel-based.

Evangelical Christians (those stressing personal faith and moral action) such as Lord Shaftesbury, called Lord Ashley until 1851, led campaigns for factory and mines reform, including the Mines Act of 1842.
George Williams founded the YMCA in London in 1844, and churches in the industrial towns ran city missions and charitable work, which responded to urban poverty with preaching, relief and education.
The churches' efforts had limits, and a census showed that many working people stayed away. The experience of Britain and France differed because of how each country organised religion.

The religious census of 1851 (England and Wales) showed that many working people, especially in the big towns, did not attend any church. Do not quote attendance figures, because sources differ widely.
William Booth began his East London mission in 1865, and it was renamed the Salvation Army in 1878. It aimed to reach poor people who did not go to church.

In France there was one Church, tied to conservatism and opposed by anticlericals. In Britain there were many denominations, with Nonconformists linked to reform and self-help, so religion and political reform were less sharply opposed there.
In both countries the churches lost much of the urban working class, so the churches' social work treated symptoms (poverty, drink, ignorance) more than the causes.
Electricity moved from laboratory experiments to a source of power in a few decades. Each scientist here built on the one before.

Michael Faraday (1791-1867), working at the Royal Institution in London, showed electromagnetic rotation in 1821. This is the principle of the electric motor, in which electricity makes a magnet and a wire turn.
In 1831 Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction, the making of an electric current by moving a magnet near a wire. It was the basis of the generator and transformer.
Faraday's laws of electrolysis (1833-34) showed that the amount of substance deposited at an electrode is proportional to the electric charge passed through the solution.
James Clerk Maxwell's theory of the electromagnetic field (1865) showed that light is an electromagnetic wave, which unified the theories of electricity and light.

Werner von Siemens's self-excited dynamo (1866-67) made practical large-scale generation of electricity possible, but its benefits came mainly after 1871. The electric light bulb belongs to a later date.
The electric telegraph used the new knowledge of electricity to send messages along wires faster than any messenger. This changed how news, trade and governments communicated.
William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone patented the British electric telegraph in 1837, and it was used on railways, on the Great Western Railway from 1838-39, where it helped signal trains.

Samuel Morse's telegraph was demonstrated in 1844 on a line between Washington and Baltimore, with the first message 'What hath God wrought'. Morse code, a system of dots and dashes, was widely adopted.

A submarine (undersea) telegraph cable was laid across the Atlantic in 1858 but failed within weeks. A lasting cable was completed in 1866, laid by the Great Eastern, so news and orders now crossed continents in minutes.

Darwin was a naturalist whose theory of evolution by natural selection transformed biology. He was a witness to nature on his voyage and a careful theorist afterwards; most Christians in 1815 believed each species was created separately and the earth was young, which is why his theory caused such uproar.

Charles Darwin was born on 12 February 1809 at Shrewsbury. He studied medicine at Edinburgh (1825-27) and then at Cambridge (1828-31) to become a clergyman, and he was keenly interested in natural history.

He sailed as naturalist on HMS Beagle (captain Robert FitzRoy) from December 1831 to October 1836, visiting South America, the Galapagos Islands (1835) and Australia. He collected fossils, rocks, plants and animals and noted variation between islands, such as finches, tortoises and mockingbirds.

Two books influenced him: Charles Lyell's Principles of Geology (1830-33) showed an earth shaped slowly over vast time, and Thomas Malthus's essay on population (1798) described a struggle for existence.

Darwin kept notebooks on the transmutation (change) of species from 1837-38, worked on the theory from 1838 and published only in 1859. Alfred Russel Wallace's letter in 1858 pushed him on, and joint papers were read at the Linnean Society in London on 1 July 1858.

On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection (24 November 1859) argued from variation, the struggle for existence, natural selection (those best suited to their surroundings survive and breed) and common descent. The first printing sold out on publication.

The theory conflicted with the Genesis account and the idea of design. At the Oxford debate (30 June 1860) Thomas Henry Huxley defended Darwin against Bishop Samuel Wilberforce, who opposed him, and Darwin was absent.
The Origin divided opinion, and Darwin let others fight in public while he wrote. Judgements of him changed from threat to founder of modern biology.
Huxley, known as 'Darwin's bulldog', Joseph Hooker and, eventually, Lyell supported him. Many churchmen and some scientists opposed him, though some Christians reconciled faith and evolution.
Describe the Oxford exchange without quotation marks for Wilberforce, because accounts of it differ and only appear in later sources.
The Descent of Man (1871) applied the theory to human evolution, the point critics found most offensive.
Darwin was a witness of nature on the voyage and a careful theorist. He took part in the debate through his books but avoided public controversy, leaving that to Huxley.

'Survival of the fittest' was Herbert Spencer's phrase (1864), which Darwin adopted in a later edition of the Origin, so he did not coin it. The misuse of his ideas as Social Darwinism was not his doing.

Darwin died on 19 April 1882 and was buried in Westminster Abbey, which showed his standing. Historians regard him as the founder of modern evolutionary biology, and his theory was completed by genetics.
Contemporaries saw him as a threat to religion, attacked by churchmen and defended by Huxley, whereas later historians rank him among the greatest figures of the century.
Biology moved from description towards explaining how living things work, with new ideas about microbes, inheritance and cells.

Louis Pasteur (1822-1895) showed from 1857 that fermentation and decay are caused by micro-organisms (living things too small to see without a microscope). This work led to the germ theory of disease, the idea that specific germs cause illness, which was established only in the 1860s-80s.

Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiments, about 1859-62 (the early 1860s), showed that micro-organisms do not appear spontaneously in sterile broth, which undermined the theory of spontaneous generation (the belief that life arises from non-living matter).
Pasteur developed pasteurisation, heating liquids to kill microbes, in the 1860s.

Gregor Mendel (1822-1884), an Augustinian friar at Brno, published experiments on pea plants in 1866, showing that inheritance follows particular patterns. His work was ignored until its rediscovery in 1900, and Darwin never knew of it, so Mendel did not influence Darwin.

Cell theory: Matthias Schleiden (plants, 1838) and Theodor Schwann (animals, 1839) showed that living things are made of cells, and Rudolf Virchow's Cellular Pathology (1858) held that every cell comes from a cell.
Before anaesthesia and antiseptics, surgery meant great pain and a high risk of infection. Two advances made operations bearable and safer.
Ether anaesthesia, which puts a patient to sleep so that surgery causes no pain, was demonstrated in Boston in 1846. James Young Simpson used chloroform in Edinburgh in 1847.
Joseph Lister introduced antiseptic surgery using carbolic acid in Glasgow in 1867, applying Pasteur's ideas about germs. Killing germs on instruments and wounds made surgery safer.
John Snow traced cholera to the Broad Street pump in London in 1854.
Steam power and photography changed how people travelled, communicated and recorded the world, linking nations and empires in a faster network.
George Stephenson's Rocket won the Rainhill trials in 1829, and the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in 1830, so steam railways quickly became the model for others.
Isambard Kingdom Brunel's SS Great Britain was launched in 1843 with an iron hull and a screw propeller. The Suez Canal opened in 1869, shortening sea routes between Europe and the East.
Nicephore Niepce made the first surviving photograph about 1826, and Louis Daguerre's daguerreotype was announced in 1839.
William Henry Fox Talbot's calotype, a negative-positive process from which many prints could be made, was patented in 1841, so it could be copied where the daguerreotype could not.
Photographs were used for portraits and to record war and cities.
Henry Bessemer's converter (1856) made cheap steel possible.
Together, railways, the telegraph and steamships brought faster communication and travel, safer surgery and a new view of nature, and science challenged religious authority.
Examiners reward judgement: what these developments achieved and where they fell short, and how contemporaries saw them compared with later historians.
Achievement: cultural nationalism gave nations symbols, languages and a shared past, and prepared the ground for political unity in Italy and Germany.
Limit: it reached mainly the educated minority, idealised the past and could not by itself win independence in Poland, the Czech lands or Hungary by 1871.
Achievement: the churches gave the poor charity, schools, temperance and moral reform, and renewed religion's role in public life.
Limit: the churches treated symptoms rather than causes, lost much of the urban working class, and in France were tied to conservatism.
Achievement: Faraday, Darwin, Pasteur and Mendel transformed knowledge, and technology such as railways and the telegraph changed daily life.
Limit: many benefits, such as electric power, germ theory in medicine and genetics, came only after 1871, and Darwin's ideas divided society.
Contemporary against later views: contemporaries saw Darwin as a threat to religion and Hugo as a controversial Romantic, but later historians rank both among the greatest figures of the century.
Overall: the period enriched national identities and expanded knowledge, but it also raised new questions about tradition, religion and national belonging that remained contested.
To judge Bismarck's foreign policy you first need the starting point: a Europe run by five Great Powers, which the new German Empire suddenly disturbed. The key idea is the balance of power.

Balance of power means that no single state, or bloc of allied states, is strong enough to dominate Europe, because the others would combine against it. A united Germany upset the old balance, and Bismarck tried to manage the new one in Germany's favour.

Germany was unified by Prussia under Bismarck through three wars: against Denmark (1864), against Austria (1866, the Austro-Prussian or Seven Weeks' War) and against France (1870-71, the Franco-Prussian War, with French defeat at Sedan in September 1870 and the siege of Paris).

Before 1871 the centre of Europe was weak and divided into many German states. This is why the five Great Powers, Britain, France, Russia, Austria-Hungary and Prussia/Germany, could balance one another.
The Eastern Question was the problem of what would happen as the Ottoman Empire (Turkey) declined in the Balkans. Russia and Austria-Hungary were rivals for influence there.
Britain wanted to keep Russia away from the Straits (the sea passage from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean) and the eastern Mediterranean, because that route guarded its own interests.

The German Empire (the Second Reich) was proclaimed in 1871 and combined a strong monarchy with an elected parliament. Its constitution put real power in the hands of the Kaiser and the Chancellor, not the Reichstag.

The Empire was proclaimed on 18 January 1871 in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, while Paris was still under siege in the Franco-Prussian War. King Wilhelm I of Prussia became German Emperor (Kaiser).

It was a federation of 25 states: four kingdoms (Prussia, Bavaria, Saxony, Württemberg), grand duchies, duchies and principalities, and three free cities (Hamburg, Bremen, Lübeck). The population was about 41 million in 1871. Because the states stayed in the federation, local rulers kept their thrones.

Prussia dominated the federation, with about two-thirds of the territory and about three-fifths of the population. Alsace-Lorraine was a Reichsland (imperial territory), ruled directly from Berlin and not a state.

The Kaiser was hereditary King of Prussia. He commanded the armed forces, appointed and dismissed the Chancellor and ministers and conducted foreign policy, and he could declare war with the consent of the Bundesrat (needed unless Germany was attacked).

The Chancellor was responsible to the Kaiser, not to the Reichstag, and ministers (state secretaries) answered to the Chancellor. Bismarck was Chancellor from 1871 to 1890 and, separately, Prussian Minister-President for almost all of that time, apart from a short break in 1873.

The Bundesrat was the federal council of delegates from the state governments, who were not elected. Prussia held 17 of its 58 votes in 1871, and 14 votes could block a constitutional amendment, so Prussia alone could do so.

The Reichstag was elected by universal male suffrage (men aged 25 and over) by secret ballot. It voted on laws and the budget, but it could not appoint or dismiss the Chancellor, which is why it was weak. This is why real power lay with the Kaiser and the Chancellor.
The peace that ended the Franco-Prussian War created a lasting French grievance. Together with the birth of a powerful Germany, it changed how the Great Powers related to one another.
The Treaty of Frankfurt (10 May 1871) made France pay an indemnity (a payment of compensation) of 5 billion francs and cede Alsace and part of Lorraine, including Strasbourg and Metz.
German troops occupied part of France until the indemnity was paid, which France achieved by 1873.
A new Great Power in the centre of Europe, with a growing population and industry, changed the balance of power. Germany now outweighed its neighbours in a way the old divided German lands never had.
France was weakened and embittered by defeat and the loss of the provinces, so it became hostile to Germany. Britain, Russia and Austria-Hungary had to adjust to a united Germany.

Bismarck governed by managing the Reichstag, working with one party after another and naming the enemies of the Reich in turn. His domestic record matters because examiners ask you to compare it with his foreign policy.

His method was to work with Reichstag parties in turn and to label groups as Reichsfeinde (enemies of the Reich): Catholics (the Centre Party), socialists, and national minorities such as the Poles, the Danes and the people of Alsace-Lorraine. The National Liberals were his main partners from 1871 to 1878.

The Kulturkampf was his struggle with the Catholic Church, begun in 1871 and wound down after Leo XIII became pope in 1878 and largely ended by 1887. It failed to break the Church, and it matters here because the assessment names it.

After attempts on the life of Wilhelm I in May 1878 (Hödel) and June 1878 (Nobiling, who badly wounded the Kaiser), Bismarck used the fear of revolution as a pretext, although neither attacker acted for the SPD. He dissolved the Reichstag, and a new election followed in July 1878.

The Anti-Socialist Law of October 1878 banned socialist associations, meetings and publications, but socialists could still stand for and sit in the Reichstag. It was renewed several times and lapsed on 30 September 1890. This means the law attacked socialist organisation, but not the party's place in parliament.
The law failed to stop the SPD (the Social Democratic Party). At the February 1890 election it won about 1.4 million votes, the largest share of any party, and 35 seats.

The tariff law of 1879 protected imported iron, steel and grain, an alliance of Junker landowners and heavy industry called 'rye and iron'. It split the National Liberals (their left wing seceded in 1880), so Bismarck turned to the Conservatives and, for the tariff, the Centre Party.
Bismarck combined repression of socialists with benefits for workers, and he fought the Reichstag over the army. At the same time he built the shared institutions of a single nation state.

To win workers away from socialism he introduced state insurance: sickness insurance (1883), accident insurance (1884) and old age and invalidity insurance (1889). Germany was the first state to create a national compulsory scheme of this kind.

This mix of repression and welfare is called 'carrot and stick' (in German, Zuckerbrot und Peitsche, 'sugar-bread and whip'). The schemes had limits: pensions were small and paid only from age 70, and the insurance failed to reduce support for the SPD.
The Septennate was the system of voting the army budget for seven years at a time (first in 1874), which kept the army outside yearly Reichstag control.

In January 1887 the Reichstag refused the new army bill, so Bismarck dissolved it. In the February 1887 election he fought on a war scare with France, and the Kartell (Conservatives, Free Conservatives and National Liberals) won a majority and passed the bill.

He also created national institutions: the mark became the single currency in 1873, and the Reichsbank was founded in 1875 (it opened on 1 January 1876). These count as domestic achievements because they made a national market possible.
After 1871 Bismarck declared Germany a satiated power, one with no wish for more European territory. His aim was to protect the new Reich from a hostile coalition, above all one that included France.

Bismarck described Germany after 1871 as a 'satiated' (saturated) power: it had what it wanted, so more expansion in Europe would only provoke the other powers. This is why he wanted peace rather than conquest.
French revanche, the desire for revenge and recovery of Alsace-Lorraine, followed the loss of the provinces. Bismarck assumed that France was irreconcilable and would never become a reliable friend.

His core aim was to keep France isolated and prevent a hostile coalition, above all a two-front war (war against France in the west and Russia in the east at once). He called this fear his 'nightmare of coalitions', his own phrase.

In the Kissingen Dictation (June 1877) he set out, as reported, that he wanted all the powers except France to need Germany and to be kept from coalitions against it by their own relations with one another.

He also wanted to keep Russia and Austria-Hungary from war with each other over the Balkans, to keep Britain friendly, and to divert rivalries to the edges of Europe, such as the Balkans and Africa, away from Germany's borders.

A later summary of this logic is that, in a Europe of five Great Powers, the aim was to be one of three, so that Germany was never the odd one out. He is reported to have said this to the Russian diplomat Saburov in 1880.
French hostility never disappeared, and several crises showed how fragile peace between Germany and France was. Bismarck also tried to ease French bitterness by encouraging French empire-building.

In the War-in-Sight crisis of spring 1875, France passed an army law (March 1875) expanding its army. An article headed 'Is War in Sight?' in the Berlin newspaper Die Post (April 1875) suggested Germany might strike first.
Britain and Russia warned Berlin, and Tsar Alexander II and his chancellor Gorchakov visited Berlin in May 1875. Historians disagree on whether Bismarck was bluffing or testing the other powers.
Either way, the lesson for Bismarck was that Britain and Russia would not allow France to be crushed a second time, which fed his fear of a hostile coalition.
In 1886-87 General Georges Boulanger, French war minister and a popular figure of revanche, stirred up feeling against Germany.

In the Schnaebelé affair (April 1887) the Germans arrested a French frontier police official on the border, and he was released about a week later. It showed how a small incident could threaten war. Such incidents mattered because French feeling was already hostile.

Bismarck encouraged France to take Tunisia, which it made a protectorate in 1881, hoping to turn French attention from Alsace-Lorraine. In 1884-85 he cooperated with the French premier Jules Ferry against Britain on African questions.
Bismarck's first attempt to keep Russia and Austria-Hungary friendly with Germany was a conservative understanding among three monarchies. It came under strain when the Balkans erupted.
The Three Emperors' League (Dreikaiserbund), completed in October 1873, linked Wilhelm I, Franz Joseph of Austria-Hungary and Alexander II of Russia.
It was a conservative understanding to consult each other and resist revolution, not a military alliance. This is why it could not bind the three emperors when their interests clashed.
The Balkan crisis of 1875-78 began with risings against Ottoman rule in Bosnia-Herzegovina (1875) and Bulgaria (1876).
Serbia and Montenegro fought Turkey in 1876, and Russia fought the Russo-Turkish War from April 1877 to early 1878.
Bismarck did not want Germany dragged in. He told the Reichstag in December 1876 that the Balkans were not worth 'the healthy bones of a single Pomeranian musketeer'.

The Treaty of San Stefano (3 March 1878, between Russia and Turkey) created a large autonomous Bulgaria under Russian influence. Austria-Hungary and Britain refused to accept it, and Britain sent its fleet to the Straits.
To prevent a European war over San Stefano, the powers met in Berlin under Bismarck's chairmanship. The settlement avoided war, but it left Russia angry with Germany.

In a Reichstag speech of February 1878 Bismarck promised that Germany would act as an 'honest broker' (ehrlicher Makler), meaning an impartial mediator. The Congress of Berlin met from 13 June to 13 July 1878 with Bismarck in the chair.
Britain was represented by Disraeli (Lord Beaconsfield) and Salisbury, Austria-Hungary by Andrássy and Russia by Gorchakov and Shuvalov.
The large Bulgaria was split into three: a smaller autonomous Principality of Bulgaria, Eastern Rumelia (autonomous under the Sultan) and Macedonia, which returned to Ottoman rule.
Serbia, Montenegro and Romania became fully independent. Austria-Hungary was allowed to occupy and administer Bosnia-Herzegovina (and garrison the Sanjak of Novi Pazar).
Russia kept southern Bessarabia and gained Kars and Batum. Britain gained Cyprus at the time of the Congress, by a separate convention with Turkey in June 1878. France was told it could take Tunisia.
War was avoided, but Russia felt cheated of the fruits of its victory over Turkey and blamed Bismarck, and the Russian press attacked Germany.

The first League lapsed, and Alexander II sent an angry letter to Wilhelm I in August 1879, the 'box on the ears' letter. This is why the Congress is judged a success for peace but a failure for Russo-German relations.
After 1878, with Russia resentful, Bismarck secured Germany by tying it to Austria-Hungary and then to Italy. These treaties became the core of his alliance system.

The Dual Alliance of 7 October 1879 was a secret defensive treaty between Germany and Austria-Hungary. If either was attacked by Russia, the other would help with all its forces; if attacked by another power, the other would stay at least neutral, unless Russia joined the attacker.

Bismarck chose Austria-Hungary to guard against a Russian attack after Russia's anger in 1878, and to bind the Habsburg state to Germany. Andrássy negotiated for Austria-Hungary. This is why the Dual Alliance became the base of his system.
Wilhelm I disliked a treaty aimed at his nephew, Tsar Alexander II, and agreed only after Bismarck threatened to resign.

The Dual Alliance was renewed regularly and lasted to the end of the war in 1918, making it the permanent core of German policy. Its danger was that it committed Germany to Austria-Hungary in the Balkans.

The Triple Alliance (20 May 1882) was a secret treaty, first for five years and renewed until 1914. Italy joined because it was angry at France's seizure of Tunisia in 1881 and wanted Great Power standing.

Its terms were that Germany and Austria-Hungary would help Italy if attacked by France, Italy would help Germany if attacked by France, and all three would fight if any member was attacked by two or more Great Powers.

It had weaknesses. Italy stated (the Mancini declaration, 1882) that the alliance could not be directed against Britain, and relations with Austria-Hungary were poor because Italian-speaking Trentino and Trieste remained under Habsburg rule.
Italy stayed neutral in August 1914 and entered the war on the Allied side in May 1915.
Bismarck repaired relations with Russia in 1881, but Balkan rivalry between Russia and Austria-Hungary wrecked the arrangement. His answer was a secret treaty with Russia alone.
The second Three Emperors' League was signed on 18 June 1881, secretly and for three years, and renewed in 1884. Each member would stay neutral if another was at war with a fourth Great Power.
Balkan changes were to be made only by agreement, which was meant to stop Russia and Austria-Hungary clashing. Austria-Hungary could annex Bosnia-Herzegovina when it chose.

In the Bulgarian crisis, Bulgaria united with Eastern Rumelia in 1885, and Serbia attacked Bulgaria and was defeated. Prince Alexander of Battenberg (not a Tsar) was forced to abdicate in 1886 under Russian pressure.
Russia and Austria-Hungary came close to war, and Russia refused to renew the League in 1887, so it collapsed. This kept Russia friendly to Germany without breaking the Dual Alliance.

Bismarck replaced it with the Reinsurance Treaty of 18 June 1887, a secret treaty between Germany and Russia for three years. Each would stay benevolently neutral if the other was at war with a third Great Power, except if Germany attacked France or Russia attacked Austria-Hungary.
A secret protocol recognised Russia's predominant influence in Bulgaria and promised German moral and diplomatic support if Russia had to defend the Straits.
Austria-Hungary and Italy were not told. It can be argued that the treaty conflicted in spirit with the Dual Alliance, since Germany was promising friendship to Austria-Hungary's rival.
In late 1887 Bismarck made two moves that pulled in different directions. One pushed Russia towards France, while the other built a loose Mediterranean barrier against Russia with British help.

In November 1887 Bismarck barred the Reichsbank from accepting Russian bonds as security for loans (the Lombardverbot). Russia raised its loans in Paris instead from 1888, which helped to bring Russia and France together. This is why Russia, for example, turned elsewhere for money.

The Mediterranean Agreements of 1887 were made by Britain, Italy and Austria-Hungary, and Germany was not a signatory. The first (February-March 1887) linked Britain and Italy, then Austria-Hungary, with Spain associated.

The second (December 1887, Britain, Austria-Hungary and Italy) kept the status quo in the Mediterranean, the Black Sea and the Near East, in effect against Russia and France. Bismarck encouraged them, which tied Britain loosely to the Triple Alliance powers.
The Reinsurance Treaty (Germany and Russia only) must not be confused with the Mediterranean Agreements. Bismarck was in effect supporting both Russia and its opponents, which only he could keep up.
Bismarck long thought colonies not worth the trouble, then changed course in 1884-85. Historians disagree about why, and the colonies strained relations with Britain.
Bismarck long regarded colonies as costly and as a source of quarrels with Britain, and Germany lacked a fleet to protect them.

In 1884 Germany took South West Africa (Lüderitz's land at Angra Pequena, April 1884), Togoland and the Cameroons (July 1884), and north-east New Guinea (Kaiser-Wilhelmsland) and the Bismarck Archipelago. In 1885 it added German East Africa (Carl Peters' German East Africa Company) and the Marshall Islands.

One explanation is pressure from merchants (such as Lüderitz of Bremen, and Hamburg trading firms) and the German Colonial Society (Kolonialverein, 1882). Colonies were also popular in the Reichstag election of October 1884, and they gave Bismarck leverage against Britain and a gesture towards France.

A.J.P. Taylor argued that the colonies were taken to quarrel with Britain and so prevent an Anglo-German liberal friendship under the future Frederick III. Hans-Ulrich Wehler argued they were 'social imperialism', a way to divert domestic discontent. Treat both as interpretations.
Bismarck preferred protectorates (Schutzgebiete) run at first by chartered companies at their own expense, rather than state-run colonies, but the state soon had to take over administration.

Gladstone was British prime minister from 1880 to 1885, and London protested about Angra Pequena and East Africa. The Berlin Conference on West Africa (15 November 1884 to 26 February 1885), called by Bismarck with France, set the rules for claiming African territory.

Relations improved with Salisbury, prime minister from June 1885 (briefly) and again from 1886, and the Mediterranean Agreements helped. In December 1888 Bismarck told the explorer Eugen Wolf, 'my map of Africa lies in Europe', with France on one side, Russia on the other and Germany in the middle.
Crown Prince Frederick had married Victoria, Queen Victoria's eldest daughter, in 1858. Both were liberal, and Bismarck distrusted their influence.
Bismarck fell because a young Kaiser who wanted to rule himself clashed with a Chancellor used to controlling everything. The quarrel centred on workers, the constitution and access to the Kaiser.

1888 is called the year of the three emperors. Wilhelm I died on 9 March 1888 aged 90, and his son Frederick III, already gravely ill with cancer of the throat, reigned 99 days and died on 15 June 1888.
Wilhelm II, born in 1859, became Kaiser aged 29. He wanted to rule personally, so he was ready to clash with Bismarck.

They quarrelled over the workers. During a miners' strike in the Ruhr in May 1889 Wilhelm II favoured concessions, and he wanted to ease the Anti-Socialist Law, which Bismarck wanted to make permanent.

In January 1890 the Reichstag rejected Bismarck's bill to make the law permanent. In the February 1890 election the Kartell lost its majority and the SPD vote rose, and Bismarck spoke of a Staatsstreich (coup) to change the constitution or suffrage.

He invoked the Prussian Cabinet Order of 1852 (ministers could approach the King only through the Minister-President), which would limit the ministers' access to the Kaiser. He also met the Centre leader Ludwig Windthorst in March 1890 without the Kaiser's consent.
Wilhelm II demanded his resignation. Bismarck sent his resignation letter on 18 March 1890, it was accepted on 20 March, and General Leo von Caprivi became Chancellor.
The Punch cartoon 'Dropping the Pilot' by John Tenniel (29 March 1890) shows Wilhelm II on deck watching Bismarck, the pilot, leave the ship.

The immediate results were that the Reinsurance Treaty was not renewed in 1890 and the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty was signed with Britain on 1 July 1890. Both were Caprivi's, not Bismarck's, and Russia moved towards France; the Franco-Russian military convention followed in 1892.

Bismarck made German unification possible in the 1860s and then governed the new Empire as Chancellor until 1890. As a participant who shaped events, and was in turn shaped by them, he is judged very differently by contemporaries and historians.

He was born on 1 April 1815 and lived until 1898 (1815-98) at Schönhausen (Brandenburg) into a Junker family (Prussian landed nobility), and became Prussian Minister-President in September 1862. He made unification possible, and his phrase 'blood and iron' belongs to those earlier years, not to the Chancellorship.

He was made a prince (Fürst) in 1871 and was Chancellor under Wilhelm I (1871-88), Frederick III (1888) and Wilhelm II (1888-90). As Chancellor he shaped the constitution, the domestic campaigns, the alliances of 1873 to 1887, the Congress of Berlin and the colonies of 1884-85.
He controlled foreign policy personally, and most of the major policy decisions of the Empire were his.

He was shaped by events as well. The War-in-Sight crisis taught him that Britain and Russia would not let France be crushed, Russian resentment after 1878 and the Bulgarian crisis forced his alliance changes, and in the end a new Kaiser ended his career.

He was a conservative monarchist defending Prussian power and the Junker order, using nationalism and the Reichstag as tools. In diplomacy he practised realpolitik, politics based on power and interests rather than principles.
Contemporaries saw the 'Iron Chancellor'. Nationalists and conservatives admired him, Catholics, socialists and many liberals hated him, and foreign observers respected him as a master diplomat.
After 1890 Bismarck became a critic of his successors, and his reputation was fought over by historians. Their verdicts divide into favourable and critical views.
He retired to Friedrichsruh, near Hamburg, and attacked the 'new course' of Wilhelm II's governments in the press, especially the Hamburger Nachrichten. He died there on 30 July 1898.

His memoirs, Thoughts and Recollections, appeared just after his death (two volumes in 1898, the third in 1921). Hundreds of Bismarck towers and monuments were built in Germany, which shows the cult that grew around him.
Favourable historians stress his diplomacy. A.J.P. Taylor (Bismarck: The Man and the Statesman, 1955) held that it was peaceful after 1871, though he also stressed his opportunism.

Lothar Gall (Bismarck: The White Revolutionary) called him a 'white revolutionary': a conservative who used revolutionary means, accepting nationalism and universal suffrage, to preserve the monarchy and the old elites.

Critics stress the flaws. Hans-Ulrich Wehler argued that his rule was a 'Bonapartist' dictatorship that kept the old elites in power through 'negative integration', uniting the majority against Reichsfeinde, and through social imperialism.
On this view he left a weak parliamentary tradition, and his system of secret, contradictory treaties needed his own skill to work, so it could not outlast him.
The usual judgement is that Bismarck was more successful abroad than at home, but both records have successes and limits. Contemporaries and later historians also judged him differently.
Foreign success: Germany fought no war between 1871 and 1890 and avoided a two-front war, while France stayed isolated. The Russo-Turkish War of 1877-78 did not become a general European war.
Foreign success: the Congress of Berlin prevented a general war in 1878 and put Germany at the centre of European diplomacy, and colonies were gained in 1884-85 without war.

Foreign limit: the system was complex, secret and partly contradictory, because the Reinsurance Treaty and the Dual Alliance pulled in opposite directions. It depended on Bismarck personally, so a successor could not keep all the balls in the air.

Foreign limit: the Dual Alliance tied Germany to Austria-Hungary in the Balkans, where Habsburg and Russian interests clashed. The treatment of Russia in 1878 and the Lombardverbot of 1887 prepared the Franco-Russian link, and French hostility never ended.
Domestic success: he created national unity, a common currency (the mark, 1873), a central bank (the Reichsbank) and the first national social insurance scheme.

Domestic limit: the Kulturkampf and the Anti-Socialist Law failed, and both the Catholic Centre and the SPD grew stronger. The Reichstag stayed weak, and he left his successors an unreformed constitution.

Contemporary view: in 1890 Germans saw a great statesman who had made Germany one of the strongest states in Europe, and foreign observers respected him as a master diplomat; the British magazine Punch's 'Dropping the Pilot' cartoon (1890) shows how large he loomed.
Later view: historians stress the flaws he left behind, a divided society and a fragile alliance system that depended on him.

To follow the alliances after 1890 you need to know what they replaced. Bismarck had built a web of agreements to keep France isolated, and his successors let part of it drop, which opened the way for new groupings.

French hostility to Germany after Germany annexed Alsace-Lorraine in 1871 (the wish for revenge, called revanche) was the fixed point of European diplomacy, so Bismarck's aim was to keep France without allies.

Bismarck's alliances were the Dual Alliance of 1879 (Germany and Austria-Hungary), the Triple Alliance of 1882 (with Italy added) and the secret Reinsurance Treaty of 1887 (Germany and Russia, for three years). Together they kept France isolated and avoided a war on two fronts.
Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in March 1890 and began a 'new course' in foreign policy. Leo von Caprivi became Chancellor (1890-94).

In 1890 Caprivi and Friedrich von Holstein (a senior Foreign Office official) let the Reinsurance Treaty lapse. They thought it inconsistent with the Dual Alliance and harmful to relations with Britain.
Letting the treaty go left Russia with no German link and no friends, which is why it looked elsewhere. This was the first step in the break-up of Bismarck's balance of power.

Russia, left without a German partner, and France, still isolated since 1871, had a shared interest in finding a friend. Their agreement ended France's isolation and was a real military alliance, unlike the later ententes.
French banks began making large loans to Russia from 1888, which gave the two countries a financial link before any political one.
A French naval squadron visited Kronstadt (Russia's naval base) in July 1891, and in August 1891 the two powers agreed a political understanding to consult each other if war threatened.

A military convention was signed in August 1892 and ratified by an exchange of letters completed in January 1894. It was secret and defensive, aimed at the Triple Alliance powers, so each ally was protected without attacking anyone.

Its terms: if France was attacked by Germany, or by Italy supported by Germany, Russia would attack Germany; if Russia was attacked by Germany, or by Austria-Hungary supported by Germany, France would attack Germany.
Both would also mobilise (call up their armies) if any Triple Alliance power mobilised, which meant a crisis involving one Triple Alliance member could draw in both allies.

Because of this, Germany now faced the danger of a war on two fronts, the very risk Bismarck had worked to avoid, and this later shaped the Schlieffen Plan (Germany's war plan against France and Russia).
French investment in Russian railways and industry cemented the alliance. It lasted until the Russian revolution and Russia's exit from the war in 1917-18.

Britain had long avoided permanent peacetime alliances, a policy called 'splendid isolation'. By 1900 that policy was costing it more than it gave, so Britain began to settle quarrels with its imperial rivals and to find partners.

Isolation lost its value because European opinion was hostile to Britain during the Boer War, and because Germany was starting to build a large navy that threatened British sea power. Joseph Chamberlain, the Colonial Secretary, sought an alliance with Germany in 1898-1901, but the talks failed.
The Anglo-Japanese Alliance (1902) gave Britain support in the Far East against Russia, so it could keep more of its navy nearer home. It was renewed in 1905 and 1911.
Théophile Delcassé, French foreign minister 1898-1905, was the French architect of an agreement with Britain, and Edward VII's visit to Paris in May 1903 helped warm opinion.

The Entente Cordiale was signed on 8 April 1904 by Lord Lansdowne (British Foreign Secretary) and Paul Cambon (French ambassador in London). France accepted Britain's position in Egypt and Britain accepted France's in Morocco.
It also settled disputes over the Newfoundland fisheries, West Africa, Siam, Madagascar and the New Hebrides, so it removed the colonial quarrels that had made the two powers rivals.

The Entente was not an alliance, because neither promised to fight for the other. It tightened over time: secret Anglo-French military staff talks began in 1906, and in 1912 a naval arrangement concentrated the French fleet in the Mediterranean and the British fleet in the North Sea and Channel.
Britain's quarrels with Russia in Asia were the last big obstacle to a grouping against Germany. Settling them completed the Triple Entente, which stood opposite the older Triple Alliance.
Russia had been weakened by defeat by Japan in 1904-05 and both Russia and Britain were worried about Germany, which is why they were ready to compromise.
The Anglo-Russian Convention (31 August 1907) was agreed by Sir Edward Grey (Foreign Secretary) and Alexander Izvolsky (Russian foreign minister).
Its terms: Persia was divided into a Russian zone in the north, a British zone in the south-east and a neutral zone between. Afghanistan was a British sphere, and both promised to keep out of Tibet.

The Triple Entente of Britain, France and Russia was therefore a loose understanding with no common military commitment. It faced the formal Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy, which had been renewed in 1887, 1891, 1902 and, for the last time, 1912.

The Triple Alliance was weaker than it looked because Italy was unreliable. In 1902 the Prinetti-Barrere agreement secretly promised France that Italy would stay neutral if France was attacked, and in 1911-12 Italy fought the Ottoman Empire for Libya.

From about 1905 the blocs hardened. Germany spoke of 'encirclement' (being surrounded by hostile powers), while Britain and France feared German ambitions, so each crisis looked like a test of strength between the blocs.
In short, the balance of power had changed from Bismarck's flexible system, built around Germany, to two armed camps.

From about 1880 to 1914 European states rushed to take colonies and spheres of influence (areas where one power claimed special rights). Historians call this the New Imperialism and ask first what economic motives drove it.
It differed from earlier empire-building in its speed, its scale, the number of powers taking part, and its targets, mainly Africa and China. It also spread beyond Europe, to the USA and Japan.
The second industrial revolution (the spread of industry using steel, electricity and chemicals) created demand for raw materials and markets, which is why industrial states looked overseas.
Industrial states needed raw materials such as rubber, cotton, palm oil, copper, gold and diamonds, and later oil.
They also wanted protected markets, because tariffs rose in Europe from the late 1870s, and outlets for investment overseas.

The British economist J.A. Hobson, who reported on the Boer War for the Manchester Guardian, argued in Imperialism: A Study (1902) that surplus capital and underconsumption (too little buying power) at home drove capitalists to invest overseas and so drove empire.
Lenin, in Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (written 1916, published 1917), called imperialism the last stage of capitalism, leading to war between capitalist states.
Historians dispute the theory. Germany's colonies took a tiny share of its trade and investment, and much British investment went to the USA and Latin America, outside the empire.

Profit was only one reason, and for many states not the main one. Strategy, prestige, religion and ideas of racial superiority also pushed governments and public opinion towards empire, and new technology made it practical.

Strategic: states sought naval bases, coaling stations and secure routes. Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 to protect the Suez Canal (opened 1869), the route to India, and then moved to control the Nile valley to keep that route safe.

Nationalist: colonies were seen as a mark of Great Power status, and the popular press, colonial societies and public opinion cheered each acquisition. After defeat in 1871 France sought compensation overseas under Jules Ferry (Prime Minister 1880-81 and 1883-85), who promoted expansion in Tunisia (1881) and Indochina (Tonkin).

Missionary and humanitarian: churches wanted to spread Christianity and end the slave trade. The Scottish missionary David Livingstone (died 1873) and the explorer H.M. Stanley, who found him in 1871, made Africa known to the public.

Ideological: Social Darwinism applied the phrase 'survival of the fittest', coined by Herbert Spencer (1864), to nations and races, so rule over others was justified as natural. Related was a belief in a duty to 'civilise' other peoples, France's mission civilisatrice.
Kipling's poem 'The White Man's Burden' (1899), written about the USA in the Philippines, expressed this duty to civilise.

Technology made conquest possible: quinine against malaria, steamships, railways, the telegraph and breech-loading rifles, and the Maxim gun (the first fully automatic machine gun, invented by Hiram Maxim in 1884) gave Europeans an overwhelming military advantage.
Competition fed on itself, which is why even poor land was claimed. Once one power claimed territory, others annexed land before they could be shut out, even where the land was of little value.
Africa was the main prize of the New Imperialism. In about thirty years almost the whole continent was divided, and a conference in Berlin gave the process its rules.

In 1880 only about a tenth of Africa was under European control, mostly coastal areas such as Algeria, the Cape and Senegal; by 1914 about nine tenths of the continent had been taken (textbook estimates).
The scramble was triggered by Leopold II's claims on the Congo, France's advance in West Africa and its protectorate over Tunisia (1881), and Britain's occupation of Egypt in 1882.

The Berlin Conference (15 November 1884 to 26 February 1885) was called by Bismarck with French agreement. Fourteen states attended, including the USA and the Ottoman Empire. Do not confuse it with the Congress of Berlin of 1878, which dealt with the Balkans.

Its General Act required powers to notify each other of claims and to show effective occupation (real control, at first of coasts), and declared free trade in the Congo basin and free navigation on the Congo and Niger rivers.
During the conference the powers recognised the claim of Leopold's association to the Congo; the Congo Free State was proclaimed afterwards, in 1885.

No African ruler took part. The Conference did not itself divide Africa, but it made the partition faster and gave it a legal shape, because anyone could now claim land by occupying it and giving notice.
Once the rules were set, the powers had competing plans. Where plans crossed they risked war, and where they could, they traded claims by agreement.

Britain's aim was a belt of territory from the Cape to Cairo under British rule. Its leading backer was Cecil Rhodes, a mining magnate (diamonds and gold) who founded the British South Africa Company in 1889 and was Prime Minister of the Cape Colony 1890-96; Rhodesia was named after him.
France sought an east-west belt linking its West African lands with Djibouti on the Red Sea. The two plans crossed at Fashoda in 1898.
Germany, a latecomer, took South West Africa, Togo, Cameroon and German East Africa (1884-85). Italy took Eritrea and Italian Somaliland and, in 1911-12, Libya. Portugal held Angola and Mozambique.
Disputes were often settled by compromise. In the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty (1 July 1890) Britain gave Germany the North Sea island of Heligoland and Germany recognised British control of Zanzibar.
Africans resisted, for example Ethiopia, under Emperor Menelik II, defeated Italy at the Battle of Adwa (1 March 1896), which kept it independent.
By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia were independent African states.
The Congo shows the New Imperialism at its worst. Its ruler was a king acting as a private owner, and the system he set up brought a public scandal that forced change.
Leopold II, King of the Belgians 1865-1909, founded the International African Association in 1876, and Stanley worked for him in the Congo from 1879.
The Congo Free State was proclaimed in 1885 as Leopold's personal state, not a Belgian colony, on promises to end slavery and keep free trade.
From the 1890s Africans were forced to collect wild rubber under quotas, because demand for bicycle and later motor-car tyres made it very profitable. This is known as the 'red rubber' system.
Failure to meet quotas was punished by taking women as hostages, flogging with the chicotte (a whip), cutting off hands, and burning villages.

The Force Publique, the colonial army of African soldiers under European officers, enforced the system. The population fell by millions from violence, disease, flight and famine, because the system destroyed villages and food supplies, but estimates vary widely.

E.D. Morel, a shipping-company clerk in Liverpool, noticed that ships brought rubber and ivory from the Congo but carried back mostly guns and ammunition. This suggested forced labour, and he campaigned on it.
Roger Casement, an Irish-born British consul, wrote a report on the Congo published in 1904. Morel, with Casement, founded the Congo Reform Association in 1904.

Writers helped the campaign: Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness (1899) drew on his own Congo journey of 1890, and Mark Twain wrote King Leopold's Soliloquy (1905). Under international pressure Belgium annexed the colony in 1908 as the Belgian Congo, and Leopold died in 1909.
In Asia the powers competed less for conquest than for ports, trade and influence, and China was the main target because it was too weak to resist. Two newer powers, the USA and Japan, joined in.

In South-East Asia France formed French Indochina in 1887 (Vietnam and Cambodia, with Laos added in 1893). Britain annexed Upper Burma in 1886 and extended control over Malaya; the Dutch held the East Indies.
Japan defeated China in the Sino-Japanese War (1894-95) and won Taiwan (Formosa). In the Triple Intervention of 1895 Russia, France and Germany forced Japan to give back the Liaodong peninsula.

The powers then scrambled for concessions (1897-98). Germany seized Kiaochow (Jiaozhou) in 1897 after two German missionaries were killed, and leased it in 1898; Russia leased Port Arthur, Britain Weihaiwei and France Guangzhouwan (1898-99).
Each claimed a sphere of influence: Russia in Manchuria, Germany in Shandong, Britain in the Yangtze valley and France in the south.

The USA defeated Spain in the Spanish-American War (1898) and took the Philippines, Guam and Puerto Rico. In 1899 its Secretary of State, John Hay, sent the Open Door notes asking for equal trading rights for all in China.

The Boxer Rising (1899-1901) was a Chinese uprising against foreigners and Christians. The foreign legations (embassies) in Beijing were besieged from June to August 1900 and relieved by an eight-nation force of Britain, France, Germany, Russia, Japan, the USA, Italy and Austria-Hungary.

Japan began to modernise after the Meiji Restoration of 1868, building a strong army and navy. It defeated Russia in the Russo-Japanese War (1904-05, ended by the Treaty of Portsmouth), the first time an Asian power beat a European Great Power in modern times.
The defeat turned Russia's attention back to the Balkans and Europe, contributed to the revolution of 1905, and opened the way to the 1907 Entente with Britain.
Fashoda was the sharpest colonial clash between two European powers in this period. It nearly caused war between Britain and France, but it ended in a settlement that led towards friendship.
Britain had occupied Egypt in 1882 and treated the whole Nile valley as its sphere, while France wanted an east-west belt across Africa, so the two plans collided on the Upper Nile.
In July 1898 Captain Jean-Baptiste Marchand's small French expedition reached Fashoda on the Upper Nile in Sudan.
Kitchener defeated the Mahdist army at Omdurman on 2 September 1898, then reached Fashoda in September with a much larger force. Both sides refused to withdraw and war was feared.
France agreed to withdraw in November 1898. Delcassé judged that France could not risk war with Britain's navy; France was isolated and facing the Dreyfus Affair at home.
An Anglo-French agreement of March 1899 set the boundary between the two spheres: the Nile valley British and the area west of it French.
Fashoda was the worst Anglo-French crisis of the period, but it showed the danger of colonial clashes and convinced both sides to settle disputes, which led to the 1904 Entente Cordiale.
Britain's war against the Boer republics was a colonial war that damaged Britain's reputation in Europe. It exposed how few friends Britain had, which helped push it out of isolation.

The Boer republics were the Transvaal (South African Republic, under President Paul Kruger) and the Orange Free State. Gold found on the Witwatersrand in 1886 drew in Uitlanders (foreign, mostly British, settlers in the Transvaal, who were denied the vote), and this led to disputes with Britain.

The failed Jameson Raid (December 1895 to January 1896), an armed incursion into the Transvaal led by Rhodes's associate Leander Starr Jameson, soured relations, and Rhodes resigned as Cape Prime Minister. Wilhelm II's Kruger telegram of January 1896, congratulating Kruger, caused outrage in Britain.
The war began on 11 October 1899. The Boers won early successes, including Black Week in December 1899 (three British defeats) and sieges of Ladysmith, Kimberley and Mafeking.
Britain sent large reinforcements under Lord Roberts, and from late 1900 under Kitchener. Mafeking was relieved in May 1900, and the Boers turned to guerrilla war (small raids and ambushes).

From 1900, and especially under Kitchener, the British burned Boer farms and moved Boer civilians into concentration camps. Over 20,000 Boer civilians died in them, most of them children. Black Africans were held in separate camps where many thousands died (figures uncertain).
Emily Hobhouse exposed the camps. The Treaty of Vereeniging (31 May 1902) made the Transvaal and Orange Free State British colonies.

The war showed Britain's isolation and aroused hostility in Europe, damaged British prestige and military reputation, and pushed Britain to end splendid isolation. Hobson's critique of imperialism arose from it.
At home it fed popular excitement: when Mafeking was relieved in May 1900 there were wild celebrations in London (Mafeking night).
Morocco was one of the last independent states in Africa. When France moved to control it, Germany tried to test the new Entente, and the result was the opposite of what Germany wanted.
The 1904 Entente gave France a free hand in Morocco. Germany aimed to test or break the Entente, to win compensation, and to assert its say in colonial questions.
Wilhelm II landed at Tangier on 31 March 1905 and declared support for the Sultan's independence. This was a challenge to France.
German pressure forced Delcassé to resign in June 1905.
The crisis ended at the Algeciras Conference (January to April 1906). France and Spain were given the policing of Morocco's ports, and France's influence over Morocco's finances was recognised.
It was a diplomatic defeat for Germany, because Germany was supported only by Austria-Hungary, while Britain and Russia backed France.
The crisis strengthened the Entente: British and French generals began secret staff talks in 1906, so a colonial settlement became closer to a quasi-alliance.
Five years later France tightened its hold on Morocco and Germany challenged it again. This time Britain's warning showed how closely it now stood by France.
In May 1911 French troops entered Fez. Alfred von Kiderlen-Wachter, the German foreign secretary, directed German policy.
The German gunboat Panther arrived at Agadir on 1 July 1911. Germany demanded compensation.
David Lloyd George, Chancellor of the Exchequer, gave the Mansion House speech on 21 July 1911, warning Germany that Britain would not be pushed aside.

The crisis was settled by a Franco-German agreement on 4 November 1911: Germany accepted French control of Morocco in return for a strip of the French Congo added to Cameroon. The Treaty of Fez (30 March 1912) made Morocco a French protectorate.
Many Germans saw the settlement as a humiliation because Germany had gained only a strip of the Congo. It drew Britain and France closer, and the Anglo-French naval arrangement followed in 1912.
Italy seized the moment, for example, to attack the Ottoman Empire in September 1911.
Colonial rivalry did not stay overseas. It shaped relations between the Great Powers, the mood of public opinion and even the way governments counted the cost of empire.
Imperial rivalry produced crises that raised tension and caused war scares between Great Powers: Fashoda, the Boer War and Morocco.
It was also settled by compromise: Heligoland-Zanzibar (1890), Fashoda (1899), and the agreements of 1904 and 1907. These colonial settlements became the basis of the ententes.

It changed the balance of power, so alignments shifted. Britain moved from isolation into the Entente, and Germany's clumsy colonial diplomacy, such as its challenges in Morocco, left it more isolated.
It fed nationalism, jingoism (aggressive patriotism) and militarism at home, through the popular press, celebrations such as Mafeking night (1900), and demands for bigger navies and armies.
Economic effects were mixed. Colonies supplied raw materials and returns on investment, but they often cost more than they earned: Germany's colonies took a tiny share of its trade.
Humanitarian opinion reacted. The Congo and Boer-camp scandals showed that public opinion could expose and restrain abuses.
Examiners want a judgement with both sides. Colonial quarrels created friction, but they were mostly resolved, so the question is how much they mattered beside Europe's own rivalries.
For tension: imperial rivalry created crises (Fashoda, the Boer War and Morocco) that raised tension and made Britain and Germany suspicious of each other.
Against: imperial agreements also reduced tension, as the Entente Cordiale and the Anglo-Russian Entente show; the powers were often able to settle colonial quarrels by compromise.
For: the Moroccan crises hardened the blocs, turning the Entente Cordiale from a colonial settlement into a quasi-alliance.
Against: colonial disputes were mostly settled peacefully, so war in 1914 came from the Balkans and Europe's own alliance system rather than from colonial clashes.
Contemporaries differed: Germans blamed British and French encirclement for their insecurity, while the British and French blamed German pressure for the Moroccan crises.

Hobson and Lenin, writing from different positions, saw capitalism and imperialism as an underlying cause of war. Later historians see imperialism as one factor alongside alliances, militarism and nationalism.
On the alliance system, it helped keep the balance of power and deter war by making each side cautious, but it also tied powers to each other, so that a local crisis could become a general war.

To judge Wilhelm II's policies you need to know what he inherited: a constitution that gave the Kaiser great power, a cautious foreign policy that he rejected, and a world in which Britain ruled the seas.

Under the 1871 constitution the Kaiser appointed and dismissed the Chancellor, was supreme commander of the armed forces and directed foreign policy, so a strong-willed Kaiser could in theory rule personally.

The Reichstag (the elected parliament, chosen by universal male suffrage) voted laws and the budget, so every Navy Law and every naval tax needed a Reichstag majority, however much the Kaiser wanted a fleet.

Bismarck called Germany a satiated power after 1871, meaning it wanted no more territory in Europe. He kept France isolated, and Germany's first colonies date only from 1884–85, so his policy was cautious and centred on Europe.
Wilhelm II forced Bismarck to resign in March 1890 (the resignation letter was dated 18 March and accepted on 20 March). This gives the contrast with Weltpolitik, the later policy of world ambitions.

Britain was an island empire that depended on sea trade and imported food, so it treated naval supremacy as a matter of survival. The two-power standard, set by the Naval Defence Act of 1889, required the Royal Navy to be at least equal to the next two largest navies combined.
Britain stayed out of alliances in a policy called splendid isolation, and its first peacetime alliance of this era was with Japan in January 1902.
Europe was already divided into two blocs: the Triple Alliance of 1882 (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the Franco-Russian alliance (a military convention in 1892, an alliance in 1894).

Naval terms: a battleship (or capital ship) is the heaviest warship and a cruiser is lighter and faster. A battle fleet is built to fight a decisive battle in home waters, whereas a cruiser fleet protects trade and colonies overseas.
Wilhelm II was Kaiser from 1888 to 1918. His family ties, his disability and his restless temperament shaped how he ruled and why he loved the navy.

He was born in Berlin on 27 January 1859, the eldest son of Crown Prince Frederick (later Frederick III) and Victoria, the eldest daughter of Queen Victoria, which made him her grandson. A breech birth damaged his left arm, which stayed withered and shorter.
1888 was the year of the three emperors. Wilhelm I died on 9 March, Frederick III reigned 99 days and died on 15 June, and Wilhelm II became Kaiser that day, aged 29.
Do not confuse the three rulers: Wilhelm I was Kaiser from 1871 to 1888, Frederick III only in 1888, and Wilhelm II from 1888 to 1918.
He was energetic, intelligent, impulsive, theatrical, militaristic and easily influenced, so his enthusiasms could swing quickly and his public words often embarrassed his ministers.

His feelings about Britain mixed love and hate. George V and Tsarina Alexandra (the wife of Nicholas II) were his first cousins, and Nicholas II was a more distant relative, while he admired the Royal Navy but resented British power.
His passion for the navy was long-standing: Queen Victoria made him an honorary Admiral of the Fleet of the Royal Navy in 1889, and he attended the Spithead naval review that year.

Contemporaries were divided. Nationalists and navalists admired him as the symbol of Germany's rise, abroad he was regarded as erratic and a threat (foreign cartoonists drew him as a menace), and after 1908 he was criticised at home too.
Wilhelm wanted to rule himself, which made a clash with the old Chancellor almost certain. After Bismarck went, a new course under Chancellor Caprivi changed German policy at home and abroad.

Wilhelm's aim was personal rule (Persönliches Regiment): to govern himself rather than through a strong Chancellor. He forced Bismarck to resign in March 1890, a moment Punch marked with John Tenniel's cartoon "Dropping the Pilot".
