How far he really achieved personal rule is debated, because the Reichstag held the budget and his own changeable moods undermined his control.
His Chancellors were Caprivi (1890–94), Prince Hohenlohe-Schillingsfürst (1894–1900), Bernhard von Bülow (1900–09) and Theobald von Bethmann Hollweg (1909–17).

The new course (Neuer Kurs) was Caprivi's policy of 1890–94, not Weltpolitik. Abroad, the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia was not renewed in 1890, and the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty with Britain (1 July 1890) gave Germany Heligoland and Britain Zanzibar.
At home Wilhelm began by easing the Anti-Socialist Law, which lapsed on 30 September 1890, and sponsored the workers' protection law of 1891 (Sunday rest, limits on child and women's labour).
Caprivi's trade treaties of 1891–94 lowered tariffs on grain, which angered the agrarians (the landowners who wanted grain protected from foreign competition).
The SPD kept growing, so Wilhelm then turned against it, and Caprivi fell in 1894.
Wilhelm liked to act as his own diplomat, but his impulsive words and private deals repeatedly damaged Germany's image. Three separate indiscretions, and one failed treaty, show the pattern.
First came the Kruger telegram of 3 January 1896, which angered British opinion because it congratulated the Boer president on defeating the Jameson Raid into the Transvaal.

Second was the Hun speech, given on 27 July 1900 to troops leaving Bremerhaven for China. He told them to give no quarter and to make the name German feared as the Huns had made theirs, which damaged Germany's image abroad.

Third was the Daily Telegraph interview, published on 28 October 1908. He said most Germans were hostile to Britain but that he was its friend, and claimed he had sent Queen Victoria a plan for the Boer War.
He also said the fleet was aimed at the Far East, which offended Japan as well as Britain.

There was uproar in the Reichstag and press across all parties. Bülow did not defend him, Wilhelm promised in November 1908 to respect his constitutional responsibilities, and he suffered a nervous collapse. He then withdrew from many public roles.
He never fully trusted Bülow again, and Bülow resigned in July 1909. The direct cause was the defeat of his finance reform, but the loss of the Kaiser's trust meant he had no support to carry on.
Wilhelm also practised personal diplomacy through the Willy-Nicky letters and telegrams, written in English, to Nicholas II.

In July 1905 the two men signed the Treaty of Björkö, a defensive alliance, on Nicholas's yacht. It was never put into effect because the Russian government and Bülow objected, which shows how limited personal diplomacy was.
Wilhelm's last years of real influence run from the war council of 1912 to defeat in 1918. Historians still argue about how far he controlled events and how much blame he carries.
On 8 December 1912 Wilhelm met his army and navy chiefs, Moltke and Tirpitz, without the Chancellor, after a British warning that Britain would not stand aside if France were attacked.

Moltke said war the sooner the better, Tirpitz asked for more time for the navy, and no decision for war was recorded. Röhl and Fischer's followers treat the meeting as evidence of planning, while others, such as Clark, see bellicose talk without consequence.
In July 1914 he gave Austria-Hungary the blank cheque (5–6 July).

He lost the army's confidence in autumn 1918. Chancellor Prince Max of Baden announced his abdication in Berlin on 9 November 1918, he crossed into the Netherlands on 10 November, and he abdicated formally on 28 November.
He lived at Doorn in the Netherlands from 1920 and died there on 4 June 1941.

He was a participant, not a bystander: he chose Tirpitz and Bülow and backed the fleet throughout. Yet he worked within pressures from nationalist groups, industry and the military, so he both shaped events and was shaped by them.
John Röhl (a three-volume biography, 1993–2008) argues that Wilhelm exercised genuine personal rule and bears heavy responsibility for 1914.

Christopher Clark (Kaiser Wilhelm II, 2000, and The Sleepwalkers, 2012) portrays him as erratic and often sidelined, with responsibility shared among all the Great Powers, while Fritz Fischer's school places German leadership at the centre of 1914.
Weltpolitik, meaning world policy, was the attempt to turn Germany from a European power into a world power. It grew from economic need, domestic politics and national pride.

Weltpolitik was the attempt from about 1897 to make Germany a world power through colonies, trade, influence and a battle fleet, as opposed to Bismarck's Europe-centred (continental) policy. It is usually dated from 1897, when Bülow and Tirpitz were appointed.
In January 1896, at the 25th anniversary of the Reich, Wilhelm said the German Empire had become a world empire. In 1898 at Stettin he declared "Our future lies on the water."

Economic causes: by 1900 Germany had overtaken Britain in steel production, and by 1914 its merchant fleet was second only to Britain's. A growing industry needed markets, raw materials and secure sea routes, and feared being shut out as Britain, France and Russia expanded.

Sammlungspolitik (the politics of rallying together), associated with Johannes von Miquel, the Prussian finance minister, from 1897, aimed to unite industrialists, landowners and the middle classes behind the monarchy and against the SPD.

Social imperialism is a historians' term, used by Wehler and others, for using overseas expansion to divert domestic discontent. Conservatives and many liberals hoped imperial success would unite the classes behind the monarchy and distract from the SPD.
Pressure groups pushed the policy: the Colonial Society (founded 1887), the Pan-German League (founded 1891, named the Pan-German League from 1894) and the German Navy League (founded April 1898).

Nationalism in Germany meant pride in the new Reich and a belief that a great nation needed colonies, world influence and a fleet. Germany felt late to empire and resented the empires of Britain and France.
Social Darwinist ideas (that nations compete like species and only the strong survive) made rivalry between nations seem natural.
Weltpolitik was carried out through a series of moves between 1896 and 1903. Each gave Germany little, but each alarmed another power.

Bernhard von Bülow was appointed Foreign Secretary in June 1897 (formally in October) and was Chancellor from 17 October 1900 to July 1909. In his Reichstag speech of 6 December 1897 he said Germany wanted to put no one in the shade but demanded "a place in the sun".

On 3 January 1896 Wilhelm sent the Kruger telegram, congratulating President Paul Kruger of the Transvaal on defeating the Jameson Raid (29 December 1895 to 2 January 1896) without appealing to the help of friendly powers, as it was reported. British press and public were outraged.

Two German Catholic missionaries were murdered in Shandong province, China, on 1 November 1897. German ships seized Kiaochow Bay, with the port of Tsingtao, that month, and a 99-year lease was signed in March 1898.

In the Boxer rising of 1900 the German minister in Peking, Baron von Ketteler, was killed in June. Field Marshal von Waldersee commanded the international relief force, which arrived after Peking had already been relieved.

In 1899 Germany bought the Caroline, Mariana (except Guam) and Palau islands from Spain. Samoa was partitioned that year between Germany and the USA, with Britain withdrawing in return for compensation elsewhere.
In October and November 1898 Wilhelm toured the Ottoman Empire (Constantinople, Jerusalem and Damascus), and at Damascus he declared himself the friend of the world's Muslims.

The Baghdad Railway had a preliminary concession in 1899 and a full convention in 1903. It was meant to tie the Ottoman Empire to Germany and rival British and Russian influence in the Middle East, so both powers were suspicious; it was still unfinished in 1914.
The balance of power means that no single state or bloc is strong enough to dominate. Weltpolitik brought Germany small gains but alarmed every other power, so it weakened Germany's own position.

Britain had traditionally opposed any power dominating the Continent and treated naval supremacy as its own security. Germany's growing power, and later its fleet, threatened both, which pushed Britain towards France and Russia.

Talks between Joseph Chamberlain, the British Colonial Secretary, and Germany in 1898–1901 for an Anglo-German alliance came to nothing. Bülow and Holstein thought Britain would have to pay a higher price later, so they did not press for agreement.
Britain then turned to Japan (the alliance of January 1902) and France (the Entente Cordiale of April 1904) instead.

Wilhelm's visit to Tangier on 31 March 1905 began the first Moroccan crisis. At the Algeciras Conference of 1906 Germany was isolated, backed only by Austria-Hungary, so the result was humiliation and a stronger Entente.

In July 1911 Germany sent the gunboat Panther to Agadir, Morocco. After Lloyd George's Mansion House speech (July 1911) warned Germany, it accepted part of the French Congo in November 1911 in return for recognising French control of Morocco.
Germans came to believe that Britain, France and Russia were hemming Germany in, a belief called Einkreisung (encirclement). Critics say German policy itself caused it.
In short, Germany's gains were small, but it alarmed every other power, pushed Britain into the Entente and left Germany relying on Austria-Hungary.

Before 1897 Germany's strength lay in its army and its navy was small. The decision to build a great battle fleet, taken in 1897-98, came from the Kaiser's enthusiasm, a book on sea power and a determined admiral.
Before 1897 the German navy was small and largely a coastal defence force, and its earlier leaders favoured cruisers. Germany's strength was its army.

Wilhelm was personally enthusiastic about a navy to rival Britain's. He admired the Royal Navy (he was an honorary British admiral from 1889 and attended the Spithead review that year) and wanted a fleet that matched Germany's new status.

Alfred Thayer Mahan, a US naval officer, argued in The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1660–1783 (1890) that national greatness depended on a strong battle fleet and command of the sea. Wilhelm said he was devouring it and had copies placed on his warships.

Alfred von Tirpitz was appointed State Secretary of the Imperial Navy Office (Reichsmarineamt) in June 1897 and held the post until March 1916. His memorandum of June 1897 named Britain as the most dangerous naval enemy.

He called for a battle fleet concentrated in the North Sea, aimed in practice at Britain, rather than a cruiser fleet for overseas, because only a fleet in home waters could threaten the Royal Navy where it was most vulnerable.
Wilhelm chose Tirpitz and backed the fleet throughout, so the Kaiser's enthusiasm and the admiral's plan reinforced each other.
Tirpitz needed a reason why a smaller fleet could still work, and reasons at home to win Reichstag money. His risk theory and his domestic aims explain how the fleet was designed and sold.

The risk theory (Risikogedanke) held that the fleet need not beat the Royal Navy, only be strong enough that a battle would cost Britain so much that it would be left exposed to other powers, France and Russia. Britain would therefore avoid war and treat Germany as an equal.

Tirpitz's target is often given as a ratio of about 2:3 against Britain, which the Kaiser and Tirpitz judged enough to make the theory work. He also hoped the fleet would win an alliance or colonial concessions from Britain.
The danger zone was the building period, when Britain might strike first before the fleet was strong enough. Germans feared a Copenhagen, after Britain's seizure of the Danish fleet in 1807.
The fleet was also a national project to rally the middle classes behind the Reich and isolate the SPD, an example of Sammlungspolitik and social imperialism.
The Navy Laws fixed the size of the fleet and the replacement of ships in law, so later Reichstags had to fund them and could not easily cut the programme.
The Navy Office's News Bureau organised press and lecture campaigns, and academic supporters who lectured and wrote for the fleet were called Flottenprofessoren (fleet professors).
The German Navy League (Deutscher Flottenverein), founded in April 1898 and funded in part by industrialists including Krupp, was a mass organisation promoting the fleet.
Industry gained from the programme: Krupp of Essen supplied armour plate and guns, and Blohm & Voss of Hamburg built warships, so heavy industry gained orders.
Germany turned the plan into law in 1898 and 1900. Britain at first reacted by reorganising its fleet rather than racing.
The First Navy Law, passed by the Reichstag on 26 March 1898, provided for 19 battleships, with cruisers and coastal armoured ships, to be built by 1904. Spending was fixed in law up to 1904.
The Second Navy Law (June 1900) doubled the battleship target to 38, to be reached over about twenty years, plus more cruisers.

German anger helped pass it. From late December 1899 to January 1900 the Royal Navy stopped and searched German mail steamers (Bundesrath, Herzog and General) off south-east Africa, suspecting contraband for the Boers during the Boer War.
The Bundesrath was stopped off Delagoa Bay on 29 December 1899, so the outrage that helped the Second Navy Law was German anger at Britain, not British anger at Germany.

The Admiralty's attention turned increasingly to Germany. Sir John Fisher, First Sea Lord from October 1904 to 1910, scrapped many obsolete ships, brought warships home from distant stations and concentrated them to face the North Sea, and British naval estimates grew.
Fisher's redeployment in 1904–05 was possible because the Anglo-Japanese Alliance of 1902 let Britain reduce its Far East fleet and the Entente Cordiale of 1904 settled disputes with France.

Invasion-scare literature spread British alarm: Erskine Childers's novel The Riddle of the Sands (1903) about a German invasion plan, and William Le Queux's The Invasion of 1910 (1906), serialised in the Daily Mail. A British Navy League had existed since 1894.
In 1906 a new British ship changed the race. Germany answered with more building, and by 1909 the race had become a public scare in Britain.
HMS Dreadnought was launched at Portsmouth on 10 February 1906 by Edward VII and completed in December 1906. She carried ten 12-inch guns, had steam turbines and reached a speed of about 21 knots.

Dreadnought became the name for all battleships of her type, and pre-dreadnought for older ones, which she made obsolete. This cut Britain's existing lead but also gave Germany a chance to compete on equal terms.
However, Britain still had a head start in building dreadnoughts and a far larger fleet overall, so the Dreadnought did not put Germany level with Britain.

Germany answered with its own dreadnoughts. SMS Nassau, its first, was launched in March 1908. The supplementary law (Novelle) of 1906 added large cruisers and provided for widening the Kiel Canal so that dreadnoughts could use it.
The 1908 law cut the life of a battleship from 25 to 20 years, so Germany would build four capital ships a year for 1908–11. The widened Kiel Canal reopened in June 1914.
In 1908–09 a naval scare broke out in Britain over fears that Germany was building faster than announced. The public demanded eight new dreadnoughts with the slogan "We want eight and we won't wait."

Asquith's Liberal government, with Reginald McKenna as First Lord of the Admiralty, agreed to eight dreadnoughts in the 1909–10 programme (four at once, four more later). Britain had decided to out-build Germany at any cost.
Lloyd George's 1909 People's Budget had to pay for both the navy and social reform, so the race strained Britain's finances too.
Both governments tried to talk their way out of the race, but each wanted the other to move first. After 1912 Germany gave up the race in practice.

Britain proposed arms limitation at the Second Hague Conference (1907), but Germany refused to discuss it. In the talks of 1906-08 and up to 1911, Germany wanted a British neutrality promise before limiting building, while Britain wanted limits first.
Bethmann Hollweg, Chancellor from July 1909, sought a naval and political agreement in 1909–11 but none was reached.

Richard Haldane, British Secretary of State for War, visited Berlin on 8–11 February 1912, arranged through the shipping magnate Albert Ballin and the banker Sir Ernest Cassel. Germany asked for a pledge of British neutrality if Germany became involved in a war.

Britain would promise only not to join an unprovoked attack on Germany, and wanted building slowed first. Neutrality would have left France and Russia to face Germany alone. Wilhelm also announced a new Navy Law in his Reichstag speech of 7 February 1912, just as the mission began.

The 1912 supplementary law added three more battleships and a third active battle squadron. Winston Churchill, First Lord of the Admiralty from October 1911 to May 1915, told the Commons in March 1912 that Britain would keep a 60 per cent superiority in dreadnoughts over Germany.

Churchill proposed a naval holiday (a pause in building) in 1912 and again in 1913, but Germany did not accept. In 1912 British battleships moved from the Mediterranean to home waters while France concentrated its fleet in the Mediterranean; the Grey-Cambon letters (November 1912) promised consultation, not alliance.

From 1912–13 Germany shifted money to the army, which received large increases in 1912 and 1913. In 1913 Tirpitz told the Reichstag budget committee that Germany accepted a 16:10 ratio in battleships in Britain's favour, and in August 1914 Britain had a clear lead in dreadnoughts.

A limited detente followed in 1913–14: an agreement on the future of the Portuguese colonies was initialled in 1913 and a Baghdad Railway agreement in June 1914. Mistrust remained, and the naval and military preparations of each side continued.
The fleet failed to achieve its aims abroad and it also cost Germany heavily at home. The money problem fed straight into party politics.

The fleet cost vast sums and absorbed resources that could have gone to the army, at a time when Germany's land frontiers were threatened by France and Russia. The navy took a growing share of the defence budget until 1912.
Rising naval spending raised the national debt and taxation and led to the Reich finance crisis of 1908–09.

In June 1909 Bülow's finance reform, which included an inheritance tax, was defeated in the Reichstag by the Conservatives and the Centre Party. Bülow resigned in July 1909, having lost the Kaiser's trust.
The dispute sharpened the quarrel between the Conservatives, who opposed the inheritance tax, and the left. The SPD and left-liberals also opposed the cost of the fleet.
The fleet rallied the right for a time, but it did not halt the SPD's growth: in the January 1912 Reichstag election the SPD won 110 seats and became the largest party.
After 1912 Germany could no longer afford to compete in both navy and army, so the army received large increases in 1912–13 and the naval race slackened.
The fleet failed in its main aim. It did not deter Britain; it turned a possible partner into an opponent, and in the war itself it achieved little.

The fleet turned a possible partner into an opponent. Britain's agreements with Japan (1902, which let it reduce its Far East fleet), France (1904, settling Egypt and Morocco) and Russia (1907, covering Persia, Afghanistan and Tibet) formed, with the Franco-Russian alliance, the Triple Entente.
Historians debate how far the navy, rather than colonial issues, caused these agreements. The 1904 Entente was mainly a colonial settlement, so the navy's role is disputed.

The fleet did not deter Britain. It helped make Britain regard Germany as the main threat and bound Britain more closely to France, so Britain declared war on 4 August 1914, after Germany invaded Belgium.

In the war the navy stayed mostly in harbour. At Jutland (31 May-1 June 1916) Britain lost more ships and men, about 6,000 British and about 2,500 German dead, but the German High Seas Fleet returned to port and rarely came out again, and the British blockade was never broken.

Many sailors resented the fleet's inactivity and harsh discipline. The mutinies at Wilhelmshaven (late October 1918) and Kiel (from 3 November 1918) helped start the revolution that overthrew the Kaiser.
The interned German fleet was scuttled at Scapa Flow on 21 June 1919 on the orders of Admiral Ludwig von Reuter.
People at the time judged the fleet very differently depending on where they stood. A document question will often turn on spotting the writer's side.

British contemporaries regarded the German fleet as a challenge to the Empire. The Admiralty, the public and the press spread alarm, including invasion scares and the Daily Mail, and the British Navy League added to it.
German nationalists were proud of the fleet and presented it as essential for the defence of overseas trade, and they explained Britain's hostility through the encirclement view.
The SPD and left-liberals objected to the cost of the fleet.
The two nations' views were mirror images: Germany saw a peaceful trading nation needing protection, Britain saw a fleet in the North Sea aimed at itself.
Historians disagree about why Germany built the fleet and what it caused. Match each historian to a clear view.

Eckart Kehr (Battleship Building and Party Politics, German 1930) argued that the fleet served the domestic interests of industry and the middle classes, a view known as the primacy of domestic politics (Primat der Innenpolitik).

Volker Berghahn (Der Tirpitz-Plan, 1971) argued that Tirpitz aimed to strengthen the monarchy against the Reichstag and to deter or blackmail Britain. Social imperialism is a term associated mainly with Wehler, not with Berghahn.

Fritz Fischer (Griff nach der Weltmacht, 1961; in English Germany's Aims in the First World War, 1967) and War of Illusions (German 1969) argued that Germany's leaders deliberately sought world power, first by the fleet and then by war. Critics say he exaggerated the coherence of German aims.

Paul Kennedy (The Rise of the Anglo-German Antagonism, 1860–1914, 1980) argues that the naval race was central to the breakdown of Anglo-German relations, though rooted in wider economic and political rivalry.
Niall Ferguson (The Pity of War, 1998) argues that Britain had clearly won the naval race by about 1912, so it was not a direct cause of war in 1914.
Other historians doubt that the race caused the war, because Anglo-German relations were improving in 1913–14 and the Entente was formed first because of colonial concerns.
A judgement answer needs achievements set against limits. These paired points give the balance examiners reward.
Achievement: Germany built the world's second-largest navy in under two decades, winning national pride and support for the Kaiser.
Limit: the fleet never came near matching Britain, and the risk theory failed because Britain out-built Germany and made friends with its rivals.
Achievement: Weltpolitik won Kiaochow, the Pacific islands, Samoa and the Baghdad Railway concession, and gave Germany a voice in world affairs.
Limit: the gains were small and unprofitable, the Morocco crises ended in humiliation, and Germany became more isolated, relying on Austria-Hungary.
Domestic achievement: the fleet and the colonial movement helped rally the right for a time, bringing Conservatives and National Liberals together behind the government.
Domestic limit: its cost caused the 1908–09 finance crisis and did not halt the SPD's growth, since the SPD became the largest party in 1912.
Contemporary view: German contemporaries regarded Weltpolitik and the fleet as a necessary national project, while British contemporaries regarded them as a direct threat.

Later view: most historians judge Weltpolitik and the fleet a strategic mistake that helped make the Triple Entente and brought Britain into the war, though some stress that Anglo-German relations were improving by 1914.
To see why a quarrel with a small state could start a world war, you first need the setting. The Ottoman Empire was losing control of the Balkans, and two larger empires wanted to fill the gap.
The Eastern Question was the problem of what would happen as Ottoman power in the Balkans declined. The decline left a vacuum, so Austria-Hungary and Russia both wanted to fill it and became rivals.

Austria-Hungary was a multinational empire of Germans, Hungarians, Czechs, Poles, South Slavs and others. Any nationalist movement therefore threatened its survival, because each nationality could claim the right to leave.
Pan-Slavism was the idea that Russia, the largest Slav and Orthodox Christian power, should protect and lead the Slavs of the Balkans. This gave Russia a reason to take Serbia's side.

By 1907 Europe was split into two blocs: the Triple Alliance of 1882 (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the Triple Entente (Britain, France, Russia). A Balkan quarrel could therefore draw in several Great Powers.
Russia was weakened by defeat in the Russo-Japanese War (1904-05) and by the revolution of 1905. This is why it was less able to stand up to Austria-Hungary and Germany in the crises that followed.
Serbia was a young state whose independence was won through the Great Powers, and it stayed economically tied to its larger neighbour. Its nationalism soon pulled against that tie.
The Congress of Berlin (1878, the Balkan settlement, not the African Berlin Conference of 1884-85) recognised Serbia's full independence from the Ottoman Empire and gave it extra territory.
At the same Congress Austria-Hungary was given the right to occupy and administer Bosnia-Herzegovina, which stayed under nominal Ottoman rule. This set up the later crisis over Bosnia.

Serbia became a kingdom in 1882 under Milan Obrenović. It was a client of Austria-Hungary (dependent on it and under its influence), whose market took Serbia's main exports of pigs and other livestock.

Serbian nationalists, like other South Slav nationalists, dreamed of uniting the South Slavs (Serbs, Croats, Slovenes and the Slavs of Bosnia) in one state. This is why Serbia and Austria-Hungary were bound to clash.

Millions of South Slavs lived inside Austria-Hungary, so a strong Serbia that attracted them threatened to break up the empire. Vienna saw Serbian nationalism as a danger to its survival, not just a foreign matter.
A fulcrum is the pivot a lever turns on. After 1903 Serbia turned from Vienna to Russia, and from then on its disputes with Austria-Hungary pulled the bigger powers in behind it.

In June 1903 army officers murdered King Alexander Obrenović and Queen Draga in Belgrade; Dragutin Dimitrijević (Apis) was one of the conspirators. Peter I of the Karadjordjević dynasty became king. Sources differ on the day, so give the month only.
The new regime turned away from Vienna and towards Russia and France. The Obrenović dynasty had been pro-Austrian; the Karadjordjević dynasty was pro-Russian.

Russia saw itself as protector of the Balkan Slavs and wanted to stop Austria-Hungary dominating the Balkans. It also wanted its warships to be able to pass through the Straits (the Bosporus and Dardanelles).

The Pig War began in 1906, when Austria-Hungary closed its border to Serbian livestock. It wanted to punish Serbia for a customs agreement with Bulgaria (1905) and for ordering artillery from France rather than from Austria-Hungary.
Serbia found other markets, so the Austrian economic hold weakened and Serbia became less dependent on Vienna. Sources disagree on when the Pig War ended, so give no end date.

Franz Conrad von Hötzendorf, Chief of the Austro-Hungarian General Staff from 1906 (briefly removed 1911-12), repeatedly urged preventive war against Serbia. His fear was that a strong Serbia could encourage the empire's Slav nationalities to leave.
Serbia was a fulcrum because a small state's quarrel with Austria-Hungary drew in Russia, its protector, and through the alliances Germany (behind Austria-Hungary) and France (behind Russia).
In 1908 Austria-Hungary turned its occupation of Bosnia into outright annexation. This humiliated Russia and Serbia, who both resolved not to back down again.

Austria-Hungary had occupied and administered Bosnia-Herzegovina since 1878, though it remained under nominal Ottoman rule. The Young Turk revolution of July 1908 in the Ottoman Empire raised the chance that Bosnia would be reclaimed, so Austria acted.

In September 1908 the Austrian foreign minister, Count Aehrenthal, met the Russian foreign minister, Izvolsky, at Buchlau in Moravia. They discussed a swap: Austria would annex Bosnia, and Russia would gain support for opening the Straits to its warships.
Austria announced the annexation on 6 October 1908, before Russia had won anything on the Straits, so Russia felt cheated. Bulgaria declared full independence at the same time.

Serbia regarded Bosnia as having a large Serb population, so it was outraged. It protested, prepared for war and demanded compensation. The Narodna Odbrana (National Defence), a nationalist society, was founded in 1908 in reaction to the annexation.

In March 1909 Germany demanded that Russia accept the annexation and drop its support for Serbia. Russia, still weak after the war with Japan and the revolution of 1905, gave way, and Serbia formally accepted it that month.
The crisis humiliated Russia and Serbia and left both determined not to back down again. Russia accelerated its rearmament, and Austria-Hungary and Germany drew closer.
Germany's backing of Austria-Hungary in the Balkans set a precedent, which is why it mattered again in July 1914.
The Balkan states used the Ottomans' weakness to grab land, and then fought over the spoils. Serbia emerged much bigger, which alarmed Austria-Hungary.
In 1912 the Balkan League was formed by Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece and Montenegro, with Russian encouragement. Italy's war for Libya (1911-12) had exposed Ottoman weakness, so the League struck.
The First Balkan War began in October 1912 and was ended by the Treaty of London in May 1913. The League defeated the Ottomans, who lost most of their European lands.

A conference of ambassadors met in London in 1912-13 under Sir Edward Grey, the British Foreign Secretary. It created an independent Albania, backed by Austria-Hungary and Italy, which denied Serbia the Adriatic port it wanted.

The League then quarrelled over the spoils. In the Second Balkan War (June to August 1913) Bulgaria attacked Serbia and Greece and was beaten, with Romania and the Ottomans joining against it. The Treaty of Bucharest followed in August 1913.
Over the two wars Serbia almost doubled its territory, gaining Kosovo (in the First Balkan War) and much of Macedonia (confirmed at Bucharest).

In October 1913 an Austro-Hungarian ultimatum forced Serbia to withdraw its troops from Albania, and Serbia complied. A stronger Serbia, backed by Russia and unsatisfied over the Adriatic, alarmed Austria-Hungary further, and Conrad pressed for war.
Conference diplomacy had contained the wars, but Austria-Hungary concluded that next time it must fight. Russia's prestige now depended on Serbia, so it too would find it hard to give way.
Serbian nationalism now had a violent wing. Officers in Serbia armed young Bosnians, and one of them killed the heir to the Habsburg throne.

The Black Hand (official name Unification or Death) was a secret society founded in May 1911 by Serbian army officers. Its leader was Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević, known as Apis, head of Serbian military intelligence by 1914. It aimed at a Greater Serbia.
Young Bosnia was a movement of young South Slav nationalists in Bosnia, mostly Bosnian Serbs. They were armed and trained with Black Hand help because both wanted to end Habsburg rule.
Do not confuse the groups. The Black Hand was a secret society of officers (1911), the Narodna Odbrana was a public nationalist society (1908), and Young Bosnia was Princip's group of Bosnian youths.

Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Habsburg throne, visited Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 after army manoeuvres. That day is Vidovdan (St Vitus's Day), the anniversary of the Serbian defeat by the Ottomans at Kosovo in 1389.

In the morning Nedeljko Čabrinović threw a bomb that missed the Archduke's car. Later the car took a wrong turn and stopped near Gavrilo Princip, who shot Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg. Both died.
The assassins were arrested. Princip, born in 1894, was 19, so he was under 20 and could not be executed. He was sentenced to 20 years and died of tuberculosis in prison in 1918.
The conspirators' pistols and bombs came from Serbia via the Black Hand. How much the Serbian government, headed by Prime Minister Nikola Pašić, knew of the plot is disputed.

Austria-Hungary decided to use the murder to crush Serbia, but first sought Germany's backing. Count Berchtold was the foreign minister, while Count Tisza, the Hungarian Prime Minister, at first opposed war. Count Hoyos was sent to Berlin on 5 July 1914.
In the five weeks after Sarajevo each step made the next harder to avoid. First Austria-Hungary secured German support, then it set Serbia terms designed to be refused.

On 5 July Wilhelm II promised Austria-Hungary support, and on 6 July Chancellor Theobald von Bethmann Hollweg confirmed it. This 'blank cheque' was unconditional support in whatever action it took against Serbia. Berlin hoped for a short, localised war.
French President Raymond Poincaré and Prime Minister René Viviani visited St Petersburg from 20 to 23 July 1914. This reaffirmed French support for Russia, which encouraged Russia to stand by Serbia.

On 23 July Austria-Hungary delivered an ultimatum (a final demand with a deadline) to Serbia: ten demands and a 48-hour deadline. They included the suppression of anti-Austrian propaganda and organisations, and Austrian officials to take part in the inquiry inside Serbia. It was meant to be refused.

On 25 July Serbia accepted most demands but refused Austrian officials a part in the judicial inquiry on Serbian soil. Serbia began mobilising the same day, and Austria-Hungary broke off relations that day.

On 26 July Grey proposed a conference, but Germany declined. The Tsar and Kaiser also exchanged the 'Willy-Nicky' telegrams in late July, but mediation failed. Sazonov was the Russian foreign minister.
Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914, three days after breaking off relations, and Belgrade was shelled from 29 July.
Once Austria-Hungary was at war with Serbia, the alliances and military timetables turned a Balkan war into a European one within a week.

Russia ordered partial mobilisation (against Austria-Hungary only) on 29 July and general mobilisation on 30 July. Germany demanded on 31 July that Russia stop, and treated general mobilisation as a cause of war.
Germany and France ordered general mobilisation on 1 August. Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August, and Austria-Hungary declared war on Russia on 6 August.

Alfred von Schlieffen, German Chief of the General Staff until 1906, drew up the Schlieffen Plan and Helmuth von Moltke the Younger modified it in 1914. It aimed to defeat France in about six weeks through Belgium before Russia was fully mobilised, then turn east.
This is why Russian mobilisation meant war in the west. Germany had to strike France first and could not wait, so it would attack through Belgium whether or not France was the aggressor.
Germany sent Belgium an ultimatum on 2 August and Belgium refused on 3 August. Germany declared war on France on 3 August and invaded Belgium on 4 August.

Britain was a guarantor of Belgian neutrality under the Treaty of London of 1839 and used the invasion of Belgium as its reason. It was also concerned for the balance of power and had the Entente with France. Its ultimatum to Germany expired at 11 pm on 4 August 1914.

Bethmann Hollweg called the 1839 treaty 'a scrap of paper' to the British ambassador, Sir Edward Goschen, on 4 August 1914. Britain's entry made it a European war and, through the empires, a world war.
Italy declared neutrality in early August 1914 because the Triple Alliance was defensive and Austria-Hungary had not consulted it. It entered the war on the Entente side in 1915.

The Second International was a federation of socialist and labour parties. Its members believed that workers had more in common across borders than with their own ruling classes, and it looked strong on paper before 1914.

Marxism holds that society is divided by class struggle and that workers of all countries share interests. Its aim is to replace capitalism with socialism. The SPD (the Social Democratic Party of Germany) was Germany's Marxist party.

The Second International was founded in Paris in July 1889, the centenary of the French Revolution, as a federation of socialist and labour parties. It had a permanent International Socialist Bureau in Brussels from 1900. It believed in workers' solidarity across borders.

The German SPD was the largest and most respected party. In the 1912 Reichstag election it won 110 seats and became the biggest party. Other members were French socialists under Jean Jaurès, British Labour, and Russian and Polish Marxists such as Lenin and Luxemburg.

Its parties were divided over reform or revolution. Eduard Bernstein, an SPD revisionist, wanted socialism by gradual reform, while revolutionary Marxists such as Luxemburg and Lenin rejected this. August Bebel led the SPD until his death in 1913.
They also disagreed over how to stop a war. Jaurès and Keir Hardie supported a general strike against war, but the SPD leaders opposed making it binding.

The Stuttgart Congress (1907) resolved that socialists should do everything to prevent war and, if it broke out, to work to end it quickly and use the crisis to hasten the fall of capitalism. The last part came from an amendment by Luxemburg, Lenin and Martov.
An extraordinary Congress at Basel on 24-25 November 1912, held during the First Balkan War, issued a manifesto against war. It warned governments that war could bring revolution.
The International's pledges to stop war were put to the test in the last days of July 1914. They failed, and the failure is the most examined part of its story.

The International Socialist Bureau met in Brussels on 29-30 July 1914, and Jaurès spoke there. He was shot dead in a Paris café by a nationalist, Raoul Villain, on 31 July 1914, which removed the leading French advocate of a general strike.

On 4 August 1914 the SPD Reichstag group voted for war credits (money for the war), in the party truce known as the Burgfrieden. Karl Liebknecht was the only Reichstag deputy to vote against war credits, in December 1914.

In France the union sacrée (sacred union) brought socialists such as Jules Guesde and Marcel Sembat into the government in August 1914. In Britain Labour largely backed the war, and Ramsay MacDonald resigned as leader of the Labour MPs.

It collapsed because nationalism proved stronger than class loyalty. German socialists feared repression and Tsarist Russia, French socialists feared German invasion, and ordinary workers were patriotic themselves. There had also been no agreed plan to stop a war.
Socialists split into those who backed their governments, pacifists, and a revolutionary minority including Luxemburg, Liebknecht and Lenin. This minority opposed it as an imperialist war.

Anti-war socialists met at Zimmerwald in Switzerland (September 1915) and at Kienthal (April 1916). The split helped produce the communist parties and the Third (Communist) International, the Comintern, founded in Moscow in March 1919.

Luxemburg was a Marxist theorist, speaker and journalist on the left of the SPD, a participant in the International's debates and a leading opponent of the war. She was a witness to the SPD's vote of 1914 and to the Russian Revolution.

She was born on 5 March 1871 in Zamość, Russian-ruled Poland, into a Jewish family. A childhood hip condition left a limp that did not stop her speaking in public. She studied at the University of Zurich (doctorate 1897).

In 1893 she co-founded the Social Democracy of the Kingdom of Poland (later the SDKPiL), opposing Polish independence as a goal because she put class before nation. In 1898 she moved to Germany, gained citizenship by a marriage of convenience, and joined the SPD on its left.

In Reform or Revolution (1899) she attacked Bernstein's revisionism. She went to Warsaw in December 1905 to join the Russian revolution and was arrested in March 1906. Her pamphlet The Mass Strike, the Party and the Trade Unions (1906) argued for the mass strike as a revolutionary weapon.

She taught at the SPD party school in Berlin (1907-14) and wrote The Accumulation of Capital (1913), an economic theory of imperialism. At the Stuttgart Congress in 1907 she helped amend the anti-war resolution with Lenin and Martov.

For anti-war speeches in 1913 urging workers not to take up arms against other nations she was tried and sentenced to a year in prison in February 1914; she began the sentence in February 1915. The SPD's vote for war credits on 4 August 1914 horrified her.

With Karl Liebknecht, Franz Mehring and Clara Zetkin she formed the International group (1915), which became the Spartacus group (1916). In prison from February 1915 to February 1916, and again from July 1916 in 'protective custody' until November 1918, she wrote the Junius pamphlet (1915, published 1916), condemning the war.

She welcomed the Russian Revolution of 1917 but criticised Bolshevik dictatorship and the closing the Constituent Assembly: 'Freedom is always the freedom of the one who thinks differently.' She co-founded the KPD (30 December 1918-1 January 1919), thought the January 1919 rising premature but backed it once begun.

Freikorps soldiers murdered her and Liebknecht in Berlin on 15 January 1919 and threw her body in the Landwehr Canal. To the SPD leaders and conservatives she was a dangerous agitator, and enemies called her 'Red Rosa'; supporters saw a courageous internationalist, Lenin's praise was mixed. Historians admire a major Marxist thinker who opposed both militarism and dictatorship, but debate her practicality.
The war had no single cause. Long-term pressures made Europe dangerous, and a chain of Balkan events from 1908 to 1914 set them off.
Alliances: Europe was divided into the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente, so a local quarrel could bring in all the Great Powers.
Militarism and war plans: the powers built large conscript armies and had mobilisation timetables that left little time for diplomacy. The Schlieffen Plan required a swift attack on France.
Naval and colonial rivalry: the Anglo-German naval race and the Moroccan crises poisoned relations between the powers.

Nationalism: South Slav nationalism threatened Austria-Hungary, French revanche (revenge) aimed to recover Alsace-Lorraine, which Germany annexed in 1871, and pan-Slavism and pan-Germanism pushed Russia and Germany towards confrontation.

Short-term causes were the Bosnian crisis (1908-09), the Balkan Wars, the assassination at Sarajevo, the blank cheque, the ultimatum, the mobilisations and Belgium. Each made the next crisis more dangerous.
The Balkans were where Austrian and Russian interests met. Neither could back down without losing Great Power status, which is why a regional quarrel could not be left alone.
Each government acted out of a fear as well as an aim. Pairing what each did with what it feared shows why none backed down.
Austria-Hungary issued the ultimatum and declared war on Serbia because it feared that Slav nationalism would break up the empire and cost it Great Power status.
Germany gave the blank cheque and hoped for a short, localised war. It feared encirclement, and the Schlieffen Plan meant it could not wait once Russia mobilised.
Russia backed Serbia and mobilised, because it feared losing prestige and status after the humiliation of 1909.
France reaffirmed support for Russia in the visit of 20-23 July and mobilised, because it feared a German attack and wanted to keep its ally.
Britain declared war on 4 August after the invasion of Belgium, because it was concerned for the balance of power and had the Entente with France.
Serbia accepted most of the ultimatum but refused Austrian officials on its soil, because it feared losing its sovereignty. It had begun mobilising on 25 July.
Who started the First World War has been argued over since 1914. Examiners reward paired views and a reasoned conclusion, not a one-sided verdict.

Contemporary German view: Germany was encircled and forced into a defensive war by Russian mobilisation. Entente view: Germany and Austria-Hungary were aggressors (blank cheque, ultimatum, Belgium). This fed the war-guilt clause, Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles (1919).
Interwar view: David Lloyd George, in his War Memoirs, said the nations 'slithered over the brink' into war. This suggests shared responsibility rather than one guilty power.

Fritz Fischer, a German historian, argued in Germany's Aims in the First World War (German edition 1961) that German leaders deliberately risked or sought war for world-power aims. His view raised an enduring debate about German war aims.
Christopher Clark, in The Sleepwalkers: How Europe Went to War in 1914 (2012), argues that all the powers, Serbia included, share responsibility. He stresses contingency and Balkan politics.

Austria-Hungary's decision to crush Serbia, Serbian nationalism, Russian backing of Serbia, German backing of Austria and military planning were all links in the chain. Historians differ on the weight of each, so weigh them.

Could organised workers have stopped the war? On paper the International was strong, as Stuttgart (1907) and Basel (1912) showed. It failed because nationalism was stronger, there was no agreed plan and workers feared repression.

Luxemburg's achievements were her theory, her consistent opposition to war and the founding of the KPD. Her limits were a small following, the failed rising and her murder before she could shape events.

The war of 1914-1918 set two coalitions against each other and spread across the globe and the oceans, which is why it is called a world war. Knowing who was on which side, and a few army terms, makes the battles that follow easier to read.

The Allies (the Entente) began as France, Russia and Britain. They were joined by Italy in May 1915, Romania in August 1916 and the USA on 6 April 1917, which fought as an associated power, meaning alongside the Allies but without a formal alliance.
The Central Powers were Germany and Austria-Hungary, joined by the Ottoman Empire (which entered in October-November 1914) and Bulgaria (October 1915).

A world war is a war fought on several continents and at sea that draws in empires, whole economies and populations. This war shows it through its many fronts: Western, Eastern, Italian, Balkan, Middle East, the colonies and the sea.

A front is the line where two armies face each other, and an offensive is a large attack. A salient is a bulge in the line surrounded on three sides, so its defenders can be shelled from three directions.
A division is a large army unit of many thousands of men, and a corps is a still larger unit made up of several divisions. BEF stands for British Expeditionary Force, Britain's army in France.
Casualties means every man an army loses: killed, wounded, missing and captured, not just deaths. This is why a figure for casualties is always larger than the figure for those killed.

All the Great Powers expected a short war. Germany's plan was to defeat France quickly by marching through Belgium and then turn on Russia, but the plan failed and by the end of the year the Western Front was a stalemate (a deadlock in which neither side can advance).

Germany invaded Belgium on 4 August 1914 and the Liege forts fell in mid-August. The Germans then swept through Belgium and northern France under the Schlieffen Plan, which the younger Moltke, German chief of staff, modified; the traditional view is that he weakened the right wing.
The British Expeditionary Force, a small professional army under Sir John French, fought its first major action at Mons on 23 August 1914. It then retreated alongside the French.

The First Battle of the Marne (5-12 September 1914), fought under the French commander Joffre, halted the Germans after they had come close to Paris. They fell back to the River Aisne and dug in, so the Schlieffen Plan had failed. Moltke was replaced by Falkenhayn.

Both sides then tried to outflank each other (get round the enemy's open end) in the race to the sea. This is why a line of trenches ran from the Belgian coast on the North Sea to the Swiss frontier by late 1914.

The First Battle of Ypres (October-November 1914) was a hard-fought defensive success for the British and French. The old regular BEF was largely destroyed, so Britain had to depend on volunteers from then on.
At Christmas 1914 troops in parts of the line took part in unofficial truces. The high commands forbade a repeat.

Once the armies dug in, the Western Front became a fixed network of earthworks that lasted for years. Trench warfare is fighting from such lines of trenches, and it shaped how millions of soldiers lived.

A trench system had a front line, support and reserve trenches behind it, and communication trenches linking them, so men and supplies could move without crossing open ground. Dugouts gave shelter underground.
Barbed wire and no man's land, the shell-torn ground between the opposing lines, kept the enemy at a distance, which is why a surprise attack was so hard to make.
Soldiers lived with mud, rats, lice, cold, and the constant danger of shelling and snipers. Wet conditions caused trench foot, a painful rotting of the feet from standing in water.
Shell shock, now called combat stress or post-traumatic stress, was a breakdown caused by prolonged bombardment and fear. It is one of the conditions to learn.
On the Western Front the weapons of defence were stronger than the means of attack. This is why battles produced very high casualties for small gains.
The machine gun and quick-firing artillery, together with barbed wire, made frontal attacks (charges straight at the enemy) very costly. Most battle casualties were caused by artillery.
Railways brought the defenders' reserves to a threatened point faster than attackers could advance across broken ground, so a breakthrough was usually sealed off before it could grow.
Attackers relied on long preliminary bombardments, which warned the enemy where the attack would come, churned up the ground and often failed to cut the wire.
From 1916 the creeping barrage, a curtain of shellfire that moved ahead of the infantry as they advanced, gave attackers more protection.
Poor communications added to the problem. Without radio at the front, commanders could not quickly learn what was happening or change orders, so a battle was hard to control once it began.
Both sides searched for a way to break the deadlock. New weapons helped, but none won the war alone, and by 1918 the answer lay in using them together.

Germany first used poison gas on a large scale at the Second Battle of Ypres on 22 April 1915, releasing chlorine against French and French colonial (Algerian) troops. Canadian troops were gassed in the same battle days later.
Phosgene followed from late 1915 and mustard gas from July 1917. Gas masks reduced its effect, so gas caused terror and suffering more than a breakthrough.

Britain first used tanks at Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916, during the Somme. They were slow and unreliable. At Cambrai (20 November 1917) about 400 were used together, a sign of what massed tanks could do.
Aircraft were used for reconnaissance and artillery spotting, then for fighter combat and bombing. Germany attacked Britain with Zeppelin raids from 1915 and Gotha bomber raids on London in 1917.

By 1918 both sides used combined arms, meaning different weapons working together. Germany developed stormtrooper infiltration tactics, in which small groups slipped past strong points, and the Allies coordinated tanks, aircraft, artillery and infantry.
After the stalemate set in, generals on both sides still believed a breakthrough was possible. When it did not come, the war turned into one of attrition.

A war of attrition is a struggle to win by wearing down the enemy's men and resources rather than by one decisive battle. Verdun, the Somme and Passchendaele are the main examples, and the blockade at sea was attrition by starvation.
In 1915 the Allies launched offensives at Neuve Chapelle (March), in Artois (French) and at Loos (September), and the Germans used gas at Ypres. None broke the line.

A shortage of shells, the shell scandal of May 1915, caused a political crisis in Britain. It helped bring a coalition government and a Ministry of Munitions under Lloyd George, so the army's needs changed British politics.
In 1916 Germany tried to win by hurting France where it would not retreat. The result was a long, costly battle.

Verdun lasted from 21 February to 18 December 1916. The German chief of staff Falkenhayn attacked the symbolically important French fortress, intending, according to his post-war account, to bleed France white.
Each side lost over 300,000 casualties, about 700,000 in total, and the French held.

General Petain took command in late February 1916. He rotated divisions through the battle so no unit was worn out, and supplies reached the front along the Voie Sacree (Sacred Way), the road from Bar-le-Duc.
Verdun became the symbol of French endurance, and the French held.
The Somme was a joint British-French offensive planned partly to relieve the pressure on Verdun. It became the most famous battle of the British Army in the war.
The Somme lasted from 1 July to 18 November 1916. A bombardment of about a week, from 24 June, was meant to destroy the German defences and wire before the infantry advanced.
On the first day the British suffered about 57,000 casualties, of whom about 19,000 were killed. It was the worst day in the history of the British Army, and the 57,000 are casualties, not deaths.
The Allied line advanced up to about 10 kilometres at the deepest point, and far less on most of the front. Total casualties were over a million across all armies, and German losses were also heavy.

It was the first big battle for Kitchener's volunteer Pals battalions, men who enlisted together from the same town. Heavy losses fell at once on particular towns, such as Accrington, home of the Accrington Pals.
Tanks were used for the first time at Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916.
Historians judge it as failure (the first-day losses and small gains) or as partial success, because it relieved Verdun, wore down the German army and taught the BEF.
Irish soldiers served in large numbers in the British Army, and two Irish divisions took part in some of the best-known battles of 1916 and 1917.
The 36th (Ulster) Division attacked at Thiepval on 1 July 1916, the first day of the Somme, so Irish units shared in its heaviest day.
The 16th (Irish) Division took Guillemont and Ginchy on 3 and 9 September 1916. Tom Kettle was killed at Ginchy on 9 September.
At Messines in June 1917 the two divisions fought side by side and took Wytschaete. Major Willie Redmond MP was killed there.
In 1917 the Allies tried again to break through. The year began with another costly failure and French collapse of morale, and then moved to more limited British operations.
Nivelle's offensive on the Chemin des Dames began on 16 April 1917. It failed with heavy losses, and mutinies spread through many French divisions in May-June 1917.
Petain replaced Nivelle in May 1917 and restored morale by improving conditions and avoiding big attacks, and the French army recovered.
At Arras, from 9 April 1917, the British attacked. The Canadian Corps captured Vimy Ridge on 9-12 April.
At Messines on 7 June 1917, 19 mines exploded under the ridge. It was a limited success and came before Passchendaele.
The British offensive in Flanders in the summer of 1917 became the most notorious battle of the war, but Cambrai later showed what tanks could achieve.

Passchendaele, also called the Third Battle of Ypres, ran from 31 July to 10 November 1917. Its aims were to break out of the Ypres salient and reach the Belgian coast and the German U-boat bases there.
Heavy rain and shell damage turned the ground to mud. Men and guns sank in it, so the advance slowed to a crawl and the final gain was only about 8 kilometres.
Canadian troops took the village of Passchendaele in November 1917, but the gain was so small for the cost that the battle became a symbol of waste.
At Cambrai on 20 November 1917, about 400 tanks attacked by surprise. The gains were mostly lost to a German counter-attack from 30 November.
On the Eastern Front the armies moved over far greater distances than in the west. Russia was large but poorly supplied, and German commanders exploited this.

Russia's invasion of East Prussia drew German troops east at the time of the Marne. At Tannenberg (26-30 August 1914) Hindenburg and Ludendorff destroyed the Russian Second Army under Samsonov and took about 90,000 prisoners.
At the Masurian Lakes in September 1914 the Germans defeated Rennenkampf's First Army.
The Central Powers broke the Russian line at Gorlice-Tarnow in May 1915, forcing a great Russian retreat from Poland and Galicia. Warsaw fell to Germany in August 1915.

The Brusilov Offensive, begun on 4 June 1916 against Austria-Hungary, was the most successful Allied attack of the year. It took many prisoners and forced Germany to move troops east, but it could not be sustained and Russia suffered very heavy losses.
Romania declared war on 27 August 1916 to join the Allies, but Germany and its allies largely overran it, and Bucharest fell in December 1916.
Defeat and strain at home brought Russia down. Its exit from the war freed Germany to turn west.

Defeats, losses, shortages and the failure of the Tsar's government led to the February Revolution of 1917 (March by the Western calendar). The Provisional Government that replaced the Tsar continued the war, but the Kerensky Offensive of July 1917 collapsed.

After the Bolsheviks seized power in October 1917 they signed an armistice with Germany in December 1917. By the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on 3 March 1918, Russia gave up Poland, the Baltic lands, Ukraine and Finland.
The treaty freed dozens of divisions for the West and so helped Germany's offensives of 1918, but Germany still kept large forces in the occupied east.

After the Ottoman Empire joined the Central Powers, Britain and France tried to knock it out quickly by attacking the Dardanelles, the narrow strait to Constantinople. The plan failed, and the campaign had lasting political and national effects.
The Ottoman Empire entered the war in October-November 1914. The naval attempt to force the Dardanelles came on 18 March 1915 and failed.

Landings followed on 25 April 1915 by British, French and ANZAC (Australian and New Zealand) troops, at ANZAC Cove and Cape Helles. The Royal Dublin Fusiliers and Royal Munster Fusiliers landed at V Beach, Helles.

The 10th (Irish) Division fought at Suvla Bay in August 1915. The campaign was stalemated, with the Ottoman commander Mustafa Kemal (later Ataturk) making his name there, and the troops were evacuated by 9 January 1916.
Gallipoli damaged Churchill, First Lord of the Admiralty, who had promoted it, and he left the Admiralty in May 1915.
It became a founding moment for Australian and New Zealand national identity, remembered each year as Anzac Day on 25 April.
The war reached well beyond France and Russia. These campaigns show why it was a world war.
Italy entered the war on the Allied side in May 1915 under the Treaty of London (April 1915), which promised it territory from Austria-Hungary. Eleven battles on the Isonzo brought little gain.

Italy suffered a disastrous defeat at Caporetto on 24 October 1917, then recovered on the Piave and won at Vittorio Veneto (October-November 1918). Do not confuse the 1915 Treaty of London with the 1839 treaty on Belgium.

In the Middle East the British fought the Ottomans in Mesopotamia, where Kut surrendered on 29 April 1916, and in Palestine. Allenby took Jerusalem in December 1917 and won at Megiddo in September 1918.
The Arab Revolt began in June 1916 under Sharif Hussein of Mecca, with T. E. Lawrence as British liaison officer, so Britain gained Arab help against the Ottomans.
Serbia was overrun in October-December 1915 after Bulgaria joined the Central Powers. The Allies kept a front at Salonika, and Bulgaria asked for an armistice on 29 September 1918.
Most German colonies were captured by the Allies early. German East Africa under Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck held out until he surrendered on 25 November 1918, after the armistice in Europe.
Britain's navy could not easily win a decisive battle, but it could strangle German trade.

Britain used its fleet to blockade Germany, stopping imports of food and raw materials. Germany suffered shortages, and the winter of 1916-17, the turnip winter, was especially severe. This was attrition at sea.

The German High Seas Fleet, built in the pre-war naval race, was cautious. The only major fleet engagement was Jutland (31 May-1 June 1916), between the British Grand Fleet under Jellicoe and Beatty and the German fleet under Scheer.
Britain lost 14 ships and about 6,000 men, and Germany 11 ships and about 2,500 men. The British fleet kept control of the North Sea and the German fleet remained mostly in port.
Unable to beat the Royal Navy on the surface, Germany turned to submarines (U-boats). The campaign nearly starved Britain but brought the USA into the war.
The liner Lusitania was sunk on 7 May 1915 off the south coast of Ireland, near the Old Head of Kinsale, Co. Cork. About 1,200 died, more than 120 of them American, which outraged American opinion.
As a result Germany restricted its campaign, giving the Sussex pledge in May 1916.

On 1 February 1917 Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare, sinking ships without warning, hoping to starve Britain into surrender within months. April 1917 was the worst month for Allied shipping losses, and Britain faced a serious food crisis.
Convoys, adopted from mid-1917, grouped merchant ships under naval escort, which made them harder for submarines to find and attack. Together with better anti-submarine methods they cut losses.
The campaign failed to knock Britain out of the war and it brought in the USA.
Mass war needed mass armies. Continental states already had conscription, which is compulsory military service, but Britain had relied on volunteers and had to change.
Germany, France, Russia and Austria-Hungary called up trained reservists under their pre-war systems of conscription.
In Britain, Kitchener, Secretary of State for War, raised over two million volunteers by the end of 1915, but losses grew and numbers fell.

The Military Service Act, passed in January 1916 and in force from 2 March 1916, conscripted unmarried men aged 18 to 41 because volunteers were no longer enough. It was extended to married men in May 1916.

Conscientious objectors, men who refused to fight on grounds of conscience, appeared before tribunals. About 16,000 claimed the status, and some were jailed while others were sent to non-combatant work.

The 1916 Act did not apply to Ireland. An attempt in April 1918 to extend conscription there caused the Conscription Crisis, with an anti-conscription pledge on 21 April and a one-day general strike on 23 April 1918. It was never enforced.
The USA introduced conscription through the Selective Service Act of May 1917. Germany passed the Auxiliary Service Law in December 1916, requiring men aged 17 to 60 to do war work.
Governments had to keep skilled workers in reserved occupations such as munitions, mines and railways, and women replaced many men.
The USA stayed neutral for nearly three years. Two German decisions in 1917 changed that.

Unrestricted submarine warfare sank American ships. The Zimmermann Telegram, sent in January 1917, was a secret German offer of an alliance to Mexico against the USA. British intelligence intercepted it and it was published in the American press on 1 March 1917.
Wilson asked Congress for war on 2 April 1917, and the USA declared war on Germany on 6 April 1917. Keep these two dates distinct.

General John J. Pershing commanded the American Expeditionary Forces, which arrived in strength during 1918. Their coming raised Allied morale and changed German calculations, because Germany could not match the new men and resources.
With Russia out, Germany had one chance to win before the Americans arrived. The offensive almost succeeded, but its failure left the German army exhausted.
Ludendorff's Spring Offensive (Kaiserschlacht) began on 21 March 1918 with Operation Michael. It made large gains and came close to Amiens, but did not break the Allied line.
Haig issued his backs to the wall order on 11 April 1918, calling on the British army to stand and fight because the line was under severe pressure.
Foch was given coordinating authority at Doullens on 26 March 1918 and made Supreme Allied Commander in April 1918, so the Allies at last had a unified command.
German troops were exhausted and short of supplies. The Allied counter-attack at the Second Battle of the Marne from 18 July 1918 turned the tide.
From August 1918 the Allies advanced almost continuously. Germany's allies collapsed one by one, and it asked for peace.

The Hundred Days began with the Battle of Amiens on 8 August 1918, which Ludendorff called the black day of the German army. Allied tanks, aircraft and artillery pushed the Germans back, and the Hindenburg Line was broken at the end of September.
On 29 September 1918 Ludendorff told the Kaiser that Germany needed an armistice. In early October Germany sent a note to Wilson asking for terms on the basis of the Fourteen Points.
Germany's allies had already collapsed: Bulgaria signed an armistice on 29 September, the Ottoman Empire on 30 October (Mudros) and Austria-Hungary on 3 November 1918.
The armistice was signed in a railway carriage at Compiegne at about 5 a.m. on 11 November 1918 and took effect at 11 a.m. Foch led the Allied delegation.
Military deaths are put at about 9 to 10 million, though some estimates are lower at about 8.5 million. Many more were wounded and civilian deaths ran into the millions.
Douglas Haig commanded the British Expeditionary Force in France from December 1915 until the end of the war. He is the most controversial British commander of the war.
Haig was born in Edinburgh in 1861 into the Haig whisky-distilling family. He studied at Oxford (Brasenose College) and Sandhurst, and became a cavalry officer in the 7th Hussars.
After Staff College he served in the Sudan (Omdurman, 1898) and the Boer War (1899-1902). In 1914 he commanded I Corps in the BEF at Mons, the retreat and First Ypres.

He led the First Army from December 1914, which fought at Neuve Chapelle (March 1915) and Loos (September 1915). He succeeded Sir John French as commander-in-chief in December 1915 and became field marshal on 1 January 1917.
His battles in 1916-17 were the Somme (1916) and Arras and Passchendaele (1917).

In 1918 he directed the defence against the Spring Offensive and issued his backs to the wall order on 11 April. He then led the Hundred Days, in which the BEF played the leading part and took many prisoners.
Haig believed in attrition and in a decisive breakthrough exploited by cavalry. His diary on the eve of the Somme shows confidence, but he also supported new weapons such as tanks.

He was a participant shaped by events. The need to support France (Verdun, the French mutinies), the strength of defences and poor communications, with no radio at the front, limited what any commander could do.
After the war he was made Earl Haig in 1919 and voted 100,000 pounds by Parliament. He was one of the founders and first president of the British Legion in 1921.
He supported the poppy appeal (the Haig Fund) for ex-servicemen and died on 29 January 1928, with huge public mourning at his funeral.
People judged Haig very differently in his own time and afterwards. The argument is the part of the topic examiners most like to set as a judgement.

Contemporaries divided. King George V and much of the army trusted him. Lloyd George distrusted him, thought his offensives wasteful and kept reserves in Britain over the winter of 1917-18. Ex-servicemen and the public mourned him in 1928.

Critics came first in memoirs. Lloyd George's War Memoirs, published in the 1930s, attacked him. Alan Clark's The Donkeys (1961) popularised the phrase "lions led by donkeys", a phrase about British soldiers and generals, not a quotation from Haig.
Clark presented the phrase as an exchange between German generals, but no such source has been found, and similar phrases were used of other armies before 1914.
Oh! What a Lovely War (stage 1963, film 1969) and Blackadder Goes Forth (1989) fixed the popular image of foolish generals.
Denis Winter (Haig's Command, 1991) and Gerard De Groot (a critical biography, 1988) portrayed Haig as a callous, unimaginative butcher.

Defenders such as John Terraine (Douglas Haig: The Educated Soldier, 1963) and Gary Sheffield (Forgotten Victory, 2001, and The Chief, 2011) argue that the BEF learned and improved its tactics, which won in 1918 under Haig.
Examiners reward a clear judgement that weighs strengths against limits. These paired points give the evidence for both sides.
Allied strength: the blockade, attrition, American troops and resources, and the combined-arms victory of 1918 wore down Germany's capacity to fight and broke its army.
Allied limit: the Western Front battles of 1915-17 produced casualties out of proportion to gains, and the Somme and Passchendaele became symbols of waste.
German success: Germany held the Western Front for four years, knocked Russia out of the war and nearly won in spring 1918.
German failure: the Schlieffen Plan failed in 1914, the U-boat gamble of unrestricted submarine warfare brought in the USA, and the army was exhausted by 1918.
Contemporary view: the troops and many officers criticised the high command. Later views range from Clark's donkeys to Sheffield's Forgotten Victory.
Judging Haig means weighing what he achieved against what he failed to avoid. A clear verdict, kept up throughout, is what examiners look for.
Achievements: victory in 1918, a record of adapting and learning new tactics, and loyalty to the coalition, which held the Allied alliance together.
Limits: the first day of the Somme, the mud of Passchendaele, over-optimism and slowness to stop failing attacks.
Contemporary view: trusted by George V and the army, distrusted by Lloyd George and mourned in 1928. Later view: the donkeys image against the learning curve argument that the BEF improved and won.
Many historians now accept that his attritional strategy was shaped by circumstances: strong defences, the need to support France and poor communications.

To understand the revolution and the peace, you first need to know who was fighting, why Germany was losing, and how Germany was governed. The old system collapsed because it had been built around a war that was now lost.

The war was fought between the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria) and the Allies (Britain, France, Russia until 1917, Italy from 1915 and the USA from 6 April 1917).

By 1918 Germany was losing. Russia had left the war by the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (3 March 1918), but the German spring offensive from March failed, and Allied counter-attacks began at Amiens on 8 August, which Ludendorff called the 'black day of the German army'.

American troops were arriving in large numbers, so Germany could not replace its losses. At home the British naval blockade had caused food shortages throughout the war, including the 'turnip winter' of 1916-17, so civilians were exhausted and hungry.

In the Kaiserreich (the German Empire) the Chancellor answered to the Kaiser, not to the Reichstag (the elected parliament). From 1916 the army leaders Hindenburg (Chief of the General Staff) and Ludendorff (First Quartermaster General) dominated government, so the army's failure discredited the whole system.

German socialism had split. The Majority SPD (Social Democratic Party; Ebert and Scheidemann) had backed the war; the Independent Social Democrats (USPD) broke away in April 1917; the Spartacists on the far left (Luxemburg and Liebknecht) wanted revolution.
Austria-Hungary was a multinational empire, and by 1918 its Czechs, Slovaks, Poles, South Slavs, Romanians and others increasingly wanted independence, which weakened it as the war went badly.

Germany's allies gave way one by one in autumn 1918, and the German army leaders then admitted they could not go on. This pushed Germany into asking for an armistice (an agreement to stop fighting) and into political change.
Bulgaria signed an armistice at Salonika on 29 September 1918. The Ottoman Empire followed with the armistice of Mudros on 30 October 1918, so Germany lost two allies in a month.

On 29 September 1918, at army headquarters in Spa, Ludendorff told the Kaiser and the government that Germany must seek an armistice at once. Allied attacks had broken into the Hindenburg Line (the main German defensive position in France) and Bulgaria had given up.
To please Wilson, the Kaiser appointed the liberal Prince Max of Baden as Chancellor on 3 October 1918. His government included Social Democrats (Scheidemann) and Centre Party members (Erzberger).
On the night of 3-4 October Germany asked Wilson for an armistice on the basis of the Fourteen Points.

Wilson's replies insisted that Germany must end its military autocracy (rule by the army and Kaiser), which encouraged calls for the Kaiser to go. The constitution was changed in late October (28 October) to make the Chancellor responsible to the Reichstag.
Ludendorff resigned on 26 October 1918, so the man who had demanded the armistice was gone before it was signed.

Austria-Hungary was defeated by Italy at the battle of Vittorio Veneto (late October to early November 1918) and signed the armistice of Villa Giusti on 3 November 1918, which came into force on 4 November.

Defeat turned into revolution within a fortnight. A naval order sparked a mutiny, the mutiny spread, and by 9 November the Kaiser's rule had ended and two rival republics had been proclaimed in Berlin.
At the end of October the naval command ordered the High Seas Fleet to sail for a last battle. Sailors at Wilhelmshaven refused.
A mutiny at Kiel, from 3 November, spread within days to ports and cities across Germany. The SPD sent Gustav Noske to Kiel on 4 November to regain control.

Sailors, soldiers and workers formed councils on the Russian model, local bodies that took over authority from the old officials. Kurt Eisner (USPD) declared a Bavarian republic in Munich on 7 November.
On 9 November, with a general strike and crowds in Berlin, Prince Max announced the Kaiser's abdication without his consent and handed the chancellorship to the Social Democrat Friedrich Ebert.

Two republics were proclaimed that day. Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed a parliamentary German republic from a window of the Reichstag, and Karl Liebknecht later proclaimed a 'free socialist republic' from the Berlin palace.
Wilhelm II crossed into the Netherlands on 10 November and signed a formal abdication on 28 November. He lived there until his death in 1941.

The armistice was signed at about 5 am on 11 November 1918 in a railway carriage in the forest of Compiègne, in force at 11 am. Matthias Erzberger of the Centre Party led the German delegation; Marshal Foch signed for the Allies.

Its terms: evacuate occupied France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Alsace-Lorraine; hand over large amounts of weapons, the submarines and much of the fleet; Allied occupation west of the Rhine with bridgeheads; Brest-Litovsk cancelled; blockade kept on until July 1919.

With the Kaiser gone, someone had to run Germany. Ebert's government had to decide whether to build a new order from the revolution or to keep the old institutions working, and its choices shaped the republic's weaknesses.

The Council of People's Representatives, the provisional government set up on 10 November 1918, had three Majority SPD members (including Ebert and Scheidemann) and three USPD members. It ruled until elections; the USPD members resigned on 29 December 1918.
Do not confuse it with the workers' and soldiers' councils, which were local bodies formed during the revolution.
The Ebert-Groener pact, made by telephone on 10 November: General Groener (Ludendorff's successor) pledged the army's support against Bolshevism, and Ebert's government respected officers' authority.

The pact helped the republic survive, because the army would defend order against the far left. It was also a weakness, because it left the old army, civil service and judiciary in place, still loyal to the old order rather than the republic.

The Stinnes-Legien agreement of 15 November 1918 was made between the industrialist Hugo Stinnes and the trade union leader Carl Legien. Employers recognised the unions and accepted the eight-hour day, which won workers' cooperation and helped to block revolution.
The central choice was between a council republic on the Russian model, which the far left wanted, and an elected parliament, which the SPD leaders wanted.
The split on the left turned violent in January 1919. The government used the army and volunteer units to crush the radicals, and this left a lasting bitterness on the left.

The KPD (Communist Party of Germany) was founded at a congress from 30 December 1918 to 1 January 1919 by the Spartacus League and other left-radical groups. They wanted a council republic like Russia's.
The trigger for the rising was the dismissal on 4 January 1919 of Emil Eichhorn, the USPD police chief of Berlin, whom the left saw as a defender of the revolution.
In the Spartacist or January rising (5-12 January 1919) radicals occupied newspaper buildings in Berlin, including the SPD paper Vorwärts.
It was crushed by government troops and Freikorps (volunteer units of ex-soldiers) under Gustav Noske, the SPD member of the government in charge of military affairs.
Luxemburg and Liebknecht were arrested and murdered by Freikorps officers in Berlin on 15 January 1919, so the KPD lost its leaders at once.
Eisner was assassinated on 21 February 1919. A Bavarian Soviet republic existed in Munich in April 1919 and was crushed by government troops and Freikorps in early May 1919.
Once the left was beaten, the SPD could hold elections and write a constitution. The republic was democratic, but it started with heavy handicaps.

In the National Assembly election of 19 January 1919 women voted nationally for the first time (votes for men and women over 20). The SPD was the largest party with about 38 per cent. The Weimar coalition was the SPD, the Catholic Centre Party and the German Democratic Party (DDP).
The Assembly first met at Weimar on 6 February 1919, away from Berlin's unrest. Ebert was elected Reich President on 11 February, and Scheidemann became head of the first government.
