The Weimar constitution was passed by the Assembly on 31 July 1919 and signed by Ebert on 11 August. The president was elected for seven years, there was proportional representation, and Article 48 gave emergency powers.

The 'stab in the back' (Dolchstoss) myth claimed that the army had not been beaten in the field but betrayed by socialists, Jews and revolutionaries at home. It was false, because the army leaders themselves had asked for an armistice. Hindenburg repeated it to a Reichstag committee in November 1919.
Nationalists called the politicians who accepted the armistice and the republic the 'November criminals', so the republic was tied in people's minds to defeat.
The Kapp Putsch of March 1920 showed the right's hostility: Wolfgang Kapp and Freikorps units seized Berlin and the army did not resist them. It was defeated within days by a general strike.

While Germany had a revolution, the Habsburg empire simply fell apart along national lines. It broke up in October and November 1918, before the peace treaties, and the treaties then confirmed what had happened.
Emperor Charles I issued a manifesto on 16 October 1918 offering to turn Austria into a federation of nationalities. It came too late, because the peoples now wanted independence.

Czechoslovakia declared independence in Prague on 28 October 1918, with Tomas Masaryk as its first president. A State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs was declared on 29 October, and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (later Yugoslavia) was proclaimed on 1 December.
Poland declared independence in November 1918 (11 November is its independence day; Jozef Pilsudski was its leader), and Hungary became a separate state.
Charles withdrew from state affairs in Austria on 11 November 1918. German-Austria proclaimed a republic on 12 November, and its assembly declared it part of the German republic.

Hungary was in turmoil. Bela Kun's Hungarian Soviet Republic (March to August 1919) ended after a Romanian invasion, when Romanian troops entered Budapest. Admiral Horthy then took power and became regent in 1920.
The Fourteen Points were Wilson's programme for a just peace. Germany asked for an armistice on their basis, so what they promised mattered when the Germans saw the treaty.

Wilson set out the Fourteen Points in an address to Congress on 8 January 1918, as a statement of American war aims and a basis for peace. It was partly a reply to the Bolsheviks, who had published the Allies' secret treaties and called for peace.

Points 1 to 5 called for open covenants (public agreements) of peace openly arrived at, freedom of the seas, removal of economic barriers (free trade), reduction of armaments, and an impartial adjustment of colonial claims in which the interests of the peoples concerned counted equally.
Points 6 to 8 dealt with the evacuation of Russia and Belgium and the return of Alsace-Lorraine to France.

Points 9 to 13 set Italy's frontiers on lines of nationality, called for autonomous development for the peoples of Austria-Hungary, and covered the Balkans and the Ottoman Empire (Turkish parts sovereign, others autonomous, the Dardanelles open). They also demanded an independent Poland with access to the sea.
Point 10 asked for 'autonomous development', not independence, for the peoples of Austria-Hungary. By 1918 Wilson came to back independence for the Czechoslovaks and South Slavs.

Point 14 called for a general association of nations to guarantee independence and territorial integrity (the right of a state to keep its borders) to great and small states alike. This became the League of Nations.

In the pre-armistice agreement (the Lansing note, 5 November 1918) the Allies accepted the Points as the basis of peace. Britain reserved its position on freedom of the seas, and the Allies demanded compensation for damage done to the civilian population.
Many Germans later believed that the harsher Treaty of Versailles broke this agreement.

The conference opened in Paris on 18 January 1919, the anniversary of the German Empire's proclamation in 1871. About thirty states took part, but the leaders of four of them took the decisions, and each had a different aim.

The defeated powers were excluded and Soviet Russia was not invited. A Council of Ten (two leading delegates each from the USA, Britain, France, Italy and Japan) took decisions at first, then the Council of Four (the Big Four) from March 1919. Commissions drafted the terms.
The Big Four were Woodrow Wilson (USA), David Lloyd George (Britain), Georges Clemenceau (France) and Vittorio Orlando (Italy).

Wilson wanted a just peace based on self-determination, with the League built into the treaty. He arrived in France on 13 December 1918 and was the first US president to travel to Europe while in office.
Clemenceau, French Prime Minister, nicknamed 'the Tiger', wanted security for France, which had been invaded in 1870 and 1914. He wanted a weak Germany, a Rhineland buffer and heavy reparations.
France at first wanted the Rhineland separated from Germany. It accepted occupation and demilitarisation of the Rhineland in return for a promised Anglo-American guarantee of French security.

Lloyd George, British Prime Minister, had won the general election of 14 December 1918 amid popular demands to make Germany pay and to try the Kaiser. He nevertheless wanted a peace that would not provoke revenge.

His Fontainebleau memorandum (25 March 1919) warned against a peace that would drive Germany to revenge or Bolshevism. He also wanted to protect British trade, empire and naval power, and to avoid French dominance in Europe.
Other states came to Paris with claims of their own, and most were disappointed. The Germans were given no chance to negotiate, which shaped how they saw the result.

Orlando wanted what the secret Treaty of London (April 1915) had promised Italy to bring it into the war: South Tyrol (Trentino to the Brenner), Trieste, Istria and much of Dalmatia. Fiume was not among the promises, but Italy claimed it as well.
Orlando left the conference in April 1919 over Fiume and returned in May. Italian nationalists, including Gabriele d'Annunzio, spoke of a 'mutilated victory'.
Japan, an ally, proposed a racial equality clause, which was rejected in April 1919. It received Germany's rights in Shandong (China).
Ireland's Sinn Fein sent Seán T. O'Kelly as Dáil Éireann's envoy to Paris in 1919 to ask for a hearing for Irish self-determination. Wilson and the Allies refused to admit the Irish case.
The terms were presented on 7 May 1919 to the German delegation, led by Foreign Minister Ulrich von Brockdorff-Rantzau. There was no negotiation: German counter-proposals were mostly rejected.
In June 1919 the Allies issued an ultimatum to sign or face renewed war, so Germany had no real choice.

The treaty was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, five years to the day after the assassination at Sarajevo. The Hall of Mirrors was also where the German Empire had been proclaimed in 1871, so the setting was deliberate.

Article 231, the war guilt clause, said that Germany accepted responsibility for itself and its allies for causing all the loss and damage suffered by the Allies in a war imposed on them by the aggression of Germany and its allies. It was the legal basis for reparations.
The word 'guilt' does not appear in Article 231; Germans called it the war guilt clause because they read it as blaming Germany alone.
In the west and north, Alsace-Lorraine went to France, Eupen and Malmedy to Belgium, and North Schleswig to Denmark after a plebiscite (a vote on a border) in 1920.

In the east, most of West Prussia and Posen went to Poland, forming the Polish Corridor to the Baltic, which separated East Prussia from the rest of Germany. Plebiscites were held in Upper Silesia and in East Prussian districts.
Danzig became a Free City under League of Nations protection, so it was neither German nor Polish, and Memel was placed under Allied control (Lithuania seized it in 1923).
The Saar was governed by the League for fifteen years, its coal mines went to France, and a plebiscite was due in 1935.
Germany lost about 13 per cent of its European territory and about a tenth of its population, which is why many Germans saw the treaty as national humiliation.
The rest of the treaty stripped Germany of its colonies, its military strength and its wealth. It was also imposed, which explains the German reaction.

All Germany's colonies were taken and made League mandates (territories run by a victor state on the League's behalf), held by Britain, France, Japan, Belgium, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand.

Disarmament, so that Germany could not attack again: the army was limited to 100,000 long-service volunteers, conscription was banned, and there were to be no tanks, military aircraft or submarines. The navy was limited to six battleships and small craft, and the General Staff was abolished.
The Rhineland was demilitarised (the left bank and a 50 km zone on the right bank), and the Allies occupied the left bank for up to fifteen years, to give France security.
Union of Germany and Austria (Anschluss) was forbidden without the consent of the League Council (Article 80).

Reparations (payments for war damage): no total was set in the treaty. Germany was to pay 20 billion gold marks by May 1921 as an interim payment. In May 1921 the London Schedule fixed 132 billion gold marks in A, B and C bonds.
The C bonds (about 82 billion) were not expected to be paid, so the real obligation was about 50 billion.
Article 227 called for the trial of the Kaiser, but the Netherlands refused to hand him over. Part I of the treaty was the Covenant of the League of Nations.

Germans called it a 'Diktat' (a dictated peace) because they had not been allowed to negotiate. Scheidemann's government resigned on 20 June 1919 rather than sign; the Assembly voted to sign on 23 June under the threat of invasion. Hermann Müller and Johannes Bell signed.
Versailles dealt only with Germany. Separate treaties dealt with Germany's allies, and together they redrew the map of central and south-eastern Europe and the Middle East.

The Treaty of St Germain with Austria (10 September 1919) recognised the new states, limited Austria's army to 30,000 and forbade union with Germany. Austria lost South Tyrol to Italy, the Sudeten German areas to Czechoslovakia and Galicia to Poland.

The Treaty of Trianon with Hungary (4 June 1920) cost Hungary about two-thirds of its territory: Transylvania to Romania, Slovakia (and Ruthenia) to Czechoslovakia, Croatia to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and Burgenland to Austria.
Over three million Hungarians were left outside Hungary, which caused bitter and lasting resentment.
The Treaty of Neuilly with Bulgaria (27 November 1919) gave Western Thrace to Greece, which cut Bulgaria off from the Aegean. It also imposed reparations and limited the army to 20,000.

The Treaty of Sèvres with the Ottoman Empire (10 August 1920) divided up the empire, with Armenia and a Kurdish area promised. Mustafa Kemal's nationalists rejected it and defeated Greece (the Greek-Turkish war, 1919-22), and the Treaty of Lausanne (1923) replaced it.
In the Middle East, mandates were allocated at the San Remo conference (April 1920). Britain received Palestine (including Transjordan) and Iraq; France received Syria and Lebanon.

Self-determination is the principle that peoples should choose the state they belong to. Wilson used it as a guide at Paris, but it was applied in some places and not others, which is why the settlement was criticised.

Applied: the settlement created or restored Poland, Czechoslovakia and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, which broke away from the Russian Empire in 1917-18, became independent.

Plebiscites in contested areas: Schleswig (1920: the north voted for Denmark, the middle zone for Germany), Allenstein and Marienwerder (July 1920: large majorities for Germany), and Carinthia (October 1920: voted to stay in Austria).
Upper Silesia voted in March 1921 with a majority for Germany, followed by a Polish rising. The League partitioned it in October 1921, giving Poland most of the industrial area.

Denied to Germans: union of Germany and Austria was forbidden although Austria's assembly had voted for it in November 1918. About three million Germans (the Sudeten Germans) were placed in Czechoslovakia, and Germans lived in the Corridor and Danzig.
Denied elsewhere: German-speaking South Tyrol went to Italy to give it a strategic frontier on the Brenner, and Hungarians were left in Romania, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia without a choice.

The new states were multinational. Poland had large Ukrainian, Jewish, Belarusian and German minorities, and Czechoslovakia large German and Hungarian minorities. Minority treaties, starting with Poland on 28 June 1919, protected them under League guarantee.
The principle was not applied to the colonies, which became mandates, nor to Ireland, Egypt or India, a fact nationalists there noted.
It could not be applied fully because populations were mixed, states needed ports, railways and defensible frontiers, the victors had their own interests, and wartime promises had been made.
Wilson's central aim was a League that would keep the peace. It was created, but the country whose president had invented it refused to join, which weakened it from the start.

The League of Nations came into force on 10 January 1920, with its seat in Geneva. Its main organs were the Assembly, the Council and the Secretariat. It also had the Permanent Court of International Justice (The Hague) and the International Labour Organisation (1919).

Its Covenant promised collective security, meaning states acting together against an aggressor. Members were to respect and preserve each other's territorial integrity and political independence (Article 10) and to settle disputes by arbitration.

Under Article 16 members applied economic sanctions, and possibly force, against a member that went to war in breach of the Covenant, so aggression was meant to be deterred by the threat of joint action.
Germany and Soviet Russia were excluded at first. Germany joined in 1926 and the USSR in 1934.

Republicans won control of Congress in the November 1918 elections. The treaty needed a two-thirds majority in the Senate, and the Republican chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Henry Cabot Lodge, proposed reservations, chiefly to Article 10, which could oblige the USA to defend other states.

Wilson refused to compromise. He toured the USA in September 1919 to rally support, collapsed at Pueblo, Colorado, on 25 September and had a stroke on 2 October 1919. The Senate rejected the treaty on 19 November 1919 and again on 19 March 1920.
The USA never joined the League and made a separate peace with Germany (the Treaty of Berlin, August 1921). The Anglo-American guarantee of France lapsed when the Senate did not ratify it.
Without the USA, the strongest Western power, France and Britain were left to enforce the settlement alone.

Woodrow Wilson was President of the USA from 1913 to 1921. He moved from neutral mediator to war leader to peacemaker, and his Fourteen Points and the League shaped the settlement, but he could not win American support for it at home.

Thomas Woodrow Wilson was born on 28 December 1856 in Staunton, Virginia. A historian and political scientist, he was President of Princeton University (1902-10) and Governor of New Jersey (1911-13), then Democratic President from 1912 (in office 1913-21). He won the 1919 Nobel Peace Prize.

He kept the USA neutral from 1914, even after the Lusitania was sunk on 7 May 1915 (128 Americans died), and in January 1917 called for 'peace without victory'. He was re-elected in November 1916 on the slogan 'He kept us out of war'.

Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February 1917, and the Zimmermann Telegram (a German offer to help Mexico regain lost US territory) was published on 1 March. So on 2 April Wilson told Congress that 'the world must be made safe for democracy'; war came on 6 April.

He announced the Fourteen Points in January 1918 and in February said that self-determination was 'not a mere phrase'. The USA fought as an 'associated power', not a formal ally. He pressed for the Kaiser's removal in the armistice exchanges, so he was a participant, not a witness.

In Paris he was welcomed by huge crowds in December 1918 and January 1919, chaired the commission that drafted the League Covenant and insisted it be in the treaty. To win the League and mandates he compromised on reparations, Article 231, the Saar, the Rhineland, Shandong and South Tyrol.

At home he lost control: Republicans won Congress in November 1918, and he refused Lodge's reservations. His tour ended in a stroke in October 1919, after which his wife Edith controlled access to him, and the Senate rejected the treaty. He died on 3 February 1924.

Contemporary views: Europeans hailed him as a prophet of a new order, while Clemenceau and others were sceptical of his idealism. Keynes portrayed him as outmanoeuvred, and Germans felt disillusioned. Many Americans felt he had entangled the USA in Europe, and nationalists in Ireland and Egypt were disappointed.

Historians: admirers see the founder of liberal internationalism, whose League foreshadowed the United Nations. Critics find him self-righteous, inconsistent on self-determination and politically inept with the Senate, so he was both architect and casualty of the settlement.
The peace did not end Europe's troubles. The war and the treaties left problems that can be grouped as human, economic, political and territorial, each linked to the war or the settlement.

Human cost: about 9-10 million soldiers were killed (estimates vary), and millions were wounded and disabled, leaving widows and orphans. The 1918-19 influenza pandemic killed tens of millions worldwide.
Refugees and minorities: the new borders and the break-up of empires left many people living in states ruled by another nationality, or moving across frontiers.

Economic dislocation: governments owed war debts, inflation hurt savings, regions of France and Belgium were damaged, and trade links between the successor states (the new states that replaced the old empires) were broken. The reparations dispute made matters worse.

Political instability: fear of Bolshevism was real, because Soviet republics appeared in Bavaria and Hungary in 1919 and there were risings in Germany. The new democracies were fragile, and the Kapp Putsch showed that the right also threatened them.

Disputed borders led to wars: the Polish-Soviet war of 1919-21 (the battle of Warsaw in August 1920 and the Treaty of Riga in 1921), the Russian Civil War of 1918-21, the Greek-Turkish war, and d'Annunzio's seizure of Fiume with volunteers in September 1919.

Revisionist states, which wanted the treaties revised (Germany, Hungary, Bulgaria and Italy, a disappointed victor), faced status quo states that wanted them kept (France and the new states). This division weakened the peace.

Historians and examiners judge both the German revolution and the Peace Settlement by weighing what they achieved against what they failed to do. The key to a top answer is pairing each achievement with a limit and reaching a conclusion.
Revolution, achievement: Germany became a democratic republic with the women's vote and the eight-hour day, and the revolution avoided a Bolshevik-style regime.
Revolution, limit: the old elites in the army, civil service and judiciary were kept, the left was split and embittered by the Freikorps killings, and the republic was tied to defeat and Versailles.

Settlement, achievement: new national states appeared where empires had ruled, and the League provided a forum for settling disputes, such as the Aaland Islands (Finland and Sweden) in 1921. Germany was disarmed but kept as a united state.
Settlement, limit: the new states contained large minorities, and revision was demanded by Germany, Hungary, Bulgaria and Italy, who felt cheated.

The core judgement: the treaty was too harsh to be accepted by Germany but not harsh enough to stop it recovering. Enforcement was left to Britain and France, who disagreed, while the USA and Russia were outside the system.

Contemporary view: Keynes, a Treasury adviser in the British delegation who resigned in June 1919, argued in The Economic Consequences of the Peace (December 1919) that the reparations were unrealistic and would ruin recovery. Foch is credited with saying: 'This is not peace. It is an armistice for twenty years.'
Germans, for their part, resented the Diktat and the war guilt clause, so the treaty gave nationalists a grievance to exploit.

Later view: some historians say Germany's grievance was exaggerated and its terms were milder than Brest-Litovsk. Others, such as Margaret MacMillan in Peacemakers (2001), see a serious attempt at a difficult task and argue that later failures, not the treaty itself, led to the Second World War.
To see how fast Germany industrialised, you need to know where it started in 1871. Britain was still ahead, and Germany had only just become one state.

The first industrial revolution (based on coal, iron, textiles and steam power) began in Britain, which was still the leading industrial power in 1871. Germany was catching up, which is why its later growth looks so dramatic.

The Reich was proclaimed in January 1871 as a federation of states dominated by Prussia. The Reichstag was elected by universal male suffrage, but the Chancellor answered to the Kaiser, not to the Reichstag.

Prussia kept its own three-class franchise (voters grouped by the taxes they paid, so the rich counted for more) until 1918. This matters later because it shut workers out of power in the largest state.

The Zollverein (a customs union led by Prussia, founded in 1834, which Austria did not join) had already removed most customs barriers between the German states, so unification built on an existing common market.
By the Treaty of Frankfurt (1871) France gave Alsace and part of Lorraine to Germany and paid an indemnity of 5 billion francs. Both the territory and the money helped German industry.
Germany had the raw materials, the people and the transport that heavy industry needs. Unification then turned many small markets into one large one.

Germany's population grew from about 41 million in 1871 to about 65 million in 1910 and about 67 million in 1914, which supplied both workers for the factories and a large home market to buy their goods.

Coal and iron were the base of heavy industry. The Ruhr (in Westphalia) was the heart of it, with more coal in the Saar and Upper Silesia, and iron ore (called minette) in Lorraine, the part annexed from France in 1871.

Unification created a single market. The mark became the one currency in 1873, the Reichsbank (the central bank) was founded in 1875 and opened in 1876, and commercial law was made common, so firms no longer faced different rules in each state.

Railways grew from about 20,000 km around 1870 to more than 60,000 km by 1913, linking the Ruhr to cities and ports. They were also a huge market in their own right, because tracks and engines used vast amounts of coal and steel.
From 1879 Prussia bought out most private railway companies, so the state owned most of the network.
The French indemnity gave the new Reich a financial boost, and the early 1870s boom (the Gründerzeit, 'founding years') followed. It ended in the stock market crash of 1873.
After the crash, prices and profits stayed depressed for much of the period to the mid-1890s. This long depression pushed firms towards cartels and the state towards tariffs.
Resources alone do not build an industry. German firms also had access to long-term money, trained engineers, organised markets and a supportive state, and as a late starter they could build new.

Universal banks, such as Deutsche Bank (founded 1870) and Dresdner Bank (1872), lent to industry for long periods and sat on company boards. This let firms raise the capital that heavy investment in plant needed.

Technische Hochschulen (technical universities), found in cities such as Berlin (Charlottenburg), Munich and Aachen, and technical schools trained engineers and chemists. Chemical and electrical firms ran their own research laboratories, so science and industry were closely linked.

A cartel is an agreement among firms to fix prices, share markets or limit output. They spread after the 1873 crash and long depression because firms wanted to protect profits, and there were several hundred by the early 1900s.
Examples of cartels include the Rhenish-Westphalian Coal Syndicate (1893), which controlled most Ruhr coal, and the Steel Works Association (Stahlwerksverband, 1904).
Large combined firms also grew, with mines, ironworks and engineering under one owner. August Thyssen built such a concern in the Ruhr, covering coal, iron and steel.
The state helped industry. The protective tariff of 1879 taxed imported iron, steel and grain, and the army, navy and state railways were large customers for steel and equipment.
Germany also gained from a late start. Its firms built new plant with the latest technology, instead of patching up older works as British firms often had to.
The result of these causes was growth that alarmed Germany's rivals. In steel, chemicals and electricals Germany overtook Britain, though not in every industry.
Hard coal output rose from about 30 million tonnes in 1871 to about 190 million tonnes in 1913, about a six-fold increase. Britain, however, still mined more coal than Germany in 1913.

In 1913 Germany produced about 17 million tonnes of steel, against about 8 million for Britain, so more than twice as much. Remember that Germany overtook Britain in steel, chemicals and electricals, not in coal.
By 1914 Germany was the second industrial power in the world after the USA. On most estimates its share of world manufacturing roughly matched or slightly exceeded Britain's by 1913.

Exports of machinery, chemicals and electrical goods competed with British goods across the world. Britain's Merchandise Marks Act (1887) required goods to show where they were made, and E. E. Williams's book 'Made in Germany' (1896) warned of German competition.

The Hamburg-America Line (HAPAG, led by Albert Ballin) and North German Lloyd of Bremen carried this trade. HAPAG was the world's largest shipping company by 1914, and Germany's merchant fleet was second only to Britain's.
German emigration, mostly to the USA, peaked in the 1880s and fell steeply after the early 1890s. This is because industry was by then creating jobs at home.

From about the 1880s new industries based on steel, chemicals and electricity grew faster than the older coal and textiles. This is called the second industrial revolution, and Germany was often the leader.

Steel: the basic (Thomas-Gilchrist) process was invented by two Britons, Sidney Gilchrist Thomas and Percy Gilchrist, in 1878-79. It made the phosphoric iron ore of Lorraine usable for steel, and German steelmakers took up the licence quickly, so steel output soared in the Ruhr.
Chemicals: BASF (Ludwigshafen, 1865), Bayer (1863) and Hoechst (1863) led the world. By 1914 Germany made the great majority of the world's synthetic dyes, and Bayer marketed aspirin from 1899.
Fritz Haber synthesised ammonia from nitrogen in 1909, and Carl Bosch scaled the process up at BASF, with the first plant at Oppau in 1913. Before 1914 it was used for artificial fertilisers.

Electricals: Werner von Siemens and Johann Georg Halske founded Siemens & Halske in Berlin in 1847, at first making telegraphs. Siemens built a dynamo (a machine that generates electricity) in 1866-67.
Siemens showed an electric railway at the Berlin trade exhibition in 1879 and ran an electric tram at Lichterfelde, Berlin, in 1881.

Emil Rathenau founded the Deutsche Edison-Gesellschaft in 1883, renamed AEG (Allgemeine Elektricitäts-Gesellschaft) in 1887. Electric lighting, trams and power stations spread in cities from the 1880s and 1890s, and by 1914 Siemens and AEG dominated the industry.
Engines and motor cars: Karl Benz and Gottlieb Daimler built motor cars in the 1880s, and Rudolf Diesel developed the diesel engine in the 1890s.

The Krupp works at Essen grew from a small steel workshop into one of the largest industrial enterprises in Europe, and its name became linked with German arms and industry. Alfred Krupp, the Cannon King, made it so.
Friedrich Krupp founded a cast steel works at Essen in 1811 and died in 1826. His son Alfred Krupp (1812-87) then took charge aged 14, when the firm was small and in debt.
At the Great Exhibition in London in 1851 Alfred showed a flawless cast steel ingot of about 2 tons, which won him international attention. He also showed a steel cannon.

He developed seamless steel railway wheel tyres, patented in the early 1850s. Their three interlocking rings became the firm's trademark. He took up the Bessemer process in the early 1860s and made steel for railways.

Alfred moved into artillery. Prussia adopted his breech-loading steel guns (loaded from the rear) in the 1860s, and in 1870-71 they outranged and outperformed French bronze muzzle-loaders in the war against France.
He sold guns to many states, including Russia and the Ottoman Empire, which earned him the nickname 'the Cannon King' (Kanonenkönig).
Welfare: from the 1860s Alfred built housing estates (colonies) for workers and provided sickness and pension funds, schools, shops (including a co-operative store) and a hospital.

Control: in 1877 he issued an appeal urging his workers to stay out of politics, and known socialists were dismissed. Historians call this paternalism, meaning care that is given in return for obedience.
He completed Villa Hügel, the family house above the Ruhr, in 1873. By his death in July 1887 the works employed about 20,000 workers.
Alfred's son Friedrich Alfred took the firm from guns for armies into armour and ships for the new German navy. Do not confuse him with the founder, Friedrich Krupp, who died in 1826.
Friedrich Alfred Krupp (1854-1902) headed the firm from 1887 to 1902.
In 1893 he bought the Gruson works at Magdeburg, which made armour plate. Krupp nickel-steel armour plate was widely used by navies, so the firm profited as fleets grew.
He took over the Germania shipyard at Kiel from 1896 (it was renamed Fried. Krupp Germaniawerft in 1902), which gave the firm shipbuilding. It later built U-boats there.
Wilhelm II was a personal friend and frequent visitor, and the fleet was a major customer. This shows how the firm and the state depended on each other.
In mid-November 1902 Vorwärts (the SPD newspaper) printed allegations about his private life on Capri. He died on 22 November 1902, officially of a stroke, though suicide was widely suspected.
Wilhelm II attended the funeral in Essen and then publicly attacked the SPD, which shows how closely the Kaiser, the firm and the political struggle with socialism were linked.
After 1902 the firm passed to a young heiress and her diplomat husband. Under them Krupp became the arms maker whose guns were used in the first months of the First World War.
Bertha Krupp (1886-1957) inherited the firm in 1902 aged 16. In 1903 it became a joint-stock company, Fried. Krupp AG, and Bertha held almost all the shares.

Gustav von Bohlen und Halbach (1870-1950), a Prussian diplomat, married Bertha in October 1906 with Wilhelm II present. The Kaiser allowed him the name Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach, so he was not born a Krupp. He ran the firm, chairing its supervisory board from 1909.

The Kornwalzer scandal (1913): the SPD deputy Karl Liebknecht exposed in the Reichstag that Krupp's Berlin agent had bribed War Ministry clerks for secret information. A trial followed in 1913, and the affair took its name from a code word used.

In August 1914 the 42 cm howitzer nicknamed 'Big Bertha' (Dicke Bertha), usually said to be named after Bertha Krupp, was used against the Belgian forts of Liège and Namur. Do not confuse it with the Paris Gun of 1918.
In the war the firm made guns, shells, armour and U-boats (built at Kiel). Its workforce passed 100,000, and many women worked in its shell shops.
The Krupps both shaped German history and were shaped by it. Contemporaries and historians judged them very differently depending on their politics.
Shaped events: the Krupps armed Prussia and the Reich, and profited from unification, the naval race and war. Krupp was often described as the largest industrial firm in Europe before 1914.
Shaped by events: the firm also depended on state orders and on the Kaiser's favour, so its success was tied to Prussian and German power.
Contemporaries: to nationalists and the Kaiser, Krupp was a national symbol of German industrial and military strength.
To socialists, the Krupps were exploiters who profited from armaments and controlled their workers. Socialists attacked the firm for profiting from armaments.

To historians Krupp is the leading example of the link between heavy industry, the army and the state before 1914, which some call a military-industrial complex, and as the model of industrial paternalism.
The firm's later role under the Nazis falls outside this period.
Industry needed workers, and they came from the countryside. This created a large urban working class, with new problems and new political strength.

Millions moved from the countryside, especially from the agrarian east (the 'flight from the land'), to Berlin and the Ruhr, because industry offered work. Polish-speaking migrants to the Ruhr were nicknamed 'Ruhrpolen'.
About a third of Germans (about 36 per cent) lived in towns of 2,000 or more in 1871. By 1910 the figure was about 60 per cent.
Berlin grew from about 830,000 (under a million) in 1871 to about 2 million in 1910. Essen grew from about 50,000 to about 300,000, with suburbs absorbed, so Ruhr towns grew many times over.

Berlin's workers lived in Mietskasernen ('rental barracks'), large tenement blocks around courtyards. They were overcrowded, with poor sanitation and disease, though public health and city services improved from the 1890s.
Working conditions meant long hours, strict factory discipline and insecurity, and women and children worked too. Real wages rose slowly from the 1890s.
The Labour Protection Law of 1891 gave Sunday rest, a maximum 11-hour day for women and banned factory work for children under 13.
Strikes showed workers' strength. In May 1889 about 90,000 Ruhr miners struck and Wilhelm II received a delegation of miners. A second, larger Ruhr strike came in January-February 1905.

The working class was divided. Catholic workers were often loyal to the Centre Party and Christian unions, Polish workers faced pressure to become German (Germanisation), and skilled workers differed from unskilled.

A large urban working class gave a party based on Marxism its chance. Marxism teaches that society is a class struggle between owners and workers, and aims at common ownership of industry. The SPD became Germany's Marxist party.
The General German Workers' Association was founded by Ferdinand Lassalle in 1863. The Social Democratic Workers' Party was founded at Eisenach in 1869 by August Bebel and Wilhelm Liebknecht.
They united at Gotha in May 1875 as the Socialist Workers' Party, which took the name SPD (Social Democratic Party) in 1890.
The Anti-Socialist Law (passed October 1878, lapsed 30 September 1890) banned socialist organisations and press. Socialists could still stand for the Reichstag, and their vote rose.

The Erfurt Programme (October 1891), drafted mainly by Karl Kautsky (theory) and Eduard Bernstein (demands), combined a Marxist analysis of capitalism with immediate demands such as democratic suffrage, the eight-hour day and social reforms.

Revisionism: Bernstein, in 'The Preconditions of Socialism' (1899), argued for gradual reform instead of revolution. The party congress at Dresden in 1903 condemned his ideas, but in practice the party acted as a reformist party.
In 1890 the SPD won about 1.4 million votes and 35 seats. In 1912 it won about 4.25 million votes (about a third of the total) and 110 of 397 seats, becoming the largest party in the Reichstag.
Despite its votes the SPD could not win power, and employers and the state fought the labour movement. Yet the movement built a world of its own.
The SPD was strongest in the Reichstag, but the Chancellor was not answerable to the Reichstag, and the Bundesrat (the council of state governments) also limited it.

Constituencies had not changed since 1871, which favoured the countryside over the growing cities. The Prussian three-class franchise kept the SPD almost out of the Prussian parliament, and no SPD member was in government before 1918.
The Free Trade Unions (socialist) had about 2.5 million members in 1913, far more than the Christian (Catholic-led) unions and the liberal (Hirsch-Duncker) unions.
Employers replied with associations, lockouts and blacklists. The police and courts were also used against strikes.
The SPD built a socialist subculture of party newspapers, clubs, choirs, sports and education societies. This gave members a community, which helps explain why the party grew despite repression.
Critics called the SPD a 'state within a state', and its members were treated as outsiders (Reichsfeinde, 'enemies of the Reich'). Repression created martyrs and so kept loyalty strong.
Industrial growth changed the balance of power between landowners, factory owners and workers. Tariffs, which were taxes on imports, were the sharpest dispute.

The Junkers were landowning nobles of the Prussian lands east of the Elbe. They dominated the army officer corps, the Prussian civil service and the Prussian parliament, where three-class voting gave the rich more weight.
From the late 1870s cheap US and Russian grain threatened Junker profits. The tariff of 1879 protected grain and iron, creating the 'iron and rye' alliance of heavy industry and Junkers.

Caprivi (Chancellor 1890-94) lowered grain duties in trade treaties (1891-94). The Agrarian League (Bund der Landwirte), founded in 1893, campaigned against them. Bülow's tariff, passed in 1902 and in force in 1906, raised grain duties again.
Tariffs had losers. Dearer bread angered workers and consumers, and exporting and finished-goods industries and the left opposed high duties. 'Bread usury' was an SPD theme.

Sammlungspolitik (the 'policy of rallying together'), associated with Johannes von Miquel from 1897, aimed to unite landowners and industrialists behind the monarchy, the fleet and Weltpolitik (world policy), against the SPD.

Industrialists resented aristocratic privilege, but many copied the nobility with titles, estates and reserve-officer commissions. Hans-Ulrich Wehler (The German Empire 1871-1918) called this the 'feudalisation of the bourgeoisie' and saw it as part of a German 'special path' (Sonderweg).
David Blackbourn and Geoff Eley replied in 'The Peculiarities of German History' (1984) that the German middle class was confident and the Reich a modern society.

The middle classes also feared socialism, which led many to support nationalist pressure groups and the monarchy. Other tensions were the Kulturkampf against Catholics, and the position of Poles and the Alsace-Lorraine population.
The state tried both to win workers over and to hold them down, a mix described as carrot and stick. Employers copied the carrot with welfare of their own.

Bismarck's social insurance created sickness insurance (1883), accident insurance (1884) and old age and invalidity insurance (1889). Its aim was to win workers from the SPD, a mix of welfare and repression known as 'carrot and stick'.

In 1890 Wilhelm II's 'new course' let the Anti-Socialist Law lapse. In February 1890 he issued decrees on workers' protection, and an international labour conference met in Berlin in March 1890. The Labour Protection Law followed in 1891.

The state then turned back to repression. The Subversion Bill (Umsturzvorlage, rejected 1895) and the Penitentiary Bill (Zuchthausvorlage, penalties for pressuring workers to strike, rejected 1899) both failed in the Reichstag. The Kaiser turned against the SPD because it kept winning votes.
Social insurance was consolidated in the Imperial Insurance Code (Reichsversicherungsordnung) of 1911.
Companies provided welfare too. Krupp's housing, schools and funds are the best-known example, and Siemens set up a pension fund in the 1870s. Employers wanted loyalty and no strikes.
Welfare did not stop the SPD vote from rising, because many workers were more loyal to their unions and party than to the state or firm.
No political reform followed economic change, and the Prussian three-class franchise survived to 1918.
Judgement questions reward weighing achievement against limit, and contemporary views against later ones. The points below are set out in pairs.
Achievement: Germany became continental Europe's leading industrial economy and led in steel, chemicals and electricals.
Limit: growth was uneven, because agriculture and the east lagged, and the economy suffered boom and slump, as with the crash of 1873 and the long depression.
Achievement: Germany built the first national social insurance system, and real wages rose and emigration fell from the 1890s.
Limit: welfare was paternalist and paired with repression, the political system stayed closed to the largest party, and class, religious and regional tensions were unresolved in 1914.
Impact abroad: industrial power fed militarism, the arms industry and the naval race, and also trade rivalry with Britain.
Contemporary views: nationalists saw industrial power as proof of German greatness, while socialists saw exploitation.
Later views: historians debate whether Germany had a modern economy with an unreformed political system (Wehler) or was a normal modern society (Blackbourn and Eley).

Russia was the largest state in Europe, but it was poor, overwhelmingly rural and ruled by an autocratic tsar. To see why it later faced crisis and revolution, you need to know how it was governed and how far behind the West it had fallen.

Autocracy means the tsar ruled with no parliament and no constitution before 1905. He was backed by the Orthodox Church, the nobility, the army, the bureaucracy and the secret police (the Okhrana), so there was no legal way to challenge him.
Defeat in the Crimean War (1853-56) convinced the government that Russia must modernise, because its army and economy could not match Britain and France. This led to the reforms of Alexander II.

The emancipation of the serfs (peasants bound to their landlords) in 1861 was Alexander II's greatest reform. Peasants had to make redemption payments to the state over 49 years for the land they received, which left many in debt.

Most peasants held land in the mir (the village commune), which periodically redistributed strips among households. This discouraged investment, because no one kept the same land long enough to improve it, so farming methods stayed backward.
The census of 1897 showed about 126 million people, about four-fifths of them peasants. Russia was a multinational empire, and ethnic Russians were under half the population.
In 1871 Russia had little heavy industry, few railways for its size and a weak banking system. It exported grain and relied on foreign capital (money invested from abroad) and technology.

Alexander II's other reforms, such as the zemstva (elected local councils, from 1864), the courts and the army, were limited. He was assassinated in St Petersburg on 13 March 1881 (1 March in the Russian calendar) by the revolutionary group People's Will (Narodnaya Volya).

Alexander III (1881-94) and Nicholas II (1894-1917) upheld autocracy and pursued Russification, forcing the Russian language and officials on minorities such as Poles and Finns. In January 1895 Nicholas told zemstvo delegates that hopes of a share in government were 'senseless dreams'.

Russian dates and names can confuse you, because Russia ran on a different calendar and its capital changed names. Getting these right explains why the 'February' and 'October' revolutions happened in March and November.

Russia used the old (Julian) calendar, which was 12 days behind the Western (Gregorian) calendar in the nineteenth century and 13 days behind in the twentieth. The Bolsheviks adopted the Western calendar in February 1918, when 31 January was followed by 14 February.
Western dates come first with the Russian date in brackets. This is why the February Revolution took place in March 1917 and the October Revolution in November 1917.
St Petersburg was renamed Petrograd in 1914, so use the name that is correct for the date. The capital moved from Petrograd to Moscow in March 1918.
With no parliament and no legal opposition, those who wanted change had to organise in secret. By 1905 three main groups had formed, and they shaped everything that followed.

Marxism sees history as a class struggle. Capitalism creates an industrial working class (the proletariat) that will overthrow it, which is why Russian Marxists welcomed industrialisation: it was creating the class that would make revolution.
The Russian Social Democratic Labour Party was Marxist and was founded in 1898. At its second congress in 1903 it split into the Bolsheviks under Lenin and the Mensheviks under Martov.

The Socialist Revolutionary Party (SRs), founded in 1901-02, was based on the peasantry, because its members believed Russia's revolution would rest on the land-hungry peasants rather than on factory workers.
The Union of Liberation, founded in 1903-04, was made up of liberals who wanted a constitution, meaning written rules limiting the tsar's power.

Sergei Witte, Finance Minister from 1892 to 1903, led a state-directed 'great spurt' of industrial growth. Russia had little private capital, so the state had to find the money and direct the effort itself.

Witte believed industry was needed for Russia to remain a Great Power, because military strength rested on factories and railways. The state built railways, placed orders with factories and protected industry with tariffs (taxes on imports), including the high tariff of 1891.

Foreign loans and investment paid for mines, ironworks and railways. They came chiefly from France, also from Belgium, Britain and Germany. The Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894 was the channel that made French money flow.
Russia put the rouble on the gold standard in 1897. This meant the rouble could be exchanged for a fixed amount of gold, which reassured foreign investors that their money would keep its value.
Heavy indirect taxes (taxes on goods such as sugar and vodka, paid by everyone) and grain exports provided the rest of the money. Peasants bore most of this burden.
Witte's predecessor, Ivan Vyshnegradsky (Finance Minister 1887-92), had already pushed grain exports. The remark 'We shall go hungry, but we shall export' is usually attributed to him.
Railways were the heart of the spurt. They tied a vast country together, carried raw materials and goods, and created demand for iron, coal and steel.
The Trans-Siberian Railway was begun in 1891. A through route to Vladivostok was open by about 1904, running partly across Manchuria, and the all-Russian route along the Amur was completed in 1916.
The railway network nearly doubled in the 1890s, from about 30,000 km to about 53,000 km, which is why iron and coal industries grew so fast.
Coal and iron grew in the Donbas (the Donets basin) in Ukraine, oil in Baku in the Caucasus, and engineering and textiles in St Petersburg and Moscow.
Industrial output grew at about 8 per cent a year in the 1890s. Coal and pig-iron output (iron fresh from the furnace, the raw material for steel) roughly tripled between 1890 and 1900.
Rapid growth brought real power but also real strain. The same policies that built factories squeezed the peasants and gathered discontented workers together.

Industry was concentrated in huge factories such as the Putilov works in St Petersburg, which had about 12,000 workers in 1905 and tens of thousands during the war. Large crowds of workers made organisation and protest easier.
The peasantry carried the burden through taxes, and grain was exported even in hungry years, so the countryside paid for the towns.
The industrial depression of 1900-03 caused unemployment and strikes. Witte moved out of the Finance Ministry in August 1903.
Growth was rapid again from about 1908 to 1914. By 1914 Russia was often ranked the fifth industrial power in the world by total output, which is an estimate.

Output per head was still low, because the huge peasant population produced little, and dependence on foreign capital was high. Germany's industry, by contrast, grew through private banks and firms rather than the state.
Most Russians were peasants, and their lives were getting harder. In 1891 a harvest failure turned long-running poverty into a national disaster that damaged the regime's standing.
Peasants faced small plots, old methods, rapid population growth and redemption payments. Land hunger (too many people for too little land) grew as families increased.

The harvest failed in 1891 across the Volga and the central black-earth provinces (the rich soil belt), causing famine in 1891-92. Cholera and typhus followed in 1892, and deaths are estimated at about 375,000 to 500,000.

Government relief was slow. Zemstvo and private volunteers, including Leo Tolstoy and Anton Chekhov, organised famine relief, which showed that educated Russians were doing what the state failed to do.
The famine discredited the regime and revived opposition among educated Russians, such as the liberals of the Union of Liberation (1903-04) and the SRs (1901-02).
Peasant unrest grew, with attacks on estates in Kharkov and Poltava provinces in 1902 and far wider violence in 1905-06.
Workers were mostly first-generation peasants who kept links with their villages. This spread discontent between town and country.
Russia's rivalry with Japan in the Far East led to a war it was confident of winning. Defeat instead exposed the regime's weakness and set off revolution at home.
Russia and Japan were rivals over Manchuria and Korea. Russia had leased Port Arthur from China in 1898, and the Trans-Siberian Railway gave it a route east.

Vyacheslav von Plehve, Minister of the Interior from 1902 until he was assassinated in July 1904, is reported to have wanted 'a short victorious war'. Instead, defeat in the war helped trigger the 1905 revolution.
Japan attacked the Russian fleet at Port Arthur on the night of 8-9 February 1904, before declaring war. Port Arthur surrendered on 2 January 1905.
Russia lost the land battle of Mukden in February-March 1905. The Baltic Fleet, which had sailed right around the world, was destroyed at Tsushima on 27-28 May 1905.

The Treaty of Portsmouth (New Hampshire, USA) of 5 September 1905 was mediated by President Theodore Roosevelt. Japan gained southern Sakhalin, the Port Arthur lease and recognition of its control of Korea.
Defeat humiliated the autocracy and exposed the weakness of the army, transport and administration, so it was the trigger of the 1905 revolution.
Defeat abroad and hardship at home produced a year of revolt. The tsar's response moved from bullets to concessions in a matter of months.

On 22 January 1905 (9 January in the Russian calendar) Father Georgy Gapon led a procession to the Winter Palace to petition the tsar. Troops fired on it. The official figure was about 130 dead, though other estimates run to several hundred or more.

Bloody Sunday broke the people's faith in the tsar as their protector, the 'little father'. Strikes, peasant risings, the mutiny on the battleship Potemkin (Black Sea Fleet, June 1905) and national movements in Poland and the Caucasus followed.
In October 1905 a general strike paralysed the railways and cities. The St Petersburg Soviet (council) of Workers' Deputies was formed, with Trotsky as its leading figure.

On Witte's advice the tsar issued the October Manifesto on 30 October 1905 (17 October in the Russian calendar). It promised civil liberties, an elected Duma (parliament) with power over laws, and a wider franchise (more people able to vote).
Witte then became the first chairman of the Council of Ministers, in effect prime minister, serving from October 1905 to April 1906.
Despite a year of revolt, the regime held on. It split its enemies, kept the army, found money abroad and then took back much of what it had promised.

The Manifesto split the opposition. The Octobrists (led by Alexander Guchkov) accepted it. The Constitutional Democrats or Kadets (led by Pavel Milyukov) wanted a constituent assembly and more power for the Duma, and the socialists rejected it.
The army stayed loyal once peace had been made with Japan, so the tsar could use force. The Soviet's leaders were arrested in December 1905 and the Moscow armed rising was crushed that month.
Redemption payments were halved for 1906 and abolished from 1 January 1907, a concession to the peasants announced in November 1905.
A very large French-led international loan in April 1906, about 2,250 million francs, let the government survive without depending on the Duma for money.
The Fundamental Laws of 6 May 1906 (23 April in the Russian calendar) were published shortly before the First Duma met. The tsar remained 'Supreme Autocrat', since the word 'unlimited' was dropped.
He appointed ministers, controlled the army and foreign policy and had an absolute veto over laws. He could dissolve the Duma and issue emergency decrees when it was not sitting (Article 87).
An upper house, the State Council, was half appointed, so it balanced the elected Duma in the tsar's favour.
Peter Stolypin, Prime Minister from July 1906 to September 1911, combined repression with reform. The Dumas show how little real power the elected parliament had.
The First Duma (May-July 1906) demanded land reform and ministers responsible to it. It was dissolved after about 72 days. The Second Duma (February-June 1907) was also dissolved.
In June 1907 the electoral law was changed by decree (the 'coup of 3 June'). Landowners and the wealthy then dominated the Third Duma (1907-12) and the Fourth Duma (1912-17).
The Duma became a place for criticism but not control, because the tsar kept his veto and could still dissolve it.

Stolypin, also Minister of the Interior, crushed disorder with field courts-martial from August 1906. More than a thousand people were executed, and the hangman's noose became known as 'Stolypin's necktie'.
Stolypin wanted to win the peasants over by making them owners. He needed time, and he did not get it.
The land decree of November 1906 let peasants leave the commune, own land privately and consolidate their strips into single farms. The Peasant Land Bank lent them money to buy land.
Resettlement of millions of peasants in Siberia was encouraged. The aim was a loyal class of prosperous peasants, often called a 'wager on the strong', meaning the sober and hardworking peasants.
By 1914 about two million households, roughly a fifth to a quarter depending on how they are counted, had left the commune. Most peasants stayed in it.
Stolypin said that if the state gave him twenty years of peace, Russia would be transformed. This is a paraphrase, not a quotation.
Dmitri Bogrov, a revolutionary who was also a police informer, shot Stolypin at the Kiev opera in September 1911 with Nicholas II present. Stolypin died a few days later.
Protest revived after 1912. Troops shot striking miners at the Lena goldfields in Siberia in April 1912, killing well over a hundred, and large strikes broke out in St Petersburg in July 1914.

A world war is a war between great alliances that spreads across continents and draws on a country's whole economy and population. Russia's economy and government could not stand that strain, and the war pushed an already weak regime towards collapse.

Russia mobilised a huge army, but it was poorly equipped. It lost at Tannenberg in August 1914 and the Masurian Lakes in September 1914, both German victories in East Prussia. The great retreat of 1915 lost Russian Poland.
The Brusilov offensive of June-September 1916 against Austria-Hungary succeeded but at heavy cost. Over the war Russia suffered millions of dead, wounded and prisoners.
About 15 million men were mobilised between 1914 and 1917, which took labour from the farms and cut food output. Railways were overloaded, so food and fuel could not reach the cities.

Inflation rose as the government printed money. The state also lost revenue when the sale of vodka was banned in 1914, because the vodka monopoly had been a major source of income. Food and fuel were short in the cities by winter 1916-17.

Nicholas II took personal command at army headquarters in September 1915. This left Empress Alexandra, who was German-born and so suspected, and Rasputin influential in government, and ministers changed rapidly.
The Progressive Bloc, formed in the Duma in August 1915, demanded a government with public confidence.

Grigori Rasputin was a peasant mystic whom the empress trusted because he seemed to ease the haemophilia of the heir, Alexei. Prince Felix Yusupov and other aristocrats murdered him in December 1916, a sign of the regime's isolation.
The regime that had survived 1905 fell in a few days in 1917. The key difference was that this time the soldiers refused to fire on the crowds.
On 8 March 1917 (23 February in the Russian calendar), International Women's Day, women textile workers in Petrograd demanded bread. Their strikes grew into a general strike in the city.
The garrison regiments mutinied on 12 March (27 February) and joined the crowds instead of firing on them. This was the key difference from 1905, when the army stayed loyal.
On the same day the Duma set up a Provisional Committee and the Petrograd Soviet of Workers' and Soldiers' Deputies was revived.
The generals advised abdication. Nicholas II abdicated on 15 March (2 March) at Pskov, for himself and Alexei, and his brother Grand Duke Michael declined the throne the next day.
This ended about 300 years of Romanov rule, which had begun in 1613.
After the tsar fell, two bodies claimed authority. The new government's decisions on war and land gave the Bolsheviks their chance.

Prince Georgy Lvov headed the Provisional Government from March to July 1917, and Alexander Kerensky from July. It shared authority with the Petrograd Soviet, an arrangement called 'dual power' (dvoevlastie).
The Soviet's Order No. 1, issued in March 1917, told soldiers to obey the Provisional Government's military orders only if the Soviet agreed. This weakened the government's control of the army.

The government granted civil liberties but kept fighting the war and postponed land reform until a Constituent Assembly could meet. The failed July (Kerensky) offensive of 1917 brought more desertions, and peasants began to seize land.
Lenin returned to Petrograd's Finland Station in April 1917 (16 April; 3 April in the Russian calendar), crossing Germany by train with German permission. He issued the April Theses.
The Theses demanded 'All power to the Soviets' and promised 'Peace, land and bread'. These slogans appealed to soldiers, peasants and hungry workers.
Within months of the April Theses the Bolsheviks went from a small party to the rulers of Petrograd. Failure by their opponents and careful organisation by Trotsky made this possible.
The July Days of July 1917 were a failed Bolshevik-backed rising, and Lenin went into hiding in Finland.

General Lavr Kornilov, commander-in-chief, moved troops towards Petrograd in mid-September 1917 (late August / early September in the Russian calendar). Kerensky armed the Petrograd workers (Red Guards) and released Bolshevik prisoners. The Kornilov affair thus armed the Red Guards and boosted the Bolsheviks.

The Bolsheviks won majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets in September. Trotsky became chairman of the Petrograd Soviet from October (late September) and organised its Military Revolutionary Committee.

The rising began on 6-7 November (24-25 October in the Russian calendar). Bolshevik forces seized the stations, bridges and telegraph, and the Winter Palace was taken in the early hours of 8 November (26 October).
The Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets met on 7-8 November (25-26 October). It approved the Council of People's Commissars (Sovnarkom), with Lenin as chairman.

The Decree on Peace and the Decree on Land followed on 8 November (26 October), together with the Declaration of the Rights of the Peoples of Russia. The Cheka (the Bolshevik secret police) was founded in December 1917 under Felix Dzerzhinsky.

In the Constituent Assembly election of November 1917 the SRs won about 40 per cent of the vote and the Bolsheviks about 24 per cent, about a quarter. The Assembly met once, on 18-19 January 1918 (5-6 January), and was dispersed by Red Guards.
The Bolsheviks had promised peace, but Germany demanded a high price. The treaty shows how weak the new government was.

An armistice (a halt in fighting) with Germany was agreed in December 1917. Trotsky, Commissar for Foreign Affairs, stalled at Brest-Litovsk with a policy of 'neither war nor peace', hoping revolution would spread.
Germany advanced again in February 1918, so the Bolsheviks gave in. A Soviet delegation signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on 3 March 1918.

Russia lost Poland, the Baltic provinces (Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia), Finland and Ukraine. This was about a third of the population of European Russia, with much of its coal, industry and farmland.
The treaty was cancelled after Germany's defeat in November 1918.
The capital moved from Petrograd to Moscow in March 1918, away from the German threat.
Within months the Bolsheviks faced armed enemies at home and abroad. They won, and the reasons why are a favourite exam question.
The Romanovs, Nicholas II, Alexandra and their children, were shot at Ekaterinburg on 16-17 July 1918, so no tsar could become a rallying point for the Whites.

The civil war was fought between the Reds (the Bolsheviks) and the Whites, a loose mix of generals, monarchists and liberals: Admiral Kolchak in Siberia, General Denikin in the south, General Yudenich in the north-west against Petrograd and General Wrangel in the Crimea in 1920.

Trotsky, Commissar for War from March 1918, built the Red Army and used tens of thousands of former tsarist officers, watched by political commissars. The Czech Legion, former prisoners of war, revolted along the Trans-Siberian Railway in May 1918.
Britain (at Murmansk and Archangel), Japan and the USA (at Vladivostok) and France in the south landed troops from 1918. Their effect was limited.
War Communism (1918-21) meant seizing grain from peasants, nationalising industry and rationing. The Red Terror was launched in September 1918 after an attempt on Lenin's life in August 1918.

Kolchak was defeated in 1919 and executed in February 1920. Yudenich was turned back near Petrograd in October 1919. Denikin's advance on Moscow was defeated in autumn 1919 and he resigned in 1920. Wrangel was evacuated from the Crimea in November 1920.
The Reds held the central core with its railways, industry, the capitals and the largest population, so they could move troops. They had one command and one aim.

The Whites were divided and scattered, and were linked to landlords and foreign powers, so many peasants feared their return. In the Polish-Soviet war of 1919-20 the Red Army's advance on Warsaw was defeated in August 1920.
Self-determination was one of the most powerful ideas of the period, and the revolution gave it a particular Russian shape. Examiners ask how it was applied and how it was denied.
Self-determination is the right of a people to choose its own government and state.

The Bolsheviks applied it in the Declaration of the Rights of the Peoples of Russia in November 1917, which recognised the right of peoples to self-determination. Finland declared independence in December 1917 and the Soviet government recognised it at the end of December 1917 or January 1918.
Poland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania became independent in 1918, confirmed by treaties with Soviet Russia in 1920. Poland's border was settled in 1921.
It was denied elsewhere: the Red Army brought Ukraine and other borderlands back under Bolshevik rule. For Lenin, self-determination came second to the revolution.
Tsarist Russia was changing fast, but its political system could not keep up. Judgement questions reward answers that weigh achievements against limits and long-term against short-term causes.
Achievement: Witte built railways and heavy industry, growth resumed after 1908, and Stolypin began to create a class of independent farmers.
Limit: growth rested on foreign capital and a poor peasantry, and it created a discontented working class in huge factories.

Limit: political reform stopped short, because the Dumas were weak. Nicholas II mistrusted reformers, with Witte let go in 1906 and Stolypin's position weak by 1911, and he wasted the chance of 1905-06.

Why the regime survived 1905 but fell in 1917: in 1905 the army stayed loyal and the opposition was split. In 1917 the army was exhausted, the cities were starving and the soldiers joined the strikers.
Long-term causes (economic backwardness, autocracy, the peasantry) set against the short-term cause (the war) is the central judgement. Decide which mattered most and show how one led to the other.

Historians: the 'optimists' argue Russia was modernising and the war caused the collapse. The 'pessimists' argue revolution was likely anyway. Leopold Haimson pointed to the 1912-14 strike wave, and Orlando Figes stresses the regime's failure to reform.

Alexander Gerschenkron argued that in a backward country the state substitutes for missing private capital, with Witte as the example. Richard Pipes sees October as a coup by a minority party, while Soviet historians saw a popular workers' revolution.
Contemporary views: liberals blamed the tsar's obstinacy, and the Bolsheviks presented October as a workers' revolution. Opponents called it a seizure of power by a minority party.
By 1914 the great powers expected a short war. Instead it became a long struggle that drew in whole societies, which is why historians call it a total war.
It was a world war because it was fought across several continents, and its effects reached civilians and economies as well as armies.

On the Western Front the war became one of attrition (wearing the enemy down), so armies needed millions of men and huge quantities of shells for years. This need, not ideology, is why states took over their economies and why women were needed.
Total war means that whole societies and economies are mobilised: the state directs industry, labour, food and public opinion, and civilians become targets.

Conscription is compulsory military service. France and Germany already had it before 1914, but Britain relied on volunteers until the Military Service Act of January 1916, which conscripted single men aged 18 to 41 and came into force in March 1916.
The Act was extended to married men in May 1916. Conscription took men out of factories and offices, so it created the demand for women's labour.
The scale and length of the war forced the British government to direct the economy and people's daily lives, far beyond anything seen in earlier wars.

The Defence of the Realm Act (DORA), passed in August 1914 and extended repeatedly, gave the government power over property, labour, the press and public behaviour. It allowed censorship of news and restricted pub opening hours.
British Summer Time was introduced in 1916 to save energy and daylight. It came from a separate act, not from DORA.
The government took control of the railways from August 1914 and of all the coal mines by 1917, and it also took over shipping, so that supplies could be coordinated.
New ministries were created: Munitions in 1915, and Labour, Food and Shipping in 1916. Each gave the state direct control of a part of the war effort.
The Shell Crisis of spring 1915 was a shortage of shells for the army. It brought down the Liberal government, which was replaced by a coalition under Asquith in May 1915.
David Lloyd George became Minister of Munitions in 1915 and led the new ministry that took charge of the supply of war material.
Germany also put its economy under state direction. Every government had to keep soldiers recruited, civilians fed and morale up, and the war reached civilians directly.

In 1914 Germany set up the War Raw Materials Department under Walther Rathenau to control scarce raw materials. The Hindenburg Programme of 1916 aimed to increase munitions production and mobilise labour.
The Auxiliary Service Law of December 1916 compelled men aged 17 to 60 into war work. Because it drew male workers into industry, it increased the pressure on women to fill other gaps.
Propaganda was used to recruit soldiers, as in Kitchener's 1914 'Your Country Needs You' poster, to sell war bonds and to encourage civilians to accept shortages.
Governments also censored newspapers and letters, so that bad news and criticism did not damage morale.

Rationing (sharing out scarce food by rule) came at different times. Germany introduced bread rationing from 1915, with a wider system of price controls. Britain brought in compulsory rationing of sugar, meat and butter only in 1918, after the submarine campaign cut supplies.
Britain's Corn Production Act of 1917 was passed to raise food output at home.
Civilians became targets. German warships shelled Scarborough, Hartlepool and Whitby in December 1914, Zeppelin airships raided Britain from 1915 and Gotha bombers attacked in 1917-18.
Fighting a war of this size cost enormous sums, and paying for it changed the position of whole countries.
States paid for the war through borrowing, war loans and printing money rather than taxation alone, so the national debts of the belligerents multiplied.
Britain, once the world's greatest creditor, became a debtor to the USA because it borrowed heavily to pay for the war, which became the leading financial power.

Inflation (a general rise in prices) meant that prices rose faster than wages in most countries and savings lost value. In Germany, where the war was funded mainly by loans and money creation, this laid the ground for later inflation.
Industry converted to war production, and new industries such as chemicals, aircraft and engineering expanded.
Peacetime trade collapsed, and Europe lost export markets to the USA and Japan.
Agriculture lost men and horses to the army, so governments pushed food production, as in the Corn Production Act of 1917.
Some economies were damaged far more than others, depending on whether they were blockaded or fought over.
Germany's blockaded economy suffered severe shortages. After a poor potato harvest the 'Turnip Winter' of 1916-17 forced people to eat turnips in place of potatoes.
Estimates of German civilian deaths linked to the blockade and malnutrition-related causes range from about 400,000 to about 750,000, so it is safest to say hundreds of thousands.
Areas fought over, such as northern France and Belgium, were devastated.
Russia's economy collapsed under the strain of the war, which contributed to revolution.
The war killed and disabled millions and shook old social patterns, while also strengthening some groups and the state.
About 9 to 10 million soldiers died in all. Germany lost about 2 million, France about 1.4 million and Britain about 700,000 to 750,000 (nearly 900,000 with the Empire).
Many survivors were disabled, and there were very many widows and orphans, so families and welfare systems were put under heavy strain.
Class barriers loosened a little because of shared danger in the trenches, the need for national unity and wider state welfare. Soldiers from town and country also met people from other regions.

Trade unions gained strength and government recognition because governments needed their cooperation. British union membership roughly doubled, from about 4 million in 1914 to about 8 million in 1920, though strikes continued over pay and conditions.
The Education Act 1918 (the Fisher Act) raised the school-leaving age to 14.
The influenza pandemic of 1918-19 killed tens of millions worldwide, with estimates ranging from about 17 million to 50 million or more. It struck young adults weakened by the war.
In 1919 demobilisation (releasing soldiers from the army) brought fears of unemployment, strikes and some army mutinies over slow demobilisation.
Before the war most women who earned wages were young and unmarried and worked in a narrow range of badly paid jobs. This is the starting point against which any change must be judged.
Domestic service was the largest employer of women in Britain, with well over a million servants. Textiles and clothing came next.
Women's pay was about half of men's or less. They were excluded from most skilled trades and professions and from many trade unions, and married women were expected to stay at home.
In France many women worked on family farms and in textile and clothing workshops.
In Germany women worked mainly in agriculture, domestic service and textiles. They were barred from political associations until 1908, which held back their organisation.
The German women's movement was split between middle-class feminists and the SPD women's movement led by Clara Zetkin.
Women could not vote in national elections in Britain, France or Germany before the war. This matters because the vote later became the clearest measure of what the war changed.
The WSPU (Women's Social and Political Union) was founded in 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst. Its members were suffragettes, and from 1905 they used militant tactics.
The NUWSS (National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies), led by Millicent Fawcett, were suffragists who campaigned peacefully.
Remember the difference: suffragettes were militant and followed Pankhurst, while suffragists were peaceful and followed Fawcett.
Once the war began, men left their jobs for the army and women were drawn in to replace them.
Men volunteered in huge numbers and then conscription emptied workplaces, so employers faced a labour shortage.
After the Shell Crisis, the new Ministry of Munitions (1915) turned to women to make the shells the army needed.
Skilled men's unions feared that employers would replace them with cheaper workers. Dilution means employing unskilled workers, including women, on tasks done by skilled men.
In the Treasury Agreement of March 1915 the unions accepted dilution for the duration of the war.
The Munitions of War Act of July 1915 backed dilution and banned strikes in munitions work, so the government could keep production going.
Munitions (shells, fuses and explosives) was the largest and best-known area of women's war work, and also one of the most dangerous.

Hundreds of thousands of women worked in munitions by 1918, filling shells and fuses and making cordite (an explosive propellant). They worked at places such as Woolwich Arsenal and the national filling factories, and were known as 'munitionettes'.
Women in paid work in Britain rose from about 6 million in 1914 to about 7.3 million in 1918.
Conditions were hard: shifts of 10 to 12 hours, night work and the constant risk of explosion.
At Silvertown in east London a huge explosion in January 1917 killed 73. At the Chilwell national filling factory in Nottinghamshire an explosion in July 1918 killed over 130.
TNT poisoning (toxic jaundice) turned the skin yellow, which is why women munition workers were called 'canary girls'. It caused illness and some deaths.
The government responded with welfare supervisors and canteens, and set up the Health of Munition Workers Committee in 1915, because poor conditions reduced output.
Women in France and Germany also took over from men, though their experience differed in important ways.
France lost its men to the army early in the war, and the 1914 harvest was brought in largely by women, children and old men. Women ran family farms and businesses for the rest of the war.

From 1915 Albert Thomas, in charge of French munitions, encouraged women into arms factories. By 1918 women were about a quarter of French munitions workers, known as 'munitionnettes', including at Renault's Billancourt works.
Because so many men were at the front, French women also worked as tram conductors, postal workers, clerks and nurses.

In Germany the National Women's Service (Nationaler Frauendienst) was organised in August 1914 by middle-class feminists including Gertrud Bäumer. It organised food distribution and welfare, so it is a key example of women's voluntary war work.
More women worked in metal, chemical and engineering firms, with Krupp and Siemens employing many more women.
The Auxiliary Service Law of December 1916 took more men into war work, so it increased the pressure on women to fill gaps.
In Germany women bore the burden of food shortages, queuing for food, and from 1915 women led food protests and riots in German cities.
Women also entered many jobs outside munitions, which showed how far the war opened work that had been closed to them.
Women replaced men in banks, government offices and shops, and the numbers of women clerks and typists rose greatly in Britain, France and Germany.
Women worked on trams, buses and railways as conductors, ticket collectors and porters, and as postal workers. Some became women police and firefighters.
The Women's Land Army was formed in Britain in 1917, because the submarine campaign had made food a priority. At its peak it had about 16,000 to 23,000 members.
Voluntary Aid Detachments (VADs, founded 1909) supplied nurses and ambulance drivers. Vera Brittain served as a VAD nurse and later wrote Testament of Youth.
Edith Cavell, a British nurse in Brussels, was executed by a German firing squad on 12 October 1915 for helping Allied soldiers escape. Allied propaganda used her as a symbol.
Auxiliary services were created: the Women's Army Auxiliary Corps (1917), the Women's Royal Naval Service (1917) and the Women's Royal Air Force (April 1918).
In these services women worked as clerks, drivers, cooks, mechanics and telephonists, releasing men for the front.
Women's wartime work did not mean equality, because both pay and union attitudes held it back.
Women's pay rose compared with pre-war women's work, especially for former domestic servants. It stayed below men's for the same work.
Trade unions feared that employers would use women to undercut men's wages and skilled status.
So they agreed to dilution only for the duration of the war, with pre-war practices to be restored afterwards.
The war split the suffrage movement and changed how the public and politicians saw women.
In August 1914 Emmeline and Christabel Pankhurst suspended the WSPU's militant campaign, and the government released suffragette prisoners.
The Pankhursts backed the war. In July 1915 the WSPU held a 'Right to Serve' march in London, funded by the government (Lloyd George), to demand war work for women.
Sylvia Pankhurst opposed the war and worked among women in London's East End. Emmeline and Christabel formed the Women's Party in 1917.
Contemporary opinion changed: ministers and newspapers praised women's war work.
H. H. Asquith, long an opponent of women's suffrage, declared his support in the Commons in March 1917, citing women's war service.
