The most visible gain from the war years was the vote, though it was won on different terms in each country.
The Representation of the People Act of February 1918 gave the vote to men over 21 and to women over 30 who met a property qualification, about 8.4 million women. The Act applied to Ireland.
In December 1918 Constance Markievicz was elected as the first woman to Westminster, but she did not take her seat.
The Equal Franchise Act of 1928 gave women the vote at 21, on the same terms as men, so the wartime Act's age and property limits were removed.
In Germany a decree of 12 November 1918 gave women over 20 the vote and the right to stand.
Women voted in January 1919 and 37 women were elected to the National Assembly. The Weimar constitution made men and women equal in civic rights 'in principle'.
France gave women the vote only in 1944, despite war work equal to or greater than that of British women.
When the fighting ended, men needed their jobs back and women were pressed to leave. Only some legal gains remained.
German demobilisation decrees of 1918-19 made women give up jobs to returning soldiers.
Britain's Restoration of Pre-War Practices Act of 1919 reinstated the old trade rules, in line with the promise given to the unions.
Many women were dismissed from munitions, and some returned to domestic service, which was still a major employer in the 1920s.
The Sex Disqualification (Removal) Act of 1919 opened some professions and jury service to women in Britain.
However, marriage bars (rules forcing women to leave a job on marrying) remained in many jobs.
Examiners reward judgement, so each gain should be set against its limit and against how historians and contemporaries saw it.
Achievement: war work showed that women could do skilled and heavy jobs and increased their public presence and confidence. It helped win the vote in Britain and Germany and brought some legal gains.
Limit: most war jobs ended in 1918-19 and women's pay remained below men's. Traditional views of women's roles returned, and the British vote was limited to women over 30.
Contemporary view: many people thought women's war work proved their worth as citizens. Others, including many male workers, regarded it as a temporary emergency.
Arthur Marwick (The Deluge, 1965) argued that war was a catalyst of social change, including the status of women.
Gail Braybon (Women Workers in the First World War, 1981) and others argued that change was limited and temporary, and that the vote owed much to pre-war campaigning and political calculation.
Differences between countries: war work and the vote were linked in Britain and Germany, whereas French women gained the vote only in 1944.
The war enlarged the state and strengthened some groups, but at a very high human and economic cost.
Gains and growth: it was the first total war, and it enlarged the state, increased union power and widened welfare, including the Fisher Act's rise in the school-leaving age to 14.
Costs: casualties of about 9 to 10 million soldiers dead, devastation in northern France and Belgium, inflation, mounting debts and lost export markets.
Britain moved from creditor to debtor while the USA became the leading financial power.

Nationalism is loyalty to the nation and the belief that each nation should be united, strong and self-governing. Between 1871 and 1914 artists turned that belief into music, buildings and poetry, which is why culture matters in the story of the nation states.

Cultural nationalism used history, myth, folk tradition (the songs and tales of ordinary country people), language and landscape to prove that a people had a distinct identity, so a nation's art became evidence for its right to exist.

There were two kinds. Established, imperial states such as Germany and Britain used culture to express pride and power. Peoples without their own state, such as the Czechs, Finns and Norwegians, used it to assert an identity that their rulers did not recognise.

Across Europe, governments and nationalist societies spread national identity by founding national museums, galleries and theatres, teaching national history in schools and fostering national languages, so ordinary people absorbed it as well as artists.
Pre-1914 cultural nationalism fed the patriotic mood of 1914, because a generation had grown up taught that the nation deserved loyalty and sacrifice. It also shaped the idealistic early war poetry.
In Germany and Britain, nationalist culture celebrated a state that already existed and was powerful. It turned myth, history and empire into sources of pride.

Richard Wagner built his operas on Germanic myth, so they presented the Germans as heirs to an ancient heroic tradition. His Ring cycle (Der Ring des Nibelungen) was first staged in full at his own Bayreuth theatre in August 1876.

Wagner died in Venice in 1883, but the Bayreuth Festival continued under his widow Cosima as a shrine of German culture. His anti-Jewish essay 'Judaism in Music' (1850, republished under his name in 1869) links him to the anti-Semitism of the age.

The Hermann Monument in the Teutoburg Forest, completed in 1875, honours Arminius (Hermann), the Germanic leader who defeated three Roman legions in AD 9. The new Reich thus claimed a heroic ancestry of resistance to foreign rule.
The Monument to the Battle of the Nations at Leipzig was unveiled in 1913, the centenary of Napoleon's defeat there in 1813, so it tied German identity to the memory of a national victory.

Edward Elgar's Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1 (1901) supplied the tune for 'Land of Hope and Glory' in the Coronation Ode (1902), with words by A. C. Benson. Together they expressed British imperial confidence, for example in the praise of a great Empire.
Rudyard Kipling, who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1907, celebrated British soldiers and the Empire in Recessional (1897, refrain 'Lest we forget') and The White Man's Burden (1899).

Kipling's only son John was killed at the Battle of Loos in 1915. Kipling later worked for the Imperial War Graves Commission and chose the inscription 'Their Name Liveth for Evermore', so his life links imperial pride to the grief of the war.
For peoples ruled by an empire, music could say what politics forbade. Composers drew on their own history, landscape and folk tunes to show that the nation existed.

Bedřich Smetana's Má vlast ('My Country'), six symphonic poems (orchestral pieces that tell a story or paint a scene) composed in 1874-79, includes Vltava ('The Moldau'). It celebrated Bohemian history and landscape when Bohemia was part of Austria-Hungary and the Czechs sought more autonomy.

Jean Sibelius's Finlandia (1899, revised 1900) was written for a protest against Russian censorship of the Finnish press. Finland was a grand duchy of the Russian Empire, so the piece became a symbol of Finnish resistance to Russification (imposing Russian language and control on minorities).

Edvard Grieg wrote incidental music (music played during a play) for Henrik Ibsen's Peer Gynt, first performed in 1876, using the Norwegian folk idiom. Norway was in union with Sweden until 1905, so the music expressed a distinct Norwegian identity.
Because these peoples had no state of their own, culture was often their main means of proving they were a nation, which made art a form of political resistance.

War writing is best understood as a story of changing attitudes: patriotic idealism in 1914-15, then disillusionment, anger and pity, then a disenchanted post-war view. The reasons lie in how the war was fought.
On the Western Front (the line of trenches across France and Belgium), trench deadlock, gas, shelling and huge casualties from 1915 turned the hope of a short heroic war into years of mass death.
The Battle of the Somme (1 July to November 1916) shows the scale: on its first day the British army suffered about 57,000 casualties, about 19,000 of them dead.
Writers also felt a gap between home-front propaganda, which kept praising glory, and what soldiers experienced, so much later writing is angry at those who had not been there.

Censorship limited what soldiers could say in letters and the press. It did not stop protest being published during the war, because Le Feu appeared in 1916 and Sassoon's statement and The Old Huntsman in 1917.

In short, there are three phases: patriotic idealism (1914-15), disillusionment, anger and pity (1916-18), and the post-war 'disenchanted' view of the late 1920s, when a boom in war books ran from 1928 to 1933.
At first many writers saw the war as a noble cause and death for one's country as a fulfilment. This mood drew on the cultural nationalism of the pre-war years.

Rupert Brooke's 1914 sonnets, published in 1915, include The Soldier, in which he imagines that if he dies, some corner of a foreign field will be 'for ever England'. They expressed idealism about dying for England.

Brooke died of blood poisoning on a hospital ship off the Greek island of Skyros on 23 April 1915, on the way to Gallipoli. He never saw major combat, but his early death made him celebrated as the ideal patriot.
Julian Grenfell (Into Battle, 1915; died of wounds in May 1915) and John McCrae, a Canadian army doctor (In Flanders Fields, written in 1915), wrote in a similar spirit.
Contemporaries preferred this patriotic verse, because it matched the mood of the time. The protest poets were read widely only after 1918.
By 1917 officers who had survived the trenches began to write against the war. Siegfried Sassoon was the first to turn protest into a public act.
Siegfried Sassoon won the Military Cross in 1916, so when he protested he did so as a decorated officer, not a shirker.
In July 1917 he made a statement against the war, read out in the House of Commons and printed in The Times. It said the war was being 'deliberately prolonged' by those who had the power to end it.

Instead of a court martial he was sent to Craiglockhart War Hospital in Edinburgh in July 1917, after Robert Graves arranged a medical board. The army thus treated a decorated officer as ill rather than as a rebel.
His satire in The Old Huntsman (1917) and Counter-Attack (1918) attacked generals and the home front, which is why he is the model of the angry protest poet.
Other soldier-poets included Isaac Rosenberg (killed in April 1918), Edmund Blunden, who wrote Undertones of War (1928), and Ivor Gurney.
Sassoon survived the war and died in 1967, whereas Owen was killed in 1918.
Prose writers carried the argument beyond the poets, from a French infantryman's view written during the war to German and British bestsellers of the late 1920s and early 1930s.

Henri Barbusse, who served as a private soldier, wrote Le Feu (Under Fire, 1916) during the war. It won the Prix Goncourt, showed the suffering of ordinary French infantrymen in the trenches and turned against the war.

Ernst Jünger's In Stahlgewittern (Storm of Steel, 1920) gave the viewpoint of a German officer who found meaning in combat. It contrasts with the protest writers, so war literature did not speak with one voice.

Erich Maria Remarque served on the Western Front and published Im Westen nichts Neues (All Quiet on the Western Front) in 1929. This post-war German novel showed a lost generation of young soldiers ruined by the war and became a worldwide bestseller. The Nazis burned it in 1933.
In the boom in war books of 1928-33, Robert Graves published the memoir Goodbye to All That (1929). Vera Brittain published Testament of Youth (1933), a woman's view of the war.
Together, Remarque, Graves and Brittain shaped later memory of the war. This is why the post-war view is called disenchanted: it looked back on the war as a loss rather than a cause.
Historians use war literature as a source, but it is not a simple record of what soldiers thought. Its value and its limits both matter when you judge it.
Its strengths are eyewitness detail and strong feeling, so poems and memoirs convey the sights, sounds and emotions of the trenches in a way official reports do not.
Its limits are that the best-known writers were mostly educated officers and wrote for effect, so they may not speak for ordinary soldiers.

Many soldiers kept their belief that the war was justified. This is why revisionist historians such as Dan Todman, in The Great War: Myth and Memory (2005), argue that the poets' view became the 'myth' of a futile war which most soldiers did not share.

Wilfred Owen fought as an officer and wrote as a witness for the men he led. He became the English poet most closely linked with the suffering of the war, yet almost nothing he wrote was published in his lifetime.

Owen was born on 18 March 1893 in Oswestry, Shropshire (in England, near the Welsh border, not in Wales), the eldest of four children of a railway worker. He was lay assistant to the vicar of Dunsden, Oxfordshire (1911-13), then taught English in Bordeaux from 1913.

He enlisted in the Artists Rifles in October 1915 and was commissioned in the Manchester Regiment in June 1916. In January 1917 he joined the 2nd Manchesters on the Somme sector, near Beaumont-Hamel, in severe winter conditions.

In March 1917 he suffered concussion. In April a shell blew him into the air and he lay for several days near the remains of a fellow officer. He was diagnosed with neurasthenia (shell shock, a nervous breakdown caused by the strain of bombardment).

He arrived at Craiglockhart War Hospital in Edinburgh in June 1917 and edited its magazine, The Hydra. He met Siegfried Sassoon there in August 1917, and Sassoon encouraged him. He met Robert Graves there in October 1917.

Between autumn 1917 and autumn 1918 he wrote or revised his best poems: Dulce et Decorum Est (drafted October 1917), Anthem for Doomed Youth (autumn 1917, opening 'What passing-bells for these who die as cattle?'), Strange Meeting, Futility and Exposure.
He was both participant and witness: an officer who fought, and who wrote on behalf of the men he led, so his poems carry the authority of experience.
Owen's poems attack the idea that war is glorious, using the detail of what he had witnessed. His fame came after his death, and historians still debate what he represents.
Dulce et Decorum Est attacks 'The old Lie: Dulce et decorum est / Pro patria mori' (from Horace: it is sweet and fitting to die for one's country). Owen aims it at those at home who spread the idea.

His method was graphic detail of gas, mud and death, and pararhyme (matching consonants with a changed vowel instead of full rhyme, as in Strange Meeting), which sounds uneasy and unresolved. His draft preface says 'My subject is War, and the pity of War. The Poetry is in the pity.'
He returned to France in late summer 1918 and won the Military Cross for action at Joncourt on 1 October 1918. It was announced only after his death.
He was killed on 4 November 1918 crossing the Sambre-Oise canal near Ors, aged 25, a week before the armistice. The telegram reached his parents in Shrewsbury on 11 November 1918.
Owen was almost unknown in his lifetime, with only about five poems published. Poems (1920) was edited by Sassoon with Edith Sitwell, and Edmund Blunden produced a fuller edition in 1931.

Contemporaries: in the 1920s he was one of several war poets, and the public were drawn at first to Brooke. In 1936 W. B. Yeats excluded him from The Oxford Book of Modern Verse. Interest grew after the 1930s as pacifist feeling spread.

Later reputation: Benjamin Britten's War Requiem (1962), written for the consecration of the new Coventry Cathedral, sets nine Owen poems, and Owen became the best-known English poet of the war, taught in schools.

Historians: the biographers Jon Stallworthy (1974) and Dominic Hibberd (2002) stress his craft and development. Revisionists such as Dan Todman argue that the war poets' view became a myth of futile war not shared by most soldiers, and the poets' view came from an educated officer class.
The new German Reich was divided by religion. Chancellor Bismarck came to see the Catholic Church as a rival loyalty, and the conflict that followed was called the Kulturkampf.

The Reich, proclaimed in January 1871, was a Protestant-led state under Prussia. Protestants were about two-thirds of its people and Catholics about a third, living mainly in the south, the Rhineland and the Polish east.

In July 1870 the First Vatican Council (a gathering of the Church's bishops) declared papal infallibility, the doctrine that the Pope cannot err when defining Church teaching. Bismarck feared that German Catholics now owed their loyalty to Rome rather than to the Reich.

The Catholic Centre Party, founded in December 1870 and led by Ludwig Windthorst, defended Catholic interests. Bismarck called Catholics, socialists and national minorities 'Reichsfeinde' (enemies of the Reich) and saw the Centre as an enemy of the new state.
He also feared Polish Catholics in the east, because as a national minority whose faith set them apart from Protestant Prussia they seemed disloyal.

The National Liberals, his allies in the Reichstag, were anticlerical (opposed to Church influence in public life). They welcomed an attack on the Church as a defence of modern secular society, so the campaign had liberal support.
The conflict took its name in 1873 from Rudolf Virchow, a Progressive (liberal) deputy and scientist, who called it a Kulturkampf ('struggle for civilisation' or culture).
Between 1871 and 1875 the Prussian and Reich governments passed laws that put schools, clergy and marriage under state control. The order matters, because each step escalated the conflict.

In July 1871 the Catholic department of the Prussian Ministry of Culture was abolished, and in December 1871 the Reich's Pulpit Law (Kanzelparagraph) made it an offence for clergy to criticise the state in sermons.

The School Supervision Law (Prussia, March 1872) put schools under state inspection, so the state rather than the clergy checked them. The Jesuit Law (July 1872) expelled the Jesuits (a Catholic religious order seen as loyal to the Pope) from Germany.
In May 1872 Bismarck told the Reichstag, 'We will not go to Canossa' (Nach Canossa gehen wir nicht), a vow not to give way to the papacy.

The May Laws of 1873 (Prussia), piloted by Adalbert Falk, Prussian Minister of Culture 1872-79, required priests to be educated at state universities and pass state exams, and made state approval necessary for church appointments.

Further laws followed. Civil marriage (a state ceremony instead of a church one) became compulsory in Prussia in 1874 and in the whole Reich in 1875. The Breadbasket Law of 1875 stopped state payments to the clergy, and most religious orders were dissolved in 1875.
Take care with names, because several laws share a label: these are the Prussian May Laws of 1873, not the Russian anti-Jewish May Laws of 1882 or the Anti-Socialist Law of 1878.
The laws did not break Catholic loyalty to the Church. They drove Catholics together, and within a few years Bismarck needed peace.
Pope Pius IX's encyclical Quod Nunquam (February 1875) declared the Prussian laws invalid. An encyclical is a formal letter from the Pope to the Church, known by its opening Latin words.
By 1876 every Prussian bishop was in prison or exile, and many parishes had no priest, because priests could not be appointed without state approval.

Catholics rallied behind the Centre under Ludwig Windthorst. In the Reichstag election of 1874 the Centre's vote roughly doubled, to about 1.4 million, and it won about 90 seats, making it the second-largest party.

Bismarck had reasons to end it. The policy had failed and strengthened the Centre. He needed Centre votes for the tariff law of 1879 and against the socialists, the new enemy (the Anti-Socialist Law of 1878), and he had broken with the National Liberals.
Pius IX died in February 1878 and Leo XIII was elected on 20 February 1878. The new pope was ready to negotiate, and Falk resigned in July 1879.
After negotiations with Leo XIII, mitigation laws (1880-83) and peace laws (1886-87) repealed or relaxed most of the measures.
Civil marriage, state school inspection and the Pulpit Law stayed. The Jesuit Law was relaxed in 1904 and repealed in 1917.
The Kulturkampf began as an attempt to subdue the Church and ended with the state giving way. Its results show the limits of Bismarck's power.
It was a political defeat for Bismarck, so he had to compromise with the Church and rely on the Centre Party he had set out to crush.
The Centre became a permanent, large party in the Reichstag, because the attack had united Catholics behind it.
Catholics felt alienated from the Protestant-led Reich, which left a lasting religious division in German politics.
Many people saw it as a model of state-church conflict and as a failure of liberalism, because liberals had welcomed state force against a religious minority.
In Italy the quarrel ran the other way round. The state was not attacking the Church; the Pope refused to accept a state that had taken his territory.

Until 1870 the Pope ruled central Italy as a temporal (worldly) ruler over the Papal States. The Kingdom of Italy, proclaimed in March 1861, took most of them, and Italian troops entered Rome on 20 September 1870 (the breach at Porta Pia). Rome became the capital in 1871.
The First Vatican Council had declared papal infallibility only in July 1870, just before Rome was lost, so the Pope lost his territory at the moment he claimed greater spiritual authority.

The Law of Guarantees (May 1871) declared the Pope's person inviolable (he could not be attacked or arrested), gave him use of the Vatican, the Lateran and Castel Gandolfo, and offered a yearly payment.

Pius IX rejected the law and refused the payment, because accepting a law made by the Italian parliament would have meant recognising the state that had taken Rome. He described himself as a prisoner in the Vatican.

This unresolved dispute over the Pope's loss of Rome and his status was the Roman Question. The papacy's refusal to accept the loss divided Italians between the liberal, anticlerical state and the Catholic population.
The Pope's refusal also shaped Italian politics, because he told Catholics to keep away from the state's elections. Catholics responded by building a separate world of their own.
Non expedit ('it is not expedient') was an instruction of 1868, confirmed in 1874, that Catholics should neither vote in nor stand for parliamentary elections.
As a result most Catholics stayed outside national politics, which left a narrow liberal ruling class in control of parliament.
Catholics remained active in local government and in social organisations: the Opera dei Congressi (founded 1874), Catholic Action, banks, newspapers and cooperatives.
The liberal state meanwhile expanded civil marriage and secular state schooling and closed religious houses, which deepened the divide.

Leo XIII kept the hard line on Rome. Pius X relaxed non expedit from 1905, and in the Gentiloni Pact of 1913 Catholic voters backed the liberal candidates of Giovanni Giolitti who promised to defend Catholic interests.

In January 1919, for example, Don Luigi Sturzo founded the Italian Popular Party (Partito Popolare Italiano). The Roman Question was settled only by the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, beyond this period.

Compare the two countries. Germany's conflict was an attack by the state on the Church and was ended by compromise by 1887. Italy's was the Church's refusal to accept the state, and it lasted until 1929.
France's own quarrel between church and state is the setting for both Leo XIII's ralliement and the Dreyfus Affair, so its background has to be clear.

After defeat by Prussia in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870-71, France lost Alsace and part of Lorraine to Germany (Treaty of Frankfurt, 1871) and the Third Republic began in 1870. The army became the symbol of national pride and revenge.
The Third Republic was divided between republicans, who were often anticlerical (hostile to the Church's role in public life), and monarchist Catholics, who distrusted the republic.

The republic passed anticlerical laws: Jules Ferry's education laws of 1881-82 (free, compulsory, secular primary schooling), the Law of Associations (1901) and the Law of Separation of Church and State (December 1905). The Dreyfus Affair sped them up, because much of the Church sided against Dreyfus's defenders.
Leo XIII was pope from 1878 to 1903. After the confrontational reign of Pius IX he tried to renew the Church's relations with governments and the modern world.

Gioacchino (Vincenzo) Pecci was born on 2 March 1810 at Carpineto Romano. He was nuncio (the Pope's ambassador) to Belgium in 1843-46, Archbishop of Perugia 1846-78 and a cardinal from 1853, and was a diplomat and scholar.

He was elected pope on 20 February 1878, after Pius IX's reign (1846-78, marked by infallibility, the 'prisoner in the Vatican' stance and the Kulturkampf at its height). He remained pope until his death on 20 July 1903, aged 93.

He ended the Kulturkampf by negotiation with Bismarck in the 1880s, and the Centre Party's cooperation with the government helped to repeal most of the laws. In 1885 Bismarck referred the Caroline Islands dispute between Germany and Spain to him for arbitration.
He encouraged scholarship. His encyclical Aeterni Patris (1879) urged the study of Thomas Aquinas, and in 1881 he opened the Vatican archives to researchers.
In April 1888 the Holy Office (a Vatican department) issued a decree condemning the Plan of Campaign and boycotting in Ireland, which gives his papacy an Irish link.
He refused to accept the loss of the Papal States and kept the 'prisoner in the Vatican' stance and non expedit in Italy, so the Roman Question remained open. He was also conservative on doctrine.

Leo XIII is best known for two initiatives, a statement on workers' rights and a call for French Catholics to accept the republic. Both show how he tried to move the papacy from lost territory to moral influence.

Rerum Novarum (15 May 1891), an encyclical on 'the condition of the working classes' (the rights and duties of capital and labour), answered the social question in general terms. It rejected socialism and class war and defended private property.

It upheld the right of workers to a just wage, decent conditions and trade unions, and called on states to protect workers and the poor. It thus offered Catholics a route between socialism and unregulated capitalism.

Rerum Novarum became the foundation of modern Catholic social teaching and encouraged Catholic trade unions and Christian democratic parties in Germany, Belgium, Italy and elsewhere. Pius XI marked its fortieth anniversary with Quadragesimo Anno (1931), which shows its lasting influence.

The ralliement ('rallying') of 1890-92 urged French Catholics to accept the republic and work within it. It began with Cardinal Lavigerie's toast to the republic at Algiers in November 1890 and was set out in the encyclical Au milieu des sollicitudes (February 1892).

Monarchist Catholics largely refused. The Dreyfus Affair and the anticlerical laws of the early 1900s, ending in the 1905 separation of church and state, wrecked the policy, because much of the Church sided with the anti-Dreyfusards.

Contemporaries: governments and many workers respected him as a moderate reformer. Conservative Catholics distrusted his accommodation with republics, and socialists opposed his rejection of socialism.

Historians regard him as the first modern pope, who moved the papacy from lost temporal power to moral and social influence. Critics regard Rerum Novarum as cautious and paternalist, and the ralliement as a failure.
Anti-Semitism is hostility to Jews as a people. After 1870 older religious prejudice was joined by political and racial forms, which is why it matters in this period.

Anti-Jewish prejudice was old in Europe and had been mainly religious. After 1870 political and racial anti-Semitism spread. Wilhelm Marr popularised the word 'anti-Semitism' and founded the League of Antisemites in 1879; the term existed before him.
Economic depression from the stock-market crash of 1873 made many people resent Jewish success in finance, trade and the professions, and look for scapegoats.

Nationalism that defined the nation by blood or religion treated Jews as outsiders, and pseudo-scientific race theory (claims, without scientific basis, that humans divide into biologically different races) gave prejudice a modern look.
Jews were blamed at once for modernity, capitalism and socialism, so anti-Semites of very different politics could all find a target.
French Jews were a small, assimilated minority, yet after 1870 nationalists and journalists made them scapegoats. The Dreyfus Affair grew out of this mood.

French Jews had been full citizens since 1791. Defeat in 1870-71, the Panama Canal Company scandal of 1892 and economic fears gave anti-Semites targets, and nationalists blamed Jews and Freemasons for the country's weakness.
Édouard Drumont's La France juive (1886) was a bestseller that portrayed Jews as a threat to France. In 1892 he founded the newspaper La Libre Parole to carry on the campaign.

Captain Alfred Dreyfus, born in Mulhouse, Alsace, in 1859, was a Jewish artillery officer on the General Staff. Arrested on 15 October 1894, he was accused of passing secrets to Germany; the evidence was a memorandum, the bordereau.

A court martial sitting in closed session convicted him in December 1894, after the judges were shown a secret file not given to the defence. He was publicly degraded on 5 January 1895 and sent to Devil's Island in French Guiana.
The case became an Affair when evidence of Dreyfus's innocence emerged and the army refused to admit its mistake. Public opinion then split France in two.

In 1896 Lieutenant-Colonel Georges Picquart, head of army intelligence, identified Major Ferdinand Walsin-Esterhazy as the real author of the bordereau. The army suppressed this: Picquart was posted to Tunisia, and Esterhazy was acquitted by court martial on 11 January 1898.

On 13 January 1898 Émile Zola published the open letter 'J'accuse...!' to President Félix Faure in the newspaper L'Aurore (its editor Georges Clemenceau chose the headline), accusing the army of covering up the truth. Zola was convicted of libel in February and fled to England in July 1898.

France divided. Dreyfusards, who defended Dreyfus, included Zola, Clemenceau, the socialist leader Jean Jaurès, many republicans and intellectuals, and the League of the Rights of Man (founded 1898). Anti-Dreyfusards included army leaders, much of the Catholic press, nationalists, monarchists and anti-Semitic leagues.
Anti-Jewish riots broke out in French cities and in Algeria in 1898, which shows how far the prejudice had spread.
In August 1898 the forgery by Lieutenant-Colonel Henry was exposed, and he cut his throat in prison.
A second court martial at Rennes (August-September 1899) again found Dreyfus guilty, 'with extenuating circumstances', and gave him ten years. President Émile Loubet pardoned him in September 1899.
In July 1906 the Cour de cassation (France's highest appeal court) quashed the Rennes verdict, and Dreyfus was reinstated in the army as a major and given the Legion of Honour.
The Affair changed French politics, and it also had an effect beyond France through the birth of political Zionism.
It was a republican victory and ended in justice for one man, because the courts and a free press could finally correct the army's error.

It discredited the army, whose leaders had covered up the truth, and the Church, much of whose press had sided with the anti-Dreyfusards. It led to the anticlerical laws of the early 1900s and the 1905 separation of church and state.
A new nationalist right emerged, such as Action Française (founded 1899), and anti-Semitism survived the Affair.
Theodor Herzl reported on the case for the Vienna Neue Freie Presse and later said it convinced him that Jews needed a state of their own. Historians debate how much it mattered.
Herzl published Der Judenstaat (The Jewish State) in 1896, and the First Zionist Congress, the first meeting of the movement for a Jewish national home (Zionism), met at Basel in August 1897.
In the Russian Empire anti-Jewish prejudice was backed by the state. Laws confined Jews and kept many poor, and violent attacks on them were tolerated.

The Empire was a tsarist autocracy (rule by a tsar with unlimited power) with the Orthodox Church as the state church and a policy of Russification (imposing Russian language and control on minorities).
About five million Jews lived in the Empire in the late 1800s (the 1897 census), the largest Jewish population in the world. Many were poor artisans and traders.
Most were confined to the Pale of Settlement, the western provinces where Jews were allowed to live, created in 1791 under Catherine the Great and abolished in 1917.

Alexander II was assassinated on 13 March 1881 (1 March in the Russian calendar), and rumours blamed Jews. Pogroms (violent attacks on Jewish communities) began at Elizavetgrad in April 1881 and spread across the south, including Kiev and Odessa, continuing to 1884.
Officials were slow to act or blamed the victims, so the violence spread unchecked.

The May Laws (Temporary Regulations) of May 1882 banned new Jewish settlement in rural areas and restricted Jews from acquiring land and property outside towns. Though called temporary, they remained in force until 1917.
Under Alexander III and Nicholas II discrimination became settled government policy, and violence continued.

From 1887 quotas (numerus clausus) limited the number of Jewish students in secondary schools and universities. About 20,000 Jews were expelled from Moscow in 1891-92, and there were limits on the professions.

Konstantin Pobedonostsev, Over-Procurator of the Holy Synod (the state official in charge of the Orthodox Church) from 1880 to 1905 and tutor and adviser to Alexander III and Nicholas II, supported discrimination and Russification. Alexander III and Nicholas II were themselves personally hostile to Jews.
Some clergy spread anti-Jewish propaganda. From 1905 the Union of the Russian People, whose street gangs were called the Black Hundreds, did the same.

The Kishinev pogrom in Bessarabia, at Easter on 6-7 April 1903 (19-20 April in the Western calendar), killed about 49 Jews and injured hundreds, and caused international outrage. Hayim Nahman Bialik wrote his poem 'In the City of Slaughter' in response.
More pogroms followed in 1905-06 during the revolution, after the October Manifesto of 1905, and were worst in Odessa.
For example, in the Beilis case Menahem Mendel Beilis, a Kiev Jew, was arrested in 1911 and tried for 'ritual murder' (the false claim that Jews murder for religious rites). He was acquitted in 1913.
Forged propaganda spread the myth of a Jewish plot, while Jews responded by leaving, organising or joining revolution. The legal system ended only in 1917.

The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, which claimed a Jewish plot to dominate the world, was forged in Russia. It was first serialised in the St Petersburg paper Znamya in 1903 and appeared in book form in 1905 (Sergei Nilus).
In 1921 The Times showed that it was plagiarised from Maurice Joly's satire of Napoleon III (1864). It spread worldwide after 1917.
About two million Jews left the Russian Empire between 1881 and 1914, most to the USA and others to Britain and Palestine, because persecution and poverty made life there hard.

The General Jewish Labour Bund, a Jewish socialist party, was founded in Vilna in 1897. Zionism, the movement for a Jewish national home, was separate: it was a national movement, not a socialist one.
Many young Jews also joined revolutionary parties, so persecution pushed some towards revolution as well as emigration.
The Provisional Government removed all legal restrictions on Jews in March and April 1917, ending the Pale and the legal disabilities. Pogroms returned in the civil war.
Examiners reward judgement, so each theme from national identity to anti-Semitism needs both a success and a limit. Each point pairs them.

National identity in the arts: it liberated peoples without a state, such as the Czechs, Finns and Norwegians, but in Germany and Britain it fed imperial pride, exclusive nationalism and the war spirit of 1914.

War literature: 1914-15 patriotism against 1917-18 protest. Contemporaries preferred Brooke, later generations Owen and Sassoon. The literature is valuable as eyewitness evidence, but the 'myth' argument reminds us that most soldiers did not share the protest view.
Kulturkampf: a success in state control of schools and marriage, but a political failure, because the Centre was strengthened and Bismarck was forced to compromise.
Italy: the liberal state survived and kept Rome, but there was a lasting split from Catholic Italy until 1929.
Leo XIII: achievements in ending the Kulturkampf, Rerum Novarum and papal prestige, against limits in the failed ralliement and the unresolved Roman Question.

Anti-Semitism compared: in France a popular and press movement that a republic finally defeated in the courts, giving justice to Dreyfus. In Russia a state-backed policy of laws and tolerated violence that drove mass emigration. Prejudice survived in both.

Marie Curie was a Polish-born physicist and chemist who worked in France. Her research on radioactivity made her one of the most important scientists of the period and the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.

Maria Skłodowska was born in Warsaw on 7 November 1867, when Poland was under Russian rule. Women could not attend university there, so in 1891 she went to study physics and mathematics at the Sorbonne (the University of Paris).

In 1895 she married the physicist Pierre Curie. After Henri Becquerel found in 1896 that uranium gave off penetrating rays, she researched them for her doctorate and coined the word 'radioactivity'. Atoms were thought unchangeable, but radioactivity showed atoms could break down and give off energy.

She found pitchblende more radioactive than its uranium could explain, so it must hold new elements: polonium, named after Poland (July 1898), and radium (December 1898). Separating radium salt from tonnes of it in a shed took until 1902; pure radium metal followed with André Debierne in 1910.

She shared the 1903 Nobel Prize for Physics with Pierre Curie and Becquerel, the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. After Pierre was killed in a Paris street accident in April 1906, she took over his post as the first woman professor at the Sorbonne.

She won the 1911 Nobel Prize for Chemistry, alone, for polonium and radium, the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences. In 1911 the French Academy of Sciences rejected her by a narrow vote, and the press attacked her over Paul Langevin, partly on xenophobic (anti-foreign) grounds.

In the First World War she organised about 20 mobile X-ray vehicles, called 'petites Curies', for the front, plus about 200 fixed radiological posts. Her daughter Irène helped train women to run them, and she learned to drive to take the units out.

The Radium Institute in Paris was completed in 1914, and radium was later used against cancer (radiotherapy). She died on 4 July 1934 of aplastic anaemia, probably caused by long exposure to radiation, whose dangers were not understood in her working life.

Contemporaries admired her as a great scientist and national hero in France and Poland, but some resented a foreign woman in a leading post. Historians see her as a founder of the study of radioactivity, opening the way to atomic physics and radiotherapy, and a pioneer for women in science.
Before 1870 most doctors blamed disease on 'miasma' (bad air from filth). The discovery that microbes cause disease changed that, and it is the basis of the medical progress of 1870 to 1920.

Louis Pasteur showed in the 1860s that microbes cause fermentation and decay, and argued that they also cause disease; this is germ theory. Pasteurisation (heating liquids to kill microbes) came from this work.

Pasteur made vaccines from weakened microbes, so the body learns to resist the real disease: against chicken cholera (about 1879) and anthrax (1881, shown in a public trial). In July 1885 he treated a nine-year-old boy, Joseph Meister, bitten by a rabid dog, and the boy survived.
The Pasteur Institute in Paris was founded in 1887 and opened in 1888 so that research could continue and vaccines could be made in quantity.

Robert Koch in Germany developed pure cultures (growing one kind of bacterium alone) and staining methods, which let others identify the germs of many diseases. He found the anthrax bacterium (1876), the tuberculosis bacillus (announced 24 March 1882) and the cholera bacterium (1883).
Koch won the Nobel Prize for Medicine in 1905. The rivalry of Pasteur (French) and Koch (German) had a national edge after the war of 1870-71, so science also became a source of national prestige.

Emil von Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburo developed antitoxins (substances that neutralise a germ's poison) against diphtheria and tetanus in 1890. Behring received the first Nobel Prize for Medicine in 1901.
Paul Ehrlich developed Salvarsan, effective against syphilis, in 1909-10. It was the first modern chemotherapy (a chemical aimed at killing a disease germ), based on his 'magic bullet' idea.
Surgery before anaesthetics and antiseptics was fast, painful and often fatal from infection. Three steps made it safer: stopping pain, killing germs, then keeping germs out altogether.

Anaesthetics (drugs that stop pain) came first: ether in 1846 and chloroform in 1847. Queen Victoria's use of chloroform in childbirth in 1853 made it acceptable, and longer operations became possible.

Joseph Lister, a surgeon working in Glasgow, used carbolic acid on wounds, dressings and instruments from 1865 and published his results in 1867. He built on Pasteur's work, and deaths from infection after surgery fell sharply.

This is antisepsis: killing germs that are already present. From the 1880s, especially in German hospitals, surgeons moved on to asepsis, which keeps germs out of the wound at all, because prevention is safer than killing germs already there.
Asepsis used steam sterilisation of instruments and gowns, and later rubber gloves. With anaesthetics and asepsis together, surgery became much safer.

Public health measures such as clean water supplies, sewers, and better food and housing cut deaths from cholera and typhoid in European cities, with clean water and sewers built from the 1850s. Germ theory explained why these worked, since they stopped microbes spreading.
Between the 1870s and 1914 new physics and new machines changed medicine and everyday life. X-rays, electric power and wireless are the examples to know.

Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays at Würzburg in November 1895, famously making an X-ray image of his wife's hand. Doctors quickly used them to find broken bones, since the rays pass through flesh but not bone, and he won the first Nobel Prize for Physics in 1901.
In the First World War X-ray equipment became standard in military hospitals, used to locate bullets and shrapnel (metal fragments from shells). Curie's mobile units took it close to the front.
Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone in 1876, and telephone exchanges and networks spread in cities in the 1880s and 1890s.

Thomas Edison invented the phonograph in 1877 and a long-lasting electric light bulb in 1879, while Joseph Swan in England worked on the bulb at the same time. The first public power stations opened in 1882 (London and New York), so electric lighting, trams and underground railways spread in cities.

Guglielmo Marconi, whose mother was Annie Jameson of the Irish whiskey family, developed wireless telegraphy (signals sent without wires) from 1895-96 and patented it in Britain in 1896. He shared the 1909 Nobel Prize for Physics.
On 12 December 1901 a signal sent from Poldhu, Cornwall, was received in Newfoundland, proving wireless could cross the Atlantic. A station at Clifden, Co. Galway, opened in 1907.
Wireless mattered at sea and in war: distress calls brought rescue ships when the Titanic sank in April 1912, and it was used for military communication in the First World War.
The Nobel Prizes were first awarded in 1901 under the will of Alfred Nobel, a Swedish chemist who invented dynamite. Early prizes were dominated by German and French scientists.
Powered flight arrived at the start of the twentieth century and was developed quickly by war. Alongside it came advances in engines, chemistry and physics.

Count Zeppelin's first rigid airship flew in 1900. The Wright brothers, Orville and Wilbur, made the first controlled, powered, sustained flight of a heavier-than-air machine at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on 17 December 1903.
Louis Blériot flew across the English Channel on 25 July 1909. Flying displays and prizes in Europe attracted publicity, so public interest in aviation grew.
In the First World War aircraft were used for reconnaissance, artillery spotting, bombing and air combat. Production rose from hundreds to tens of thousands, so engines improved fast.
John Alcock and Arthur Whitten Brown made the first non-stop transatlantic flight in June 1919, from Newfoundland to a bog near Clifden, Co. Galway.
Rudolf Diesel applied for a patent in 1892 for his compression-ignition engine, in which fuel ignites from the heat of compressed air rather than from a spark.

Fritz Haber (laboratory synthesis in 1909) and Carl Bosch (industrial process, first plant 1913) made ammonia from the air. This allowed artificial fertilisers and, in the war, explosives for Germany despite the blockade.
Albert Einstein published the special theory of relativity in 1905 and the general theory in 1915.
Karl Benz was the engineer who designed the first practical car as a complete machine. He was a participant, not a witness: he designed and built it himself, with his wife Bertha as partner.

Karl Benz was born on 25 November 1844 near Karlsruhe (at Mühlburg), the son of a locomotive driver who died when Karl was a small child. He studied mechanical engineering at the Karlsruhe Polytechnic.

A first engineering business in Mannheim failed. To earn money he built a working two-stroke gas engine, running in 1879, and in 1883 he founded Benz & Cie in Mannheim, building stationary gas engines, which paid for his car work.
He designed the car as a whole, not as an engine added to a carriage: a light three-wheeled vehicle with a single-cylinder four-stroke petrol engine at the rear, running in 1885.
He applied for a patent on 29 January 1886 for the 'Benz Patent-Motorwagen' (motor carriage), and it was granted in November 1886. It is often called the birth certificate of the car.
Bertha Benz was his wife and business partner, and her money helped fund the firm. Her 1888 drive gave publicity and showed faults he then fixed, such as the need for a lower gear for hills.
The Benz Velo of 1894 was the first car built in series (many copies of one design). By about 1900 Benz & Cie was among the largest car makers in the world, and France was its biggest early market.

Benz was cautious about faster, more powerful designs, so he fell behind the Daimler company's Mercedes after 1901, and he left day-to-day management in the early 1900s. In 1926 Benz & Cie merged with the Daimler company to form Daimler-Benz, and he died in 1929.

He is honoured in Germany as the inventor of the car. Historians credit him with the first practical car designed as a whole, but stress that Daimler and Maybach's engine, French manufacturers and Ford's mass production were equally needed to make the car a success.

Before the car, road transport meant horses and carriages and, from the 1880s, the bicycle, while railways carried long-distance traffic. The car emerged in Germany and France in the 1880s from the internal combustion engine and from the bicycle and carriage industries.
The bicycle trade supplied skills, light frames, chain drive and tyres to the early car makers, which is why the car grew out of it rather than out of the railway.

Steam road vehicles and electric cars had been tried earlier. Petrol won because its engine was light, it gave a long range, and refuelling was quick, whereas steam needed time to raise steam and electric cars needed slow recharging.

Nikolaus Otto built the first practical four-stroke gas engine in 1876 at the Deutz company near Cologne. Its four strokes are intake, compression, power and exhaust, and it became the basis of the petrol engine.

Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach, formerly of Deutz, developed a small, light, high-speed petrol engine in the 1880s. It was fitted to a wooden motorcycle in 1885 and to a four-wheeled carriage in 1886, which was a converted coach, not a car designed as a whole.

They founded the Daimler company, Daimler-Motoren-Gesellschaft, in 1890. Benz's three-wheeled Motorwagen, patented in 1886, was the first vehicle designed as a whole, and Benz and Daimler worked separately, about 100 km apart.
After 1886 the car had to prove itself on the road and then find makers and customers. Publicity from a famous journey, French manufacturers and new tyres all helped in the 1880s and 1890s.
In August 1888 Bertha Benz drove a Motorwagen from Mannheim to Pforzheim, about 100 km, with her sons Eugen and Richard and without telling Karl. This showed that a car could travel a long distance.
On the way she bought fuel (ligroin, a light petroleum) at a pharmacy in Wiesloch and made roadside repairs. The journey proved the car practical, and the publicity helped sales.

In France, Panhard et Levassor and Peugeot began building cars in 1890-91 with Daimler-licensed engines. France led early car production, with trials such as Paris-Rouen (1894) boosting interest, and it was the biggest car producer in Europe before 1914.
Louis Renault built his first car in 1898 and the Renault company followed in 1899.

John Boyd Dunlop, a Scottish vet in Belfast, patented the pneumatic (air-filled) tyre in 1888 for his son's tricycle. It made bicycles and cars run more smoothly, and the Michelin brothers brought out a detachable pneumatic tyre in 1891.
By 1900 cars were still handmade and slow, and law held them back in Britain. A new design, new rules and new makers in the next decade moved the car forward.
In Britain the 'red flag' laws, which required a man with a flag to walk in front of early vehicles, limited them to walking pace.
The Locomotives on Highways Act of 1896 raised the speed limit and ended the red-flag rules. It was celebrated by the Emancipation Run from London to Brighton on 14 November 1896.

Daimler died in 1900. In 1901 the Daimler company produced the Mercedes, designed by Maybach and named after Mercédès, the daughter of the businessman Emil Jellinek. It was lighter, more powerful and lower than earlier cars, so it set the pattern for later cars.
The Mercedes was a Daimler car, not a Benz car, until the two firms merged in 1926.
Charles Rolls and Henry Royce met in 1904, and the Rolls-Royce Silver Ghost (1906-07) made Britain known for luxury cars.

In Ireland the Gordon Bennett motor race was held on 2 July 1903 in Co. Kildare, Queen's County (Laois) and Co. Carlow. The Motor Car Act 1903 brought registration plates, driving licences and a 20 mph limit for Britain and Ireland, in force from 1904.
Early cars were handmade, expensive and uncomfortable, so motoring before 1914 was for the rich. You need this detail to place a document such as an advertisement or a motorist's account.
Cars were luxury goods for the wealthy, and advertisements were aimed at the upper classes. Drivers were often employed as chauffeurs, and motoring clubs and early tourism grew.
There were no filling stations, so fuel was bought in cans from chemists, shops or hotels. This is why a journey needed planning, as Bertha Benz's drive showed.
Cars were open, with no roof or windscreen, so drivers wore protective goggles and dust coats. Unsurfaced roads threw up dust, and candle or acetylene lamps gave poor light.

Breakdowns and punctures were frequent, and poor oil made engines unreliable. Early motorists also met hostility from farmers, carters, cyclists and pedestrians, who disliked the noise, dust and danger.
Doctors, salesmen and country clergy were among the early users of cars before 1914, because they travelled far and could make use of the speed.

Ford turned the car from a luxury into a product ordinary people could buy by cutting the cost of making it. The Model T (1908), the moving assembly line (1913) and the five-dollar day (1914) are three different steps to keep apart.
Henry Ford founded the Ford Motor Company in Detroit in 1903, because he wanted to build a cheap, simple car for ordinary people.

The Model T, launched in October 1908, was simple, strong and easy to repair. It cost about 850 dollars at launch, and the price was cut again and again as output rose, falling by more than half within about eight years, so far more people could buy one.

In 1913 Ford introduced the moving assembly line at Highland Park, Michigan: the chassis (the car's frame) moved past workers, who each did one task, using standard interchangeable parts. Chassis assembly time fell from over 12 hours to about 90 minutes.

Dull, repetitive work caused very high staff turnover. In January 1914 Ford announced the five-dollar day, about double the usual pay for an eight-hour day, which kept workers and meant they could become customers.
By 1920 the USA had millions of cars and made most of the world's cars. Ford also began assembly at Trafford Park, Manchester, in 1911, and in 1917 founded a factory at Cork.
European firms studied Ford's methods, later called 'Fordism'. About 15 million Model Ts were made by 1927, which is outside the topic's dates.
The car created new industries and changed roads and war transport, but by 1920 it had changed everyday life in Europe much less than in the USA.
The car industry drove demand for steel, rubber, glass, petrol and machine tools, and created jobs in factories, garages and repair. Oil and tyre firms grew.
Roads were improved and tarred for motor traffic, since cars raised dust on unsurfaced roads. Governments passed traffic laws, licences and speed limits.

In the First World War motor transport was vital. About 600 Paris taxis took troops to the Marne in September 1914, and lorries carried supplies to Verdun along the Voie Sacrée (Sacred Way) in 1916, as well as ambulances.
War production made engines and lorries more powerful, and the war gave rise to the tank and the armoured car (first tanks in action in 1916), as well as aircraft engines.
After the war surplus army lorries and trained drivers fed bus services and road haulage, which began to compete with the railways in the 1920s.
Cars stayed rare and expensive in Europe by 1920, so they were far less common than in the USA, where the Model T made them part of everyday life.

The period's science and technology saved lives and changed daily life, but their benefits were uneven and they also made war deadlier. Examiners reward a judgement that sets these against each other.
Achievement: germ theory, vaccines, antiseptics and X-rays saved many lives, and X-rays changed diagnosis.
Limit: knowledge of radiation dangers came too late for pioneers such as Curie, and the benefits of medicine reached the poor slowly.
Achievement: electricity, the telephone and wireless changed communication, and the car and aeroplane changed transport.
Limit: the same science made the war deadlier, because aircraft, motor transport, chemistry and wireless were all used in the First World War.

Contemporary view: people saw science as progress and as a source of national prestige, as in the Pasteur and Koch rivalry and the honours given to Curie in France and Poland. Later view: it was also a weapon.
The car's history shows the difference between inventing a machine and making it widely available. By 1920 its importance was greater for industry and war than for daily life in Europe.
Invention versus innovation: Germany invented the car (Benz, Daimler and Maybach), France developed and raced it, and the USA, through the Model T, mass-produced it.
Importance by 1920: greater for industry, engineering and war than for everyday European life, since cars were still too expensive for most Europeans.
Contemporary view: an exciting luxury or a dangerous nuisance, as the hostility of farmers, cyclists and pedestrians shows.
Later view: historians stress that its mass social effects came mostly after 1920.
To see why fascism took hold, start with the state it replaced and what the First World War did to it. Italy's war ended in debt, grief and disappointment.

Before 1922 Italy was a constitutional monarchy under King Victor Emmanuel III, with an elected Chamber of Deputies. The King appointed the Prime Minister and commanded the army, which is why his decisions mattered so much in 1922 and 1943.

Italy entered the First World War in 1915 on the Allied side under the secret Treaty of London, which promised it territory from Austria-Hungary. This promise is the yardstick Italians later used to judge the peace.

The war cost heavy casualties and heavy debt, and the peace settlement gave Italy less than the Treaty of London had promised. This fed the sense of a 'mutilated victory' (vittoria mutilata, the poet D'Annunzio's phrase): Italians felt they had won the war but been cheated of the prize.

The Russian Revolution of 1917 made socialists and communists across Europe look like a real threat to property, the Church and the monarchy. Italy's propertied classes therefore watched Italian socialism with fear.

The League of Nations, set up by the peace settlement, was meant to settle disputes between states and could impose sanctions (economic penalties) on an aggressor. Its weakness in Mussolini's later foreign policy depends on this role.
Fascism grew where parliamentary government seemed weak and where fear of revolution and economic hardship had left people frightened and angry.

Italy had five prime ministers between 1919 and 1922 (Orlando, Nitti, Giolitti, Bonomi and Facta). Proportional representation, introduced in 1919, gave parties seats in line with their share of the vote and so produced weak coalitions dependent on the Socialists and the Catholic Popolari (the Catholic People's Party).

The Biennio Rosso (1919-1920, the 'two red years') brought strikes, peasant land seizures and factory occupations in the north. Landowners, industrialists and the middle classes feared a socialist revolution, so they were ready to back anyone who promised order.
Inflation, unemployment and food shortages added to the anger of ex-servicemen, who believed the state had failed to reward them for their sacrifice.
Fascism drew support from ex-servicemen, the lower middle class, large landowners in the Po valley and industrialists. The last two wanted an end to strikes and socialist organisation.

The poet Gabriele D'Annunzio seized Fiume with volunteers (September 1919 to December 1920). This showed the weakness of the state and gave Fascism its style: black shirts, balcony speeches, the Roman salute and mass ritual.
Fascism was not a single fixed doctrine, but its movements shared a recognisable set of beliefs and methods. Each of these can be illustrated from Mussolini's Italy.
Fascism combined nationalism, a single party, a leader, violence against opponents, and hostility to socialism and liberal democracy.
Extreme nationalism: the nation is placed above the individual, so personal rights and interests count for less than the nation's greatness.
The leader principle and personality cult: power is concentrated in one leader who is said to embody the nation, and propaganda presents him as infallible and heroic.
One party and a totalitarian state: Mussolini's own formula, from a 1925 speech, was 'everything within the state, nothing outside the state, nothing against the state'.
Fascists were hostile to communism, socialism and liberal democracy, which they blamed for class conflict and national weakness.
Fascism glorified violence, war and youth, through uniformed squads and mass rallies, because it saw struggle as the way to make a strong nation.
Fascism promised corporatism, in which employers and workers would co-operate in state-controlled corporations instead of fighting a class conflict.

Comparison only: other inter-war authoritarian regimes included Horthy's Hungary (1920), Primo de Rivera's Spain (1923-30), Pilsudski's Poland (1926), Salazar's Portugal (1932) and Metaxas's Greece (1936). Most were conservative military or clerical dictatorships rather than mass fascist movements.
Three further terms recur in every answer on Mussolini, and examiners expect them to be used precisely.

Dictatorship is rule by one leader or party without free elections, an independent parliament or a free press. Mussolini's rule fits this from 1925-26, once opposition parties and the free press had gone.
A personality cult presents the leader as infallible and heroic through propaganda, ritual and his image. Mussolini was Il Duce (the leader).

Totalitarianism means the state seeks to control all public and private life through one party, secret police and propaganda. The word was first used by an opponent, Giovanni Amendola, in 1923, and Mussolini then adopted it.
Italy was not fully totalitarian, because the King, the Church, the army and big business kept independent power. This is why the King was able to dismiss Mussolini in 1943.
The Fascist movement gained power through organised violence against its opponents, often tolerated by local police and army commanders.

Benito Mussolini, a former editor of the socialist newspaper Avanti!, founded the Fasci di Combattimento in Milan in March 1919. Its programme mixed radical and nationalist ideas, and it was a movement, not yet a party.

The squadristi were armed squads, often led by ex-servicemen, who attacked socialist offices, trade union halls and Popolari premises, especially in the Po valley and Tuscany. They were often tolerated by local police and army commanders.

Their violence was aimed at the organisations that had led the 1919-1920 unrest, so Fascism presented itself as the defender of order against socialism. Frightened property owners therefore welcomed it.

In the May 1921 election the Fascists, standing inside Liberal leader Giovanni Giolitti's electoral bloc, won 35 seats and Mussolini himself was elected. Giolitti underestimated them and believed he could control them.

Mussolini signed a Pacification Pact with socialist leaders in August 1921 to end the violence, but local squads ignored it and the pact collapsed. The movement was becoming too big for one man to restrain.
Mussolini founded the National Fascist Party (PNF) in November 1921, turning the Fasci movement into a party.
By 1922 the Fascists had taken control of many local councils in northern and central Italy. This gave them local bases of power independent of Rome.
The March on Rome was a show of force that persuaded the King to hand power to Mussolini rather than declare a state of siege (emergency military rule).

Between 27 and 30 October 1922, about 30,000 Fascists converged on Rome under four leaders, the quadrumvirs: Italo Balbo, Emilio De Bono, Cesare Maria De Vecchi and Michele Bianchi. Estimates range from about 25,000 to 30,000.
Mussolini himself waited in Milan. Prime Minister Luigi Facta asked the King for a state of siege so that the army could stop the march.

King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign the state of siege decree, fearing civil war and doubting the army's loyalty. He invited Mussolini to form a government on 29 October, and Mussolini took office on 30 October 1922.

The March succeeded because it was a show of force and a bluff. The King handed power over legally, with the support or acceptance of conservatives, so in form it was an appointment rather than a coup.

Mussolini's first government was a coalition in which Fascists held only a minority of posts alongside Liberals, Popolari and nationalists, so he needed parliament's support. Parliament granted it emergency powers for a year in November 1922.
Once in office Mussolini set about turning a minority coalition into a Fascist-controlled state. He created party and armed bodies loyal to himself and changed the electoral rules.
The Fascist Grand Council (December 1922) became the party's governing body, so that the party had a command centre of its own.
The Fascist militia (MVSN, the Voluntary Militia for National Security, January 1923) turned the squads into a state-paid force loyal to Mussolini rather than the King.

The Acerbo Law of 1923 gave two-thirds of the seats in the Chamber of Deputies to the list with the most votes, provided it had at least 25 per cent. Such a rule made a Fascist majority almost certain.
In the April 1924 election the Fascist-led national list won about 65 per cent of the vote (about two-thirds), in a campaign marked by intimidation and violence against opponents.
The murder of a socialist deputy in 1924 threatened Mussolini's government. He survived the crisis and used it to remove parliamentary and press freedom.
On 30 May 1924 Giacomo Matteotti, a Socialist deputy, denounced electoral fraud and violence in the Chamber of Deputies.
Matteotti was abducted in Rome on 10 June 1924 by men connected to the Fascist squads and was murdered, so Fascist violence now reached a parliamentarian. His body was found in August.

Opposition deputies walked out of the Chamber in what became known as the Aventine Secession (1924), hoping the King would dismiss Mussolini. The King did not act, and the walkout left Mussolini free to dominate parliament.
On 3 January 1925 Mussolini told the Chamber that he accepted political responsibility for the violence, which marked the start of his open dictatorship.

The Leggi Fascistissime (1925-26) made Mussolini responsible only to the King and let him rule by decree. They banned opposition parties, censored the press, and replaced elected mayors with appointed podesta (1926).

The same laws set up a Special Tribunal for the Defence of the State (1926). Political prisoners were sent to confino (internal exile) on islands such as Lipari, and the OVRA secret police hunted opponents.
Violet Gibson, an Irishwoman and the daughter of a Lord Chancellor of Ireland, shot Mussolini in Rome on 7 April 1926 and wounded his nose. The attack was used to justify further repression.

A 1928 electoral law let the Grand Council draw up a single list of 400 candidates for voters to accept or reject. The 1929 plebiscite (a yes or no vote) approved it with about 98 per cent voting yes.
Mussolini aimed to bring industry and labour under state direction through fascist unions and corporations, so that class conflict would end. In practice the system remained more theory than reality.

The Rocco Law of 1926 allowed only state-recognised syndicates (unions and employers' bodies) to represent workers and employers, and it banned strikes and lockouts. Workers thus lost their independent unions.
The Charter of Labour of 1927 set out the principles of the corporate system, in which employers and workers would be organised together under the state, so that class conflict would end.

Corporations covering the main economic sectors were set up in 1934, so that each sector had a state-controlled body. In 1939 the Chamber of Deputies was replaced by the Chamber of Fasces and Corporations.
The corporate state existed largely on paper, because employers kept control of production and the corporations had little real power.
Mussolini fought a series of publicised 'battles' to show that Fascism could make Italy strong. Most gave prestige rather than real success.
The Battle for Grain (from 1925) aimed at self-sufficiency in wheat by raising tariffs and expanding cereal production on poor land. It did not make Italy self-sufficient in food.
The Battle for Births, promoted from about 1927, offered rewards for large families and taxed bachelors, aiming at a bigger population for a stronger nation. The population target was not met.

Quota 90 (the Battle for the Lira) was announced in Mussolini's Pesaro speech of August 1926 and reached in 1927. It revalued the lira to 90 to the pound sterling for national prestige, but it made exports dearer, deflated the economy and cut wages.

The Pontine Marshes south of Rome were drained and resettled in the 1930s, for example, a project presented as a triumph of the regime. Autostrade (motorways) and rail electrification were other visible successes.

After the 1929 crash the state rescued banks and industry through the Institute for Industrial Reconstruction (IRI, 1933), which left the state owning a large share of banking, shipbuilding and steel.
The regime used mass organisations, the press and film to win consent and to present Mussolini as the embodiment of the nation. Consent was backed by fear.

The Opera Nazionale Balilla (1926) brought boys and girls into a state youth organisation, so that children were taught fascist values from childhood. It was reorganised as the Gioventu Italiana del Littorio in 1937.
The Dopolavoro (after-work) organisation from 1925 provided, for example, sport, excursions and leisure for adult workers under fascist supervision, extending party influence into free time.
Elementary schools used a single state textbook from 1929, and university professors had to swear an oath of loyalty to the regime in 1931. Only about a dozen of over 1,200 refused.

The Istituto Luce, founded in 1924, produced newsreels and documentary films, which reached ordinary people and showed Mussolini at work, at rallies and at public works. The Ministry of Popular Culture (Minculpop, 1937) controlled the press, radio, cinema and theatre.

The cult of Il Duce used posters, photographs of him harvesting grain or bare-chested, and balcony speeches from the Palazzo Venezia in Rome, his office. Wall slogans included 'Mussolini is always right' and 'Believe, obey, fight'.

The regime used the Catholic Church and public ritual to build legitimacy, although the Church kept its own youth and press organisations. The Lateran Treaties of 11 February 1929 settled the Roman Question and created Vatican City, a success for the regime.
Consent was won by propaganda and public works, while the militia, the Special Tribunal, the OVRA and confino deterred opposition. This is why propaganda and terror must be explained together.
Mussolini used foreign adventures to build prestige. In these years he was also wary of Hitler, and he acted first against weak neighbours.

The Corfu incident of August 1923 began when General Enrico Tellini of an Italian boundary commission was murdered on the Greek-Albanian border. Italy bombarded and occupied Corfu until Greece paid compensation.
Italy annexed the port of Fiume in 1924 under a treaty with Yugoslavia, which ended a long dispute left over from the peace settlement.
After Austrian Nazis murdered the Austrian Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss in July 1934, Mussolini moved troops to the Brenner Pass, showing he opposed German control of Austria at that time.
In April 1935 Italy joined Britain and France in the Stresa Front, an agreement to resist German challenges to the peace settlement.
The invasion of Abyssinia was Mussolini's biggest foreign gamble. It exposed the weakness of the League of Nations and pushed Italy towards Germany.

After the Walwal incident (December 1934), a clash on the Abyssinian border, Italy invaded Abyssinia (Ethiopia) on 3 October 1935. The attack was also revenge for Italy's defeat by Ethiopia at Adowa in 1896.
Italy used poison gas against the Abyssinians, a breach of the rules of war that shocked opinion abroad. Emperor Haile Selassie appealed to the League of Nations in 1936.
The League imposed sanctions, but they excluded oil, so they did not stop the invasion.

The Hoare-Laval Plan of December 1935, devised by the British Foreign Secretary Samuel Hoare and French Prime Minister Pierre Laval, would have given Italy much of Abyssinia. It was abandoned after public protest in Britain and France.
Addis Ababa was captured on 5 May 1936, so Victor Emmanuel III was proclaimed Emperor of Ethiopia.
Isolated by the sanctions, Mussolini drew closer to Hitler. Step by step this alliance committed Italy to a war it was unprepared to fight.
Italy and Germany drew together after German support during the Abyssinian war. They also intervened jointly for Franco in the Spanish Civil War (1936-39).
Mussolini announced the Rome-Berlin Axis in a Milan speech on 1 November 1936. It was only an understanding between the two states, not a formal alliance.
Italy joined the Anti-Comintern Pact in 1937 and accepted the Anschluss (Germany's union with Austria) in 1938, although in 1934 it had opposed German control of Austria.
Mussolini posed as a peacemaker at the Munich Conference (September 1938), which won him prestige, and invaded Albania in April 1939.
On 22 May 1939 Italy signed the Pact of Steel, a military alliance with Germany. Yet when war began in September 1939 Italy declared itself non-belligerent.
Italy declared war on Britain and France on 10 June 1940, when France was already beaten. Defeats in Greece (invaded from October 1940) and North Africa then made Italy dependent on German help.
Military defeats and an Allied invasion of Sicily brought the regime down in 1943. Mussolini's rule in northern Italy continued under German control until 1945.

Allied forces landed in Sicily on 10 July 1943, and the defeat made Fascist leaders doubt Mussolini. At a meeting on the night of 24-25 July the Fascist Grand Council passed Dino Grandi's motion to return command of the armed forces to the King.
King Victor Emmanuel III dismissed Mussolini on 25 July 1943 and had him arrested. Marshal Pietro Badoglio formed a new government.
Italy's armistice with the Allies was announced on 8 September 1943, so German forces, fearing Italy would change sides, took control of much of the north and centre.
German paratroopers and SS commandos, among them Otto Skorzeny, rescued Mussolini from a mountain hotel at Gran Sasso on 12 September 1943.

Mussolini headed the Italian Social Republic, known as the Salo Republic after its seat on Lake Garda. It was a German puppet state, and it executed his son-in-law Galeazzo Ciano and other Grand Council members at Verona in January 1944.
Mussolini and his mistress Clara Petacci were shot by partisans near Lake Como on 28 April 1945, and their bodies were displayed in Piazzale Loreto in Milan.
Mussolini led Italy from 1922 to 1943 and was the founder and leader of the Fascist movement.
Born in 1883 at Predappio in the Romagna region, he trained as a teacher, became a socialist journalist, and edited Avanti! from 1912.
He was expelled from the Socialist Party in 1914 for supporting Italian entry into the First World War. He served in the army and was wounded in 1917.

As founder of the Fasci di Combattimento (1919) and the National Fascist Party (1921), he led the movement that took power in 1922. He was Prime Minister from 1922, ruled as dictator from 1925 and was deposed in 1943.

He was a participant who shaped events: he organised the March on Rome from Milan, took personal responsibility for the violence in January 1925 and made the key decisions on Abyssinia, the Axis and entry into the war.

Contemporaries were divided. Many conservatives, the Vatican and foreign statesmen admired him for defeating socialism (Churchill praised him on a visit to Rome in 1927). Socialists, Popolari and liberals such as Giovanni Amendola, who died in 1926 after a Fascist beating, denounced his violence.

Historians differ: Renzo De Felice argued that the regime enjoyed real popular consent in 1929-1936, while Denis Mack Smith portrayed Mussolini as an opportunist and propagandist more concerned with image than with real achievement.

Many historians now regard Italian Fascism as an incomplete totalitarianism, since the King, the Church, the army and big business kept independent power. This is why the King was able to dismiss him in 1943.
Judgements of the regime depend on whether its stability and public works are weighed against its violence, economic failures and disastrous war.
Achievement: Mussolini ended parliamentary rule and established a one-party state by 1926, with little open resistance for most of the 1920s.
Limit: the corporate state existed largely on paper, as employers kept control of production and the corporations had little real power.
Achievement: the Lateran Treaties of 1929 settled the Roman Question, and the Pontine Marshes scheme, the autostrade motorways and rail electrification gave the regime visible successes.
Limit: the Battle for Grain did not make Italy self-sufficient in food, and the deflationary policy of Quota 90 damaged industry and jobs.
Achievement: Italy gained territory in Abyssinia and Fiume, which the regime presented as the fulfilment of national destiny.

Limit: the Abyssinian war was costly, the alliance with Germany drew Italy into a war it was ill-prepared to fight and left it dependent on Germany, and the regime collapsed in 1943 after defeats in North Africa and Sicily.

Contemporary view: many Italians and foreign conservatives saw Mussolini as the saviour of order who had defeated Bolshevism. Later view: his regime is judged by its violence, its alliance with Hitler, the 1938 racial laws and the defeat it brought on Italy.
Overall, Mussolini was very effective at winning and keeping power (1922-1926) but much less effective at transforming the economy, society or Italy's place in the world.

The Weimar Republic was born out of defeat, and that shaped how many Germans judged it from the start. To follow the rest of the story you need the basic machinery of the new state and the parties that competed inside it.
Germany lost the First World War: the Kaiser (Wilhelm II) abdicated on 9 November 1918 and a republic was proclaimed the same day, and the armistice of 11 November 1918 ended the fighting.

Democracy means government by elected representatives, with free elections and the rule of law. Weimar was Germany's first democracy, and it was fragile because it was created in defeat and many powerful people never accepted it.

The system had an elected President as head of state and a Chancellor as head of government, who needed the support of a majority in the Reichstag (parliament). Because no party won a majority alone, the Chancellor usually led a coalition of several parties.

The main parties, from left to right, were the Communists (KPD), the Social Democrats (SPD), the Catholic Centre Party, the liberal parties (including Stresemann's DVP), the nationalist DNVP and the Nazis (NSDAP). The SPD, Centre and liberals were the parties that supported the republic.
Reparations are payments that a defeated state makes to the victors for war damage; they became a lasting source of bitterness in Germany.
A putsch is an attempt to seize power by force. Several were tried against the republic, from both left and right.
The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 began the worldwide Depression, which later ended Germany's recovery.
The National Assembly drew up a democratic constitution in 1919, but some of its features and some of the people left in charge of the state made it easy to undermine.
