The National Assembly met at Weimar, away from the unrest in Berlin, and adopted a constitution on 31 July 1919 creating a federal republic. All men and women over 20 could vote.
The President was elected by the people for seven years and the Chancellor was responsible to the Reichstag.
Proportional representation for the Reichstag (seats shared out in line with each party's share of votes) produced many small parties, so stable majority government was very difficult to form.

Article 48 allowed the President to issue emergency decrees and to rule without the Reichstag. This power was meant for emergencies, but it became central after 1930, when governments no longer had Reichstag majorities.

Many judges, civil servants, army officers and university teachers from the imperial era stayed in post and remained hostile to the republic, so the state's own servants could not be relied on to defend it.

The 'stab in the back' myth claimed that Germany had not really been beaten and that the politicians who made peace in November 1918, labelled the 'November criminals', had betrayed the army. It blamed these politicians, not the army, for defeat.
The republic's first leaders and its peace settlement set the scene for its early troubles. Many Germans blamed the republic for a treaty that it had been forced to sign.
Friedrich Ebert was the first President, from 1919 until his death in 1925.
Paul von Hindenburg, a former field marshal, succeeded Ebert in 1925 and was re-elected in 1932. He was President, never Chancellor,.

The Treaty of Versailles of June 1919 returned Alsace-Lorraine to France, took away Germany's colonies, limited the army to 100,000 men with no air force, demilitarised the Rhineland and imposed reparations.
Article 231, the war-guilt clause, placed the blame for the war on Germany, and was felt as a national humiliation.

The London Schedule of 1921 set Germany's reparations at 132 billion gold marks, a sum that many Germans regarded as impossible and humiliating, so parties promising to overturn Versailles gained appeal.

In its first years the republic faced armed challenges from left and right. Its judges and army officers were often sympathetic to the right, so the threats from the right were treated far more lightly.

The Spartacist rising of January 1919 (a communist uprising in Berlin) and the murders of Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg by Freikorps soldiers (volunteer units of ex-soldiers) were put down with the help of Freikorps units.

The Kapp Putsch of March 1920 was led by Wolfgang Kapp with General Walther von Lüttwitz and the Ehrhardt Brigade, a Freikorps unit. They seized Berlin, and the army refused to defend the government, which left Berlin.
The putsch collapsed after four days because the trade unions called a general strike, so the government was saved by workers rather than by its own army.

Political murders by the far right, including the killing of Matthias Erzberger in 1921 and of Foreign Minister Walther Rathenau in June 1922, showed the weakness of the state's protection of its leaders.
The judiciary favoured the right: the statistician Emil Gumbel counted 354 political murders by the right and 22 by the left between 1919 and 1922, with far heavier sentences for left-wing killers.

In 1923 a dispute over reparations led to a crisis that destroyed the value of German money. This is hyperinflation, the extreme form of inflation, in which prices rise so fast that money loses nearly all its value.
Germany fell behind on reparations deliveries of timber and coal, so in January 1923 France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr, the main industrial region, to take coal and goods.
The German government under Chancellor Wilhelm Cuno called for passive resistance in the Ruhr (workers refusing to co-operate with the occupiers), which the government funded by printing money.

Printing so much money made it worth less and less, which is the cause of the hyperinflation of 1923. Before the war there were about 4.2 marks to the US dollar; by November 1923 there were about 4.2 trillion.
Prices rose by the hour, so workers were paid daily or twice daily and rushed to spend their wages before they lost value, and barter replaced money in many places.

Middle-class savings, pensions and war loans were largely wiped out, because they were fixed sums in a currency that no longer bought anything. This left many people who had supported the old order resentful of the republic.

Debtors, speculators and large industrialists such as Hugo Stinnes, who borrowed to buy assets, gained from the inflation, because they repaid their debts in worthless money, while people on fixed incomes and savers lost most.
Once passive resistance ended and a new currency was issued, the republic recovered. The Dawes Plan then gave Germany a workable way to pay reparations, but it tied recovery to foreign money.
Gustav Stresemann became Chancellor in August 1923 (he held the post only until November) and called off passive resistance in the Ruhr in September.
The Rentenmark, introduced on 15 November 1923, was backed by a mortgage on land and industry, which gave people reason to trust it, and it ended the hyperinflation.
Hjalmar Schacht, as currency commissioner and then Reichsbank president, kept the supply of Rentenmarks tightly limited. It was a temporary currency, replaced by the permanent Reichsmark in 1924.

The Dawes Plan of 1924, drawn up by a committee chaired by the American Charles Dawes, set reparations payments that rose with Germany's capacity to pay and provided a loan of 800 million gold marks. It did not reduce the total.
Under the Dawes Plan the French left the Ruhr by 1925, which ended the occupation.
The German recovery of 1924 to 1929 depended on American money lent under the Dawes Plan, so it collapsed when the loans were withdrawn after the Wall Street Crash began in October 1929.
Hitler built a small Bavarian party into a movement with its own private army, and in 1923 tried to use it to seize power by force.

Hitler joined the small German Workers' Party in Munich in September 1919. It was renamed the National Socialist German Workers' Party (NSDAP) in February 1920 with a 25-point programme, and Hitler became its leader with dictatorial powers in July 1921.
The party's early support came from Bavarian ex-soldiers and anti-communist groups, who were angry at defeat and afraid of revolution.
The Sturmabteilung (SA), a paramilitary force founded in 1921, whose street violence gave the Nazis a reputation for strength.
On 8 to 9 November 1923 Hitler and Erich Ludendorff tried to seize power in Munich, starting in the Bürgerbräukeller beer hall, as a first step to a march on Berlin.
The Munich (Beer Hall) Putsch failed: Bavarian police fired on the marchers, killing sixteen Nazis, and four police officers died.

The failed putsch turned out to help Hitler, because the trial made him famous and convinced him to change tactics. His party stayed small in the prosperous years, until a campaign on reparations gave it respectability.

Hitler was tried for high treason in early 1924 and used the trial as a national platform. The sympathetic court gave him five years, the minimum sentence, and he served only about nine months in Landsberg prison.
He wrote Mein Kampf in prison, setting out his views on race, Lebensraum (living space) and the need to destroy Marxism and the Jews. The first volume was published in 1925.
The party had been banned after the putsch. Hitler refounded it in February 1925 and adopted a strategy of winning power legally through elections.
The strategy had little effect while Germany was prosperous: in the 1928 Reichstag election the Nazis won only 12 seats and 2.6 per cent of the vote.

Hitler's prominence in the 1929 campaign against the Young Plan, alongside Alfred Hugenberg's nationalist DNVP and its newspapers (Hugenberg was the owner), gave the Nazis national publicity and respectability on the right.
Gustav Stresemann was Chancellor only from August to November 1923, but as Foreign Minister he won back Germany's place among the powers. Most of his achievements belong to this later role.
As Foreign Minister from 1923 until his death in October 1929, Stresemann pursued the revision of Versailles by negotiation rather than force, a policy of fulfilment.
The Locarno Treaties of October 1925 confirmed Germany's western borders (not its eastern ones), which reassured France, and led to Germany's entry into the League of Nations in 1926.
Stresemann shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1926 with the French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand, in recognition of this improved relationship.
The Young Plan of 1929, chaired by the American Owen D. Young, reduced the total of reparations and spread payments to 1988, so it lowered the annual burden on Germany.
Between 1924 and 1929 Germany enjoyed relative prosperity, and many historians see these as the republic's best years. Look closely, though, and the recovery was less secure than it seemed.
Weimar governments built a welfare state: the eight-hour day (1918) and large state-funded housing programmes in the later 1920s.
The 1927 Act created national unemployment insurance, but it was funded for far fewer claimants than the Depression produced, so it broke down after 1929.
The recovery depended on American loans, which meant that Germany had no reserves of its own when the loans were called in.
Agriculture and the middle classes did not share fully in the prosperity, so discontent remained beneath the surface.
Stresemann died in October 1929, and his successors could not secure the political support needed to continue his policies.
The Depression is the slump after 1929, with falling output, bank failures and mass unemployment. In Germany it ended the recovery and brought down the coalition governments.

Unemployment rose from an annual average of about 1.9 million in 1929 to about 6 million registered unemployed by early 1932, because American loans were called in and exports fell. It was above three million by 1930.
The grand coalition of Social Democrats, Centre and liberal parties broke down in March 1930 over unemployment insurance contributions and the budget.
Heinrich Brüning of the Centre Party, the new Chancellor from March 1930, governed through Article 48 emergency decrees, cutting wages, pensions and welfare to balance the budget.
These deflationary policies (cutting spending and prices) raised unemployment and gave the impression that the government was making the crisis worse, so support for the republic weakened.
The banking crisis of 1931 deepened the slump: the Creditanstalt in Vienna collapsed in May and the Danat Bank in Germany in July.

Brüning hoped deflation would prove that Germany could not pay reparations. Hoover's moratorium (a pause in payments) suspended them in 1931, and the Lausanne Conference of 1932, under his successor, effectively ended them.
Middle-class and farming groups, badly hit by falling prices, turned to parties that promised radical solutions.
Brüning, Papen and Schleicher in turn governed through the President, with emergency decrees, rather than through a Reichstag majority. These were the presidential cabinets.

The Nazi party's rapid electoral growth came from its appeal to unemployed people, farmers, small business owners and Protestant voters, especially in rural areas, and from skilful propaganda backed by the SA.

In the September 1930 Reichstag election the NSDAP won 107 seats and 18.3 per cent of the vote, up from 12 seats in 1928, becoming the second largest party after the SPD. The Communists also gained, winning 77 seats.

Nazi propaganda combined attacks on the Versailles settlement, the Weimar parties and communism with promises of jobs, bread and national revival, so it appealed to people who felt let down by the republic.

Goebbels, Gauleiter (regional party leader) of Berlin from 1926, ran propaganda with mass rallies, posters, newspapers such as Der Angriff and film. In 1932 Hitler toured the country by aeroplane, speaking at several rallies a day.

The SA's street violence against communists and Social Democrats gave the party a reputation for strength, and it drew unemployed young men into its ranks, which gave them uniforms, meals and shelter.
Nazi voters were disproportionately Protestant, rural and small-town, middle-class (shopkeepers, farmers, white-collar workers, civil servants and pensioners) and young.
Catholic areas loyal to the Centre Party and industrial workers loyal to the SPD and KPD were less receptive, though the Nazis did win many working-class votes.
Through 1932 the Nazis reached their highest vote in a free election, but they never won a majority, and by the end of the year their support was slipping.
Hitler became a German citizen in February 1932 so that he could stand for President. In the first round in March he won about 30 per cent to Hindenburg's 49.6 per cent.
In the run-off on 10 April Hindenburg won about 53 per cent to Hitler's 37 per cent, so Hindenburg was re-elected.
In the July 1932 election the NSDAP won 230 seats and about 37 per cent of the vote, making it the largest party in the Reichstag.
Hitler refused any post below Chancellor, and Hindenburg refused to appoint him in August 1932.

In the November 1932 election the NSDAP lost about two million votes and 34 seats, falling to 196 seats and about 33 per cent, although it remained the largest party. The party was also short of money.
After Brüning, government depended on the President's favour and on private intrigue, and the SA's violence made politics even less stable.

Brüning banned the SA and SS in April 1932, but Hindenburg dismissed him in May. Franz von Papen, Chancellor from June, lifted the ban, which led to street battles such as the Altona 'Bloody Sunday' of July 1932.
Papen's government removed the Social Democrat government of Prussia in July 1932, in what became known as the Prussian coup, so a major state government lost its elected leaders.
Kurt von Schleicher became Chancellor on 3 December 1932 and tried to split the Nazis by offering the Vice-Chancellorship to Gregor Strasser, and to win trade union support with job-creation schemes.
He failed to build a majority and resigned on 28 January 1933.
The final step to power came through a deal among conservatives who believed they could use the Nazis' popularity for their own purposes.
Papen met Hitler at the banker Kurt von Schröder's house in Cologne on 4 January 1933, and then persuaded Hindenburg to appoint Hitler Chancellor.
Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933, in a cabinet with only three Nazis (Hitler, Wilhelm Frick and Hermann Göring), because the conservatives believed they could control him.
Papen was Vice-Chancellor and Hugenberg was also in the cabinet, so the conservatives held most posts.
This entry covers Hitler's route to the Chancellorship, from his early life to 30 January 1933.
Born in 1889 at Braunau am Inn in Austria, he served in the German army in the First World War and was awarded the Iron Cross.
He joined the German Workers' Party in September 1919 while working as a political informant for the army in Munich, and became its most effective speaker.
As leader of the NSDAP from 1921, he used rallies, a private army (the SA) and personal charisma to make the party the main vehicle of the far right.
He was a participant who learned from failure: after the Munich Putsch he chose the legal road to power through elections, while using the SA's street violence to show strength.

Contemporaries were divided: millions of voters saw him as a national saviour, the left saw him as a tool of big business, and conservatives such as Papen saw a demagogue whom they believed they had hired and could control.
Historians agree that he was appointed legally, but differ on why. Alan Bullock, in Hitler: A Study in Tyranny (1952), stressed his opportunism and will to power.
Henry Ashby Turner, in Hitler's Thirty Days to Power (1996), showed that his appointment depended on intrigues among a few men around Hindenburg in January 1933.
Weimar governments faced war debts, housing shortages, inflation and then mass unemployment. Their responses moved from welfare spending to deflation to emergency job creation, with mixed success.

After 1918 the republic recognised trade unions and collective bargaining. The Stinnes-Legien agreement of November 1918 gave the eight-hour day and union recognition in return for employers' co-operation.
The Hauszinssteuer, a tax on house owners who had gained from inflation, funded large municipal housing estates in Berlin and Frankfurt in the later 1920s.

Stresemann's government ended hyperinflation in 1923 by ending passive resistance, balancing the budget and issuing the Rentenmark, but the middle classes who lost their savings were never compensated in full.
The 1927 Unemployment Insurance Act gave benefit to workers who paid contributions, but it was designed for about 800,000 claimants and was overwhelmed when unemployment passed three million.
Brüning's emergency decrees of 1930 and 1931 cut civil service pay, unemployment benefit and wages and raised taxes in order to balance the budget, a deflationary policy that deepened the slump.
The Voluntary Labour Service (Freiwilliger Arbeitsdienst) of 1931 gave unemployed young men work on public projects for pocket money, and it was widened under Papen and Schleicher.

Papen's September 1932 programme offered tax certificates to employers who hired extra workers, and Schleicher's emergency job-creation programme of December 1932 tried to win union support, but neither had time to take effect before January 1933.
Social strain was severe by 1932: millions of families lived on reduced benefit or on poor relief, and thousands of young unemployed men joined the SA, which provided uniforms, meals and shelter.
Judgements of the republic divide between blaming its structure and the Treaty of Versailles, and emphasising the impact of the Depression and the choices of its leaders.

Structural view: proportional representation, Article 48 and the lack of a stable parliamentary majority left the republic dependent on emergency government. Against this, the constitution worked in the stable years of 1924 to 1929.

Versailles view: contemporaries on the right blamed the treaty for national humiliation, and this shaped the appeal of parties promising revision. Against this, Stresemann succeeded in revising reparations and winning acceptance for Germany by negotiation.
Achievement: Stresemann's policies produced a recovery between 1924 and 1929, with inflation defeated and Germany admitted to the League of Nations.
Limit: that recovery depended heavily on American loans, so the Wall Street Crash exposed its fragility and left no reserves to cushion the unemployment that followed.
The Depression was the decisive trigger: the Nazis won 12 seats in 1928 but became a mass party by 1930. Others stress long-term causes such as hostile elites, Versailles and the weak constitution.

Later historians such as Henry Ashby Turner stress that Nazi electoral support was falling by late 1932 and that Hitler's appointment was not inevitable but resulted from decisions by a small group of conservative politicians.
Contemporary left-wing and liberal critics blamed the conservative elite for undermining the republic, while the Nazi party presented itself as the only force able to restore order.

Everything the Nazi state did between 1933 and 1939 makes sense only against what Hitler wanted and the position he started from. He came to power through a deal with conservatives, but he had a programme that he had already written down.

Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933 by President Hindenburg, at the head of a coalition. Only three Nazis (Hitler, Frick and Göring) sat in the first cabinet, so Papen, the Vice-Chancellor, and the conservatives expected to control him.

In Mein Kampf (two volumes, 1925 and 1926, mostly written in Landsberg prison after the Munich Putsch) Hitler set out his aims: overturn Versailles, unite all Germans in one state, win Lebensraum (living space) in the east, and fight a racial struggle.

The Treaty of Versailles (1919) limited the German army to 100,000 men and banned conscription, an air force, tanks and submarines, which is why rearmament was Hitler's first goal. The Rhineland was demilitarised and the Saar placed under League of Nations rule for 15 years from 1920.

Versailles also forbade union (Anschluss) with Austria, made Danzig a Free City under the League, and used the Polish Corridor to separate East Prussia from the rest of Germany. Each of these became a Hitler target between 1933 and 1939.
While Germany was weak, Hitler was cautious: he needed time to rebuild the army and economy, so his first steps were presented as demands for fair treatment, not as plans for conquest.

Within months of his appointment Hitler removed the legal and political limits on his power, using emergency decrees, intimidation and a vote of the Reichstag itself. Each step built on the one before.

The Reichstag fire of 27 February 1933 was blamed on a Communist plot, because Marinus van der Lubbe, a young Dutch communist (later executed), was found in the building. This gave the Nazis the excuse they needed to attack their left-wing opponents.

The Decree for the Protection of People and State (the Reichstag Fire Decree) of 28 February 1933 suspended freedom of speech, press and assembly and allowed arrest without trial, so opponents could be locked up with no legal protection.
Thousands of Communists were arrested after the fire, and the Communist Party was effectively destroyed in early 1933, removing one of the Nazis' main rivals before the next vote.

In the election of 5 March 1933, despite terror and propaganda, the Nazis won only about 44 per cent of the vote. They had a majority only with their Nationalist (DNVP) allies, so Hitler still needed another way to rule freely.

The Enabling Act of 23 March 1933 (formally the Law for the Removal of the Distress of People and Reich) let the cabinet make laws without the Reichstag, even ones departing from the constitution, for four years.

The Act passed 444 to 94. The Communist deputies had been arrested or had fled, the Catholic Centre Party voted for it, and only the Social Democrats voted against, which shows how far intimidation had worked.
Do not mix up the two measures: the Reichstag Fire Decree suspended people's rights, while the Enabling Act removed the Reichstag's law-making role.

After the Enabling Act Hitler used Gleichschaltung (coordination: bringing every institution into line with Nazi aims) to take over the rest of German life. It ended in a state where only one party and one organisation for workers were allowed.

Reich governors (Reichsstatthalter) were appointed over the German states in April 1933, and the Law for the Reconstruction of the Reich of 30 January 1934 abolished the state parliaments, so power was concentrated in Berlin.

The Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service of 7 April 1933 removed Jews and political opponents from the civil service. This put the officials who ran the country under Nazi control and made loyalty the test for a job.
Gleichschaltung also brought the courts, universities and cultural bodies under Nazi control, which meant that teaching, law and the arts could no longer act independently of the regime.

On 2 May 1933 the SA and SS occupied trade union offices and the unions were dissolved. Their members were not abolished by law but seized and absorbed, with workers then pushed into the German Labour Front, set up in May 1933 under Robert Ley.

The Law against the Formation of New Parties of 14 July 1933 made the NSDAP the only legal party. The Communists and Social Democrats had already been banned, and the other parties dissolved themselves in June and July 1933.

By 1934 Hitler's remaining rival at the heart of the movement was his own storm-troop army, the SA. Removing its leadership in one weekend won him the army's support and cleared the way to supreme power.

Ernst Röhm, the SA chief of staff, led an organisation of several million members by 1934, far more than the 100,000-man army. He talked of a "second revolution" and wanted the SA to form the core of a new people's army.

Conservatives were alarmed by SA violence. Vice-Chancellor Papen's Marburg speech of 17 June 1934 criticised that violence and the calls for a second revolution, adding to the pressure on Hitler to act.
Between 30 June and 2 July 1934, Hitler ordered the murder of Röhm and other SA leaders. The killings were carried out by the SS and Gestapo with army help.

Hitler also used the purge to settle other scores: Gregor Strasser (a former Nazi leader), Kurt von Schleicher (former Chancellor) and his wife, Gustav von Kahr, Erich Klausener and Edgar Jung (author of the Marburg speech) were killed.
At least 85 people were killed, possibly more, because the true total is uncertain.
On 3 July 1934 the Law on Measures of State Self-Defence declared the killings legal after the event, which gave murder a cover of legality.
The army leadership, under Defence Minister Werner von Blomberg, approved the purge in return for the removal of the SA as a rival force, which tied the army to Hitler.
Hindenburg's death gave Hitler the last piece of formal power. From then on the state rested on his person, and the law, the army and the party all swore obedience to him.

President Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934. The offices of President and Chancellor were merged and Hitler took the title Führer and Reich Chancellor. He was never called President. A plebiscite on 19 August 1934 approved the change, with about 90 per cent in favour.
On 2 August 1934 soldiers swore an oath of unconditional obedience to Hitler personally, as Führer, rather than to the constitution. This tied the armed forces to Hitler personally.
The Führer principle (Führerprinzip) meant authority flowed from the top down, with absolute obedience upward, and propaganda built a cult of Hitler's personal leadership around it.

In practice the state was a polycracy: overlapping party and state bodies (ministries, Gauleiters, the SS, the Four Year Plan office) competed for power and for Hitler's favour. This rivalry meant decisions could be chaotic.

A dictatorship is rule by one person or party without legal limits or free elections. By August 1934 Hitler had removed the Reichstag's law-making role, rival parties and independent organisations and so fitted this definition.
The regime did not rely on consent alone. A police system outside the law, led by Heinrich Himmler, gave it the power to detain anyone it chose.

Heinrich Himmler was Reichsführer-SS (head of the SS, the party's elite force) from 1929. By 1934 he controlled the political police of almost all the states, and in June 1936 he became Chief of German Police, which merged party and state police power in his hands.
Reinhard Heydrich led the SD (Sicherheitsdienst), the SS Security Service, which watched for opponents and gathered intelligence on the population.
The Gestapo (Secret State Police) was founded in April 1933 in Prussia by Hermann Göring. Himmler and Heydrich took it over in April 1934.

The Gestapo could arrest people without trial or appeal, a procedure the regime called protective custody (Schutzhaft). Because there was no legal challenge, nobody could force the police to explain or end a detention.

Historians such as Robert Gellately have shown that the Gestapo was small and relied heavily on denunciations by ordinary Germans. Its reach therefore depended partly on people reporting their neighbours, not on police numbers alone.

Do not confuse the organisations: the SA were the brownshirts under Röhm, sidelined after 1934; the SS was the party elite force under Himmler; the SD was SS intelligence under Heydrich; the Gestapo was the secret state police.
Detention and the courts completed the system. Camps held people the regime wanted out of sight, and the courts were changed so political cases could be decided without legal protection.

Dachau, near Munich, opened in March 1933 and was the first concentration camp run by the SS and the model for later camps. The SA also ran makeshift early camps in 1933, which is why Dachau is called the first SS camp.
Other camps followed: Sachsenhausen in 1936 and Buchenwald in 1937, so the system grew as the regime's controls hardened.

The first prisoners were political opponents such as Communists, trade unionists and Social Democrats. Later Jehovah's Witnesses, "asocials", homosexuals and Jews were held too, so the camps widened as the idea of who threatened the community widened.

Special Courts (Sondergerichte) were set up in March 1933 and the People's Court (Volksgerichtshof) in 1934 for treason cases. Political verdicts came with little legal protection for defendants, so courts reinforced terror instead of limiting it.
The regime's popularity depended on jobs, and its foreign aims depended on arms. Its economic policy tried to deliver both, and hide how much it was spending on rearmament.

Hjalmar Schacht was Reichsbank president from March 1933 and Economics Minister from August 1934. He financed rearmament through Mefo bills, credit notes issued through a dummy company (Mefo) to pay arms firms, which kept military spending off the budget.

The New Plan of September 1934 controlled foreign trade through bilateral trade agreements and exchange controls (limits on buying foreign money), which gave priority to imports of raw materials for rearmament.

Public works, including autobahns, housing and military building, created jobs. The first autobahn section, Frankfurt to Darmstadt, opened in May 1935. The Nazis expanded and publicised the autobahns, but plans and a first stretch (Cologne to Bonn, 1932) predate 1933.

The Reich Labour Service (RAD) became compulsory for young men in June 1935, with six months' work, and conscription was reintroduced in March 1935. Both took young men out of the job market, which helped to lower the unemployment figures.
Unemployment fell dramatically, but the figures hide a more complicated story, and from 1936 the economy was steered openly towards war.

Registered unemployment was about six million in January 1933 and under one million by 1937. By 1938-39 labour shortages had replaced unemployment, because rearmament and conscription absorbed workers.
The figures hide a lot: women and Jews were removed from them, conscription and the Labour Service took men out of the labour market, wages were held down and there were no free unions to bargain.
Recovery had begun before 1933 and world trade was recovering, so Nazi policy alone did not end the Depression in Germany. Historians therefore debate how much credit the regime deserves.

The Four Year Plan, announced in September 1936 with Hermann Göring as Plenipotentiary, aimed to have the army ready for action and the economy fit for war within four years. This priority is often paraphrased as guns before butter.

It also aimed at autarky (self-sufficiency, so Germany would not depend on imports in wartime), through synthetic oil from coal, synthetic rubber (buna) and the state-owned Reichswerke Hermann Göring (1937), which mined low-grade German iron ore.
The plan missed its targets, and Germany still relied on imports in 1939.

Schacht resigned as Economics Minister in November 1937 after clashing with Göring over the pace and cost of rearmament. He was dismissed from the Reichsbank in January 1939, and by 1939 the economy was strained.

The Volksgemeinschaft (people's community) was the idea of a racially pure national community that stood above class. The regime tried to win workers and shape children so that they would belong to it.
The German Labour Front under Robert Ley replaced the free unions, so workers had an organisation controlled by the party instead of one that could bargain for them.

Its Strength Through Joy (Kraft durch Freude) section, set up in November 1933, offered cheap holidays, cruises, concerts, theatre and sport, so workers felt rewarded. Its Beauty of Labour section improved factory canteens, lighting and washrooms.
The Volkswagen ("people's car", the KdF-Wagen) scheme had workers pay weekly instalments, but the factory turned to war production and no savers received a car.

The Hitler Youth, led by Baldur von Schirach (Reich Youth Leader from 1933), had four sections: the Jungvolk (boys 10-14), the Hitler Youth (boys 14-18), the Jungmädelbund (girls 10-14) and the League of German Girls, the BDM (girls 14-18).

The Hitler Youth Law of 1 December 1936 made the Hitler Youth the only legal youth organisation, and membership became compulsory from 1939, so by the end of the decade almost no young person could avoid its training.

Schools taught racial science and nationalist history, and textbooks were rewritten. Teachers were pressed to join the National Socialist Teachers' League, and teachers who were Jewish or politically unreliable were dismissed.

The national community was defined by who it left out as much as who it included. Women were given a fixed role, those judged outsiders were excluded, and the regime relied on consent as well as terror.

Nazi ideology assigned women the roles of wife and mother, often summed up as "Kinder, Küche, Kirche" (children, kitchen, church). The slogan is older than the Nazis, who did not coin it, but it describes their policy.

Marriage loans from 1933 (Law for the Reduction of Unemployment, June 1933) gave 1,000 marks, with a quarter cancelled for each child born. The wife was expected to give up work, which also freed jobs for men.
The Cross of Honour of the German Mother, instituted in December 1938, rewarded large families: bronze for four children, silver for six and gold for eight.
Married women were pushed out of civil service posts from 1933, and from 1936 women could not be judges or public prosecutors. But labour shortages in the late 1930s drew many women back into work.

The regime excluded those it judged inferior. The law of 14 July 1933 on hereditarily diseased offspring led to about 400,000 people being forcibly sterilised by 1945, and the Nuremberg Laws of 15 September 1935 took citizenship from Jews and banned marriage and sexual relations between Jews and Germans.
Opponents and "asocials" were sent to camps, so belonging to the community depended on conforming.

The regime was also popular. Jobs, order and foreign successes won consent, while opposition was limited and mostly passive. After the Anschluss, the slogan "One People, One Reich, One Leader" summed up the mood.
Hitler's first foreign moves rejected the Versailles restrictions step by step. Each time the western powers protested but did not act, which taught him how far he could go.

On 14 October 1933 Germany left the Geneva Disarmament Conference and the League of Nations, claiming unequal treatment. A plebiscite in November 1933 approved the move, with about 95 per cent in favour.
The German-Polish non-aggression pact of 26 January 1934, for ten years.

On 25 July 1934 Austrian Nazis murdered Chancellor Dollfuss in a failed coup in Vienna. Mussolini moved troops to the Brenner Pass, so Hitler backed off and disowned the coup. Kurt Schuschnigg succeeded Dollfuss.
The Saar, governed by the League since 1920, held a plebiscite on 13 January 1935 in which about 90 per cent voted to return to Germany. It was reunited on 1 March 1935, a major propaganda success.

In March 1935 Göring revealed the existence of the Luftwaffe (the German air force) to foreign journalists, and on 16 March Hitler announced conscription, with the army to grow to 36 divisions (about 550,000 men). Both breached Versailles.

The Stresa Front of Britain, France and Italy condemned German rearmament in April 1935 and promised to uphold Locarno and Austrian independence, but took no effective action and broke down after Italy invaded Abyssinia in October 1935.

The Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 18 June 1935 allowed Germany a surface fleet up to 35 per cent the size of the British. Britain accepted it without consulting France, so a Versailles limit was broken with British consent.
The agreement gave Hitler the diplomatic recognition he had sought and weakened the united front against him, which encouraged him to test the western powers further.
From 1936 Hitler moved from undoing Versailles to open expansion, supported by new friends and a growing army. The western powers' failure to resist the Rhineland set the pattern for what followed.

On 7 March 1936 German troops reoccupied the demilitarised Rhineland (the reoccupation), breaking Versailles and the Locarno Treaties of 1925. France, in the middle of an election campaign, and Britain did not resist; the League only condemned it. Hitler offered new peace pacts the same day.
It was a gamble, and the generals were nervous, but its success increased Hitler's popularity at home and his confidence that Britain and France would not fight.

The Rome-Berlin Axis (agreed in October 1936 and named by Mussolini in a speech on 1 November 1936) and the Anti-Comintern Pact between Germany and Japan (25 November 1936, with Italy joining in November 1937) aligned Germany with Italy and Japan.
The German Condor Legion (air and ground units) fought for Franco in the Spanish Civil War from 1936 to 1939 and bombed Guernica in April 1937.

At the Hossbach meeting of 5 November 1937 Hitler told Blomberg, Fritsch, Raeder, Göring and Neurath that Germany's need for space could be solved only by force, at the latest by 1943-45 and earlier if chances arose, starting with Austria and Czechoslovakia.
The minutes were written up days later by Colonel Friedrich Hossbach, so the meeting is known as the Hossbach Memorandum.

In February 1938 Blomberg and Fritsch were removed after personal scandals. Hitler took personal command of the armed forces through a new High Command (OKW), and Joachim von Ribbentrop replaced Neurath as Foreign Minister.

The Anschluss followed: Hitler pressed Schuschnigg at Berchtesgaden in February 1938 to admit Austrian Nazis, including Seyss-Inquart as Interior Minister. Schuschnigg announced a plebiscite for 13 March, cancelled it under pressure and resigned on 11 March; German troops entered Austria on 12 March 1938.
After Austria, Hitler turned to Czechoslovakia. The Sudeten crisis showed how far Britain and France would go to avoid war and how Czechoslovakia was left to pay the price.
Austria was declared part of the Reich on 13 March 1938, and a plebiscite on 10 April 1938 showed over 99 per cent approval, a result produced in an atmosphere of Nazi control.

Konrad Henlein's Sudeten German Party, backed and funded by Berlin, demanded autonomy and then union with Germany for the three million Sudeten Germans, giving Hitler a pretext to threaten Czechoslovakia.
Chamberlain flew to meet Hitler at Berchtesgaden on 15 September 1938 and again at Bad Godesberg on 22 September, where Hitler raised his demands to immediate occupation.

The Munich conference met on 29 September 1938 and the agreement was signed in the early hours of 30 September by Chamberlain, Daladier (France), Hitler and Mussolini. Czechoslovakia was not represented and the Soviet Union, which had a treaty with Czechoslovakia, was not invited.
Czechoslovakia had to hand over the Sudetenland to Germany between 1 and 10 October 1938, and lost its frontier fortifications, leaving it defenceless.
Chamberlain and Hitler also signed a declaration that Britain and Germany would never go to war again. On his return Chamberlain said it was "peace for our time".
Churchill told the Commons in October 1938 that Munich was "a total and unmitigated defeat".
Hitler's seizure of Prague in 1939 broke the logic of appeasement, and within months the road to war was open.

On 15 March 1939 German troops occupied Prague. Bohemia and Moravia became the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, and Slovakia, which declared independence on 14 March, became a German client state.
Memel was taken from Lithuania in March 1939, and Italy invaded Albania in April 1939.
Prague broke the Munich promises and was Hitler's first seizure of non-German land. It ended the belief that his claims were limited to Germans and led Britain to abandon appeasement.

Hitler demanded Danzig and a road and rail link across the Polish Corridor. Britain announced a guarantee of Polish independence on 31 March 1939, with France joining it, and the Anglo-Polish alliance followed on 25 August 1939.

The Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact (the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact) was signed in Moscow on 23 August 1939 by Ribbentrop and Molotov. It promised ten years of non-aggression, and a secret protocol divided Poland and placed the Baltic states and Bessarabia in spheres of influence.
The pact removed the danger of a war on two fronts and was surprising because the two regimes were ideological enemies.
Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and Britain and France declared war on 3 September.
Hitler's foreign policy was driven by racial ideas and by the goal of Lebensraum in the east. Historians argue over whether this meant a plan for war from the start or opportunism.

Lebensraum (living space) was Hitler's goal: Germany needed land in Eastern Europe, to be settled by a racially pure population, with the Slavs to be subjugated. This made war with the east, not just revision of Versailles, the aim.
Herrenvolk (master race) was the idea that Germanic people were racially superior. It underpinned both domestic policy and plans for the conquest and resettlement of Eastern Europe.
Totalitarianism and dictatorship: Hitler's ideology claimed to reach every part of life, which is why the regime tried to control work, schools and families as well as politics.
Appeasement was British and French policy to satisfy Germany's grievances through concessions, based on the belief that Versailles had been unfair and that war must be avoided.

Historians disagree on whether Hitler planned a general war from 1933 or responded to opportunities. Trevor-Roper argued Hitler pursued consistent war aims set out in Mein Kampf (the plan or programme view).
A.J.P. Taylor's The Origins of the Second World War (1961) argued that Hitler was an opportunist with traditional German aims and that the war was a blunder. The book was widely attacked.
The terms intentionalist (Hitler's plan) and functionalist (circumstances and rival agencies) are borrowed from the wider debate about the Nazi state.
Appeasement was the policy of giving way to Hitler's demands to keep the peace. It was supported for several reasons and judged very differently at the time and afterwards.

Britain and France appeased Hitler for several reasons: guilt over Versailles, a horror of another war, a fear of bombing, rearmament that was not ready, reluctant dominions, a belief that communism was the greater threat, and the cost to the economy.

Neville Chamberlain, Prime Minister from May 1937 (succeeding Stanley Baldwin) to May 1940, was its main practitioner, so Munich is linked to his name. Churchill, out of office in the 1930s, was its main critic.
At the time appeasement was popular: Chamberlain was cheered on his return from Munich.
Later it was condemned: the pamphlet Guilty Men (1940), by "Cato" (Michael Foot and others), blamed the appeasers, but some historians defend it as buying time to rearm.
The war gave the regime new radical powers, and Germany's economy and society were geared to total war.
Albert Speer, Hitler's architect, became Minister for Armaments and Munitions in February 1942 after the death of Fritz Todt. Arms output rose sharply until 1944 despite bombing.
After the surrender at Stalingrad, Goebbels called for total war in his Sportpalast speech in Berlin on 18 February 1943. In January 1943 women aged 17 to 45 were required to register for war work.
Millions of foreign forced labourers and prisoners of war worked in Germany by 1944.

On 20 July 1944 Colonel Claus Schenk von Stauffenberg planted a bomb at Hitler's headquarters, the Wolf's Lair near Rastenburg, East Prussia. Hitler was only injured, the coup in Berlin collapsed that night and Stauffenberg was shot.
Thousands were arrested and many executed after the July plot.
Hitler stayed in command to the end and killed himself in his Berlin bunker on 30 April 1945.
Hitler's rule from 1933 to 1939 combined a consolidated dictatorship at home with a foreign policy of rearmament, expansion and war. He directed each stage himself.
Hitler was born on 20 April 1889 at Braunau am Inn, Austria. He served in a Bavarian regiment from 1914 to 1918 and won the Iron Cross First Class in 1918.
He led the Nazi Party from July 1921, attempted the Munich (Beer Hall) Putsch in November 1923, wrote Mein Kampf in Landsberg prison in 1924, and became Chancellor on 30 January 1933.

From 1933 to 1939 he built a dictatorship, rearmed, left the League, took the Rhineland, achieved the Anschluss with Austria, received the Sudetenland under the Munich Agreement, occupied Prague and invaded Poland.
He set the aims and took the key decisions on the purge, the Rhineland, the Anschluss, Czechoslovakia and Poland. He was a participant who directed each stage, not a witness.
His style of rule was to rise late, avoid paperwork and encourage rivalry between subordinates, who competed to anticipate his wishes: what Ian Kershaw calls "working towards the Führer".

At home, he was popular after the Saar, the Rhineland and the Anschluss. Abroad, David Lloyd George visited him in September 1936 and praised him, and many saw a reasonable revisionist, but Churchill warned repeatedly of German rearmament and saw a threat.

Historians' views have changed. Alan Bullock (Hitler: A Study in Tyranny, 1952) saw an opportunist adventurer seeking power, a view later revised. Trevor-Roper stressed consistent war aims, and Taylor argued Hitler was an opportunist.

Hans Mommsen called Hitler a "weak dictator", and Martin Broszat (The Hitler State) saw a chaos of rival agencies. Kershaw's two volumes (1998 and 2000) combine the views through "working towards the Führer".
Examiners reward judgement more than narrative. For each theme, set the achievements against the limits, and be ready to weigh Hitler's own responsibility against other causes.

Totalitarian state: totalitarian aims and terror (SS, Gestapo, camps, courts) show control, but polycracy, a small Gestapo dependent on denunciations, and consent won by jobs and success show it was less total than it looked.
Economy, achievement: unemployment was cut, recovery was achieved and rearmament was built up.
Economy, limit: hidden unemployment, controlled wages, strain and shortages by 1939, and a recovery that had begun before 1933.
Foreign policy, achievement: by 1939 Hitler had overturned Versailles and gained territory without war.
Foreign policy, limit: it led to a general war that Germany was not ready for in 1939 and to the destruction of Germany.

Causes of the war: Hitler's aims and decisions (Mein Kampf, Hossbach, Prague, Poland) made war likely, while Versailles resentment, the weak League, appeasement, the Nazi-Soviet Pact and Mussolini shaped when and how it came.
Plan or opportunism: the usual balanced verdict is fixed long-term aims with opportunist timing and methods, which fits both Trevor-Roper's programme and Taylor's opportunism.

Munich: contemporaries felt relief and cheered Chamberlain in 1938, but it is now generally judged a failure that gave away Czechoslovakia's defences and left Hitler convinced that the western powers would not fight.

Everything Lenin and Stalin did rests on a few starting ideas and facts: the Marxist theory the Bolsheviks believed, the poor country they ruled, and the party machine they used to rule it. Exam questions take these basics for granted.

The Bolsheviks seized power in Petrograd on 7-8 November 1917 (25-26 October by the old Russian calendar) and set up the Council of People's Commissars (Sovnarkom, the new government) with Lenin as chairman.

Marxism says history is a struggle between classes. The working class (the proletariat) would overthrow capitalism, and a 'dictatorship of the proletariat' (rule in the workers' name) would come before a classless communist society. Lenin added that a disciplined party of professional revolutionaries must lead the workers.

Russia was backward: about four-fifths of the people were peasants living on the land, and it had little modern industry compared with Britain, Germany or the USA. This is why Stalin later pushed so hard for industrialisation.

The party ruled through a ladder of bodies. The Party Congress and the Central Committee sat above the Politburo, the small group that made the real decisions, while the General Secretary ran the party machine and its appointments.

The party controlled the soviets (the elected councils that were supposed to hold power) and the government, so whoever controlled the party controlled the state. This is why the post of General Secretary mattered so much in the succession struggle.
The Western (Gregorian) calendar was adopted in February 1918, so every date here is a Western date unless stated, which avoids confusion with the old Russian calendar.
Communism, as used here, is the Marxist ideology and system in which the state owns land, industry and banks and one party claims to rule for the working class.
Lenin held on to power by force. In these years the Bolsheviks created a secret police, banned their rivals and won a civil war, and these methods became the foundation of the Soviet state.

The Cheka, the Bolshevik secret police, was set up in December 1917 under Felix Dzerzhinsky. It used arrest and execution against opponents, including the Socialist Revolutionaries (SRs) and Mensheviks, rival socialist parties.
Lenin was shot and wounded on 30 August 1918. The Red Terror, a campaign of mass arrests and executions, was proclaimed in September 1918.
The Constituent Assembly (the elected parliament) met once in January 1918 and was dispersed by force. This is background, but it shows the Bolsheviks would not share power.

Kadets (a liberal party), Mensheviks and SRs were suppressed and rival parties banned during the civil war. By its end the Communist Party, as the Bolsheviks were renamed in 1918, was the only legal party, so one-party rule was set in place.

The Russian Civil War (1918-1921, with fighting continuing in the Far East until 1922) pitted the Red Army, led by Leon Trotsky as Commissar for War from 1918, against the White armies (anti-Bolshevik forces) and foreign intervention by Britain, France, Japan and the USA.
The White leaders were Kolchak, Denikin, Yudenich and Wrangel. The Reds won because they held the central position, were united and disciplined, and used terror, while the Whites were divided.
To win the civil war Lenin ran the economy like a army supply system. The result was a crisis in 1920-1921 that threatened the Bolsheviks' own supporters.

War Communism (1918-1921) nationalised industry and banks (took them into state ownership), forced peasants to hand over grain at fixed low prices (requisitioning) and rationed food to towns. Private trade was banned, which cut the incentive to grow food.

Peasants hated requisitioning because the state took their grain for little in return. For example, the Tambov peasant rising of 1920-1921, led by Alexander Antonov, was the best known of many peasant revolts, and strikes and economic collapse followed, because the towns were starved of food and goods.
The famine of 1921-1922 on the Volga and elsewhere killed about 5 million people. The American Relief Administration fed millions, which showed how far the policy had failed.

In March 1921 sailors and workers at the Kronstadt naval base near Petrograd rose against Bolshevik rule. They had backed the Bolsheviks in 1917, and now demanded free elections to the soviets, freedom of speech and an end to the monopoly of power.
The Red Army under Tukhachevsky crushed the rising by crossing the frozen Gulf of Finland. The rebels were sailors and workers who had backed the Bolsheviks in 1917.

Faced with revolt, Lenin retreated. The New Economic Policy (NEP) loosened the economy to save the regime, while the party tightened its own discipline, and the state took the form it kept until 1991.

At the Tenth Party Congress in March 1921 the Bolsheviks adopted the NEP. A tax in kind (a fixed share of the crop) replaced grain requisitioning, peasants could sell their surplus, and small private trade and small-scale industry were allowed.
The state kept the 'commanding heights' of the economy, meaning large industry, banks and foreign trade. This is why the NEP was a retreat to save the regime, not a new socialist policy.
The same congress banned factions, so no organised groups could exist inside the party. This was meant to protect unity at a dangerous time, and so Stalin later used the rule against his rivals.

The NEP restored food supplies and output, and the economy recovered by the mid-1920s. It also produced Nepmen (private traders) and better-off peasants called kulaks, so many Communists saw it as a retreat from socialism.

Lenin's slogan of December 1920 was 'Communism is Soviet power plus the electrification of the whole country'. GOELRO, the state electrification plan of 1920, aimed so that electric power could drive industry and modernise a backward country.
The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was formally created on 30 December 1922, bringing together the Russian, Ukrainian, Belorussian and Transcaucasian republics.

Lenin suffered strokes in May 1922, December 1922 and March 1923, and died on 21 January 1924. His embalmed body was displayed in a mausoleum in Red Square, Moscow, and Petrograd was renamed Leningrad that January. He left no clear successor.
Cheka, GPU/OGPU and NKVD are different names for the police at different dates: the Cheka (1917), the GPU/OGPU (1922-34) and the NKVD from 1934. Do not call the 1920s police the NKVD.
Lenin's illness opened a contest to rule the USSR. Stalin won not because he was the best known, but because he controlled the party machine and played his rivals against each other.

Stalin was Commissar for Nationalities from 1917 to 1923 and General Secretary from April 1922. The post gave him control of party appointments, and the 'Lenin enrolment' of 1924 brought in large numbers of new members who owed their places to the party leadership.

Lenin's Testament, dictated from December 1922 to January 1923, criticised all the leading candidates (Trotsky, Zinoviev, Kamenev, Bukharin and Stalin). Its postscript of January 1923 called Stalin 'too rude' and proposed his removal as General Secretary, but it was read to delegates in 1924 and not published.
Trotsky was brilliant and had created the Red Army, but he had joined the Bolsheviks only in 1917, seemed arrogant and was feared as a possible 'Bonaparte' (a general who might seize power).
For example, Zinoviev led the Leningrad party and the Comintern, Kamenev the Moscow party, and Bukharin edited Pravda and was the party's leading theorist.

The policy debate: Trotsky's 'permanent revolution' (spreading revolution abroad) and rapid industrialisation, against Stalin's 'socialism in one country' of 1924. Stalin's idea appealed to party members tired of waiting for world revolution.
With the contest set, Stalin used the party machine to remove his rivals in turn. He first allied with some against others, then adopted the policy of those he had beaten.

Stalin, Zinoviev and Kamenev formed a triumvirate (a ruling trio) against Trotsky in 1923-25. When Zinoviev and Kamenev joined Trotsky in the United Opposition of 1926, it was defeated, Trotsky and Zinoviev were expelled in November 1927, and the Fifteenth Congress expelled the opposition in December 1927.
Trotsky was exiled to Alma-Ata, Kazakhstan, in January 1928 and deported from the USSR in February 1929. Ramon Mercader, an NKVD agent, killed him in Mexico in August 1940 on Stalin's orders.
The Right Opposition (Bukharin, Alexei Rykov, head of the government, and Mikhail Tomsky, trade unions) backed the NEP and gradual growth.

After the grain procurement crisis of 1927-28 Stalin adopted forced industrialisation and grain collection, so the Right was defeated in 1928-29, with Bukharin removed from the Politburo in November 1929.

Stalin had beaten the Left with the Right's help, then took up the Left's policy. He won because of his control of the party machine, his rivals' mistakes and underestimation of him, the ban on factions and his skill in using one faction against another.
Stalin made industrialisation the centre of Soviet policy. The Five-Year Plans were central targets set by the state, and they changed the landscape and the lives of workers.
Stalin wanted to end backwardness, build socialism, strengthen the USSR against attack and secure his power.
In February 1931 he warned managers: 'We are fifty or a hundred years behind the advanced countries. We must make good this distance in ten years. Either we do it, or they will crush us.'

Gosplan, the state planning agency, drew up the First Five-Year Plan, which ran from October 1928 and was declared fulfilled in four years and three months, at the end of 1932. It aimed to turn the USSR into an industrial power.
Targets were set for coal, steel, oil, electricity and machinery, with heavy industry given priority over consumer goods, because heavy industry built the economy and the army.
The showpiece projects were Magnitogorsk, a steel city in the southern Urals built from 1929, the Dnieper dam in Ukraine (completed 1932) and the Moscow Metro (opened 1935).
Magnitogorsk became a symbol of the drive for industrialisation and of the labour that went into it, because it was built quickly by workers drawn from the villages.

Labour came from the villages. Wage differences and bonuses rewarded effort, discipline for lateness and absence was harsh, internal passports controlled movement, and propaganda praised 'shock workers' (workers who exceeded targets).

Alexei Stakhanov, a Donbas coal miner, was reported on 31 August 1935 to have cut 102 tonnes of coal in one shift, about fourteen times the norm. The shift was specially prepared with helpers, and the movement was resented because it raised the norms (the output required) for ordinary workers.

Engineers and managers were blamed for failures as 'wreckers' (people accused of sabotage), beginning with the Shakhty trial of 1928, when engineers in the Donbas mining town of Shakhty were accused of sabotage. This gave Stalin scapegoats for the plan's difficulties.
The plans brought real growth but at enormous human cost, so examiners expect every achievement to be paired with its price.

The Second Five-Year Plan (1933-1937) was more realistic and gave some attention to consumer goods and transport. The Third (1938-1941) shifted to armaments as war approached and was cut short by the German invasion in 1941. The economy was militarised by the late 1930s.
Steel output rose from about 4 million tonnes in 1928 to about 18 million in 1940, and coal from about 35 million tonnes to about 165 million. These are official figures and some were inflated.
There were large rises in oil and electricity too, and the USSR was one of the world's leading industrial powers by 1940. New industrial regions in the Urals and Siberia proved vital in the war.
The costs were high: real wages and living standards fell in the early 1930s, housing was overcrowded, goods were of poor quality, and there was waste and inflated statistics.
Forced labour by Gulag prisoners was used on projects such as the White Sea-Baltic Canal, built in 1931-33, and many of the prisoners died.
Stalin saw the peasants as the obstacle to industrialisation. Collectivisation was meant to give the state control of grain, but it caused one of the worst disasters of the period.

The reasons were the grain procurement crisis of 1927-28, the need to feed the growing towns and to export grain to pay for machinery, a wish to bring the peasants under state and party control, and ideological hostility to private farming and the kulaks.

Collectivisation was launched at the end of 1929 when Stalin called for the 'liquidation of the kulaks as a class' (December 1929). Peasants were forced into kolkhozy (collective farms where land and livestock were pooled and members shared income) that delivered quotas to the state.
Sovkhozy were state farms with paid workers. Machine tractor stations (MTS) supplied machinery to collective farms and also gave the party political control over them.

Dekulakisation was the campaign against kulaks, the better-off peasants. In practice the label was applied to anyone who resisted, and families were shot, sent to camps or deported to Siberia, the Urals and Kazakhstan.
Peasants resisted by slaughtering livestock, burning crops and revolting and there were also women's protests.
In March 1930 Stalin's article 'Dizzy with Success' in Pravda blamed local officials for excesses and allowed peasants to leave the collectives. Many left, but pressure resumed later in 1930.

The famine of 1932-1933 came when high requisitions were taken despite poor harvests. It killed several million people, mainly in Ukraine (where it is called the Holodomor), the North Caucasus, the Volga and Kazakhstan. Estimates differ widely, and whether it was a genocide is debated.
The law of 7 August 1932 punished theft of collective farm property, movement was restricted, the famine was officially denied and grain was still exported.
Collectivisation succeeded in giving the state control of grain, but it did not improve farming.
Over 90 per cent of peasant households were collectivised by the late 1930s, so the state controlled the grain supply.
Livestock numbers and farm output fell and took years to recover. Output was below 1928 levels for years, so the main gain was control, not abundance.
Peasants' small private plots produced a large share of the country's vegetables, milk and meat, which shows how weak the collective farms were.

A personality cult presents a leader as infallible and heroic through propaganda, ritual and images. Stalin's cult built on the Lenin cult that followed Lenin's death in 1924, which gave it a precedent.
The cult began with the celebrations of Stalin's fiftieth birthday in December 1929, when he was hailed as Lenin's heir, a claim that gave him legitimacy against rivals.

Official history was rewritten. The History of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (Bolsheviks): Short Course of 1938 put Stalin at the centre of the revolution, while Trotsky and other fallen leaders were written out and removed from photographs.

Portraits, statues, poems, songs and films presented Stalin as the wise 'father of the peoples' and Lenin's true heir. Towns and places were named after him, and Tsaritsyn was renamed Stalingrad in 1925.
The cult gave Stalin legitimacy as Lenin's successor, produced unity behind one leader during upheaval, and was a substitute for religious and tsarist loyalties.
The Stalin Constitution of December 1936 promised universal suffrage, a secret ballot and civil rights on paper, while one-party rule and the NKVD were unchanged.

Behind the cult stood a machine of fear. Control of everyday life by the secret police is why historians call the USSR a leading example of totalitarianism, a state that tries to control every part of public and private life through one party, an ideology, secret police, terror and propaganda.
The OGPU was absorbed into the NKVD in 1934, and the NKVD ran the secret police and the Gulag camp system, whose prisoners built canals, railways and mines.
The Gulag held more than a million prisoners at a time by the late 1930s, and millions passed through it. Many were peasants and political prisoners.
Internal passports, introduced from December 1932, and registration of residence controlled movement, so peasants were tied to the countryside and 'undesirables' were kept out of the cities.
The Kirov murder, the Moscow trials, the army purge and the Great Terror of 1936-1938 belong to a separate topic. There is more on this in Stalin's show trials.
The regime tried to remake society as well as the economy, aiming at a new Soviet man and woman who valued collective achievement. Some changes widened opportunity while others closed freedom.

Mass literacy campaigns and the expansion of schools and technical colleges trained workers and engineers. After 1931 schools returned to discipline, exams and uniforms, and education also served as indoctrination.
The Young Pioneers and the Komsomol, the Communist youth league, brought children and young people into party organisations, so the party could shape them from an early age.

Women gained legal equality, easy divorce and legal abortion (1920). The Zhenotdel, the party's women's department, ran from 1919 to 1930, and Alexandra Kollontai was a leading Bolshevik campaigner for women's rights.
Women were drawn into industry and the professions, but carried a 'double burden' of work and housework. A 1936 law banned abortion and made divorce harder, to raise the birth rate.

Church property was seized, clergy arrested and churches closed or destroyed. Moscow's Cathedral of Christ the Saviour was blown up in December 1931, the League of the Godless was founded in 1925 and became the League of the Militant Godless in 1929, and atheism was taught in schools.

The 1920s were a time of experiment, for example Sergei Eisenstein's film Battleship Potemkin (1925). In April 1932 a Central Committee decree dissolved independent literary groups and set up a single Union of Soviet Writers.

The First Congress of Soviet Writers in 1934 adopted socialist realism (art showing the heroic building of socialism) as the official method, with Maxim Gorky prominent. Cultural life was controlled by the party.
Pravda attacked Shostakovich's opera Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk in January 1936, and the poet Osip Mandelstam was arrested in 1934 for a poem mocking Stalin and died in a transit camp in 1938.
The regime sought collective values, and its claims of progress during the Depression made it attractive to some foreign observers, while others were horrified. Opinion at the time was divided.
The 'new Soviet man' was a citizen with collective values. Heroes of labour, parades and posters, and public monuments expressed a culture of collective achievement.

The Soviet alternative appealed in the Depression because the West had mass unemployment and falling output, while the USSR claimed full employment, rapid growth and planning. The planned economy looked attractive to some socialists, intellectuals and trade unionists in Britain, France and the USA.

Lincoln Steffens, an American journalist, said after visiting in 1919: 'I have seen the future, and it works.' George Bernard Shaw visited and met Stalin in 1931, and some Western visitors toured factories and collective farms and returned with favourable reports.
Sidney and Beatrice Webb, British socialists, published Soviet Communism: A New Civilisation? in 1935, presenting the system as a model for social planning.
Walter Duranty of the New York Times denied there was a famine. Gareth Jones and Malcolm Muggeridge reported it in 1933 and were attacked for doing so.
Liberals, conservatives, the churches and many socialists pointed to the famine, the lack of freedom and the show trials. Fear of communism also helped fascism in Europe.
Recognition by the United States in November 1933 and membership of the League of Nations in September 1934 gave the regime growing respectability and international standing.
Soviet foreign policy swung between isolation, co-operation with Germany, collective security and finally a pact with Hitler, shaped by fear of attack.
The Treaty of Rapallo with Germany (April 1922) restored relations between two outcast states, and secret military co-operation, including German rearmament on Soviet soil, followed.
The Comintern (Communist International), founded in March 1919, controlled foreign communist parties. Its 'social fascist' line against Social Democrats split the German left before 1933.

After Hitler's rise the USSR turned to collective security (joint resistance to aggression). Maxim Litvinov was Foreign Commissar from 1930 to 1939, the USSR joined the League in 1934, signed pacts with France and Czechoslovakia in May 1935 and backed Popular Fronts of left-wing co-operation.
Soviet aid went to the Spanish Republic from October 1936, but the USSR was excluded from the Munich Conference in September 1938, and Molotov replaced Litvinov in May 1939.

The Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact of 23 August 1939, signed by Molotov and Ribbentrop, had a secret protocol dividing eastern Europe. It was a non-aggression pact, not a military alliance, and it gave Stalin time and a buffer.
The Red Army entered eastern Poland on 17 September 1939. In spring 1940 the NKVD shot about 22,000 Polish officers, police and others in the Katyn massacre, and the USSR blamed Germany until 1990.
The Winter War with Finland (November 1939 - March 1940) exposed Red Army weakness, and Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were annexed in 1940.
The USSR was unready in June 1941 because Stalin ignored repeated warnings of a German attack, and the army was weakened by the purges.
The German invasion tested the Soviet system. After disastrous early errors, Stalin took charge and the state was reorganised for total war.
Germany invaded on 22 June 1941 in Operation Barbarossa. The Red Army suffered huge early losses of men, territory and aircraft, and Leningrad was besieged from September 1941 to January 1944.

Stalin withdrew briefly in late June 1941 before taking charge. He chaired the State Defence Committee (GKO), set up on 30 June 1941 to direct the war economy, and in a radio broadcast on 3 July 1941 addressed listeners as 'brothers and sisters'.

Stalin became Supreme Commander in August 1941 and stayed in Moscow during the German advance of autumn 1941. The German advance was stopped before Moscow, and a Soviet counter-offensive under Georgy Zhukov followed in December 1941.
About 1,500 industrial enterprises were moved east to the Urals, Siberia and Central Asia, mostly in the second half of 1941. There was total mobilisation of labour, including women.
Output of tanks and aircraft rose sharply by 1942 and soon exceeded Germany's, including the T-34 tank.
After the crisis, the Soviet Union turned the tide, but the regime kept terror alongside appeals to patriotism, and the war left it a superpower.

The Battle of Stalingrad, from August 1942 to 2 February 1943, was the turning point in the east. A Soviet counter-encirclement in November 1942 trapped the German Sixth Army under Paulus, which surrendered.
Kursk in July 1943 followed, so the Soviets kept the initiative, and the Red Army advanced west to Berlin in April-May 1945, with German surrender in May 1945.

Order 227 of 28 July 1942, 'Not one step back', led to blocking detachments behind the front line and penal battalions for those who retreated. The NKVD enforced discipline behind the lines, including executions of deserters and punishment of soldiers who had been captured.
Lend-Lease supplies from Britain and the USA, such as trucks, food and equipment, were a significant support to the Red Army, because they eased shortages of transport and food.

Stalin appealed to patriotism over ideology. The conflict was called the 'Great Patriotic War' from 1941, appeals were made to Russian history and heroes, the Orthodox Church was allowed a patriarch again in September 1943 and the Comintern was dissolved in May 1943.

Whole peoples accused of collaboration were deported: Volga Germans in 1941, Chechens and Ingush in February 1944 and Crimean Tatars in May 1944. Returning prisoners of war were treated as suspects and many were sent to camps.
Soviet deaths in the Second World War were about 27 million, military and civilian combined, far more than any other combatant, which shows the scale of the sacrifice behind the victory.

Stalin made disastrous early errors by ignoring warnings and forbidding retreat in 1941, then relied more on able generals such as Zhukov. He was given the rank of Generalissimo in June 1945, and most German army losses were on the Eastern Front.
By 1945 the USSR had survived, and victory was turned into political capital for Stalin.
The USSR emerged as a superpower because the Red Army was in control of eastern Europe.
Victory was used to strengthen Stalin's authority and to claim that the system had been proved right.
Stalin attended wartime conferences at Tehran (1943), Yalta (February 1945, with Churchill and Roosevelt) and Potsdam (July-August 1945, with Truman, and Churchill then Attlee).
Lenin led the Bolsheviks from the 1903 split until 1924, and he created the institutions that Stalin inherited.
Born Vladimir Ulyanov in 1870 at Simbirsk, he had an elder brother, Alexander, who was executed in 1887 for plotting against Tsar Alexander III.

He returned to Russia in April 1917 and issued the April Theses, calling for power to pass to the soviets. He led the Bolsheviks in seizing power in October 1917 and headed Sovnarkom, the first Soviet government.
He then set up the Cheka and terror, introduced War Communism, and made the retreat to the NEP in 1921 and created the USSR in 1922.
He shaped events as architect of the one-party state, but was flexible enough to retreat to the NEP to save the regime. He also banned factions and wrote his Testament.
He was a participant, not a witness: he led and decided at every stage until his strokes.
To the party he was the unquestioned authority on Marxism, while to opponents (Mensheviks, SRs, Kronstadt sailors) he was a dictator. After his death in 1924 the Lenin cult grew.

Historians divide: the continuity view (Richard Pipes is a leading example) holds that Lenin's terror, one-party rule and ban on factions made Stalinism possible, while the discontinuity view holds that the NEP and the Testament show a different path that Stalin abandoned.
Stalin ruled from the late 1920s until his death in 1953, and he transformed the Soviet economy and society and built a cult around himself.

Born Ioseb Dzhugashvili in 1878 at Gori, Georgia (Soviet sources later gave 1879), he trained for the priesthood at the Tiflis seminary. He became a Bolshevik revolutionary, was several times exiled to Siberia, and took the name Stalin, from the Russian for steel.

He became General Secretary in 1922 and defeated his rivals by 1929. He directed the Five-Year Plans from 1928 and collectivisation from 1929, carried out the Terror of 1936-38, signed the Nazi-Soviet Pact in 1939 and was war leader from 1941 to 1945. He died on 5 March 1953.
He drove a 'revolution from above', but was also shaped by the grain crisis, fear of foreign attack and the Bolshevik tradition of terror.

Contemporaries differed. Lenin warned against him in the Testament, the cult called him 'father of the peoples', Western admirers such as Shaw and the Webbs praised him, and critics included Trotsky in exile.
Nikita Khrushchev denounced the cult in his secret speech to the 20th Party Congress in February 1956, which is why the cult is seen as ending officially only after his death.

Robert Conquest (The Great Terror, 1968, and The Harvest of Sorrow, 1986, on collectivisation and the famine) took the totalitarian view. Isaac Deutscher (Stalin: A Political Biography, 1949) saw a brutal moderniser, and social historians such as Sheila Fitzpatrick (Everyday Stalinism, 1999) studied everyday life and pressures from below.

Judgements of the Soviet system balance achievements against the human costs of its methods. Examiners reward a stated verdict in the introduction and conclusion that pairs each achievement with its limit.
Lenin, achievement: he won the civil war, held the state together and the NEP produced recovery.
Lenin, limit: terror, one-party rule, the famine of 1921-1922 and Kronstadt.
Industry, achievement: an industrial and military power by 1941, so it could out-produce Germany in the war.
Industry, limit: low living standards, waste, forced labour and inflated statistics.
Agriculture, achievement: state control of grain, so towns and exports could be supplied, and mechanisation through the MTS.
Agriculture, failure: the famine, the destruction of the kulaks and output below 1928 levels for years.
Society, achievement: literacy, education, and women's work and professional opportunities. Limit: no political freedom, persecution of religion and the arts, and the 1936 reversal on family policy.

Foreign policy and war: survival, victory and superpower status, against the Nazi-Soviet Pact leaving the USSR unready in 1941 and about 27 million dead. Views differ: the totalitarian school against social historians, and continuity against a break between Lenin and Stalin.

By 1934 Stalin had already beaten every rival in the party and controlled a powerful secret police. The public trials of 1936 to 1938 copied a pattern that earlier trials had tested on engineers and foreigners.
Stalin had been General Secretary of the Communist Party since 1922, which let him shape the party machine and its appointments.
In the succession struggle he defeated Trotsky (expelled from the party in 1927, deported from the USSR in 1929), then Zinoviev and Kamenev, expelled in 1927 and later readmitted.

He also defeated the Right, Bukharin, Rykov and Tomsky, in 1928-29, and Bukharin was removed from the Politburo in 1929. This is why the later trials could present all of them as old enemies of his leadership.

The First Five-Year Plan (from October 1928) and collectivisation (from late 1929) brought shortages, accidents, missed targets and the famine of 1932-33. These costs created a need for someone to blame.

The secret police had passed from the Cheka to the OGPU, which was merged into the NKVD (the People's Commissariat for Internal Affairs) in July 1934. The Gulag, the Main Administration of Camps, had been set up in 1930.

The Shakhty trial of 1928 tried engineers from a Donbas coal town on charges of sabotage and foreign conspiracy. The Industrial Party trial of 1930 repeated the charges against leading technical specialists, so the regime had already shown that sabotage claims could be staged.

In April 1933 six British engineers of the Metropolitan-Vickers company were among those tried in Moscow for espionage and wrecking, a case that showed the regime blaming foreigners for industrial failures.

A party purge or chistka (a cleansing of the membership) began in 1933, when members judged unreliable were expelled. In 1935 a check on party documents led to further expulsions. These purges were not at first fatal, which separates them from the Terror that followed.
Historians list several causes at once, and examiners reward ranking them. Some are about Stalin's own power, some about blame for economic failure, and some about fear of the outside world.

Stalin's suspicion, often called paranoia, and his wish for unchallenged personal power meant that anyone with independent standing in the party looked like a threat. This is why even loyal veterans were treated as dangerous.

Rivals: Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin were old Bolsheviks who kept the prestige of 1917 and of Lenin's time. With Trotsky in exile abroad, they could be presented as a potential alternative leadership.
