Scapegoats: the costs of the plans needed an explanation other than bad policy, so managers, engineers and officials were accused of 'wrecking' (deliberate damage to industry) and sabotage.

Fear of war: as Nazi Germany and Japan grew stronger, and Hitler rose, Stalin feared a 'fifth column' (secret traitors who would help an invader), and the trials charged defendants with plotting with those powers. This is why the charges so often named Germany and Japan.
Signs of discontent inside the party: in 1932 Martemyan Ryutin circulated a platform calling for Stalin's removal, and he was expelled and imprisoned (he was shot in 1937).

The 17th Party Congress of January and February 1934, known as the Congress of Victors, celebrated the success of the plans. Of its 1,966 delegates, 1,108 were later arrested, so the Congress became a target rather than a triumph.

Historians differ on motive. Robert Conquest (The Great Terror, 1968) and Oleg Khlevniuk, working from the opened archives, stress Stalin's central direction. J. Arch Getty (Origins of the Great Purges, 1985) stresses disorder, local initiative and real tensions.

Others point to real tensions over the pace of industrialisation, fear of foreign attack, and pressure on local officials to find enemies. In short, the debate is central planning against pressure from below, and paranoia against calculation.
The shooting of a leading Stalinist gave Stalin the pretext for the repression that followed. Whoever planned it, he used it to claim that a network of conspirators existed.

Sergei Kirov, party leader in Leningrad and a member of the Politburo, was shot dead on 1 December 1934 at the Smolny Institute, the party headquarters in Leningrad. The killer was Leonid Nikolaev, a young party member who had lost his job and had been briefly expelled.

A decree issued on the evening of the murder, on Stalin's initiative, ordered that terrorism cases be investigated within ten days, heard without defence lawyers, with no appeal and with death sentences carried out at once. This removed every legal protection for the accused.

The NKVD first blamed 'white guard' terrorists (supporters of the old order), then former supporters of Zinoviev in Leningrad. Nikolaev was tried in secret and shot in December 1934. This is why the blame kept shifting towards Stalin's old rivals.
Zinoviev and Kamenev were tried in secret in January 1935 and given prison terms of ten and five years. In 1936 they were brought back for a public trial on much graver charges.

Historians disagree about the murder. Conquest suspected that Stalin or the NKVD arranged it, while Getty and Matthew Lenoe (The Kirov Murder and Soviet History, 2010) find that Nikolaev acted alone. No document proving Stalin's involvement has been found.
Either way, Stalin exploited the killing. He claimed that a network of conspirators existed and that the opposition had been drawn into terrorism, and he used this claim to justify the show trials.
The Trial of the Trotskyite-Zinovievite Terrorist Centre opened the public series and showed that even Lenin's closest colleagues could be made to confess.

The trial was held from 19 to 24 August 1936 at the House of Unions in Moscow, with sixteen defendants led by Grigory Zinoviev and Lev Kamenev, two of Lenin's closest colleagues and former members of the Politburo.

They were charged with forming a terrorist centre under Trotsky's direction, murdering Kirov, and plotting to kill Stalin and other leaders. These charges tied the old opposition to Kirov's death, so that they looked like murderers rather than critics.

Before the trial Zinoviev and Kamenev had held out for months. Stalin reportedly promised that their lives and their families would be spared if they confessed (the source is later testimony, not a document), and the NKVD interrogators told them that confession would serve the party.

All sixteen defendants confessed in open court and were sentenced to death on 24 August. They were shot on 25 August 1936, within hours of the verdict, despite the reported promise. This is why the verdict served as a warning to every other oppositionist.

Trotsky, then living in Norway, and his son Lev Sedov were named as the organisers of the plot and were condemned in their absence. Naming him linked the accused to Stalin's chief enemy abroad, so that the plot looked like a foreign one.
Mikhail Tomsky, the trade union leader and former Right Oppositionist, was named during the trial and shot himself on 22 August 1936 before he could be arrested.
The trial opened a campaign against 'Trotskyite-Zinovievite' enemies and led to the arrest of thousands of former oppositionists.
The trial of the so-called Anti-Soviet Trotskyite Centre moved the charges from terrorism to industrial sabotage. This gave a ready explanation for the failures of the Five-Year Plans.

It was held from 23 to 30 January 1937 and tried seventeen defendants, among them Yuri Pyatakov, a deputy commissar for heavy industry, and the journalist Karl Radek. This meant the trial worked as an excuse for industrial failure.

The defendants were accused of wrecking in factories and mines, causing railway accidents and plotting with Trotsky, Germany and Japan to restore capitalism. These charges explained the failures of the plans as the work of traitors.

Pyatakov testified that he had flown to Oslo in December 1935 to meet Trotsky. The Norwegian authorities stated that no foreign aircraft had landed at the airfield then, an inconsistency that foreign critics noticed.
Thirteen defendants, including Pyatakov, were shot. Radek and Grigory Sokolnikov received ten years in prison, and two others received eight years. Radek had co-operated with the prosecution.

Radek died in prison in 1939. The usual account is that a fellow prisoner killed him on NKVD orders, though the circumstances are unclear. The uncertainty is why historians describe it as 'the usual account'.
Sergo Ordzhonikidze, Commissar for Heavy Industry and Pyatakov's superior, died on 18 February 1937. The official cause was heart failure, but it is generally believed that he shot himself.
The NKVD itself changed hands. Genrikh Yagoda, its head from 1934, was replaced by Nikolai Yezhov in September 1936, and Yagoda later became a defendant in the third trial.
The Trial of the Right-Trotskyite Bloc was the last and the largest of the public trials. It brought the leaders of the old Right Opposition and the former head of the secret police into the dock.

It was held from 2 to 13 March 1938 and tried twenty-one defendants. They included Nikolai Bukharin (former editor of Pravda and Comintern chairman), Alexei Rykov (former head of the Soviet government), the former NKVD chief Genrikh Yagoda, and Nikolai Krestinsky.

The defendants were charged with treason, spying for foreign powers, wrecking, planning to break up the USSR, and murder plots, including against Lenin in 1918, Stalin and Kirov. They were also accused of killing the writer Maxim Gorky, who died in 1936.
Yagoda and a group of doctors were accused of causing deaths by 'medical murder'.

On the first day Krestinsky denied his confession, saying it was false, but he withdrew the denial the next day after a night in NKVD hands. This shows how the NKVD could make a defendant change his mind overnight.

Bukharin admitted general political responsibility for the 'bloc' but denied the specific charges of espionage and murder. This has been read as an attempt to signal his innocence to a careful reader.

Eighteen defendants, including Bukharin, Rykov and Yagoda, were shot on 15 March 1938, and three others received prison terms. This made the third trial the most deadly of the three, with eighteen of twenty-one shot.
Bukharin was rehabilitated (officially declared innocent) by the Soviet government in 1988, as were Zinoviev and Kamenev.
The trials were scripted from start to finish, and Stalin himself oversaw the charges and the testimony. The aim was to make a confession look like proof, since there was no documentary evidence.

The prosecutor Andrei Vyshinsky, Procurator-General of the USSR and a former Menshevik, prepared the cases with the NKVD and argued that a confession was sufficient proof of guilt. In 1936 he demanded that the defendants be shot as 'mad dogs'.

Vasily Ulrikh, chairman of the Military Collegium of the Supreme Court, presided over all three trials as judge and helped to keep the proceedings tightly controlled. This is why the verdicts were never in doubt.

The NKVD obtained confessions by sleep deprivation, endless interrogation, threats against family members and false promises of leniency. Stalin's telegram of January 1939 confirms that physical pressure had been allowed from 1937. Such methods explain why defendants confessed to crimes they could not have committed.
The evidence for physical torture is strongest from 1937, and methods varied, so you should not say that every defendant was tortured.

Defendants rehearsed their parts. Some seem to have been persuaded that confession served the party's interest, an argument used by interrogators on loyal communists who had given their lives to the party.

The trials took place in public at the House of Unions in central Moscow before an invited audience, with foreign journalists and diplomats present and the transcripts published in several languages. The aim was to convince the world as well as the Soviet people.
Soviet newspapers and mass meetings demanded death for the 'enemies of the people' before the verdicts were given. For example, the demand for death was public before any court had spoken.

Weaknesses in the evidence were noticed abroad: the Oslo flight, a defendant's claim in the first trial to have met Sedov in 1932 at the Hotel Bristol in Copenhagen, a hotel that had been demolished in 1917, and the near-identical wording of confessions.
Because foreigners were allowed into the courtroom, the trials were judged by observers who disagreed sharply. Their views are the evidence behind many documents questions.

Joseph Davies, the American ambassador in Moscow from January 1937, attended parts of the 1937 and 1938 trials and reported to Washington that the defendants appeared guilty. This is why Soviet propaganda could quote a foreign diplomat in the trials' favour.

The German exile writer Lion Feuchtwanger visited Moscow, attended the January 1937 trial and defended the trials in his book Moscow 1937. Ivan Maisky, the Soviet ambassador in London from 1932 to 1943, defended them to British visitors.
Western communist parties defended the trials as necessary to destroy fascist agents. Some members left the party over the issue. Their defence mattered because they were loyal to Moscow.

Some other diplomats and journalists were doubtful. Fitzroy Maclean, a junior British diplomat, attended the 1938 trial and described it later in Eastern Approaches (1949). Many liberals and socialists condemned the proceedings as a travesty of justice.

In 1937 a commission of inquiry chaired by the American philosopher John Dewey heard Trotsky's evidence at Coyoacán, Mexico, in April. It announced in December 1937 that the trials were frame-ups, and its report was published as Not Guilty in 1938.
The trials damaged the reputation of the Soviet Union among liberals and the left, at the very time of the Popular Fronts (alliances of left-wing parties against fascism).
Stalin used the verdicts to discredit Trotsky. On 20 August 1940 Trotsky was attacked in Mexico by the NKVD agent Ramón Mercader and died the next day, which ended the campaign against him.
The destruction of the army leadership took place largely in secret, unlike the public trials. It was a closed tribunal, not a show trial, so keep the two separate.

Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky, former First Deputy Commissar for Defence and the leading advocate of mechanised warfare, was arrested in May 1937 with other senior officers. He was a dangerous figure to Stalin because of his rank and prestige in the army.
He and seven other senior commanders were tried by a closed military tribunal on 11 June 1937 on charges of treason and spying for Germany, and were shot on 12 June 1937.
The evidence was fabricated and relied on confessions, and holding the trial in secret meant that foreign observers could not test it.

Three of the five Marshals of the Soviet Union died in the purge: Tukhachevsky and Alexander Yegorov were shot, and Vasily Blyukher died in custody in 1938. Most army commanders were arrested, as were many naval and air force officers.
Estimates of officers dismissed in 1937-38 are around 30,000 to 35,000. Many were arrested, but some were later reinstated, and political commissars regained control of the army.
The purge left the Red Army poorly led at the time of the Winter War against Finland (November 1939 to March 1940) and the German invasion of 22 June 1941.
Historians debate how much the purge explains the defeats of 1941.
Show trials were the visible tip of a mass campaign run by the NKVD and carried out largely in secret. Most of its victims were not famous communists.
Nikolai Yezhov replaced Yagoda as head of the NKVD in September 1936, and the years 1937 and 1938 are known as the Yezhovshchina ('the Yezhov times').
NKVD Order 00447 of 30 July 1937 set quotas by region for arrests of 'former kulaks, criminals and anti-Soviet elements'. The first category was to be shot and the second sent to camps.
Local NKVD chiefs asked for higher quotas and the totals were exceeded. This is why the Terror reached far beyond the party, because local chiefs competed to show zeal.

National operations in 1937-38 targeted ethnic groups with foreign connections, such as Poles, Germans and Latvians, who were suspected of loyalty to other states. The Polish operation was the largest. This is why the Polish operation hit so many ordinary families.

NKVD records show about 1.5 to 1.6 million arrests in 1937-38 and about 680,000 executions (archives opened after 1989). Deaths in camps and prisons are additional, so some historians believe the true total of deaths was higher.
The archives and Khrushchev's 1956 speech give the scale of the Terror, and its mass phase ended only when Stalin turned on the NKVD itself.
Many victims were ordinary workers, peasants and minorities rather than officials, so fear spread through the whole of society and not only the party.
Neighbours and colleagues were encouraged to denounce 'enemies of the people', and the families of the arrested were stigmatised and often arrested too.

According to Khrushchev's secret speech of 25 February 1956, 1,108 of the 1,966 delegates to the 17th Congress were arrested, and 98 of the 139 members and candidates of the Central Committee elected there were arrested and shot.
By 1939 the Gulag held well over a million prisoners, whose forced labour was used on the economy's projects. This shows that the Terror also fed the economy with forced labour.
The Terror slowed in late 1938. Yezhov was removed in November 1938 and replaced by Lavrentiy Beria, and Yezhov was arrested in April 1939 and shot in February 1940.
The trials show three of the syllabus concepts working together. Each one explains how Stalin could stage a lie and make people believe it.

Totalitarianism (a state that leaves no area of life outside political control): the secret police, the control of the courts and the press, and the ability to make leading communists confess to invented crimes show it at work.

Propaganda (the deliberate shaping of opinion): newspapers, radio and public meetings across the USSR demanded death for the 'enemies of the people', and the published transcripts and confessions were used to explain shortages and accidents.

Personality cult (the building of a leader into a heroic, near-infallible figure): the trials presented Stalin as the vigilant leader who protected the people and as Lenin's true heir, while the old Bolsheviks were written out of the revolution.

The Short Course history of the party, published in 1938, carried this further by presenting the defendants as agents of foreign powers from the beginning of the revolution. This is why the defendants could be called traitors even in the history books.
The trials changed every part of Soviet life: the party, the army, the economy and society. A strong answer gives a dated fact for each and ends with a judgement.
The party: the old Bolshevik leadership was destroyed. Stalin's rivals and potential rivals were dead or in exile, and no organised opposition was left.
Younger men promoted into the vacancies in the party, army and industry owed their careers to Stalin, which made the new elite loyal to him alone.

The army: the loss of experienced commanders, and the fear and caution in the officer corps that followed, are widely linked to the poor performance against Finland in 1939-40 and the German advance in 1941.

The economy: managers, engineers and planners were lost, and fear of being accused of wrecking made officials cautious, so they avoided decisions or falsified results. Gulag labour was used on the economy's projects.

Society: fear, denunciation and the arrest of relatives bred silence and broke families, and the families of those arrested were stigmatised as relatives of 'enemies of the people'. This is why it was safer to say nothing.

Stalin's personal power became absolute. History was rewritten in the Short Course (1938), the History of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (Bolsheviks), to make the old Bolsheviks traitors from the start and Stalin Lenin's true heir, so that no rival could claim a share of the revolution.

Later, in his secret speech to the 20th Party Congress in February 1956, Khrushchev condemned the Terror. Mass rehabilitations followed, including Tukhachevsky in 1957, and Bukharin's in 1988 was one of the last.
Judgements balance the consolidation of Stalin's personal power against the damage the Terror did to the state. Examiners reward paired points and a clear verdict.

Achievement for Stalin: by 1939 the party, army and state were in the hands of officials loyal to him, his rivals were gone, and no organised opposition survived. This is why the Terror can be called a success in terms of power.
Limit for the regime: the loss of officers, managers and specialists weakened the army, the party and the economy in the years before the German invasion of 1941.
Contemporary supportive view: Soviet propaganda and foreign communists presented the trials as the exposure of real traitors, and visitors such as Davies and Feuchtwanger accepted the evidence.
Contemporary critical view: the Dewey Commission, liberal and socialist critics and many diplomats treated the trials as frame-ups.

Later view: after the archives opened in the 1990s, historians agree that the trials were stage-managed fabrications, though they still debate how far Stalin planned the Terror and how far it reflected paranoia or political calculation. This is why the later view differs from the contemporary views.
Later revisionist view: Getty and others stress the disorder and local initiative in the Terror, while Conquest and Khlevniuk emphasise central planning by Stalin.
Link to the economy: the trials served as the explanation of the plans' failures, since managers and engineers were blamed as wreckers.
The Third Republic was France's parliamentary democracy from 1870 to 1940. Its institutions and parties explain why so much of the politics of the 1920s and 1930s looked the way it did.

The Republic was proclaimed in 1870, after France's defeat by Prussia, and its constitutional laws date from 1875. Democracy here means government by elected representatives answerable to the voters, with free elections, parties and civil rights, although only men could vote.
Parliament had two houses: an elected Chamber of Deputies and an indirectly elected Senate, which could block laws, so reforms needed to pass both. Women had no vote until 1944-45.

The President, elected for seven years by the Chamber and Senate meeting together, had a largely ceremonial role. Real power lay with the Prime Minister (called the President of the Council) and the ministers.
Governments needed a majority in the Chamber and fell when they lost a vote, so ministers lived at the mercy of the deputies.
No single party ever won a majority, so every government was a coalition. The right was made up of conservative and Catholic groups, and the Radical Party stood in the centre-left.

The Radical Party, anticlerical (opposed to the Church's influence) and strong among small-town and rural voters, was the hinge of most coalitions because governments needed its votes whether they leaned left or right. It was the largest force in most governments of the 1920s and early 1930s.
The left consisted of the Socialists (the SFIO) and, from 1920, the Communists (the PCF), founded at the Congress of Tours in December 1920 after a split in the Socialist party.

French society was deeply divided: left against right, Catholic against secular (anticlerical) France, workers against employers, Paris against the provinces. These divisions shaped every crisis of the period, because each camp distrusted the other's government.

France won the First World War but paid heavily for it, and its politics after 1919 were dominated by the demand that Germany pay. The first post-war government, the Bloc National, was built around that aim.

About 1.4 million French soldiers were killed in 1914-1918, and the north-east, where much of the fighting took place, was devastated, with many villages and farms destroyed. A falling birth rate and heavy war debts added to the damage.
Alsace-Lorraine returned to France by the Treaty of Versailles in 1919. Even so, France felt a deep fear of Germany, so it wanted the treaty enforced in full.

Reconstruction of the devastated areas was financed by borrowing, in the expectation that German reparations (payments for war damage) would repay the loans. The slogan of the early 1920s, 'Germany will pay' ('L'Allemagne paiera'), summed up this hope.
The Bloc National, a coalition of conservative, centre and Catholic parties, won the November 1919 election and governed until 1924. It took a firm line on Germany and against the left.
Clemenceau left politics, his career ended, after he was defeated in the presidential election of January 1920 by Paul Deschanel.
Budget deficits, large debts and a falling franc marked the early and mid 1920s. This made the government's reliance on German payments a financial gamble as well as a political one.
When Germany fell behind with reparations, France chose force. The result showed the limits of French power and left it short of friends.
Raymond Poincaré was Prime Minister from January 1922 to June 1924 and took a hard line towards Germany, which suited the parties of the Bloc National.
In January 1923, after Germany defaulted on reparations (failed to pay what was due), French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr, a German industrial area.
Germany answered with passive resistance, refusing to co-operate with the occupiers. Britain disapproved openly and refused to take part.
The Dawes Plan of 1924 reorganised German payments, so the French troops were no longer needed and were withdrawn by 1925.
The occupation brought some payments, but also isolation, cost and a weaker franc, so it ended without securing full reparations.
While governments argued about money, French foreign policy pursued one aim: protection against a revival of German power.
France made an alliance with Poland in 1921 and a treaty with Czechoslovakia in 1924, to gain friends against Germany in eastern Europe.
Aristide Briand was Foreign Minister for most of the years 1925 to 1932 and favoured agreement with Germany rather than force, in contrast to Poincaré's hard line.
The Locarno treaties of 1925, which aimed to keep the peace in western Europe, and the Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928, in which states renounced war, were his best-known achievements.
Briand shared the 1926 Nobel Peace Prize with the German statesman Stresemann.
France also decided in this period to build a fortified line along the German border, the Maginot Line, as a further guarantee of security.
Voters turned left in 1924, but a financial crisis undid the new government. Poincaré's return then restored confidence and gave France a few calm, prosperous years.
The Cartel des Gauches, a coalition of Radicals and Socialists, won the May 1924 election, and Édouard Herriot, a Radical, was Prime Minister from June 1924 to April 1925.

The Cartel fell in April 1925 after a run on the franc (people rushing to sell francs) and a financial crisis. It was called the 'wall of money': banks and investors had lost confidence in a left-wing government.
A run of short governments followed in the next years, and the franc crisis of July 1926 brought Poincaré back at the head of a Government of National Union.
Poincaré raised taxes and cut spending, which restored confidence, so the franc was stabilised in practice by late 1926.
The 'Poincaré franc' was fixed in law in June 1928 at about one-fifth of its 1914 gold value. The late 1920s were prosperous, and Poincaré retired in July 1929 because of ill health.
Governments in the Third Republic were short-lived, which made steady policy difficult. Several features of the system, working together, explain why.
There were many parties and no majority party, so governments were fragile coalitions that lasted only as long as every partner agreed.
The Radicals switched between left and right partners, so withdrawing their support could topple a government quickly.
The Chamber held frequent votes of no confidence, and governments changed very often, many lasting only months. Ministers were often replaced after a few months in office.
The President had the power to dissolve the Chamber, but it was not used after 1877, so deputies could bring down governments without facing an election themselves.
The Senate blocked reforms, so reforming governments lost momentum, and financial crises, especially in 1924-26, brought governments down.

The President's role was largely ceremonial, so policy was decided by the Prime Minister and the parliamentary majority, and when the majority broke up there was no one else to hold the government together.
France's economy was less affected by the Depression at first than Britain's or Germany's, but the slump arrived later and was prolonged by government policy.
France's economy rested on small family farms and small family firms, and the country held large gold reserves, which cushioned it against the immediate effects of the Wall Street Crash.

The slump hit in earnest from 1931, with industrial production falling sharply. It then lasted longer than in Britain or Germany, and recovery was slow until the late 1930s. Farmers and small businesses suffered most.
Official unemployment stayed lower than in Britain or Germany, partly because foreign workers left and some unemployed returned to the land. It still remained a serious problem.

Governments kept the franc at its 1928 gold value, and France led the 'gold bloc' of countries that stayed on gold. To defend the currency they used deflation, cutting spending, wages and prices, which deepened the slump and hurt industry and farming.
Pierre Laval, Prime Minister from June 1935 to January 1936, issued decree-laws in 1935 that cut public spending and salaries, so the policy of deflation continued.
The franc was devalued (its gold value lowered) only under the Popular Front in autumn 1936, after which exports recovered slightly.

The left (Radicals and Socialists) won the May 1932 election and Herriot was Prime Minister again, but governments fell in quick succession. Contempt for parliament and 'the politicians' grew, which prepared the ground for the leagues.
As faith in parliament fell, leagues offered an alternative. These were anti-parliamentary, nationalist and mostly right-wing movements.

Action française was founded in 1899 and led by Charles Maurras. It was monarchist and anti-Semitic, had opposed the republic since before 1914, and its street militants were called the Camelots du Roi.
The Jeunesses Patriotes were led by Pierre Taittinger, and the Solidarité française was funded by the perfume maker François Coty, so the leagues had wealthy backers as well as street militants.
The Croix-de-Feu was a veterans' league led by Colonel François de La Rocque. It was the largest league, with hundreds of thousands of members by 1936.
Francisme, led by Marcel Bucard, was a smaller group that was openly fascist, which made it different from the larger leagues that claimed only to defend the nation.

Economic hardship and fear of war split French opinion into left and right camps, so the leagues found support on the right while Communists and Socialists gained from the unity forged after February 1934.

Historians disagree on how far the leagues threatened democracy. René Rémond argued that they belonged to France's traditional right, while Zeev Sternhell (Neither Right nor Left, 1983) argued that fascist ideas had deep roots in France.
After the leagues were dissolved in 1936, the Croix-de-Feu re-formed as the Parti Social Français, which grew into a large party.
A financial scandal in January 1934 gave the leagues their chance. The riot that followed brought down a government and pushed the left to unite.
Alexandre Stavisky was a swindler with political protection who sold worthless bonds through the municipal pawnshop (the Crédit municipal) of Bayonne.
He was found shot dead in January 1934. The police called it suicide, but left and right both suspected he had been silenced, and the affair suggested corruption reaching into the Radical Party.
The scandal forced the resignation of the Radical Prime Minister Camille Chautemps in January 1934, and the leagues used it to attack the republic as corrupt.
The new Prime Minister, Édouard Daladier, dismissed Jean Chiappe, the Paris Prefect of Police, who was favoured by the right. This angered the right further.

On 6 February 1934 the leagues, including the Croix-de-Feu, Action française and the Solidarité française, and veterans' groups marched on the Chamber of Deputies. Police opened fire and about 15 people were killed and over a thousand injured.
Daladier resigned on 7 February, the first government brought down by street violence. A government of national union under Gaston Doumergue, with Pétain as War Minister, was formed to restore order.
The left read 6 February as an attempted fascist coup. It responded with a general strike and mass demonstration on 12 February 1934, which led to left unity.
Fear of fascism did what years of argument had not, and brought Socialists, Communists and Radicals together. Their alliance, the Popular Front, won power in 1936.

The Socialist-Communist unity-of-action pact of July 1934 was possible because the Comintern, the international body of Communist parties directed from Moscow, had reversed the Communists' hostility to other left parties. Its Seventh Congress confirmed the popular front line in 1935.
The Radicals joined in 1935, shown at the mass rally of 14 July 1935, and a joint programme followed in January 1936. The slogan was 'Bread, Peace and Liberty' ('Pain, Paix, Liberté').
The Popular Front won a majority in the elections of 26 April and 3 May 1936, and Léon Blum became Prime Minister on 4 June 1936. Socialists and Radicals sat in the cabinet.
The Communists supported the government in parliament but took no ministries, so they should not be listed as ministers.
Blum was the first Socialist and the first Jewish Prime Minister, but not the first left-of-centre one, because Herriot, a Radical, had led the Cartel in 1924.
Blum was attacked by the anti-Semitic right and was beaten up by Action française supporters in February 1936.
Three women became under-secretaries, Cécile Brunschvicg, Irène Joliot-Curie and Suzanne Lacore, although women could not yet vote.

Workers expected a Popular Front government to improve their lives, and they pressed the point with strikes. The employers gave way, and the Matignon Agreements and the June laws were the biggest social gains of the period.

The strikes began in May 1936 (from about 11 May), before Blum took office. The main wave and the factory occupations came after he formed his government on 4 June, and they peaked in early-to-mid June.
Many were sit-down strikes, in which workers occupied their factories instead of leaving them, and about two million workers were out at the height of the wave.

The pressure of the wave pushed the employers into the Matignon Agreements, reached on 7-8 June 1936 in the middle of the wave to end it. They were signed at the Hôtel Matignon, the Prime Minister's residence, with Blum chairing the talks between employers and unions.
The agreements gave wage rises of about 7 to 15 per cent, union recognition (the right of unions to represent workers), collective agreements and elected workers' delegates.
Laws that month brought in the 40-hour week and two weeks' paid holiday, which meant that for the first time many workers could take a holiday.
Beyond Matignon, the government used its majority to reshape the economy, farming, schools and leisure, and to deal with the leagues.
The leagues were dissolved in June 1936, because the government feared the threat they had shown on 6 February 1934.
The Wheat Office was set up in 1936 to stabilise farm prices, which helped farmers hurt by deflation, for example wheat growers.
The state gained greater control of the Bank of France, and the arms industry was part-nationalised (partly taken into state ownership).
The school-leaving age was raised to 14 in 1936 by the education minister Jean Zay.
Léo Lagrange, under-secretary for sport and leisure, developed a leisure and sport policy that included cheap rail tickets for holidays.
A rearmament programme began in September 1936, and the franc was devalued in autumn 1936.
The plans for public works spending were limited by financial pressure and capital flight.
The Popular Front's gains were soon eroded by economic trouble, and the Spanish Civil War split the coalition itself.
Capital fled abroad because investors distrusted the government, and rising prices ate up the wage gains of workers.
Industrial output was slow to recover, and the 40-hour week limited production, including the production of arms.

Blum adopted a policy of non-intervention in the Spanish Civil War in August 1936. This angered the Communists and much of his own party, but Britain backed non-intervention and the Radicals opposed intervening, so he feared splitting the coalition and the country.
Roger Salengro, the Interior Minister, killed himself in November 1936 after a campaign against him in the right-wing press.

The anti-Semitic right hated Blum, and a phrase attributed to parts of the right said they preferred Hitler to Blum. The origin of the phrase is unclear, so do not treat it as anyone's recorded words.
Economic pressure and the Senate's opposition ended the Popular Front's reforming period. Its social gains were then undone one by one.
Blum announced a pause in reform in February 1937, because financial pressure made further spending impossible.
He resigned in June 1937 when the Senate refused him emergency financial powers. Governments under Chautemps followed.
Blum led a brief second government in March and April 1938, and Daladier became Prime Minister in April 1938 (he held office until March 1940), which ended the coalition.
The finance minister Paul Reynaud's decree-laws of November 1938 undid the 40-hour week.
The general strike of 30 November 1938 failed, and its failure ended the Popular Front era.
France's defences in the 1930s reflected memories of the First World War and a fear of losing another generation of young men. The result was a defensive strategy with fatal weaknesses.

The Maginot Line was named after André Maginot, the War Minister. A law funding it passed in January 1930, and it was built mainly in the 1930s, so it was funded from 1930 and built mainly in the 1930s. It was very expensive.
It was a system of concrete forts and underground works along the Franco-German border, designed to hold an invader while the army mobilised.
It reflected defensive thinking after Verdun and the shortage of manpower, because France could not afford the huge casualties of attacking again.
It did not extend along the Belgian border, because Belgium was an ally until it declared neutrality in 1936. It was also weak opposite the Ardennes, a wooded region thought unsuitable for tanks.
The army's doctrine was slow, methodical and defensive. Tanks were spread among infantry units instead of being concentrated.
De Gaulle's book of 1934, Vers l'armée de métier (in English The Army of the Future), argued for a professional armoured force. It was ignored.
As Hitler's Germany rearmed, France looked for allies but did not act alone. Its caution helped to make war more likely.
France signed the Franco-Soviet Pact in May 1935, because it hoped for an ally against Germany.
When Hitler remilitarised the Rhineland on 7 March 1936, France took no action, and its reliance on Britain grew.
Daladier signed the Munich Agreement on 29-30 September 1938, which showed how far France followed Britain's policy of appeasement.
France declared war in September 1939 but did little fighting for eight months. When the German attack came in May 1940, the French plan collapsed within weeks.

France declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939, after the invasion of Poland. During the Phoney War (the drôle de guerre) there was little fighting, and the army under General Maurice Gamelin, the commander-in-chief, waited behind the Maginot Line.
The Communist Party was banned in September 1939 after the Nazi-Soviet Pact, which the Communists had to defend. Paul Reynaud replaced Daladier as Prime Minister in March 1940.
The German attack began on 10 May 1940. Gamelin and Pétain thought the Ardennes forest difficult terrain for tanks, so the main French and British forces moved into Belgium on the Dyle plan.
German armoured divisions came through the Ardennes and crossed the Meuse at Sedan on 13 May and reached the Channel coast at Abbeville on 20 May, cutting off the northern armies.
Maxime Weygand replaced Gamelin on 19 May. The British Expeditionary Force and many French troops, about 338,000 Allied troops in all, were evacuated from Dunkirk between 26 May and 4 June.
Once the northern armies were cut off, resistance collapsed. Within six weeks the government had asked for peace and the Republic was at an end.
Italy declared war on France on 10 June 1940. Paris was declared an open city (undefended) and occupied on 14 June, and millions of civilians fled south in the 'exodus'.
The government left Paris for Bordeaux, and Reynaud resigned on 16 June. Pétain became Prime Minister and asked Germany for an armistice on 17 June.

The armistice was signed with Germany on 22 June 1940 at Compiègne, in the same railway carriage as the 1918 armistice, so that Germany's humiliation of 1918 was reversed. A separate armistice with Italy followed on 24 June.
France was divided into an occupied zone, the north and the Atlantic coast, about three-fifths of the country, and an unoccupied zone in the south. Alsace-Lorraine was in practice annexed by Germany.
France had to pay the costs of occupation, at first 400 million francs a day, and prisoners of war were to stay in Germany.
The armistice army was limited to 100,000 men, and the fleet was to be disarmed but kept by France.
About 1.8 million French soldiers were taken prisoner in 1940, and well over a million were still in Germany years later.
The Third Republic did not fall to a coup. Its own parliament voted away its powers, which makes 10 July 1940 a key date in the story of democracy in France.
After the armistice the government settled at Vichy, a spa town in the unoccupied zone, in July 1940.

On 10 July 1940 the National Assembly, the Chamber and Senate meeting together in the Grand Casino at Vichy, voted by 569 to 80, with about 20 abstentions, to give full powers to Marshal Philippe Pétain to draw up a new constitution.
The vote did not itself create the Vichy regime. The next day, 11 July, Pétain's constitutional acts made him Head of the French State.

The order of events is therefore armistice (22 June), vote (10 July), Head of State (11 July). The Third Republic had survived the Depression and the leagues, but it ended by its own parliament's vote.
The speed of the defeat shocked contemporaries and has been argued over ever since. Explanations fall into two schools, military and political.

Military explanations stress the army's slow defensive doctrine, slow command and communications, and the gamble that the Ardennes was unsuitable for tanks. German air power and surprise also mattered.

France had roughly as many tanks as Germany, but it spread many of them among infantry units instead of concentrating them in armoured divisions as Germany did, so the Germans could break through at one point.
The Maginot Line did not extend along the Belgian frontier or through the Ardennes, so the Germans simply went round it.
Ernest May (Strange Victory, 2000) stresses poor intelligence, slow command and German skill rather than moral failure.
Political and moral explanations stress instability, division, defeatism and 'decadence' (a decline in the nation's will). The historian Jean-Baptiste Duroselle took this view in La Décadence (1979).
Marc Bloch, a historian and army officer, wrote the contemporary witness account Strange Defeat in 1940 (published 1946). He later joined the Resistance and was shot by the Germans in 1944.
Contemporaries blamed the political decadence of the Third Republic, and Vichy used that explanation. Today most historians stress the military failures of May 1940.
Pétain was the most admired soldier in France in 1940 and became the ruler of the Vichy state. His reputation has fallen from saviour to collaborator.
Pétain was born in 1856 and became known as the 'victor of Verdun' for his part in the battle of 1916, which gave him huge prestige.
He was War Minister in 1934, in Doumergue's government, and ambassador to Franco's Spain in 1939.
He became Prime Minister in June 1940 at the age of 84, asked for the armistice, and was Head of the French State from 1940 to 1944.
He was taken to Sigmaringen in Germany in 1944 and was later tried in France. He was sentenced to death in August 1945, but de Gaulle commuted the sentence to life imprisonment, and he died in 1951.
Many saw him in 1940 as a saviour who would shield France, because he had been a hero in 1916.
Historians now judge him a collaborator who bore responsibility for persecution under his regime.
De Gaulle began 1940 as a little-known general and ended the war as the leader of liberated France. He also built the image of France that lasted for decades.
De Gaulle was born in 1890 and argued in the 1930s for armoured warfare, which was later shown to be the German method, but his ideas were ignored.
He commanded the 4th Armoured Division in May 1940, and became Under-Secretary of State for War in Reynaud's government from early June 1940.
His appeal of 18 June 1940 led to the Free French, and he led the Provisional Government from 1944. A Vichy court sentenced him to death in his absence in 1940, so his regime was a rival to Vichy.
He resigned in January 1946, and the Fourth Republic's constitution was approved by referendum in October 1946.
He built the post-war image of a France united in resistance, an image later historians challenged.
Blum led the Popular Front government of 1936 and was the target of the anti-Semitic right. Vichy then put him on trial for the defeat.
Blum was born in 1872 and was a Socialist leader. He was Prime Minister in 1936-37 and briefly in 1938.
He was the first Socialist and the first Jewish Prime Minister, and was attacked by the anti-Semitic right, which beat him up in February 1936.
Vichy tried him at Riom, with Daladier and Gamelin, in a trial that opened in 1942 and was suspended when it embarrassed the regime.
He was held by the Germans from 1943 to 1945, near Buchenwald, and survived.
Laval held office under both the Third Republic and Vichy, and he is remembered above all as the man of collaboration.
Laval was born in 1883 and was Prime Minister in 1931-32 and 1935-36, so he led governments under the Third Republic as well as under Vichy.
His 1935 decree-laws cut spending and salaries, and the Hoare-Laval Pact of December 1935 concerned Abyssinia.
He became Pétain's deputy in 1940, but he was dismissed in December 1940. Admiral Darlan, not Laval, led the Vichy government in 1941.
He returned as head of government from April 1942 until 1944, and was executed in October 1945 after being convicted of treason.
Pétain's regime rejected the Republic and its values. It called itself the French State and set out to remake France through what it called the National Revolution.
The regime renamed the state the French State (the État français). Pétain, aged 84, held executive and legislative power, and there was no parliament and there were no elections.

The capital was the spa town of Vichy. The regime governed all France in law, except Alsace-Lorraine, and was based in the unoccupied zone, but the Germans ruled the occupied zone directly through their military administration.

Instead of a single party, Vichy relied on the Legion of French Combatants, a veterans' organisation founded in August 1940. A cult of Pétain grew, with portraits and the song 'Maréchal, nous voilà!'.
Vichy's own press and radio supported the National Revolution, and its youth organisations, including the youth camps (Chantiers de la jeunesse), aimed to instil discipline and loyalty to Pétain.
The National Revolution blamed the defeat on the Republic, the left, the Popular Front and 'anti-French' groups, so it presented defeat as a punishment for decadence.
The motto 'Travail, Famille, Patrie' (Work, Family, Fatherland) replaced the republican 'Liberté, Égalité, Fraternite'.
It favoured the Catholic Church, the family and large families, women's place in the home, and a return to the land and rural life.
Vichy was an authoritarian regime that silenced opposition and punished groups it blamed for the defeat.
The trade union confederations were dissolved and strikes were banned. The Labour Charter of October 1941 replaced the unions, so workers lost the rights won in 1936.
Freemasons, Communists and Jews were excluded from public life or persecuted, because the regime held them responsible for France's decline.
De Gaulle was sentenced to death in his absence in 1940.
The Riom trial of Blum, Daladier and Gamelin opened in February 1942, to blame the Republic's leaders for the defeat, but it was suspended in April 1942 when it embarrassed the regime.

Collaboration means co-operation with the occupying power. In France there was state collaboration by the Vichy government, and collaborationism, the open support for Nazism of fascist groups, was a separate phenomenon.
On 24 October 1940 Pétain met Hitler at Montoire, and on 30 October he announced in a broadcast: 'I enter today on the path of collaboration.'
Laval was dismissed on 13 December 1940, and Admiral François Darlan headed the government from February 1941 to April 1942.
Laval returned as head of government in April 1942 and in a broadcast in June 1942 said: 'I wish for a German victory.' This led to ever closer co-operation with Germany.

The British attack on the French fleet at Mers-el-Kébir in Algeria on 3 July 1940, to stop it falling into German hands, killed about 1,300 French sailors. It fed anti-British feeling and helped Vichy.
Vichy hoped for a better place in a German-dominated Europe, wanted the release of prisoners, saw a chance to carry out the National Revolution, and was anti-communist.
Defenders argued that Pétain acted as a 'shield' protecting the French from harsher German rule, whereas critics said Vichy collaborated willingly.
The occupation touched daily life in every part of France. It brought hardship and then, in 1942, ended Vichy's limited independence.
France had to pay the costs of the German occupation, set at 400 million francs a day at first, and its food, raw materials and industrial output were directed to Germany.
Rationing, queues, shortages and the black market (illegal trading at high prices) affected daily life, because so much was sent to Germany.
Well over a million French prisoners of war remained in Germany for years, so thousands of families lacked fathers and sons.
In 1942 the relève was announced in June: skilled workers went to Germany in return for the release of prisoners. It was voluntary and a failure.
After the Allied landings in French North Africa on 8 November 1942 (Operation Torch), the Germans occupied the southern zone on 11 November, so the 'free' zone ended.
The fleet was scuttled (sunk by its own crews) at Toulon on 27 November 1942, so that Germany could not seize it. Vichy lost what independence it had left.
Some French people went further than the Vichy government, and wanted a fascist France allied to Nazi Germany. They are called collaborationists.
These were Paris-based fascist parties, more pro-Nazi than Vichy itself.
Jacques Doriot, an ex-Communist turned fascist, led the Parti Populaire Français, founded in 1936.
Marcel Deat led the Rassemblement National Populaire, founded in 1941.
The Legion of French Volunteers against Bolshevism, founded in 1941, fought on the Eastern Front, so it was an armed force of collaboration.
Vichy persecuted Jews on its own initiative, and later its police helped to deport them. French people also saved many.
The first Statute on Jews of October 1940 was issued without any German demand. It excluded Jews from public service and many professions, so thousands lost their livelihoods.

A second statute followed in June 1941. The Commissariat-General for Jewish Questions was set up in March 1941, first led by Xavier Vallat, and Jewish businesses were 'aryanised', that is taken over. Foreign Jews were interned in camps.
From 1942 Vichy's police, under Rene Bousquet's agreements with the SS, carried out arrests in both zones. Foreign Jews in the southern zone were handed over in August 1942.
On 16-17 July 1942, in the Vel' d'Hiv round-up, French police arrested about 13,000 Jews in Paris, including about 4,000 children.
Families were held in the Vélodrome d'Hiver cycling stadium and then sent through camps such as Drancy, a transit camp near Paris, to Auschwitz.
About 76,000 Jews were deported from France and about 2,500 survived. About three-quarters of the Jews in France survived the war, many helped by ordinary people and churches.
By 1943 Vichy was becoming a police state. It created its own armed force and sent French workers to Germany.
The Milice, led by Joseph Darnand, was founded in January 1943. It was Vichy's paramilitary police, so French men hunted fellow French resisters and Jews and fought the maquis.
It carried out reprisals against civilians, which was a sign of Vichy becoming a police state by 1943-44.
The Service du Travail Obligatoire (STO), a compulsory labour service, was introduced in February 1943 after the voluntary relève had failed. It sent young French men to work in Germany.
Many went into hiding in the maquis to avoid it, which swelled the Resistance.
Vichy's police and administration carried out many arrests and deportations, so French officials were directly involved, and collaboration extended to the economy, with supplies sent to Germany.
Historians since Robert Paxton's Vichy France of 1972 have argued that Vichy's collaboration was active and not merely a shield against harsher German policy.
Resistance means organised opposition to the occupier and to Vichy. It began outside France, with a single general in London.

Charles de Gaulle, a brigadier-general and Under-Secretary for War in Reynaud's government in June 1940, broadcast an appeal on the BBC from London on 18 June 1940, calling on the French to continue the fight.
Churchill recognised him as leader of the Free French on 28 June 1940. French Equatorial Africa, led by Chad, rallied to him in August 1940.
His Free French forces fought alongside the British.
His relations with Churchill and especially Roosevelt, who preferred General Henri Giraud, were difficult.
De Gaulle won control of the French Committee of National Liberation, formed in Algiers in June 1943, and it became the Provisional Government of the French Republic in June 1944.
Inside France resistance began with small groups and grew into an organised movement, which depended on the Communists and on Jean Moulin to unite it.
In 1940-41 the early groups were small and made up of volunteers. They produced underground newspapers, ran escape lines for Allied airmen and gathered intelligence for Britain.
In the south the main movements were Combat (Henri Frenay), Libération (Emmanuel d'Astier de La Vigerie) and Franc-Tireur.
The Communists joined armed resistance after Germany invaded the USSR on 22 June 1941. The Francs-Tireurs et Partisans, formed in 1942, became one of the largest armed groups.
The Germans took hostages and shot them in reprisal, for example at Châteaubriant in October 1941, hoping to frighten people away from resistance.
The Resistance was divided among Gaullists, Communists and other political groups, so unity was hard.

Jean Moulin, de Gaulle's representative, was parachuted into France in January 1942 and united the main groups. He chaired the first meeting of the National Council of the Resistance in Paris on 27 May 1943.
Moulin was arrested at Caluire near Lyon in June 1943 and died after torture in July 1943. The Council's programme of March 1944 set out plans for post-war social reform.
In 1943-44 armed resistance grew, and the Germans and the Milice answered with terror. Ordinary people also took risks to save others.
The maquis, groups of guerrillas in rural areas, grew as young men fled the STO in 1943 and 1944. In 1944 the armed groups were united as the French Forces of the Interior (FFI).
Sabotage of railways and telephone lines helped the Normandy landings, because it slowed German reinforcements. The Vercors maquis was crushed in July 1944.
The Gestapo and Milice used torture and executions, and Klaus Barbie was the Gestapo chief in Lyon.
On 9 June 1944 the SS Das Reich division hanged 99 men at Tulle, and on 10 June it massacred more than 600 villagers at Oradour-sur-Glane (642 is the usual figure).
The village of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon, where Protestant villagers led by Pastor André Trocmé sheltered thousands of Jews and refugees, became a symbol of civilian rescue.
The Resistance was always a minority, as was active collaboration. Most people tried to survive (attentisme, 'wait and see').
Allied landings and a rising in Paris freed France in 1944.
D-Day was on 6 June 1944, and there were landings in Provence on 15 August 1944, in which French forces under General de Lattre de Tassigny took part.

The Paris rising began on 19 August, and General Leclerc's 2nd Armoured Division, a Free French unit, entered the city. The German commander von Choltitz surrendered, and Paris was liberated on 25 August 1944.
On 26 August 1944 de Gaulle walked down the Champs-Élysées as head of the Provisional Government.
The Allies recognised his Provisional Government in October 1944. It prevented civil war between Gaullists and Communists and restored the Republic's authority.
After the liberation France settled accounts with collaborators. It then wrote a new constitution, and Vichy was finally buried.
In the purge (the épuration) there were summary executions of collaborators, about 9,000-10,000 though estimates vary, and women accused of relations with Germans were publicly shaved.
Resistance groups also carried out executions of collaborators and informers, and these reprisals were a source of political tension. Trials followed.
Pétain was sentenced to death in August 1945, but de Gaulle commuted the sentence to life imprisonment. Laval was shot on 15 October 1945.
An ordinance of April 1944 gave women the vote, first used in 1945.
De Gaulle resigned on 20 January 1946, and the Fourth Republic's constitution was approved by referendum in October 1946.
How the French remembered Vichy changed over time. After the war a comforting myth took hold, and later historians and film-makers challenged it.
After the war the 'sword and shield' view held that de Gaulle was the sword and Pétain the shield (Robert Aron, History of Vichy, 1954).
Robert Paxton (Vichy France: Old Guard and New Order, 1972) argued that collaboration was Vichy's own choice and its anti-Jewish laws were home-grown.

The Gaullist myth of a nation united in resistance, which suited a country eager to forget, was challenged from the 1970s by Marcel Ophuls's film The Sorrow and the Pity (made 1969, shown in French cinemas in 1971, banned from French television until 1981) and by Paxton.
Henry Rousso's The Vichy Syndrome (1987) studied how France struggled to face this past.
Maurice Papon, a Vichy official, was convicted in 1998, and in a speech on 16 July 1995 President Jacques Chirac acknowledged the French state's responsibility for the Vel' d'Hiv round-up.

Judgements of the Third Republic weigh its survival and its reforms against its instability and its failure to resist invasion. Judgements of Vichy and the Resistance depend on whether you take the contemporary or the later view.
Achievement: the Third Republic stabilised the franc under Poincaré, survived the Depression and the leagues' challenge in 1934 without a coup, and its institutions held until 1940.
Limit: governments changed very often, the response to the Depression was slow, and France stayed divided. The failure to modernise the army left it unprepared for the German attack of 1940.
Achievement: the Popular Front brought paid holidays and shorter working hours to French workers in 1936.
Limit: the Popular Front's economic policies failed to reduce unemployment, the 40-hour week was undone in 1938, and it could not agree on how to respond to the Spanish Civil War.
Contemporary view: many French conservatives in 1940 saw the armistice and Pétain's rule as a necessary response to military defeat and the failures of the republic, and Pétain as a shield.
Later view: historians stress that Vichy was not forced into collaboration, and that its anti-Jewish policies went beyond German demands in some areas.
The Resistance was a minority but important, and it helped the Republic return in 1944-46.
Verdict: the problems were overcome only in part. Finance, survival of the Republic and social reform were achievements, but instability, division and defence were not solved before defeat in 1940.

Britain entered the inter-war years with an economy that the First World War had weakened, and with a run of governments that tried different answers to the same problems. Knowing who governed when lets you match each policy to the right Chancellor and party.

Before 1914 Britain's wealth rested on exports from the staple industries (the long-established heavy industries: coal, cotton, shipbuilding, iron and steel), which sold to the whole world and gave Britain its lead.

The First World War cost Britain export markets to the USA, Japan and others, whose industries grew while Britain's factories made weapons, and it left large war debts. This is why the staple industries struggled to recover afterwards.

Governments were: Lloyd George's coalition to October 1922; Conservative governments under Stanley Baldwin in 1923 and 1924-29; minority Labour governments (without a majority in the Commons) under Ramsay MacDonald in 1924 and 1929-31.
From August 1931 the National Government, a cross-party coalition, ruled until 1940. MacDonald was Prime Minister to 1935, Baldwin 1935-37 and Neville Chamberlain 1937-40.
The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 began a world depression, in which world trade, prices and investment all collapsed. Britain, which lived by selling goods abroad, was hit hard.
A short post-war boom gave way to a sharp slump from late 1920, and the government's cuts in public spending deepened unemployment in the early 1920s.

The boom of 1919-20 came because demand held back during the war was released once wartime controls were removed; prices rose sharply and speculation spread. Lloyd George's 1918 promise of 'homes fit for heroes' raised hopes of a better Britain.
The slump began in late 1920, when prices and exports collapsed. Registered unemployment passed two million by mid-1921 and, after 1921, did not fall below one million until the Second World War.

The Geddes Axe of 1922 was named after Sir Eric Geddes, who chaired the Committee on National Expenditure. It recommended deep cuts in public spending on education, housing and the armed forces, which deepened the slump.
Unemployment insurance began in 1911 for a few trades and was extended in 1920 to most manual workers, about 12 million people, though farm workers and domestic servants were left out.

Benefit, known as 'the dole', ran only for limited periods, so long-term unemployed people fell back on extra payments or Poor Law relief (the old system of local charity for the destitute). In the 1920s claimants also had to prove they were 'genuinely seeking work'.
Wartime government control of the coal mines ended on 31 March 1921. The mines had always been privately owned, so the owners cut wages and locked miners out (refused to let them work).

On 'Black Friday', 15 April 1921, the railwaymen's and transport workers' unions of the Triple Alliance, an agreement of three unions to strike together, called off their support, leaving the miners to be defeated.

The staple industries had been the basis of the Victorian economy, and between the wars they shrank. Because each was concentrated in particular regions, the decline produced a country split between struggling areas and prosperous ones.

The staple industries declined for several reasons: lost export markets, foreign competition, old equipment and methods, many small firms, falling world demand (oil and electricity replaced coal) and, after 1925, a pound that was too high for exporters.
Coal lost exports, and the worst-hit coalfields were South Wales, Durham and Northumberland, and Lanarkshire. Whole villages depended on a single pit, so when it closed there was no other work.
Lancashire's cotton industry lost markets in India and the Far East to Indian and Japanese mills, and suffered a long decline with many mills closed by the 1930s.
Shipbuilding yards on the Clyde, Tyne and Wear were short of orders after the post-war boom and again after 1929, and many closed in the 1930s. Iron and steel suffered with them.

'Rationalisation' means closing surplus capacity to save the rest. National Shipbuilders' Security Ltd, set up in 1930 with the Bank of England's backing, bought up and closed yards it judged surplus.

The 'distressed' or 'depressed' areas were South Wales, the north-east, Lancashire, west Cumberland and central Scotland. In 1932 more than a third of insured workers in Wales were unemployed, against about one in seven in London and the south-east.
In the worst towns, such as Merthyr Tydfil and Jarrow, over half the insured workers were unemployed in the early to mid 1930s, while the south-east and the Midlands stayed comparatively prosperous.

The unemployed did not simply move to where work was because moving and housing cost money, family and community ties held them, and older skilled men were unsuited to new work. The Industrial Transference Board (1928) helped some to move.
In 1925 the government fixed the pound to gold at the pre-war rate. This made life harder for exporters such as the coal industry, and it set the scene for the General Strike.
Under the gold standard a currency is fixed to gold, so its exchange rate is fixed too. A high rate makes a country's exports dearer abroad and its imports cheaper.
Churchill, Chancellor of the Exchequer from 1924 to 1929, announced the return to gold in his April 1925 budget, at the pre-war rate of 4.86 dollars to the pound.

Keynes argued in The Economic Consequences of Mr Churchill (1925) that the pound was overvalued, by about 10 per cent in his estimate, so exports would be dearer and wages, above all miners' wages, would be forced down.
Owners tried to protect profits by cutting wages and lengthening hours. The miners' leader A.J. Cook gave them their slogan: 'Not a penny off the pay, not a minute on the day'.
On 'Red Friday', 31 July 1925, the government agreed a nine-month subsidy to the coal industry, buying time, and set up a Royal Commission under Sir Herbert Samuel.

The Samuel Commission reported in March 1926. It rejected nationalisation (state ownership of the mines) and recommended wage cuts, which the miners refused. The owners locked them out from 1 May 1926.

When the coal dispute reached a lock-out, the Trades Union Congress (TUC), the central body of the trade unions, called out its members in support. The strike lasted nine days and ended in defeat for the unions.

The TUC called the General Strike, which ran from 4 to 12 May 1926, in support of the locked-out miners. About one and a half to one and three-quarter million workers, including transport, printing, iron and steel and power workers, came out.
The government was prepared. The Organisation for the Maintenance of Supplies (OMS), set up in 1925, recruited volunteers, and troops guarded convoys of food. The strike was largely peaceful.

The government published the British Gazette, edited by Churchill, while the TUC produced the British Worker. The BBC, then new, was under the government's influence and gave little voice to the strikers.
The TUC called the strike off on 12 May, after nine days, without any guarantees for the miners. It was Britain's only general strike, and it was not an attempt at revolution.
The miners stayed out until late 1926 and then returned on lower wages and longer hours.

Union membership fell, and the Trade Disputes and Trade Unions Act of 1927 made general and sympathetic strikes illegal. It also made members 'contract in' (choose to join) to pay the political levy to Labour, a rule repealed in 1946.
The strike showed that the labour movement worked through constitutional, not revolutionary, politics, which is one reason Britain's democracy held in the 1930s.

The world depression struck a minority Labour government that held to orthodox finance. A budget crisis in 1931 split the party, brought in the National Government and ended in Britain leaving the gold standard.

The second Labour government (from June 1929) was the largest party with 287 seats but had no majority. Philip Snowden, the Chancellor, kept to balanced budgets and free trade, the 'Treasury view' that state spending only crowds out private investment.
As exports fell, registered unemployment rose from just over one million in 1929 to about two and a half million by the end of 1930, and the unemployment insurance fund ran into debt.
In 1930 the Labour minister Sir Oswald Mosley proposed public works, protection and earlier retirement in the Mosley Memorandum. It was rejected, and he resigned in May 1930.

The May Report (Sir George May's Committee on National Expenditure), published on 31 July 1931, forecast a budget deficit (spending above income) of about 120 million pounds and recommended cuts of about 96 million pounds, including 20 per cent off unemployment benefit. A run on the pound followed.

The Cabinet split over a 10 per cent cut in benefit. On 24 August 1931 MacDonald formed a National Government with the Conservatives and some Liberals, and Labour went into opposition and expelled him, Snowden and the others who joined.

The emergency budget of September 1931 cut benefit by 10 per cent, cut public-sector pay and raised taxes. On 15 and 16 September sailors of the Atlantic Fleet at Invergordon, Scotland, refused duty over pay cuts, the Invergordon mutiny.
Britain left the gold standard on 21 September 1931 and the pound fell by about a quarter against the dollar. This made exports cheaper and allowed interest rates to fall.
In the general election of 27 October 1931 National Government candidates won 554 seats and Labour fell to about 50.

Once off gold, the National Government dropped free trade and kept money cheap, while Chamberlain held to balanced budgets. Recovery came, but chiefly from these policies, private building and later rearmament.

The Import Duties Act (passed February 1932, in force 1 March) set a general tariff (a tax on imports) of 10 per cent on most imports, higher on some. Empire goods were exempt. This ended free trade and is Britain's example of protectionism.
Protection helped industries such as steel and motor vehicles, but it raised the cost of food and materials for consumers.

The Ottawa Agreements, made at the Imperial Economic Conference in July-August 1932, gave preference to trade within the Empire (imperial preference). This helped trade with the Empire but cost trade with the USA and Europe.

Bank Rate, the central bank's basic interest rate, was cut to 2 per cent on 30 June 1932 and kept there until August 1939. This 'cheap money' made borrowing cheaper, so mortgages were cheap and housebuilding boomed.
In 1932 about 2 billion pounds of 5 per cent War Loan was converted to 3.5 per cent, lowering the government's own interest bill.
The Wheat Act of 1932 gave a subsidy to wheat growers, and marketing boards such as the Milk Marketing Board (1933) helped farmers.
Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor from November 1931 to May 1937, kept to balanced budgets and no large public-works programme. The 1931 cuts in benefit were restored in 1934.
Rearmament from the mid-1930s, speeded up from 1936, brought orders for steel, shipbuilding, engineering and aircraft. It helped some depressed areas more than any regional policy did.

How the unemployed were paid mattered as much as how many there were. From 1931 the household means test, which judged claims by the whole family's resources, became the most hated feature of the system.

The Local Government Act of 1929 abolished the Boards of Guardians (the local bodies that ran Poor Law relief) and passed relief to the Public Assistance Committees (PACs) of county and county borough councils from April 1930.

In November 1931 the household means test began. After 26 weeks on insurance benefit, unemployed people received 'transitional payments' from the PACs only after a test of the whole household's income and savings.

The test was hated because inspectors came into the home, the earnings of sons and daughters and savings were counted, furniture might have to be sold, and families split up as young earners left home. It brought humiliation and stigma.
Some councils applied it leniently. Labour-controlled authorities in County Durham and Rotherham were among those whose committees were replaced by government commissioners in 1932.

The Unemployment Act of 1934 restored insurance benefit and ran it separately. It created the national Unemployment Assistance Board (UAB) to pay the long-term unemployed from January 1935 on national scales.

Many payments fell under the UAB's new scales, causing mass protest, largest in South Wales in early 1935. The government suspended the cuts by the Unemployment Assistance (Temporary Provisions) Act of 1935, known as the 'Standstill' Act.
The unemployed did not only wait for help. The National Unemployed Workers' Movement organised protest, and hunger marches to London brought the issue to public attention.

The National Unemployed Workers' Movement (NUWM), founded in 1921 and led by the Communist Wal Hannington, organised protests, helped people with benefit claims and resisted evictions. The Labour Party and the TUC distrusted it because of its Communist leadership.
National hunger marches to London took place in 1922, 1929, 1930, 1932, 1934 and 1936. Marchers walked from the depressed regions to demand work and an end to the means test.
The authorities often met the marches with police and government hostility. The 1932 march saw clashes with police in London, in Hyde Park, though the marchers also won public sympathy.
The Jarrow March of 5 to 31 October 1936, with about 200 marchers, became the best-known protest. It was organised by the council, not the NUWM. There is more on this in the Jarrow March notes.

The government's regional help was small, but housebuilding and the new light industries of the south-east and the Midlands changed the economy and created jobs. This is why the 1930s were prosperous for much of Britain even while the staple regions suffered.

The Special Areas (Development and Improvement) Act of December 1934 named four Special Areas: South Wales, Tyneside and Durham, west Cumberland, and central Scotland (Clydeside and Lanarkshire). London and the other areas were excluded.
The Act appointed two commissioners, one for England and Wales and one for Scotland, with only 2 million pounds at first, and the power to aid industry but not to compel it to move.

The Special Areas (Amendment) Act of 1937 offered firms help with rent, rates and taxes. Trading estates (planned industrial sites) such as Team Valley, Gateshead, and Treforest, near Pontypridd in South Wales, followed, but results were small before rearmament.

Council housing acts were: Addison (1919), subsidies for council houses; Chamberlain (1923), subsidies mainly for private builders; Wheatley (1924), subsidies for council houses to rent; Greenwood (1930), slum clearance; and the 1935 Act on overcrowding.

About 4 million houses were built in Britain in 1919-39, about 1.1 million by councils and the rest privately. In the 1930s cheap money, building societies and suburban semi-detached houses, mostly in the south and Midlands, made building a source of jobs.

New industries grew in the south-east and Midlands: motor cars (Morris at Cowley, Oxford; Austin at Longbridge, Birmingham; Ford at Dagenham from 1931), electrical goods, chemicals (ICI, formed 1926), rayon and aircraft.

The Central Electricity Board (1926) and the National Grid, largely complete by 1933, let factories locate anywhere, so they chose sites near the London and Midlands markets, far from the depressed regions.
Those in work saw rising living standards: prices fell, real wages rose and hours shortened. Families bought radios, vacuum cleaners and cars and enjoyed holidays and the cinema.

Between the wars Britain was in effect two countries: a prosperous south-east and Midlands, and depressed regions where long unemployment destroyed health and morale. Contemporary writers and investigators recorded the contrast, and their works are sources you may meet in a documents question.

The J.B. Priestley book English Journey (1934) described three Englands: the old rural England, nineteenth-century industrial England, and the new England of by-passes, factories and suburbs. His contrast of old and new England is the 'two Britains' idea.

Long-term unemployment meant poverty, poor diet and health, bad and overcrowded housing and high infant mortality. It also meant loss of self-respect, and women bore the burden of managing the household on the dole.

Contemporary witnesses included Walter Greenwood's novel Love on the Dole (1933) and John Boyd Orr's Food, Health and Income (1936), which showed that much of the population could not afford a healthy diet.
George Orwell's The Road to Wigan Pier (1937) and the Pilgrim Trust's survey Men Without Work (1938) also recorded life on the dole. All were written at the time, so they are contemporary sources.
Registered unemployment peaked at about three million, over a fifth of insured workers, in 1932-33. It fell with recovery but stayed above one million until 1939.
Trade unions were weakened after the General Strike, but the employed majority gained: real wages rose, so many families in work enjoyed a rising standard of living.

Britain's Depression was milder than in Germany or the USA, and Britain kept its parliamentary democracy. Extremist movements won little support, and the contrast with Germany explains much of the examiners' interest.
Sir Oswald Mosley founded the New Party in 1931 and, in October 1932, the British Union of Fascists (BUF). He is evidence that British democracy held because his movement stayed marginal.
On 4 October 1936 at the Battle of Cable Street in East London, anti-fascists blocked a BUF march. The Public Order Act of 1936 banned political uniforms and gave police the power to ban marches.
The small Communist Party of Great Britain, founded 1920, had just one MP, Willie Gallacher, from 1935.

Extremism failed for several reasons: a long parliamentary tradition, Labour and the TUC committed to constitutional methods, the broad support for the National Government, the dole (however mean) and real prosperity in much of the country.

Compared with Germany, Britain's problems were long-term decline in particular regions and industries, with no hyperinflation and no collapse of democracy. The Depression was milder than in the USA or Germany.

John Maynard Keynes was a Cambridge economist and government adviser who argued that governments should spend to create demand when jobs are scarce. Governments ignored him in the 1930s, but his ideas shaped policy after 1945.
Keynes was born in Cambridge on 5 June 1883 and became a Fellow of King's College, Cambridge. He belonged to the Bloomsbury group and in 1925 married the Russian ballerina Lydia Lopokova.

He worked at the Treasury from 1915 and was its chief representative at the Paris Peace Conference. He resigned in June 1919 over reparations (payments demanded from Germany), a participant who became a critic.

His book The Economic Consequences of the Peace (December 1919) was a best-seller. It called the reparations unpayable and damaging to Europe, because a ruined Germany could not trade with its neighbours.

In the 1920s he attacked orthodox policy: A Tract on Monetary Reform (1923), with the line 'In the long run we are all dead', and The Economic Consequences of Mr Churchill (1925) against the return to gold.

In 1929 Lloyd George's Liberal programme We Can Conquer Unemployment promised to cut unemployment through public works. Keynes backed it and with Hubert Henderson wrote Can Lloyd George Do It?. He sat on the Macmillan Committee and the Economic Advisory Council (1930) and wrote A Treatise on Money (1930).

The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (February 1936) argued that unemployment comes from too little total demand, so an economy can stay stuck in a slump. The government should then borrow and spend on public works.
The multiplier (each pound spent creates further spending) spreads the effect. This challenged the Treasury view and balanced budgets, so it was a direct attack on orthodox policy.

He wrote an open letter to President Franklin D. Roosevelt in the New York Times in December 1933. Harold Macmillan's The Middle Way (1938) and other planners drew on his ideas, though they had little effect on British policy before 1940.

In the war Keynes moved from critic to insider, helping plan how Britain would pay for the conflict and the peace. His legacy is judged both by what he achieved and by how far his ideas could have worked earlier.
