How to Pay for the War (1940) proposed compulsory saving to curb inflation, because heavy spending with few goods to buy would push prices up. He became adviser to the Chancellor at the Treasury from 1940.

His approach shaped the 1941 budget, which used national income figures to set taxation against inflation. He was made Baron Keynes in 1942. He led the negotiations for the American loan to Britain, agreed in December 1945 (about 3.75 billion dollars), and died on 21 April 1946.

He led the British delegation at the Bretton Woods conference in New Hampshire in July 1944, which set up the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank (the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development).
His own plan for an international clearing union was largely set aside for the American plan of Harry Dexter White, because the USA was the strongest creditor and could insist on its own plan.

Contemporaries thought him brilliant and persuasive, but the Treasury, the Bank of England, Snowden and Chamberlain resisted his ideas of deficit spending. Lloyd George, Mosley and some in the Labour Party welcomed them.

His ideas shaped the 1944 Employment Policy White Paper, in which the government accepted responsibility for 'a high and stable level of employment'. They also shaped the post-1945 'Keynesian' consensus of managed demand and full employment.
Later critics blamed Keynesian policies for the inflation of the 1970s.

Historians debate whether Keynesian spending could have cured unemployment in 1930s Britain, given its dependence on trade and the very large scale that would have been needed. Do not credit his ideas with the 1930s recovery or with Roosevelt's New Deal, which was not built on the General Theory.

Judgements of the government's response weigh the recovery after 1932 and the survival of democracy against persistent unemployment in the depressed areas. A clear overall verdict, such as partial success, repeated in each paragraph, scores better than a narrative.
Achievement: recovery came after 1932, with housebuilding, new industries and rising real wages for those in work, and democracy was preserved through a severe crisis.
Limit: unemployment never fell below one million, the depressed areas were neglected, the means test was hated and the Special Areas budget was small.
Limit: recovery owed more to cheap money, private building and rearmament than to any planned regional policy.

Contemporary view: the left and the writers of the time painted the 'hungry thirties' or 'devil's decade', pointing to the means test and the depressed areas. Supporters of the National Government argued instead that its policies protected the currency and prevented a worse slump.

Later view: since the 1970s historians such as John Stevenson and Chris Cook (The Slump, 1977) have stressed the prosperity of the employed majority, while agreeing that the depressed areas suffered badly.

Britain against Germany: Britain's decline was slower and regional, while Germany suffered hyperinflation and collapse in the Depression. Britain's democracy survived, so it dealt with its problems better, although it faced lesser ones.
Keynes against other responses: Keynes changed economic thinking in the long run but not 1930s policy, while the Jarrow March won sympathy but no immediate help.
Jarrow's story only makes sense against the national picture. After the world slump of 1929, Britain had mass unemployment that fell unevenly, and the government believed time would cure it.

Registered unemployment in Britain peaked at nearly three million in 1932-33 and was under two million in 1936. The Depression (the world slump in trade and production after 1929) hit hardest in the old staple industries such as shipbuilding.

Recovery was uneven: the north of England, South Wales and central Scotland, where the staple industries were concentrated, stayed depressed, while the south-east and Midlands recovered. This is why Jarrow could be in crisis while the nation's figures improved.

Stanley Baldwin, the Conservative leader, was Prime Minister of the National Government from 1935, and it held a large majority. His government kept to orthodox finance and balanced budgets, believing general recovery would in time reach the depressed areas, so it saw no need for special action.

The long-term unemployed were paid by the Unemployment Assistance Board, set up under the Unemployment Act 1934. It paid benefit, the dole, only after a household means test, which examined the whole family's income.
The Special Areas Act 1934 designated depressed areas, including Durham and Tyneside, where Jarrow lay. Commissioners were appointed, but with limited funds, so the town got little help.
Before the march the government's attitude was summed up by Walter Runciman, President of the Board of Trade, who told Jarrow it must "work out its own salvation".
Jarrow was a one-industry town, so its fortunes rose and fell with a single shipyard. When the yard failed, almost everything else in the town failed with it.
Jarrow lies on the south bank of the River Tyne in County Durham and had a population of about 35,000.

Charles Mark Palmer founded the shipyard in 1851. The firm later became Palmers Shipbuilding and Iron Company, with its own blast furnaces and steelworks, so it grew into a combined shipyard and iron and steel works that dominated the town.
Almost the whole local economy depended on the yard's wages, so when orders collapsed, the shops, trades and families that lived off those wages collapsed with it.
Palmers' last ship, the destroyer HMS Duchess, was launched in 1932, and a receiver (an official appointed to take over a failed company's affairs) was appointed in 1933.
Palmers did not simply fail by accident. A world slump in shipbuilding, then a deliberate scheme by the industry itself, closed the yard, and a second body then blocked the one plan to replace it.
World trade fell and foreign competition grew, so British yards had far more capacity than orders. This is the thinking behind the scheme that closed Palmers.

National Shipbuilders Security Ltd (NSS) was formed in 1930 by the shipbuilding firms, with Bank of England support. It bought and closed redundant yards, financed by a levy (a compulsory charge) on shipbuilders.
NSS bought Palmers in 1934 and dismantled the yard. The site could not be used for shipbuilding for forty years, which ruled out any revival of shipbuilding in Jarrow.
In 1934 T. Vosper Salt proposed a modern steelworks on the Palmers site. The British Iron and Steel Federation opposed it, because it wanted no new competitor, and the scheme was dropped.
Wilkinson's later book blamed NSS, the steel interests and the government for what happened to the town.
The closure left Jarrow with unemployment far above the national level and the poverty that goes with it.
In the mid-1930s about two-thirds to over 70 per cent of Jarrow's insured workers were unemployed. Figures quoted vary, so give the range, not one exact figure.
National insured unemployment in 1936 was about 13 per cent, so Jarrow's rate was several times the national one.
Jarrow had one of the worst records in Britain for poor and overcrowded housing, poverty, hunger, ill health and high death rates.
J.B. Priestley visited Jarrow for his book English Journey (1934) and described it as a town without work or hope, which makes his book a useful source on conditions.
Wilkinson later called her book on Jarrow The Town That Was Murdered, because she held that the town had been killed by decisions made elsewhere.
The march was run by the town council with cross-party support, and its public face was the town's Labour MP, Ellen Wilkinson.

Ellen Wilkinson (1891-1947), known as Red Ellen for her politics and red hair, was an early member of the Communist Party of Great Britain, which she left in the 1920s. She was a trade union organiser and Labour MP for Middlesbrough East from 1924 to 1931.
She was elected Labour MP for Jarrow in 1935, so she spoke for a constituency in the Commons.

Wilkinson was an experienced campaigner, and she used the march to dramatise the plight of her constituents in the Commons, where she argued that private industry could not be left to decide the fate of towns.
She backed the march and did much of the publicity, speeches and parliamentary work, including presenting the petition in the Commons. She was a participant, but not on foot for the whole way.

She left the march early on to attend the Labour Party conference in Edinburgh and rejoined it later. She did not share the men's sleeping quarters, so her account is that of an organiser, not an ordinary marcher.
Councillor David Riley was the marshal and leader of the marchers on the road, so Wilkinson led the campaign and Riley led the column.
Jarrow Borough Council organised the march, and Labour, Conservatives and Liberals on the council supported it, so it was presented as an appeal by the whole town, not a party or Communist protest.

Wilkinson wrote The Town That Was Murdered in 1939, partly blaming NSS, the steel interests and the government. After the war she became Minister of Education in the Labour government of 1945 and died in 1947.
Historians treat her book as the account of a partisan participant, written in 1939 with hindsight, which gives it great value as a source but means it needs care.
The organisers called the march a crusade, not a hunger march, and prepared it carefully so that it would look respectable and non-political.
The aim was a petition asking the government to provide work for Jarrow, above all by bringing new industry such as a steelworks, and to make the town's distress known.
About 200 men were chosen from many more volunteers and each was medically examined, so that only fit men set out.
The men carried a petition of about 11,000 signatures in an oak box. Their banner read Jarrow Crusade, and a mouth-organ band kept up their spirits and set the pace.
They were organised and disciplined to show that the unemployed were respectable men who wanted work. A public appeal raised funds, and supporters gave boots, clothing and food.

The national Labour Party and the TUC (the Trades Union Congress, the federation of trade unions) gave no official support, because they feared Communist links and preferred action through Parliament.
The Labour conference in Edinburgh in October 1936 criticised the march, although many local Labour parties and trades councils helped it.

The Communist-led National Unemployed Workers' Movement (NUWM) had a tradition of hunger marches that the government and the Labour leadership distrusted. Jarrow kept apart from it, which is why the town called its march a crusade.

The churches gave a service and the Bishop of Jarrow's blessing at the start, and churches along the route gave food and shelter. Herbert Hensley Henson, Bishop of Durham, condemned the march as revolutionary mob pressure.
The men walked from the north-east to London, relying on the hospitality of the towns along the way, and the sympathetic press turned their walk into a national story.
The marchers left Jarrow on 5 October 1936 after a church service and a send-off by crowds.

They walked about 300 miles by way of Chester-le-Street, Darlington, Ripon, Harrogate, Leeds, Barnsley, Sheffield, Chesterfield, Nottingham, Leicester, Market Harborough, Northampton, Bedford, Luton and St Albans.
They marched in stages with rests and Sundays off, and slept in drill halls, schools, church halls and sometimes workhouses, relying on supporters for meals.

They were welcomed and fed by councils, Co-operative societies, churches and local parties of all sides. At Leicester, Co-operative boot workers repaired the marchers' boots, although some officials and Conservatives were cool.
The march was widely covered by the press and by newsreels (short films shown in cinemas), mostly sympathetically, which made it a national story.
They reached London (Marble Arch) on 31 October 1936, and a meeting was held in Hyde Park on 1 November 1936.
The government met the march with a refusal to act. The petition was presented, but it brought no new commitment.
In October 1936 the government stated that marches on London were undesirable and that grievances should be raised through MPs, because processions had no constitutional influence.
Stanley Baldwin, the Prime Minister, refused to receive a deputation of the marchers.
Ellen Wilkinson presented the petition in the House of Commons on 4 November 1936. It led only to a brief exchange and no action.
The Unemployment Assistance Board reduced the marchers' benefit, the dole cut, because they had not been available for work while they were marching.
The marchers returned to Jarrow by train on 5 November 1936. They were welcomed home, but there was bitter disappointment among the men.
The government's argument was that national recovery would restore jobs in time, and it questioned whether special help for one town was fair when many areas suffered.
The march brought no immediate results. What helped Jarrow later came from other causes, chiefly rearmament.
In the short term there was no steelworks, no shipyard and no new commitment from the government, so unemployment in Jarrow stayed high.

Sir John Jarvis, Conservative MP for Guildford, organised help through a fund raised in Surrey. He brought shipbreaking (including the liner Olympic, broken up partly at Jarrow from 1935) and small metal works to the Palmers site, but they employed only a fraction of the jobless.
The Special Areas (Amendment) Act 1937 gave tax, rent and rate reliefs to firms in the special areas. There is no evidence that the march caused it.
Rearmament from the later 1930s and the Second World War brought work back to Tyneside, and this, not the march, ended mass unemployment in Jarrow.
Wilkinson published The Town That Was Murdered in 1939, and became Minister of Education in 1945 and died in 1947.
Many marchers felt they had failed.
The march is remembered far more than it achieved. It became a symbol of the Depression and of how a democracy handled a peaceful protest.
The march became the best-known symbol of the hungry thirties and of government failure on unemployment.
Memories of the 1930s fed the post-1945 commitment to full employment and the welfare state.
The march was re-enacted in 1986, its 50th anniversary, and in 2011, its 75th anniversary, which shows its place in the memory of the labour movement.
The Depression: Jarrow was the extreme case of structural unemployment, meaning lasting joblessness caused by the decline of a whole industry, here shipbuilding, not a temporary dip.
Democracy: the march was a peaceful, lawful protest within a parliamentary democracy, in contrast to the extremism of the dictatorships and the violence of Cable Street in the same week.
It also showed the limits of democracy, since a petition could be ignored.
Some note that the NUWM's national marches were larger but are less remembered.
The march took place in a month of major events, which helps date and judge any source about it.
The march set out the day after the Battle of Cable Street in London on 4 October 1936, when anti-fascists stopped a march by Oswald Mosley's British Union of Fascists.
The Spanish Civil War, which began in July 1936, was also in the news.
The NUWM's own national hunger march reached London in November 1936, and the Jarrow organisers had deliberately kept apart from it.
The abdication of Edward VIII in December 1936 pushed Jarrow from the headlines soon after the marchers had gone home.
Unemployment nationally was falling to under two million by late 1936, which strengthened the government's argument that special help was unnecessary.
Documents questions reward you for saying who wrote or issued a source, when and why, because that decides how far you can trust it.
Wilkinson's book of 1939 is a primary source by a participant, but it is partisan and was written after rearmament had begun to revive the town, so it combines a campaigner's anger with hindsight.
Government statements aimed to show that recovery was under way and to discourage marches on London, so they argue from recovery and constitutional practice.
Newspaper editorials written during the march are opinion, not a full account, so they show attitudes at the time more than they tell you what happened.
Photographs of the disciplined column with its banner support the image of respectability the organisers wanted.
Conservative and some local newspapers questioned the march as a political stunt, while sympathetic papers described crowds and gifts along the route.
Later textbooks are secondary sources, written by people who did not take part and who can use hindsight.
Labour and TUC leaders were cautious because they wished to avoid association with Communist-led marches and preferred action through Parliament.
The judgement depends on whether the march is measured by its immediate aims or by its long-term effect on opinion.
Failure: the government refused to receive the marchers, no steelworks or shipyard was secured and the men lost benefit for the weeks they marched.
Failure: the real cause of recovery in Jarrow was rearmament and war, not the march.
Success: the march made Jarrow a national symbol, kept the problem of the distressed areas before the public and showed that the unemployed were disciplined and honest.
Success: it won wide sympathy across party lines in the town, and its memory shaped postwar attitudes to unemployment.
Contemporary view: supporters saw a moral victory, with dignity. Critics, among them Henson and Labour leaders, saw political theatre with no solution.
Later view: historians see it as a failure in its immediate aims but a lasting success in publicity and memory.

The Second World War began because Hitler's demands on Poland met a British and French promise to defend it, after Germany and the Soviet Union had agreed to share eastern Europe. It was fought at first with weapons and ideas still shaped by the First World War.
In March 1939 Britain and France guaranteed Poland's independence, which meant that a German attack on Poland would bring them into the war. Hitler's demands on Poland were what tested that promise.

On 23 August 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union signed the Nazi-Soviet Pact (also called the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact). Its secret protocol divided Poland and eastern Europe into German and Soviet spheres, so each side could take its share without fighting the other.

Tanks, military aircraft, submarines and poison gas were all used in 1914-18, and the British first used tanks in battle on the Somme on 15 September 1916. But tanks were slow and unreliable, so the war stayed mostly static trench warfare (armies dug in along fixed lines).
Blitzkrieg is German for 'lightning war'. It names a way of fighting designed to win quickly and so avoid the long trench stalemate of 1914-18.

Its core was the concentrated Panzer division (a German armoured division, with tanks massed together rather than spread out), working with motorised infantry, meaning foot soldiers carried in vehicles so that they could keep up with the tanks.

Close air support came from dive-bombers such as the Junkers Ju 87 Stuka, which attacked enemy positions as the tanks advanced, and radio communication let commanders direct tanks and aircraft together at speed.

The method depended on speed and breakthrough: armour broke through a weak point in the enemy line and then encircled the defenders, which meant they were cut off and forced to surrender instead of fighting a drawn-out war.
'Blitzkrieg' was a label popularised by the Western press in 1939-40. German commanders did not use it as the name of an official doctrine, so it is best understood as a description of a method.
Poland in 1939 showed the method, although that campaign was largely a conventional advance with tanks in support. France in 1940 is the classic example of blitzkrieg, where it was perfected.
Germany's first campaigns showed how fast armoured forces could win. Britain and France, though at war with Germany, made no major attack in the west for months.
Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939.

The Soviet Union invaded eastern Poland on 17 September 1939 under the Nazi-Soviet Pact, and the two powers divided the country between them. Warsaw surrendered at the end of September and the last Polish forces in early October, about five weeks in all.

During the Phoney War, from September 1939 until the German offensive in the west in May 1940, Britain and France made no major attack on the Western Front (the border between France and Germany). It was called phoney because so little fighting took place.
Germany invaded Denmark and Norway on 9 April 1940. Denmark surrendered the same day.
British, French and Polish forces landed in Norway, including at Narvik, but were withdrawn by early June 1940, and Norway capitulated that month.
Victory gave Germany naval bases and secured the route for Swedish iron ore, the raw material for steel, which was shipped through Narvik.
The failure in Norway led to the Norway debate in the House of Commons on 7-8 May 1940, which led to Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain's resignation on 10 May 1940.
In six weeks in the spring of 1940 German armour defeated France. The speed of the defeat is the standard example of blitzkrieg.
The German offensive in the west began on 10 May 1940, with attacks on the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg and the main armoured thrust through the Ardennes (a hilly, wooded region).
This bypassed the Maginot Line, the chain of French fortifications along the German border, so the fortifications were outflanked rather than attacked.
The plan is known as the 'sickle cut' (Sichelschnitt) and is associated with Erich von Manstein, because the armour swung like a sickle blade through the Ardennes to the sea.
German tanks reached the Channel coast near Abbeville on 20 May 1940, cutting off the British and French forces in the north.

From 26 May to 4 June 1940 Operation Dynamo evacuated over 330,000 Allied troops from Dunkirk. Almost all their heavy equipment was left behind, so the army was saved but its tanks and guns were lost.
Italy declared war on Britain and France on 10 June 1940, although it was not ready for war.

The Franco-German armistice (ceasefire agreement) of 22 June 1940 ended the fighting in France. The collapse of the French government and the setting up of the Vichy regime followed, but the military defeat itself took only six weeks.
With France beaten, Britain stood alone. Hitler's plan to invade depended on first winning control of the skies, so the Battle of Britain became the first major campaign fought entirely in the air.

The Battle of Britain was fought from July to October 1940. The Luftwaffe (the German air force) attacked RAF airfields and aircraft factories to gain air superiority, meaning control of the air, which was needed before an invasion called Operation Sea Lion could be risked.

RAF Fighter Command, flying Hawker Hurricane and Supermarine Spitfire fighters and using the Chain Home radar early-warning system, defeated the attempt to win air superiority. Chain Home gave warning of raids so that fighters could be sent up in time.
Operation Sea Lion was postponed in September 1940 (indefinitely, on 17 September) and then abandoned.
Germany then switched to bombing London and other cities in the Blitz, which began on 7 September 1940 and continued until May 1941.
Italy's failures dragged Germany into campaigns it had not planned. This widened the war to the Balkans and North Africa.
Italy invaded Greece in October 1940 and was driven back. British forces defeated the Italians in Libya between December 1940 and February 1941.

Germany had to intervene to rescue its ally: Erwin Rommel and the Afrika Korps (the German force in North Africa) were sent there in February 1941, and Germany invaded Yugoslavia and Greece in April 1941.

German intervention in the Balkans and North Africa stretched German resources. Historians debate whether the Balkan campaign delayed the invasion of the Soviet Union in a way that mattered, because the late spring and supply problems also caused delay.
Nazi Germany and communist Russia were bitter ideological enemies, yet from August 1939 until June 1941 they co-operated because each gained from it.
The two powers jointly partitioned Poland in September 1939, so each gained territory at Poland's expense.
German-Soviet trade agreements supplied Germany with Soviet oil, grain and raw materials until 22 June 1941, which meant the Soviet Union was helping to feed and fuel the German war effort.
Operation Barbarossa, the German invasion of the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941, ended the partnership. It had been a convenience for both sides rather than a real friendship.
Hitler's invasion of the Soviet Union opened the largest front of the war. It ended the Nazi-Soviet partnership and committed Germany to a long war in the east.
Operation Barbarossa began on 22 June 1941 along a front of about 3,000 kilometres from the Baltic to the Black Sea.
German forces advanced rapidly in the first months and reached the outskirts of Moscow and Leningrad by late 1941. Leningrad was besieged from September 1941 (until January 1944).
The Germans were halted before Moscow by the winter and by the Soviet counter-offensive that began in December 1941. The hoped-for quick victory, the aim of blitzkrieg, had failed.
By the end of 1941 the wars in Europe and Asia had merged. Japan's attack on the United States brought America in, and Germany and Italy joined the fight against it.
Japan had been at war with China since 1937. It occupied northern French Indochina (France's colony in south-east Asia) in 1940 and the south in July 1941.
The United States responded with an oil embargo in the summer of 1941, which pushed Japan towards the attack of December 1941.
On 7 December 1941 Japan attacked the US Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, which brought the United States into the war.
Germany and Italy declared war on the United States on 11 December 1941, turning two separate wars into one global conflict.
Japan's early victories were rapid, but they were halted within six months by American carrier power. The United States then advanced island by island towards Japan.

Within months Japan captured Hong Kong (25 December 1941), Malaya, Singapore (which Britain surrendered on 15 February 1942), the Dutch East Indies, the Philippines and Burma, so most of these conquests were complete by mid-1942.

The American victory at the Battle of Midway in June 1942, in which four Japanese aircraft carriers were sunk, ended Japan's advance. The Guadalcanal campaign, from August 1942, began the American counter-offensive.
The United States used an island-hopping strategy, capturing chosen islands as stepping stones towards Japan, backed by submarines and carrier air power. B-29 bombers later attacked Japanese cities.

The Soviet Union declared war on Japan on 8 August 1945, between the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Japan announced its surrender on 15 August, and the formal surrender was signed on 2 September 1945 aboard USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay.
Between late 1942 and mid-1943 the Allies stopped the Axis advance on every major front. After this the Axis powers were mostly on the defensive.

The Second Battle of El Alamein, from 23 October to early November 1942, was won by Montgomery's Eighth Army against Rommel's Axis forces in North Africa. It was the second of two battles there, and the decisive one.
Operation Torch, the Anglo-American landings in Morocco and Algeria, took place on 8 November 1942. The Axis forces in Tunisia surrendered in May 1943, so the Axis was expelled from North Africa.
The Battle of Stalingrad, from August 1942 to 2 February 1943, ended with the surrender of the German Sixth Army under Paulus. It was the turning point of the war in the east.
The Battle of Kursk in July 1943 was the last major German offensive in the east and one of the largest tank battles in history.
The Allies invaded Sicily on 10 July 1943, and Italy's armistice was announced on 8 September 1943. Germany occupied northern and central Italy, so the fighting there continued.
The Battle of the Atlantic, the naval war over Allied supply routes, lasted from 1939 to 1945 and was the longest campaign of the war.
Its turning point came in May 1943, when the U-boats (German submarines) suffered such losses that they were withdrawn from the North Atlantic for a time.
The Normandy landings opened a second front in the west while the Red Army advanced from the east. Germany was squeezed between them until it collapsed in May 1945.
D-Day, 6 June 1944, was Operation Overlord, the Allied landings on five beaches in Normandy. Dwight D. Eisenhower was supreme commander and Montgomery commanded the land forces in the landings.

Landing an army from the sea needed special equipment: landing craft, Mulberry harbours (prefabricated floating harbours towed to Normandy) and PLUTO (Pipe-Line Under The Ocean), a fuel pipeline across the Channel.
Allied forces broke out of the beachheads and liberated Paris on 25 August 1944.
The Soviet Red Army advanced into Poland and the Balkans in 1944, and the Soviet offensive on Berlin began on 16 April 1945.
Hitler killed himself in Berlin on 30 April 1945, and the Berlin garrison surrendered on 2 May.
German forces surrendered in May 1945: the surrender was signed at Reims on 7 May and in Berlin on 8 May, which became VE Day (Victory in Europe Day).
The Allies did not win by one battle or one weapon. Once the Soviet Union and the United States were both fighting Germany, the balance of resources and mistakes decided the outcome.

The United States and the Soviet Union together far out-produced Germany and Japan in tanks, aircraft and ships, and they had far greater manpower, so the Axis could not replace its losses as fast as the Allies.
The Axis made strategic mistakes: Germany fought on too many fronts, and it declared war on the United States in December 1941, adding the strongest industrial power to its enemies.
Allied intelligence and technology, such as radar and Ultra (intelligence from decoded enemy signals), helped the Allies make better use of their strength.
The Axis powers of Germany, Italy and Japan were linked by treaties, but their war aims were not coordinated and they often acted separately.

The Rome-Berlin Axis of 1936 was the forerunner. The Pact of Steel of 22 May 1939 then bound Germany and Italy into a military alliance, although Italy was not ready for war when it entered on 10 June 1940.
The Tripartite Pact of 27 September 1940, signed in Berlin, added Japan to the Axis. It recognised the leadership of Germany and Italy in Europe and of Japan in East Asia.

Hungary, Romania and Slovakia joined in November 1940 and Bulgaria in March 1941. Finland fought alongside Germany against the Soviet Union from June 1941 (the Continuation War) without signing the pact.
The Axis had no joint strategy or command. Italy was a drain on German resources, because its defeats in Greece and North Africa in 1940 and 1941 forced Germany to send help.

Japan and the Soviet Union signed a Neutrality Pact in April 1941, and Japan did not attack the Soviet Union until the Soviet Union attacked it in August 1945. Germany was not consulted over Pearl Harbor, so the two did not coordinate their attacks.
Churchill called the coalition of Britain, the Soviet Union and the United States the 'Grand Alliance'. It grew in stages as each power was drawn into the war.
After June 1940 Britain stood alone, with its Empire and Commonwealth. The Soviet Union joined the coalition after Barbarossa in June 1941, and the United States after Pearl Harbor in December 1941.
In the destroyers-for-bases agreement of September 1940, the United States gave Britain 50 old destroyers in return for leases on British bases.

The Lend-Lease Act of March 1941 (signed by Roosevelt on 11 March) allowed the United States to supply Britain with weapons and equipment without immediate payment. It was extended to the Soviet Union later in 1941.
Arctic convoys carried supplies to Murmansk and Archangel in the Soviet Union from August 1941.

The Atlantic Charter of 14 August 1941 was agreed by Churchill and Roosevelt at Placentia Bay, Newfoundland, aboard warships. It was a statement of principles: no territorial gains, no territorial changes against the wishes of the peoples concerned, and the right of peoples to choose their government.

The Charter also promised restoration of self-government to those deprived of it (self-determination), freer trade and disarmament of aggressors. The Declaration by United Nations of 1 January 1942 was then signed by 26 nations.

At the Washington ('Arcadia') conference of December 1941 to January 1942 the Allies confirmed 'Germany first', meaning the decision to defeat Germany before Japan, and set up the Combined Chiefs of Staff.
As the Allies moved towards victory, their leaders met to settle strategy and the shape of post-war Europe. The decisions they reached at each meeting were different, so the order matters.
At the Casablanca Conference in January 1943, Roosevelt and Churchill demanded the unconditional surrender of the Axis, meaning no negotiated peace. Stalin did not attend.
The Tehran Conference of 28 November to 1 December 1943 was the first time Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin met together. They agreed the invasion of France (Overlord) for 1944.
At Tehran Stalin promised to enter the war against Japan after Germany's defeat, and Poland's eastern frontier, roughly on the Curzon Line, was discussed.

In October 1944 in Moscow, Churchill and Stalin agreed the percentages agreement on spheres of influence in the Balkans. Churchill proposed, for example, 90 per cent British influence in Greece and 90 per cent Soviet influence in Romania, and Stalin ticked the note.
At the Yalta Conference of 4-11 February 1945, in the Crimea, Germany was divided into four occupation zones, including one for France. The Declaration on Liberated Europe promised free elections.

Yalta also set Poland's eastern frontier on the Curzon Line, with compensation in the west, and agreed that the Soviet-backed Lublin government should be broadened. The Soviet Union would enter the war against Japan within three months of Germany's defeat.
A conference to found the United Nations was also agreed at Yalta and held at San Francisco in April 1945.

The Potsdam Conference of 17 July to 2 August 1945 brought together Truman (Roosevelt having died on 12 April 1945), Stalin, and Churchill, who was replaced by Attlee during it after the British election result. It ended the wartime alliance.
The Allies were united by the need to beat Germany, but they distrusted each other. Disputes over strategy and Poland foreshadowed the Cold War.

Stalin repeatedly demanded a second front, a major Allied invasion of western Europe that would draw German forces away from the Red Army. The Western Allies delayed it, and the Allied delay was a constant source of Soviet resentment.
The Dieppe raid of August 1942, a mainly Canadian landing, failed with heavy losses. Britain also preferred a Mediterranean strategy, which put off a cross-Channel invasion.

In April 1943 Germany announced the discovery of mass graves of Polish officers killed by the Soviet NKVD (secret police) in 1940, the Katyn revelation. The Soviet Union then broke relations with the Polish government-in-exile in London.
In July 1944 the Soviet Union set up the Polish Committee of National Liberation (the Lublin Committee), a Soviet-sponsored rival to the London Poles.
During the Warsaw Uprising of August to October 1944 the Red Army did not help the Polish fighters, and Stalin at first refused Allied aircraft landing rights.
Mutual suspicion and Soviet control of eastern Europe foreshadowed the tensions of the Cold War.
The 1920s and 1930s produced the ideas and machines that were used in the Second World War. Theorists asked how to avoid another stalemate, and the answer was armour and air power.

British writers J.F.C. Fuller and Basil Liddell Hart argued for armoured warfare. Heinz Guderian, the leading German tank commander and theorist, wrote Achtung - Panzer! (1937), and the first three German Panzer divisions were formed in October 1935. Britain and France instead spread their tanks among infantry units.

The Italian theorist Giulio Douhet argued in The Command of the Air (1921) that bombers would decide wars. Stanley Baldwin, in 1932, said that 'the bomber will always get through', expressing the fear that cities could not be defended.
The Spanish Civil War was a testing ground for aircraft and tactics. The German Condor Legion bombed Guernica on 26 April 1937, which shocked world opinion.
Fighter design improved. The Hawker Hurricane first flew in November 1935 and the Supermarine Spitfire in March 1936, and the Messerschmitt Bf 109 entered service in Germany in 1937.
Several technologies that decided the war were first developed in the 1930s: ways to detect aircraft, read enemy messages, fly without propellers and launch rockets.

In February 1935 Robert Watson-Watt demonstrated that radio waves reflected from an aircraft could detect it. Chain Home stations were built along the east and south coasts from 1936, and a chain was in operation by 1939.
Several countries developed radar in the 1930s, so Britain's advantage was an integrated warning system linking Chain Home to fighter control.
Enigma was the German cipher machine. Polish mathematicians led by Marian Rejewski broke it from 1932, and in July 1939 they passed their methods and replica machines to the British and French.
Frank Whittle applied for his jet engine patent in 1930, and the patent was granted later. The Heinkel He 178, the first jet aircraft to fly, flew on 27 August 1939.
Wernher von Braun worked on army rockets from 1932. The Peenemunde research centre on the Baltic coast opened in 1937 and later developed the V-2 rocket.
ASDIC (sonar), which detects submarines by sound, was developed by Britain from the end of the First World War, and aircraft carriers, ships that launch aircraft, were also developed after 1918.
In 1939-45 the ideas of the 1930s were tested at scale. On land, tanks and mass production gave armies speed and weight, while in the air strategic bombing carried the war to cities.

German Panzer divisions used radio communication and combined armour with motorised infantry. The Soviet T-34 tank, in production from 1940, and the American M4 Sherman, of which about 50,000 were built, show that mass production mattered as much as invention.
Armies answered tanks with the anti-tank gun and, from 1942, the American bazooka, a shoulder-fired anti-tank rocket.

Strategic bombing means attacking an enemy's cities and industry from the air. RAF Bomber Command under Arthur Harris, head of the command from February 1942, practised area bombing at night, aiming at whole city districts. The first thousand-bomber raid was on Cologne on 30-31 May 1942.
The US Army Air Forces flew B-17 Flying Fortress bombers by day, in what was called precision bombing. From early 1944 long-range P-51 Mustang escort fighters protected them over Germany.

Hamburg in July 1943 (Operation Gomorrah) suffered a firestorm, a fire so intense that it drew in air and spread on its own, which killed tens of thousands (estimates are about 35,000-45,000). Dresden, on 13-15 February 1945, lost about 25,000 people.
The morality and effectiveness of strategic bombing are still debated, because it caused fires and many civilian deaths in German cities.
Intelligence and detection did as much as weapons to decide the war. At sea they decided the Battle of the Atlantic, where German submarines tried to cut Britain's supply line.
Radar gave early warning of attacks. The British Chain Home system worked in the Battle of Britain.

The cavity magnetron, developed by John Randall and Harry Boot at Birmingham University in 1940 and shared with the United States in the Tizard Mission that year, allowed small airborne and ship-borne sets.
Small radar sets made night fighters and the hunting of U-boats possible. Bomber Command also used H2S ground-mapping radar from 1943 as a bombing aid.

At Bletchley Park, Buckinghamshire, the home of the Government Code and Cypher School, the British decrypted German Enigma messages. Alan Turing designed the bombe (first in use in 1940), a machine to find Enigma settings.
Ultra was the code name for the intelligence from decrypted high-level enemy signals. It was used in the Battle of the Atlantic and the North African campaign.
Colossus (1944), designed by Tommy Flowers, broke the German Lorenz cipher, not Enigma.
German U-boats hunted in 'wolf packs' under Admiral Karl Donitz and sank large numbers of Allied merchant ships in the Atlantic.

The convoy system (merchant ships sailing together under guard), escort groups, long-range aircraft, radar and Ultra reduced losses from 1943, and in May 1943 the U-boats were withdrawn from the North Atlantic for a time.

In the last year of the war Germany produced rockets and jet aircraft that were far ahead of their time, but too late to change the result. The United States produced the atomic bomb, which ended the war against Japan.

The V-1 flying bomb, a pilotless aircraft that could be shot down, was launched against London from 13 June 1944. The V-2 ballistic rocket, which had no defence against it, was first fired at London on 8 September 1944 and also at Antwerp.
The V-weapons were too late and too few to change the outcome. They were built by forced and concentration-camp labour in the Mittelwerk underground factory.
The Messerschmitt Me 262 jet fighter entered operational service in 1944, and the British Gloster Meteor jet fighter entered service in July 1944. The Me 262 came too late to change the outcome.

The Manhattan Project, the American atomic bomb programme from 1942, was run by General Leslie Groves, with J. Robert Oppenheimer directing the Los Alamos laboratory in New Mexico. The first test, the Trinity test, took place in New Mexico on 16 July 1945.

The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 ('Little Boy', a uranium bomb) and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945 ('Fat Man', a plutonium bomb). Tens of thousands died immediately and many more later from injuries and radiation.
Japan announced its surrender on 15 August 1945. The bombs marked the start of the nuclear age.
Churchill's wartime fame followed a long career in which he was both admired for his energy and distrusted for his judgement.

He was born on 30 November 1874 at Blenheim Palace, Oxfordshire, into an aristocratic family, the son of Lord Randolph Churchill. He served as a soldier and war correspondent in the Sudan in 1898 and in the Boer War, where he escaped from captivity in 1899.
He became an MP in 1900 as a Conservative, joined the Liberals in 1904 and rejoined the Conservatives in 1924-25.

As First Lord of the Admiralty (the minister in charge of the Royal Navy) from 1911 to 1915, he resigned in 1915 after the failure of the Dardanelles or Gallipoli campaign, a setback that damaged his reputation for years.
As Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) from 1924 to 1929 he returned Britain to the gold standard in 1925.
He was out of office from 1929 to 1939, the 'wilderness years'. He opposed the Government of India Act of 1935 and warned against Hitler and appeasement, the policy of giving way to Hitler's demands.
He called the Munich agreement of October 1938 'a total and unmitigated defeat'.
Churchill came to power on the day Germany attacked in the west, and in 1940 his leadership turned Britain's isolation into determination to fight on.
He became First Lord of the Admiralty again on 3 September 1939. After the Norway debate he succeeded Neville Chamberlain as Prime Minister on 10 May 1940, the same day Germany attacked in the west.

He led a coalition (a government of several parties) that included Labour's Clement Attlee, Deputy Prime Minister from 1942, and Ernest Bevin, Minister of Labour. Churchill also made himself Minister of Defence, so he directed the war effort himself.
He refused to seek a negotiated peace in 1940.

His speeches on the radio and in Parliament sustained morale after Dunkirk and during the Blitz: 'I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears and sweat' (13 May 1940), 'we shall fight on the beaches' (4 June 1940) and 'their finest hour' (18 June 1940).
During the Battle of Britain he said, on 20 August 1940, 'Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few', which made him a symbol of national resistance.

Churchill was a participant who made the key decisions on British strategy and diplomacy. He worked to bring the United States and the Soviet Union into partnership with Britain, though Britain became the junior partner.

He courted Roosevelt through the destroyers-for-bases deal, Lend-Lease, the Atlantic Charter and the policy of Germany first. When Germany invaded the Soviet Union he welcomed it as an ally in a broadcast on 22 June 1941, despite his anti-communism.

He met Roosevelt at Placentia Bay (August 1941), Washington (December 1941 and later), Casablanca (January 1943, where unconditional surrender was announced) and Quebec (August 1943 and September 1944), and both leaders at Tehran and Yalta.
He met Stalin in Moscow in August 1942 and in October 1944, when he proposed the percentages agreement on spheres of influence in the Balkans. This has been seen as wartime realism or as cynicism.
He attended the Potsdam Conference in July 1945 until the election result replaced him with Attlee.
His strategy favoured the Mediterranean and North Africa, supported strategic bombing and was cautious over a cross-Channel invasion.
There were setbacks in 1942: Singapore and, in June, Tobruk, which fell to Rommel. In July 1942 he won a vote of no confidence in the House of Commons by a very large majority.
By 1944 Britain was the junior partner, because the United States and the Soviet Union supplied far more men and resources.
Churchill won the war but lost the election that followed, because voters in 1945 wanted a government they trusted to deliver post-war reform.

In the 1945 general election, with polling on 5 July and results on 26 July, Labour won a landslide and Attlee became Prime Minister, replacing Churchill at Potsdam. Voters trusted Labour more on post-war reform.

He returned as Prime Minister in 1951-55. His 'iron curtain' speech (Fulton, Missouri, March 1946) warned of the division of Europe, and he won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953. He died in January 1965 and was given a state funeral.
Churchill divided opinion in his own time and still divides historians. The same record looks like triumph or failure depending on what is weighed.
Contemporaries admired him as the voice of national resistance. Before 1940 he had been distrusted for his judgement, over Gallipoli, the return to gold, India and the abdication crisis.

Field Marshal Alan Brooke (Lord Alanbrooke), Chief of the Imperial General Staff from December 1941, wrote diaries, published after the war, that show admiration mixed with exasperation at Churchill's interference. Some generals and Labour also criticised him, and voters rejected him in 1945.
Historians such as Andrew Roberts (Churchill: Walking with Destiny, 2018, largely admiring) praise his resolve in 1940, his strategic leadership and his alliance-building.

John Charmley (Churchill: The End of Glory, 1993) argued that the war ruined Britain financially and made it dependent on the United States, so Churchill's critics say the war cost Britain its empire.
Historians also criticise the bombing of German cities such as Dresden, the diversion of forces to the Mediterranean and Greece in 1941, and his attitude to India and the empire.
They debate his government's response to the Bengal famine of 1943, in which about 2 to 3 million died (estimates vary). How far Churchill's government was responsible is disputed.
Judgements of Churchill and the alliances weigh the British war effort and the coalition's success against its divisions and its costs.
Achievement: Britain's refusal to negotiate a peace in 1940 kept open a base from which the Allies could later invade Europe.
Limit: British strategy relied heavily on American resources after 1941, and Britain lost Hong Kong in December 1941 and Malaya, Singapore and Burma in 1942, although it kept India.
Achievement: the Grand Alliance defeated the Axis powers and produced the United Nations as a post-war organisation.
Limit: the alliance concealed deep divisions over Eastern Europe, and these became the Cold War once Germany was defeated.
Contemporary view: many British people saw Churchill as the embodiment of national resistance, while critics on the left and in his own party questioned his judgement.
Later view: historians still debate how far Churchill's leadership was essential, with some stressing his role in 1940 and others emphasising the decisive contribution of Soviet and American forces.
Technology changed how the war was fought, but historians disagree about how far it decided the result compared with production, manpower and strategy.

Technology brought speed and mobility on land, a new war in the air and at sea, and intelligence from codebreaking, and it made civilians targets through strategic bombing, the V-weapons and the atomic bomb.
Some technology was decisive at key moments: radar in 1940, and Ultra and convoys in the Atlantic.
Some came too late: the V-weapons and the Me 262 could not change the outcome.
Mass production mattered as much as invention, because the American Sherman and the Soviet T-34 were built in huge numbers, and Allied industrial production and manpower outweighed Axis technology.

The morality and effectiveness of strategic bombing and the atomic bomb remain disputed, because they killed large numbers of civilians, and the atomic bombs are linked to the end of the war against Japan.

In the Second World War the fighting was not confined to soldiers on distant fronts. Whole populations and economies were put to work for the war, and civilians became targets, so what ordinary people did and endured is part of the history of the war itself.

Total war means a war in which a state mobilises its whole population and economy, and in which civilians become targets. This is why the Second World War, more than the First, made the Home Front decisive: factories, farms, food supplies and morale mattered alongside the fighting.

For civilians the war ran in stages. Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939. The Phoney War followed (months with little fighting), then the fall of France (armistice 22 June 1940).
The Battle of Britain and the Blitz came next, and by 1942 most of Europe was occupied. The Allied bombing offensive and liberation in 1944-45 came last.
Before 1939 governments expected air attack on cities to cause huge casualties and panic. This fear is why Britain planned evacuation, shelters and the blackout in advance.
Nazi racial ideology ranked peoples, so occupation in the east was far harsher than in the west. This shaped rationing, forced labour and resistance, as the later blocks show.

Britain's government expected German bombers to devastate the cities, so it planned to move the people it thought most at risk, above all children, out to the countryside before the war began. The first movement took place in the first days of September 1939.

Operation Pied Piper, the government's evacuation scheme from London, Birmingham, Liverpool, Manchester and other big cities, began on 1 September 1939. It moved schoolchildren with their teachers, mothers with young children, expectant mothers and the disabled, because these groups were judged most at risk and least able to protect themselves.

Evacuees travelled by train,  with luggage labels on their coats and gas masks in boxes. The government organised billeting (the placing of evacuees in private homes), and householders could be required to accept them.
About 1.5 million people were evacuated in the first few days, most of them children. This was a vast movement of people, planned in advance because of the expectation of air raids.
Operation Pied Piper, the evacuation of civilians in September 1939, is not Operation Dynamo, the Dunkirk evacuation of troops in May-June 1940.
Evacuation did not go smoothly, because it threw together families from very different backgrounds. Its results ran from lasting friendships to a new awareness of how poor much of urban Britain was.
Reception was mixed. Some hosts and evacuees formed lasting bonds, while others met homesickness, culture clash and hostility. Evacuees were received unevenly in the countryside.
Some middle-class hosts were shocked by lice, poor clothing, poor hygiene and unfamiliar behaviour, and by the poor health of children from poor urban homes.
When the expected bombing did not come during the Phoney War, many evacuees drifted back to the cities, and most had gone home by early 1940.
There were further waves of evacuation in 1940, after the fall of France and when the Blitz began, and again in 1944 against the V-1 flying bombs.
Overseas evacuation was a separate scheme, run by the Children's Overseas Reception Board (CORB) in 1940, to send children to the Dominions and the USA.
The overseas scheme ended after the liner City of Benares was sunk by a U-boat in September 1940, because 77 of the 90 CORB children on board died.

Evacuation showed the comfortable classes the poverty of the inner cities. Reformers used its social findings to argue for better health and education services, so it strengthened the case for social reform after the war.
Britain imported much of its food, and German U-boats sank the merchant ships that carried it. Rationing, a fixed allowance for each person, shared scarce food fairly and helped keep prices down.
Each household registered with a shopkeeper and received ration books. Shoppers handed in coupons as well as money, so everyone had a fixed weekly allowance whatever their income.
Petrol was rationed from September 1939. Bacon, butter and sugar were rationed on 8 January 1940, and meat followed in March 1940, each with a fixed weekly allowance.
Tea and margarine were rationed in July 1940, and clothing on 1 June 1941, by coupons. A points system for tinned and dried goods began in December 1941, and sweets were rationed in 1942.
Rationing lasted beyond the war because shortages continued. Bread was rationed in 1946-48, though never during the war, and all rationing ended in 1954, with meat last in July 1954.
The government did more than ration. It organised food supply, standardised everyday goods and asked people to grow their own, so that a nation short of imports could stay healthy.

The Ministry of Food, led by Lord Woolton from April 1940, controlled food imports, supply and prices. It also ran publicity and recipes, and basic foods included National Dried Milk and the wholemeal National Loaf (from 1942).
Children and mothers received extra milk and vitamins, such as orange juice and cod liver oil. British Restaurants were subsidised communal restaurants serving cheap meals.

Utility goods were standard designs of clothing (from 1941-42) and furniture (from 1943) sold at controlled prices, with minimum standards of design and quality. The Make Do and Mend campaign urged people to repair clothes rather than buy new.
The Dig for Victory campaign, from 1939, encouraged families to grow vegetables in gardens, allotments and parks, so that less food had to be imported and more land was ploughed.
The Women's Land Army, re-formed in 1939, recruited women, called Land Girls, to work on farms. This raised home food production.

Most people accepted rationing as fair. The diet of the poorest improved, and children's health held up or improved. There were still shortages, queues and a black market, run by dealers known as spivs.
From September 1940 German bombers attacked British cities by night. The Blitz tested the country, and the shelters and the blackout were the everyday defences against it.
The blackout, enforced from 1 September 1939 by ARP (Air Raid Precautions) wardens, hid cities from bombers. It also raised road deaths sharply in the first winter,.

Anderson shelters were garden shelters, issued from 1939 and free to households below an income limit, while others paid. Morrison shelters were indoor shelters from 1941. Public shelters and London Underground stations were also used, and people took over the Underground despite official reluctance.

The Blitz began on 7 September 1940 with raids on London's docks and the East End. London was bombed on 57 consecutive nights, and raids continued until May 1941, the heaviest on London being 10-11 May 1941.

Other cities suffered too. Coventry was bombed on 14 November 1940, which destroyed the city centre and cathedral and killed about 550 to 600 people. Clydebank was hit in March 1941, and Belfast in April and May 1941, with about 900 killed in the raid of 15-16 April 1941.
Liverpool, Birmingham, Glasgow, Bristol, Plymouth and Hull were also heavily bombed.

The Blitz of September 1940 to May 1941 killed over 40,000 civilians, about half of them in London. About 60,000 civilians were killed by bombing in Britain in the whole war, though sources give 60,000-70,000.
Many homes were destroyed, which left people homeless and dependent on rest centres, places where bombed-out families were given shelter and help.

Surviving the Blitz depended on thousands of volunteers and on keeping up spirits. The government used propaganda and the media, and later historians have questioned how united the people really were.

Civil defence was staffed by ARP wardens, the Auxiliary Fire Service, fire-watchers, and ambulance and rescue workers, many of them part-time volunteers. The Women's Voluntary Service (WVS), founded in 1938 and led by Lady Reading, provided welfare work, including meals and clothing for bombed-out families.

The Local Defence Volunteers were formed in May 1940 after Anthony Eden's broadcast appeal, so that ordinary men could help resist invasion, and renamed the Home Guard in July 1940. Mostly older men and those in reserved jobs, they guarded against invasion and supported civil defence.
The Home Guard stood down in 1944.

The Ministry of Information used posters and slogans such as Careless Talk Costs Lives, and censorship, to shape opinion. BBC news, Churchill's broadcasts, comedy such as ITMA (It's That Man Again, starring Tommy Handley) and cinema newsreels and films carried official messages.
Mass Observation, a social research organisation founded in 1937, was independent of the government. Its reports on morale and public opinion were used by the Ministry of Information.
From June 1944 V-1 flying bombs, and from September 1944 V-2 rockets, fell on London and the south-east, killing thousands of civilians. About 6,000 were killed by V-1s and about 2,700 by V-2s.

The 'Blitz spirit' is the idea of a united, cheerful people under the bombs, and it was contemporary propaganda. Historians such as Angus Calder (The People's War, 1969; The Myth of the Blitz, 1991) show fear, looting, class anger (especially at the East End's suffering) and complaints alongside real endurance.
In short, morale bent but did not break. The shared danger and rationing also encouraged support for government planning and the welfare reforms after 1945.
Fighting a total war meant directing labour. Men were conscripted, workers were steered into war industry, and women entered work and service on a new scale.

Ernest Bevin, a trade union leader, was Minister of Labour and National Service from May 1940 to 1945 in Churchill's coalition. He had power to direct workers into war industries, and reserved occupations kept key workers out of the forces.

Men were conscripted (called up by law) under the National Service (Armed Forces) Act of 3 September 1939. From December 1943 some conscripts, the Bevin Boys, were chosen by ballot to work in the coal mines.

Women's war work grew greatly, so women worked in factories making munitions and aircraft, and in transport, farms and offices. Women also served as nurses and in anti-aircraft batteries, but not in front-line combat.

The women's auxiliary services were the ATS (Auxiliary Territorial Service, the army), the WAAF (Women's Auxiliary Air Force) and the WRNS (Women's Royal Naval Service, 'Wrens'). The Women's Land Army was a civilian service for farms.

The National Service (No. 2) Act of December 1941 made unmarried women and childless widows aged 20 to 30 liable to conscription (call-up) into the auxiliary services, civil defence or industry. It was later extended, though married women with young children were exempt.

Change had limits. Women were usually paid less than men for the same work, and nurseries were limited. Most women expected, or were expected, to leave paid work after the war, but attitudes had begun to change.
Northern Ireland was part of the UK Home Front, with Belfast's Harland and Wolff shipyard, Short Brothers aircraft works and the 1941 Blitz, but conscription was not applied there.
The war made ordinary people want a better country afterwards. Beveridge's report gave that wish a plan, and the governments of 1944-48 turned the plan into law.
Sir William Beveridge's report, Social Insurance and Allied Services, was published on 1 December 1942. It named five giants to be defeated: Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness.

It proposed a single national insurance scheme, in return for weekly contributions, often summed up as 'from the cradle to the grave'. It also proposed family allowances, a national health service and the aim of full employment.
The report sold hundreds of thousands of copies, which shows huge public interest. Churchill's coalition was cautious, while Labour was enthusiastic.
The report was a plan, not law, and it did not itself create the welfare state. The coalition's Education Act 1944 (R.A. Butler) came first, then the Family Allowances Act 1945.

Labour won the general election of July 1945, and Clement Attlee became Prime Minister. The National Insurance Act 1946 followed, and the National Health Service began on 5 July 1948 under Aneurin Bevan, Minister of Health.
The war had made state planning and 'fair shares' acceptable, which helps explain why the reforms had such wide support.

Germany's civilians faced the same demands of war as Britain's, but the Nazi regime handled them differently. It took food and labour from occupied Europe and was cautious about asking Germans to sacrifice, until defeat at Stalingrad.

Rationing began at the end of August 1939, just before the war. Rations were relatively adequate until the later war years because Germany took food from occupied Europe, but they were cut in 1942 and there was severe shortage in 1944-45.
Ration scales were graded by work and by race, so that German civilians received higher rations than foreign workers and occupied populations, and Jews and eastern workers received far less.
Germany entered the war with a shortage of labour, yet Nazi ideology kept women's call-up limited in 1939-42, and the regime preferred foreign labour.
Many German women already worked in 1939, so the number in paid work rose little in the war. Historians such as Richard Overy stress this; the older claim that German women hardly worked is wrong.
After Stalingrad, where the German Sixth Army surrendered in early February 1943, Goebbels made his total war speech at the Berlin Sportpalast on 18 February 1943.

The regime then, because manpower was running out, registered women for labour service and closed non-essential businesses. Albert Speer, Minister of Armaments from 1942, drove up armaments output, and the Volkssturm (a home militia of men aged 16 to 60) was formed in October 1944.
Women's employment rose less than in Britain, so Britain mobilised its own people, women included, more fully.

Control and terror kept order at home. The SD (the SS security service) reported on public mood, 'defeatism' was punished harshly and listening to foreign radio was a crime, and terror rose as defeat neared. The July 1944 plot was part of the opposition.
Because the regime held back its own women and drafted its men, Germany filled factories and farms with foreign workers. From 1942 its cities were also bombed, and civilians suffered both ways.

By 1944 about seven to eight million foreign civilian workers and prisoners of war, from all over occupied Europe, were in the German economy. Fritz Sauckel was in charge of labour recruitment from 1942.

Western workers were treated better than eastern ones, because Nazi racial ideology ranked eastern peoples lower. Ostarbeiter ('eastern workers') from the USSR, and Poles, wore badges (Ostarbeiter an 'OST' badge), lived in camps and suffered hunger, beatings and high death rates from disease, overwork and mistreatment.
Firms also used concentration-camp prisoners as labour.

RAF area bombing of cities began in 1942 under Arthur Harris, head of Bomber Command, and was joined by American daylight raids. The Hamburg firestorm of late July 1943, killed about 40,000 (estimates 35,000 to 45,000).

Dresden was bombed on 13-15 February 1945, killing up to about 25,000. German civilian deaths from bombing in the whole war are estimated at about 350,000 to about 600,000, with great loss of housing and many left homeless.
Morale was damaged but the regime did not collapse, and production rose until 1944. The effect on production is debated.

The Kinderlandverschickung (KLV), run with the Hitler Youth from 1940, evacuated millions of children and families from bombed cities to the countryside. It is not the Kindertransport or British evacuation.
War and occupation uprooted millions of people. Whether they were fleeing, interned, exiled or freed, their fate depended on the policies of the governments they met.
Before the war, about 10,000 mainly Jewish children reached Britain on the Kindertransport in 1938-39, fleeing Nazi persecution.

In May and June 1940, millions of Belgians, Dutch and French fled the German advance, the French 'exodus'. They crowded and blocked the roads of northern and central France and were strafed from the air.

After the fall of France, Britain interned about 27,000 German, Austrian and Italian 'enemy aliens' in 1940, many of them Jewish refugees from Nazism. Most were held on the Isle of Man, and some were shipped overseas to Canada and Australia. Most were released by 1941.
The Arandora Star, carrying German and Italian internees to Canada, was sunk by a U-boat on 2 July 1940, and over 800 died.

London hosted governments in exile: Poland (from 1940), Norway, the Netherlands, Belgium and Czechoslovakia. De Gaulle's Free French were in London from June 1940, and exiles served in the Allied forces.
In the east, Germans were settled in annexed Polish lands and Poles were expelled, and in 1941 the Soviet Union moved people and industry eastward.
In 1945 millions of displaced persons (DPs) were found: former forced labourers, prisoners of war, camp survivors and people who had fled the Red Army.

UNRRA (the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, set up in November 1943) and the Allied armies ran DP camps and repatriation, though many eastern Europeans and Jewish survivors would not or could not go home.
More than ten million Germans fled or were expelled from eastern Europe in 1944-47.
Most occupied countries were run, at least in part, with the help of some of their own people. To judge collaboration fairly we need to know the forms it took and the reasons people gave.

Collaboration means cooperation with the occupier. It ranged from state collaboration by governments and officials, through economic collaboration by firms and workers, to collaborationism, which is ideological support for Nazism, including joining German units.

Collaboration forced by circumstance must be kept apart from willing collaboration, because a worker obeying orders is not the same as a volunteer for the SS. Attentisme (waiting to see what happens) is neither collaboration nor resistance.
People collaborated out of belief in Nazism or fascism, anti-communism, ambition and profit, a wish to protect their country or job, fear, and the belief in 1940 that Germany had won.
Waffen-SS units recruited volunteers in western Europe, including Norwegians, Dutch, Belgians and French. Auxiliaries also served in the east.

The occupied states show collaboration in different forms, from a puppet government in Norway to a 'model protectorate' in Denmark. In each case it carried consequences for Jews and for the country after liberation.

Norway: Vidkun Quisling led the fascist party Nasjonal Samling (founded 1933). He proclaimed himself head of government on 9 April 1940, the day of the German invasion, but the Germans soon set him aside.
Quisling was Minister-President from 1 February 1942 under the real ruler, Reichskommissar Josef Terboven, with little popular support. His name became a word for traitor.

The Netherlands: the civil service and police kept working under Reichskommissar Arthur Seyss-Inquart. Anton Mussert's NSB (National Socialist Movement) cooperated, and Dutch police helped round up Jews. About three-quarters of the Jews of the Netherlands were killed.

Belgium: King Leopold III surrendered the Belgian army on 28 May 1940 and stayed in Belgium. Léon Degrelle's Rexists (Rex) and Flemish nationalists collaborated, and Degrelle fought on the Eastern Front in the Waffen-SS.

Denmark was occupied on 9 April 1940 and was a 'model protectorate'. The Danish government and parliament carried on until the government resigned in August 1943. This collaboration by negotiation spared Danes the worst until then.
Vichy France was the largest case of state collaboration. Pétain met Hitler at Montoire in October 1940, and Laval headed the Vichy government from April 1942.
Vichy helped in the deportation of Jews (the Vel' d'Hiv round-up in Paris, July 1942) and supplied labour to Germany. The Milice, formed in January 1943, carried out reprisals against resisters.
After liberation there were trials and executions, purges and summary revenge. Laval and Quisling were executed in October 1945, and Mussert in 1946.
Resistance was not only armed. Most of it was small acts of defiance, and it depended on help from outside that kept it supplied and connected.

Resistance ranged from passive and symbolic acts, such as go-slows, jokes and refusing to cooperate, to underground newspapers, intelligence, escape lines for airmen, hiding Jews, strikes, sabotage and armed partisan war.

Britain's Special Operations Executive (SOE, set up in July 1940) and later American agents supplied arms, radios and agents, because resisters could not make these themselves. The BBC carried messages to resisters, and the resistance supplied intelligence in return.
The French Resistance and the Polish Home Army were both linked to Allied intelligence and special operations, which provided weapons, radio equipment and training.
The cost was high. Reprisals and hostage shootings, the destruction of villages, and the torture and execution of captured resisters followed.
The strength, politics and risks of resistance depended on the country and on the occupier. These four cases are the ones examiners most often name.

France: the Free French (de Gaulle's forces abroad) and the internal Resistance, including the maquis (rural armed groups, swollen by evaders of the STO, the compulsory labour service of February 1943), carried out sabotage before D-Day. Jean Moulin united the movements and died in 1943.
Reprisals followed, for example at Oradour-sur-Glane on 10 June 1944, where the SS killed more than 600 villagers.

Poland: the Home Army (Armia Krajowa, AK), formed in February 1942, was usually described as the largest underground army in occupied Europe. It was loyal to the Polish government in exile in London, and part of a Polish Underground State with underground schools and courts.

The Warsaw Uprising ran from 1 August to 2 October 1944. About 150,000 to 200,000 civilians were killed. The Red Army stood on the far bank of the Vistula and did not help, and the Germans then largely destroyed the city.

Yugoslavia: Josip Broz Tito's Communist partisans fought the Germans, Italians and the Croatian Ustaša (the fascist regime under Ante Pavelić) from 1941, after Germany invaded in April 1941. They also fought a civil war, because of rivalry, against Draža Mihailović's royalist Chetniks.
Britain switched its support to Tito in 1943. The partisans liberated most of the country, with the Red Army helping take Belgrade in October 1944, and Tito then ran a post-war Communist state.

Germany: the White Rose was a group of Munich University students who distributed six leaflets against the regime in 1942-43. Hans and Sophie Scholl were arrested on 18 February 1943 and executed on 22 February 1943.

Other German opposition included Communist groups, youth gangs such as the Edelweiss Pirates (working-class youths, some executed in Cologne in 1944), the churches, and the July 1944 plot (20 July 1944). Resistance was hard in a police state among one's own people.
Some of the best-known acts of resistance came from small countries and happened in a single moment. Taken together they show both what resistance achieved and why historians weigh its limits.
Norway: Norwegian commandos trained by SOE sabotaged the Vemork heavy-water plant in February 1943, and teachers refused to join a Nazi union.
The Netherlands: the February Strike in Amsterdam on 25-26 February 1941 was a protest against the round-up of Jews, for example a rare mass act of public defiance.

Czechoslovakia: Czech and Slovak parachutists trained in Britain attacked Reinhard Heydrich in Prague on 27 May 1942, and he died in June. In reprisal, the village of Lidice was destroyed in June 1942, with men shot and women and children deported.

Denmark: after a warning of a planned round-up in early October 1943, ordinary Danes ferried about 7,000 Jews, most of the community, across the Øresund to neutral Sweden. The story that the Danish king wore the yellow star is a legend.

Soviet partisans fought behind German lines. Italian partisans fought the Germans and Mussolini's Salò Republic from September 1943, and partisans shot Mussolini in April 1945. The Italian resistance became a major political force after liberation.

Resistance had military value in intelligence, sabotage and tying down German troops, especially in Yugoslavia and the USSR. It also had political value: national self-respect, post-war governments formed by resistance movements, and prestige for the Communists.
Its limits were small numbers until 1943-44 and heavy losses from reprisals.
For French civilians, occupation meant shortage, fear of reprisal and divided loyalties. Comparing this with the British experience is a standard essay.

France was divided into two zones, and the Germans occupied the southern zone as well on 11 November 1942. German soldiers requisitioned buildings and food, and curfews, identity checks and the taking of hostages made daily life uneasy.

Ration cards were issued by age and work category, and bread, meat, fat and fuel were short. There were queues and substitutes, prices rose and city dwellers went hungry, so many made trips to the countryside to buy food on the black market.
About 1.8 million French soldiers were taken prisoner in 1940, and well over a million were still in Germany years later.
Many women had to take over family farms and businesses because so many men were away. The STO (February 1943) sent young men to work in Germany or into the maquis.
Jews were persecuted and deported, which Vichy helped carry out.
Allied bombing of French industry and railways before and after D-Day, and the battles of 1944, killed tens of thousands of French civilians.

Attitudes changed over time. Most people accepted Pétain in 1940, but the compulsory labour service and the German occupation of the south in November 1942 turned many against Vichy and the Germans from 1942-43.
Attentisme ('wait and see') was the commonest response, and only minorities actively resisted or collaborated.
French women were given the vote by de Gaulle's provisional government in 1944 and first voted in 1945.
Examiners expect a judgement, not a list. The three societies shared rationing and bombing but not their fate, because Britain was never occupied.
Britain was bombed but never occupied, so it kept democracy and a free (if censored) press, and the war united society and led to reform.
France was defeated, occupied and divided by collaboration and resistance, so it emerged from the war with bitter memories.

Britain and Germany both rationed, evacuated and were bombed. Britain mobilised its own people, women included, more fully, while Germany relied on forced foreign labour and the exploitation of occupied Europe.

Judgements of wartime society balance the solidarity and sacrifice of civilians against fear, division and the wide scale of collaboration. The balance has changed as historians have looked beyond wartime propaganda.
Achievement: British society sustained the war effort through rationing, evacuation and civil defence, and the Beveridge Report reshaped post-war social policy. Morale held and production rose.
Limit: the British Home Front had class tensions and a black market, and women were paid less than men, so change for women was limited. The 'Blitz spirit' was partly a myth.
Limit: Germany's home front relied on forced foreign labour, so its civilians were protected by the systematic exploitation of occupied peoples.
Achievement: resistance movements kept political opposition alive, so they gave national self-respect and provided the bases for post-war governments in France, Italy and Yugoslavia.
Limit: most people in occupied Europe neither resisted nor collaborated actively. Resistance remained a small minority until 1943-44, and it brought heavy reprisals.
Contemporary view: the British public generally accepted the sacrifices of the war and supported the welfare plans that followed. In Britain, the 'people's war' was a widely shared picture.

Later view: Angus Calder challenged the Blitz spirit, and Robert Paxton (Vichy France, 1972) revised the post-war myth of a nation in resistance in France. Historians have since found widespread accommodation elsewhere too, and research since the 1970s shows a more complex and divided record.
In short, resistance and collaboration were two ends of a range in which most people lay in between.

Hatred of Jews was centuries old in Europe before the Nazis. What Hitler's movement added was a racial doctrine that made Jews the enemy of the German nation, and then turned that doctrine into state policy.

Anti-Semitism, hostility towards or prejudice against Jews, combined religious hostility from Christian teaching, economic resentment and, from the late nineteenth century, racial theories that claimed Jews were a separate and inferior race.
Three examples show how widespread it was before the Nazis: pogroms (violent attacks on Jewish communities) in the Russian Empire from 1881 and the Dreyfus Affair in France, which began in 1894.
