The third example is the Protocols of the Elders of Zion, a forgery first published in Russia in 1903, which invented a Jewish plot to rule the world and so gave hatred a false 'proof'.

The Nazis shifted anti-Semitism from religion to race. Under the old religious hatred a Jew could escape by converting, but under racial anti-Semitism ancestry was all that counted, so conversion or assimilation could never make a Jew 'German'.
The Nazis built their politics on the idea that races struggle for survival. This gave Jews a fixed role as the enemy, and it gave the regime a reason for its later policies.
Nazi racial ideology saw history as a struggle between races, with the so-called 'Aryans' at the top. Jews were portrayed as a racial enemy working behind both capitalism and communism.
Hitler's Mein Kampf (first volume 1925) blamed Jews for Germany's defeat in 1918, for communism and for the Versailles settlement, and it set out the aim of removing Jews from German life.

This blame built on the 'stab in the back' myth, the false claim that Germany lost the war because of betrayal at home, and on resentment of the hyperinflation of the early 1920s, so many Germans were ready to listen.

Herrenvolk, the 'master race' of Germanic people, was the key Nazi concept. It required that Jews be defined as racially alien and excluded from the German community, while Slavs were labelled Untermenschen ('subhumans'). Lebensraum (living space) in the east later brought millions more Jews under German rule.

The Nazis came to power when Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933. Their tools were the SS under Heinrich Himmler (Reichsführer-SS), the Gestapo (secret police) and concentration camps, the first of which, Dachau, opened in March 1933.
Anti-Semitism was not confined to Germany: in 1938 Italy introduced racial laws that excluded Jews from schools, the professions and the armed forces and banned mixed marriages.
Nazi ideas reached ordinary Germans through newspapers, films and classrooms. The target of this hatred was a small minority that was mostly well integrated.
Der Stürmer, the anti-Semitic weekly of Julius Streicher (founded 1923), promoted stereotypes of Jews and encouraged hostility towards Jewish neighbours.

Schools taught race 'science', so children learned that Germans and Jews belonged to different races. Two films, The Eternal Jew (Der ewige Jude) and Jud Süß, both of 1940, presented Jews as a threat.
There were about 500,000 Jews in Germany in 1933, under one per cent of the population, which shows how little real basis the 'Jewish threat' had.
Most German Jews were fully integrated into German economic, cultural and civic life, which is why the racial claims had to be imposed by law, and many had served in the First World War.
Once in power, the regime set out to push Jews out of public life, first by pressure and then by law. The Nuremberg Laws gave this exclusion a legal basis.
The boycott of Jewish shops and businesses on 1 April 1933 was announced as a one-day action and lasted one day. Public response was mixed, so the regime moved on to using the law instead.

The Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service (7 April 1933) dismissed Jewish officials. Later measures excluded Jews from the law, medicine, journalism, culture and the universities, and in May 1933 Nazi book burnings destroyed works by Jewish authors.
The Nuremberg Laws of 15 September 1935, announced at the Nuremberg rally of that year, were the Reich Citizenship Law and the Law for the Protection of German Blood and Honour.
The Reich Citizenship Law removed German citizenship from Jews, who became subjects with no political rights, and the second law banned marriage and sexual relations between Jews and Germans.

The laws did not say who counted as a Jew. A supplementary decree of 14 November 1935 defined a Jew by descent, with three or four Jewish grandparents, and people of mixed descent were classed as Mischlinge. This definition was used in later persecution.
As the economic and social exclusion tightened, Jews lost their livelihoods and many tried to leave. Leaving was hard, and this is why so many could not.

'Aryanisation' meant forcing Jews to sell their businesses and property at low prices, or confiscating them, so that wealth passed to non-Jewish Germans. Jews had to register their property in 1938, which made seizure easier, and the process accelerated that year.
After the Anschluss (union of Austria with Germany) in March 1938, the Jews of Vienna suffered public humiliation and violence.
About 280,000 Jews had left Germany by September 1939, and about 117,000 more left annexed Austria.
Emigration was difficult because emigrants lost their property and faced emigration taxes, and then needed visas and had to meet immigration limits in the countries abroad.
Kristallnacht marked the move from legal discrimination to open, state-encouraged violence. It was triggered by a chain of events in autumn 1938.

In late October 1938 Polish Jews living in Germany were expelled to the Polish border. Herschel Grynszpan, 17, whose family had been expelled, shot the German diplomat Ernst vom Rath in Paris on 7 November 1938.
Vom Rath died on 9 November. That evening Goebbels gave a speech to party leaders in Munich that launched a pogrom, an organised attack on Jews.

Kristallnacht ('Night of Broken Glass'), 9-10 November 1938, took place in Germany and Austria, so it was a violent event on a national scale. Over 250 synagogues were burned or destroyed, about 7,500 Jewish businesses and many Jewish homes were wrecked and about 90 Jews were killed.
About 30,000 Jewish men were sent to Dachau, Buchenwald and Sachsenhausen, and most were released only if they agreed to emigrate.
Jews were made to pay a collective fine of one billion Reichsmarks, so the victims paid for the damage done to them, and were then excluded from economic life and from German schools.
Violence in Germany and Austria sent thousands of Jews looking for a place to go. Other states mostly refused to take them in, which made emigration a trap for many.

The Évian Conference (July 1938, at Évian-les-Bains, France) was called on the initiative of President Franklin Roosevelt of the United States. 32 countries attended, but almost none agreed to take more refugees, so the conference achieved little.
Only the Dominican Republic offered to take a substantial number of refugees.
Immigration limits and visa rules kept most refugees out, so even Jews with the means to leave often could not find a country willing to admit them.

The Kindertransport (December 1938 to September 1939) took about 10,000 children, mostly Jewish, from Germany, Austria and Czechoslovakia to Britain. Their parents were not admitted, so most children left without them.
The war put millions more Jews under German rule. The regime responded by confining them in ghettos, where conditions killed many even before any deportation.

Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and about 3 million Jews in Poland came under German or Soviet rule. From December 1939 Jews in the General Government (the German-ruled part of occupied Poland) had to wear armbands marked with a Star of David.
Property was seized throughout the occupied territories.
The Madagascar Plan (1940) proposed deporting Jews overseas to the island of Madagascar. It was abandoned when Britain was not defeated.

Ghettos, sealed-off districts of cities, were set up in Polish cities. The Łódź ghetto was sealed in 1940, and the Warsaw ghetto, sealed in November 1940, was the largest, with about 400,000 people at its height.
Jewish Councils (Judenräte, singular Judenrat) were forced to administer the ghettos. Whether their members acted wrongly is debated, but they were coerced and are not counted as collaborators.
Ghetto conditions were marked by overcrowding, starvation rations, typhus (a disease spread by lice) and forced labour, so death rates were high before any deportation began.
When Germany invaded the Soviet Union, killing in the east became organised and open. Jews were shot in large numbers close to their homes.
The Einsatzgruppen were four mobile killing units, A to D, of the SS and police. They followed the army into the Soviet Union after the invasion (Operation Barbarossa) of 22 June 1941.
They shot Jews, Roma and communist officials, helped by German police battalions and local auxiliaries, which meant that killing could be done fast and in the open.
At Babi Yar, a ravine near Kiev, about 33,000 Jews were shot on 29-30 September 1941. It was a mass shooting, not a camp, so do not describe it as a death camp.
In Germany the yellow star became compulsory for Jews from September 1941, and deportations of German Jews to the east began in October 1941.
Mass murder grew in 1941 as the war widened. The Wannsee Conference then coordinated the machinery across the government, rather than starting the killing.

Historians agree that the murder of the Jews grew during 1941, but no written Hitler order survives. Göring gave Reinhard Heydrich a written order on 31 July 1941 to prepare a 'total solution' of the Jewish question.
Himmler, head of the SS, was overall in charge, while Heydrich, head of the Reich Security Main Office, was the organiser. Heydrich was assassinated in Prague in 1942.
The Wannsee Conference of 20 January 1942, held at a villa at Wannsee, Berlin, was chaired by Heydrich. About 15 senior officials attended, and Adolf Eichmann kept the minutes.

The conference coordinated the deportation of all European Jews. It brought the ministries into line with a policy already under way. The phrase 'Final Solution' was in use before the conference, and means the Nazi plan to murder all the Jews of Europe.
The minutes listed about 11 million Jews to be included, even in neutral and unoccupied countries. Britain was included, and Ireland was listed with 4,000.

Historians debate whether the Holocaust was planned from the start or developed step by step: intentionalists stress Hitler's early plan, and functionalists stress the growth of policy under pressure of events.
The killing now moved to camps built for the purpose. Knowing the difference between types of camp, and naming the main death camps, is basic to any answer.

A concentration camp was a prison and labour camp, such as Dachau, Buchenwald and Bergen-Belsen, where many died of disease and starvation. A death (extermination) camp was built for killing. Bergen-Belsen and Dachau were not death camps, because they were built for imprisonment, not for killing.

All six death camps were in occupied Poland. Chełmno used gas vans from December 1941, and the Operation Reinhard camps of Bełżec, Sobibór and Treblinka opened in 1942. Majdanek, near Lublin, and Auschwitz-Birkenau were both labour and death camps, which is why they are listed in both groups.
Treblinka was a pure killing centre, built only for murder, and estimates of its dead range from about 700,000 to about 900,000. The Reinhard camps killed most arrivals within hours.

Auschwitz, near Oświęcim, had three parts: the main camp (Auschwitz I), Birkenau (Auschwitz II), where the gas chambers were, and Monowitz (Auschwitz III), where prisoners did labour for IG Farben, a chemical company.
At Auschwitz Zyklon B poison gas was used. About 1.1 million people were murdered there, about 1 million of them Jews. On the arrival ramp prisoners were selected for labour or for immediate death.
Staff and gassing techniques from the T4 programme against disabled people were later used in the death camps, so the programme was a rehearsal for mass murder.
Jews were brought to the camps from across Europe by rail. The numbers lost varied sharply from country to country, which depended on who ruled and who helped.
Eichmann's office organised the deportation transports by rail from across Europe, including the round-ups of Jews in France.
Germany occupied Hungary in March 1944, and about 430,000 Hungarian Jews were deported to Auschwitz in about eight weeks between May and July 1944. Most were murdered on arrival.
As Soviet forces advanced in late 1944 and 1945, the SS forced prisoners west into Germany on death marches. Very many died of exhaustion, cold and shooting.
About six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust (the Hebrew word is Shoah, 'catastrophe'), about 3 million of them from Poland.
Losses by country varied: about 90 per cent of Polish Jews and of the Jews of the Baltic states, about 75 per cent of Dutch Jews and about 25 per cent of French Jews.
Anne Frank, who hid in Amsterdam, was deported in 1944 and died in Bergen-Belsen in 1945. Her diary, published after the war, is one individual record of the victims.
The regime's racial ideology did not stop with Jews. It also led to the persecution and murder of other groups seen as inferior or as threats to the 'national community'.
A sterilisation law of July 1933 allowed compulsory sterilisation of people with hereditary conditions, and about 400,000 people were sterilised.

The Aktion T4 programme, begun in 1939, murdered about 70,000 disabled patients in gas chambers by August 1941. It was officially halted that month after public protests, including a sermon by Bishop Galen, though killing of patients continued in secret.
Roma and Sinti, treated as racially inferior because of the same race ideas, were deported, imprisoned and murdered. Estimates of the dead range from about 200,000 to 500,000.
About 3 million of some 5.7 million Soviet prisoners of war died in German captivity, from starvation, disease and execution.
Homosexual men were arrested under Paragraph 175 of the criminal code, Jehovah's Witnesses were persecuted for refusing military service and loyalty oaths, and political opponents were imprisoned.
Slavs in Poland were treated as a labour reserve, and their intelligentsia, the educated leaders of society, was targeted.
Resistance was real but limited, because the Germans controlled weapons and information and the ghettos were sealed. It took armed and unarmed forms.

The Warsaw ghetto uprising ran from 19 April to 16 May 1943. The Jewish Fighting Organisation (ŻOB), led by Mordechai Anielewicz, resisted the attempt to deport the remaining inhabitants, after mass deportations to Treblinka in summer 1942. The ghetto was destroyed, and Anielewicz was killed in May 1943.
Prisoners revolted in the camps: at Treblinka in August 1943, at Sobibór in October 1943, where they killed guards and escaped, and in the Sonderkommando revolt at Auschwitz-Birkenau in October 1944.
Jewish partisans fought in the forests of Eastern Europe. The Bielski brothers' group in Belorussia sheltered about 1,200 Jews.
Unarmed resistance included smuggling food and arms into the ghettos, keeping diaries and maintaining schools, religious and cultural life.
Emanuel Ringelblum's secret archive (Oneg Shabbat) in the Warsaw ghetto recorded life there. It was buried in milk cans and metal boxes and was partly recovered after the war.
Whether Jews lived or died depended greatly on how other Europeans behaved. Some helped the killers, many stood by, some risked their lives, and the Allies debated how far they could act.

Collaborators were governments, police and officials who helped persecute Jews. Vichy France issued its first anti-Jewish statute in October 1940, French police took part in round-ups, Dutch officials helped, and in Lithuania most Jews were murdered in 1941 with local auxiliaries taking part.
Bystanders did nothing, out of indifference or fear. Some neighbours profited from the seizure of Jewish property, and the churches' public protest was limited.
Rescuers hid Jews, forged documents and smuggled people across borders. Yad Vashem in Jerusalem (founded 1953) honours non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews as the Righteous Among the Nations.

Oskar Schindler, a German industrialist in Kraków, saved about 1,200 Jews by employing them in his factories. Raoul Wallenberg, a Swedish diplomat in Budapest in 1944, issued protective passports to Jews.
In Denmark in October 1943 over 7,000 Jews were ferried to safety in Sweden. This showed that large-scale protection was possible where the population and the local authorities were willing to act.
The Allies knew of the mass murder by 1942, and on 17 December 1942 issued a declaration condemning the extermination of the Jews.

The Allies did not bomb Auschwitz or the railways leading to it, and immigration limits stayed in place, so rescue was left mostly to individuals. Whether more could have been done is debated, for example whether bombing would have saved lives.
Liberation revealed the scale of the crimes to the world, and trials set legal standards. The effects continued after 1945.
Soviet troops liberated Majdanek in July 1944 and Auschwitz on 27 January 1945. American troops liberated Buchenwald and Dachau, and the British liberated Bergen-Belsen on 15 April 1945.
Newsreels and photographs of the camps shocked the world, because they gave proof that could not be denied.
The International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg sat from November 1945 to October 1946 and tried 22 leading Nazis. Its charges included the new charge of crimes against humanity.
Later trials prosecuted doctors, judges, industrialists, SS and camp staff. Eichmann was captured in Argentina in 1960, tried in Jerusalem in 1961 and executed in 1962.

Raphael Lemkin coined the word 'genocide' in 1944, and the UN Genocide Convention was adopted in December 1948. Many Jewish displaced persons, survivors with no home to return to, left Europe for Palestine, and the State of Israel was founded in May 1948.
The effects reached every part of Europe, and historians weigh them as pairs: destruction against rescue, complicity against resistance, and contemporary views against later ones.
Destruction: Jewish communities and their culture were destroyed across Europe, so Europe lost much of its Jewish population. Rescue: the Righteous Among the Nations and the Danish rescue saved many.

Complicity: states, collaborators and bystanders helped or allowed the killing, for example Vichy France and Lithuanian auxiliaries. Resistance: ghetto fighters, camp revolts and partisans fought back, and Ringelblum's archive preserved the record.

Refugee crisis: Évian and immigration limits showed that most states would not solve the crisis. Legacy: Nuremberg, the idea of crimes against humanity and the Genocide Convention made genocide a crime in law.

Contemporary view: in the 1930s and 1940s many contemporaries treated persecution as Germany's internal affair or did not believe the reports. Later view: Allied governments knew of the mass killings by 1942, and historians debate whether more could have been done.
Historians debate intentionalist and functionalist explanations: was the murder planned from the start, or did it develop step by step as the war went on?

They also debate why ordinary men became killers. Christopher Browning's Ordinary Men (1992) described a German police battalion's killings, while Daniel Goldhagen's Hitler's Willing Executioners (1996) argued for a deep German 'eliminationist' anti-Semitism, a view widely criticised by historians.

Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933, and the regime soon treated control of what Germans read, heard and saw as a main tool of rule. Understanding what the propaganda was for, and which ideas it repeated, explains the choices made in every medium that follows.
By mid-1933 Germany was a one-party state, so the regime could use the whole machinery of government to push its message.
Propaganda is the organised spreading of ideas, images and information to shape opinion and win loyalty to a regime, its leader and its policies.
Its aims were to win and keep consent, build the Hitler cult, create the national community, spread racial ideas and prepare Germans for rearmament and war.

A personality cult presents the leader as an infallible, heroic saviour of the nation through propaganda, ritual and his image in daily life. For Hitler it was known as the Hitler cult or 'Führer myth'.

The same core ideas were repeated: the national community (Volksgemeinschaft, one united German people), the leader principle (all authority flows from Hitler), anti-communism, anti-Semitism, the 'shame' of the Treaty of Versailles, and the glory of the German nation.

Methods were simple themes repeated constantly, because repetition makes slogans stick, emotional appeal rather than argument, the mixing of entertainment with political messages, and the use of every new medium. Posters, parades, slogans and mass rallies bound people to the leader and the party.

Totalitarianism means a state that seeks to control all public and private life through one party, secret police, terror and propaganda. Control of the mass media and culture was one of its main tools.
Propaganda worked alongside terror (the Gestapo, the camps and the courts): persuasion won over the willing, while fear silenced those who could not be persuaded.
The Nazis did not leave the media to chance. They set up one government ministry to direct them and a compulsory membership body to decide who was allowed to work in them.

The Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda was established by decree on 13 March 1933 with Joseph Goebbels as minister (1933-1945). It took charge of the press, radio, film, theatre, music and the arts, so one man gave the orders for all of them.

Gleichschaltung ('coordination') of culture means bringing the press, radio, film and the arts into line with Nazi ideology. Here the term is used only for culture, not for the wider takeover of the state.
The Reich Chamber of Culture was created by a law of September 1933, with Goebbels as president. It had sub-chambers for the press, radio, film, music, theatre, fine arts and literature.
Anyone working in these fields, including writers, painters, musicians and actors, had to be admitted to the chamber. Jews and opponents were excluded, so exclusion meant losing one's livelihood.
Newspapers were the first medium to be brought into line. The regime did this by making editors answerable to the state, telling them daily what to print, and buying out independent owners.
The Editors' Law of October 1933 made editors responsible to the state and barred Jews, so Jewish journalists were excluded from the press.
The Reich Press Chamber and the ministry's daily press conferences told papers what to print and how to present it, so newspapers across the country carried the same line.
Max Amann, head of the party publishing house (the Eher Verlag), bought up or closed independent papers, which put much of the press in party hands.

Three papers are easy to confuse: the Völkischer Beobachter was the party daily, Der Angriff ('The Attack') was Goebbels's Berlin paper founded in 1927, and Der Stürmer was Julius Streicher's anti-Semitic weekly.
Radio could carry Hitler's voice into every home, so the regime took it over early and then made sure ordinary families could afford a set.
Broadcasting was taken under the ministry's control in 1933 when the ministry took over the broadcasting companies, so every programme could be vetted.
The Volksempfänger (People's Receiver) was a cheap radio set launched at the Berlin radio exhibition in August 1933 and priced at 76 Reichsmarks, so that ordinary households could buy one.
Loudspeakers in factories, offices and squares allowed communal listening to major speeches, so people without a set still heard the leaders.
Programmes mixed light music and entertainment with speeches and news. This kept people listening, and the political message reached them along with the music.
From September 1939 listening to foreign stations such as the BBC was a crime with heavy penalties, and some people were executed for spreading what they had heard.
Cinema was the most popular medium, so the regime controlled the film industry closely and used it to carry both entertainment and propaganda.
The Reich Film Chamber (1933) controlled the industry. Scripts were vetted, films the regime judged unsuitable were banned, and the state funded films with propaganda messages.
Most feature films were entertainment, but every programme carried a newsreel. Audiences who came for the entertainment therefore also received the regime's version of events.
From 1940 a single newsreel, the Deutsche Wochenschau, was shown across occupied Europe, so the same view of the war reached audiences in conquered countries.
Hitler Youth Quex (Hitlerjunge Quex, 1933) was an early propaganda film that glorified the movement's young followers.
Jud Süß (1940, directed by Veit Harlan) and The Eternal Jew (Der ewige Jude, 1940) were explicit anti-Semitic propaganda. Jud Süß was shown to audiences in Germany and occupied countries.
Kolberg (1945, also directed by Veit Harlan) was a costly late-war film about resistance to the end, made to stiffen morale when the war was being lost.
Alongside the big media, the regime filled everyday life with signs of loyalty to the leader. This is how the Hitler cult reached people who never went to a rally.

Posters and slogans were widely displayed. 'Ein Volk, ein Reich, ein Führer' (one people, one empire, one leader) was used around the Anschluss of 1938 and packed the regime's message into five words.
The 'Heil Hitler' greeting made an everyday exchange into a small act of loyalty to the leader, so refusing it stood out.

Hitler's portrait hung in public places, his birthday on 20 April was a public celebration, and books of photographs by Heinrich Hoffmann, his personal photographer, showed him as the saviour and father of the nation.
Youth and women's organisations, schools and the Labour Front (the state-run body for workers) were used for indoctrination, so people met the same ideas at school, at work and in their free time.
Controlling culture meant not only promoting approved work but also destroying and condemning anything that did not fit Nazi ideology. Public spectacles made the condemnation part of the propaganda.

On 10 May 1933, organised by the German Student Union, students and party members burned books by Jewish, Marxist, liberal and pacifist authors on the Opernplatz in Berlin and in other university towns. Goebbels spoke in Berlin.
Authors whose books were burned included Karl Marx, Sigmund Freud, Erich Maria Remarque (author of All Quiet on the Western Front) and Heinrich Heine, so the burning targeted ideas the regime feared.
Heine had written in 1821: 'Where they burn books, they will in the end burn people too.' The line is now inscribed at the book-burning memorial in Berlin, and it belongs to Heine, not to Goebbels.
Degenerate art was the Nazi label for modern art such as Expressionism and abstract art, which was condemned and removed from galleries.
The Degenerate Art (Entartete Kunst) exhibition opened in Munich in July 1937, the day after the Great German Art Exhibition of approved art opened in the new House of German Art.
It showed modernist works, including those by Otto Dix, George Grosz, Emil Nolde, Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and Paul Klee, as examples of decadence.

The Degenerate Art exhibition drew about two million visitors, far more than the approved exhibition beside it, so the regime's attempt to teach people to despise modern art was also a very popular show.
In music, jazz was condemned as 'degenerate' and works by Jewish composers were banned.
Hosting the Olympics gave the regime a world audience. It used the Games to present a peaceful, modern and efficient Germany to foreign visitors.
The Winter Games were held at Garmisch-Partenkirchen in February 1936 and the Summer Games in Berlin in August 1936, so say which Games you mean.
The regime wanted visitors to see a peaceful, modern, efficient Germany, and it removed anti-Semitic signs for the games so that foreign guests would not meet open racial hatred.

At the Summer Games in Berlin, Germany won the most medals (about 89, ahead of the USA), which the regime used as proof of national strength. At the Winter Games Norway, not Germany, topped the medal table.
Jesse Owens (USA) won four gold medals. His success was a limit on the racial message, because the regime claimed that some races were superior to others.
In war the aim of propaganda changed from celebrating success to holding the home front together. The message had to shift when the news turned bad.
In the early years of the war, victories were celebrated in the newsreels, which fed the idea that Hitler and the army were unbeatable.
After the German surrender at Stalingrad in early February 1943, the message shifted to endurance and fear of the enemy, because victory could no longer be promised.

On 18 February 1943 Goebbels gave his total war speech at the Berlin Sportpalast, asking the crowd 'Do you want total war?' (Wollt ihr den totalen Krieg?). It was broadcast nationally so that the whole country heard the call.
As defeats mounted, the credibility of propaganda declined, because people could compare the official claims with what they saw and heard around them.
Goebbels was the Gauleiter (party leader) of Berlin and then the head of Nazi propaganda from 1933 to 1945. He directed the machine that controlled what Germans saw and heard.

Born in 1897 in Rheydt, Rhineland, he had a club foot that kept him out of the First World War army. He gained a doctorate in literature (Heidelberg, 1921) and failed as a writer. In the mid-1920s he joined the party on Strasser's 'socialist' northern wing, until Hitler won him over in 1926.

Hitler made him Gauleiter of Berlin in November 1926. There he organised street fights with the communists, mass meetings and his paper Der Angriff (from 1927), and he made Horst Wessel, an SA man killed in 1930, a martyr whose song became the party anthem.

From 1930 he was party propaganda chief (Reich Propaganda Leader). He ran the Reichstag campaigns of 1930 and 1932 and the presidential campaign of 1932, in which Hitler flew across Germany, using posters, films, records, loudspeaker vans and radio.

As Minister of Propaganda from March 1933 he also headed the Reich Chamber of Culture and organised the book burning. His anti-Semitic films and his Munich speech of 9 November 1938, which encouraged the Kristallnacht pogrom, show his role.

In the war he gave the total war speech (1943) and became Plenipotentiary for Total War in July 1944. Hitler's will named him Reich Chancellor, and on 1 May 1945, the day after Hitler's suicide, he and his wife Magda killed their six children and then themselves in Berlin.

He was a participant who directed the propaganda machine rather than a witness to events. He claimed the creation of the Führer myth as his greatest achievement, and his diaries are a major source for historians.

Contemporaries saw a brilliant, cynical speaker and organiser who stayed loyal to Hitler. Rivals in the leadership, Göring, Himmler, Ribbentrop and Rosenberg, disliked and distrusted him, which is why his power over culture was never complete.

Historians judge him the most skilled propagandist of the age, but argue that propaganda worked best when it reinforced existing beliefs (nationalism, anti-communism, the Hitler cult) and less well when it tried to change them. His influence fell in the late 1930s and rose again from 1943.

Born in Berlin in 1902, Riefenstahl trained as a dancer, acted in 'mountain films' and directed and starred in The Blue Light (1932). She admired Hitler and met him in 1932, and her rally and Olympic films gave the regime its most lasting images.

Hitler, not Goebbels, commissioned her to film the rallies, with a large crew; she and Goebbels were on poor terms. Her films were Victory of Faith (1933 rally), Triumph of the Will (released 1935, 1934 rally) and Day of Freedom (1935, the army at the 1935 rally).

Victory of Faith was withdrawn after the murder of Ernst Röhm in 1934. Triumph of the Will opens with Hitler's aeroplane descending through clouds over Nuremberg and uses moving cameras, low angles, no narrator and music by Herbert Windt.
Triumph of the Will sets the leader against massed ranks, which gives its message of unity behind Hitler after the purge and shows Hitler and the party as the sole leadership.

Her documentary Olympia (1938) covers the 1936 Berlin Olympics in two parts, Festival of the Nations and Festival of Beauty. Its new camera techniques (underwater, tracking and slow motion) presented athletic achievement as a national triumph. It premiered on 20 April 1938, Hitler's birthday.

Contemporaries praised her art. Triumph of the Will won the German National Film Prize in 1935 and a gold medal at the Paris World Exhibition in 1937, and foreign audiences admired the films as cinema, while critics abroad recognised their propaganda purpose.

During the war she made Tiefland, for which Sinti and Roma were taken from an internment camp as extras; it was released in 1954. After 1945 she was interned and, after several denazification hearings, was classified as a 'fellow traveller' (Mitläufer), not a major offender.
She always claimed her films were art or documentary, not propaganda, and that she knew nothing of the regime's crimes. She later photographed the Nuba of Sudan and died in 2003, aged 101.

She was a willing participant who gave the regime its most lasting images. Historians and critics judge her films technically brilliant and influential but reject her claim to be non-political, as Susan Sontag did in her 1975 essay 'Fascinating Fascism', and they still debate the line between art and propaganda.
The Nuremberg Rallies were the Nazi party's yearly show of strength. Nuremberg was chosen for the setting because of what the city stood for and because it suited huge gatherings.
The Reichsparteitag (Reich party congress, or rally) was the party's annual gathering. Do not confuse it with the Reichstag, the parliament.
Earlier rallies were held in Munich (1923) and Weimar (1926). The party then met in Nuremberg in August 1927 and 1929, and every September from 1933 to 1938, each rally lasting about a week.

Nuremberg was a medieval free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire and a symbol of German history and greatness. The Nazis used its old buildings and traditions to link the Third Reich to the First (the Holy Roman Empire).
Practical reasons also counted: it had a central position and good railway links, the local party under Julius Streicher (Gauleiter of Franconia) was strong, and there was open land for vast grounds.
The grounds were built to turn the rallies into a spectacle of order and power, and they were designed around the Dutzendteich lake, away from the old city.
The grounds lay south-east of the city, around the Dutzendteich lake, on open land that could hold vast crowds.
The Luitpold Arena was used for the mass assemblies of the SA, SS and Hitler Youth, and was designed to hold large numbers of marching men. It also contained the Hall of Honour war memorial.
The Zeppelin Field had a grandstand designed by Albert Speer and modelled on the Pergamon Altar. It was used for mass parades and for Hitler's appearance before the party's formations.
The Congress Hall was begun but never completed, and the German Stadium was planned but barely begun, which shows how much grander the grounds were meant to become.
Albert Speer was the young architect who designed the grounds and staging and won Hitler's favour.
Staging used monumental stone architecture, huge swastika banners and eagles, massed standards, torchlight processions, bands and drums. The scale made each individual feel part of something vast.

The 'cathedral of light' was Speer's ring of anti-aircraft searchlights pointed into the night sky around the Zeppelin Field. Sources give about 130 to 150 lights, and it was used in the mid- to late 1930s rallies.
Each year's rally was named for what the regime wanted to celebrate, so the sequence of themes follows the regime's own progress from takeover to expansion.
The 1933 rally in September, the first held after Hitler became Chancellor, was the Rally of Victory, celebrating the seizure of power, and it was filmed as Victory of Faith.

The September 1934 rally was the first after the Night of the Long Knives (30 June 1934), when Röhm and the SA leadership were murdered. It was staged to show party, SA, SS, Labour Service and army united behind Hitler, and was filmed as Triumph of the Will.
The 1935 rally was the Rally of Freedom, celebrating the return of conscription (March 1935) and rearmament, which the regime presented as Germany breaking free of Versailles.
During that rally the Reichstag was summoned to Nuremberg and on 15 September 1935 passed the Nuremberg Laws, together with the Reich Flag Law that made the swastika flag the national flag.
The 1936 rally was the Rally of Honour, after the remilitarisation of the Rhineland in March 1936. The Four Year Plan was proclaimed at it, and Göring was put in charge in October 1936.
The 1937 rally was the Rally of Labour and included parades of workers and the Labour Service.

The 1938 rally was the Rally of Greater Germany, celebrating the Anschluss of March 1938. Hitler's closing speech attacked Czechoslovakia over the Sudetenland, only weeks before the Munich Agreement of 29-30 September 1938.
The 1939 Rally of Peace was planned but cancelled because of the invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 and the outbreak of war.
A fixed programme of set pieces made each rally feel like a ritual of loyalty rather than a party meeting.

Days were set aside for particular groups: the political leaders, the Labour Service, the Hitler Youth, the SA and SS, and the armed forces, who had their own day. Hitler gave an opening proclamation and a closing speech, and there were parades through the old city.

At the Luitpold Arena in 1934 Hitler walked between the SA and SS ranks with Himmler (head of the SS) and Viktor Lutze (SA chief of staff after Röhm) to the war memorial. This staged a reassurance to the SA and an image of the new order after the purge.

In the consecration of the standards, Hitler touched new flags with the Blood Flag (Blutfahne), the banner said to have been carried in the Munich Putsch of November 1923. This linked the new banners to the party's own founding story.
Rituals included oaths of loyalty, and in 1934 the Labour Service marched with spades. Together with the banners they gave the rallies a quasi-religious atmosphere and a sense of sacred purpose.
The night-time ceremonies, such as the political leaders' assembly under the cathedral of light and the torchlight processions, were the most dramatic part of the programme.
Hitler's speeches expressed party doctrine and foreign policy, which is why the rallies were also used to announce policies, as the Four Year Plan was in 1936.
What the rallies meant depended on who was there and who was watching. Participants, foreign diplomats and journalists left very different accounts, and the exam uses them as documents.
Hundreds of thousands of party members, workers, soldiers and youths came by special trains and lived in huge tent camps.
The camps ran under strict rules, such as passes to leave the grounds, fire safety, silence at night and the reporting of sickness, so that large numbers could be controlled.
Days were long, with drilling, marching and waiting. For many it was a powerful experience of comradeship and belonging, while for others it was exhausting.
Participants were organised into units and marched in disciplined formations, which created a visual impression of unity and order.
German participants showed enthusiasm, and foreign visitors and journalists were impressed too, some seeing evidence of the order and vitality of the new Germany.

William Shirer, an American correspondent, saw the 1934 rally and wrote about it in Berlin Diary (1941). Charles Bewley, Irish Minister (envoy) in Berlin from 1933 to 1939, was sympathetic to the regime.
Nevile Henderson, British ambassador to Germany from 1937, called the searchlight display a 'cathedral of ice', a phrase that echoes the 'cathedral of light' but with ice instead of light.
The rallies were staged for several purposes at once, and their reach went far beyond Nuremberg. Their afterlife shows how the city has dealt with that past.
The purpose was to display unity, order and strength, to build the Hitler cult and to bind the individual to the national community, which is why everyone marched, sang and swore oaths together.
Policies were announced at the rallies, including the Nuremberg Laws, the Four Year Plan and foreign policy claims, so racial ideas were presented as part of the national community.
The rallies also aimed to impress and intimidate foreign opinion by showing a disciplined, rearming Germany.
Radio, newsreels, the press and Riefenstahl's films carried the rallies to millions who never attended, and the films reached cinemas in Germany and abroad.
In April 1945 the US Army blew up the swastika on the Zeppelin Field grandstand. After 1945 the grounds were used by the US Army and the city, and parts of the Zeppelin Field survive today.
The Nuremberg war crimes trials (1945-46) were held in the city partly for its symbolism.
The unfinished Congress Hall now holds a Documentation Centre, which opened in 2001.
Judgements of Nazi propaganda weigh its success in creating consent and loyalty against its limits, and ask how far it explains support for the regime.
Achievement: the Hitler cult and genuine popularity in the 1930s, the rallies' spectacle and the films' reach gave the regime a powerful image of unity.
Limit: propaganda failed to win over many workers and churchgoers, and it depended on terror, so the police, courts and camps were needed to suppress opposition.

Limit: people tired of constant political content, which is why so much of the media was entertainment, and after 1943 propaganda focused on defence and national survival, and its credibility fell as the war turned against Germany.

Contemporary view: many Germans responded with enthusiasm, and many foreigners were impressed, seeing awe-inspiring order and unity, while exiled opponents and foreign critics saw the rallies as an exhibition of dictatorship.

Later view: historians see manipulation and a link between the rallies, the racial laws and war, and Riefenstahl's films remain among the most studied examples of film propaganda and have shaped how later film-makers use visual rhetoric.

How far propaganda explains support: Ian Kershaw (The 'Hitler Myth', 1987) stresses that propaganda reinforced existing beliefs, and that economic recovery, foreign policy success, national pride and fear also mattered.
The reports of the exiled Social Democrats (Sopade) show grumbling and limits to belief, which is evidence that many people did not accept everything they were told.
Goebbels and Riefenstahl as contributors: Goebbels was the organiser who controlled what Germans saw and heard, while Riefenstahl was the artist who created the regime's most lasting images.
Church-state relations in Italy began with a quarrel that was almost sixty years old. Mussolini inherited it and chose to settle it rather than fight the Church.

In 1870 Italian troops took Rome and ended the Papal States (the lands the popes had ruled as kings). The popes refused to recognise the Kingdom of Italy and called themselves "prisoners in the Vatican". This dispute is known as the Roman Question.
For decades Catholics were told not to take part in national politics, so the quarrel kept many devout Italians at a distance from the state that ruled them.

Mussolini became Prime Minister in October 1922 and by 1926 ruled a one-party state, a dictatorship in which only the Fascist Party was allowed, so the Church had to deal with one ruler rather than many parties.
Fascism began anticlerical (hostile to the Church), but Mussolini dropped this stance because he needed the support of Catholics and conservatives to hold power.

The Vatican let the Catholic Popular Party (the Partito Popolare, or Popolari) go, so the Church no longer had a party of its own in politics. Its leader, the priest Luigi Sturzo, resigned in 1923 and went into exile in 1924.
By the late 1920s each side had something the other could give. Neither was acting out of friendship: both were pursuing their own interests.
Mussolini wanted the support of a Catholic nation, because the Church's approval would give his regime legitimacy (acceptance as the rightful government) at home and prestige abroad.
Pope Pius XI (pope from February 1922 until his death in February 1939) wanted the Roman Question settled, so that the Church's position in Italy rested on a firm legal footing.

He also wanted Catholic life protected, including Church schools, Catholic marriage and Catholic Action (the Church's organisation for lay people, meaning ordinary Catholics who are not clergy), and he saw Mussolini as an ally against communism.
The Lateran Treaties were the great settlement between the Italian state and the papacy. They were three agreements in one, each dealing with a different part of the quarrel.

They were signed at the Lateran Palace in Rome on 11 February 1929 by Mussolini and Cardinal Pietro Gasparri, the Vatican Secretary of State (the pope's chief minister), and were ratified (formally approved) in June 1929.

The three documents were a treaty (creating Vatican City), a financial convention (dealing with compensation) and a concordat (an agreement between the pope and a state about the Church's place in that country).
The treaty made Vatican City an independent sovereign state of about 44 hectares, so the pope ruled his own territory. In return the papacy recognised the Kingdom of Italy with Rome as its capital.
The financial convention gave the Church compensation of 1.75 billion lire (750 million in cash and 1 billion in state bonds) for the Papal States lost in 1870.

Under the concordat, Catholicism became the sole religion of the state, and religious teaching was provided in state primary and secondary schools, which gave the Church a say in how the young were taught.
Church marriage became valid in civil law, so couples married in church were legally married. Bishops had to swear loyalty to the state.
Catholic Action was allowed to continue, but only if it stayed out of politics. This condition shows that the Church's gains came with strings attached.
The settlement paid off for Mussolini almost at once, and it proved more lasting than his regime.

In the plebiscite election of March 1929 voters were offered a single list of Fascist candidates and approved it by an overwhelming majority, with Catholic organisations urging a yes vote. This showed what Church backing was worth to him.
Mussolini gained the support of the Catholic majority, and the Church's endorsement helped legitimise the regime in the eyes of many Italians.
He also won prestige abroad. Pius XI publicly praised him, describing him as a man sent by Providence (God's guiding care).
The settlement is often called Mussolini's most lasting achievement. It outlived Fascism, and the concordat was revised only in 1984, when Catholicism ceased to be the state religion of Italy.
The partnership soon met its first limit. A dictatorship wants to shape the young, and the Church had its own organisations for doing exactly that.
Catholic Action's youth and student groups worried the regime, because the Fascists saw them as rivals to the Fascist youth movement.
Fascist squads attacked Catholic centres, and the regime dissolved the Catholic youth organisations in May 1931, because it would not tolerate a rival for the loyalty of the young.

Pius XI replied with the encyclical (a formal letter from the pope to the whole Church) Non abbiamo bisogno (We have no need), issued in Italian on 29 June 1931. It condemned the regime's claim to monopolise the young.

The dispute ended in a compromise agreement in September 1931. Catholic Action survived under the bishops, but it was confined to religious, cultural and charitable activities, and its youth groups were kept out of politics and sport.
Apart from this encyclical, the Church's objections were mostly made in private diplomacy and in the Vatican's press, and Pius XI rarely challenged Mussolini openly.
Italy's alliance with Nazi Germany pulled the regime towards racial policy. This tested the Church's relationship with the regime a second time.
Following the Axis (the alliance between Italy and Germany), Mussolini's regime published the Manifesto of the Race on 14 July 1938, which defined the racial basis of Italian identity.

Racial laws followed between September and November 1938, in line with Germany's policy. They excluded Jews from state schools, the professions and the armed forces, and banned marriage between Italians and Jews.
Pius XI objected above all to the marriage ban, which also covered Jews who had become Catholics, because he saw it as a breach of the marriage terms of the concordat.
In September 1938 he told Belgian pilgrims, "Spiritually, we are Semites." The remark stressed the link between Christians and Jews, but it was a spoken comment, not a break with the regime.
The Church protested but did not break with the regime.
Pius XI died in February 1939. His successor, Pius XII (Eugenio Pacelli, elected in March 1939), was more cautious.
Hitler faced a different religious map from Mussolini's. Germany was split between two large churches, and both had reasons to be wary of a Nazi government.
Germany was about two-thirds Protestant and one-third Catholic. The Protestants were divided into 28 regional (Land) churches, so there was no single Protestant Church for Hitler to deal with.
Catholics remembered the Kulturkampf, Bismarck's struggle with the Catholic Church in the 1870s, and so they knew what it was to have the state turn against them.

Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933. The Enabling Act (23 March 1933, which let him make laws without parliament) passed with the votes of the Catholic Centre Party, and Gleichschaltung began, the bringing of every organisation into line with Nazi control.
The Nazi Party programme of 1920 promised "positive Christianity". Hitler courted the churches in 1933 while planning to subordinate them (bring them under Nazi control).

Leading Nazis such as Alfred Rosenberg, Martin Bormann and Himmler were hostile to Christianity. Rosenberg's The Myth of the Twentieth Century (1930) was placed on the Church's Index of forbidden books in 1934.
The German bishops lifted their ban on Catholics joining the Nazi Party on 28 March 1933, which removed one barrier between Catholics and the new regime.
Within months of taking power Hitler offered the Catholic Church the kind of agreement Mussolini had made. For him it was a way to win respectability while ending Catholic politics.
The Reich Concordat was signed in Rome on 20 July 1933 by Cardinal Eugenio Pacelli (the Vatican Secretary of State, later Pius XII) and Vice-Chancellor Franz von Papen.
The Church kept freedom of worship, its schools, religious teaching and its religious organisations. In return clergy were barred from party politics and bishops swore loyalty to the state.
The Centre Party, the main Catholic party, dissolved itself on 5 July 1933, as the Concordat was being concluded, so Catholic organisations in Germany lost much of their political role.
Hitler's gains were international respectability, because a treaty with the Vatican made his regime look acceptable abroad, and the end of political Catholicism.
The Concordat did not protect the Church for long. The regime wanted total loyalty, so it squeezed Catholic organisations and then persecuted the clergy.
On 30 June 1934, in the Night of the Long Knives, Erich Klausener, head of Catholic Action in Berlin, was murdered, a warning that Catholic leaders were not safe.
Catholic youth groups were squeezed and then banned as the Hitler Youth became compulsory (the Hitler Youth law was passed in December 1936), because the regime wanted to claim the young for itself.
By the end of the 1930s Catholic schools had been replaced by state community schools, and the Catholic press was curbed.
In 1936-37 the regime staged morality trials of priests and members of religious orders, show trials meant to blacken the clergy's reputation.
Clergy were sent to camps, such as Dachau, where there was a priests' block.
Popular protest could win locally: the order removing crucifixes from schools in Oldenburg was withdrawn after protests in 1936.
In short, the Nazi regime violated the Concordat within a few years, closing Catholic schools and youth organisations and arresting priests and members of religious orders.
The Reichskirche (Reich Church) was Hitler's plan for the Protestants. With 28 regional churches, one Church under Nazi control looked like an easy way to bring all Protestants into line.
The Reichskirche was to be a single, centralised Protestant Church loyal to the Nazi state. It would replace the 28 regional churches and end their independence.
Its backers were the German Christians (Deutsche Christen), a pro-Nazi movement within Protestantism founded in 1932, who wanted a Christianity fitted to Nazi ideas.
Two of their demands were the Aryan paragraph, which barred pastors of Jewish descent so that Jewish Christians were excluded from church office, and talk of dropping the Old Testament.
The German Christians won about two-thirds of the votes in the Protestant church elections of July 1933, which gave them control of the church machinery.
Ludwig Müller, Hitler's adviser on church affairs, became Reich Bishop in September 1933, but his leadership was challenged within the churches.
The Reichskirche failed. Its own extremism drove moderate Protestants away, and the regime could not bring the churches to heel even when it tried direct control.
A mass German Christian rally in Berlin's Sportpalast in November 1933, demanding that the Old Testament be dropped, drove moderates away.
Müller never controlled the churches and was sidelined.
In 1935 the regime set up a Ministry for Church Affairs under Hanns Kerrl to impose control directly, with little more success.
The Protestant churches split three ways: the German Christians, the Confessing Church, and a cautious neutral majority.
Protestants who refused the Reich Church formed their own opposition. It was about defending the Church's independence, not about overthrowing Hitler.
The Confessing Church grew from Martin Niemöller's Pastors' Emergency League, formed in September 1933 with several thousand pastors.
The Barmen Declaration of 31 May 1934, mainly drafted by the Swiss theologian Karl Barth, said that the Church answered to Christ, not to the state or a Führer (the Nazi leader).
It defended the Church's independence and its teaching, and so rejected the state's claim to control what the Church taught.
It did not set out to overthrow the regime, and few of its members spoke up for Jews who were not Christians.
Two men came to stand for Protestant resistance. Their fates were very different, and examiners expect you to keep them apart.

Martin Niemöller was a U-boat commander in the First World War and then a pastor at Dahlem in Berlin. He at first welcomed the Nazis, but he founded the Pastors' Emergency League and led the Confessing Church.
He was arrested on 1 July 1937 and tried in 1938. He was held in Sachsenhausen and then Dachau concentration camps as Hitler's personal prisoner until 1945, so he survived the war.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer, born in 1906, was a Lutheran theologian of the Confessing Church. From 1935 he ran its secret seminary at Finkenwalde, which the Gestapo (the Nazi secret state police) closed in 1937.
He moved from church opposition to active resistance through contacts in military intelligence (the Abwehr) and the plotters against Hitler, and he was arrested in April 1943.
Bonhoeffer was executed at Flossenbürg concentration camp on 9 April 1945.
Catholic opposition came from the top of the Church, through the pope's encyclical and the sermons of one bishop. Both defended Catholic institutions and teaching against Nazi persecution.
Mit brennender Sorge (With burning concern), dated 14 March 1937, was an encyclical by Pius XI written in German. Cardinal Michael von Faulhaber, Archbishop of Munich, and Pacelli helped draft it.
It condemned breaches of the Concordat and the worship of race and state, so it attacked both the regime's broken promises and its ideology.
It was smuggled into Germany and read from Catholic pulpits on Palm Sunday, 21 March 1937. The Gestapo seized copies and closed the printers, and the persecution of the clergy increased.

Clemens August von Galen, Bishop of Münster from 1933 and nicknamed the Lion of Münster, attacked Gestapo seizures of church property in sermons in July and August 1941. He also attacked the killing of disabled people in the T4 euthanasia programme.
The T4 programme was officially halted in August 1941, but the killings continued in secret.
The regime did not arrest Galen, for fear of Catholic opinion in wartime.
Church protest was real but narrow. The churches mostly defended themselves, and historians still argue about how far that was a moral failure.
The churches defended their own institutions and teaching far more than the victims of the regime. Their protests were limited to defending themselves and to opposing the euthanasia programme.
There was little public protest at the persecution of the Jews. Kristallnacht (9-10 November 1938) passed without an official protest from either church.
Most clergy and churchgoers conformed, for example by staying silent, and many backed the war.

Pius XII's Christmas broadcast of 1942 spoke of people killed because of their nationality or race, without naming the Jews or Germany. Critics such as John Cornwell (Hitler's Pope, 1999) call this silence complicity.
Defenders of Pius XII say that public protest would have made things worse, and they point to Catholic help for Jews in hiding.

Bormann, Himmler and Rosenberg intended to destroy the churches' influence after the war. The German Faith Movement and neo-pagan ideas (a revival of pre-Christian religion) had little popular following.
Put side by side, the two stories follow one pattern. The difference lies in how much each dictator needed the Church.
Both dictators began with a concordat, in 1929 and in 1933, and both later clashed with the Church over youth and race.
Mussolini needed the Church and kept a working partnership, so his clashes ended in compromise in 1931 and in protest without a break in 1938.
Hitler saw the churches as rivals for total loyalty, so he moved from courtship to persecution.
The churches survived both regimes as the largest institutions outside party control.
From the early 1920s radio brought news, music, sport, comedy and the voices of leaders into the home. Governments quickly saw that it could inform, entertain and persuade all at once.
Cheap sets made radio affordable, so Britain had about 9 million radio licences by 1939.
The British Broadcasting Company was founded in 1922, with John Reith as its general manager.
On 1 January 1927 it became the British Broadcasting Corporation under a royal charter (a formal grant from the Crown), with Reith as its first director-general until 1938.
The BBC was a monopoly funded by the licence fee that listeners paid, with no advertising, so it did not depend on advertisers.
Reith's public-service ideal, broadcasting for the public good rather than profit, was to "inform, educate and entertain", and Sunday programming was strict.
The Empire Service began in 1932, so that BBC programmes reached listeners across the British Empire.
The American model was the opposite of the BBC's. Radio there was paid for by advertisers, and it challenged British ideas of what radio should be.

NBC (founded 1926) and CBS (founded 1927) were American networks, meaning chains of stations broadcasting the same programmes. They were commercial, paid for by advertisers, who sponsored whole programmes.
Programmes included comedy, variety, dance bands and serials, which were nicknamed soap operas after their soap-company sponsors.
Radio Luxembourg began English-language programmes in 1933, beamed into Britain, especially on Sundays. It played the dance music and American-style shows that the BBC avoided.
It was the most famous commercial challenger to the BBC monopoly, alongside Radio Normandy, which had been broadcasting English-language commercial programmes to Britain since 1931.
Radio changed how leaders spoke to their people. In a democracy it allowed explanation and reassurance, and it also showed how tightly a broadcast could grip an audience.
President Franklin Roosevelt gave his first fireside chat, a radio talk in a relaxed, conversational style, on 12 March 1933, during the banking crisis.
About 30 fireside chats followed, up to 1944, so Roosevelt could speak directly to listeners about the New Deal and later the war.
A democratic leader explaining and reassuring by radio contrasts with the dictators' mass rallies.
Orson Welles directed and starred in The War of the Worlds, a drama about a Martian invasion, broadcast by CBS on 30 October 1938.
Newspaper reports of mass panic were exaggerated, but the broadcast showed radio's hold on listeners.
In the Second World War the BBC became a tool of morale, information and resistance, and its reputation for truth was one of its great assets.
The BBC Home Service began in September 1939, and the Forces Programme, lighter in tone for the troops, began in January 1940.
BBC news bulletins were trusted at home and in occupied Europe, and gained a reputation for trustworthy reporting in contrast to German propaganda.
Churchill made radio broadcasts to the nation at key moments, so the whole country could hear its leader at once.
De Gaulle made a broadcast appeal to the French on the BBC on 18 June 1940, which shows how radio could reach people across a occupied frontier.
The V for Victory campaign of 1941 was run over the BBC, and broadcasts to occupied Europe included coded messages to resistance groups.
ITMA (It's That Man Again), a BBC comedy with Tommy Handley from 1939, helped to keep up spirits.
Radio was heard across the front lines. American broadcasters built sympathy for Britain, while Germany's radio used propaganda and, by accident, a song that both sides loved.
Edward R. Murrow broadcast for CBS from London during the Blitz in 1940-41, opening with "This is London", and his reports built American sympathy for Britain.
The American Forces Network began broadcasting in Britain on 4 July 1943. It played American music and gave news to troops and, unofficially, to British listeners.
Glenn Miller's American band broadcast to the forces. Miller disappeared over the English Channel in December 1944.
William Joyce, known as Lord Haw-Haw, broadcast Nazi propaganda from Germany to Britain from 1939. He was more mocked than believed, and he was hanged for treason in January 1946.
Lili Marleen, in Lale Andersen's recording of 1939, was broadcast nightly from the German forces' radio station in Belgrade from 1941. It was loved by soldiers on both sides in North Africa.
In the 1920s and 1930s going to the pictures became the most popular entertainment of the age. Then sound changed the industry almost overnight.
By the late 1930s Britain had about 20 million cinema admissions a week, many in large cinemas called picture palaces.
Audiences were strongly young, female and working-class, and going to the pictures was a weekly habit because tickets were cheap and cinemas were everywhere.

The Jazz Singer (Warner Bros, 1927), starring Al Jolson, was the first feature film with synchronised singing and speech. It was not entirely spoken, but it began the talkies and led to their rapid spread.
By the early 1930s silent films were finished.
The effects of sound included new stars and musicals, language barriers in Europe that were met with dubbing and subtitles, and the strength of English-language films in Britain.
Hollywood's world dominance came from the way the film business was organised, not only from the films themselves.

A few major studios (MGM, Paramount, Warner Bros, 20th Century Fox and RKO) controlled production, distribution and many cinemas. This is called vertical integration, meaning that one company owns every stage from making a film to showing it, so the studios could make sure their films got screens.
Stars were tied to the studios by long contracts, so the studios controlled their careers.
Genres included musicals, gangster films, westerns and comedies, as well as cartoons such as Disney's Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937).
The Production Code, known as the Hays Code, was adopted in 1930 and strictly enforced from 1934. It governed morality on screen, so studios cut scenes to avoid banned content.
The studios produced and distributed most of the films shown in Britain and Europe, so Hollywood dominated the world market.
American films filled most of the screen time in Britain, so Britain acted to protect its own industry and still produced some films of its own that succeeded.
By the late 1930s Hollywood films filled most screens in Britain and much of Europe.
The Cinematograph Films Act (1927) required distributors and cinemas to show a quota of British films, which rose over ten years, to protect the domestic industry from American competition.
The quota produced many cheap quota quickies, but it also protected a home industry.
British films that succeeded included Alexander Korda's The Private Life of Henry VIII (1933), a success in America, and Alfred Hitchcock's The 39 Steps (1935).
Gracie Fields and George Formby were popular British comedians.
For many people in the 1930s the only moving pictures of real events came from the newsreels shown in cinemas.
Newsreels were short news films shown before the main feature, so a whole cinema audience saw the same pictures of events.
The main British newsreels were British Pathé and British Movietone News (from 1929). The American newsreel The March of Time began in 1935.
They were generally patriotic and deferential (respectful towards those in authority), so they supported rather than questioned governments.
Germany and Italy used newsreels for propaganda, while the British and American newsreels were generally patriotic and deferential.
In wartime governments and studios used film to lift morale and to explain what the fighting was for.
Humphrey Jennings made the documentaries Listen to Britain (1942) and Fires Were Started (1943).
Noël Coward's naval drama In Which We Serve (1942) was a wartime morale film. It was a private production made with the Navy's help.
Laurence Olivier's Henry V (1944) was patriotic spectacle, and British films stressed a people's war of all classes.
In America, Mrs Miniver (1942) pictured an English family in the war. It won the Oscar for Best Picture and built support for Britain.
Casablanca (1942) was another Hollywood film of the war years.
Frank Capra's Why We Fight series (1942-45) explained the war to American servicemen, and the American government used films to explain the war to the public.
The dictatorships distrusted Hollywood's hold over their audiences, so they built or protected their own industries, though their cinema-goers still loved American films.
Fascist Italy built the Cinecittà studios, opened by Mussolini in 1937, and began the Venice Film Festival in 1932.
From 1938 the Italian state held a monopoly on importing foreign films, after which the major American studios withdrew from Italy.
Nazi Germany censored and restricted American films in the 1930s and banned them in the war. German cinema came to be dominated by home-made films and newsreels.
Hollywood stayed popular with audiences in both countries, which is why the regimes kept needing restrictions.
Both regimes also ran their own propaganda machines, Goebbels's ministry in Germany and Mussolini's Istituto Luce in Italy, which offer a contrast with Anglo-American radio and cinema.

Chaplin was a British-born comedian and film-maker whose Tramp character made him the most famous film star of the silent era, and whose later films criticised modern society and the dictators. He shaped popular culture rather than simply witnessing it.

Chaplin was born in London on 16 April 1889 (four days before Hitler), into poverty, and began as a child performer in the music hall. He toured the USA with Fred Karno's comedy company from 1910 and joined Mack Sennett's Keystone studio in late 1913.

The Tramp first appeared in 1914: a little man with bowler hat, cane and baggy trousers, poor but dignified. He was developed in The Kid (1921), The Gold Rush (1925) and City Lights (1931, still silent, with a music score).

In 1919 Chaplin co-founded United Artists with Mary Pickford, Douglas Fairbanks and D.W. Griffith, so he owned his films and worked independently of the major studios. He resisted talkies longer than anyone.

Modern Times (1936) showed the Tramp as a factory worker caught in the machine, in a world of unemployment and the Depression. It gave social comment through comedy, and it was the first film in which his voice was heard, in a nonsense song, and the Tramp's last appearance.

The Great Dictator (1940) was his first full talking picture. He played two parts: Adenoid Hynkel, dictator of Tomania and a parody of Hitler, and a Jewish barber who is mistaken for him. Benzino Napaloni of Bacteria parodied Mussolini.

The film ends with the barber's speech for peace and humanity. Made while the USA was still neutral, it was his biggest box-office success and won five Academy Award nominations. In his 1964 autobiography he said he could not have made it had he known the truth of the camps.

Contemporaries saw him as the world's most famous film star, loved across Europe, though the Nazis banned his films. In the United States he was attacked for his left-wing views and private life, and in 1952, while he was travelling to London, his permission to re-enter the USA was withdrawn.

He settled in Switzerland, received an honorary Oscar in 1972 and a knighthood in 1975, and died in 1977. Historians see him as a founder of film comedy as an art and proof that cinema could carry political criticism; they debate his later films' politics.
Crosby was an American singer and actor whose radio shows, records and films made him the most popular entertainer of his age, and whose songs were heard across the world during the war.
Crosby was born in Tacoma, Washington, on 3 May 1903. In the late 1920s he sang with Paul Whiteman's band as one of the Rhythm Boys.
He had his own CBS radio show from 1931. His soft crooning style used the microphone rather than projecting the voice, so it suited radio and records perfectly.

He hosted NBC's Kraft Music Hall from the mid-1930s to 1946 and recorded for Decca from 1934, becoming the best-selling recording artist of his time and making hundreds of records. Radio, records and film fed each other, a model of the modern entertainment industry.

He was a Paramount star, with the Road films with Bob Hope and Dorothy Lamour from Road to Singapore (1940). He won the Oscar for Best Actor as a priest in Going My Way (1944), awarded at the 1945 ceremony.

Irving Berlin's song White Christmas, sung by Crosby in Holiday Inn (1942), had a longing for home that made it the song of soldiers far from home. His recording is often called the best-selling single of all time.

Crosby entertained Allied troops through broadcasts for the forces, war-bond drives and a USO tour (the USO was the organisation that put on shows for American troops) of camps in England and France in 1944. His popularity with the forces was very high.

Contemporaries saw him as the most popular entertainer of the age, the relaxed, friendly face of America and an embodiment of easy-going American popular culture. His music spread the sounds of American radio into Europe.
Historians see him as central to the rise of recorded popular music and to American cultural influence in Europe, and they study his role in wartime morale alongside that of other entertainers.
American popular culture crossed the Atlantic in the 1920s and 1930s, carried by records, radio and film. Europe's young embraced it, while their elders often worried.
The jazz age came to Europe with the Original Dixieland Jass Band in London (1919) and Josephine Baker in Paris (1925), and with dance crazes such as the Charleston.
American slang, clothes, hairstyles and film-star glamour were copied especially by the young.
British critics feared Americanisation, the spread of American habits and tastes, and worried about its effect on speech, taste and morals.
The film quota and the BBC's public-service ethos were partly defences against it. Audiences went on choosing American films and dance music anyway.
The dictatorships treated American culture as a threat to their control and tried to ban it. The bans did not work as they hoped.
Nazi Germany banned jazz from German radio in 1935. In 1938 it showed jazz at the Degenerate Music exhibition in Düsseldorf as racially alien.
The Swing Youth (Swingjugend) of Hamburg and other cities defied the regime, for example by dancing to banned music, and faced arrest from 1941, with some sent to camps.
Fascist Italy promoted Italian films against Hollywood, for example through Cinecittà and the 1938 import monopoly.
Bans did not end American culture's appeal, because young people simply listened and danced in secret or in defiance.
The war put millions of Americans in Britain and put American music into British ears. This brought both admiration and resentment.
The first American troops arrived in Britain (in Northern Ireland) in January 1942, and there were well over a million by 1944. They brought swing music, chewing gum, nylons, cheap goods and money.
The reaction was admiration and resentment, summed up in the wartime British saying that they were "overpaid, oversexed and over here".

Vera Lynn, known as the Forces' Sweetheart, sang We'll Meet Again (1939), which became a symbol of separation and hope for servicemen and their families and was the British counterpart to White Christmas.
After 1945 American music and film dominated western Europe.
Judgements of church-state relations weigh the agreements and the Church's survival against the regimes' control of religious life. The best answers argue throughout who gained more.
Achievement for Mussolini: the Lateran Treaties ended the dispute with the papacy, brought Catholic support for a decade and prestige, and solved the Roman Question.

Limit for Mussolini: the Church kept its own youth organisations, press and moral authority, and there were open disputes in 1931 and 1938. It was the one large organisation in Italy that stayed outside Fascist control, which set a limit on Italian totalitarianism.

Achievement for Hitler: the Concordat gave him prestige and ended the Centre Party and political Catholicism, the regime avoided a rupture with the Catholic population in the early 1930s, and most churchgoers conformed.
Limit for Hitler: the Reichskirche failed to unify the Protestant churches. The Confessing Church and Galen showed that totalitarian control stopped at the church door.
Survival against failure: the churches survived both regimes as the largest institutions outside party control, but they did not defend the regimes' victims.
Judgements of popular culture weigh its appeal against state control and cultural reaction. The same media could serve both freedom and propaganda.
Entertainment against persuasion: the same media served morale and propaganda, from BBC bulletins and Mrs Miniver to Lord Haw-Haw's broadcasts.
Democratic use against dictatorial control: BBC news, fireside chats and Chaplin's satire contrast with Nazi and Fascist bans and monopolies.
Americanisation as liberation for the young against a threat to national cultures: young people copied American music and film, while critics and dictators tried to restrict them.
Impact in war: radio and film lifted morale, and songs such as White Christmas, We'll Meet Again and Lili Marleen reached troops, while the BBC gave information to occupied Europe.
Chaplin's satire and Crosby's morale-building contrast with Riefenstahl, whose film work served the Nazi state as propaganda.
Views of these events changed with time. What contemporaries welcomed, later historians often questioned.
Contemporary view: the Lateran Treaties were welcomed by Catholics in 1929, including Catholics around the world.
Later view: critics say the Church lent Fascism respectability by signing, a bargain that made it complicit.
The Reich Concordat and Pius XII's wartime silence remain a continuing historians' debate.
Chaplin and Crosby were entertainers in their day, and they are now also historical evidence of the new mass culture.
Later historians stress that American popular culture spread widely in Europe in the 1930s and became a key influence on European youth, despite the dictatorships' attempts to restrict it.

The Cold War grew out of a wartime partnership that was always uneasy. The USA, Britain and the Soviet Union were allies against Hitler, but they stood for opposite systems and never fully trusted one another.

The Grand Alliance began in 1941, when Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June and the USA entered the war in December. The allies fought together because they shared an enemy, not because they shared aims.

Distrust was old. The West had intervened against the Bolsheviks after 1917, and Stalin had signed the Nazi–Soviet Pact with Hitler in August 1939, so each side suspected the other of putting its own interests first.
Capitalism means private ownership and production for profit in a market economy; it was the system the USA defended. Western democracy added free elections and several parties competing for power.

Communism, as practised in the Soviet bloc (the group of states under Soviet leadership), meant a single party controlling the state, with industry publicly owned and centrally planned. The two systems each claimed to be the future, which made lasting friendship unlikely.

Soviet war dead numbered over 20 million (estimates go up to about 27 million), and Germany had invaded Russia through Poland in 1914 and again in 1941. This is why Stalin demanded security on his western frontier.

The Cold War is the rivalry of the two blocs short of direct war between the superpowers (the USA and the Soviet Union). It was fought by propaganda, aid, alliances, arms and crises, and is dated about 1945 to 1991.
The term was used by the American financier Bernard Baruch in a 1947 speech and popularised by the journalist Walter Lippmann's book The Cold War (1947).
Even while Germany was still undefeated, quarrels over strategy and over Poland showed that the allies wanted different things from the peace. These disputes shaped the bargaining at Yalta.

The second front argument: Stalin pressed the Western allies to open a second front in western Europe to relieve the Red Army, and resented the delay because the Soviet Union was bearing the brunt of the fighting.

Katyn: Polish officers had been murdered by the Soviet NKVD (secret police) in 1940. In 1943 the Polish government-in-exile in London asked for an inquiry, so the Soviet Union broke off relations with it.

The Warsaw Rising of August–October 1944 was a Polish revolt against the Germans. The Red Army did not come to its aid, which Poles and the West read as Stalin letting non-communist resistance be crushed.
