In August 1980 the pope's picture hung on the Gdańsk shipyard gate during the strike, which shows that his election and visit had given many Poles the confidence to organise.

He returned to Poland in June 1983, when he met Lech Wałęsa, and in June 1987. His sermons defended workers' rights and human dignity without calling for revolt, which gave Solidarity moral support while the authorities tried to suppress it.
He was shot in St Peter's Square, Rome, on 13 May 1981 by Mehmet Ali Ağca, a Turkish gunman, and recovered. Claims of Bulgarian or Soviet involvement have never been proven.

The Polish and Soviet governments saw him as a threat, and the Polish secret police monitored the Church closely. On 1 December 1989 he received Gorbachev in the Vatican, the first Soviet Communist Party leader (General Secretary) to meet a pope.

Historians debate how far he caused 1989: many see a moral leader who strengthened Polish civil society (groups organised outside the state), others stress economic and Soviet factors. Gorbachev wrote in 1992 that events in eastern Europe would have been impossible without the pope.

Poland's economic troubles produced the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc. Solidarity grew from a shipyard strike into a national movement, forcing the communist state to deal with an organised opposition.

In December 1970 price rises caused strikes on the Baltic coast (Gdańsk, Gdynia, Szczecin); troops fired on workers and Gomułka was replaced by Edward Gierek. Gierek borrowed heavily from the West in the 1970s, protests followed price rises in 1976, and meat-price rises came in July 1980.
The strike at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk began on 14 August 1980, sparked by the sacking of the crane operator Anna Walentynowicz.
The inter-factory strike committee made 21 demands, including free trade unions, the right to strike, the release of political prisoners, access to the media and better supplies.
The Gdańsk Agreement, signed on 31 August 1980, gave the strikers the right to form free trade unions and to strike, a concession forced on the state by the strike.
Solidarity (Solidarność) was founded in September 1980 and registered by the courts in November 1980. Its leader was Lech Wałęsa, an electrician at the shipyard who had been sacked in 1976.

At its peak in 1981 it had about ten million members, about a quarter of the population, and Rural Solidarity was formed for farmers in 1981. With Church and intellectual support, this made it a national movement rather than just a union.
The state struck back in December 1981, but it could not destroy Solidarity. Eight years later the same regime had to negotiate with it.

General Wojciech Jaruzelski, prime minister from February 1981 and party First Secretary from October 1981, declared martial law on 13 December 1981. Wałęsa and other Solidarity leaders were interned, the union was suspended, and a curfew and army rule through the Military Council of National Salvation followed.
The union was formally banned in October 1982 so that it could not revive, and martial law was lifted in July 1983.

Jaruzelski later claimed martial law was the 'lesser evil' that prevented a Soviet invasion. Moscow had pressed for firm action, but Soviet Politburo records from December 1981 suggest it was unwilling to send troops.

Historians still debate how to read those records and whether the invasion threat was real, and many add that Jaruzelski also acted to keep communist control. Martial law was control by proxy: Poles, not Soviet troops, did the repressing.

Wałęsa was released in November 1982 and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983. Father Jerzy Popiełuszko, a pro-Solidarity priest, was murdered by secret police officers in October 1984, and the officers were tried and convicted.
Strike waves in 1988 showed that Solidarity's support had survived the years of repression, which is why the government had to talk to it.

Round Table talks between the government and the Solidarity-led opposition ran from 6 February to 5 April 1989. They agreed partly free elections (a set share of Sejm, the lower house, seats reserved for the communists and their allies, and a new freely elected Senate) and a new presidency.
Solidarity was legalised again on 17 April 1989, which opened the way to the June elections because it could now stand candidates.
Mikhail Gorbachev, Soviet leader from 1985, began reforms that he meant to renew socialism but that ended with the collapse of communist rule in eastern Europe and the break-up of the USSR.
He was born on 2 March 1931 in Privolnoye, in the Stavropol region, to a peasant family. He took a law degree at Moscow State University (1955), where he met his wife Raisa.

He rose through the party in Stavropol (regional First Secretary in 1970), became Central Committee secretary for agriculture in 1978 and a full Politburo member in 1980, as a protege of Yuri Andropov.

He became General Secretary on 11 March 1985, on Chernenko's death, as the youngest Politburo member. He was head of state from October 1988 (chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet), chairman of the new Supreme Soviet in 1989 and President of the USSR in March 1990.

He was chosen by the party in 1985 and by the Congress of People's Deputies in 1990, never by popular vote; Boris Yeltsin, elected in June 1991, was the one with a popular mandate. Gorbachev resigned on 25 December 1991 and died in 2022.

His aim was to save and renew socialism, not to end it. As a participant he chose not to use force in eastern Europe, unlike Khrushchev in 1956, and most historians agree that the consequences, the end of communist rule and of the Union, were ones he did not foresee.

Contemporaries abroad welcomed him. After meeting him in December 1984 Margaret Thatcher said: 'I like Mr Gorbachev. We can do business together.' Reagan negotiated arms agreements with him, 'Gorbymania' (popular enthusiasm) swept the West, and he won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990.

At home conservatives blamed him for destroying the system, radicals such as Yeltsin (dismissed in 1987 after attacking the slow pace of reform) thought him too slow, and many Russians blamed him for shortages and economic collapse.

Historians differ. Archie Brown (The Gorbachev Factor, 1996) sees a genuine transformer of the system; Stephen Kotkin (Armageddon Averted, 2001) argues the system was already doomed and that his achievement was that it ended without war.

By 1985 the Soviet Union was stagnating, and Gorbachev set out to renew it from above. His economic policies moved from a simple push for speed to a wider restructuring, and neither cured the shortages.
Reform was needed because of economic stagnation, the cost of the arms race and of the war in Afghanistan (Soviet troops there since December 1979), and an ageing leadership.
World oil prices fell sharply in 1986, cutting Soviet export earnings, so the state had less money to meet its costs.
He relied on younger reformers, notably Alexander Yakovlev, his key adviser on reform and glasnost, and Eduard Shevardnadze, foreign minister from 1985.
His first economic slogan, in 1985-86, was uskorenie (acceleration of economic growth). It tried to speed up the existing planned economy, and when it failed he moved to perestroika.
The anti-alcohol campaign of May 1985 belonged to this early effort, but it was unpopular and cost the state tax revenue.

Perestroika (restructuring) set out to reform the economy, and later the political system, by adding limited market elements to central planning. The Law on State Enterprise (1987) gave factories more freedom over output and prices.
The Law on Cooperatives (1988) allowed small private businesses, for example restaurants and workshops, so private enterprise returned in a limited form.
Perestroika failed because it was a set of half-measures: markets were added but planning was not abandoned, so by 1990-91 there were empty shops, rationing, rising prices and falling output.
Gorbachev found that economic reform needed honest information and public pressure on officials. Glasnost opened up discussion, and democratisation then gave voters a real say.
Glasnost means openness: freer discussion, less censorship and criticism of officials and of the Soviet past. It was proclaimed at the 27th Party Congress in February-March 1986.

The reactor explosion at Chernobyl, in Soviet Ukraine (not Russia), on 26 April 1986 exposed the secrecy of the system: the authorities said nothing for about two days, until radiation was detected in Sweden. The concealment strengthened the case for glasnost.
Banned works were published, which showed the new openness, such as Boris Pasternak's Doctor Zhivago (1988) and Solzhenitsyn's writings (1989-90), and Stalin's crimes were openly discussed.
Dissidents (open critics of the regime) were released, for example the nuclear physicist Andrei Sakharov, freed from internal exile in Gorky in December 1986.
Democratisation (demokratizatsiya) meant partly free elections and the end of the party's monopoly of power.

The elections to the Congress of People's Deputies in March 1989 were the first partly free elections in the Soviet Union since 1917. Several party bosses were defeated and the sessions were televised.
In February-March 1990 the party gave up its leading role (Article 6 of the constitution was amended in March 1990), and in March 1990 Gorbachev became the first executive president of the USSR.
Glasnost also released nationalism in the republics, so the success of freeing speech carried a limit that Gorbachev could not control.
Gorbachev wanted to cut the military burden that was crippling the economy. His 'new thinking' in foreign policy, helped by Shevardnadze, ended the arms race and eased tension with the West.

He held summits with Reagan at Geneva (November 1985), Reykjavik (October 1986) and Washington (December 1987). At Reykjavik they came close to agreeing deep cuts in nuclear weapons but failed over SDI.

The INF Treaty, signed in Washington on 8 December 1987, abolished all US and Soviet intermediate-range (500-5,500 km) land-based missiles, the first treaty to remove a whole class of nuclear weapons.

In his United Nations General Assembly speech on 7 December 1988 he announced that Soviet armed forces would be cut by 500,000 men and some divisions withdrawn from eastern Europe, which signalled a lower military threat.
The last Soviet troops left Afghanistan on 15 February 1989, ending a costly war that had begun in December 1979, so the USSR no longer had to pay for it.
At the Malta summit with President George H. W. Bush on 2-3 December 1989 (Bush, not Reagan) the leaders met as the bloc collapsed, and it is often seen as marking the end of the Cold War.
START I (strategic arms reduction) was signed in July 1991 to cut the long-range nuclear weapons of both sides, which continued arms control after the INF Treaty.

In 1989 communist rule collapsed across eastern Europe in a few months, almost entirely without Soviet intervention. Poland and Hungary went first, and Hungary's actions opened a route to the West for East Germans.

The Polish elections of 4 and 18 June 1989 were not fully free, because a set share of Sejm seats was reserved for the communists and their allies. Solidarity won all but one of the Sejm seats it could contest (161) and 99 of the 100 Senate seats.

Jaruzelski was elected president by parliament in July 1989. In August 1989 Tadeusz Mazowiecki, a Catholic journalist and Solidarity adviser, became prime minister of the first non-communist-led government in the Soviet bloc in over forty years.
Wałęsa was elected President of Poland in December 1990.

In Hungary János Kádár, leader since 1956, was removed in May 1988. The dismantling of the border fence with Austria began on 2 May 1989, and on 27 June the Hungarian and Austrian foreign ministers, Gyula Horn and Alois Mock, cut the wire publicly.

Imre Nagy, leader of the 1956 uprising, was reburied with honours in Budapest on 16 June 1989 before a huge crowd, which turned the memory of 1956 into a national symbol and a challenge to the regime.

At the Pan-European Picnic near Sopron on 19 August 1989 several hundred East Germans crossed to Austria, and on 11 September 1989 Hungary opened its border to East Germans so that they could escape west.

Round-table talks agreed multi-party elections, the party renamed itself the Hungarian Socialist Party in October 1989, and the Republic of Hungary was proclaimed on 23 October 1989, the anniversary of 1956.
Free elections in March-April 1990 were won by the Hungarian Democratic Forum, and József Antall became prime minister.

East Germany's government collapsed under pressure from its own people, who first left in thousands and then marched. The opening of the Berlin Wall became the symbol of the end of the division of Europe.
Thousands of East Germans fled through Hungary and Czechoslovakia and camped in the West German embassy in Prague, until they were allowed to leave for the West at the end of September 1989.

New Forum, an opposition group, was founded in September 1989, and the Leipzig Monday demonstrations began that month. On 9 October about 70,000 marched and the security forces did not fire, which showed that the regime had lost the will to shoot.
Gorbachev attended the GDR's 40th anniversary celebrations on 7 October 1989 and urged reform, a sign that Moscow would not back the hardliners with force.
Erich Honecker, East German leader since 1971, resigned on 18 October 1989 because the demonstrations could not be stopped, and Egon Krenz succeeded him.
A mass rally in East Berlin on 4 November 1989 followed. The slogan 'We are the people' later became 'We are one people', showing the shift from demanding reform to demanding unity.

On the evening of 9 November 1989 Günter Schabowski, Politburo spokesman, told a press conference that new travel rules applied 'immediately'. The announcement was confused, and crowds gathered at the crossings.
Guards at Bornholmer Strasse opened the gate that night, so the Wall was opened, not knocked down; demolition came in 1990.
The last regimes fell in a rush in November and December 1989. Czechoslovakia's change was peaceful, Bulgaria's came from inside the party, and Romania's was the only violent revolution of 1989.
The Velvet Revolution began on 17 November 1989, when police beat a student march in Prague. It is called 'velvet' because it was peaceful.
Mass demonstrations and a general strike on 27 November followed. Civic Forum, with Havel, led the opposition in the Czech lands, and Public Against Violence did so in Slovakia.
The party gave up its leading role at the end of November, and Husák resigned as president in December 1989.
Dubček was elected chairman of the Federal Assembly on 28 December and Václav Havel president on 29 December 1989, so the leader of 1968 and the Charter 77 spokesman stood together at the end.
In Bulgaria, Todor Zhivkov, leader since 1954, was removed by his own party on 10 November 1989 and replaced by Petar Mladenov.
In Romania protests began in Timișoara on 16 December 1989 over the eviction of the Hungarian Protestant pastor László Tőkés, and security forces fired on the crowds.
A rally in Bucharest on 21 December turned against Nicolae Ceaușescu. He fled by helicopter on 22 December, the army changed sides, and there was fighting with Securitate (secret police) loyalists.
The National Salvation Front, led by Ion Iliescu, took power. Nicolae and Elena Ceaușescu were tried by a military court and shot on 25 December 1989. About 1,100 people died in the revolution.
The speed and calm of 1989 need explaining, because earlier risings had been crushed. The central change was that Moscow no longer backed its allies with force.

In October 1989 Gennady Gerasimov, the Soviet foreign ministry spokesman, said the Brezhnev Doctrine had been replaced by the 'Sinatra Doctrine' (after the song 'My Way'), meaning that eastern European states could choose their own path.
Non-intervention was Gorbachev's choice. He meant to renew socialism, not to free eastern Europe, so the fall of the regimes was a consequence he did not foresee.
The economic failure of the regimes had already cost them public support, so there was little loyalty left to defend them.
Each neighbour's example mattered: success in Poland and Hungary showed that change was possible, which encouraged protesters in East Germany and Czechoslovakia.
Television and travel showed eastern Europeans the prosperity of the West, which made their own living standards look worse.
The regimes lost the will to shoot because they knew Soviet tanks would not come, so the police and army did not fire on the crowds.

Glasnost let the republics of the USSR (the Soviet Union was a federation of fifteen republics) air grievances that had long been suppressed. National demands and a rival leader in Russia weakened Gorbachev's authority.
Nagorno-Karabakh was the scene of an Armenian-Azerbaijani conflict from 1988, which showed that glasnost let old ethnic quarrels resurface.
In Tbilisi, Georgia, in April 1989, troops killed peaceful demonstrators, which hardened nationalist feeling.
On 23 August 1989, the 50th anniversary of the Nazi-Soviet Pact, about two million people formed a human chain across Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, called the Baltic Way.

Lithuania, led by Vytautas Landsbergis, declared independence on 11 March 1990, and other Soviet republics followed in demanding sovereignty. In January 1991 Soviet troops killed fourteen people at the Vilnius television tower.

Boris Yeltsin, Moscow party chief, attacked the slow pace of reform and was dismissed in 1987. He was elected chairman of the Russian parliament in May 1990, left the Communist Party in 1990, and Russia declared its sovereignty in June 1990.
On 12 June 1991 Yeltsin was elected President of the Russian republic by popular vote. This gave him a mandate Gorbachev lacked and made Russian sovereignty a rival to Soviet authority.
In 1991 the institutions of the Soviet system fell apart one after another. A coup by hardliners meant to save the Union instead hastened its end.
Comecon was dissolved in June 1991 and the Warsaw Pact was formally dissolved on 1 July 1991 in Prague. Soviet troops left Hungary and Czechoslovakia in 1991, and the last left Germany in 1994.
The coup of 19-21 August 1991 came on the eve of a new Union Treaty giving the republics more power, which hardliners feared would break up the Union.

It was staged by the State Committee for the State of Emergency, eight hardliners including Vice-President Gennady Yanayev, KGB chairman Vladimir Kryuchkov and Defence Minister Dmitry Yazov. Gorbachev was held at his holiday home at Foros, Crimea.
Yeltsin spoke from a tank outside the Russian parliament (the White House) in Moscow and rallied opposition. Troops would not attack, three civilians were killed, and the coup collapsed.
Gorbachev returned on 22 August, weakened, and resigned as General Secretary on 24 August 1991. The Communist Party was suspended, and Yeltsin banned it in Russia in November 1991.
The republics declared independence. The USSR recognised Estonian, Latvian and Lithuanian independence on 6 September 1991, and all three were admitted to the UN on 17 September 1991.
After the coup the Union had no authority left, and the republics negotiated their way out. The end came in a few weeks.
On 1 December 1991 Ukraine held an independence referendum with about 90 per cent in favour, which made it hard to keep the Union together.

On 8 December 1991 the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus met at Belovezha (the Minsk agreement), declared the USSR at an end and founded the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), a loose association of former republics.
More republics joined the CIS at Alma-Ata on 21 December 1991, so the CIS replaced the Union.
Gorbachev resigned as Soviet president on 25 December 1991 because the Union he led no longer existed in practice, and the red flag over the Kremlin was lowered that evening.
The USSR was formally dissolved on 26 December 1991, a day after his resignation, leaving fifteen independent successor states.
The fall of the Wall put unity on the agenda within weeks. Chancellor Helmut Kohl moved quickly, and Gorbachev's consent allowed a united Germany to remain in NATO.
Helmut Kohl, West German chancellor from 1982 to 1998, pushed for rapid unity after the Wall fell, so he set out a Ten-Point Plan on 28 November 1989.
In the first free East German election on 18 March 1990 the Kohl-backed Alliance for Germany won, and Lothar de Maizière became prime minister, which showed that East Germans wanted unity.
Monetary, economic and social union came into force on 1 July 1990, so that the Deutsche Mark became East Germany's currency.
In July 1990 Gorbachev accepted that a united Germany could be in NATO, in return for German aid and limits on German forces.
The Two Plus Four Treaty was signed in Moscow on 12 September 1990 by the two German states plus the USA, the Soviet Union, Britain and France.
It gave Germany full sovereignty, confirmed the Oder-Neisse border, left a united Germany free to stay in NATO and required Soviet troops to leave.
Unification took place on 3 October 1990, when the territory of the GDR joined the Federal Republic. Kohl won the first all-German election in December 1990.
Yugoslavia was a federation of republics held together under Tito. When communism fell, nationalism broke it apart, and unlike most of 1989 the change was violent.
Tito died in May 1980, and a rotating collective presidency followed, so no single leader held the federation together. Economic crisis and rising nationalism followed.
Slobodan Milošević, Serbian leader from 1987 (president of Serbia from 1989), stirred Serb nationalism, and from 1991 Serbia opposed the secession of Slovenia and Croatia.
Slovenia and Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991, and Macedonia declared independence in 1991 too.
The Ten-Day War in Slovenia (June-July 1991) ended with the Yugoslav army withdrawing, so Slovenia's break was brief.
War in Croatia began in 1991 because Serbia opposed secession, with the siege and fall of Vukovar in November 1991.
The European Community recognised Slovenia and Croatia on 15 January 1992, after Germany pressed for it.
Bosnia-Herzegovina voted for independence in a referendum in February-March 1992, boycotted by most Bosnian Serbs, and was recognised in April 1992. War and the siege of Sarajevo began that month.
The war in Bosnia lasted until 1995 and was the bloodiest in Europe since 1945.
With the Soviet bloc gone, the former satellites and the Baltic states looked west, Czechoslovakia split peacefully, and the CIS took shape in the east.
The Visegrád group of Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary, which was founded on 15 February 1991, coordinated their approach to integration with the West.

The former satellites and the Baltic states turned to Western institutions: the Council of Europe, the European Community and NATO. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic later joined NATO in 1999, and most of them and the Baltic states joined the EU in 2004.
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania regained independence in 1991 and sought membership of Western institutions.
In the east the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) linked former Soviet republics loosely, so Russia kept some influence without the old Union.

Czechoslovakia divided peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 1 January 1993, agreed in 1992 after the June elections won by Vladimír Mečiar's party in Slovakia and Václav Klaus's in the Czech lands.
Examiners reward a judgement that weighs what Gorbachev achieved against what he lost. His record was far stronger abroad than at home.
Success abroad: the INF Treaty, the UN troop cuts and START I ended the arms race. Failure at home: the economy got worse, with empty shops, rationing and falling output by 1990-91.

Success: the withdrawal from Afghanistan in February 1989 ended a costly war, which freed money and effort for reform. Limit: shortages made him unpopular at home, so foreign admiration did not translate into support.

Success: non-intervention let eastern Europe change peacefully and let Germany unite within NATO. Failure: the loss of the Union he meant to save, as nationalism grew in the republics and the August 1991 coup failed.
Success: glasnost brought freedom of speech and partly free elections. Limit: it released nationalism, and he reformed the party's monopoly of power too slowly to keep control.
Contemporary views: Western leaders welcomed him, while conservatives at home blamed him for destroying the system and radicals such as Yeltsin for being too slow.
Later views: Archie Brown credits him as a genuine transformer, while Stephen Kotkin argues the system was already doomed and that his achievement was that it ended without war.
Compared with Khrushchev, Gorbachev also reformed from above, met resistance and fell, but unlike Khrushchev he refused to use force, and his reforms ended the bloc and the Union.
Historians explain the collapse through long-term failure, short-term triggers and the decision not to use force. The best answers rank these causes and weigh internal against external ones.

Long-term causes: the command economy failed to deliver, and the regimes lacked legitimacy because they had never ruled by consent. Nationalism, the burden of the arms race, which the West pressed on through defence spending, and Western prosperity seen on television added to the pressure.
Short-term causes: Gorbachev's reforms and non-intervention removed the threat of Soviet force, which had held the regimes up since 1953.
Opposition movements such as Solidarity and Charter 77, and the Church, kept reform alive through repression, and the domino effect of 1989 carried change from one country to the next.
Internal view: Stephen Kotkin and others stress the structural weakness of the system, while Archie Brown stresses Gorbachev's personal role.

External view: contemporary Western conservatives credited Reagan's pressure, including the arms build-up, SDI and his 'tear down this wall' speech in Berlin in June 1987. This is one view, not proven fact, and later historians give more weight to the Soviet system's internal crisis.
Soviet control of eastern Europe was kept by force in 1953, 1956 and 1968 and by proxy in 1981, but never by consent, and it was lost within months once Moscow would not use force.

In 1945 Western Europe was in ruins and its old rivalries had just caused a second world war. Leaders turned to unity for three reasons: to stop another war, to stand together against the Soviet Union and to rebuild their economies.

The Second World War left Western Europe devastated and dependent on the USA. France and Germany had fought three wars in seventy years (1870-71, 1914 and 1939), so ending their rivalry was the first aim of unity.

The Cold War split Europe by the Iron Curtain into a Soviet bloc in the East and a Western side, which formed NATO (the US-led military alliance) in April 1949. Integration here was Western European only, and its supporters saw it as strength against the Soviet threat.
Marshall Aid (1948-52) and the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC, set up in 1948 to share it out) made the USA a sponsor of European cooperation.

Economic recovery was a third motive: a larger market allows more efficient production, and the Benelux customs union (Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, in force 1 January 1948) was an example that cooperation worked.

The Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany) was founded in 1949 under its first chancellor, Konrad Adenauer (in office 1949-63). How to rebuild and rearm it safely, the 'German question', lay behind both the Schuman Plan and the European Defence Community.
Ideas mattered too. Altiero Spinelli, an Italian federalist, wrote the Ventotene Manifesto in 1941 while interned by Mussolini's regime.

Christian Democrat leaders such as Robert Schuman (France), Adenauer and Alcide De Gasperi (Italy) shared a wish to bind their countries together, and Europe's decline as a world power made unity look necessary.

The history of European unity is a debate between two ways of organising it, and a handful of terms describe the choices. Knowing them lets you say exactly what each treaty did and what each leader wanted.
A federal Europe means a united Europe with a central, supranational government above the national governments. Federalists such as Spinelli, Spaak, Monnet, Hallstein and Delors wanted this.
Supranational means that the institutions' decisions bind member states, even against their wishes. Examples are the ECSC High Authority, the Commission and the Court of Justice.

Intergovernmental means cooperation decided by national governments, each keeping a veto (the power to block a decision). The Council of Europe, EFTA, de Gaulle's Europe of states and Thatcher's view all follow this model.

A customs union has no tariffs (taxes on imports) between members and one common tariff on goods from outside. It is the first stage of a common market, which adds free movement of goods, services, capital and people. In Britain and Ireland the EEC was commonly called 'the Common Market'.

The single market is the completion of the common market by removing physical (border), technical (standards) and fiscal (tax) barriers, the 1992 programme. Do not confuse it with the customs union, completed in 1968.
Qualified majority voting means decisions in the Council of Ministers by a weighted majority rather than unanimity, so one state cannot block everything. The Single European Act extended it.
The Six were France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, the members of the ECSC and the founders of the EEC.
Between 1946 and 1950 Europeans tried loose cooperation first. It produced a forum for debate, not a government, and its limits pushed the federalists to look for another route.

Winston Churchill, then leader of the opposition, called at the University of Zurich on 19 September 1946 for 'a kind of United States of Europe' built on a partnership between France and Germany. He saw Britain and the Commonwealth as friends and sponsors outside it, not members.

The Congress of Europe at The Hague (May 1948) brought together several hundred delegates, with Churchill as chairman. It called for a European assembly and a charter of human rights, and it led to the creation of the Council of Europe the following year.
It split between federalists, who wanted real authority, and unionists, who wanted cooperation between governments, so it showed the argument that ran through the whole period.

The Council of Europe was founded by the Treaty of London on 5 May 1949 by ten states: Belgium, Denmark, France, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and Britain. Its seat is Strasbourg.

Its Consultative Assembly could only debate and recommend, so it was a forum rather than a source of binding law. This disappointed federalists, and Paul-Henri Spaak, the Assembly's first president (1949), resigned in 1951 in frustration at its lack of power.
Its main achievement was the European Convention on Human Rights, signed in Rome on 4 November 1950 and in force in 1953. The European Court of Human Rights was set up in Strasbourg in 1959.
The Council of Europe is not an EEC institution, and its Court of Human Rights is not the EEC's Court of Justice (which sits in Luxembourg). Do not confuse either with the Council of Ministers.
Monnet was a French planner and persuader who designed the first European communities and is widely called a 'father of Europe'. He never held elected office, so he worked through politicians.
He was born in Cognac, France, in 1888, worked in the family cognac business and then in international finance, and was deputy secretary-general of the League of Nations from 1919 to 1923.

In the Second World War he coordinated Anglo-French war supplies (1939-40) and helped draft the offer of a Franco-British union in June 1940, which the French government did not accept before France's surrender. He later worked on war supplies in Washington.

From 1946 he headed the French planning commission. The Monnet Plan of that year modernised coal, steel, electricity, transport and other basic industries through state investment, partly financed by Marshall Aid.

He drafted the Schuman Declaration, announced by the foreign minister Robert Schuman on 9 May 1950. His method was to unite Europe sector by sector, 'through concrete achievements', so that each small step created a reason for the next.
He was the first president of the ECSC High Authority (1952-55), based in Luxembourg. He then left it to campaign for further integration.

In 1955 he founded the Action Committee for the United States of Europe, which brought together political parties and trade unions from the Six. It pressed for Euratom, the EEC and later British membership, so he kept shaping events without office.
Contemporaries were divided. Federalists and American leaders admired him, while de Gaulle and the Gaullists opposed him because they rejected supranational institutions. He died in 1979.
Historians call him the architect of the 'Monnet method' of gradual, functional integration, but debate how much credit he deserves compared with the national governments that took the decisions.
The first supranational community pooled the coal and steel of France and West Germany.

Coal and steel were the basis of war industries, and they were a sore point: the Ruhr (in West Germany) had been under an International Authority for the Ruhr since 1949, and the Saar was under French economic control after the war (it returned to West Germany in 1957).

The Schuman Declaration of 9 May 1950 proposed a joint authority for French and West German coal and steel, open to other states. It said pooling them would make war between France and Germany 'not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible'. 9 May is now celebrated as Europe Day.

Reactions differed. Adenauer accepted at once, because the plan treated West Germany as an equal and offered an end to international control of the Ruhr (that authority was wound up only when the ECSC began in 1952). Italy and the Benelux countries joined.
Britain's Labour government under Clement Attlee refused to join, because it would not hand control of its nationalised coal and steel industries to a supranational body.
The Treaty of Paris was signed on 18 April 1951 by the Six (the signatories) and came into force on 23 July 1952, to run for fifty years.
It had four institutions: the High Authority (a supranational executive), the Common Assembly, the Special Council of Ministers and the Court of Justice.
The High Authority could take decisions binding on firms and governments, raise a levy on coal and steel production and fine firms that broke the rules.

Results: a common market in coal and steel, an institutional model that the EEC later copied, and Franco-German reconciliation in practice, since the two countries now ran their war industries together.
After success in coal and steel, the French tried to extend the same supranational method to defence. The attempt failed, and integration turned back to the economy.

The Korean War (from June 1950) led the USA to press for West German rearmament. In October 1950 the French prime minister René Pleven proposed a European Defence Community (EDC), a European army, so that West Germany could rearm without having a national army.
The EDC Treaty was signed on 27 May 1952 by the Six. A plan for a European Political Community (1953) depended on it and fell with it.
The French National Assembly rejected the EDC on 30 August 1954, by a procedural vote. It was the Assembly, not the government, that killed a plan the French government itself had proposed.

The reasons were fear of German rearmament, opposition from Gaullists and communists, and reluctance to lose sovereignty over the army. Britain had refused to join, and the death of Stalin in March 1953 and the Korean armistice of July 1953 had eased the sense of threat.

West Germany was rearmed another way. The Paris Agreements of October 1954 extended the 1948 Brussels Treaty to West Germany and Italy, creating the Western European Union (from 1955), and West Germany joined NATO in May 1955.
The result was that integration turned back to economics, and defence stayed national and Atlantic. This is why the Treaties of Rome were about trade, not armies.
Having failed in defence, the Six returned to the economy in 1955. The result, the Treaties of Rome, created the EEC, which became the centre of European integration.

The Messina conference of the six foreign ministers (1-3 June 1955) relaunched the project. It was prepared by the Benelux governments and chaired by Italy; Monnet was not its organiser but worked through his Action Committee.
Spaak chaired the committee whose report (April 1956) proposed a common market and an atomic energy community. It was approved at Venice in May 1956.

The Treaties of Rome were signed on 25 March 1957 by the Six and came into force on 1 January 1958. They created the European Economic Community (EEC) and the European Atomic Energy Community (Euratom).

The EEC was to build a customs union in stages over twelve years, with a common external tariff, and to bring free movement of goods, services, capital and workers (the 'four freedoms'). It also planned common policies in agriculture and transport.
The preamble speaks of 'an ever closer union among the peoples of Europe', which shows that the long-term aim was political as well as economic.
Euratom was for civil nuclear cooperation among the Six. It was less important than the EEC.

Four institutions ran the EEC: the Commission (based in Brussels, which proposed legislation), the Council of Ministers, the Assembly and the Court of Justice. The Assembly renamed itself the European Parliament in 1962, and its members were appointed from national parliaments until direct elections in 1979.

Walter Hallstein of West Germany, a federalist, was the first Commission president (1958-67). The Merger Treaty (signed 1965, in force 1 July 1967) merged the executives of the ECSC, EEC and Euratom into one Commission and one Council.
The EEC was not the European Union or a single currency. Those date from Maastricht (1992, in force 1993) and the euro from 1999.
In its first decade the EEC proved it could deliver. It built its customs union early and launched a common farm policy, while a rival group tried a looser path.

The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) was agreed in January 1962 and operated from 1962, designed by the Dutch commissioner Sicco Mansholt. It gave farmers common guaranteed prices, protected them with a levy on cheaper imports and paid export subsidies, all financed from a common fund.

Benefits were secure incomes for farmers and food security. Costs were that the CAP became by far the largest item in the Community budget, and guaranteed prices produced surpluses nicknamed 'butter mountains' and 'wine lakes'. Milk quotas were introduced in 1984 to limit them.
The customs union was completed on 1 July 1968, eighteen months ahead of schedule, with the common external tariff in place the same day. Trade among the Six grew rapidly.

The European Free Trade Association (EFTA) was set up by the Stockholm Convention in January 1960 (in force May 1960) by Britain, Austria, Denmark, Norway, Portugal, Sweden and Switzerland. It was a free-trade area in industrial goods only, with no common external tariff and no supranational institutions.

EFTA was Britain's alternative to the EEC for states that rejected supranationalism. Its weakness was that it lacked the EEC's large common market and common policies. Britain, Ireland and Denmark applied to join the EEC in 1961.

Charles de Gaulle, president of France from 1959 to 1969, wanted a Europe of cooperating states, not a supranational one. He used vetoes and a boycott to block British entry and to defend national sovereignty.
De Gaulle favoured a Europe of states or nations, cooperation between sovereign governments, which contrasted with Monnet's supranational model.
The Élysée Treaty of Franco-German friendship, signed on 22 January 1963 by de Gaulle and Adenauer, showed that he wanted a French-led partnership with West Germany at the heart of Europe.

Britain applied to join in 1961 under Harold Macmillan (the negotiator was Edward Heath), as did Ireland under Seán Lemass and Denmark. De Gaulle announced his veto at a press conference on 14 January 1963.

His reasons were Britain's ties to the USA (the Nassau agreement of December 1962 on American Polaris missiles for Britain) and to the Commonwealth, and its different farming and trading system. He feared Britain would weaken the Community and French leadership of it.
He vetoed Britain, not Ireland. Ireland's application lapsed because its trade depended on the British market, so it would not join without Britain.
Britain reapplied in 1967 under Harold Wilson, with Ireland and Denmark, and de Gaulle used his second veto on 27 November 1967.

The empty chair crisis began when France stopped attending Council of Ministers meetings from 30 June / 1 July 1965. The causes were the financing of the CAP, plans to give the Commission and Assembly control of Community money, and the coming move to majority voting.

The Luxembourg Compromise of January 1966 was an informal political agreement, not a treaty change. Where a member said very important national interests were at stake, the Council would try for unanimity. In practice a state could block such decisions, so unanimity became the norm for about twenty years.
After de Gaulle resigned in April 1969, his successor Georges Pompidou allowed the Community to grow. The 1970s brought new members and new institutions, but also slow progress.

The Hague summit of 1-2 December 1969 agreed on 'completion, deepening, enlargement': finishing the common policies, moving towards monetary union and admitting new members. Do not confuse it with the Hague Congress of 1948.
Britain (prime minister Edward Heath), Ireland (Taoiseach Jack Lynch) and Denmark joined on 1 January 1973. Norway's voters rejected membership in September 1972.

Irish voters approved membership in a referendum on 10 May 1972 by about 83 per cent. Britain confirmed its membership in a referendum on 5 June 1975 under Harold Wilson, when about two-thirds voted to stay in. Britain joined in 1973, not 1975.
The European Regional Development Fund was set up in 1975 to help poorer regions. Ireland later became a large net beneficiary of the CAP and the structural funds.

The European Monetary System (EMS) began on 13 March 1979, with the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), which kept currencies within bands, and the ECU, a unit of account. Roy Jenkins, Commission president 1977-81, promoted it, backed by Helmut Schmidt and Valery Giscard d'Estaing.
Ireland joined the ERM, and the Irish pound's one-to-one link with sterling ended in March 1979. Britain stayed out until October 1990 and left in September 1992.
The first direct elections to the European Parliament were held in June 1979, giving it a democratic mandate for the first time.
Eurosclerosis was the name for the slow progress of the Community in the 1970s and early 1980s, during recession.
In the 1980s the Community widened to twelve members and then deepened, setting a deadline for a true single market. Britain's budget quarrel had to be settled first.

Greece joined on 1 January 1981, after military rule ended in 1974. Spain and Portugal joined on 1 January 1986, after the fall of dictatorship (Franco died in 1975; Portugal's dictatorship fell in 1974). Membership became twelve, and the Community supported these new democracies.
At the Fontainebleau summit in June 1984 a permanent rebate for Britain on its budget contribution was agreed, which settled a dispute that had dogged the Community.

The Single European Act was signed in February 1986 and came into force on 1 July 1987. Its entry into force was delayed by the Irish Supreme Court's Crotty judgment, which required a referendum, and the Irish referendum of May 1987 approved it.

The Act set 31 December 1992 for the single market, extended qualified majority voting, gave the Parliament more say and put European Political Cooperation (foreign policy) on a treaty basis. Structural funds doubled afterwards.
Germany reunified on 3 October 1990, and the former East Germany became part of the Community through the united Germany.
Delors was the French socialist who led the European Commission for ten years and relaunched integration through the single market and the plan for monetary union.
He was born in Paris in 1925 and worked at the Banque de France and in French planning. A socialist influenced by Catholic social thought, he joined the Socialist Party in 1974.

He advised prime minister Jacques Chaban-Delmas (1969-72), was an MEP (1979-81) and was French minister of the economy and finance under President Mitterrand (1981-84), so he came to Brussels with government experience.
He was president of the European Commission from January 1985 to January 1995, three terms, about ten years.

The single market was his first project: the 1985 White Paper listed about 300 measures to remove physical, technical and fiscal barriers by 31 December 1992, and the Single European Act of 1986 gave it legal force.

He added a social dimension, because he thought a single market needed protection for workers. In September 1988 he told the British Trades Union Congress to expect one, and the Social Charter was adopted in December 1989 by eleven of the twelve members, Britain refusing.
In July 1988 he told the European Parliament that within ten years about 80 per cent of economic legislation would come from the Community.
The Delors Report of April 1989 set out economic and monetary union in three stages. He took part in the Maastricht negotiations of 1991 and the Treaty of 1992, which built on his plan.

Contemporaries credited him with relaunching the Community after Eurosclerosis. Thatcher saw him as the leader of a drive towards a European super-state, and the Sun newspaper's headline 'Up Yours Delors' (1990) showed British tabloid hostility.
Historians rate him one of the most influential Commission presidents, but debate whether his federal ambitions outran what member states and voters wanted, as the Danish 'no' of 1992 suggested.
Maastricht turned the Community into a union with the aim of a single currency. It also exposed how far voters and governments were willing to go.

The Treaty on European Union was agreed at Maastricht in December 1991, signed on 7 February 1992 and in force on 1 November 1993. It created the European Union, so the term dates from here, not from Rome.

The Union had three pillars: the European Communities, a Common Foreign and Security Policy, and cooperation in justice and home affairs. The principle of subsidiarity (decisions taken at the lowest suitable level) was added.
Economic and monetary union would come in three stages, with a single currency by 1 January 1999 at the latest, and the treaty introduced European citizenship.
Britain opted out of the single currency and the Social Chapter (the Maastricht protocol on social policy, not to be confused with the 1989 Social Charter declaration). Denmark later gained opt-outs.
Danish voters rejected the treaty on 2 June 1992 (approving it in a second vote in 1993), while Irish voters approved it in June 1992.
Throughout the period people disagreed about what unity should be. The split was between those who wanted a federal Europe and those who wanted cooperation between states.

Federalists (Spinelli, Spaak, Monnet, Hallstein and Delors) wanted supranational institutions. Intergovernmentalists (de Gaulle, Thatcher and British governments generally) wanted states to keep control. This split explains most disputes in the period.

Thatcher, British prime minister 1979-90, supported the single market and signed the Single European Act, but opposed federalism, the social dimension and a single currency. She demanded a refund of what she called Britain's own money.
In her Bruges speech of 20 September 1988 she said Europe should be a family of sovereign nations and warned against 'a European super-state' exercising power from Brussels.
Britain was called an 'awkward partner', the title of a book by the historian Stephen George (1990), because of its late entry, the referendum, the budget dispute and the opt-outs.
Unity changed Western Europe's economy, politics and society, but not equally for everyone. Weigh the benefits against the costs.

Economic: trade between members grew rapidly, markets and investment grew, farmers got guaranteed prices under the CAP, and the regional and structural funds helped poorer regions such as Ireland. The costs were CAP surpluses and food prices.

Political: there was Franco-German reconciliation and no war between members of the Community in the period. Spain, Portugal and Greece joined as new democracies, and Europe gained a stronger voice in world trade.
Social: free movement of workers and common rules on working conditions and equal pay (women's rights belong elsewhere) gave new opportunities to countries such as Ireland.

Limits: unity was Western Europe only, there was no common defence, national vetoes remained, the CAP was costly, and there was a 'democratic deficit' (the Parliament had limited power over decisions). This is why unity did not reach every area.
A good answer opens with a judgement. Economic unity went far, but political and defence unity did not, and Europe was supranational in coal, steel and trade but intergovernmental in most else.
Achievements: peace between France and Germany, a customs union and single market, growth from six to twelve members and democracy anchored in the south.
Limits: no common defence (the EDC failed), de Gaulle's vetoes and the empty chair, the CAP's costs, Britain's reluctance, and unity confined to Western Europe.
Contemporary view: federalists hoped that Maastricht was the start of a political union, while critics such as Thatcher feared a super-state.
Later view: historians stress that integration came from compromises between national governments, not from the triumph of the Monnet method alone.

On Monnet and Delors, contemporaries saw them as builders of peace or as threats to sovereignty, while historians ask how far they or the governments deserve the credit and whether Delors's ambitions outran voters.

To understand the post-war boom you need to know what Europe was recovering from and what its governments were determined to avoid. They rebuilt a capitalist system, but one with a much bigger role for the state than before the war.

The Second World War ended in 1945 with much of Europe in ruins, while the USA emerged as the leading economy in the world. From 1947 the Cold War (the hostile standoff between the USA and the Soviet Union) began to divide Europe.

Post-war planners remembered the inter-war years: the Great Depression, protectionism (high tariffs to keep foreign goods out) and mass unemployment. Governments wanted growth, open trade and full employment so that this would not happen again.

Capitalism means private ownership, competitive markets and profit. Western Europe stayed capitalist, in contrast to communism, but ran a mixed economy, with state planning, nationalisation (state ownership of key industries) and welfare provision.
The welfare state means the state provides health care, pensions, unemployment benefit and education, paid for through taxation and insurance contributions.
A common market means free movement of goods, services, capital and workers inside a group of countries, with a common external tariff (the same import tax on goods from outside the group).

Western Europe emerged from the war with damaged cities, disrupted trade and food shortages, which made reconstruction the first priority. Its weakness also made the USA's economic and political help decisive.
Much of the industrial capacity of Germany, France and Italy was damaged or destroyed, and transport networks, bridges and ports had to be rebuilt before trade could restart.
Food and fuel were scarce, so rationing continued in several countries into the late 1940s.
The winter of 1946–47 was exceptionally severe. Coal and fuel shortages slowed factories and transport across Western Europe, including British and continental industry.
Europe suffered from a dollar gap: it needed American goods, such as food and machinery, but had no dollars to pay for them, so it ran a large trade deficit with the USA.

Britain borrowed heavily from the USA, including an Anglo-American loan of about 3.75 billion dollars agreed in December 1945. It stayed dependent on dollars and devalued the pound from 4.03 dollars to 2.80 dollars in September 1949.

Several million German refugees and expellees from the east settled in West Germany by the early 1950s. At first they were a burden because they worsened housing shortages, but they later supplied labour for industry.

The Cold War shaped recovery. In 1947 France and Italy had strong communist parties, and American leaders feared that poverty would increase their support, so the Marshall Plan aimed to prevent economic collapse from strengthening communism.

The USA offered large-scale aid to rebuild Western Europe, partly out of generosity but mainly to bring stability and block the spread of communism. The aid came with conditions that pushed European states to work together.

US Secretary of State George Marshall offered aid in a speech at Harvard on 5 June 1947. The Soviet Union refused and pressed its satellites (the states under its control) to refuse, and Molotov left the Paris talks in July 1947.

Sixteen states took part in the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC), set up on 16 April 1948, and received aid. Recipients had to draw up plans for recovery, and the OEEC coordinated the allocation of aid.

The Economic Cooperation Act passed in April 1948. The European Recovery Programme ran from 1948 to 1952 and provided about 13 billion dollars, mostly as grants, which means money that did not have to be repaid.
The largest recipients were Britain, France and West Germany. Aid paid for food, fuel, raw materials and machinery, which helped solve the dollar gap.
Counterpart funds were local currency raised by selling the American goods inside each country. Governments used them to finance investment in industry and housing.
The OEEC later became the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) in 1961, when the USA and Canada joined. Do not confuse the OEEC with the EEC.
Marshall Aid was meant to do more than supply dollars. It tied recipients to cooperation and to open trade, and historians still argue about how much it really achieved.
Aid was linked to conditions: removing trade barriers, controlling inflation and keeping finances stable. This pushed European states away from the protectionism of the 1930s.

The European Payments Union of 1950 introduced multilateral clearing of members' trade balances. In other words, countries settled their trade accounts together instead of one pair at a time, which helped to revive trade between members.
Aid also promoted American-style productivity methods, such as more efficient factory organisation and management.
Aid gave the USA political leverage. It was meant to strengthen stability and weaken communism's appeal, which fits the American policy of containment (stopping the spread of communism).
The historian Alan Milward, in The Reconstruction of Western Europe, 1945–51 (1984), argued that aid was a modest share of national investment and that domestic policy mattered more.

The case for aid is that it supplied dollars and confidence when Europe was short of both. The case against is that its money was a small part of total investment, so recovery depended mostly on European effort.
Alongside regional recovery, the Western powers rebuilt the rules of world money and trade. Their aim was stable exchange rates and falling tariffs, the opposite of the inter-war chaos.

The Bretton Woods conference of July 1944 created the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank. It fixed currencies to the US dollar, which was convertible into gold at 35 dollars an ounce.

The fixed exchange rate system gave Western economies stable conditions for trade and investment, because firms could trade without fearing sudden currency swings. It lasted until the strains of the 1960s undermined it.

The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) was signed at Geneva on 30 October 1947 by 23 states and came into force on 1 January 1948. It provided a framework for reducing tariffs through successive rounds of negotiation.
The GATT rounds, including the Kennedy Round (talks 1964–67, concluded 1967), reduced tariffs on industrial goods across the Western world.

In December 1958 the main Western European currencies became convertible, which meant they could be freely exchanged for dollars. This ended the controls on trade payments that had survived from the war.
Within Western Europe, states went further than GATT by forming trading blocs. Each one lowered barriers between its members in a different way.

The Benelux customs union (Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg) was agreed by a convention signed in London in 1944 and began operating on 1 January 1948. A customs union removes tariffs between members and sets a common tariff against outsiders.
The European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) was created by the Treaty of Paris in 1951 and came into force in 1952. It covered trade in coal and steel only.

The European Economic Community (EEC) was created by the Treaty of Rome, signed on 25 March 1957 and in force from 1 January 1958. Its six members were Belgium, France, West Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.

The EEC abolished internal industrial tariffs on 1 July 1968, 18 months early, and had the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) in operation from 1962. The CAP set common farm prices, so the 1968 date relates to industrial tariffs and common farm prices, not the start of the CAP.

The European Free Trade Association (EFTA) was set up by the Stockholm Convention of 1960. Its members were Britain, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Austria, Switzerland and Portugal. They removed tariffs on industrial goods, but not on farm produce, and had no common external tariff.
West Germany's recovery was so rapid that it became known as an economic miracle. Reform of money and prices released the market, and a distinctive economic model kept it stable.
The currency reform of 20 June 1948 introduced the Deutsche Mark in the Western zones. It was an Allied measure, not a German one, and it restored confidence in money.
Days later Ludwig Erhard, then director of economic administration, ended most price controls. He was economics minister from 1949 to 1963. Do not confuse him with Adenauer, who was chancellor.
Erhard's social market economy combined free markets with social insurance and trade union rights, so it gave West Germany a stable framework.
Together these reforms created the basis of the economic miracle, the Wirtschaftswunder.
West Germany's economy grew at more than 7 per cent a year on average in the 1950s. Unemployment was about 1.3 per cent in 1960 and under 1 per cent from 1961.
France and Italy also grew rapidly but in different ways: France through state planning and Italy through industry and the movement of labour. Britain, by contrast, grew more slowly.
In France the state planning system began with the Monnet Plan of 1946–47, led by the Commissariat général du Plan. Its priorities were coal, electricity, steel, cement, transport and farm machinery.
The Commissariat set targets for key industries through successive national plans. The state also owned key firms, so Renault was nationalised in 1945.
The French economy grew strongly through the 1950s and 1960s. The economist Jean Fourastié later coined the name trente glorieuses (the thirty glorious years, covering about 1945–75).

Italy's boom ran roughly from 1958 to 1963 and was built on exports of Fiat cars, domestic appliances and textiles. The south (the Mezzogiorno) stayed poor, so many people moved to Turin, Milan and abroad, straining housing and services in the north.
Britain grew more slowly than the continental economies, and balance-of-payments crises produced stop-go policy (swings between expansion and restraint).

Common features were reconstruction, catching up with American methods, cheap oil from the Middle East, skilled and mobile labour, rising exports and rising domestic demand. The adoption of American production methods and the reintegration of trade sustained productivity growth.
Fast growth created more jobs than local workers could fill, so Western Europe turned to workers from abroad. West Germany's guest worker system is the clearest example.

Labour was short for several reasons. The war had killed many working-age men, growth created many new jobs, and rising education and living standards meant fewer locals wanted low-paid, heavy or dirty work.
West Germany recruited guest workers, the Gastarbeiter, under agreements with Italy in 1955, Spain and Greece in 1960, Turkey in 1961 and Yugoslavia in 1968.
Until the Berlin Wall was built in August 1961, workers had also come from East Germany. Once the Wall ended that flow, guest workers became more important to West German industry.
Recruitment was halted in November 1973, by which time there were well over two million foreign workers.
Many guest workers were expected to return home, but many stayed and their families joined them, which made Western Europe multicultural in the later decades.

France and Britain drew many workers from their former empires, who often had citizenship or settlement rights, unlike temporary guest workers. This brought economic benefits and also social tensions.
France drew workers from its former colonies in North Africa (Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia) and from Portugal, and Belgium from Italy and Spain. They worked in construction and car factories.
Algeria became independent in 1962, and several hundred thousand pieds-noirs (settlers of European origin) moved to France.

Britain admitted workers from the Commonwealth. The arrival of the Empire Windrush at Tilbury on 22 June 1948, with over 1,000 passengers, several hundred of them from the Caribbean, marked a major stage in Commonwealth migration.
The British Nationality Act of 1948 gave Commonwealth citizens the right to enter and settle in Britain. The Commonwealth Immigrants Acts of 1962 and 1968 restricted this right.
Commonwealth migrants from the Caribbean, India, Pakistan and Bangladesh worked in the NHS, transport and textile factories. They faced discrimination in housing and employment.
Immigration brought social tensions, and the Race Relations Act of 1965 was Britain's first law against racial discrimination in public places.
The Netherlands received migrants from Indonesia, its former colony, from 1945 onwards, and Italy and Spain exported workers to northern Europe.
Overall, migrants brought economic benefit by filling jobs and supporting growth, but they met discrimination and caused housing pressure. Settled families made the societies multicultural.
The welfare state gave citizens protection against sickness, unemployment and old age.

The Beveridge Report of December 1942, by Sir William Beveridge, identified five giant evils: want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness. It proposed a system of national insurance, in which workers pay contributions to get benefits.
Clement Attlee was prime minister from 1945 to 1951. His Labour government passed the National Insurance Act of 1946.
Britain's National Health Service (NHS) was founded on 5 July 1948 by Aneurin Bevan, the minister of health, and provided free treatment at the point of use.
Attlee's government also nationalised the Bank of England (1946), coal (1947) and the railways (1948).
The Education Act of 1944 made secondary education free, and universities grew in the 1960s.
Other Western European states built their own welfare systems, often from older traditions. Welfare was accepted by parties of left and right, so it grew steadily.
France's social security system was created by ordinances of October 1945. It combined health insurance, family allowances and pensions for workers.

West Germany's welfare system was closely tied to the social market economy. Social insurance dates from Bismarck's laws of the 1880s and was revived, and it provided compulsory insurance funded by employers and employees.

The Scandinavian countries developed universal welfare systems, meaning benefits for all citizens. In Sweden, Social Democratic governments from the 1930s to the 1970s combined social security with active labour market policies.
Christian Democratic governments in West Germany, Italy and Belgium also supported social insurance, which showed that the welfare state was favoured by parties of both left and right.
Welfare spending rose steadily across Western Europe in the 1950s and 1960s, and it became a permanent feature of the political consensus.
The boom had many causes, and some things also slowed it. Group the factors by type, such as state action, foreign aid and trade, and labour and energy, then judge which mattered most.

Helped, investment and labour: high investment in industry, the move of workers from farms into factories in Italy, France and West Germany, and the supply of labour from refugees and later guest workers.
Helped, energy and technology: access to cheap oil, which kept factory costs low, and the catching up with American technology and management methods.
Helped, trade and aid: Marshall Aid, freer trade and growing export markets, because exports paid for imports and gave factories steady demand.
Helped, state action: governments accepted responsibility for full employment, using the ideas of John Maynard Keynes to manage demand, and political stability supported long-term investment.
Helped, war: the Korean War boom of 1950–53 raised demand for European exports of steel and machinery.
Hindered, early: war damage, which cut output, and the shortage of dollars in the late 1940s, and the cost of rearmament and Cold War defence spending.
Hindered, Britain: weak productivity and frequent strikes, and balance-of-payments crises that led governments to alternate between expansion and restraint, known as stop-go policies.
Hindered, late 1960s: inflation and pressure on currencies as wages rose, and Vietnam War spending and American deficits, which weakened the dollar.
The boom of 1945–1973 is judged as the most prosperous period in Western Europe's modern history, but its causes and its end are debated. Weigh achievements against limits.
Achievements: unprecedented growth, rising living standards, full employment in many countries, welfare provision, the spread of home ownership and a large expansion of education.
Limits: dependence on cheap oil and on the dollar-based system, inflation in the late 1960s, uneven growth (Britain, southern Italy) and the difficult position of migrants.

The Bretton Woods system broke down after US president Richard Nixon suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold on 15 August 1971, and by early 1973 currencies were floating (their values set by the market).
Western Europe's growth rate between 1950 and 1973 was far higher than in any earlier period, but it slowed sharply after 1973.
Historians disagree on how far Marshall Aid caused recovery. Some stress American aid and pressure for cooperation, while Milward and others stress domestic policy and economic structure.
Contemporaries saw the boom as the result of good management. Later historians stress that it was partly a catching-up with the American economy that could not continue indefinitely.

The oil crisis struck an economy that had grown rapidly for almost thirty years on cheap energy and stable exchange rates. To judge how much damage the shock did, you need to know what was already shaky before October 1973.

From 1945 to 1973 Western Europe enjoyed a post-war boom of rapid growth, full employment, Marshall Aid (American money for rebuilding), free trade and a growing welfare state. People came to expect that prosperity would simply continue.

Keynesian economics was the guiding idea: governments should manage demand, by spending more or cutting taxes, to keep employment high. In Britain it produced a post-war 'consensus', meaning both main parties accepted full employment and the welfare state.

Western European oil consumption had risen sharply since the 1950s, and most imported oil came from the Middle East. Oil became the main energy source in the 1950s and 1960s, supplying around half or more of Western Europe's energy by 1973.
Oil was bought cheaply in dollars, at about three dollars a barrel in 1973. Because economies were built around cheap oil, any large price rise would hit every importing country.

The Bretton Woods system fixed exchange rates, so that currencies kept a stable value against the dollar. It collapsed in 1971–73, when the USA ended dollar convertibility to gold in August 1971, and currency values became less predictable.
Inflation, a general rise in prices, had begun to rise in the late 1960s. This is why many historians argue the boom was already weakening before the oil shock.
The oil shock was a political act as much as an economic one. Arab oil producers had grievances over prices and over land Israel held, and in 1973 they found a way to turn oil into a weapon.
Israel was created in 1948, and the Arab–Israeli conflict that followed shaped Middle East politics for decades.

In the Six-Day War of June 1967 Israel occupied Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights. Arab states wanted this land back, so Israeli withdrawal from the occupied territories became the producers' main political demand.
OPEC (the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) was formed in 1960 and includes producers of all regions. Its Arab members had long sought higher prices for their oil.
OAPEC (the Organisation of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries) was formed in 1968 and includes Arab members only, so it could act on Arab political aims such as the occupied territories.
An 'oil shock' means a sudden, large rise in the price of oil that hits the economies importing it. The crisis of 1973 was the first of two such shocks.
On 6 October 1973 the Arab–Israeli conflict turned into open war. Within two weeks the oil producers had used the war as the occasion to raise prices and cut supply.
The Yom Kippur War began on 6 October 1973 when Egypt and Syria attacked Israel. It was the trigger for the oil crisis.
The USA resupplied Israel with arms during the war. This led the Arab states to use oil as a weapon against supporters of Israel.

On 16 October 1973 OPEC's Gulf members raised the posted price (the official price set by the producers) by about 70 per cent. This rise affected every importing country, not just those later singled out.

On 17 October OAPEC announced output cuts of 5 per cent a month, to continue until Israel withdrew from the occupied territories. Cutting supply pushed prices up further because buyers competed for less oil.
The embargo was aimed at particular countries, while the price rise hit everyone. Together they ended the era of cheap oil.
An embargo is a ban on supplying particular countries. One was placed on oil exports to the USA from 19–20 October 1973 and on the Netherlands from 21 October, as supporters of Israel.
The Netherlands was targeted because its government supported Israel and because Rotterdam was Europe's main oil port, so cutting it off hurt Europe's whole supply network.
The Yom Kippur War ended with a ceasefire in late October 1973, following UN Security Council Resolution 338 of 22 October. Western governments then reassessed their dependence on imported energy.
The price was raised again at the end of 1973. Taken with the October rise, this meant that by early 1974 oil cost about four times its pre-war price, so prices roughly quadrupled.
The embargo was lifted in March 1974, but the new higher prices stayed in place. This is why the economic damage outlasted the political crisis.
Governments and households reacted to shortages and soaring prices by using less fuel. The measures were visible and are easy to illustrate with named examples.
Car-free Sundays were introduced in the Netherlands and West Germany in the winter of 1973–74, so that private motoring, a big user of petrol, was cut.
Governments reduced speed limits, because cars burn less fuel at lower speeds, and asked households to turn down their heating.
The Netherlands also issued ration coupons for petrol, so rationing is a Dutch example.

In Britain, Edward Heath's government introduced a three-day working week for industry from January to March 1974. A miners' overtime ban and dispute added to the power shortage, which cut electricity supplies.
Higher oil prices fed through the whole economy. Western Europe faced rising prices and falling output at the same time, a combination that its economic thinking had not prepared it for.
Inflation rose sharply, because oil is used in transport, heating and manufacturing, so higher energy costs pushed up the price of almost everything.
Industrial production fell and unemployment rose from the low levels of the 1960s, with the sharpest increases in heavy industry.
The balance of payments of oil-importing states went into deficit. That means they paid out more for imports than they earned from exports, because they now had to pay far more for oil.
The Arab producers gained huge revenues, known as petrodollars (oil income in dollars), which were recycled through Western banks.
Stagflation is the combination of stagnation (no growth, falling output and rising unemployment) with rising prices. It is different from an ordinary recession and from inflation on its own.
Conventional Keynesian policies struggled with stagflation. Boosting demand to cut unemployment would push prices up further, but cutting demand to reduce inflation would deepen unemployment.
A second shock in 1979 meant the first was not a one-off. Together they produced the long recession and unemployment of the early 1980s.
The Iranian revolution of 1979 caused the second oil shock, which is different from the first shock of 1973–74 that followed the Yom Kippur War. Oil prices roughly doubled between 1978 and 1980.
The second shock pushed many economies back into a second recession in 1980–82, just as they were recovering from the first.
Unemployment across the EEC rose from low levels in the early 1970s to above 10 per cent by the mid-1980s. Spain and Ireland suffered much higher rates.
The rise was worst in heavy industry and in the north of Britain, Scotland and Wales, where coal, steel and shipbuilding were concentrated. British unemployment reached about three million in 1982.
Riots in English cities in 1981, including Brixton and Toxteth, came during this period of recession.
Rising unemployment also strained the welfare state, because more people needed benefits while fewer paid taxes.
Recession and costly energy exposed industries that could no longer compete. The result was deindustrialisation, the long-term decline of manufacturing and heavy industry and the jobs it provided.
Britain's steel, coal and shipbuilding industries declined sharply, and the loss of these jobs changed the regional economies of the north and Scotland.
Older industries such as coal, steel and shipbuilding were cut back across Europe, because demand fell and competitors elsewhere produced more cheaply.
The EEC introduced steel quotas in 1980, known as the Davignon Plan after Étienne Davignon, the commissioner for industry. Quotas limited how much steel each producer could make.
West Germany contrasts with Britain: its industry moved up-market into machinery and cars, which kept it competitive.
The shock made energy independence a political goal. Governments looked for new sources and for ways to use less oil.
France announced a nuclear power programme in 1974, the Messmer Plan, named after Prime Minister Pierre Messmer. By the late 1980s nuclear power gave about 70 per cent of French electricity.
North Sea oil began to flow in the mid-1970s. By about 1980 Britain was self-sufficient in oil and Norway a major exporter, which cushioned both economies against the second oil shock.
The International Energy Agency was set up in 1974 under the OECD to coordinate oil stocks and policy among importing states.
Energy conservation and the development of coal and nuclear power were promoted as ways to reduce dependence on imported oil.
The crisis ended the long boom, but historians disagree about how much of that was the oil shock's doing. Examiners ask how lasting the impact was.
The crisis ended the long boom and exposed the dependence of Western prosperity on cheap energy. It shifted political attention from growth to inflation and unemployment.
It strengthened the case for the EEC to act together, leading to the European Monetary System in 1979.
Contemporaries blamed the Arab embargo and OPEC for the economic troubles.

Many economists later argued that inflation, the end of Bretton Woods and falling productivity were already weakening the boom, so the oil shock hastened the end of the boom rather than solely causing it.
The embargo also gave oil-producing states a new role in world politics and led Western states to look for energy independence, through nuclear power, North Sea oil and conservation.
Its impact was lasting in some ways, as energy policy changed. Unemployment and industrial decline also remained long after the embargo ended.
Thatcher's policies make sense only against a few ideas. These terms are used throughout the rest of the notes, so each is defined as it applies to this period.
Capitalism is an economic system based on private ownership, competitive markets and profit. Thatcher's aim was to extend it, through privatisation and free markets.

The welfare state is state provision of health, pensions, benefits and education. It was strained by unemployment and cost after 1973. Thatcher cut the growth in spending but did not dismantle its core.
Monetarism is the policy of controlling inflation by controlling the money supply, the amount of money circulating in the economy. It is the opposite of Keynesianism, which manages demand.
Privatisation means selling state-owned firms to private owners. Deregulation is different: it means removing rules, as in the City of London in 1986.
Trade union laws were the Employment Acts of 1980 and 1982 and the Trade Union Act of 1984, which limited union power.

Thatcher led the Conservative Party from 1975 and was Prime Minister from 1979 to 1990, pursuing monetarist and free-market policies. She was a direct participant in almost every episode that follows, as well as someone shaped by the failures of the 1970s.

She was born in Grantham on 13 October 1925, the daughter of a grocer, Alfred Roberts. She studied chemistry at Somerville College, Oxford, and was called to the bar in 1953, so she was a barrister, before becoming MP for Finchley in 1959.
She was Secretary of State for Education and Science in Edward Heath's government from 1970 to 1974.
