Heath lost two general elections in 1974, in February and October, and her break with him followed. Keith Joseph, whose policy ideas lay behind monetarism, founded the Centre for Policy Studies in 1974 with her.
On 11 February 1975 she was elected Conservative leader. Heath was knocked out in the first ballot, and she then won the second ballot against Willie Whitelaw.
She became Prime Minister on 4 May 1979, defeating James Callaghan's Labour government after the 1978–79 'winter of discontent'. Note that she was leader from 1975 but Prime Minister only from 1979.
She won the general elections of 1979, 1983 and 1987. Her term of about eleven and a half years was the longest continuous premiership of the twentieth century.
She was shaped by Heath's failure, the crisis of the 1970s and Joseph's ideas, and shaped events as Prime Minister in every episode that follows.
Thatcher's central aim was to defeat inflation, even at the cost of unemployment. Her government used monetarism to do so, and the results were mixed.

Her Chancellor, Geoffrey Howe, applied monetarism, an approach associated with Milton Friedman. The Medium Term Financial Strategy (1980) was the plan for cutting inflation by controlling the money supply.
Howe's 1981 budget raised taxes in the middle of a recession, which shocked many experts: 364 economists signed a letter of protest.
Inflation fell from double figures in 1980, about 18 per cent, to under 5 per cent by 1983, so the main aim was achieved.
Unemployment passed three million in 1982, and the early 1980s recession hit manufacturing in the north, Scotland and Wales hardest, with riots in English cities in 1981.
Under her government, fighting inflation replaced full employment as the main priority, which marked a break with the post-war consensus.
Thatcher wanted a freer market economy with less state ownership and weaker unions. Her government passed a series of measures between 1979 and 1986 to achieve it.
Exchange controls, which had limited moving money abroad, were abolished in October 1979.
The Housing Act 1980 gave council tenants a right to buy their homes, spreading property ownership.
Privatisation sold state assets to private owners: British Telecom in 1984, British Gas in 1986 and British Airways in 1987.
The City of London was deregulated in October 1986, the 'Big Bang', when old rules were removed from financial trading. This was deregulation, not privatisation.
The Employment Act 1980 limited secondary picketing (pickets at a workplace not involved in the dispute) and restricted the closed shop (a workplace where all workers must join the union).
The Employment Act 1982 added further limits on the closed shop and made unions liable for damages, so unions risked heavy costs when strikes broke the law.
The Trade Union Act 1984 required secret ballots for strikes and for union executives.
The Falklands War gave Thatcher a victory at a time when her policies had made her unpopular. It helped to transform her political position.
Argentina invaded the Falklands on 2 April 1982. Thatcher sent a task force, and Argentine forces surrendered on 14 June 1982.
She was the Prime Minister who sent the task force, not a combatant, so describe her as the leader who took the decision.
Her popularity recovered, and she won a landslide in the general election of June 1983.
The strike was the most severe test of Thatcher's trade union policy. It followed the pit closure plans of the National Coal Board and ended in defeat for the miners.
The strike began in March 1984 with the announcement of the closure of the Cortonwood pit, when the National Coal Board chairman, Ian MacGregor, announced a closure programme.
Arthur Scargill's National Union of Mineworkers called the strike without holding a national ballot.
The government had built up coal stocks, so power supplies could continue, and it used mass policing. Violent clashes occurred at Orgreave on 18 June 1984.
The miners returned to work in March 1985 without a settlement. The defeat weakened the union movement and speeded up the closure of coal mines.
Abroad, Thatcher combined a close alliance with the USA with a cautious readiness to deal with the Soviet Union. She also signed a significant agreement on Northern Ireland.
Her relationship with President Ronald Reagan was close, and the two leaders coordinated the Western response to Soviet policy in the early 1980s.
US cruise missiles were deployed at Greenham Common from 1983, and US aircraft flew from British bases in the raid on Libya in April 1986. Both showed her support for Reagan.
A Soviet newspaper nicknamed her the 'Iron Lady' in January 1976. She later adopted the name with some pride.
She met Mikhail Gorbachev at Chequers in December 1984, before he took power, and said he was a man she could 'do business with'. She then helped to persuade Reagan that he was sincere.
She signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement with the Taoiseach, Garret FitzGerald, at Hillsborough on 15 November 1985. It gave the Irish government a consultative role in Northern Ireland.
Thatcher backed the EEC as a market but resisted its move towards political union. Her attitude shows in a run of dated episodes.
She negotiated the British budget rebate at the Fontainebleau European Council in June 1984, which reduced Britain's net contribution to the EEC budget. This showed her hard line on money.
She approved the Single European Act in 1986 because it supported the single market, a free market in goods and services across the EEC.
In her Bruges speech of 20 September 1988 she criticised plans for a federal Europe while supporting a single market.
She opposed the Social Charter and economic and monetary union.
Britain joined the Exchange Rate Mechanism only in October 1990, shortly before her fall.
Thatcher won three elections but was removed by her own party. Europe and the poll tax were the underlying causes.
The poll tax (Community Charge), a flat-rate local tax, was introduced in Scotland in 1989 and in England and Wales in 1990. It became a major cause of the challenge to her.
Geoffrey Howe resigned on 1 November 1990 over her European policy, and he made a critical speech on 13 November.
Michael Heseltine then challenged her for the leadership. She won the first ballot on 20 November 1990 but not by the margin required, so the contest was not settled.
She announced her resignation on 22 November 1990 and left office on 28 November, when John Major succeeded her.
Judgements on Thatcher were sharply divided at the time and remain so. You need both sides, as examiners reward a balanced verdict.
Admirers praised her resolve and credited her with ending the 'British disease' of industrial conflict and decline.
Critics pointed to unemployment passing three million in 1982, deindustrialisation, social division and the North–South gap. They also pointed to the poll tax.

Historians debate whether her policies were a decisive break with the post-war settlement or the continuation of trends already under way, such as the oil shock, the decline of heavy industry and the rise of finance.
'Thatcherism', her combination of free markets, privatisation and union reform, is seen as a lasting legacy.
The record of the Western economies after 1973 is judged on whether they restored growth and whether the costs of adjustment were fair. Thatcher's record is judged the same way.

Achievements: inflation was reduced, trade union power was curbed, privatisation and a more flexible labour market in Britain followed, and Britain's profile rose in Europe and with the USA, and the single market deepened in the EEC after 1986.
Limits: mass unemployment, the decline of manufacturing and mining communities, regional inequality, the poll tax and her fall in 1990.
Supporters of Thatcher say she reversed Britain's relative decline, while critics say the decline of manufacturing was a heavy and lasting cost.

The oil shock hastened the end of the boom but did not solely cause it, since inflation and industrial change were already under way. Its energy impact was lasting, but unemployment and industrial decline remained.

Contemporaries blamed the embargo and OPEC, while later economists stress earlier weaknesses. Contemporaries saw Thatcher as either resolute or divisive, while historians ask whether she broke with or continued earlier trends.

After 1945 Europe split into a capitalist west and a communist east, and the two sides competed over whose economic system could deliver more. To follow the problems of the communist economies, you first need the system they were built on and the dates of the leaders who ran it.
Communism, as used here, means one-party rule combined with a publicly owned, centrally planned economy, in which the state rather than private owners decides what is made and at what price.

Capitalism rests on private ownership, markets and profit, whereas communism rests on public ownership and state direction. This difference made the economy a central battleground of the Cold War, because each side claimed to offer people a better life.
After 1945 the Soviet Union dominated eastern Europe, and communist parties took power there in 1945–48. Sovietisation means remodelling these states, their economies included, on the Soviet pattern.

The Marshall Plan (1947) offered American aid to rebuild Europe and deepened the division of the continent, because the Soviet bloc refused Marshall aid and set up its own economic arrangements instead.

Stalin died in March 1953. Khrushchev then led the Soviet Communist Party from 1953 until he was removed in October 1964, Brezhnev led from 1964 to 1982 (he died in November 1982), and Gorbachev became General Secretary on 11 March 1985.

Communist economies were run by central planning, in which the state set production targets and allocated resources instead of leaving decisions to markets. The system was built in the Soviet Union first, at enormous human cost.

Gosplan, the Soviet state planning committee (set up in 1921), drew up five-year plans that set output targets for industry, agriculture and trade. Prices were also set by the state, so there were no market signals telling factories what people wanted.
Priority was given to heavy industry (steel, coal, machinery and armaments), while consumer goods and housing were neglected, because the plans aimed to build industrial and military strength first.
Stalin's first Five-Year Plan began in 1928 and built heavy industry and cities at great human cost.

Collectivisation, the forcing of peasants to give up private farms and work in large state-controlled farms, was carried through in the Soviet Union in the early 1930s. Together with the famine of 1932–33 it killed millions, though estimates of the total vary widely.

Output was driven by pressing workers to exceed their norms (set work quotas). The Stakhanovite campaigns, which began in the Soviet Union in 1935 and were named after the miner Alexei Stakhanov, held up record-breaking workers as models, and they were copied in eastern Europe from the late 1940s.
Once communist parties held power in eastern Europe, the Soviet economic model was copied there. This tied the satellite economies, the states under Soviet influence, closely to Moscow.

In eastern Europe, industry, banks and large estates were nationalised (taken into state ownership) in 1945–48. Plans on the Soviet pattern followed from about 1949–51, for example Poland's Six-Year Plan (1950–55) and East Germany's first Five-Year Plan (1951).

Showpiece new industrial towns were built to symbolise the new system, such as Nowa Huta, a steel town and combine near Kraków begun in 1949, and Stalinstadt in East Germany, a steel town founded in 1950 and renamed Eisenhüttenstadt in 1961.

Collectivisation was imposed on most eastern European farms after 1945, and was pressed hard in Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria, Romania and East Germany. Poland was the major exception, because most Polish farms stayed in private hands.

Comecon, founded in January 1949 in Moscow (the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance), coordinated trade and planning among the Soviet bloc. It is usually seen as a Soviet answer to the Marshall Plan.

Comecon trade used a non-convertible accounting currency, one that could not be exchanged for Western money (bilateral clearing at first, then the transferable rouble from 1963), at prices set by planners.
In practice the Soviet Union supplied cheap raw materials and energy and took manufactured goods from the satellites. This is why the east European economies became dependent on Soviet supplies.

In the early years the Soviet Union also took resources out of the region through reparations (payments in goods) and Soviet-controlled joint companies in Hungary, Romania and East Germany in the late 1940s and early 1950s. In 1949–53 eastern Europe's trade shifted from the West to the Soviet Union.

Central planning produced chronic shortages of goods, poor quality and slow adoption of new technology. Each problem had a cause in how the system rewarded managers, and together they undermined the economies over time.

Planners set targets in gross output terms, meaning the total quantity produced. This encouraged factories to produce heavy and low-quality goods rather than goods that consumers wanted, because quantity was what earned the reward.

Prices were fixed by the state rather than by supply and demand, so shortages in shops coexisted with surpluses of unwanted goods in warehouses. Nothing in the system adjusted production to what people would actually buy.
Shortages of consumer goods, meat, housing and cars were common, and long queues and black markets (illegal trade in scarce goods) were a permanent feature of daily life.

Innovation was slow because managers had little incentive to adopt new technology, and the state discouraged risk-taking. A manager who changed methods risked missing the target and gained little if the change worked.

Housing was built in standard blocks and was often overcrowded. In East Germany buyers had to wait many years for a car such as the Trabant, which shows how little the system answered consumer demand.

Beyond the daily shortages, the system had deeper structural weaknesses. Agriculture stayed unproductive, industry damaged the environment, growth depended on adding more inputs, and military spending drained resources.

Soviet agriculture remained unproductive, with a large share of the labour force employed on farms. The Soviet Union bought large amounts of Western grain after the poor harvest of 1963 and again in the 1970s.
Environmental damage was severe. Industrial regions such as northern Bohemia and Upper Silesia were polluted by heavy industry, and in the Aral Sea basin irrigation for cotton shrank the Aral Sea.

The economies relied on extensive growth, which comes from adding more labour and raw materials, and could not move to intensive growth, which comes from better technology and productivity. Once the supply of new workers dried up in the 1970s, growth slowed.

The arms race and the cost of maintaining an army and military industries absorbed a large share of national output, especially in the Soviet Union. This was at the cost of consumers and investment, because resources spent on weapons could not be spent on housing or modern factories.
Soviet leaders knew the system performed badly, and tried to improve it without giving up central control. Both main reforms were partial, and neither lasted in its original form.

Khrushchev's reform of 1957 replaced industrial ministries with regional economic councils (sovnarkhozy), aiming to bring decisions closer to local industry. Ministries were restored after he fell in October 1964, so the reform was reversed.

Khrushchev also tried to lift the production of consumer goods and housing. He launched a mass housebuilding drive from the mid-1950s and in 1957 pledged to overtake the USA in output of goods such as meat, milk and butter, but this was not achieved.

Alexei Kosygin, Soviet prime minister from 1964 to 1980, announced his economic reform in September 1965. It gave enterprises more control over profits and pricing, but central control of investment stayed in place, and the reform also restored the ministries.

By the late 1960s Kosygin's reform had been watered down and it faded. A common explanation is that ministries and the party feared losing control, and the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968 also discouraged further experiment.
Some bloc states went further than the Soviet Union in introducing market elements. Even so, none gave up one-party rule, which limited how far reform could go.

Czechoslovakia's New Economic Model of the mid-1960s was designed by the economist Ota Šik and proposed market mechanisms. The Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968 ended it, and also warned other bloc states against going too far.

Hungary's New Economic Mechanism came into force on 1 January 1968. It allowed limited market prices and private enterprise in services, and it survived in part into the 1980s, which made it a model of partial reform.

Hungary's policy under János Kádár, who led the country from 1956 to 1988, was nicknamed goulash communism. It tolerated small private plots and enterprises and gave citizens more consumer goods than in other bloc states.
Hungary's reforms gave managers more freedom and allowed a second economy, private work done after hours alongside the official one, but the state kept control of the main industries and prices.

Yugoslavia under Tito was expelled from the Cominform (the Soviet-led communist bloc organisation) in 1948. It left Soviet alignment and was never a full member of Comecon. From 1950 it developed worker self-management and market socialism, and it allowed its citizens to travel and work abroad.
Yugoslavia's system had costs. It ran up heavy foreign debt and suffered high inflation in the 1980s.

Reforms stalled because they threatened the control of the party and the ministries. Under Leonid Brezhnev, who led from 1964 to 1982, the Soviet leadership avoided reform and the economy grew more slowly.
Fear of losing party and ministry control is a common explanation of why reforms stopped, and the 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia served as a warning of the risks of loosening central control.

Growth in the Soviet economy slowed in the 1970s, as the labour force grew more slowly and the rise in productivity fell. The period became known as stagnation (zastoi), a label applied later, especially by Gorbachev.

The Soviet Union earned large hard currency (convertible Western money) revenues from oil and gas exports after the oil price rises of 1973 and 1979. This let the leadership buy Western grain and technology and postpone reform.
When oil prices fell sharply in 1986 this support vanished, so the economy's weaknesses were exposed. Living standards for most people had improved only slowly during the 1970s.

Under Brezhnev the Soviet Union reached rough nuclear parity with the USA and increased its military spending, which took a large share of national output at the cost of consumer goods and investment. Soviet forces entered Afghanistan in December 1979, which added to the burden.
Rewarding party loyalty rather than performance led to corruption and an ageing leadership.
Consumers experienced shortages of basic goods. The black market, bribery and blat, the use of personal contacts and favours to obtain scarce goods and services, became part of ordinary life.

Poland's attempts to raise living standards by borrowing from the West ended in debt and repeated waves of protest. Three price-rise crises, in December 1970, June 1976 and summer 1980, mark the story.

Price rises announced in December 1970 led to riots and strikes in Gdańsk, Gdynia and Szczecin on the Baltic coast. They brought the fall of Władysław Gomułka, who was replaced by Edward Gierek on 20 December 1970.
Gierek borrowed heavily from Western banks to finance imports of machinery and consumer goods. These were intended to modernise industry and win public support.
Price rises announced on 24 June 1976 led to strikes and riots, notably at Radom and Ursus. The government withdrew the increases the next day.

Gierek's strategy failed for several reasons. The new factories produced goods that were not competitive in Western markets, so export earnings did not pay off the loans, and agricultural output suffered from a lack of investment.
Poland's debt to the West was over 20 billion dollars by 1980. By then it had become unsustainable, the economy had shrunk and shops were bare of meat.

Price rises announced on 1 July 1980 set off strikes that spread to Gdańsk in August. The shipyard strike there began in mid-August, the Gdańsk Agreement was signed on 31 August 1980, and Solidarity, led by Lech Wałęsa, was founded in September 1980.
Poland's economic crisis was a cause of Solidarity, and the economic collapse in the 1980s helped to bring the communists to the Round Table talks with Solidarity, which began in February 1989.
Mikhail Gorbachev tried to rescue the Soviet economy by restructuring it. His reforms weakened the old system without putting a working new one in its place.

Gorbachev launched perestroika, meaning restructuring of the economy, in 1986 (27th Party Congress, February–March 1986). It coincided with falling oil prices in 1986, which cut the Soviet Union's hard currency earnings.
The Law on State Enterprise, passed in 1987 and in force from 1988, gave factories more freedom. The 1988 law on cooperatives allowed private business.
These laws weakened central control without creating a functioning market. Planners no longer directed supply reliably, but prices and competition did not yet replace them.
By 1989–90 the Soviet economy was suffering from shortages, a growing budget deficit and falling output, and rationing (coupons) for basic goods appeared in several cities.

By the late 1980s the gap between the communist states and the West was plain to see, and several bloc economies survived only on Western credit or severe austerity. Their end left problems for the successor states.
Romania under Nicolae Ceaușescu announced in 1989 that its foreign debt was repaid. The cost was cuts in imports and in food, heating and electricity for the population, who suffered shortages.

East Germany was the strongest industrial economy in the bloc by common assessment, but it depended on West German credit and trade concessions, including a billion-mark loan arranged in 1983, with a second in 1984.
The German economic, monetary and social union of 1 July 1990 exposed East German industries to competition and led to mass closures.

The gap with the West was visible by 1989. East German and Czechoslovak citizens could see how much better West Germans and Austrians lived on television and through travel, and living standards in the Soviet Union lagged far behind.
The end of the Soviet bloc's economic system left a legacy of obsolete industry, environmental damage and unemployment that the successor states had to address.
The bloc was not uniform, and examiners reward comparison of different states. Each started from a different level of development and handled planning differently.
Czechoslovakia was the most industrialised state in the region before the war, because the Czech lands were the industrial heartland of the Habsburg Empire and of interwar Czechoslovakia.
Czechoslovakia's living standards were among the highest in the bloc in the 1950s, but it stagnated under rigid planning in the 1960s and was the home of Ota Šik's reform.

East Germany was among the most advanced economies in the bloc and the showcase of socialism, but it lost skilled workers to the West until the Berlin Wall was built in August 1961, after millions of people had left since 1949.

Bulgaria and Romania were still largely agricultural in 1945 and were industrialised rapidly. Romania developed heavy industry, oil and chemicals and pursued an independent foreign policy under Ceaușescu.
Ceaușescu's Romania exported food and fuel to pay its debts and rationed food and electricity in the 1980s. His systematisation programme, announced in 1988, planned to demolish villages.

Hungary's partial reforms and Poland's private farming made those states more flexible than the Soviet Union. However, their dependence on Western credit made them vulnerable when interest rates and prices rose around 1980.
Communist economies achieved rapid industrialisation and social welfare, but they failed to sustain growth or satisfy consumers. Judgement answers need both sides and a clear verdict.
Achievements: rapid industrialisation, near-universal literacy, free health care and education, full employment including high employment of women, and cheap housing and basic goods.
Limits: chronic shortages, low quality, poor housing, environmental damage and a standard of living that fell further behind the West.
Eastern Europe's communist states did expand education, cheap housing and health care, but their living standards fell behind West European levels by the 1970s.
Contemporary Western accounts often stressed the failure of the planned economy, while Soviet and bloc officials emphasised the achievements of industrialisation and social welfare.
Later historians stress both the system's real successes in mobilising resources and the structural limits that made it impossible to sustain growth without political reform.
The final judgement of historians is that the planned economy could build basic industry, but could not adapt to the information-based economies of the 1980s.
Reform within the bloc was partial, because leaders would not give up party control. Economic failure was one cause, not the only cause, of the events of 1989.

To understand the changes after 1945, you need to know where families and women started from. Europe was damaged and short of homes, but its economy was about to grow fast, and that growth paid for most of what follows.
The Second World War left Europe devastated, with serious housing shortages and millions of men returning from military service, so families had to be rebuilt and homes found for them.

Western Europe's post-war economic growth is what paid for rising incomes, welfare states (governments providing benefits such as family allowances) and the consumer goods that filled homes in the 1950s and 1960s.
Before 1945 most European women had few legal rights in marriage and were paid less than men, which is why later reforms of family law and pay mattered so much.

Women had gained the vote only recently in many countries: French women voted for the first time in 1945, the right having been granted by ordinance in 1944, and Italian women voted in 1946, the right having been granted in 1945.

De Beauvoir was a French philosopher and writer whose 1949 study The Second Sex became a founding text of modern feminism. Feminism is the argument for equal rights and opportunities for women, and a challenge to the roles society assigns them.

She was born in Paris on 9 January 1908 and died there on 14 April 1986. She was a philosopher and writer and the partner of Jean-Paul Sartre, with whom she shared a close intellectual life for decades.

She passed the highly competitive agrégation (the French state examination for teaching posts) in philosophy in 1929, placed second to Sartre and, at 21, the youngest candidate to have passed. She then taught for some years.

The Second Sex (Le Deuxième Sexe) was published in two volumes in 1949 and translated into English in 1953. It argued that women were treated as the 'Other' while men were taken as the norm by a male-centred society.
She argued that women's inferior position was created by history, law, religion and education, not by biology, so it could be changed, and that economic independence was the key for women.
Her best-known line, from The Second Sex, is "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman." It separated biological sex from the roles society gives women, which is the idea behind the word gender.

She lived through the Second World War and the Occupation of Paris as a witness. Later she became a participant in the feminist movement of the 1970s, joining the Women's Liberation Movement (MLF) in France and campaigning for the legalisation of abortion.

In April 1971 she signed the Manifesto of the 343, in which women declared that they had had abortions, and she co-founded the pro-choice group Choisir with the lawyer Gisèle Halimi. She did not sponsor the 1975 abortion law.

Contemporaries were divided. The Vatican placed her works, including The Second Sex, on the Index of Forbidden Books in 1956, and male intellectuals on both left and right attacked or mocked it, yet younger women read it as a guide to their own position.

Historians now treat the book as a foundational text of second-wave feminism. Later critics questioned its assumption of a universal experience of womanhood, pointing to differences of class and race.
After 1945 marriage and childbirth rose, and a domestic model of family life became the norm in much of Western Europe. Governments, churches and the media all backed it.

The baby boom (a sharp rise in the number of births) in Western Europe ran from about 1946 to the mid-1960s, with birth rates higher than in the 1930s. Marriage was also earlier and more common than before the war.
The nuclear family, meaning two parents and their children, with a male breadwinner and a housewife-mother, became the ideal.
Housing shortages after the war meant that many young couples lived with relatives, so public housing programmes were used to increase family accommodation.
Welfare states paid family allowances (regular payments to families with children).
The emphasis on the housewife and mother reflected a wish to restore stability after the war, so conservative parties and churches promoted the family as the basis of society.
Cinema, magazines, television and advertising presented the ideal of the happy housewife surrounded by labour-saving appliances, which reinforced the idea that her place was in the home.

Inside marriage, women were legally unequal. In France a law of 13 July 1965 allowed a married woman to work and open a bank account without her husband's permission, which shows that she needed it until then.
In West Germany the marriage law kept a clause until 1977 that a wife was to run the household and could work only if that was compatible with her family duties.
From the 1950s more married women took paid jobs, but they were concentrated in low-paid work. Equal pay laws were the first real attempt to close the gap.
The number of married women in paid employment rose steadily from the 1950s, especially in service work and clerical (office) work, because these sectors grew as economies expanded.
Women's work was mostly in low-paid jobs such as teaching, nursing, secretarial work and factory assembly, and women were paid less than men and barred from many professions.
Article 119 of the Treaty of Rome (1957) required equal pay for equal work for men and women, but at first it was weakly enforced.

In the second Defrenne case (Defrenne v Sabena), decided on 8 April 1976, the European Court of Justice ruled that Article 119 had direct effect, which means individual women could rely on it in their national courts.
In Britain the Equal Pay Act 1970 came into force on 29 December 1975, alongside the Sex Discrimination Act 1975.

Second-wave feminism of the 1960s and 1970s demanded equal pay, nurseries and an end to confinement in the home. A central demand was control over childbearing, and the pill and new laws made this possible. This is different from first-wave feminism, which campaigned mainly for the vote.
The contraceptive pill was approved in the USA in 1960 and became widely used in Western Europe in the 1960s, so women could now plan whether and when to have children.
France legalised contraception with the Neuwirth Law of December 1967, named after Lucien Neuwirth. Do not confuse it with the Veil Law on abortion.
The Veil Law of 17 January 1975 legalised abortion in France within the first ten weeks of pregnancy. It was sponsored by the health minister Simone Veil.

Elsewhere, Britain's Abortion Act of 1967 legalised abortion on medical grounds in England, Scotland and Wales, but not Northern Ireland. Italy legalised abortion in 1978, and West Germany reformed its abortion law in the 1970s.
The Catholic Church opposed contraception and abortion. Pope Paul VI's encyclical (a formal papal letter) Humanae Vitae in 1968 reaffirmed the ban on artificial contraception.

Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963), an American book, helped start second-wave feminism by arguing that confinement to the home left women unfulfilled. The Mouvement de libération des femmes (MLF) was formed in France in 1970.

The Manifesto of the 343, published in Le Nouvel Observateur in April 1971, carried the names of 343 women who declared that they had had abortions, so it called publicly for legalisation. Choisir, a pro-choice group founded in 1971, continued the campaign.

From 1969 divorce became easier in several Western European countries, and family law moved from the husband as head of the household towards equality between spouses. Change came at very different speeds.
The Divorce Reform Act of 1969 in England and Wales took effect in 1971 and made irretrievable breakdown of the marriage the sole ground for divorce.
Italy legalised divorce in December 1970 under the Fortuna-Baslini law. In a referendum on 12 May 1974 voters chose to keep it, with about 59 per cent against repeal.
Italy's family-law reform of 1975 gave spouses equal rights, replacing the idea of the husband as head of household.

West Germany's marriage and family law reform of 1 July 1977 introduced divorce by breakdown instead of fault, so one partner no longer had to be proved guilty. It also dropped the clause that a wife was to run the household.
Later and slower cases include Spain, which legalised divorce in 1981, and Ireland, whose constitution banned it, approved divorce only by a narrow referendum vote in November 1995.
Divorce rates rose across the region in the 1970s, and single-parent households became a growing category.
The rise in divorce and in working mothers led to debate about the future of the family, with conservatives blaming the changes on permissiveness.

Economic growth raised incomes in the 1950s and 1960s. Families could now buy goods once thought luxuries, and this created a consumer society, one built around buying and owning goods, which critics soon attacked.
Households acquired consumer durables (goods that last for years), such as refrigerators, washing machines and televisions. These saved housework and changed daily routines.

Cars became affordable: the Volkswagen Beetle, mass-produced in West Germany from the late 1940s, was a huge success in the 1950s and 1960s, the Citroën 2CV was launched in 1948, the Fiat 500 in 1957 and the Mini in 1959.
Self-service supermarkets spread across Western Europe in the 1960s, and they changed how families shopped and the goods available to them.
Hire purchase (paying for goods in instalments) and consumer credit made it possible for families to buy goods before they could afford them outright.
Advertising and television encouraged consumption. Television spread rapidly in the 1950s and 1960s, becoming the centre of the home and the main form of evening leisure.
Vance Packard in The Hidden Persuaders (1957) argued that advertising manipulated consumers.
John Kenneth Galbraith in The Affluent Society (1958) argued that private affluence went with public squalor, meaning rich households but poor public services.

Herbert Marcuse in One-Dimensional Man (1964) argued that consumer society encouraged conformity and suppressed critical thought. The French Situationists, whose leader Guy Debord wrote The Society of the Spectacle (1967), also attacked the 'spectacle' of consumption.
Higher incomes came with more free time. Together they created mass leisure industries, above all mass tourism to the Mediterranean.
Working hours fell and paid holidays grew. In France paid holiday was two weeks from 1936, a third week was added in 1956 and a fourth in 1969, so workers had more time away from work.

Package holidays (flights, hotel and transfers sold as one price) and charter flights to the Spanish coast (the Costa Brava and Costa del Sol), the Balearic islands, Italy and Greece boomed from the 1960s and brought the Mediterranean within reach of workers from northern Europe.
Club Méditerranée (Club Med), founded in 1950, offered all-inclusive holidays.
Car ownership made domestic holidays and weekend trips possible, and camping and caravanning became popular in Britain and Scandinavia.
Leisure at home and nearby included spectator sport, cinema, television, record-buying and home improvement, which show the rise of mass leisure industries.

In the communist states of Eastern Europe, women's employment and legal equality were promoted by the state, but there was little consumer choice and no free feminist movement. Comparing East and West is a good way to show what these changes meant.
In the East many more women went out to work, backed by state childcare and the expectation that they would work. Communist states promoted equal rights in law.
Domestic responsibilities for housework and childcare remained largely with women, who therefore carried a double burden of paid work and housework.
East Germany offered state nurseries, paid maternity leave and a 'baby year' from 1976. Abortion was legalised there in 1972, and the divorce rate was high.

In the Soviet Union abortion was legalised again in 1955, and women formed a large part of the workforce, including doctors and engineers. Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in June 1963, an achievement, but women still did most of the housework.
There was no independent feminist movement in the East, so the Western movement of the 1960s and 1970s had no equivalent there.

Consumer goods in the East were scarcer and of lower quality, so the consumer society was far less developed than in the West. East German cars such as the Trabant and Wartburg had waiting lists of many years.
East German holidays were organised by the trade union federation in union holiday homes and Baltic resorts, and Black Sea resorts served the Soviet bloc, while travel to the West was restricted.
East Germans could watch West German television, so they were conscious of the gap in goods.
Historians debate whether the changes of the period liberated women and families or extended consumer pressures into private life. Good answers set achievements against limits and give a judgement.
Achievements: legal and employment equality, access to contraception and abortion in many states, easier divorce and more choice in marriage.

Limits: women still bore most domestic work, a pay gap persisted, many women worked in low-paid jobs, and gains were uneven across countries and social classes. In the East there was equality in law but not at home.
Consumerism brought higher living standards and more leisure, but critics argued that it encouraged conformity, debt through credit and pressure to buy, and that it tied family life to paid work.
Contemporaries disagreed: churches and conservatives defended the traditional family, while feminists demanded new rights.
Later historians see the 1960s and 1970s as a turning point, but they stress that the gains were uneven.

To understand why writers mattered so much in this period, you need to know what they were up against. In the communist states writing was a political act, and in the West the Cold War shaped what intellectuals argued about.
Stalin's terror (the 1930s to his death in 1953) filled the Gulag, the Soviet system of labour camps, so the camps were a fact of life that the state did not want discussed.

In 1956 Khrushchev, Stalin's successor, denounced Stalin's crimes in his secret speech. The loosening of controls that followed is called the thaw, and it made the 1962 publication of One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich possible.

Communist states controlled publishing and the press through censorship and the official Writers' Unions, and the KGB (the Soviet secret police) policed dissent, so a writer who criticised the system risked losing the right to publish, prison or exile.
A dissident writer is a writer who openly opposed a communist state's policy or ideology and faced censorship, prison or exile as a result.
The Cold War divided Europe, and Western intellectuals argued fiercely over communism, the USA and colonialism, which is why many Western writers of this period took political sides.

Before 1945 Western Europe was largely Christian in practice, whereas the communist parties in the East were officially atheist, so religion was a matter of habit in the West and of conflict with the state in the East.

Solzhenitsyn was the Soviet novelist whose writing on the Gulag made the camp system known to the world and made him the most famous dissident in the Soviet Union. His own years as a prisoner gave him his subject.
He was born in Kislovodsk on 11 December 1918 and served as an artillery officer (a captain) in the Red Army in the Second World War.
In February 1945 he was arrested at the front for criticising Stalin in private letters to a friend, which shows how far the terror reached, since even private remarks were punished.

He was sentenced to eight years in labour camps and then to internal exile (forced residence inside the USSR) in Kazakhstan from 1953. The exile ended in 1956, so he spent eight years in camps and about three in exile.
In 1954 he was treated for cancer in a hospital in Tashkent and was cured, an episode that lies behind his novel Cancer Ward.
One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich appeared in the Soviet journal Novy Mir in November 1962 with Khrushchev's personal approval, which was possible because of the thaw.

The novel describes a single day of a camp prisoner, Ivan Denisovich Shukhov, in a Stalin-era camp. It brought the camps into Soviet public discussion because it was an officially approved publication.

After Khrushchev fell in October 1964 censorship tightened, so The First Circle and Cancer Ward could be published only abroad, in 1968, and he was expelled from the Soviet Writers' Union in November 1969.
He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1970, but he did not travel to receive it, fearing that he would not be allowed back into the USSR.

Once his official publishing stopped, Solzhenitsyn wrote the book that made him an enemy of the state. Its publication abroad led straight to his expulsion, and he continued to write and speak from exile.
The Gulag Archipelago is non-fiction: a work of testimony, history and reflection on the camp system, drawing on the accounts of many prisoners. Unlike Ivan Denisovich, it was banned in the USSR.
The KGB seized a copy of the manuscript in 1973, and this led him to authorise publication. It appeared in Paris at the end of 1973 and had a major impact in the West.
He was arrested on 12 February 1974 and flown the next day to West Germany, where he was stripped of his citizenship. The expulsion therefore followed the Archipelago, not Ivan Denisovich.
In exile he lived first in West Germany, then in Switzerland, and from 1976 in Vermont in the USA.
In his Harvard commencement address of June 1978 he criticised Western materialism and weakness as well as communism, which disappointed many of his Western admirers.
From Vermont he continued to write The Red Wheel, his multi-volume historical cycle on the Russian Revolution.
He returned to Russia in 1994 and died in Moscow in August 2008.
Solzhenitsyn fits the definition of a dissident writer exactly, and both his contemporaries and later historians judged him in divided ways.

He is a dissident writer because he opposed the Soviet system through his writing, exposing the camps that the state wanted hidden, and he was punished for it with censorship, expulsion from the Writers' Union and exile.
The Soviet authorities called him a traitor and expelled him, while many Western intellectuals admired him, though some later disliked his nationalist and religious views.

Historians regard his work as central to Western understanding of Soviet terror, because he gave the West evidence from the inside, although some question the reliability of his testimony and his later political stances.
In Russia after 1994 his reputation was divided between admirers who saw him as the nation's conscience and critics who disliked his Russian nationalism and his religious conservatism.

Beauvoir (1908-1986) is best known for The Second Sex, but she was also a novelist, memoirist and critic who questioned Western society and its values from the Paris intellectual left. Here she is the writer and critic.
In 1945 she joined Jean-Paul Sartre in founding the review Les Temps modernes, which became the leading journal of left-wing intellectuals in France.
Her novel The Mandarins portrayed the Parisian intellectual left after the Second World War and won the Prix Goncourt, a leading French literary prize, in 1954.
Her memoirs, including Memoirs of a Dutiful Daughter (1958), described her youth, and they also describe her relationship with Sartre.
That relationship was a lifelong partnership by choice without marriage. Admirers presented it as a model of equality, while critics called it a privilege of the elite.
When Sartre died in 1980 she wrote about his death in Adieux: A Farewell to Sartre (1981).
Her essay La vieillesse (The Coming of Age, 1970) attacked the way society treated the elderly, so her criticism reached beyond politics to everyday attitudes.
The Second Sex (1949), which described women as defined as the Other, made her a founder of modern feminism.
Beauvoir used her reputation to take public stands, especially over Algeria, and her view of communism changed as she saw it at first hand.
She took part in the political debates of the 1960s and 1970s, supporting the left and speaking out for the rights of women and of prisoners.
In September 1960 she signed the Manifesto of the 121, which supported French conscripts who refused to fight in the Algerian war.
She campaigned against torture by the French army and in 1962 championed the case of Djamila Boupacha, an Algerian woman who alleged torture by French forces.
With Sartre she visited the Soviet Union, China (1955) and Cuba (1960), where she observed communism at first hand, and her views on it changed over time.
Contemporaries praised her as a writer and public intellectual, while conservative critics attacked her for challenging traditional morality.
Historians now judge her as one of the most influential critics of the twentieth century, though her later political views are contested.

Writers in the communist states could not publish freely, so they found other ways to reach readers. They circulated unofficial copies, sent work abroad and relied on Western radio to carry banned works back.

Samizdat (Russian for self-published) was the system by which typed and copied manuscripts were passed from hand to hand in the Soviet Union and Czechoslovakia. The authors' work could thus circulate without passing the censor.
Some writers instead smuggled their work abroad to be published there. Western radio stations such as Radio Free Europe and the BBC then broadcast banned works to the East.
Boris Pasternak's Doctor Zhivago was first published in Italy in 1957. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1958 and, under pressure from the Soviet authorities, declined it.

In 1966 Andrei Sinyavsky and Yuli Daniel were sentenced to labour camps (seven and five years) for publishing satires abroad under pseudonyms, and in 1964 Joseph Brodsky was tried for social parasitism. Both cases drew international protest.
Andrei Sakharov, the physicist central to the Soviet hydrogen bomb, became a human rights campaigner. He was exiled to Gorky in January 1980 and released in December 1986 under Gorbachev.
Dissident writers faced expulsion, imprisonment or exile, and Solzhenitsyn's expulsion in 1974 was the most famous example.
Outside the Soviet Union, writers in Czechoslovakia and Poland also challenged the state. In the 1970s international agreements gave dissidents a new standard to appeal to.

Milan Kundera's novel The Joke (1967) and the Czechoslovak Writers' Union congress of June 1967, which criticised censorship, were part of the intellectual ferment that came before the Prague Spring of 1968.
Václav Havel, a Czech playwright, wrote The Power of the Powerless in 1978. He argued that ordinary people could resist by "living within the truth", as it is reported.

Havel helped to found Charter 77, a human rights manifesto of January 1977, and he was imprisoned from 1979 and released in early 1983, so most of 1979-83 was spent in jail. He became president of Czechoslovakia in December 1989.
Polish writers also took part: Czesław Miłosz, who defected in 1951, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1980, the same year as Solidarity's rise.

The Helsinki Final Act of 1975, in which the signatories (the USSR included) accepted human rights commitments, gave dissidents a standard of rights to appeal to, since their government had signed it.

Social criticism means writing that attacks the faults of a society. Western writers were free to publish, and they used that freedom to criticise totalitarianism (a state that controls every part of life) and the conformity of their own societies.
George Orwell's Animal Farm (1945) and Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) criticised Stalinism and the abuse of power, and both became standard texts in the Cold War.
Aldous Huxley's Brave New World (1932) was read alongside Nineteen Eighty-Four as a warning against conformity and totalitarian control, whether communist or consumerist.
Albert Camus's The Plague (1947) used an epidemic as an allegory (a story with a hidden political meaning) for resistance to tyranny, and he received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1957.
Camus broke with Sartre in 1952, after his book The Rebel (1951), over the question of communism and violence. He was killed in a car crash in January 1960.
In France, Germany and Britain, writers also turned their criticism on their own societies, on their national pasts and on class.

Jean-Paul Sartre's existentialism, expressed in Being and Nothingness (1943) and in his plays, argued that people are free and responsible for their choices. It dominated French thought in the late 1940s and 1950s.
Sartre's plays and essays also criticised bourgeois society (the comfortable middle class) and colonialism, and in 1964 he declined the Nobel Prize in Literature by his own choice.
Günter Grass's The Tin Drum (1959) examined Germany's wartime past and the moral compromises of ordinary people, and he received the Nobel Prize in 1999.
Heinrich Böll's novels criticised the restoration of West German society after 1945 and he received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1972.
In Britain, John Osborne's play Look Back in Anger (1956) and the writers known as the Angry Young Men attacked class and complacency in post-war society.

Secularisation means religion losing belief, practice and influence in public life. In much of Western Europe it advanced quickly from the 1960s, and the authority of the churches over everyday life declined.
Attendance at Mass and other religious services fell in most Western European countries from the 1960s, and the fall was sharpest among young people.
There were national differences: attendance fell sharply in Britain, the Netherlands, France and Scandinavia, while in Ireland and Poland religious practice remained high for longer.
The Netherlands is a striking case, because Catholic Mass attendance fell dramatically between the 1960s and 1980s and many left the Church.
Secularisation meant that the state, education and family life increasingly ran without reference to religious authority.
The decline of clergy vocations (people choosing to become priests, monks or nuns) was visible by the 1970s, when seminaries and religious orders in many countries recruited far fewer men and women.
No single event caused the decline of religion. Several social changes worked together, and the Catholic Church was also divided from inside.
Rising affluence and growing education were causes of secularisation.
Television brought new ideas and entertainment into the home, and urban life loosened the close communities in which church attendance had been a habit.
The welfare state took over services once run by the churches, so people needed the church less.
In the 1960s people questioned authority of all kinds, including the authority of the churches, and this was one cause of secularisation.
The reforms of the Second Vatican Council (a Catholic Church council) and the controversy over contraception created divisions in the Church.
In Humanae Vitae (July 1968) Pope Paul VI reaffirmed the ban on artificial contraception, which many Catholics found hard to accept.
While Christian practice declined, migration brought a new religion into Western Europe. It made religion visible in public life again in societies that were becoming more secular.
Muslim communities grew in Western Europe through migration from North Africa (especially to France), Turkey (especially to West Germany) and South Asia (especially to Britain).
These communities set up prayer rooms and mosques, so a new religion became a visible part of many European cities.
In the East, churches faced persecution or state control rather than the gradual decline seen in the West. Some, however, kept real influence and became centres of resistance.
The Catholic Church in Czechoslovakia was suppressed after the communist takeover of 1948, and bishops were imprisoned.

In Poland the Church retained real independence and mass support. Cardinal Stefan Wyszyński was interned from 1953 to 1956, but its influence grew after the election of the Polish pope, Karol Wojtyła (John Paul II), in 1978.

In Hungary Cardinal József Mindszenty was arrested in December 1948 and sentenced to life imprisonment in February 1949. He was freed in the uprising of October 1956 and took refuge in the US legation in Budapest from November 1956 until 1971, about 15 years.
The Evangelical (Protestant) Church in East Germany adopted a policy of coexistence with the state while maintaining its own institutions and social work.
In East Germany church-led peace prayers in Leipzig in autumn 1989 preceded the mass demonstrations, so the churches provided a protected space where protest could begin.
The Russian Orthodox Church was permitted to operate under tight state control and KGB infiltration. Khrushchev's anti-religious campaign of 1959-64 closed thousands of churches.
The contrast with the West is that religion in the East was persecuted or controlled by the state, whereas in the West it declined by voluntary choice.

The ecumenical movement means cooperation and moves towards unity among Christian churches of different denominations. After 1945, as Christian practice fell in the West, the churches cooperated more closely than at any time since the Reformation.

The World Council of Churches was founded at Amsterdam in August 1948 by Protestant, Anglican and Orthodox churches. The Roman Catholic Church did not join, and the Russian Orthodox Church joined in 1961.
Taizé, an ecumenical community in Burgundy, France, founded in 1940 by Brother Roger (Roger Schutz), drew young people from many countries in the 1960s and 1970s.
In January 1964 Pope Paul VI met Patriarch Athenagoras of Constantinople in Jerusalem, a step towards reconciling the Catholic and Orthodox churches.
In December 1965 the mutual excommunications of 1054, by which the two churches had condemned each other, were lifted.
Historians debate how far writers and religious movements shaped political change and how far they merely reflected it. The judgement is balanced on both sides.
Achievement: dissident writing kept the truth about Stalin's crimes alive and gave the West evidence, which helped to create an intellectual opposition in the communist states.
Limit: samizdat had a small readership, and most citizens were not directly reached by dissident writing, so the regimes survived until 1989-91 for other reasons.
Contemporaries: Soviet authorities called Solzhenitsyn a traitor, while many in the West praised dissident writers as heroes of freedom.

Later views: historians rate Solzhenitsyn and Beauvoir as hugely influential, though his testimony and politics and her later political views are questioned. Beauvoir was praised by contemporaries and attacked by conservative critics.
Religion: secularisation in the West was a broad social trend with several causes, not the result of a single event or movement.
In the East, religion was a source of resistance in Poland and East Germany, which is the reverse of the Western trend.

In the 1950s the Catholic Church was run from Rome and felt under pressure from the modern world. Pope John XXIII called a Council (a meeting of the bishops of the Church) to renew the Church and bring it into closer contact with that world.

In the 1950s the Church was led by the pope from Rome, the Mass was in Latin, power lay with a centralised Roman Curia (the Church's central administration), and priests and bishops were clearly separate from the laity (ordinary lay Catholics).

Pius XII (pope 1939–58) had centralised authority in Rome and ruled in an authoritarian style. By the 1950s the Church also faced secularisation (the decline of religion in society), the loss of the working class in industrial Europe, communism and modern ideas.

The Reformation had split Christianity into Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches, and the Catholic Church had long viewed the others with suspicion. The Church also faced the division between Catholics and other Christians, and the Holocaust and the long history of Christian anti-Judaism made Catholic–Jewish relations an urgent question.

Angelo Roncalli, patriarch of Venice, was elected Pope John XXIII on 28 October 1958, aged 76. He was seen as a caretaker pope, a short-term holder of the office, so his decision to call a Council surprised many.

He announced the Council on 25 January 1959 at the Basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls, to a group of cardinals, and this surprised them. It was the twenty-first ecumenical council (a Council of the whole Church) and the first since Vatican I (1869–70).

He used the Italian term aggiornamento, meaning bringing up to date, for its aim. He wanted a pastoral Council to renew the Church's teaching and practice rather than condemn errors, so that it could speak to ordinary people in a world of nuclear weapons, television and rapid change.

He also wanted Christian unity: the Council was meant to deal with the Church and the modern world, the liturgy (the Church's public worship) and relations with non-Catholic Christians. In 1960 he set up a Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity under Cardinal Augustin Bea.

Preparatory commissions began work in 1960 and were dominated by Curia officials, including Cardinal Alfredo Ottaviani, head of the Holy Office and of the theological commission. They expected a short Council that would simply approve prepared drafts, which set up the clash at the opening.
The Council met in four autumn sessions in Rome. John XXIII opened it, but he died in June 1963 and Pope Paul VI carried it to its close, so be clear which pope did what.

The Council opened on 11 October 1962 in St Peter's Basilica, with about 2,500 bishops (the Council fathers) from all continents attending, along with observers from other Christian churches. About 2,500 is the figure for the opening only.

1. First session (autumn 1962): on 13 October the bishops, led by Cardinals Liénart of Lille and Frings of Cologne, asked for time before electing commission members, so the Curia's prepared drafts were not adopted. Reformers such as Frings, Suenens (Belgium) and Léger (Canada) gave it its own direction.
John XXIII died on 3 June 1963, and Cardinal Giovanni Battista Montini was elected Paul VI on 21 June 1963. Paul VI kept the Council going.

2. Second session (September to December 1963): the bishops debated the nature of the Church and collegiality, the idea that the bishops share authority with the pope. Sacrosanctum Concilium was promulgated (formally issued) on 4 December 1963.

3. Third session (September to 21 November 1964): Lumen Gentium and Unitatis Redintegratio were promulgated on 21 November 1964. The final tense week, when a conservative minority and last-minute papal changes caused conflict, was called Black Week.

4. Fourth session (September to 8 December 1965): Nostra Aetate (28 October), Dei Verbum (18 November), and Dignitatis Humanae and Gaudium et Spes (7 December) were promulgated. The Council closed on 8 December 1965, and Paul VI set up the Synod of Bishops in September 1965 to continue consultation.

Joseph Ratzinger, later Pope Benedict XVI, attended as a theological adviser, so the Council drew on expert theologians; and Karol Wojtyła (later John Paul II) took part as a bishop. Observers from Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant churches attended, and the press, radio and television covered the proceedings widely.

The Council produced sixteen documents: four constitutions, nine decrees and three declarations. A constitution is the top rank of Council document, so the four constitutions set out its main teaching.
Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963), a constitution, reformed the liturgy. It allowed the use of local languages in the Mass so that people could take a fuller part in worship.

Lumen Gentium (1964), a constitution whose title means light of the nations, described the Church as the people of God. This gave a larger role to the laity and to the bishops collectively, which is the idea of collegiality.
Dei Verbum (1965), a constitution, addressed revelation (how God makes himself known) and Scripture, and it encouraged Catholics to study the Bible.
Gaudium et Spes (1965), a constitution whose title means joy and hope, addressed the Church in the modern world, including economic life, marriage, peace and social justice.
Unitatis Redintegratio (1964) was a decree, not a declaration. It committed the Church to ecumenism, the search for unity with other Christian churches.
Nostra Aetate (1965), a declaration, addressed non-Christian religions, including Judaism, and rejected the charge of collective Jewish guilt for the death of Christ.
Dignitatis Humanae (1965), a declaration, affirmed religious liberty, the right of people to follow their conscience in religion.
The Council's decisions changed Catholic worship and the Church's relations with other faiths. These were its most visible results.

Local languages were used in parts of the Mass from 1964–65, and the new Roman Missal (Missal of Paul VI), issued in 1969 and in use 1969–70, completed the reform. The old Mass had been in Latin, so the vernacular Mass (in everyday language) made worship understandable.
The Council did not order the priest to face the people. The 1969–70 Missal made this common practice, so don't present it as a Council rule.
Lay Catholics were encouraged to take a more active part in worship, reading the Scriptures and serving as ministers. The laity's wider role also included parish councils.

The Church began dialogue with other Christian churches, and observers from those churches attended the sessions. This is the ecumenical movement, the movement among Christian churches to cooperate and move towards unity, which the Council endorsed in Unitatis Redintegratio.

On 7 December 1965 Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras of Constantinople lifted the mutual excommunications of 1054, which had marked the East–West split between the Catholic and Orthodox churches. They had met in Jerusalem in January 1964.

Nostra Aetate became the basis for improved Catholic–Jewish dialogue. John Paul II visited the Great Synagogue of Rome on 13 April 1986, widely described as the first papal visit to a synagogue, and called Jews the elder brothers of Christians.
Priests and religious orders were asked to return to their founders' ideals and to adapt their dress and rules, so many nuns changed their habits.

Dignitatis Humanae accepted the principle of religious liberty, that the state should not coerce people in matters of faith. This was a shift from the Church's earlier hostility to such liberty, though historians and theologians dispute how far it was a break rather than a development.
The Council divided Catholics. Its reforms produced a traditionalist reaction, progressive demands for more change, and then a crisis over contraception.

Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre, a French archbishop and a leading conservative at the Council, founded the Society of St Pius X in 1970. It rejected the Council's teaching on religious liberty and the new liturgy.
Lefebvre was excommunicated in 1988 after consecrating four bishops without papal approval. Keep the two dates apart: the Society dates from 1970 and the excommunication from 1988.
Progressive Catholics felt the reforms had stalled, because they argued the Council had not gone far enough on the role of women, on collegiality and on sexual ethics.

Humanae Vitae, issued by Paul VI on 25 July 1968, reaffirmed the ban on artificial contraception. It came after the Council closed and is Paul VI's teaching, not the Council's. It was widely rejected by Catholics in the West.

A papal commission on birth control reported in 1966 with a majority favouring a change after the introduction of the pill in the early 1960s. Paul VI did not follow it, so the ban's confirmation in 1968 came as a shock to many Catholics.
Theologians and bishops' conferences in the Netherlands, Belgium and West Germany voiced open dissent, and in practice many Catholic couples used contraception.
Humanae Vitae is seen as a turning point because it opened a gap between the Church's teaching and the practice of lay Catholics, and it weakened the authority of the clergy.

The Dutch Church, which held a pastoral council in 1968–70, was seen as the most progressive in Europe, and Rome moved to restore control under Paul VI and John Paul II. Many Western Catholics also attended Mass less often after the 1960s, a trend historians link to wider secularisation.

Karol Wojtyła, a Polish bishop who took part in the Council, was elected pope on 16 October 1978, the first non-Italian pope since 1523. He led the Church until his death on 2 April 2005, and his religious role shaped how the Council was interpreted.

Born in Wadowice, Poland, on 18 May 1920, Wojtyła became a priest, then auxiliary bishop of Kraków in 1958 and archbishop in 1964. He took part in the Second Vatican Council as a bishop and contributed to the drafting of Gaudium et Spes.

He made over a hundred foreign journeys (about 104), more than any previous pope, and drew huge crowds in Poland, Latin America, Africa and Europe. His first visit to Poland as pope, in June 1979, linked the Church with Polish national identity.

His 1979 visit and his support for Solidarity (founded in Poland in 1980) made him a political figure, so communist rulers saw him as a challenge. He met Gorbachev at the Vatican on 1 December 1989, a sign the Church had outlasted the communist regimes.

He visited Ireland from 29 September to 1 October 1979, the first papal visit to Ireland, saying Mass before about a million people in the Phoenix Park, Dublin. He also visited Drogheda, Galway, Knock and Limerick, and at Drogheda he appealed to paramilitaries to end violence.

He reaffirmed traditional teaching on contraception, abortion and the priesthood, and he opposed the ordination of women, liberation theology and a change to clerical celibacy. Under him the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, led by Cardinal Ratzinger from 1981, disciplined theologians.

He launched World Youth Days in the mid-1980s and promoted new movements such as Opus Dei and the Neocatechumenal Way. He also reached out beyond the Church, with the 1986 synagogue visit and a public act of repentance for the sins of Christians in the Jubilee year 2000.
He was shot in St Peter's Square on 13 May 1981 by Mehmet Ali Ağca and visited his attacker in prison in December 1983.

Contemporaries divided: supporters and crowds admired him, while critics saw a conservative turn after the Council. Historians disagree: supporters see a defender of human dignity and a world figure, while critics argue he resisted reform and handled abuse scandals badly.

The Council's effect on practice is hard to judge because it coincided with wider social change such as secularisation, prosperity and the influence of the media. This makes the cause of decline disputed.

Attendance at Mass and vocations (calls to become a priest or member of a religious order) fell in Western Europe from the 1960s. Mass attendance fell steeply in the 1960s and 1970s, but Protestant churches declined too without any Council, which suggests social causes.
Vocations to the priesthood and religious life fell in the 1970s, as many priests and nuns left their orders in the years after the Council and fewer young people entered.

Attendance fell sharply in countries such as France and the Netherlands, while Poland and Ireland stayed relatively high. The cause of the decline is disputed, because social change coincided with the Council.
In Ireland practice stayed high into the 1980s, but vocations and Mass attendance later began to fall, and the authority of the Church was shaken later still.

The Council did lead to increased lay involvement, in parish councils, readers and Eucharistic ministers (lay people who help give communion), and to a stronger Catholic interest in social justice and in peace.

Historians differ on whether Vatican II was a successful renewal or a cause of decline. The judgement depends on which measure is used, so compare what the Council intended with what happened in practice.
Achievements: the vernacular liturgy, new relations with other faiths and churches, and a more open style of Church leadership.
Limits: falling practice, declining vocations to the priesthood, the conflict between traditionalists and progressives that continued after 1965, and the dispute over Humanae Vitae.
Contemporaries in the Church were divided: some saw the Council as a new beginning, while others saw it as a betrayal of tradition.
Later historians stress that the changes in religious practice were part of wider social trends, and that the Council's effects differed between countries.
Traditionalists blame the Council for the decline. Progressives argue instead that the Church failed to implement its reforms, especially on the role of women and collegiality.

John Lennon was a founding member of The Beatles, the band that turned British pop into a worldwide phenomenon and made its members the first global pop stars (mass-audience performers made famous by records, television and press coverage).

Lennon was born in Liverpool on 9 October 1940. He formed the Quarrymen in 1957, and the group later became The Beatles (the name was adopted in 1960) with Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr, who joined in 1962.
The Beatles played long residencies in Hamburg from 1960 to 1962 and at the Cavern Club in Liverpool, which gave them years of live experience before they were nationally famous.
Brian Epstein became their manager in 1962 and polished their image, while George Martin produced their records. Their first UK number one, From Me to You, came in 1963.

The Ed Sullivan Show on 9 February 1964 put them on American television and gave them a mass audience in the USA, the start of the 'British invasion' of American pop. Beatlemania, the screaming crowds and saturation press coverage that followed the band, spread across Western Europe.

Lennon and McCartney wrote most of the Beatles' songs. Albums such as Rubber Soul (1965) and Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967) showed that pop music could be an art form and not just disposable entertainment.

In June 1967 the Beatles performed All You Need Is Love on Our World, the first live global television broadcast by satellite, which was watched by hundreds of millions of people. This shows how television and pop music together created a worldwide audience.
In 1966 Lennon remarked that the Beatles were more popular than Jesus. This provoked protests and record burnings in parts of the USA, and it showed the controversy his fame attracted.

Epstein died in August 1967, which weakened the group, and the Beatles broke up in 1970. Disputes about business and music contributed to the split, so Epstein's death was one cause and not the only one.
After the Beatles became world famous, Lennon used that fame for the anti-war cause. His protests and his solo career brought him both admirers and enemies, and his life ended violently in 1980.
In March 1969 he and Yoko Ono held a 'bed-in' at the Amsterdam Hilton to promote peace. His song Give Peace a Chance (1969) became an anthem of the anti-war movement.
He returned his MBE (a British honour) in November 1969 in protest at British support for the US in Vietnam and the Nigerian civil war, a gesture that made his protest a public act.
He and Yoko Ono ran peace campaigns including the War Is Over billboard campaign of December 1969, which used advertising-style posters to spread an anti-war message.
His solo career produced the Plastic Ono Band records and Imagine (1971), a song that is judged both radical and commercially successful.
The US authorities tried to deport him from 1972 because of his anti-war activity. He won the right to stay, and he was granted a green card (permanent residence) in 1976.
From 1975 he spent five years as a househusband caring for his son Sean, who was born in 1975, before returning to music with the album Double Fantasy (1980).
He was shot dead outside his home in New York on 8 December 1980, and his death was widely mourned across Europe and America.
Lennon divided opinion in his lifetime, and historians still weigh his importance. Examiners on the Higher paper reward a judgement on impact, controversy and legacy.
Contemporaries saw him as a symbol of youthful rebellion: to fans he was an idol and a hero of the peace movement, while to critics such as those who burned Beatles records he was a danger to morals.
The American authorities treated him as a political danger, which is why they tried to deport him in 1972 because of his anti-war activity.
Historians present him as a symbol of the 1960s counterculture, meaning a culture that rejected the dominant values of society, and they treat the Beatles as the first global pop stars.
The Beatles are also seen as the model for later artists who wrote their own songs, because Lennon and McCartney showed that a group could write as well as perform its material.
Historians judge his post-Beatles work as both radical and commercially successful, and critics note that his radicalism was sometimes self-contradictory.

After 1945 young people became a distinct group in society with money, music and style of their own. This happened because of post-war prosperity, more schooling and new media that were aimed at them.
The word teenager (a young person treated as a distinct group with its own spending power and culture) was in common use in the USA from the 1940s, and the idea spread to Europe from there.

Post-war recovery and the 'economic miracle' brought rising wages and full employment in Western Europe in the 1950s and 1960s, so young people had more spending money for records, clothes and cinema.

The baby boom after 1945 and the expansion of secondary and university education kept young people in school longer and put more of them together with others their own age. This gave them a shared identity, which helped to fuel youth rebellion.

The Cold War division of Europe shaped what young people could hear, wear and watch. In the West they were free to follow American and British trends, while in the East the authorities tried to restrict them.
The 45 rpm single, introduced by RCA in the USA in 1949, made records cheap enough for teenagers to buy with their own money.
Radio Luxembourg, funded by advertising, broadcast pop music in English to Britain and Europe, so teenagers could hear music that official stations did not play.
Teenage magazines and dances created a youth media and a social scene of their own, so young people became a market that businesses competed to serve.
Rock 'n' roll came from America and reached Europe in the mid-1950s. It alarmed many adults, and later pop events showed how youth culture could be used for a cause.
The USA's cultural influence on Europe after 1945 reached young people through films, music, jeans and consumer goods, which made American style attractive.
Rock 'n' roll arrived in Europe in the mid-1950s. Bill Haley's Rock Around the Clock reached the UK singles chart in 1955, and Elvis Presley's first UK hits came in 1956.
Films about rebellious youth, The Wild One (1953) and Rebel Without a Cause (1955), made rebellion look glamorous to teenagers.
Many adults feared that rock 'n' roll and these films encouraged delinquency (youthful law-breaking), so critics saw the music as a threat to order and morals.

Live Aid, organised by the Irish singer Bob Geldof, was held at Wembley in London and in Philadelphia on 13 July 1985 to raise money for famine relief in Ethiopia. A very large global television audience watched, so it was a late example of youth culture used for a cause.
Dress and music were how young people marked themselves out from their elders. A subculture is a youth group with its own style, music and values, and several of them sparked public debate.
Teddy boys in 1950s Britain wore Edwardian-style jackets and became associated with delinquency, so their critics treated them as proof that rock 'n' roll was a threat.
The Mods and Rockers of Britain clashed at English seaside resorts in 1964, beginning at Clacton at Easter and followed by Margate and Brighton at Whitsun (May 1964).
The press coverage of these clashes exaggerated them and created a 'moral panic', a wave of public alarm about youth out of proportion to the events.
Fashion expressed the new youth market. Mary Quant of London helped to make the miniskirt famous in the 1960s, and Carnaby Street in London became a centre of fashion.
Hippies of the late 1960s adopted long hair, flowers and communal living. They were part of the counterculture, which rejected the dominant values of society.
Youth style was also political and national. Jeans carried a message about America and freedom, and later styles expressed the anger of a generation hit by economic hardship.
Jeans symbolised America and freedom. They were worn by young people across Europe and highly valued in the East, where they were scarce.
Punk arose in 1976–77 with the Sex Pistols and The Clash. It expressed the anger of unemployed young people in the recession.
The Sex Pistols' God Save the Queen was released on 27 May 1977, about ten days before the Silver Jubilee bank holiday on 7 June. It was in the charts during Jubilee week, when it reached number 2.

Skinheads and later the new romantics, mostly in Britain, were other styles that fused fashion, music and class identity. They show that each generation's subculture reflected its own social conditions.
