The war left a lasting refugee problem and new borders that no one fully accepted. It also shaped Israel as a state of immigration.
About 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled from what became Israel; estimates range roughly from 600,000 to 750,000. Some left in fear, as after Deir Yassin, and some were driven out.

UN General Assembly Resolution 194 of December 1948 said refugees who wished to return and live in peace should be allowed to. Israel has not accepted a general right of return, so the refugee question stayed unresolved.
The armistice agreements of 1949 ended the fighting without a peace. Jordan held the West Bank, which it annexed in 1950 although few states recognised this, and Egypt administered the Gaza Strip.
Israel's Law of Return of 1950 gave Jews the right to immigrate, which brought large numbers to the new state. Many Jews also left or were pushed out of Arab states after 1948.
Nasser took power in Egypt in 1952 and set out to free Egypt from British influence. His clashes with Britain, Israel and the West then led towards the Suez Crisis.
The Free Officers overthrew King Farouk on 23 July 1952. Gamal Abdul Nasser became the leading figure, became prime minister in April 1954 and was elected president by referendum in June 1956.
The Anglo-Egyptian Agreement of October 1954 provided for British troops to leave the Suez Canal base, a British military base beside the canal. They had left by June 1956.

Nasser attended the Bandung Conference of Asian and African states in April 1955 and supported anti-colonial movements in Algeria and elsewhere, so Arab nationalism for him meant opposing Western control.
The Baghdad Pact of 1955 linked Britain, Iraq, Turkey, Iran and Pakistan. Nasser saw it as an attempt to isolate Egypt, so he opposed it.

Egypt barred Israeli ships from the canal and the Straits of Tiran. Fedayeen (Palestinian raiders) attacked Israel from Gaza, and an Israeli raid on Gaza in February 1955 killed 38 people. This pushed Nasser to look for arms.
In 1955 Nasser bought arms from the Soviet bloc through Czechoslovakia. This made Egypt a point of Cold War rivalry, because Western powers now feared Soviet influence in the Middle East.
In 1956 the loss of Western funding for the Aswan High Dam pushed Nasser into a bold response. The canal he seized mattered greatly to Britain and France.
Egypt recognised communist China in May 1956. The United States withdrew its offer to finance the Aswan High Dam on 19 July 1956 and Britain followed within days.

The Suez Canal opened in 1869. Britain bought the Khedive's shares, about 44 per cent, in 1875 under Disraeli, and in the 1950s about two-thirds of Western Europe's oil passed through it. It was the sea route between Europe and Asia.

On 26 July 1956 Nasser announced the nationalisation of the Suez Canal Company, the private company that owned the canal. The dam was to be financed from canal revenues, so the nationalisation answered the Western withdrawal.
Anthony Eden was Britain's prime minister. Guy Mollet, France's prime minister, blamed Nasser for backing the Algerian rebels. Israel wanted the Tiran blockade ended and the fedayeen raids stopped.
Diplomacy came first, but attempts to negotiate a settlement failed, so the three countries moved to military plans. The Anglo-French plan was called Operation Musketeer.
The Soviet Union later helped to build the dam, so the Aswan project became a symbol of Egypt's turn towards the Soviet bloc.
Britain, France and Israel prepared the attack in secret and gave it a public excuse. The invasion then followed in a set order.

The Protocol of Sèvres was signed secretly near Paris on 24 October 1956 by Britain, France and Israel, with Ben-Gurion attending. Israel would attack Sinai; Britain and France would then demand that both sides withdraw and occupy the canal to ‘separate’ the combatants.
This pretext was false, because the attack had been planned together. The secrecy later made the collusion a political scandal, which is why critics at home condemned it.
2. On 30 October Britain and France issued an ultimatum telling both sides to withdraw about 10 miles from the canal. Israel accepted and Egypt refused.
3. On 31 October the Anglo-French bombing of Egyptian airfields began.
4. On 5 November British and French paratroopers landed at Port Said and Port Fuad, and on 6 November seaborne landings followed.
5. A ceasefire took effect at midnight on 6-7 November, while the Anglo-French force was still advancing down the canal.
The invasion was stopped by pressure from the two superpowers and by the UN rather than by Egypt's army. Britain, dependent on American support, could not carry on.

President Eisenhower of the United States opposed the action. Britain faced a run on the pound (heavy selling of the currency), and the US withheld support at the IMF (the International Monetary Fund) until Britain agreed to withdraw.
Soviet leaders threatened rocket attacks on London and Paris on 5 November, and the Soviet Union supported Egypt in the UN.
Soviet troops crushed the Hungarian rising on 4 November 1956. This weakened the Anglo-French complaint against Soviet behaviour at the UN and made Eisenhower angrier at his allies.

The UN set up the United Nations Emergency Force (UNEF) in November 1956 on the proposal of Lester Pearson, Canada's foreign minister, to supervise the withdrawal. General E. L. M. Burns commanded it.
Suez ended in political defeat for Britain and France and a victory for Nasser, although his army had lost. It also moved power in the Middle East to the United States.

Eden resigned on 9 January 1957, in ill health and politically discredited, and Harold Macmillan succeeded him. The crisis showed that Britain could not act against American wishes, so Britain became more dependent on the US.

Britain and France lost their position as the main Western powers in the Middle East. The Eisenhower Doctrine of January 1957 pledged US help to Middle Eastern states against communism, so the US took over the role.
Egypt's army was beaten in Sinai, but Nasser kept the canal and became a hero of Arab nationalism. His prestige in the Arab world rose sharply because he had defied Britain, France and Israel.
Egypt blocked the canal with a number of sunken ships. A UN clearance operation reopened it in April 1957, under Egyptian control, and Egypt seized British and French property.
Israel withdrew from Sinai and Gaza by March 1957 after US assurances about the Straits of Tiran, so Israel gained some security. UNEF was stationed on the Sinai frontier.
The Iraqi monarchy, Britain's close ally, was overthrown in July 1958, and Iraq left the Baghdad Pact in 1959. This showed how British influence among Arab states was falling.
Ben-Gurion led the Jewish community in Palestine and became the first prime minister of Israel. He was a labour Zionist leader who shaped the state as it was founded.
Born David Grün in 1886 in Plonsk in the Russian Empire, he emigrated to Ottoman Palestine in 1906 and became a leader of labour Zionism.
He led the Jewish Agency executive from 1935 and accepted the UN partition plan of 1947 as a first step towards a Jewish state.
He was shaped by events: the Holocaust and the White Paper shaped his outlook, and the war of 1948 tested the new state.
He proclaimed Israel on 14 May 1948 as a participant and was prime minister in 1948-54 and 1955-63, also holding the defence ministry. He retired for a time to Sde Boker kibbutz.

He created the Israel Defence Forces in May 1948 and ordered the shelling of the Irgun arms ship Altalena in June 1948 to assert a single army. In October 1956 he attended the secret talks at Sèvres with Britain and France.
Contemporaries differed: most Jews saw him as the founder of the state, while Arabs and Palestinians saw him as the architect of a state that displaced them.

Historians of the ‘new history’ school such as Benny Morris argue there was no overall expulsion plan in 1948 but that expulsions took place, including from Lydda and Ramle in July 1948. How far Ben-Gurion approved them is debated.
Nasser led Egypt from 1952 and became the most important figure of Arab nationalism. The Suez Crisis was the central event of his career.
Born on 15 January 1918 in Alexandria, he trained as an army officer and was one of the Free Officers who overthrew King Farouk in 1952.
He was prime minister from 1954 and president from 1956. He pursued land reform and the Aswan High Dam, and nationalised the canal. He formed the United Arab Republic with Syria in 1958-61.
He was shaped by events: the Gaza raid, the Baghdad Pact and the withdrawal of the dam offer each pushed him towards confrontation.
In the Suez Crisis he was a participant. His army was defeated in Sinai, but he survived the attack with control of the canal confirmed.
Eden and some British commentators compared him with Mussolini and Hitler, because he seemed an aggressive dictator, while Arab nationalists saw a hero who had defied the West.
Historians credit him with land reform, the dam and Arab self-confidence. They criticise his one-party rule, the suppression of the Muslim Brotherhood and the defeat of 1967.
He intervened in the Yemeni civil war from 1962 and blocked the Straits of Tiran in 1967. Egypt lost Sinai in the Six-Day War of June 1967.
He offered to resign after the defeat, withdrew the offer after mass demonstrations, and died on 28 September 1970.
Examiners want a judgement about how far Britain caused the troubles of the Middle East and how far its actions succeeded. Use each pair of points to argue both sides.
Britain's contribution, limit: the Mandate's contradictory promises, its handling of immigration, the 1939 White Paper and the abrupt withdrawal in 1948 all left a legacy of refugees and hostility.
Britain was not the only cause, because Arab and Jewish nationalism, the Holocaust, the US and UN, Arab rejection of partition and Nasser's own actions also drove events.
Withdrawal, achievement: Britain ended a costly commitment and passed the question to the UN instead of fighting both communities, as the attacks on British forces had become too great.
Withdrawal, limit: the Mandate's conflicting promises to Arabs and Jews were not reconciled, so the 1948 war left refugees and hostility.
Suez, achievement: Israel overran Sinai in days and the Anglo-French force was advancing down the canal before the ceasefire, so the operation was largely successful as far as it went.
Suez, limit: the operation failed politically. The ceasefire was forced by the United States, the Soviet threat and the UN, and the canal remained in Egyptian hands.

Contemporary view: Eden presented the action as a police action to separate Israel and Egypt, while Labour leader Hugh Gaitskell condemned it and Anthony Nutting, a Foreign Office minister, resigned in protest.
Later view: many historians treat Suez as the moment that exposed the end of Britain's great-power pretensions, while others argue that decolonisation was already under way.

After the Second World War the old empires were harder to hold than before. Britain and France had to decide whether to fight for their colonies or let them go, and France's own recent history shaped its choices.

Empires lost both the power and the will to continue: war-weariness at home, the weakness of Britain and France after the war, and hostility to empire from both the United States and the Soviet Union all made colonial rule harder to defend.

The new United Nations gave colonial peoples a public place to raise their grievances, and nationalist movements (organised groups demanding self-rule) grew stronger, so every colony became a potential problem for its ruler.

France was defeated in 1940 and the Vichy regime governed France afterwards, which damaged French prestige. De Gaulle's appeal of 18 June 1940, made from London, began the Free French movement that fought on.
The Fourth Republic (1946–58) was unstable, with weak governments that rarely lasted long, so France found it hard to settle on a firm colonial policy.
Britain's withdrawal from India in 1947 and France's defeat in Indochina in 1954 had already shown that empires could be ended, so nationalists in Africa could point to real examples.

The French Union, created by the 1946 constitution, kept the empire under Paris. It was replaced in the 1958 constitution by the French Community, which gave territories internal self-government but left foreign affairs, defence and currency with France.
Before the Algerian war ended, change had already begun elsewhere. Reform in French Africa and independence for Ghana and Guinea showed that independence was becoming possible.

The Brazzaville Conference of January–February 1944, a Free French gathering, promised reforms for the empire but ruled out self-government, so it admitted that change was needed while keeping French rule intact.
Tunisia and Morocco, France's neighbours to Algeria's east and west, became independent in March 1956. Their independence mattered to the Algerian war because both later sheltered FLN forces.

The Loi-cadre (framework law) of June 1956, introduced by the minister Gaston Defferre, gave the French African territories elected assemblies and governments with wider powers, an early step towards self-government.

Ghana (the former Gold Coast, a British colony) became independent on 6 March 1957 under Kwame Nkrumah, the first sub-Saharan colony to do so, which gave other African nationalists an example to point to.
During an African tour de Gaulle spoke at Brazzaville on 24 August 1958 and offered the territories a choice between the Community and independence.

Guinea, under Sékou Touré, rejected the 1958 constitution (and so the Community) in the referendum of 28 September 1958 and became independent on 2 October 1958, the first French colony in sub-Saharan Africa to leave. Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Tunisia and Morocco had already left French rule.
In 1960 independence came in a rush. A British prime minister gave the movement its best-known phrase, and France's Community broke up in practice.
Harold Macmillan, the British prime minister, told the South African Parliament in Cape Town on 3 February 1960 that 'the wind of change is blowing through this continent'.
Seventeen African states became independent in 1960, so it is known as the Year of Africa. Examples include the Ivory Coast, Nigeria and the Congo.

Most French West and Equatorial African territories, along with Madagascar, became independent by negotiation in 1960 and signed co-operation accords with France on defence, currency and aid, so independence did not mean a clean break.
In practice the French Community therefore broke up within two years of its creation, because its members chose independence instead of internal self-government.

Britain chose negotiated transfers of power in most of its colonies. France's policy in Algeria was contested by about a million settlers and an armed nationalist movement, which made a negotiated settlement far harder.

Algeria was not an ordinary colony in French eyes. It had been conquered long before, was treated as part of France itself, and was home to a large settler community, which is why giving it up was so painful.

France began its conquest of Algeria in 1830. By the 1848 constitution Algeria was divided into three départements (administrative districts like those of mainland France) that were treated as part of metropolitan France.

The settlers, known as pieds-noirs, numbered about one million out of about nine million people by 1954. They dominated the economy, land and local administration, so they had much to lose from any change.
The French aim was assimilation: making colonial subjects French in language, law and culture. Few Muslim Algerians accepted this in practice, and most never won full equality.

Most Muslim Algerians were subjects rather than full citizens. Those who wanted full French citizenship had to give up their Islamic personal status (Muslim family law), a condition few chose to meet before 1954.

The Sétif and Guelma uprising of 8 May 1945 killed about 100 Europeans. French repression killed thousands of Algerians: the official French figure is about 1,500, Algerian nationalists claim 45,000, and historians generally accept a figure in between.
Messali Hadj founded the Movement for the Triumph of Democratic Liberties (MTLD) in 1946 to campaign for independence. It split in 1954 between moderates and the armed nationalists.

The Statute of 1947 created an Algerian Assembly with two colleges (voting groups) of equal size. Europeans, with a small number of Muslims, elected the first and the Muslim majority the second, which favoured the settlers because far fewer people elected as many members.
On 1 November 1954 a new nationalist movement chose armed force. France answered with its army, and by 1957 the war was being fought in the cities, the countryside and along the borders.
The National Liberation Front (FLN) launched a rising on 1 November 1954 with attacks on police and military targets across Algeria, which began the Algerian war.

The French government sent conscripts (young men called up for compulsory service), reaching about 400,000 troops at the peak. Under Guy Mollet's government in 1956 the Special Powers law gave the army wide powers.
The FLN held the Soummam Valley Congress in August 1956, which set up its political leadership, so the movement had an organised direction beyond its fighting units.
The Morice Line, built from 1957, was a barrier of wire, mines and fencing along the Tunisian border, intended to stop arms and fighters crossing from Tunisia, where the FLN found shelter.

In the Battle of Algiers (January to October 1957) French paratroopers under General Jacques Massu broke the FLN's network in the city through arrests, interrogation and torture. It was a military success won by methods that damaged France's reputation.
As the war grew, both sides used methods that shocked observers. How the war was fought turned it into a political problem for France at home and abroad.
French forces used torture. Henri Alleg's La Question, an account of his own torture, was banned in France in 1958, but as a first-hand account it brought the issue before French opinion.

Terrorism means violence against civilians to spread fear and win a political aim. The FLN used it, with bombings in Algiers cafés from September 1956 onward, and it also killed Algerian rivals and Muslim opponents.
French forces also killed civilians in reprisal operations (revenge attacks), so civilians suffered at the hands of both sides.

From 1955, and especially after 1957, the French army moved more than a million rural Algerians into fenced regroupement camps as part of its counter-insurgency strategy (the effort to defeat a guerrilla rising).
French military deaths numbered about 25,000. Estimates of Algerian deaths range from about 300,000 to the Algerian official figure of 1.5 million, so historians still debate the figures.
Support for the FLN abroad grew. Tunisia and Morocco sheltered its fighters, Egypt supplied arms, and the UN General Assembly debated Algeria from 1955, so the war was never only a French matter.
On 8 February 1958 French aircraft raided the Tunisian village of Sakiet, which damaged France's reputation with the US and the UN.
By 1958 the Fourth Republic could neither win the war nor settle on a policy. A revolt by settlers and army officers in Algiers gave Charles de Gaulle his chance to return to power.
Between 1946 and 1958 the Fourth Republic had more than twenty governments, which made it hard to sustain a consistent policy on Algeria and helped bring about its fall.
On 13 May 1958 settlers and army officers seized government buildings in Algiers and demanded that Algeria stay French. They formed a Committee of Public Safety.
The government of Pierre Pflimlin, the last prime minister of the Fourth Republic, lost the confidence of the army, and President René Coty then called on de Gaulle to form a government.
The National Assembly invested de Gaulle on 1 June 1958 as prime minister, not president, because he became president only in January 1959.
Speaking to the crowd in Algiers on 4 June 1958 de Gaulle said 'Je vous ai compris' (I have understood you). At Mostaganem on 6 June he cried 'Vive l'Algérie française'.
These words led the settlers to believe he would keep Algeria French, which is why they later felt betrayed when he changed course.
De Gaulle's first task was to rebuild the state. The new constitution gave France the strong government the Fourth Republic had lacked, and it set out a new relationship with the colonies.

A new constitution was approved by referendum on 28 September 1958, establishing the Fifth Republic with a strong presidency, which gave France stable government after the Fourth Republic's constant changes of government.
The constitution also set up the French Community, which gave the colonies internal self-government but kept foreign affairs, defence and currency with France.
De Gaulle was elected president in December 1958 (on 21 December) by an electoral college, a limited group of electors rather than a popular vote, and he took office on 8 January 1959.
Once in office de Gaulle moved step by step away from the settlers' hopes. Each step provoked a violent reaction from those who wanted Algeria to stay French.

On 16 September 1959 de Gaulle announced that Algerians would be offered self-determination (the right to decide their own future), with a choice among independence, close association with France and full integration.
Settler militants staged Barricades Week in Algiers from 24 January to 1 February 1960, a revolt against this policy that de Gaulle put down with the army.
Talks with the FLN at Melun in June 1960 failed, so the war went on.
On 4 November 1960 de Gaulle spoke of an Algerian Republic in the future, a clear sign that independence was now a real prospect.

In the referendum of 8 January 1961 about 75 per cent of votes cast overall approved self-determination, and about 70 per cent in Algeria itself, which gave de Gaulle a clear mandate (authority from the voters).

In the Algiers putsch (a seizure of power by force) of 21–26 April 1961, four generals who opposed independence, Challe, Salan, Jouhaud and Zeller, took Algiers. It collapsed in about four days because conscripts and most of the army stayed loyal to de Gaulle.
The Secret Army Organisation (OAS), formed in early 1961 by settlers set on stopping independence, carried out bombings and assassinations in Algeria and in France, and it attacked de Gaulle himself.
After years of war France and the FLN finally negotiated a settlement. Independence came in stages, which is why several dates are given for it.
The Évian Accords were signed on 18 March 1962 after negotiations between the French government and the FLN, and a ceasefire took effect on 19 March.
The Accords guaranteed the rights of the French minority (the settlers), kept the Mers-el-Kébir naval base for France for a time, and gave France access to Saharan oil and gas.
The Accords were approved in a referendum in France on 8 April 1962 (about 91 per cent yes) and in Algeria on 1 July 1962 (an overwhelming yes), so signing them was not the end of the process.
Algeria became independent after the 1 July vote: France recognised it on 3 July, and 5 July is the date celebrated as independence.
After a struggle with rival nationalist leaders in the summer of 1962, Ahmed Ben Bella became prime minister in September 1962 and president in 1963.
The OAS tried to wreck the settlement by violence, and the settlers' anger peaked in the weeks after Évian. Its defeat ended the settlers' armed resistance.

On 26 March 1962 French troops fired on pro-French demonstrators in the rue d'Isly in Algiers, killing about 50 people, which deepened the settlers' sense of betrayal because the shots came from French soldiers.
The OAS was defeated in Algiers and in France, and its leaders were tried. General Raoul Salan, a leader of the 1961 putsch, was arrested in April 1962 and received a life sentence.

The OAS ambush of de Gaulle's car at Petit-Clamart on 22 August 1962 failed. Its organiser, Jean Bastien-Thiry, was executed in March 1963, the last person executed by firing squad in France for a political offence.
A general amnesty in 1968 freed those OAS members still in prison.
Independence did not end the links between the two countries, but the new state steadily took control of what France had kept.
Ben Bella was overthrown by his defence minister Houari Boumediene in June 1965.
France handed over the Mers-el-Kébir naval base in 1968, ending the military presence that the Évian Accords had allowed it to keep for a time.
In 1971 Algeria nationalised (took into state ownership) French oil and gas holdings, reversing the access to Saharan oil and gas that the Accords had given France.
Independence turned into flight for the European settlers and tragedy for many of the Algerians who had served France.
On 5 July 1962, the day celebrated as independence, violence against Europeans broke out in Oran. Estimates vary, but hundreds were killed or went missing, and many settlers fled the city.
About 800,000 settlers left Algeria in 1962, many within a few months and most for France, which had to absorb them into an already strained economy. Nearly a million had gone by the mid-1960s.
The departure of the settlers ended the French presence in Algerian agriculture and administration, and many farms were taken over by the new state.
The harkis were Algerians who had served as auxiliaries (helpers) in the French forces.
The French government refused or obstructed organised rescue of the harkis, and officers who helped them were punished. About 90,000 reached France with their families.
Tens of thousands of harkis were killed in reprisals (revenge killings) after independence, with estimates ranging widely from about 30,000 to 150,000.

Most harkis who reached France were placed in camps and forest hamlets. Recognition and compensation remained a political issue: President Chirac paid national tribute to them in 2001 and President Macron asked their forgiveness in 2021.
De Gaulle led the Free French in the Second World War and then ended the Algerian war as president of the Fifth Republic. His career shows both a leader shaping events and one pushed by them.
Born on 22 November 1890 in Lille, he was a career army officer who became undersecretary for war in June 1940. His appeal of 18 June 1940 from London made him leader of the Free French.

He headed the provisional government from 1944 to January 1946, resigned, founded the Rally of the French People (RPF) in 1947, and withdrew from politics in the 1950s before returning to power in 1958.

As the key decision-maker he took the major steps himself: the return in 1958, the Fifth Republic, the 1959 offer of self-determination, putting down Barricades Week and the putsch, and the path to Évian.

In 1958 the settlers welcomed him because they believed he would keep Algeria French, but his 1959 turn showed events shaping him too. He moved from 'Je vous ai compris' in 1958 to self-determination in 1959.
Contemporaries split sharply: the settlers, the army and the OAS called him a traitor, while many in France and Algeria saw him as the leader who ended a costly war.

Some historians argue that he planned withdrawal from early on and moved slowly to avoid civil war. Others argue that he moved step by step as the war's costs, the army's attitude and international pressure became clear.

He used the Community and, after 1960, bilateral co-operation accords (agreements between two countries) to keep French influence in sub-Saharan Africa, working through Jacques Foccart, his adviser on African affairs.
He resigned as president in April 1969 after losing a referendum, and died on 9 November 1970.
De Gaulle's record and the wider retreat from empire can be judged by pairing achievements against limits, and contemporary views against later ones.
Achievement: de Gaulle ended a war that the Fourth Republic had failed to win, and he gave Algerians the right of self-determination.

Limit: the war cost many lives, caused the exodus of about a million people and divided the French army and political class. His policy was also delayed and ambiguous, which left the settlers feeling deceived.
Achievement: the Fifth Republic's constitution gave France a stable government that could take the decision to withdraw.

Limit: the French Community did not hold the colonies together, yet most independent states of West and Equatorial Africa kept close ties with France through co-operation accords, with French troops stationed in several of them.

Explanations for withdrawal: the cost and unpopularity of the Algerian war, the independence of Tunisia and Morocco in 1956, UN General Assembly debates on Algeria from 1955, American pressure, world opinion and the growth of African nationalist parties.
The British and French cases differed: Britain's transfers were mostly negotiated, while France fought a war in Algeria before accepting independence.
Later view: the war divided the army, the political class and French society, and many judge that de Gaulle's greatest achievement was to end it without a collapse of the Republic.
Contemporary view: settlers, the OAS and the generals of the 1961 putsch saw withdrawal as betrayal, while about 91 per cent of French voters approved the Évian Accords in April 1962.

To understand what went wrong and right after independence, you need three starting facts: how the colonial borders were drawn, why the colonial powers let go, and how the Cold War shaped the new states.
Colonial rule means control of a territory by an external power, governed for the benefit of the imperial state rather than of the people who lived there.

European powers partitioned Africa in the later nineteenth century, at the Berlin Conference of 1884-85. They drew borders that cut across peoples and joined rival ones together, which is the root of later ethnic tension.

The Second World War weakened the standing of Britain, France, Belgium and Portugal, and African nationalism (the demand for self-government) grew after 1945. Ghana became independent on 6 March 1957 and led the wave.
About seventeen African states became independent in 1960 alone, so independence came to many territories in a very short time.
The Cold War (the rivalry between the USA and the USSR) meant both superpowers competed for influence in the new states. This shaped events in the Congo and Angola in particular.
Several terms recur in every case in this subsection. Knowing exactly what each means as historians use it lets you write precise answers.

Tribalism was the colonial officials' term for ethnic loyalty (loyalty to your own ethnic group). Colonial policy often defined, fixed and exploited ethnic identities, so the label described something that colonial rule itself had hardened.
The (British) Commonwealth is an association of Britain and its former colonies, and many of them joined on independence, which kept a link with Britain after rule had ended.

Indirect rule meant governing through existing local rulers instead of replacing them. Lord Lugard used it in Nigeria, where the colonial government ruled much of the north through its emirs (Muslim rulers).
A federation is a state in which regions keep their own governments and powers under a central government. Nigeria's regions are the main example.
Secession means a region breaking away from a state to form its own. Katanga seceded from the Congo in 1960 and Biafra from Nigeria in 1967.

The Force Publique was the Belgian Congo's colonial army, and ONUC was the UN operation in the Congo. The Estado Novo was Portugal's authoritarian regime under Salazar, in place from the 1930s until 1974.

The MPLA was one of Angola's three nationalist movements. The Carnation Revolution was the 1974 overthrow of the Portuguese regime in Lisbon, and Zairianisation was Mobutu's 1973 transfer of foreign-owned businesses to Zairian owners.

Nigeria began as a British creation that joined very different peoples. How Britain governed it, and how the regions were later organised, set up the rivalries that would break the country in the 1960s.
Lord Lugard united the Northern and Southern territories of Nigeria into one colony in 1914. Under indirect rule, the colonial government ruled much of the north through its existing emirs.
Nigeria's three main groups were the Hausa-Fulani in the north, the Yoruba in the west and the Igbo in the east. This mattered because each group was concentrated in one part of the country.
The north was predominantly Muslim and the south had large Christian populations, so religion deepened the divide between north and south.
The 1954 federal constitution created three regions, Northern, Western and Eastern, with Lagos as a federal territory.
The regions had their own parliaments and revenue, and the regional parties drew their support on ethnic lines, which made federal politics tense.

The main parties were the Northern People's Congress (NPC), the Action Group (Yoruba west) and the National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC, led by Azikiwe, Igbo east), each rooted in one region.
Nigeria's oil came from Oloibiri in the Niger Delta, discovered by Shell-BP in 1956, and exports began in 1958. The oil lay in the Eastern Region, so it later became a source of dispute.
Independence in 1960 handed power to a federation whose largest party came from the north. The first years showed both how the system was meant to work and where it was already under strain.
In the federal elections of December 1959 the NPC won the most seats and formed a coalition with the NCNC, and its leader Abubakar Tafawa Balewa became federal prime minister.

Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960 as a member of the British Commonwealth, with Balewa as prime minister. The Queen remained head of state, represented by a governor-general, Nnamdi Azikiwe from November 1960.
Nigeria became a republic on 1 October 1963 with Azikiwe as president, so the Queen was no longer head of state. A fourth region, the Mid-West, was also created in 1963.

Regional tension grew in the early 1960s. A political crisis in the Western Region began in 1962, and the elections of 1965 were violently disputed, which weakened trust in the federal system before the army acted.
In 1966 the army took over, and ethnic violence turned a political crisis into a break-up. The order of events matters, because each step pushed the Igbo-dominated east closer to leaving.

1. On 15 January 1966 army officers led by Major Chukwuma Nzeogwu killed Prime Minister Balewa, the Northern premier Ahmadu Bello and the Western premier Samuel Akintola. The coup was seen as dominated by Igbo officers, which made northerners suspicious of the Igbo.
2. Major-General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi became the first military head of state in January 1966. He was killed in a counter-coup in July 1966, and Lieutenant-Colonel Yakubu Gowon became head of state.
3. Massacres of Igbo people in the north in 1966, in May and again in September-October, killed many thousands. Large numbers fled to the east, which hardened Igbo feeling against the federation.
4. At Aburi in Ghana in January 1967 an attempt to settle the crisis was made, but it failed.
5. On 27 May 1967 Gowon decreed twelve states. This broke up the Eastern Region and cut the Igbo off from most of the oil.

6. Three days later, on 30 May 1967, Lieutenant-Colonel Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu (later called Colonel) declared the east the Republic of Biafra. The federal government responded with a blockade of the east.
The Biafran War was a secession and a famine crisis, not simply Nigeria against itself. Biafra had very little international recognition, but the suffering of its people drew worldwide sympathy.
The war lasted from July 1967 to 15 January 1970. It caused widespread famine in Biafra, because the blockade cut off supplies.
Estimates of the death toll vary widely, from several hundred thousand to over a million, most of them from starvation and disease. No single figure is reliable.
Only five states recognised Biafra: Tanzania, Gabon, the Ivory Coast, Zambia and Haiti. Recognition was limited to a few states, which left Biafra isolated.
Britain and the Soviet Union supplied arms to the federal government, while France gave covert (secret) support to Biafra.

Many people outside Nigeria were moved by images of starving Biafran children. Joint Church Aid flew relief into Biafra, and Irish missionaries (Holy Ghost Fathers) were prominent, so supplies kept reaching the enclave.

Gowon announced reconciliation, rehabilitation and reconstruction at the end of the war on 15 January 1970. He said there was "no victor, no vanquished", which aimed to bring the Igbo back into the federation.
Belgium ran the Congo as a colony for profit and gave Congolese people almost no training for government. That is why independence in 1960 arrived so suddenly and so badly prepared.

King Leopold II ruled the Congo Free State from 1885 as his personal possession. Forced rubber collection caused widespread abuses, which Roger Casement and E. D. Morel exposed, and this led to international protest.

The Belgian government took over the colony in 1908. It was ruled by a paternalistic administration (one that treated Congolese like children to be looked after), which gave them little political role.
The colony's wealth lay in minerals including copper, cobalt and diamonds. The Belgian company Union Minière du Haut-Katanga ran the mines of Katanga, mining copper and cobalt.
By 1960 only a handful of Congolese had a university degree. The Force Publique had no Congolese officers, so the new state would have almost no trained administrators or commanders.
Congolese political parties emerged in the late 1950s, including Patrice Lumumba's National Congolese Movement (MNC), which won the most seats in the May 1960 elections.
Riots in Léopoldville in January 1959 shocked Belgian opinion, and King Baudouin soon promised independence but gave no date.
The Round Table at Brussels in January-February 1960 fixed independence for 30 June 1960, only months later, which left almost no time to prepare.
Within weeks of independence the new state had a mutiny, two secessions and a UN intervention. The speed of the collapse is the main evidence for how unprepared it was.
On 30 June 1960 Joseph Kasa-Vubu became head of state and Patrice Lumumba became prime minister.
At the independence ceremony King Baudouin praised Belgium's colonial work. Lumumba replied with a speech attacking the humiliations of colonial rule, which offended Belgian opinion.
Soldiers of the Force Publique mutinied on 5-6 July 1960. Attacks on Europeans followed, so Belgium sent troops back to the Congo in July 1960.
Katanga, led by Moïse Tshombe, seceded on 11 July 1960 with Belgian backing, and South Kasai declared its own state in August 1960.
The UN Security Council authorised the UN operation in the Congo (ONUC) in July 1960. It had about 20,000 troops at its height and withdrew in 1964.
Kasa-Vubu dismissed Lumumba on 5 September 1960 and Lumumba tried to dismiss Kasa-Vubu. Colonel Joseph Mobutu, the army chief of staff, took power on 14 September 1960.
Lumumba, who had appealed to the Soviet Union for help, was confined to his residence under UN guard. He left it in late November 1960 and was captured in December.
Lumumba was flown to Katanga and murdered there on 17 January 1961 with Belgian officers present. Belgium later accepted moral responsibility.

Mobutu first took power in 1960 and then seized it again in 1965, this time to rule for over thirty years. His rule shows how a Cold War ally could keep a weak state together while ruining its economy.
Mobutu seized power in a second coup on 24 November 1965, deposing Kasa-Vubu and putting the army in charge of the state.
The country was renamed Zaire in 1971. Mobutu's authenticité campaign banned Christian first names and replaced European suits with the abacost, to stress African identity.
In 1973 Zairianisation transferred foreign-owned plantations and businesses to Zairian owners, mostly Mobutu's associates. The economy collapsed as the copper price fell in 1974-75.
The Popular Movement of the Revolution (MPR) was the only legal party, so political opposition was suppressed.
The United States, Belgium and France supported Mobutu as a barrier to communism in central Africa. Their help repelled the Shaba invasions of 1977 and 1978 by Katangan exiles from Angola.
Mobutu announced the end of the one-party state in April 1990, under pressure from protests and the end of Cold War support. He stayed in power until he fell in 1997.
Tanganyika moved to independence without armed conflict under Julius Nyerere and then united with Zanzibar. It is the main example of the opportunities of independence.
Tanganyika was German East Africa until 1918, then a British mandate and, from 1946, a UN trust territory. In both cases Britain governed it on behalf of an international body.
Julius Nyerere founded the Tanganyika African National Union (TANU) in 1954 and led it to a majority in the 1960 elections.
Tanganyika became independent on 9 December 1961 with Nyerere as prime minister. It became a republic with Nyerere as president in December 1962.
Zanzibar became independent in December 1963, but a revolution in January 1964 overthrew its Arab-led government. The Afro-Shirazi Party dominated the new regime.
Tanganyika and Zanzibar united on 26 April 1964, and the union was renamed Tanzania in October 1964. Zanzibar kept its own government and its president, Abeid Karume.
In January 1964 the Tanganyika Rifles mutinied against British officers. Nyerere asked Britain for help, Royal Marines put down the mutiny, and the army was then rebuilt.
With no dominant ethnic group, Nyerere built a national identity instead of letting ethnic politics take hold. In foreign policy he was willing to quarrel with Britain over principle.
Tanzania was a multi-ethnic state with more than a hundred ethnic groups and no dominant majority, so no single group could claim to speak for the nation.
Nyerere made Swahili the national language and avoided ethnic parties. A shared language and a national identity reduced ethnic conflict after independence.

Nyerere broke off diplomatic relations with Britain in December 1965 over its failure to act against the white minority regime in Southern Rhodesia. The break was over Rhodesia, not over Tanzania's own affairs.
Tanzania nevertheless stayed in the Commonwealth, so it kept the association while criticising British policy.

Portugal refused to decolonise, so Angola's nationalists had to fight. The nationalists were divided among three movements (the MPLA, founded in 1956, the FNLA and UNITA, founded in 1966) with different regional and ethnic bases, and this division later fed a civil war.
Portugal under the Estado Novo regime of António de Oliveira Salazar regarded Angola as an overseas province rather than a colony, and it refused to grant independence.

Armed attacks in Luanda on 4 February 1961 began the Angolan war of independence. A rising in the north followed on 15 March 1961, in which many Europeans and Africans were killed and Portuguese reprisals were severe. The war lasted until 1974.
The MPLA, led by Agostinho Neto and founded in 1956, was strongest among the Mbundu and in Luanda.
The FNLA, led by Holden Roberto, was based among the Bakongo in the north.
UNITA, founded in 1966 and led by Jonas Savimbi, was based among the Ovimbundu.
The Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974 in Lisbon overthrew the Portuguese regime, and the new government agreed to grant independence to Angola.
Independence came in 1975 without agreement between the movements, so the anti-colonial war turned straight into a civil war that the Cold War powers fed.
The Alvor Agreement of January 1975 set up a transitional government in which the three movements shared power, but it broke down into fighting.
Angola became independent on 11 November 1975, with the MPLA under Neto holding Luanda.
The civil war between the MPLA and UNITA and the FNLA lasted until 2002. Cuban troops and Soviet aid supported the MPLA, while South African and American support went to its opponents.
Most of the roughly 300,000 Portuguese settlers left Angola in 1975, taking skills and capital with them. This left the new state short of skilled people.
Oil from Cabinda and diamonds became the main sources of revenue.
Independence did not end the link with the old rulers. Each power kept a different kind of influence, and this is what examiners mean when they ask whether the colonial powers helped or hindered.

Britain and Nigeria: Nigeria kept the Queen as head of state until becoming a republic in 1963 and stayed in the Commonwealth. British companies such as Shell-BP dominated the oil industry, and Britain supplied arms to the federal side in the Biafran War.
Belgium and the Congo: Belgium kept large economic interests through the Union Minière and backed Katanga's secession in 1960. Belgium later supported Mobutu.
Mobutu nationalised the Union Minière's Katanga assets in 1966-67, before reaching a settlement with it in 1969.
Portugal and Angola: Portugal's refusal to decolonise until 1974 meant Angola faced a long war, and Portugal's exit left Angola with few trained administrators.

Tanzania and Britain: Tanzania remained in the Commonwealth and received British aid, but Nyerere pursued non-alignment (not taking sides in the Cold War) and criticised Western economic influence. He also broke relations over Rhodesia in 1965.
France kept influence in its former colonies through co-operation accords, the franc zone and military agreements. This pattern was later called Françafrique.
Ethnic loyalty did not simply survive from the past. Colonial rule shaped it, and after independence politicians in several states built their support on it.

Colonial rulers defined and fixed ethnic identities through census categories, languages and indirect rule. Colonial officials then used the term tribalism to describe the ethnic loyalty that this policy had helped to harden.

In Nigeria, each of the three main parties drew its support from one region and one ethnic group. The army's officer corps also divided on regional lines, which contributed to the coups of 1966 and the massacres that followed.

In the Congo, the leading politicians drew support from particular regions and ethnic communities. Lumumba's base was in the east, Kasa-Vubu's party ABAKO drew on the Kongo people in the Léopoldville region in the west, and Tshombe's Conakat drew on the Lunda of Katanga.
Katanga's secession was partly based on the claim that the Katangan people had a separate identity from the rest of the Congo. The national government rejected this claim.

Tanzania's single language, Swahili, and the policy of building a national identity were among the factors that reduced ethnic conflict after independence. This gives a contrast to Nigeria and the Congo.
Independence brought real gains and serious dangers, and the balance differed from country to country. The best answers state a judgement and support it with a paired example on each side.
Opportunity: independence gave Africans control of their own governments. Nyerere's Tanzania pursued national unity and African development without a civil war.
Problem: the Belgian Congo's rapid independence left the new state with almost no trained administrators or officers, and the army's mutiny and the secession of Katanga followed within weeks.
Opportunity: Nigeria's oil revenue, which grew rapidly after the 1973 oil price rise, gave the federal government resources for reconstruction after the Biafran War.
Problem: the Biafran War and the 1966 coups showed how the federal structure could fail to hold ethnic groups together.
Problem: Angola's long war of independence ended in civil war because the three movements had different ethnic bases and different foreign backers.
Contemporary view: many African leaders saw independence as the end of colonial domination, while the former colonial powers often saw it as the start of a new relationship of trade and aid.
Later view: historians stress that colonial borders, ethnic policies and the Cold War constrained the new states, but they also stress African agency in shaping the outcomes.
Overall judgement: outcomes differed by country, with Tanzania stable, Nigeria and Angola at war and the Congo in crisis, so a balanced answer compares them.

Katanga was the richest province of the Belgian Congo, and its wealth was in the hands of a Belgian company. That wealth, and the ethnic politics that grew up around it, explain why the province tried to break away as soon as the Congo became independent.

Belgian rule had been paternalistic (the colonial power treated Africans like children to be guided): the Congo was Leopold II's Congo Free State and then the Belgian Congo from 1908. Few Congolese were educated, so there were almost no African officers or professionals at independence.

The Congo became independent on 30 June 1960 under President Kasa-Vubu and Prime Minister Lumumba, with its capital at Léopoldville. The army, the Force Publique, mutinied in early July and Belgian troops returned, so the new state was unstable from the start.

The crisis also unfolded during the Cold War, when the United States and the Soviet Union competed for influence in new states. The United Nations, led by its Secretary-General, tried to keep the Congo out of that rivalry.

Katanga, later called Shaba, was the copper-mining heart of the Congo and also produced cobalt and uranium. It was the richest province and supplied a very large share of the country's revenue, which gave its leaders a strong reason to want to keep that money.

The Union Minière du Haut-Katanga, a Belgian-controlled company, ran the mines. This is a transnational economy (companies and capital operating across borders): a foreign company shaped the province's economy, administration and politics.

Mining towns such as Élisabethville (now Lubumbashi), Kolwezi and Jadotville had a large European population, and Congolese workers lived in segregated housing. Belgian and settler interests backed Conakat because they wanted to keep Belgian influence.

Conakat (Confédération des associations tribales du Katanga) was formed in 1958 and came to be led by Moïse Tshombe, who was linked by marriage to the Lunda ruling family. It was strongest among the Lunda and campaigned for autonomy, even federalism, so that Katanga would keep its own revenue.

The rival Balubakat party, led by Jason Sendwe, drew support from the Baluba of northern Katanga and had links to Lumumba. Their rivalry is what the colonial and later term tribalism (ethnic loyalty) describes, though historians stress that politics and economics mattered as well as ethnicity.

Only eleven days after independence, Katanga declared itself a separate state. A secession is the breaking away of part of a state, and this one was backed by Belgium, so it became an international problem at once.
Tshombe proclaimed Katanga independent on 11 July 1960, eleven days after the Congo's independence. This is separate from the South Kasai secession of August 1960 and from the army mutiny.

In the May 1960 provincial elections Conakat formed the provincial government with Tshombe as president of the province, while in the national results Lumumba's allies were strong. Katanga's leaders therefore feared being ruled by Lumumba's government in Léopoldville.

Tshombe's reasons were to keep Katanga's revenue in the province, because it was so large, and to avoid a centralising government in Léopoldville which he called Communist and controlled by outsiders.

Belgian troops intervened from 10 July 1960, the day before the proclamation, and Belgium gave Katanga military and technical help. Belgian officers and advisers and paid foreign mercenaries trained and led the Katanga Gendarmerie (Katanga's army and police).
No state recognised Katanga, and Lumumba's government saw the secession as a threat to the unity of the Congo.
Lumumba appealed to the United Nations to help restore the Congo's territory. The Security Council set up ONUC, the UN force in the Congo, in July 1960 (resolution of 14 July).

On 9 August 1960 the Security Council called on Belgium to withdraw from Katanga, and UN troops entered the province on 12 August. Belgian troops withdrew after the UN arrived, but Belgian officers and advisers stayed on in the Katangan forces.

The Katanga crisis destroyed Lumumba. When the UN would not defeat the secession, he looked to the Soviet Union, which alarmed the West. He was dismissed in September 1960 and killed in Katanga in January 1961.

Lumumba was angry that ONUC would not use force against Tshombe. In August 1960 he accepted Soviet transport aircraft and trucks, which were used in an offensive in South Kasai, and this raised Western alarm about Cold War involvement in the Congo.
President Kasa-Vubu dismissed Lumumba on 5 September 1960. Lumumba declared Kasa-Vubu deposed, and on 14 September Colonel Mobutu's coup 'neutralised' both men, meaning it put both out of action.
Lumumba was confined to his residence under UN guard, left UN protection in late November 1960 and was arrested by Mobutu's troops in early December.
On 17 January 1961 he was flown to Katanga and killed, with Belgian officers present and Katangan leaders taking part. His death was announced on 13 February 1961.
The murder provoked Soviet and African protests and riots in several capitals. It also led to Security Council Resolution 161 of February 1961, which authorised the use of force as a last resort.
Lumumba became a martyr of African nationalism, which means he was honoured as a hero who died for African independence.

ONUC was meant to restore order, not to take sides. Its rule of staying out of internal disputes left it unable to end the secession, until events in 1961 pushed it into force and put Irish soldiers in the front line.

ONUC was the UN force sent to the Congo under Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld. It lasted 1960–64, and the UN declared it would not intervene in internal disputes except to prevent civil war, which is why Lumumba was angry that it would not use force against Katanga.
On 8 November 1960 an Irish patrol was ambushed at Niemba by Baluba tribesmen, and nine Irish soldiers were killed. Niemba was an ambush in 1960, whereas Jadotville was a siege in 1961.

Security Council Resolution 161 of 21 February 1961 authorised force as a last resort to prevent civil war, and called for foreign military personnel and mercenaries to leave. Resolution 169 of 24 November 1961 explicitly authorised action against the secession and the mercenaries.

Conor Cruise O'Brien, an Irish diplomat and the UN representative in Katanga in 1961, pushed for a firmer policy. Operation Rumpunch on 28 August 1961 was followed by Operation Morthor, launched on 13 September 1961 to arrest the foreign officers and take control of Élisabethville. Morthor failed.

At Jadotville, 155 men of A Company, 35th Battalion, under Commandant Pat Quinlan, were besieged from 13 September 1961 by Katangan gendarmes with foreign mercenaries. With no relief, little water and low ammunition they surrendered on 17 September.
No Irish soldier was killed at Jadotville, and the men were held prisoner for about a month.
O'Brien later wrote of his Katanga experience in To Katanga and Back (1962). The UN's Congo operation cost about 250 lives, among them about 26 Irish soldiers.
After Morthor failed, the UN lost its Secretary-General in a plane crash and then, under his successor, finally defeated Katanga's forces. The Cold War also hung over this period.

At the UN General Assembly in autumn 1960 Nikita Khrushchev attacked Hammarskjöld's handling of the Congo and proposed replacing the Secretary-General with a three-man body (a troika). This was a sign of Soviet hostility to the UN's role.

Hammarskjöld's plane crashed near Ndola in Northern Rhodesia in the night of 17–18 September 1961, while he was travelling to meet Tshombe. The cause remains disputed, so do not state that it was sabotage.

Fighting between UN and Katangan forces in Élisabethville in December 1961 ended with the Kitona Declaration of 21 December 1961. Tshombe seemed to accept Katanga's place in the Congo, but he later repudiated it (rejected it).
U Thant succeeded Hammarskjöld as Secretary-General and continued the operation. Operation Grand Slam against the Katangan forces began on 28 December 1962.
Tshombe announced the end of the secession at Kolwezi on 14 January 1963, and UN troops entered Kolwezi a week later. He announced this after Operation Grand Slam, not as a negotiated settlement.
Tshombe then left for exile. The secession had lasted about two and a half years, and its end removed the largest threat to the central government's authority.
Defeating the secession did not bring stability. Tshombe returned as national prime minister, the east rose in rebellion and the army, under Mobutu, took over.
Tshombe was recalled as prime minister of the Congo in July 1964 and held the post until Kasa-Vubu dismissed him in October 1965. The UN force left in 1964, leaving the army more important.

The Simba rebellion of 1964, by supporters of Lumumba, spread through the east. Stanleyville fell in August 1964, and in November 1964 Belgian paratroopers, carried by American aircraft, rescued hostages there. The rebellion was crushed in 1964-65 with the help of mercenaries.
Mobutu seized power on 24 November 1965, so this was his second coup, after that of 14 September 1960 which handed power back to Kasa-Vubu in 1961.
Tshombe went into exile in Spain. His plane was hijacked to Algeria in 1967 and he died in custody there in 1969.
The secession had shown the importance of the army and of foreign support, and Mobutu's coup used the army to end the factional fighting of the 1960s.

In 1977 and 1978 former Katangan gendarmes based in Angola invaded Shaba province. The 1977 invasion was repelled with Moroccan troops and a French airlift, and in 1978 French and Belgian paratroops retook Kolwezi.
The United States supported Mobutu's regime with military aid after 1965, which made the army a key instrument of Cold War policy in central Africa.

Born Joseph-Désiré Mobutu on 14 October 1930 at Lisala, he served in the Force Publique (the colonial army) and worked as a journalist before independence. He rose to become dictator of the Congo, which he renamed Zaire, and ruled until 1997. Within this topic, his importance is that the crisis of 1960-65 gave him the army, Western backing and the means to take power.

He was chief of staff of the Congolese army from July 1960 and led the coup of 14 September 1960 that 'neutralised' Lumumba and Kasa-Vubu. His troops arrested Lumumba in December 1960, and he handed power back to Kasa-Vubu in February 1961.

As a direct participant he worked with the CIA station chief Larry Devlin in 1960, and the United States saw him as the best anti-communist leader. The Church Committee of the US Senate in 1975 later revealed CIA plans against Lumumba.

He was shaped by events: the crisis gave him control of the army and Western backing, and it taught him the dangers of fragmentation. He seized power again on 24 November 1965, and foreign support helped keep him in power.
He had four politicians hanged in public in June 1966, founded his Popular Movement of the Revolution (MPR) in 1967 and ruled as president under a one-party system.

He nationalised the Union Minière's Katanga assets in 1966-67, creating Gécamines. He launched the policy of authenticité (a return to African authenticity) in 1971, renamed the Congo Zaire in 1971 and took the name Mobutu Sese Seko in 1972.
Contemporaries in the West, including the United States and Belgium, regarded him as a bulwark against communism in central Africa, whereas many Congolese saw a corrupt ruler who enriched his circle.
Historians describe personal dictatorship and kleptocracy (rule by theft): he drew on mineral revenues and Western aid, rewarded loyalists and kept the state weak.

Only the period to 1990 belongs to this topic: in April 1990 he announced the end of the one-party state, and his Western support weakened with the end of the Cold War. He was overthrown in May 1997 by Laurent-Désiré Kabila and died in exile in Morocco in September 1997.
The secession mattered inside the Congo, where it tested whether the state could survive, and far beyond it, where it involved the UN, the superpowers and the African states.
Nationally, the secession tested whether the Congo could survive as one state, and the central government's victory preserved its territory. However, the state stayed weak and dominated by the army.
Internationally, the crisis was a Cold War contest in which the United States and the Soviet Union, and the former colonial power Belgium, supported different sides.
The Katanga case set a precedent for the UN's involvement in internal conflicts and for its peacekeeping role (using troops to keep order between rival forces).
This differs from Suez, where a UN force separated combatants, because in the Congo the UN used force on a member state's territory.
Mobutu nationalised the Union Minière's Katangan assets in 1966-67 and set up the state company Gécamines, so the province's mineral wealth became the central state's main source of revenue.

African states divided: the Casablanca group, including Ghana, Guinea and Egypt, backed Lumumba and the central government. The crisis was one of the first tests of African unity before the Organisation of African Unity was founded in 1963.

The cost of the operation caused a UN financial crisis because the Soviet Union and France refused to pay towards it. The death of Hammarskjöld is also part of the crisis's international significance.
Examiners reward an argument that ranks the causes and weighs success against limits, and contemporary views against later ones. These paired points give you that material.

Cause: Katanga's mineral revenues, held by the Belgian-controlled Union Minière, gave its leaders a strong economic reason to keep control of their wealth, and Belgian companies and officials supported that aim.
Cause: Conakat claimed that Katanga's peoples had a separate regional identity, and fear of Lumumba's centralising government strengthened regional loyalties.

International involvement came from Belgian self-interest in protecting its investments, Cold War rivalry (the Soviet aid to Lumumba and the CIA role) and the UN's duty to protect a member state's territory.
Achievement: the central government's victory kept the Congo's borders as drawn at independence, in line with the African principle of accepting colonial frontiers.
Limit: the Congo became dependent on foreign military support, and the Simba rebellion of 1964 and then army rule showed how much remained unstable.

Contemporary view: the central government, much of Africa and the Soviet bloc saw the secession as a neo-colonial plot, while Tshombe and his supporters saw it as self-determination against centralised rule.
Contemporary view of the UN: the Soviet bloc and some African states accused it of failing to protect Lumumba and the central government.

Later view: Ludo De Witte's book on Lumumba's murder prompted a Belgian parliamentary inquiry, which reported in 2001 that Belgian ministers and officials bore moral responsibility. Historians stress the roles of Belgium and the Union Minière in sustaining Katanga.

Most African states became independent between the late 1950s and 1960s, but political independence did not bring economic independence. Colonial rule had built economies to export raw materials to Europe, and those structures outlived the flags coming down.

Colonial economies were organised around cash crops (crops grown for sale abroad, not for local food) and minerals: cocoa in the Gold Coast, groundnuts in Senegal, cotton in Uganda and copper in Katanga.
Railways and ports were built to carry exports to the coast, so most African transport networks linked interior mines and farms to ports rather than to each other.
Colonial powers controlled trade through their own companies and currencies, so African states inherited trading patterns that tied them to a few European markets.
Colonial governments in the Belgian Congo and Portuguese Mozambique forced peasants to grow set quantities of cotton, which was bought at fixed low prices.
Raúl Prebisch and Hans Singer argued from 1950 that the terms of trade (the ratio of export prices to import prices) tend to move against primary producers, those who sell raw materials.
African countries therefore have to export more to buy the same manufactured goods, and commodity prices fell sharply in the 1980s.

Dependence on one or two commodities made African economies vulnerable to price falls, because a single bad year in world markets cut national income. Examples are copper prices in the mid-1970s and cocoa and coffee prices in the 1980s.

Multinational companies (firms operating in many countries) such as Unilever's United Africa Company, Shell-BP in Nigerian oil and Union Minière du Haut-Katanga in Katanga copper kept control of trade, oil and mining after independence.
This is why the topic is linked to the idea of a transnational economy, in which trade, finance and production cross borders through multinationals and lenders.

The European Economic Community (EEC), created by the Treaty of Rome in 1957, set up trade and aid agreements with former African colonies. These grew from an association of colonies into the Lomé Conventions, which offered a new kind of deal.
The Treaty of Rome of 1957 associated the overseas territories of the EEC members, mostly in Africa, with the Community. This gave those territories special trading links with the new EEC.

The Yaoundé Convention of 1963 (with a second in 1969) between the EEC and 18 associated African states gave their exports duty-free access to European markets in return for limited reciprocal opening of their own markets.

Lomé I was signed on 28 February 1975 in Lomé, Togo, between the EEC (then nine members) and 46 African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) states. The ACP group was formally founded by the Georgetown Agreement in June 1975.
Britain's entry in 1973 had brought in Commonwealth countries, so the group was wider than the Yaoundé states.

Lomé I gave ACP exports largely duty-free access to the EEC without requiring reciprocal concessions, meaning the ACP did not have to open its own markets in return. This was a new departure in trade relations, though agricultural products covered by the Common Agricultural Policy were treated less generously.

STABEX was a fund set up under Lomé I to compensate ACP countries when earnings from listed agricultural exports fell below a reference level. It cushioned the price falls that made single-commodity economies so vulnerable.
Lomé I also included a Sugar Protocol, which guaranteed quotas for ACP sugar at European prices. Lomé II (1979) added SYSMIN, support for mineral exporters.

Later Conventions were signed in 1979 (Lomé II), 1984 (Lomé III) and 1989 (Lomé IV). Lomé IV was revised in the mid-1990s, when human rights became an essential element, and the Conventions were replaced by the Cotonou Agreement, signed in 2000.
The Conventions had limits. ACP exports stayed concentrated on a few commodities despite the preferences, and the aid element was small against the needs of the countries involved.

In the 1970s many African governments borrowed heavily, and in the 1980s they could not repay. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank then used their loans to push through economic reforms that proved very controversial.

The IMF and the World Bank were created at the Bretton Woods conference in the United States in July 1944. The IMF lends to countries with balance-of-payments problems (when they spend more abroad than they earn), with conditions attached, while the World Bank funds development projects.

Oil price rises in 1973 and 1979 raised import costs for oil-importing African states, so many governments borrowed heavily from banks and international lenders in the 1970s to keep paying their bills.

When interest rates rose in the early 1980s and commodity prices fell, African countries earned less and owed more, so they struggled to repay. Mexico's default in August 1982 marked the start of the wider debt crisis.

From the early 1980s the IMF and World Bank made new loans conditional on structural adjustment programmes: devaluation (making the currency cheaper), cuts in public spending, removal of subsidies and the sale of state enterprises (privatisation).

The World Bank's report Accelerated Development in Sub-Saharan Africa, known as the Berg Report (1981), blamed African governments' own policies: overvalued currencies, state marketing boards and neglect of agriculture.
Critics argued that structural adjustment cut spending on health and education, so the poor paid for it. UNICEF's 1987 report Adjustment with a Human Face made the case for protecting the poor.

Ghana under Jerry Rawlings adopted an IMF-backed Economic Recovery Programme from 1983. Supporters presented it as an early success, but this view was contested because the programme brought hardship.
Aid was meant to help new states develop, but it came with strings and often kept them tied to the same partners as before. Examiners reward answers that weigh both its benefits and its costs.
Aid came in two forms: bilateral aid, given government to government by a donor state, and multilateral aid, channelled through bodies such as the World Bank and the UN.
Tied aid required recipients to spend the money on goods and services from the donor country, which increased its cost and reduced its value to the recipient.
Many former colonies received aid from their former rulers, so aid often reinforced existing trade and political links rather than diversifying them.
Aid was criticised for supporting corrupt or authoritarian governments, such as Mobutu's Zaire, which received large Western aid, and for creating dependence on donors for budgets and food.
Some African governments tried to reduce dependence by promoting local industry and regional trade, but many national markets remained small and fragmented.
The United Nations General Assembly set a target in 1970 that rich countries give 0.7 per cent of national income as aid. Most donors did not reach it.

Cold War rivalry shaped aid because both superpowers courted African states. China built the TAZARA railway from Zambia to the Tanzanian port of Dar es Salaam, with Chinese finance and labour, between about 1970 and 1975. The Soviet Union and the United States each aided their allies.

Famines in the post-colonial period were caused by war, drought and state policy, and they drew international relief efforts. Public reaction in Europe and North America, helped by television and photographs, shaped the later charity movement.
During the Biafran War (1967-70), blockade and fighting caused a famine in Biafra in 1968-70, and images of starving children drew wide attention in Europe and North America.

Relief flights into Biafra mostly ran at night from São Tomé to the Uli airstrip, and they were limited by the federal government's control of the airspace. In June 1969 a Red Cross aircraft was shot down.

A drought in the Sahel (the dry belt south of the Sahara) from the late 1960s to the mid-1970s caused famine across Mali, Niger, Chad, Mauritania, Upper Volta (now Burkina Faso) and Senegal, with large loss of livestock.
The Wollo famine of 1972-74 was in Ethiopia, not the Sahel proper. It helped bring down Emperor Haile Selassie, who was deposed in 1974.

The Ethiopian famine of 1983-85 killed hundreds of thousands, with estimates from about 300,000 to one million. Drought combined with the policies of the Derg (the military regime) and the wars in Eritrea and Tigray. A BBC report by Michael Buerk in October 1984 brought it to Western attention.

The British singer Bob Geldof organised the Band Aid charity single 'Do They Know It's Christmas?', released in December 1984. The Live Aid concerts in London and Philadelphia on 13 July 1985 followed, and Live Aid raised about 150 million pounds over time for famine relief.
Famine relief was also criticised for distorting local markets, because free food undercut local farmers, and for prolonging wars when food aid went to armed groups.
The Ethiopian government's resettlement programme of 1984-86 moved about 600,000 people from the drought-hit north. Many thousands died, though estimates vary.
Much famine relief and development work was done not by governments but by voluntary organisations, and several of the best known were Irish.
Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) are non-state charities and campaigning bodies that deliver aid and work on development projects.
Oxfam was founded in Oxford in 1942 as the Oxford Committee for Famine Relief, and it later expanded into development work across Africa and Asia.
Concern was founded in Dublin in 1968 by John and Kay O'Loughlin Kennedy in response to the Biafran famine, and it became one of Ireland's main aid agencies.

Trócaire was founded in 1973 by the Catholic bishops of Ireland as the Irish Catholic development agency, and it works through local partners in Africa. Its annual Lenten campaign raised money and awareness in Irish parishes and became one of the best-known development campaigns in Ireland.
GOAL was founded in Dublin in 1977 by John O'Shea. Médecins Sans Frontières was founded in France in 1971 by doctors, some of whom had worked in Biafra.

NGOs distinguish between emergency relief (short-term help in a crisis) and long-term development (building lasting ability to feed and educate people). Many shifted in the 1980s towards community projects and advocacy, meaning campaigning for change.
The Irish government began an official aid programme in 1974, and Irish missionary orders had long worked in Africa.
Julius Nyerere, leader of Tanzania, tried to build African socialism through state control and rural villages. The policy began as a voluntary programme and turned compulsory.

The Arusha Declaration of 5 February 1967, issued by TANU (the ruling party) under Julius Nyerere, committed Tanzania to ujamaa (familyhood, or African socialism), self-reliance and state control of the main means of production.
The government nationalised the banks and major industries in 1967. It also introduced 'Education for Self-Reliance' in 1967, a policy to shape schooling around rural work and life.
TANU's Mwongozo (guidelines) of 1971 required party members to work for their living and to avoid exploitation and privilege. It was a leadership code.
The ujamaa villages were voluntary cooperative settlements at first. But from 1973-74 the government moved millions of people into villages, often by force, in a policy called villagisation.

Villagisation disrupted farming because families were moved away from their fields, and food shortages followed. Do not confuse ujamaa (the policy), villagisation (the compulsory phase) and the Arusha Declaration (the 1967 statement).
Ujamaa produced real gains in education and health but also economic decline. How Nyerere is judged depends on which of these is stressed.

Universal primary education, launched in 1974, aimed to put every child in school by 1977, and primary enrolment rose rapidly. Tanzania's literacy and primary schooling expanded markedly, which showed what a poor country could achieve in social services.

Villagisation was not the only cause of the crisis. The oil price rise of 1979, drought and the cost of the war to overthrow Idi Amin of Uganda in 1978-79 added to it. Tanzania had to import food, and the economy was in decline by the early 1980s.
Nyerere stepped down as president in 1985. His successor Ali Hassan Mwinyi accepted an IMF agreement in 1986 that reversed many of the socialist policies.
Nyerere, known as Mwalimu (teacher), died in 1999. Supporters stress his gains in education, health and national unity and his refusal to rule by ethnic favour.
Critics stress the collapse of farm output, the use of compulsion and the one-party state, since Tanzania was ruled by TANU/CCM with no legal rival.
Development workers, including missionaries, volunteers and agency staff, carried out most of the day-to-day aid work in rural Africa from the 1960s. Aengus Finucane is a documented Irish example.

Development workers came from churches, voluntary bodies such as Britain's Voluntary Service Overseas (1958), government programmes such as the American Peace Corps (1961), and NGOs such as Concern and Trócaire.
Aengus Finucane, an Irish Holy Ghost priest (Spiritan), worked in Biafra relief during the war, 1968-70, with Concern. He later led Concern as chief executive until 1997 and died in 2009.

Their typical work included well-digging, agricultural advice, primary health care and vaccination, the supply of food in famines, and training of local staff, so that communities could manage after the workers left.
Many arrived as young volunteers on short contracts, and they often lived in remote rural communities with limited access to medicine, transport and communications.

Their problems included poor roads and supplies, cultural misunderstandings with local communities, the risk of violence during civil wars, and the difficulty of keeping projects running after the donor left.
They were participants in the aid system but also witnesses to its results, and their reports were important sources for NGO campaigns in Europe and North America.

Contemporaries in Europe often saw development workers as humanitarian heroes, while some critics saw them as agents of dependence on foreign money. Historians have criticised 'top-down' development projects of the 1960s and 1970s, and they have praised the shift in the 1980s towards projects planned with local people.
Irish missionary orders such as the Holy Ghost Fathers and the Medical Missionaries of Mary ran schools, hospitals and clinics in Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania and elsewhere.

The verdict is mixed, and examiners reward a stated judgement supported by paired achievements and limits. Colonial structures, debt, dependence and famine weigh against gains in health, education and trade terms.
Achievement: the Lomé Conventions gave ACP states preferential access to European markets and a stabilisation fund (STABEX), which was a recognised innovation in trade policy.
Limit: despite these trade preferences, most ACP exports stayed concentrated on a few primary commodities, and commodity prices fell in the 1980s.

Achievement: international health campaigns eradicated smallpox, whose last natural case was in Somalia in 1977 and which the World Health Organization declared eradicated in 1980. Aid and NGO work also improved access to water and primary schooling in many areas.
Limit: debt and structural adjustment left many governments cutting public services, and the famines of the 1970s and 1980s showed how fragile food supply remained.
Achievement: Tanzania's expansion of literacy and primary education showed what a government with limited resources could achieve in social services.
Limit: villagisation and the collapse of agricultural output showed that state-directed development could cause serious hardship.
