Later view: Walter Rodney, in How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972), blamed colonial exploitation, while the World Bank's Berg Report of 1981 blamed domestic policies. Most historians now combine colonial legacies, falling commodity prices, Cold War pressures and government choices.

After 1945 both Britain and France needed workers and both ruled or had ruled overseas peoples, so people from the colonies moved to the old imperial centres. Four ideas run through this topic and are used in the same sense throughout.

Britain after 1945 had labour shortages in reconstruction, the new National Health Service, transport and industry, and its empire was turning into a Commonwealth (a group of independent states linked to Britain), so many colonial subjects held British status.
France also needed labour for reconstruction and the post-war boom. It had colonies and territories in North and West Africa, and Algeria was treated as part of France until independence in 1962.

The Second World War had discredited racist ideas, because the Nazis had shown where they led. Even so, colour prejudice persisted in both societies, and this is the setting for the conflicts that follow.

Racism means treating people as inferior or different because of their race or colour. It shows itself in prejudice (hostile attitudes), discrimination (unfair treatment in jobs or housing) and violence.
Cultural diversity means many cultures, religions and languages living within one society, which is what migration produced in both countries.
Identity is how migrants and their children saw themselves, often caught between the culture of their family's origin and the host society they lived in.

Assimilation is the expectation that migrants adopt the majority culture, which was the French approach. Multiculturalism, or integration with diversity, accepts that distinct cultures can continue within a common framework, which became the British approach.

Britain's post-war labour shortage and the Commonwealth citizenship laws brought large numbers of migrants from the Caribbean and South Asia. They came because there was work in Britain and because the law let them in.
The British Nationality Act of 1948 made citizens of the UK and Colonies and of Commonwealth countries British subjects, with the right to enter and settle in Britain.

The SS Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury on 22 June 1948 with about 1,000 passengers, most of them from Jamaica and other Caribbean islands, and it became the symbol of the start of Caribbean migration.

Post-war labour shortages led Britain to recruit workers in the Caribbean in the 1950s, for example for the National Health Service (founded in 1948) and London Transport, and poor prospects at home made the offer attractive.
Migration from India and Pakistan grew in the 1950s and later included Bangladesh, with many migrants from Punjab and Gujarat settling in Birmingham, Leicester, Bradford and London.
Migrants were concentrated in a few big cities and industrial areas, especially London, the West Midlands and Yorkshire, where the jobs were.
Most migrants held Commonwealth citizenship, so they had the right to vote and to live in Britain, but they still faced discrimination in housing and jobs.

Caribbean migrants met a colour bar (a refusal to let rooms to black people) in lodgings. In Notting Hill the landlord Peter Rachman became notorious in the 1950s for overcrowded, exploitative lettings to newcomers.
Migration rose sharply in 1961–62 because migrants rushed to enter Britain before the 1962 Act took effect and restricted entry.

As migrants settled, hostility from some of the white population turned to violence in 1958. These were the first major riots about race in post-war Britain, and they pushed the question of racism into politics.
In August 1958 disturbances broke out in Nottingham, and in late August and September 1958 white youths attacked West Indian residents in Notting Hill, in serious racial violence.
The disturbances were caused by overcrowded housing and competition for jobs and housing, and by far-right agitation in the area, such as Oswald Mosley's Union Movement and the White Defence League.

The Trinidad-born journalist Claudia Jones organised an indoor Caribbean carnival in London in January 1959, a response that celebrated Caribbean culture and became a precursor of the Notting Hill Carnival.
Kelso Cochrane, an Antiguan-born carpenter, was murdered in a racist attack in Notting Hill in May 1959, and his death increased pressure for a legal response to racism.
From 1962 governments began to restrict entry, and public debate treated migration as a problem. Extremist groups grew, and so did campaigns against them.

The Commonwealth Immigrants Act of 1962 introduced employment vouchers, which restricted the entry of Commonwealth citizens who had no job arranged in Britain. The Irish were not covered because of the Common Travel Area.
In February 1968 a new Commonwealth Immigrants Act was passed through Parliament in a few days to restrict the entry of Kenyan Asians holding British passports, who faced discrimination in Kenya.

Enoch Powell, a Conservative MP, spoke at a Conservative meeting in Birmingham on 20 April 1968, warning that continued immigration would lead to violence. Edward Heath dismissed him from the Shadow Cabinet the next day, but some London dockers marched in his support.
The speech is known as the 'rivers of blood' speech because it referred to the Tiber 'foaming with much blood', though Powell did not use the phrase itself.
The Immigration Act of 1971 introduced patriality, the right of abode (the right to live in Britain freely) for those with a parent or grandparent born in Britain. It came into force in 1973.

President Idi Amin ordered Asians out of Uganda in August 1972, giving them 90 days to leave. About 27,000 settled in Britain, many holding British passports, helped by the Ugandan Asian Resettlement Board.

The National Front, founded in 1967, campaigned for an end to immigration but stood candidates in the general elections of 1974 and 1979 but never won a parliamentary seat. Its clashes with opponents included the Battle of Lewisham in August 1977 and the death of the teacher Blair Peach at an anti-NF protest in Southall in April 1979.

Rock Against Racism (1976) and the Anti-Nazi League (1977) organised counter-campaigns against the National Front. Overall, migration was framed as a problem and entry was restricted, while the rights of those already settled were protected by law.
While entry was being restricted, Parliament also made discrimination against people already living in Britain illegal. Each Act widened the ban and set up a body to promote it.
The Race Relations Act of 1965 banned discrimination on grounds of colour, race or ethnic or national origins in public places, and it created the Race Relations Board.
The Race Relations Act of 1968 extended the ban to housing, employment and services, which were the areas where migrants had faced the colour bar, and it created the Community Relations Commission.
The Race Relations Act of 1976 extended the law to indirect discrimination (rules that look neutral but disadvantage one group) and created the Commission for Racial Equality.
The laws were enforced through complaints and conciliation, and critics argued that they were limited because discrimination was difficult to prove in practice.
Home Secretary Roy Jenkins said in 1966 that integration should mean equal opportunity accompanied by cultural diversity, not assimilation, and this set the direction of British policy.
By the early 1980s many young black people faced unemployment, discrimination in jobs and housing, and tense relations with the police. In 1981 these tensions exploded in riots.
Young black people suffered high unemployment in the early 1980s as well as discrimination in jobs and housing, which left many with little stake in society and fed resentment.

Stop and search under the 'sus' laws (the Vagrancy Act of 1824, which let police stop people on suspicion) was used heavily against young black men, and many black residents saw it as harassment. The law was repealed in 1981.
The Brixton riots of 10–12 April 1981 followed Operation Swamp 81, in which police stopped and searched nearly a thousand people in about a week, mostly young black men. Hundreds were injured.
Riots broke out in Toxteth in Liverpool and Moss Side in Manchester in July 1981, as well as in other cities. Police used CS gas on the British mainland for the first time in Toxteth.
The Scarman Report of November 1981 (by Lord Scarman) named racial disadvantage, unemployment and poor relations between police and community as the causes of the riots.
Scarman rejected the idea that the police were institutionally racist (racist in their rules and culture), but accepted that individual officers had acted improperly.

Scarman recommended community policing and consultation, so that police would work with local people. The Police and Criminal Evidence Act of 1984 reformed police powers, and the report was one influence on it among others.

By the 1980s Britain had large Caribbean, Indian, Pakistani and Bangladeshi communities, and their culture changed British life in music, food, religion and politics. Their presence also caused tension, as the Rushdie affair showed.
Caribbean communities shaped British music, including reggae, ska and calypso, and Caribbean food and festivals became part of urban life.
Notting Hill Carnival began as a street festival in 1966 and grew into one of the largest street festivals in Europe.
Muslims from South Asia built mosques in the 1960s and 1970s, and Sikh and Hindu communities built gurdwaras (Sikh places of worship) and temples in Birmingham, Leicester and London.
Multiculturalism became British policy, supported by local councils and the Race Relations Acts, which encouraged recognition of distinct cultures within a common framework of laws.
The Rampton Report (1981) and the Swann Report (1985) on the education of ethnic minority children argued that schools should recognise those children's needs.
Black and Asian candidates entered Parliament: Diane Abbott, Paul Boateng, Bernie Grant and Keith Vaz were elected in 1987.

The Rushdie affair of 1988–89 showed the tension between religious identity and freedom of expression. Copies of The Satanic Verses (1988) were burned in Bradford in January 1989, and Ayatollah Khomeini issued a fatwa (a religious ruling) against Salman Rushdie in February 1989.

France also recruited workers after 1945, but its migrants came from southern Europe and from its former colonies in North and West Africa. Many of them lived in very poor conditions, and the Algerian war cast a long shadow over them.

Post-war reconstruction created labour shortages, and the state set up the National Immigration Office (ONI) in 1945 to recruit. Migrants came from Italy, Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Tunisia, Algeria and West Africa and worked in factories, mines and construction.
Algerians had French status until independence in 1962 and could move freely between Algeria and France, so their movement to the mainland was not immigration in the legal sense before then.

Many migrants lived in bidonvilles, shanty towns on the edges of French cities, such as Nanterre near Paris, in the 1950s and 1960s. Later migrants were housed on housing estates and in state-backed hostels for migrant workers.
On 17 October 1961 Paris police under Maurice Papon attacked an Algerian demonstration against a curfew. Dozens at least were killed, and the number remains disputed.

Algerian migration continued after 1962 and brought the legacy of the Algerian war into French politics. The harkis, Algerians who had served in the French army, came to France as refugees rather than as labour migrants and faced hostility and poor housing.
Labour immigration was suspended in 1974, but migration did not end, because families joined those already in France. This produced a new generation that was born and raised in France.
In July 1974 the French government suspended labour immigration, which stopped new recruitment of workers but not the arrival of families.
In 1976 the government allowed family reunification for migrants who had been living in France, so wives and children joined them and migrants settled permanently.
After 1977 the government offered payments to migrants who agreed to go home, but few accepted, with little effect.

Migrants from North and West Africa raised a second generation, the 'beurs' (the French-born children of North African migrants), who grew up in the banlieues (the suburbs around big cities) and by the 1980s were a focus of French debate about integration.
France treated migrants very differently from Britain. Its model rested on the idea that the state deals with individual citizens, not with ethnic or religious groups.
The French model of integration was based on universal citizenship: all citizens were equal before the law, and the state did not recognise ethnic or religious communities as such.
Assimilation meant that migrants were expected to adopt the French language, values and civic practices, and to keep their ethnic identities in private.
The law separating church and state in 1905 established laïcité, state secularism, which shaped how public religious expression was regulated. Laïcité is secularism, not assimilation itself.
France collected no statistics by ethnic origin, which meant that discrimination was harder to measure and debate than in Britain.
The Pleven law of 1972 was France's main anti-racist legislation, and it made incitement to racial hatred a criminal offence.
The two countries faced similar pressures but responded in different ways. A good comparison pairs a similarity or difference in one country with the matching fact from the other.
Similarity: both states restricted immigration in the 1970s, Britain with the Acts of 1962, 1968 and 1971 and France with the halt of 1974.

Similarity: both had far-right parties that gained support by the late 1970s and 1980s, both had racial violence in urban areas, and both saw discrimination and the concentration of migrants in poor housing.

Difference: most migrants to Britain were Commonwealth citizens with a legal right of entry, while migrants to France came from southern Europe as well as North and West Africa, and Algerians had a distinct legal status until 1962.
Difference: Britain developed multiculturalism, which recognised ethnic groups, while France used assimilation, which recognised individuals as citizens.

Difference: Britain monitored ethnic groups, which let it measure discrimination, while France collected no ethnic statistics. Britain also passed three Race Relations Acts, while France's main anti-racist law was the Pleven law of 1972.
Difference: Britain's migrants came largely from former colonies in the Caribbean and South Asia, and France's from its former North African and West African colonies.
Both countries tried to integrate migrants, with real achievements and real limits. Historians judge each model by how far it ended disadvantage.
Achievement: Britain's anti-discrimination laws gave migrants a legal basis for challenging discrimination in jobs, housing and public services.
Limit: the laws did not end disadvantage, and the 1981 riots showed that unemployment and police practices remained sources of conflict.
Achievement: France's universal citizenship gave second-generation migrants a legal claim to French nationality, and many took part fully in French public life.
Limit: the assimilation model made it difficult to recognise ethnic discrimination, and the banlieues showed the tensions it created.
Contemporary view: many politicians in both countries saw migration mainly as an economic and security problem, while migrant communities often saw discrimination as the main issue.

Later view: scholars contrast Britain's race-relations model, which counted ethnic groups and tackled discrimination through the law, with France's republican model, which counted no one by origin. Each has been criticised for failing to end disadvantage.

To follow race relations in 1980s France you need the ideas and the politics behind them. France expected everyone to become French in the same way, and the party in power changed twice in the decade.

The republican ideal says citizens are individuals, equal before the law, so the state does not recognise ethnic or religious groups. This is why France expected migrants and their children to assimilate (adopt French language, values and civic culture) rather than keep a separate group identity.
Laïcité (state secularism, based on the 1905 law separating Church and State) keeps religion out of public institutions such as state schools. It was at stake in the headscarf affair of 1989.
Jus soli means nationality by birth in the territory. It matters here because French-born children of foreign parents could become French, and the Right tried to change how this worked in 1986-87.
Racism means ranking people by race and treating them differently, shown in violence, discrimination and exclusion.

Identity, here, is the question of how the second generation (French citizens of North African heritage) saw themselves and were seen. Cultural diversity means many cultures and religions in one society, which the banlieues and the second generation made visible.

Politically, the Socialist François Mitterrand became President in May 1981 and was re-elected in 1988. The Right won the 1986 parliamentary elections, giving a Chirac government (1986-88) that shared power with a Socialist president, known as cohabitation, and Michel Rocard led the Left's government from 1988.

By the early 1980s the children of North African and West African migrants lived in the banlieues, where unemployment and policing were the main grievances. Knowing who lived there, and why they were angry, explains the events that follow.

The banlieues were the working-class suburbs and high-rise estates around French cities. Many were built from the 1950s and 1960s to house migrant families and urban workers, and by the 1980s they had become rundown.
Many families lived in HLM estates (habitation à loyer modéré, public housing), so poor housing and the condition of the estates became part of the grievance.
Les Minguettes, an estate in Vénissieux near Lyon, was one of the best-known banlieues, and it became the scene of unrest in 1981.

The second generation, known as 'beurs' (verlan, a French slang that reverses syllables, from 'arabe'), had been born or raised in France and had French citizenship or a right to it. This is why their demand was to be treated as French.

The oil shock of 1973 ended the post-war economic boom, and migrant workers in the factories were among the first to lose their jobs. Youth unemployment in the banlieues was therefore far above the national average, and many young people were in low-skilled work or outside the labour market.
Relations between young people and the police were poor, and identity checks and stop-and-search practices were a constant complaint in the banlieues.

At the 1982 census about 800,000 Algerians lived in France, making them the largest foreign nationality, ahead of Portuguese and then Moroccans. Post-war labour migration, including from the Maghreb and West Africa, and the halt to labour migration in 1974 explain how these communities came to settle.
In summer 1981 anger in the banlieues erupted at Les Minguettes. The new Socialist government had to respond, and its measures helped some people but left the main grievances untouched.
In summer 1981 young men at Les Minguettes stole and burned cars, in what the press called 'rodéos', and clashed with police, drawing national television coverage.
The unrest spread to other banlieues in Lyon and elsewhere, and it drew national attention to the living conditions of second-generation migrants.
The Socialist government of François Mitterrand, elected in May 1981, responded with social programmes for the banlieues and promised reforms to immigration law.

The government created Priority Education Zones (ZEP, giving extra help to schools in deprived areas) in 1981 and launched the 'Banlieues 89' regeneration project in 1983. Both were limited in scale, so they did not remove the causes of disadvantage.

The Dubedout report of 1983 (by Hubert Dubedout, 'Ensemble, refaire la ville') recommended local regeneration and more involvement of residents in their neighbourhoods. It led to the 'développement social des quartiers' programme, so residents' views began to shape local projects.

The government regularised the status of about 130,000 undocumented migrants in 1981-82, so they could stay legally. A law of July 1984 created a ten-year residence card, which gave long-term security.

Mitterrand's 1981 manifesto promised local voting rights for foreign residents, and he spoke of a 'right to be different' (droit à la différence). The voting-rights promise was never carried out, which left a lasting grievance.
The second generation organised a national protest in 1983. A police shooting set it off, and the march showed that beurs could run a national campaign.

The cause was the shooting and wounding of Toumi Djaïdja, a young man from Les Minguettes, by a police officer in June 1983. The priest Christian Delorme and the Protestant pastor Jean Costil helped organise the march.
The march set out from Marseille on 15 October 1983 with about 30 people. It grew as it crossed France and reached Paris on 3 December 1983 with tens of thousands of supporters.
A delegation was received at the Élysée (the presidential palace) by President Mitterrand, who promised the ten-year residence card. It was enacted in 1984.
The demands were equal treatment in jobs, housing and policing, and the right of second-generation migrants to be treated as French citizens.
The press called it the 'Marche des Beurs' because its core was second-generation young people, but its official title was the March for Equality and against Racism.
It was organised with local associations and churches, and it showed that second-generation migrants could run a national political campaign.
After the march, a new organisation turned anti-racism into a mass youth movement. It was popular and well backed, but critics doubted how much it changed.
SOS Racisme was founded in Paris in 1984, launched in October, by young activists including Harlem Désir and Julien Dray. It quickly grew into a national organisation with local branches.
Its slogan, 'Touche pas à mon pote' (Hands off my pal), appeared on a badge in the shape of a yellow open hand worn widely by young people. It expressed solidarity across ethnic lines.
It was supported by the Socialist government, by celebrities and by trade unions, and it ran concerts and campaigns against racism in schools and workplaces.
A free concert in the Place de la Concorde, Paris, on 15 June 1985 drew hundreds of thousands of young people, which shows how popular the movement had become.
Critics on the left argued that SOS Racisme focused on individual racism and did not address the social causes of disadvantage in the banlieues, such as unemployment and housing.
Some of the 1983 marchers accused the Socialists of using SOS Racisme to take over the anti-racist movement.
The Front National (FN) was a far-right party that won votes by campaigning against immigration. Its breakthrough in 1983 made it a political force.

The FN was founded on 5 October 1972 by Jean-Marie Le Pen, born in 1928, a former paratrooper who had served in Algeria. It had the backing of far-right groups including Ordre Nouveau, and it drew on supporters of Algérie française (keeping Algeria French).
Its policies were to restrict immigration, expel illegal migrants and give 'national preference' (priority for French citizens) in jobs and housing.
Its breakthrough came in the municipal election at Dreux (Eure-et-Loir) in September 1983, not a by-election. Jean-Pierre Stirbois's list won about 17 per cent in the first round on 4 September.
In the second round on 11 September the FN joined a right-wing list that took the town. This ended the taboo on the mainstream Right allying with the FN.
In the 1984 European elections the FN won about 11 per cent of the vote and 10 seats, which confirmed that Dreux was not a one-off.
The FN's national success followed. How many seats it won depended on the voting system as much as on its share of the vote, which is a point examiners like.

In the 1986 legislative elections, held under proportional representation (seats shared out according to each party's share of the vote), the FN won 35 seats in the National Assembly, with about 10 per cent of the vote.
The FN's support was strongest in the south and east of France, in areas with high unemployment and large migrant communities, such as Marseille and Nice.
In the April 1988 presidential election Le Pen won about 14.4 per cent of the first-round vote, about 4.4 million votes.
In June 1988 France had returned to single-member two-round constituency voting, which rewards parties that can win a majority locally, so the FN won only one seat.
Le Pen had been elected the youngest deputy in 1956, aged 27, for the Poujadist movement (a protest movement of small shopkeepers).
In September 1987 Le Pen said on radio that the Nazi gas chambers were 'a detail' of the history of the Second World War. The remark was widely condemned.

When the Right won in 1986, policy turned towards control. Protests forced the government to retreat on nationality and a student's death forced it to drop a bill, and the Left then changed course in 1988.
The Chirac government of 1986-88, with Charles Pasqua as interior minister, passed laws that tightened immigration controls, permitted identity checks and made deportation easier.
The Pasqua law of September 1986 made expulsion of illegal immigrants easier and required visas for most foreigners, so entering France became harder.
On 25 October 1986 a charter flight deported about 100 Malians, an example of the tougher policy.

In 1986 the government planned to end the automatic acquisition of French nationality at 18 by French-born children of foreign parents, who would instead have to make a formal declaration. This was a change to jus soli in practice.

After mass protests, including from SOS Racisme, the plan was dropped in 1987 and a commission headed by Marceau Long was set up (1987-88). The Méhaignerie law of 1993 later introduced the declaration of will to acquire nationality.

Malik Oussekine died on 6 December 1986 after being beaten by riot police (the 'voltigeurs') during student protests against the Devaquet university reform bill. The outrage led the government to withdraw the bill.

When the Left returned in 1988, the Joxe law of 1989 (Pierre Joxe, interior minister) eased some of the 1986 restrictions. The Haut Conseil à l'intégration was created in December 1989, and the Rocard government preferred the word integration to assimilation.
A dispute in one school became a national argument about what laïcité meant for Muslim pupils. The 1989 ruling and the later 2004 law show how the issue developed.

In autumn 1989 the headmaster, Ernest Chenière, of the Collège Gabriel-Havez in Creil (Oise), north of Paris, excluded three Muslim girls for wearing headscarves in class. It became a national controversy.

Education Minister Lionel Jospin asked the Conseil d'État (France's highest administrative court) for its opinion. On 27 November 1989 it ruled that headscarves were allowed unless ostentatious or used for pressure or propaganda.
Jospin's circular of 12 December 1989 told schools to apply that ruling and to accept headscarves unless they were ostentatious or used for proselytising.

The approach was case-by-case, not a ban, because each school judged whether a headscarf was ostentatious, and it lasted until the law of 15 March 2004 banned conspicuous religious symbols in state schools.
The affair showed the tension between laïcité and Muslim identity in schools, and it was debated in the press and by politicians of all parties.

The 1980s tensions were not only about the 1980s. Decolonisation and the Algerian war (1954-62), which ended in Algerian independence, shaped who the migrants were, how others saw them, and which groups supported the FN.

Algerians had been French nationals before independence in 1962, and Algerian-origin families formed the largest group among the second generation. The Algerian war shaped how many French people saw North African migrants.
Many Algerian migrants and their children were linked by family and history to the war, and the harkis (Algerians who served France in the war) and their families remained a sensitive issue.

The Évian Accords (March 1962) led to independence, and between 800,000 and a million pieds-noirs (European settlers) left Algeria, mostly in 1962. Many settled in southern France, where the FN later won much of its support, though its voters were not only former settlers.
The FN drew support from Algerian war veterans and supporters of Algérie française, and its rhetoric echoed arguments about French identity from the colonial period.
Under the 'double jus soli' rule, a child born in France to a parent born in Algeria before independence was French at birth. This shows how the colonial past was written into the nationality rules.
The government's immigration policies in the 1980s were shaped by the memory of decolonisation, so debates about migrants were never only about the present.
Britain faced similar problems in the same years but answered them differently. The contrast comes from France's assimilationist model against Britain's multicultural framework.
Similarities: both countries had urban unrest and confrontations between police and young people in the early 1980s, and both had a far-right party that gained votes from anti-immigrant feeling.

France lacked the British framework of a series of Race Relations Acts (1965, 1968, 1976) and a public body like the Commission for Racial Equality. It did have the loi Pleven of 1972, which penalised racial incitement and discrimination.
France did not record ethnic statistics, which made discrimination harder to measure, for example in jobs or housing.
France's assimilation model treated citizens as individuals, so anti-discrimination arguments were framed in terms of universal rights rather than ethnic groups.
Britain answered its unrest of 1981 (the Brixton riots) with a public inquiry, the Scarman Report of 1981, while France's response was urban regeneration programmes such as Banlieues 89.
Britain's Commonwealth citizens had the vote, whereas non-citizen residents in France did not, which made the unfulfilled promise of local voting rights a live grievance.
A good judgement weighs what the second generation achieved against what stayed unresolved. State your view early and keep to it.
Achievement: the second generation found a national voice through the 1983 march and SOS Racisme, which made racism a public issue.
Limit: government responses centred on policing, immigration control and limited regeneration, so disadvantage in the banlieues persisted and remained a source of unrest.
Achievement: the Conseil d'État's 1989 ruling gave schools a legal framework for religious expression that lasted until 2004.
Limit: the FN's success showed that anti-immigrant politics could win mainstream attention, and mainstream parties were pulled towards some of its themes.

Contemporary views: assimilationists saw banlieue unrest as a failure of integration, while activists saw it as the result of racism and exclusion. Le Pen's supporters said immigration threatened French identity.
Contemporary government view: Socialist ministers presented integration, rather than assimilation, as the aim in 1989.
Later view: historians stress that the banlieues were shaped by housing policy, deindustrialisation and the colonial past, not by immigration alone.

Between the late 19th century and the 1960s most of Africa was governed by European powers, and each tried in its own way to change how Africans lived and thought. Knowing the three main styles of rule explains why culture, religion and language became such contested ground.

Britain, France, Belgium and Portugal governed most of Africa from the late 19th century, and independence came mostly between 1956 and 1975, so the cultural effects of colonial rule were still being argued over in the period after 1945.

British indirect rule meant governing through existing local rulers, so it left more room for African institutions, whereas French assimilation aimed to make colonial subjects French in language and culture.
Belgian rule relied heavily on Christian missions to run schools and hospitals, which gave the missions great influence over how Africans were educated.

Identity means a person's or community's sense of who they are, shaped by language, religion, ethnicity and history; under colonial rule this sense was contested because rulers pressed their own culture on others.
Cultural diversity means many languages, religions and traditions within one society, and both post-colonial states and European states with migrant communities had to manage it.

Assimilation is the expectation that subjects adopt the colonial power's language and culture; French policy applied it most fully, which is why it matters so much for the French empire's schools and élites.

Colonial powers presented their rule as a civilising mission, the claim that Europe was justified in ruling because it brought Christianity, education and European values. Education was the main means of spreading European culture, and it set colonial culture against indigenous culture.
The French idea of a mission civilisatrice held that France had a duty to spread French language, law and values among its colonial subjects, which is why French policy aimed at assimilation.
Most schools in British and Belgian Africa were run by Christian missions, which taught literacy, scripture and European history and often discouraged African languages and customs.

The French system created a small educated elite trained in French and expected to adopt French culture, through schools such as the Lycée Faidherbe in Saint-Louis, Senegal, and the École William Ponty in Senegal, which trained teachers, clerks and officials for French West Africa.

In British colonies, indirect rule and mission schools produced clerks, teachers and interpreters, the people the colonial administration needed, and the education of girls lagged far behind that of boys.

Colonial curricula taught European rivers, kings and battles, and the phrase 'our ancestors the Gauls' is often cited as typical of French colonial schoolbooks, though it was not true of every school.
African historical and literary traditions were largely absent from schools until after independence.
The Négritude movement was formed among black students in Paris in the 1930s and rejected the claim that European culture was superior. It asserted pride in black and African culture.
The Négritude movement was formed among black students in Paris in the 1930s by the poet Léopold Sédar Senghor of Senegal, the Martinican poet Aimé Césaire and the Guianese poet Léon-Gontran Damas.
The journal L'Étudiant noir, founded in 1934, was one of the first publications to bring together students from Africa, the Caribbean and Guiana around the idea of a shared black identity.
Négritude celebrated African and black cultural values, and it challenged the assumption that European culture was superior to African culture.
Césaire's poem Cahier d'un retour au pays natal (1939) is the best-known early use of the word négritude, and Senghor's poetry celebrated an African sensibility based on rhythm and emotion.
Senghor was also a politician: he became the first president of Senegal in 1960 and held office until 1980, advocated 'African socialism' and kept close ties with France.

In 1983 Senghor became the first African elected to the Académie française, the French institution that guards the French language, which shows how far a poet of black pride had also become part of French culture.

Critics such as the Nigerian writer Wole Soyinka and the South African writer Es'kia Mphahlele argued that Négritude was too closely tied to European intellectual traditions and romanticised African culture.
Christianity spread in colonial Africa mainly through missionaries, but Africans did not simply accept it as it came. They took leading roles in the churches and founded their own.

Christian missions, Catholic and Protestant, were the main agents of Christian expansion in colonial Africa, and they built schools, hospitals and churches across the continent, which is why education and religion were so closely linked.
The White Fathers, a Catholic missionary order founded in Algiers in 1868 by Cardinal Lavigerie, became prominent in East and Central Africa.
The Church Missionary Society, an Anglican mission founded in 1799, was active across West and East Africa.
Irish missionaries such as the Holy Ghost Fathers and the Society of African Missions worked in Nigeria and other British colonies, running schools and hospitals.
Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a freed slave from Yorubaland, became the first African Anglican bishop in 1864, an early sign of African leadership in mission churches.

African Independent Churches, meaning churches founded by Africans, broke away from the mission churches; the Kimbanguist Church, founded by Simon Kimbangu in the Belgian Congo after his preaching began in 1921, became one of the largest.
The Aladura churches grew in Yorubaland in Nigeria in the 20th century, which shows that Africans reshaped Christianity to suit their own worship.

Islam reached Africa long before colonial rule and spread by different routes from Christianity, mainly trade and religious brotherhoods. Colonial rulers then had to deal with Muslim communities, and ordinary Africans often blended old and new beliefs.
Islam had spread across West Africa through trade and Sufi brotherhoods, which are Muslim religious orders built around a spiritual leader and his followers.

The Sokoto Caliphate, founded after the jihad (holy war) led by Usman dan Fodio from 1804, spread Islamic law across much of northern Nigeria; this is pre-colonial background rather than part of the colonial period.
The Mouride brotherhood in Senegal, founded by Amadou Bamba in the 1880s and linked with the groundnut economy, became a major political and economic force despite his exile by the French.
On the East African coast Islam had been established for centuries through trade, and it shaped Swahili language and culture.

In northern Nigeria, Lugard's indirect rule worked through the Muslim emirs and barred most Christian missions from the emirates, so western education spread much faster in the south than in the north.
Many Africans combined Christian or Islamic belief with older religious practices, a mixing called syncretism, and the relationship between religion and political authority varied widely.

Islam also became part of European life in the 20th century, first as a symbol of the imperial relationship and then through migration. The Rushdie affair showed how sharply religious identity and freedom of expression could clash in Britain.

The Grand Mosque of Paris was inaugurated in 1926 to honour the Muslim soldiers who died for France in the First World War and as a symbol of the French state's relationship with Islam in its empire; it has no link with the later immigration of the 1980s.

Muslim migration to Britain and France from the 1950s and 1960s led to the building of mosques in British cities, including Birmingham, Bradford and London, and to the establishment of Islamic cultural centres.
France had a large Muslim community, mostly of Algerian, Moroccan and Tunisian origin, and Islam became France's second religion.
1. Salman Rushdie's novel The Satanic Verses was published in September 1988, and many Muslims in Britain objected to its portrayal of the Prophet Muhammad.
2. In January 1989 Muslims in Bradford burned copies of the book in a public protest, which drew national attention to the question of blasphemy (insulting a religion) in Britain.
3. On 14 February 1989 the Iranian leader Ayatollah Khomeini issued a fatwa, a religious ruling, calling for Rushdie's death, so Rushdie went into hiding under British police protection.

The Rushdie affair raised the question of freedom of expression against religious identity in Britain, and Britain's blasphemy law protected only the Christian faith; in 1991 the courts refused to extend it to Islam, which Muslim campaigners cited after the affair.
The affair was debated alongside the headscarf question in France.
Language was the other great cultural legacy of empire. English spread widely, and the choice of which language to use for government and education became a question of identity for each new state.
English spread across the world through the British Empire and the Commonwealth, and it became the official language of many former British colonies, including Nigeria and Kenya.
In Nigeria, English was the language of government, education and the courts, and it became a second language for many Nigerians alongside the major local languages.
After 1945 the spread of English was also driven by American economic and cultural power, through films, music, business and the new international organisations.

Pidgin English, a simplified mixed language, developed in West African trading ports and became a widely spoken lingua franca (a common language between people with different mother tongues) in Nigeria and Cameroon.

Tanzania, under Nyerere, chose Swahili as its national language and language of instruction in primary schools, making it one of the few African states to adopt an indigenous language as its main national language.
In India Hindi was declared the official language in 1950 with English as an associate official language, and English was kept after anti-Hindi protests in the south (Madras State) in 1965.
France promoted its own language through La Francophonie, whose first institution, an agency for cultural and technical cooperation, was founded in 1970 by French-speaking states.
The use of English in African literature raised the question of whether colonial languages could carry African experience, and writers answered it in different ways.

Achebe was the Nigerian novelist whose work changed how Africa was represented in world literature. His career runs from the story of colonial arrival to disillusion with independent Nigeria, and the Biafran War marked it deeply.
Born 16 November 1930 at Ogidi in eastern Nigeria, he studied at University College Ibadan and worked for the Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation before becoming a full-time writer.
Things Fall Apart, published in 1958 by Heinemann, portrayed an Igbo village community before and after the arrival of British colonial rule through the story of Okonkwo.
Its title comes from W. B. Yeats's poem 'The Second Coming', and the novel became one of the most widely read African novels in English.

His later novels examined the new states: No Longer at Ease (1960), A Man of the People (1966) on corruption and the failures of independent Nigeria, and Anthills of the Savannah (1987), set in a fictional West African state under military rule.

The Biafran War (1967-70) followed the Nigerian coups of 1966 and the secession of the Igbo east; Achebe, an Igbo, supported Biafra, travelled abroad as an advocate for its cause, and wrote about the war in There Was a Country (2012).
As the first editorial adviser of Heinemann's African Writers Series from 1962, he helped to publish many other African writers.

Obi Wali argued in 1963, in 'The Dead End of African Literature?', that African writing in European languages was a dead end; Achebe replied in his 1965 essay on the African writer and the English language that English could be remade to carry African experience.
In his 1975 lecture 'An Image of Africa' he criticised Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness for portraying Africa as the opposite of Europe, and historians of literature still debate his argument.

Contemporaries praised him as the founder of modern African fiction, though critics attacked him for writing in English; he died in March 2013, and his work is now studied as a foundational text of post-colonial literature.

Gordimer was a South African novelist whose writing examined white and black lives under apartheid, the system of legal racial segregation that South Africa operated from 1948, and the limits of liberal opposition to it.
Born 20 November 1923 at Springs near Johannesburg, she was a white South African who wrote in English and lived most of her life in Johannesburg.
Her early novels, The Lying Days (1953) and A World of Strangers (1958), explored the social divisions of white and black South Africans.

The authorities used censorship, the banning of books, against her: A World of Strangers was banned in South Africa for about twelve years, and Burger's Daughter (1979), about the child of a communist activist, was banned for a short time.
The Conservationist (1974) shared the Booker Prize that year; she did not win the Booker for Burger's Daughter.

July's People (1981) imagined a revolution in which a white family shelters in the village of their black servant, and it was widely read internationally; My Son's Story (1990) explored the politics of the apartheid years through a family's divided loyalties.

She supported the African National Congress and helped Nelson Mandela with his speech at the Rivonia trial in 1964, so contemporaries in South Africa saw her as an opponent of apartheid whose work was censored.
Some black writers argued that white liberal writers were limited in their perspective.
She was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1991, gave a lecture called Writing and Being, remained an opponent of censorship after apartheid ended, and died in July 2014.

Post-colonial literature is writing from former colonies, in European or local languages, about colonial rule, identity and its aftermath. Other writers pushed the language debate further and widened the themes.
Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o of Kenya wrote his early novels in English, such as A Grain of Wheat (1967), but was held without trial in 1977-78 after a play in Gikuyu, and afterwards wrote in Gikuyu.
His book Decolonising the Mind (1986) argued that writing in colonial languages restricted African culture, because it cut writers off from ordinary people who spoke African languages.

The Nigerian playwright and poet Wole Soyinka won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986, the first African to receive it; he was detained during the Nigerian civil war, much of it in solitary confinement.
The African Writers Series, begun by Heinemann in 1962, made African novels widely available in schools and universities across the English-speaking world.
Post-colonial writers often explored the tension between traditional beliefs and the new Christian or Islamic faiths, and between village life and urban modernity.
Soyinka's novel The Interpreters (1965) and Ngũgĩ's A Grain of Wheat (1967) examined the moral failures of the independence generation.

French-language writers included Cheikh Hamidou Kane, whose novel Ambiguous Adventure (1961) explored a Senegalese Muslim boy's education in France, and Mariama Bâ, whose So Long a Letter (1979) described the lives of Muslim women in Senegal.

Judging the cultural legacy of empire means weighing what Africans created against what colonial rule took away. Examiners reward answers that pair achievements with limits and contemporary views with later ones.

Achievement: African writers and religious movements created new forms of cultural expression that combined African traditions with European and Islamic influences, and African literature won a world audience.
Limit: colonial education and missions had reduced the teaching of African languages, and many African states inherited a dependence on English or French for higher education.
Achievement: Tanzania's choice of Swahili showed that an African language could be used as the language of government and education.
Limit: the debate over writing in English or in local languages, between Achebe and Ngũgĩ, showed a continuing tension between cultural identity and the legacy of colonial education.
Contemporary view: colonial officials and missionaries often saw African culture as backward, while African nationalists argued for the revival of African traditions.

Later view: Achebe argued that English could be reshaped to carry African experience, while Ngũgĩ argued that using European languages cut African writers off from the peasants and workers who spoke African languages.

The US Constitution (drafted 1787) divides power between the federal government in Washington and the fifty state governments. That division, called federalism, shaped the civil rights and social policy fights of the period because southern states defended segregation as their own business.
The Bill of Rights (1791) added the Tenth Amendment, which reserves powers not given to the federal government to the states, so states controlled schools, policing, voting rules and marriage law.

Before the 1960s most southern states enforced segregation (the separation of black and white people, often called Jim Crow) by state law, and federal action against it was met with the argument that such matters belonged to the states. This argument is known as states' rights.

In 1948 southern Democrats angry at Truman's civil rights programme left the party and formed the States' Rights Democratic Party (the Dixiecrats) with Strom Thurmond as candidate. It carried four Deep South states: Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi and South Carolina.

The Civil Rights Act 1957 was the first federal civil rights law since Reconstruction (the years after the Civil War when the North tried to protect black rights in the South). It set up a Civil Rights Commission and let the Justice Department act over voting rights.

In September 1957 Governor Orval Faubus of Arkansas used the National Guard to stop nine black students entering Little Rock Central High School. Eisenhower replied by sending federal troops, including the 101st Airborne Division, to enforce integration, so the federal government overruled a state governor.

The Civil Rights Act, signed on 2 July 1964, rested on the federal power to regulate interstate commerce (trade between states), which allowed Congress to ban segregation in hotels, restaurants and other public places even though they were privately owned.

The Voting Rights Act, signed on 6 August 1965, suspended literacy tests used to keep black people off the voting lists and sent federal examiners to register voters. It put federal law above state practice, and it is a separate law from the 1957 and 1964 Acts.

The Constitution gives law-making, executing and judging to three different bodies, so that no one can rule alone. Each can also limit the others, a system called checks and balances, and the period from 1945 to 1989 shows each check being used.

Congress (the Senate and House of Representatives) makes laws, raises taxes and declares war; the President executes the laws, commands the armed forces as commander in chief and conducts foreign policy; the Supreme Court interprets the Constitution.

The President can veto (refuse to sign) bills, but Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds majority in both houses. The Senate must also confirm senior appointments and ratify treaties by a two-thirds vote, which stops a President acting alone.

Republicans won both houses of Congress in the November 1946 midterm elections (held halfway through a presidential term), using the slogan "Had enough?". It was the first Republican control since the 1928 elections, so Truman faced a hostile Congress until January 1949.

That Congress passed the Taft-Hartley Act in 1947, restricting trade union activity such as the closed shop (a workplace where only union members can be hired), and overrode Truman's veto in June 1947. Truman did not simply give in: he campaigned against that Congress and won in 1948.

Youngstown Sheet and Tube Co v Sawyer: Truman seized the steel mills in April 1952 during a strike without congressional authority. In June 1952 the Supreme Court ruled that he had exceeded his powers, a check on the President by the courts.

The Twenty-Second Amendment, passed by Congress in March 1947 and ratified in 1951, limits a president to two elected terms. It was a direct response to Roosevelt winning four elections, so it is a check on the length of a President's power, not on a single act.
From the 1950s the Supreme Court and Congress used their powers more boldly, first to extend rights and then to limit presidents after Nixon and during Reagan's presidency.

The Warren Court (led by Chief Justice Earl Warren, appointed by Eisenhower in 1953) used judicial review, the power to strike down acts that break the Constitution, to extend civil rights. Brown v. Board of Education (1954) rested on the Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection.
Miranda v. Arizona (1966) on the rights of arrested suspects was another Warren Court ruling, so the Court was shaping social policy as well as checking the President.
United States v Nixon (July 1974): the Supreme Court unanimously ruled that Nixon must hand over the White House tapes, and his resignation followed on 9 August 1974.

Earlier, in November 1973, Congress passed the War Powers Resolution over Nixon's veto to limit the President's power to commit troops without congressional approval, so Congress took back a power the President had been using.

The Boland Amendments (1982 to 1984) restricted US aid to the Contra rebels in Nicaragua. Officials in the Reagan administration kept the Contras supplied in breach of them, which is the core of the Iran-Contra affair.

From the 1930s the President's staff and agencies grew steadily, a development called the presidential bureaucracy. It meant that more policy was shaped inside the White House and its agencies rather than in Congress, which is why people began to worry about presidential power.

The Executive Office of the President was created in 1939 under Roosevelt, giving the President a personal staff separate from the government departments, so the President no longer depended only on cabinet departments.

The National Security Act of July 1947, signed by Truman, created the National Security Council, the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the National Military Establishment. It was renamed the Department of Defense in 1949.
The National Security Council gave the President a forum of advisers on foreign and defence policy, so decisions could be made without going through the State Department and Congress.

The Council of Economic Advisers was created by the Employment Act of 1946, which committed the federal government to promote maximum employment, production and purchasing power. This made the President responsible for the health of the economy.

Public opinion, meaning what ordinary voters think, increasingly shaped presidents as polls and media grew. Kennedy held live televised press conferences from January 1961, using them as a direct channel to the public that bypassed newspapers and Congress.

Arthur Schlesinger Jr. described the expanded executive in The Imperial Presidency (1973). The phrase became the standard label for concern over presidential power after Watergate,, which also led Congress to reassert its oversight of presidents.

Roosevelt led the US through the Depression and most of the Second World War, and his coalition and the wartime economy shaped the politics that Truman inherited in 1945. Roosevelt's New Deal (from 1933) had expanded federal power and welfare, and 'liberalism' in the US sense came to mean an active federal government promoting welfare and civil rights.
Roosevelt won four presidential elections (1932, 1936, 1940 and 1944) and served from March 1933 until his death, so Americans had known no other president for years.

The New Deal coalition combined urban workers, trade unions, Catholics and Jews, farmers, southern whites and black voters who moved to the Democrats from the 1930s. It gave the Democrats a majority, but it held together very different groups.
Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945, and Harry Truman, vice president since January 1945, became president while the Second World War and the start of the Cold War were still in progress.
Truman inherited a wave of strikes in 1945 and 1946 as the wartime economy was converted to peacetime production (reconversion), when workers wanted higher pay while prices were rising.

Truman's party was divided between northern liberals and conservative southern Democrats. The southerners often voted with Republicans in Congress (the conservative coalition) to block reform, so a Democratic president could not rely on a Democratic Congress.

Truman was a participant in the domestic politics of his presidency, and he took over a divided party and a hostile Congress, so much of his programme was blocked. His popularity swung from an upset victory in 1948 to deep unpopularity by 1952.
Born in Lamar, Missouri, in 1884, he worked as a farmer, a haberdasher (a men's clothing seller) and a county court official. He served as an artillery captain in France in the First World War.
He owed his early career to Tom Pendergast's Kansas City Democratic machine, so he reached the Senate in 1934, taking his seat in 1935.
The Truman Committee (1941 to 1944), a Senate committee he chaired, investigated waste and fraud in wartime production and gave him a reputation for careful oversight.
As vice president from January 1945 he was not told of the atomic bomb project until he became president on 12 April 1945, so he relied heavily on advisers at first.

In September 1945 he sent Congress a 21-point programme of reforms that continued the New Deal, but reconversion, inflation and strikes blocked most of it. In 1947 Congress overrode his veto of the Taft-Hartley Act.

His civil rights programme began with the report To Secure These Rights (October 1947) from the President's Committee on Civil Rights. Executive Order 9981 (26 July 1948) then ordered the desegregation of the armed forces, which a president could do without Congress.

His loyalty programme (Executive Order 9835, March 1947) required checks on federal employees for disloyalty. It fed the wider Red Scare, the fear of communists in America, and is judged damaging to civil liberties.

In January 1949 he outlined the Fair Deal: national health insurance, a wider Social Security system, a higher minimum wage and public housing. Congress blocked national health insurance and most other proposals; the Housing Act of 1949 and a rise in the minimum wage were among the main successes.

Truman's own combative style won the 1948 election against the odds, but the Korean War, prices and scandal wore down his popularity. Contemporaries and historians have therefore judged him very differently.
In 1948 he beat Thomas Dewey, 303 electoral votes to 189, even though the Democrats split three ways: Thurmond's Dixiecrats on the right and Henry Wallace's Progressives on the left.

He ran a combative cross-country whistle-stop train campaign (speaking from the back of a train at small towns) attacking the Republican Congress as a do-nothing Congress, so the hostile Congress became his best argument.
The Chicago Daily Tribune printed the headline "Dewey Defeats Truman" before the result was known, which is why the upset became famous.
Contemporaries were often dismissive: the 1946 joke "To err is Truman" mocked his handling of strikes and prices, and his Gallup approval rating fell to about 22 per cent in early 1952.

By 1952 his popularity had fallen sharply because of the Korean War, rising prices and corruption scandals in several federal agencies, and he announced in March 1952 that he would not seek re-election.
Historians since the 1970s, and David McCullough's biography Truman (1992), have generally ranked him among the stronger presidents for his decisiveness and his civil rights initiatives.
They also judge his domestic record more limited than he hoped and his loyalty programme damaging to civil liberties.

After Truman, the Republican Eisenhower accepted the New Deal's main structures rather than undoing them, and Kennedy then promised a more active government. Both presidents faced the federal-state conflict over civil rights, and Kennedy's death left his bills to Johnson.

Eisenhower, a Republican and former Allied commander in the Second World War, called his approach Modern Republicanism. He accepted most New Deal programmes rather than dismantling them, though he was not a New Dealer himself.
He extended Social Security to about 10 million more workers in 1954 and created the Department of Health, Education and Welfare in 1953, so the New Deal's welfare structures grew under a Republican.

The Federal-Aid Highway Act of June 1956 funded an Interstate Highway System of about 41,000 miles, the largest federal public works programme of the period, which shows a Republican using federal money for a national project.

In his Farewell Address (January 1961) Eisenhower warned against the "military-industrial complex", the close link between the armed forces and the arms industry, which he feared could gain too much influence.
Kennedy won the 1960 election narrowly over Richard Nixon, and his New Frontier, presented in his nomination speech of July 1960, promised a more active federal role at home and in space.

Kennedy's tax cut was proposed in January 1963 and passed as the Revenue Act of February 1964 under Johnson, cutting the top income tax rate from 91 to 70 per cent. His civil rights bill was sent to Congress in June 1963 but only passed after his assassination.

Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas on 22 November 1963; Lyndon Johnson was sworn in as president on Air Force One that afternoon, so the same day saw both the end of one presidency and the start of the next.

Johnson's domestic programme was the largest federal social effort since the New Deal. He used Kennedy's death and his own legislative skill to pass a flood of laws in 1964 and 1965, until the Vietnam War began to drain money and attention from it.
Johnson, Senate Majority Leader from 1955 to 1961, used his legislative skills (the persuasive "Johnson treatment") and the national mood after Kennedy's death to pass Kennedy's stalled bills.
The Civil Rights Act of 2 July 1964 banned segregation in public places and discrimination in employment on grounds of race, colour, religion, sex or national origin.
In a speech at the University of Michigan on 22 May 1964, Johnson set out the Great Society, a programme to end poverty and racial injustice.
The Economic Opportunity Act of 1964 launched the War on Poverty, which included Job Corps (job training for young people) and community action programmes.
In the 1964 election Johnson won about 61 per cent of the popular vote against Barry Goldwater, who carried only six states, giving him a huge majority in Congress to pass further laws.

The Voting Rights Act of 6 August 1965 suspended literacy tests and sent federal examiners to register voters in areas where discrimination was proven. Medicare for the elderly and Medicaid for the poor were signed into law on 30 July 1965.

The Elementary and Secondary Education Act (April 1965) and the Higher Education Act (1965) provided federal aid to schools and colleges, and Head Start for poor pre-school children began in 1965. The Immigration and Nationality Act (1965) ended national-origin quotas.
The Department of Housing and Urban Development was created in 1965, giving the federal government a cabinet department for cities and housing.
The cost of the Vietnam War from 1965 drained money and attention from the Great Society, and Republican gains in the 1966 midterms slowed new legislation.

Between 1969 and 1981 three presidents faced scandal, recession and inflation, and the public's trust in the presidency fell. Watergate was the turning point, because it forced a resignation and showed Congress and the Court could check a President.
Richard Nixon won the 1968 election narrowly and was re-elected in 1972 by carrying 49 states, so his fall in 1974 came soon after a landslide.

Nixon's domestic record included the Environmental Protection Agency (1970), wage and price controls (August 1971) to fight inflation, and the expansion of affirmative action (favouring minorities) in federal contracts.

Five men were arrested for burgling the Democratic National Committee headquarters in the Watergate complex on 17 June 1972, and the Washington Post's reporting kept the scandal in the news. Nixon resigned on 9 August 1974, after the Supreme Court ordered him to hand over his tapes.

Gerald Ford, who had become vice president in December 1973 after Spiro Agnew resigned, became president and pardoned Nixon on 8 September 1974. The pardon damaged his standing, and with inflation and recession in 1974 to 1975 he lost narrowly to Carter in 1976.
Jimmy Carter, a Democrat from Georgia, won the 1976 election and negotiated the Panama Canal treaties of 1977, under which the canal passed to Panama at the end of 1999.

The Camp David Accords of September 1978, brokered by Carter, led to a peace treaty between Egypt and Israel signed in March 1979. Carter also created the Departments of Energy (1977) and Education (1979).
High inflation and the 1979 oil shock undermined Carter. His televised speech of July 1979 on a "crisis of confidence", nicknamed the malaise speech, was seen by critics as blaming the public.

The Iran hostage crisis held 52 American diplomats and citizens in Iran from 4 November 1979 to 20 January 1981, 444 days. An attempted rescue in April 1980 failed, and the crisis was a major cause of Carter's defeat.

Ronald Reagan won in 1980 promising smaller government and tax cuts, reversing the liberal direction of the New Deal and Great Society. His first term set the conservative agenda, and his second was clouded by Iran-Contra.
Ronald Reagan defeated Carter in 1980 and was re-elected in 1984, carrying 49 states against Walter Mondale, which shows how popular he stayed.
In his first inaugural address (20 January 1981) Reagan said that "government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem", which summed up his case against federal power.
The Economic Recovery Tax Act of August 1981 cut income tax rates by about 25 per cent over three years and lowered the top rate from 70 to 50 per cent.
Reagan's first term combined cuts to many domestic social programmes with a large rise in defence spending, a pattern known as Reaganomics.

When air traffic controllers in the PATCO union struck in August 1981, Reagan dismissed the strikers, signalling a hard line on public sector unions, because the strikers worked for the federal government.
Iran-Contra was revealed in November 1986: the administration had sold arms to Iran and diverted the money to the Contra rebels in Nicaragua despite congressional restrictions, the Boland Amendments.
The Tower Commission (February 1987) criticised Reagan's detached management style. National Security Adviser John Poindexter and his aide Oliver North were among those prosecuted.
Reagan's popularity survived the scandal and he left office in January 1989 with high approval ratings, earning the nickname "the Teflon president" because scandals did not stick to him.

Judging presidents means weighing what each achieved against where each failed, and contemporary verdicts often differ from later ones. A good answer gives a stated judgement with dated evidence on each side.
Truman: his civil rights initiative, including desegregating the armed forces, and his leadership in the early Cold War (the Marshall Plan and NATO) are usually seen as successes.
Truman's critics point to the failure to pass national health insurance, because a hostile Congress blocked it, and to the unpopularity of the Korean War.
Johnson: the Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts and Medicare are counted as major achievements, while his Vietnam policy is widely judged a failure that drained the Great Society.

Nixon and Ford: Nixon's opening to China and his arms control agreements are credited as achievements, but Watergate and the secret bombing of Cambodia are judged serious failings, and Ford's pardon of Nixon cost him public trust.
Yet the Court's ruling and the War Powers Resolution show that Congress and the Court acted as effective checks on the President.
Carter: the Camp David Accords are judged a success, while the Iran hostage crisis, inflation and his 1980 defeat are the main charges against him.

Reagan: supporters credit his tax cuts and conservative revival, and they claim he helped to end the Cold War, which is their view and not settled fact. Critics point to the rising deficit, the 1981 to 1982 recession and Iran-Contra.
Public opinion polls made presidential popularity visible from the 1930s onwards, and the Watergate and Iran-Contra scandals led Congress to reassert its oversight of presidents.

Contemporary verdicts often differed from later ones: Truman left office in 1953 deeply unpopular, yet his reputation rose sharply in later historians' rankings, as did Eisenhower's, while Johnson's soared in 1964 and collapsed by 1968.

Before 1941 the United States kept out of most quarrels in Europe and Asia. The Second World War ended that, and by 1945 it faced a rival superpower, the Soviet Union, whose system was the opposite of its own.

Pre-war US isolationism (staying out of other countries' conflicts) was ended by Pearl Harbor and the war, so after 1945 the United States followed internationalism: active involvement in world affairs instead of withdrawal.
The war left the United States the richest industrial power and, until the Soviet test in 1949, the only atomic power, which gave it the means to lead a worldwide policy.

The wartime alliance with the Soviet Union broke down because Soviet forces held Eastern Europe at the war's end; the strain showed at the Yalta conference (February 1945) and the Potsdam conference (July to August 1945).
Churchill's "iron curtain" speech at Fulton, Missouri, in March 1946 gave the division of Europe between East and West its best-known image.
The Cold War rested on a clash of systems: communism, with the state controlling the economy under one party, against capitalism, with private ownership and markets.
In China a civil war was being fought between Mao Zedong's Communists and Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists, so Asia was drawn into the same contest as Europe.
Imperialism means domination of one country by another through political, military or economic control. In this topic it is applied to US influence in Cuba and to Soviet control of Eastern Europe.

Germany, and Berlin within it, was divided into four occupation zones or sectors (US, British, French and Soviet). Berlin lay deep inside the Soviet zone, so the three Western sectors, which became West Berlin, were cut off from the West by Soviet-held territory.
Containment means checking Soviet and communist expansion by firm resistance. It grew out of a new weapon and one diplomat's analysis of how the Soviet Union behaved.
The atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945, on Truman's authority, which left the United States as the only country with atomic weapons.
The Soviet Union tested its own bomb on 29 August 1949, which ended the American monopoly, so the United States could no longer rely on the bomb alone to hold Soviet power back.
George Kennan, a US diplomat in Moscow, sent his Long Telegram in February 1946, arguing that Soviet expansion could be checked by firm, long-term resistance rather than by negotiation.
Kennan's article "The Sources of Soviet Conduct", published in Foreign Affairs in July 1947 under the signature X, made the same case in public and gave containment its name.

Keep four terms apart: containment is the idea (Kennan), the Truman Doctrine is political and military aid to Greece and Turkey, the Marshall Plan is economic aid to Western Europe, and NATO is the alliance.
Between 1947 and 1950 a run of crises turned Kennan's idea into American policy and open commitments.
In February 1947 Britain told the United States it could no longer support Greece and Turkey, so Washington decided to take over that burden.

In the Truman Doctrine speech to Congress on 12 March 1947 Truman asked for about 400 million dollars for Greece and Turkey and committed the United States to support free peoples resisting armed minorities or outside pressure.
The Communist seizure of power in Czechoslovakia in February 1948 convinced many in Washington and Western Europe that the Soviet threat was immediate, so it made them readier to act.

Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949. Republicans asked "Who lost China?" and used the question to attack Truman's Asia policy, which made it harder for him to look weak abroad.

NSC-68, a paper by the National Security Council (the President's foreign-policy advisory body), called in April 1950 for a large rise in defence spending to meet the Soviet threat. It was approved as policy in autumn 1950, after the Korean War began.
Containment in Western Europe had an economic side. American money would rebuild damaged economies so that poverty and unrest did not push voters towards communism.
George Marshall, the Secretary of State, proposed a European recovery programme in a speech at Harvard University on 5 June 1947.
The European Recovery Program, passed by Congress in April 1948, provided about 13 billion dollars of aid to Western European countries between 1948 and 1952.
The plan had three aims: economic recovery in Western Europe, stopping the spread of communism, and rebuilding European markets for American goods.
Most aid was given as grants of food, fuel and machinery rather than as loans, so recipients received supplies they did not have to repay as ordinary debt.
The Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC) was set up in April 1948 to allocate the aid, and Britain, France and West Germany were the largest recipients.

The Soviet Union refused Marshall aid and pressed its satellite states (the Eastern European countries it controlled) to refuse too. Czechoslovakia first accepted, then withdrew in July 1947 under Soviet pressure, so Europe settled more firmly into two blocs.
Aid was matched by a military guarantee. In 1949 the defence of Western Europe and the future of Germany were both settled in ways that made the division of Europe harder to undo.
The North Atlantic Treaty was signed on 4 April 1949 by twelve countries, including the United States, Britain, France, Canada and Italy.

NATO, founded in April 1949 on the Article 5 principle of collective defence, was the first peacetime alliance of its kind that the United States had joined, a clear break from pre-war isolationism and a sign that internationalism now meant permanent commitments.
Article 5 of the treaty stated that an armed attack on one member would be treated as an attack on all, which is the basis of collective defence: any attacker would face the whole alliance.

Germany was divided as well: the Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany) was founded in May 1949 in the Western zones, and the German Democratic Republic (East Germany) followed in October 1949 in the Soviet zone.
Berlin lay inside the Soviet zone, so the Soviet Union could squeeze the Western sectors without invading. The crisis of 1948 to 1949 tested whether the West would stay.
The Soviet Union began blocking road, rail and canal access to West Berlin on 24 June 1948, aiming to force the Western powers out of the city.
The Western powers responded with an airlift that flew food, coal and other supplies into West Berlin. More than two million tons were carried before the blockade was lifted on 12 May 1949.
Truman chose the airlift rather than an armed convoy.
The result was a Western success: the Soviet Union lifted the blockade without achieving its aim, and the West held Berlin without firing a shot.
Berlin remained a flashpoint after the airlift. From 1958 the Soviet leader pressed the West to leave, and in 1961 the border between East and West Berlin was sealed.
In November 1958 Khrushchev demanded that the Western powers withdraw from Berlin within six months, and the issue was debated at the Vienna summit with Kennedy in June 1961.
More than two million East Germans had fled to the West between 1949 and 1961, mostly by crossing from East to West Berlin, which drained the East's skilled workforce.
The Berlin Wall was built from 13 August 1961, closing the border between East and West Berlin and stopping the flow of refugees.
In October 1961 American and Soviet tanks faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie, the crossing point for foreigners, in a tense standoff that ended without shots.
The Wall was a propaganda defeat for the East, because it had to wall in its own people, but the West accepted it rather than tearing it down, so the division of the city became permanent.
Kennedy visited West Berlin on 26 June 1963 and declared in German "Ich bin ein Berliner" (I am a Berliner), a statement of solidarity that was widely praised in the West.
Korea was split by the superpowers in 1945. In 1950 the split turned into war, and the United States fought under the flag of the United Nations.
Korea was divided at the 38th parallel in 1945. The Republic of Korea in the South under Syngman Rhee and the Democratic People's Republic in the North under Kim Il Sung were both founded in 1948.

US troops left South Korea in 1949, and Secretary of State Dean Acheson's speech of January 1950 placed Korea outside the American defence perimeter in the Pacific. It may have encouraged the North, though historians disagree how far.
North Korean forces invaded the South on 25 June 1950. The UN Security Council condemned the attack and recommended that members help South Korea repel it.
The Council could act because the Soviet delegate was absent (the Soviet Union was boycotting it), so Security Council resolutions could be passed.
Truman sent American forces without asking Congress for a declaration of war and described the operation as a police action, so the war was never formally declared.

Korea applied containment to Asia: Washington saw the invasion as communist expansion that had to be stopped, as the domino theory (if one country falls to communism, its neighbours follow) later argued in Vietnam.
The war swung up and down the peninsula before settling into a stalemate close to where it began.
General Douglas MacArthur led the UN forces. His landing at Inchon on 15 September 1950 cut North Korean supply lines and led to the recapture of Seoul in late September 1950.
UN forces crossed the 38th parallel in October 1950. Chinese forces entered the war in large numbers from late October and November 1950 and drove them back.
Truman dismissed MacArthur on 11 April 1951 after the general publicly argued for attacking China, because Truman wanted the war kept limited. The decision caused a major domestic row.
An armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953 and the frontier stayed close to the 38th parallel. No peace treaty was ever signed, so the two Koreas remained technically at war.
