The United Auto Workers and General Motors signed a five-year contract in 1950, often called the Treaty of Detroit. It linked wages to productivity and the cost of living and provided pensions and health insurance, while management kept control of production decisions.
Such agreements gave many manual workers rising real wages and benefits, which means pay that bought more over time, and they became a model for other unions in the core industries.

The Taft-Hartley Act of 1947 restricted union tactics such as secondary boycotts (action against a firm's customers or suppliers) and the closed shop (only hiring union members), and it allowed states to pass right-to-work laws. It also required union leaders to sign non-communist affidavits.
The American Federation of Labor and the Congress of Industrial Organizations merged in 1955 under George Meany, which created a single labour federation.
Unions were weakest in the South and among service and farm workers, who were often excluded from the postwar bargain.

Government economists believed that spending and tax policy could keep growth going, and the 1964 tax cut was the major test of that belief. The idea comes from John Maynard Keynes, who argued that governments can manage demand (the total spending in the economy) through spending and taxation.
The economic advisers of Kennedy and Johnson accepted Keynes's ideas. In practice this meant cutting taxes or raising spending to boost demand when growth slowed.

Walter Heller, chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers under Kennedy, argued for a tax cut to stimulate demand and growth, because lower taxes leave households and firms with more to spend and invest.
The Revenue Act of 1964, signed by Johnson, cut taxes and reduced the top income tax rate from 91 per cent to 70 per cent.
Strong economic growth followed in the mid-1960s, so the tax cut is often cited as a successful example of demand management before the costs of the Vietnam War appeared.
Milton Friedman, a monetarist (someone who stresses controlling the money supply), argued that governments could not fine-tune the economy.

A strong judgement weighs the scale of the boom against its dependence on temporary US dominance and on government spending. It also compares what contemporaries praised with what later critics noticed.
Achievement: between 1945 and 1968 living standards rose steadily, home ownership became widespread and a large middle class emerged, helped by the GI Bill and rising union wages.
Limit: the boom depended partly on the temporary dominance of the US economy after 1945, which was bound to decline as Europe and Japan recovered from the war.
Limit: critics argue the boom rested on defence spending and large public investment, such as the Interstate system and research funding, and not only on the free market.

Limit: some groups did not share fully in the boom. Black Americans and many southern workers faced discrimination in jobs and housing, and black veterans were often denied GI Bill benefits in practice.

John Kenneth Galbraith's The Affluent Society (1958) argued that the boom created private wealth but left public services such as schools and parks neglected, an idea summed up as private affluence and public squalor.
Michael Harrington's The Other America (1962) showed that tens of millions still lived in poverty despite the boom.

Contemporary against later views: many at the time praised corporate America for stability and rising living standards, while Whyte's critique of the Organization Man saw conformity and a loss of individualism.
From 1945 to 1968 the United States enjoyed a postwar boom. To follow what went wrong after 1968, you need the basic economic terms and the idea that the US economy was now part of a world market.

Until 1968 the US had high growth, low inflation and a dominant place in the world economy, with the dollar at the centre of the Bretton Woods system (the postwar arrangement in which other currencies were tied to the dollar and the dollar was convertible into gold).

Inflation means a general rise in prices. Recession means falling output and rising unemployment. Stagflation is the two troubles together: high inflation with stagnant growth and high unemployment, which is unusual because inflation normally comes with strong demand.

A budget deficit is one year's shortfall when government spending is above revenue. The national debt is all the borrowing built up over the years. A trade deficit means imports are above exports, so it is a different thing from the budget deficit.

Globalisation is the growing integration of national economies through trade, investment and finance. For the US it meant that industries faced Japanese and European rivals, and that the value of the dollar and the price of oil were set in a world market.

Corporate capitalism is an economy dominated by large corporations. Here the position of the big US firms in steel and cars was challenged by foreign competition, and Reagan-era deregulation (removing government controls on prices and entry) changed how some industries operated.
The rust belt is the old industrial region of the Midwest and northeast, whose factories declined. The Sun Belt is the South and West, which grew.

Johnson tried to pay for a major war (guns) and expanding social programmes (butter) at the same time, without raising taxes. This pushed up demand, prices and federal borrowing and set the pattern for the 1970s.

Federal spending on the Vietnam War rose sharply after 1965, and Johnson chose not to raise taxes to pay for it while also expanding the Great Society (his programmes against poverty and for education and health). The war was very costly.
Unemployment was already low, so the economy was near full employment. The extra demand from war and welfare spending could not be met by extra output, and so it pushed up prices.
Because spending rose faster than output, inflation, which had been about 1 per cent in 1964, passed 4 per cent in 1968. Consumer prices began to climb steadily in the late 1960s.
Johnson asked Congress for a tax increase only in 1967. Wilbur Mills, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, made agreement conditional on spending cuts, which delayed the measure.
Congress passed a 10 per cent income tax surtax in June 1968 to restrain spending and reduce the deficit, but it did not stop inflation.
The federal budget deficit grew through the late 1960s and 1970s, so deficits became a persistent feature of US government finance.

The balance of payments (the record of money flowing in and out of the country) also worsened. US military spending abroad and foreign investment sent dollars overseas faster than exports earned them.
Foreign governments, notably France, began to exchange dollars for US gold, so the strain on the dollar built through the late 1960s.
By 1971 the strain on the dollar was too great. Nixon ended the link between the dollar and gold, and the system of fixed exchange rates followed it.
On 15 August 1971 Nixon suspended the convertibility of the dollar into gold, so foreign governments could no longer swap dollars for gold. This ended the Bretton Woods system.
The same measures imposed a 90-day wage and price freeze and a 10 per cent surcharge on imports.
The US trade balance moved into deficit from 1971, and deficits grew in the 1970s. The country was now buying more from abroad than it sold.
The Smithsonian Agreement of December 1971 tried to fix new exchange rates, but it failed, and currencies were floating (their values set by the market) by 1973.
Two sudden price rises, in 1973 and 1979, hit an economy already suffering from inflation, and produced stagflation.
The Arab members of OPEC (the oil producers' organisation) began an oil embargo on the United States in October 1973 after the Yom Kippur War, and oil prices about quadrupled in 1973 to 1974.
The embargo brought petrol queues at filling stations, and in some states rationing by odd and even number plates. It was lifted in March 1974.
The recession of 1973 to 1975 was the worst since the 1930s, with unemployment about 9 per cent in 1975. Dearer oil raised costs and prices while cutting output, which is how stagflation arose.
Ford's Whip Inflation Now campaign of 1974 relied on voluntary measures and was widely mocked. Carter's first attempts at stimulus did not stop inflation rising again in 1978 and 1979.
The Iranian Revolution of 1978 to 1979 caused a second shock, with oil prices about doubling, which deepened inflation and recession.
Inflation was about 13 per cent in 1980. The combination of high inflation and stagnant growth became known as stagflation.
The oil crises made energy a central economic issue. Governments tried conservation, new institutions and the aim of self-sufficiency, but the US stayed dependent on imports.
Nixon's Project Independence (November 1973) aimed to end dependence on foreign oil by 1980, but American oil imports kept rising.
Congress passed a national maximum speed limit of 55 miles per hour in January 1974 to reduce petrol consumption, since slower driving uses less fuel.
The Department of Energy was created in August 1977 under Carter, bringing together federal energy programmes that had been spread across several agencies.
The National Energy Act of 1978 encouraged conservation and phased in higher natural gas prices. It was a compromise reached after long debate in Congress.
Domestic oil production remained below its peak, so the United States depended on imports from the Middle East and other producers for a growing share of its oil by the late 1970s.

In the 1970s American steel and car makers lost ground to Japanese and European rivals. This is globalisation at work, and the damage fell on the industrial Midwest and northeast, nicknamed the rust belt.
The steel industry lost ground to imports from Japan and Europe in the 1970s, and steel mills in the Midwest and northeast reduced production or closed.
Youngstown Sheet and Tube closed its Ohio works in September 1977, costing about 5,000 jobs. It became a symbol of the wider loss of industrial jobs in the region.
Japanese car makers such as Toyota and Honda sold small, fuel-efficient cars. After the oil shocks these were attractive, while Detroit built large cars.
Imports took about a quarter of the American car market by the early 1980s, and Japan overtook the United States as the world's largest car producer in 1980.
Chrysler was saved from bankruptcy in 1979 by federal loan guarantees of 1.5 billion dollars. Lee Iacocca led the company.
The Japanese gains led the Reagan administration to negotiate voluntary export restraints in 1981, in which Japan agreed to limit its car exports to the US.
American industry was hit by several causes at once, and the effects were uneven across the country. Some regions lost out while others gained.

Historians point to several causes of falling competitiveness: older plant (factories and machinery), weaknesses in management and quality, higher wages and costs than rivals, the high dollar in the early 1980s, and wider global change.
A high dollar makes American exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper at home, which is why it hurt manufacturers in particular.
The US trade balance moved into deficit in the 1970s, and the deficit with Japan grew steadily through the 1980s.

The Plaza Accord of September 1985, agreed by the leading industrial countries (the G5: US, Japan, West Germany, France and Britain), aimed to bring the dollar down to restore the competitiveness of American exports.
Rust belt cities such as Detroit, Cleveland and Youngstown lost jobs, population and tax revenue as factory jobs vanished, while the Sun Belt in the South and West gained.
Growth in service and high-technology jobs, in Silicon Valley in California and in defence-related industries, partly offset the losses in manufacturing.
Reagan's economic policy, known as Reaganomics, combined tax cuts, less regulation and higher defence spending. First, though, inflation had to be broken, and that brought a severe recession.
Paul Volcker became chairman of the Federal Reserve (the US central bank) in August 1979, appointed by Carter, not Reagan. He raised interest rates very sharply to bring down inflation.

These high interest rates helped to cause the recession of 1981 to 1982. Unemployment rose above 10 per cent in late 1982 (peak about 10.8 per cent), the highest since the Depression, before recovery began in 1983.
Reaganomics rested on supply-side theory, associated with the economist Arthur Laffer. It said that lower tax rates would encourage work and investment and so raise growth.
The Economic Recovery Tax Act of August 1981 cut income tax rates by about 25 per cent over three years, reducing the top rate from 70 to 50 per cent.
In 1981 Reagan also cut spending on some social programmes, such as food stamps and aid to families, while defence spending rose.
The Tax Equity and Fiscal Responsibility Act (TEFRA) of 1982 raised some taxes to reduce the deficit, which had grown as the tax cuts took effect.
Deregulation, which means removing government controls over prices and business, had begun before Reagan. The 1980s then brought a long expansion, but also costly failures and continuing weaknesses.
Deregulation continued a trend begun under Carter, including the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 and the Staggers Rail Act of 1980, which reduced government control of transport prices.

Deregulation of the savings and loan institutions (thrifts) in the early 1980s was followed by the Savings and Loan crisis. Hundreds failed, and the federal bailout of 1989 cost taxpayers tens of billions of dollars.
The Gramm-Rudman Act of 1985 tried to force deficit reduction by setting deficit targets.
The Tax Reform Act of 1986 cut the top income tax rate to 28 per cent while removing many deductions (amounts that people could subtract from taxable income).
Economic growth returned strongly in the mid-1980s and inflation fell sharply, though unemployment and the deficit remained issues for the rest of the decade.
The expansion from late 1982 to 1990 created about 18 million jobs, mostly in services, but deficits and uneven gains remained.

Tax cuts combined with rising defence spending meant that the government spent far more than it raised. The gap was financed by borrowing, much of it from abroad, which left the US in a new and weaker position.
Government spending on defence rose sharply under Reagan, and the tax cuts cut revenue, so the federal budget deficit remained large in every year of his presidency.
The national debt nearly tripled during the 1980s, reaching almost 3 trillion dollars, and the government's interest payments became a major item in the budget.
The strong dollar of the early 1980s drew in large amounts of foreign capital, which financed the deficits but hurt exporters because it made their goods dearer abroad.
In 1985 the United States became a net debtor nation, owing more to foreigners than it owned abroad.

The trade deficit reached about 150 billion dollars in 1987. The Plaza Accord of 1985 aimed to lower the dollar. The Louvre Accord of February 1987 aimed to stabilise exchange rates after the dollar's fall.
On 19 October 1987, Black Monday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by about 22 per cent in a single day. The Federal Reserve responded by providing liquidity (ready cash) to the banking system.
The steady rise in living standards of the postwar boom slowed after the early 1970s, and the gains of the 1980s were unevenly shared.
Real wages (wages adjusted for rising prices) of production workers stagnated from the early 1970s, so household incomes depended increasingly on more family members working.
The gap between high-income and low-income households widened during the 1980s, as the tax cuts of 1981 and 1986 favoured higher earners and wages for less-skilled workers fell in real terms.
The decline of manufacturing reduced the bargaining power of many manual workers, and the share of workers in unions, already falling since the 1950s, fell faster in the 1980s.
Service jobs in retail and catering paid less than the factory jobs they replaced, and the federal minimum wage was not raised from January 1981 to 1990, so its real value fell.
The poverty rate, which had fallen to about 11 per cent in 1973, rose to around 15 per cent in the early 1980s before easing.
Black unemployment was roughly double white unemployment throughout the period, and urban areas that had lost industries suffered most.

The decisive judgement is between the recovery of the 1980s and the longer-term weaknesses. A good answer separates two phases: the boom to 1968, and then stagflation, restructuring and an uneven recovery.

Success: supporters of Reagan point to the recovery of growth after 1983, low inflation and the expansion of employment in service industries. The long expansion from late 1982 created about 18 million jobs.
Limit: critics point to the rising national debt, the trade deficit and the loss of manufacturing jobs in steel and cars, which made the United States dependent on foreign capital.
Growth was limited between 1968 and 1989 by the cost of Vietnam and the Great Society, the end of Bretton Woods in 1971, the oil shocks of 1973 and 1979, foreign competition, and deficits.
Winners and losers: the 1970s brought stagflation and falling real incomes for many families, while the wealthy gained most from the tax cuts of the 1980s, so the recovery was uneven.
Historians disagree about whether the decline of manufacturing was an inevitable result of global change or of policy choices, such as the high dollar and the lack of industrial policy.

Paul Kennedy, in The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers (1987), argued that the United States was suffering "imperial overstretch". Optimists pointed to US leadership in computers, services and finance.

After 1945 Americans had wartime savings and pent-up demand, and they married early and had many children. The result was a population boom and a great movement of people, both of which created huge new demand for homes and goods.
The baby boom ran from about 1946 to 1964, with births peaking in 1957 at about 4.3 million in a single year. It followed the end of the war, a prosperous economy and early marriage.
Families were larger than in the 1930s, and the average age of first marriage fell during the 1950s, so more young couples were setting up homes and buying goods at the same time.
Dr Benjamin Spock's The Common Sense Book of Baby and Child Care (1946) sold millions of copies, which is why historians link it with how the boom generation was raised.
The suburbs, the residential rings around the edge of cities, were the fastest-growing part of the country in the 1950s, because families wanted space and could now afford new houses.
As the suburbs grew, several older northern industrial cities, such as Detroit, began losing population in the 1950s, which left the city centres with fewer of the white middle-class residents.

The Sun Belt, the South and Southwest from Florida to California, grew rapidly after 1945, helped by air conditioning, which made the hot climate liveable, and by federal defence spending, which brought jobs.
California passed New York as the most populous state in the early 1960s, a measure of how far the Sun Belt had grown.

The Great Migration, the movement of black Americans from the South to northern and western cities such as Chicago, Detroit and Los Angeles, continued after 1945, while white families moved out to the suburbs in a pattern called white flight.

Mass-produced houses on new suburban estates, financed by federal mortgage guarantees, became the physical image of the American Dream (the belief that hard work brings a home, prosperity and upward mobility). They also showed that this Dream was not open to everyone.
Wartime savings and pent-up demand in 1945, together with federal housing help for veterans under the GI Bill (1944), meant that many families wanted to buy a home as soon as houses were available.

William Levitt's firm began Levittown on Long Island, New York, in 1947, with about 17,000 houses. They were built with specialised teams for each stage on mass-production lines, which kept costs low.
The first Levittown houses were small Cape Cod style homes sold for under 8,000 dollars, so ordinary families, not only the rich, could afford to buy.
Federal Housing Administration (FHA) and Veterans Administration (VA) mortgage guarantees let buyers borrow with a small deposit or none, on long repayment terms.

Levittown leases excluded black buyers. The Supreme Court ruled restrictive covenants (clauses barring sales to certain groups) unenforceable in Shelley v. Kraemer (1948), but lending practices and private rules still kept most black families out of new suburbs.
The suburbs were built around the car, with new highways and shopping centres replacing the public transport and downtown shops of the older cities.
Television sets were in most American homes by 1960, and advertising on television promoted the goods that suburban households were expected to buy.

In the Kitchen Debate in Moscow in July 1959, Richard Nixon and Nikita Khrushchev argued in a model American house and kitchen at the American National Exhibition. Nixon claimed that suburban abundance proved the superiority of capitalism over communism.

Consumerism is a culture in which buying goods, encouraged by advertising and credit, is central to life and identity. In the 1950s mass production, instalment buying and television turned shopping into a way of showing who you were.

Diners Club, launched in 1950, was an early charge card, and BankAmericard, launched in 1958, became the forerunner of Visa. Do not confuse the two: one was a charge card, the other an early credit card.
Credit let families buy cars, appliances and furniture on instalments, so spending was no longer limited to the income they had that week.
Shopping malls, supermarkets and department stores spread through the suburbs, and goods such as dishwashers, freezers and automatic washing machines became common in middle-class homes.
Television was in about 9 per cent of homes in 1950 and about 87 per cent in 1960. Advertising reached the living room, and sponsors paid for programmes such as I Love Lucy.
Advertising agencies used television, magazines and market research (studying what buyers want) to create demand for new products, and brand loyalty became a central marketing aim.
Vance Packard's The Hidden Persuaders (1957) accused advertisers of using psychological methods to manipulate buyers.
John Kenneth Galbraith's The Affluent Society (1958) argued that private affluence sat beside neglected public services, and that advertising created wants that consumers did not really need.
Disneyland opened in California in July 1955, and leisure industries such as theme parks and motels grew with the car and the family holiday.
Rising incomes and a shorter working week gave Americans more time and money for leisure. At the same time, work in large organisations shaped how middle-class men saw themselves.
The standard working week was about forty hours, and paid holidays became more widespread in the 1950s and 1960s, which gave families time for trips and recreation.
Leisure centred on the home, television and the car, with the suburban backyard a key place of recreation and the car holiday a new family habit.
White-collar jobs (office, management, sales and service work) grew faster than manufacturing jobs from the 1950s onwards, so more workers were salaried employees rather than factory hands.

William H. Whyte's The Organization Man (1956) described the salaried corporate employee who values loyalty and conformity, and it criticised a culture in which large companies shaped how middle-class men lived.
The male breadwinner ideal, the belief that the husband should earn the family income, was celebrated by the suburban culture of the 1950s, which left the wife with the home.

The 1950s promoted domesticity for women, but in practice more and more women, including married women, took paid jobs. Their pay and range of jobs stayed limited, and family life itself began to change.
Many women left wartime industrial jobs after 1945 and were pushed out. The media then promoted the domestic ideal in magazines, films and advice literature.
From the 1950s women's share of the paid workforce rose steadily, as married women with children increasingly took jobs outside the home.
Women were about 30 per cent of the labour force in 1950 and about 38 per cent in 1970, but they were concentrated in clerical, teaching, nursing and sales jobs at lower pay.
Divorce rates rose and single-parent families increased from the 1960s and 1970s. This weakened the ideal of the traditional nuclear family of a breadwinner father and a housewife mother.
Enovid, the first contraceptive pill, was approved by the Food and Drug Administration for contraception in May 1960, which gave women greater control over the timing of births.
Griswold v. Connecticut (1965) was a Supreme Court decision that struck down a ban on contraception for married couples.

From the 1960s federal law and the courts began to challenge sex discrimination. Each measure dealt with a different area of life and had limits, and conservative women organised against the Equal Rights Amendment.
The Equal Pay Act of 10 June 1963 applied to men and women doing equal work in the same establishment. Enforcement was weak, so low pay for women continued.

Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned employment discrimination on grounds of sex as well as race, colour, religion and national origin. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission enforced it.
Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 banned sex discrimination in federally funded education. Do not confuse it with Title VII, which dealt with employment.
The Equal Credit Opportunity Act of 1974 made it illegal to refuse credit to a woman on the basis of her sex or marital status. It mattered because credit was central to consumer life.
Roe v. Wade (22 January 1973) was a Supreme Court ruling that the Constitution protects a woman's decision to have an abortion, at least in the early stages of pregnancy.
The Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) passed Congress in March 1972. The ratification deadline was extended to 1982, but only 35 of the 38 states needed had ratified, so it failed.
Phyllis Schlafly's STOP ERA campaign began in 1972 and mobilised conservative women who argued that the amendment threatened the family, which helped to block ratification.
Friedan was both a witness to and a victim of the domestic ideal she attacked, and she became a central figure in second-wave feminism (the movement for women's equal rights revived in the 1960s).

Betty Friedan was born in Peoria, Illinois, in 1921 and studied psychology at Smith College. She wrote magazine articles while she was a housewife and mother in the suburbs, so she knew the life she described.
Her survey of her former Smith College classmates about their lives formed the basis of The Feminine Mystique, published in 1963.
The Feminine Mystique argued that American women were trapped by a domestic ideal, the feminine mystique, which denied them fulfilment. She called their condition the 'problem that has no name'.
The book sold very widely and is credited with helping to start the second wave of the American feminist movement.

In June 1966 Friedan founded the National Organization for Women (NOW) and became its first president, aiming to secure equal rights for women in employment and law. NOW pressed for the ERA, which failed to be ratified by 1982.

She organised the Women's Strike for Equality on 26 August 1970, the fiftieth anniversary of the Nineteenth Amendment (which gave women the vote), and helped to found the National Women's Political Caucus in 1971.
Contemporaries were divided. Supporters admired her as a campaigner for women's rights, conservatives attacked her, and younger radical feminists found her too moderate.
Historians judge her a central figure who helped start the second wave. They criticise The Feminine Mystique for focusing on white middle-class women, and criticise her hostility to lesbians in NOW.
Monroe's screen image stood for 1950s ideals of glamour and desirability, and it was closely tied to consumer culture. Here she is treated only as an image of women.
She was born Norma Jeane Mortenson in Los Angeles in 1926 and became a model and then a film star, taking the name Marilyn Monroe.

Her films, including Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953), How to Marry a Millionaire (1953) and The Seven Year Itch (1955), presented a glamorous, sexually attractive and childlike blonde, an image that was widely copied.
Her image was used in advertisements and magazines that sold products by linking them to her appeal, which tied her closely to the consumer culture of the 1950s.

Hollywood marketed her as a sex symbol and typecast her. She resisted by founding Marilyn Monroe Productions in 1955 and studying at the Actors Studio in New York, and she won acclaim for Some Like It Hot (1959).
Contemporaries admired her beauty and screen presence, but she was criticised as a sex symbol rather than a serious actress.
Later feminist critics read her image as a product of a male-dominated film industry that limited women's roles to decorative or passive parts.
Historians now treat her as a symbol of both the glamour and the constraints placed on women in the 1950s. Her image fitted the ideal of femininity that Friedan attacked.

Examiners reward a judgement stated at the start and supported by paired points, which weigh the material gains of the period against the groups left out. The Dream was real for many but unevenly shared by race, class and sex.
Achievements: home ownership, rising incomes and the spread of consumer goods gave millions of white middle-class families a standard of living that earlier generations had not known.
Limits: lending practices and private rules excluded most black families from the suburbs, and the poor were left out of the affluence, so the Dream was unevenly shared by race and class.
Women's gains: more women, including married women, held jobs and gained new legal rights such as the 1963 Equal Pay Act and Title VII of 1964.
Women's limits: pay stayed low and the range of jobs narrow, and Friedan's evidence showed that many women felt the domestic ideal failed them.
Critics: Galbraith, Packard and Whyte questioned the quality of affluent life, arguing that it brought manufactured wants, manipulation and conformity.
Overall: by the 1970s the family and women's roles had changed, because divorce, single-parent families and women's employment had all increased.

To understand the civil rights movement you need to know how black Americans lost the rights they had briefly won after the Civil War, and why the Constitution let southern states get away with it. Pressure for change began to build only when millions of black Americans moved and fought in the Second World War.

Three Reconstruction amendments (changes to the Constitution made after the Civil War) promised equality: the 13th (1865) ended slavery, the 14th (1868) gave citizenship and equal protection of the law, and the 15th (1870) gave black men the vote.
These gains collapsed. By the 1890s southern states had taken back control of their own governments and stripped black men of the vote, so the amendments existed on paper but were not enforced.
Federalism is the division of power between the federal government in Washington and the state governments. Southern states claimed the right to run their own race laws as states' rights.
The federal government and the Supreme Court could override the states, which is why the courts and Congress became the targets of the movement.

Discrimination means unequal treatment because of race. In the South it was written into law; in the North, and in housing and jobs everywhere, it was enforced by custom, so a black family could be refused a house or a job with no law requiring it.
Jim Crow is the name for the system of laws that enforced segregation (the legal separation of the races) in the South.

The Great Migration was the movement of black Americans from the rural South to cities in the North and West. It gave black communities more votes and political weight outside the South, and it brought the northern ghettos that later exploded in riots.

The Second World War started postwar pressure for change, because black Americans who had fought for democracy abroad were no longer willing to accept segregation at home. In July 1948 Truman's Executive Order 9981 desegregated the armed forces.
Segregation was enforced by state law across the South and by custom in much of the North, and the courts were the first route to change. The NAACP chose to attack it case by case through the law.

Jim Crow in the South meant separate schools, buses, waiting rooms and water fountains. Black voters were kept off the rolls by poll taxes (a fee to vote that poor black families could not pay) and literacy tests (reading tests applied unfairly by local officials).
Intimidation by the Ku Klux Klan and local officials completed the system, because anyone who tried to register risked violence or loss of a job.
In the North discrimination in housing and jobs was enforced by custom and by restrictive covenants, which were clauses in property deeds forbidding owners to sell to black buyers.

Plessy v Ferguson (1896) upheld Louisiana's separate railway carriages under the doctrine of separate but equal facilities. In practice this meant inferior schools, transport and public services for black Americans, because the facilities were separate but never equal.

The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP, founded in 1909 and run by lawyers) led the legal campaign against segregation through cases on education and voting in the 1930s and 1940s and on into the 1950s, with Thurgood Marshall leading the cases.

Two NAACP successes show the strategy. Smith v. Allwright (1944) ended the all-white Democratic primary (the party election that decided who won in the South), and Sweatt v. Painter (1950) concerned the University of Texas law school.

Brown v Board of Education of Topeka, decided unanimously on 17 May 1954 under Chief Justice Earl Warren, overturned separate but equal in public schools and ruled that segregated public schools were unconstitutional.

Brown II in 1955 ordered desegregation "with all deliberate speed". That vague phrase let southern states delay, so progress was very slow, and by 1964 only a small fraction of southern black children attended mixed schools.
The Brown ruling did not end segregation, because white southerners resisted it and the federal government hesitated. The murder of Emmett Till and the crisis at Little Rock made the issue national.
Emmett Till, aged 14 and from Chicago, was brutally murdered in Mississippi in August 1955. Two white men were acquitted by an all-white jury in September 1955, which shocked black Americans.
His mother held an open-casket funeral so that the world could see what had been done to him, and he became a symbol of the cause.

The Southern Manifesto of March 1956 was signed by 101 members of Congress, all from the South. It pledged to resist desegregation by all lawful means, so it showed that southern political leaders would fight Brown.
At Little Rock in early September 1957 Governor Orval Faubus used the Arkansas National Guard to bar nine black students from Central High School, defying a federal court order.

President Eisenhower answered by sending federal troops (the 101st Airborne) and federalising the Guard, which took it out of Faubus's control. The nine entered under guard in late September 1957, so the federal government enforced the law by force.

The Civil Rights Act of 1957, signed in September, was the first federal civil rights law since Reconstruction. It created a Civil Rights Commission and a Civil Rights Division in the Justice Department.
It did little for voting in practice, because juries in the South often refused to convict anyone charged with keeping black citizens from voting.

From 1960 young activists turned from courtrooms to non-violent direct action, which meant peaceful protest that broke segregation rules in public and accepted the consequences. It exposed segregation to national and international audiences.

On 1 February 1960 four students from North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College sat at a Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, where black customers were not served. Sit-ins spread across the South within weeks, reaching dozens of cities.

The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC, pronounced snick) was formed in April 1960 at Shaw University, Raleigh, North Carolina, with the help of Ella Baker, to coordinate student protest across the South.

The Freedom Rides began in May 1961 and were organised by the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE, led by James Farmer). Their aim was to test a Supreme Court ruling against segregation in interstate bus terminals.
The riders met violence. A bus was burned by a mob near Anniston, Alabama, and riders were beaten in Anniston and Birmingham.

The Kennedy administration sent marshals to protect the riders, and the Interstate Commerce Commission ordered desegregated terminals in late 1961. The Rides therefore won a federal response by provoking violence.

The Albany Movement in Georgia in 1961 to 1962 was King's failure. Police Chief Laurie Pritchett arrested demonstrators in large numbers without violence and used neighbouring jails, so there were no shocking images, and King left with little achieved.
Albany showed that violence by the police helped the movement, because it won sympathy. In Birmingham the following year Bull Connor supplied that violence.

In 1963 the movement chose a city where the police were likely to use violence, and television carried the result into every home. The events of this one year turned the federal government towards a civil rights law.

The Birmingham campaign in Alabama in April and May 1963 was led by King and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC), with Fred Shuttlesworth. Commissioner of Public Safety Eugene "Bull" Connor used police dogs and fire hoses against demonstrators.

In early May hundreds of schoolchildren marched and were arrested, the so-called Children's Crusade. Photographs and television footage were shown across the world, which shocked opinion and built support for federal civil rights legislation.
An agreement on 10 May desegregated lunch counters and fitting rooms in downtown shops. Bombings and rioting followed on 11 May, so the violence came after the agreement, not before it.
In April 1963 King wrote the Letter from Birmingham Jail to eight white clergymen who had called the protests unwise and untimely. It argued for civil disobedience against unjust laws.

On 11 June 1963 Governor George Wallace made his "stand in the schoolhouse door" at the University of Alabama to block black students. The same evening Kennedy's television address called civil rights a moral issue.
Medgar Evers, the NAACP field secretary in Mississippi, was shot dead outside his home on 12 June. Kennedy sent a civil rights bill to Congress in June 1963.
Kennedy was first reluctant about the March on Washington, fearing violence, and then backed it. On 28 August 1963 about 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial.
The speakers included John Lewis of SNCC and King, whose "I Have a Dream" speech became the defining statement of the movement. Organisers included A. Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin.
Kennedy's bill of June 1963 became law only after his death and a long Senate struggle. The Act of 2 July 1964 was the first law to use federal power to end segregation in everyday life.

After Kennedy was assassinated on 22 November 1963, Johnson used the public's memory of him and his own skill as a former Senate leader to push the bill through, which is why it passed in Johnson's name.

Southern senators filibustered, which means they kept talking to delay a vote. It was the longest filibuster to that date, and the Senate ended it by cloture (a vote to close debate) on 10 June 1964, the first time cloture was used on a civil rights bill.
The Civil Rights Act was signed on 2 July 1964. Title II banned segregation in public accommodations such as hotels, restaurants and theatres.

Title VI allowed the government to withhold federal money from segregated programmes, and it enabled the Justice Department to sue segregated schools, so federal power could now end school segregation.
Title VII banned employment discrimination by race, colour, religion, sex or national origin, and the Act set up the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to enforce it.
The 24th Amendment, ratified in 1964, banned poll taxes in federal elections, removing one barrier to black voting.

Freedom Summer in Mississippi in 1964 was run by SNCC and others with northern student volunteers who registered voters. Three workers, James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner, were murdered in June 1964 and their bodies found in August.
The 1964 Act left the vote largely untouched. King's campaign at Selma was designed to force Washington to act, and it produced the second great law.
Selma, Alabama, was the scene of an SCLC voter-registration campaign in early 1965, led by King to dramatise how black citizens were denied the vote in Alabama.
On Bloody Sunday, 7 March 1965, state troopers and a sheriff's posse attacked marchers at the Edmund Pettus Bridge. Television pictures of the attack outraged the nation.
On 15 March 1965 Johnson addressed Congress to call for the Voting Rights Act and used the movement's words "we shall overcome". The march from Selma to Montgomery was completed in late March 1965.

The Voting Rights Act, signed on 6 August 1965, suspended literacy tests and similar devices in areas with a history of discrimination. It sent federal examiners to register voters and required federal approval of voting-law changes in those areas.
The results were quick. In Mississippi black voter registration rose from about 7 per cent in 1964 to about 60 per cent by 1967, and black elected officials began to take office in the South.

The Fair Housing Act, signed on 11 April 1968, a week after King's death, banned discrimination in the sale and rental of most housing. Enforcement was weak at first, so it did not quickly end residential segregation.
Liberalism is the belief in an active federal government that uses its power for civil rights and social welfare, and it was the basis of Johnson's laws.
They passed in 1964 to 1965 because of Kennedy's death, Democratic majorities in Congress after Johnson's landslide in the 1964 election, and public reaction to violence seen on television.

King was the best-known leader of the civil rights movement, both a participant who led marches and a symbol who shaped how the nation saw the cause. His role in the Montgomery bus boycott belongs to its own case study, so only a reference to it appears here.
King was born in Atlanta, Georgia, on 15 January 1929, the son of a Baptist minister, and was ordained as a Baptist minister himself. He later married Coretta Scott King.
He earned a PhD in theology at Boston University in 1955. His commitment to non-violent direct action came from Gandhi's methods and from Christian teaching on love.

His philosophy of non-violence combined these two, and he argued that the movement should win over white opinion by accepting suffering rather than returning violence. Civil disobedience (deliberately breaking an unjust law and accepting the punishment) was part of this.
He used the media deliberately. Peaceful marchers attacked by police made a powerful contrast on television, which is why he chose to protest where violence was likely.
He was a founder and first president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, formed in 1957 to coordinate church-based civil rights protest across the South.
His main successes were Montgomery (1955 to 1956), Birmingham (1963) and Selma (1965). The Albany Movement (1961 to 1962) was a setback.
He wrote the Letter from Birmingham Jail in April 1963, spoke at the March on Washington in 1963 and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964, aged 35, the youngest recipient up to that time.

He shaped events and was shaped by them. He learned from Albany to choose Birmingham, where Bull Connor's violence helped him, and in later years he was pushed to the left by the riots and by Black Power.

After 1965 King turned from southern segregation to northern housing, poverty and war, and this brought him failure and new enemies. His death in 1968 ended the career, and opinion of him has changed since.

King campaigned in Chicago in 1966 against housing discrimination, against mayor Richard Daley. White crowds attacked marchers, and an agreement achieved little, so this was his main setback in the North.

In 1967 he linked the civil rights struggle with poverty and the Vietnam War, and he spoke against the war in his Riverside Church speech on 4 April 1967, exactly a year before his death. This lost him the support of Johnson and of some civil rights leaders.

His Poor People's Campaign was planned to bring poor Americans of all races to Washington in 1968. In Memphis, Tennessee, in March and April 1968 he was supporting a strike by sanitation workers when he was killed.
He was shot at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis on 4 April 1968. James Earl Ray pleaded guilty to the murder in March 1969, and riots followed in many cities.

Contemporaries were divided. Supporters admired him, but many southern whites opposed him, and Malcolm X criticised the March on Washington and non-violence. Later Black Power leaders judged him too moderate.
The FBI under J. Edgar Hoover wiretapped King and tried to discredit him through its COINTELPRO operations, which were exposed in the mid-1970s. Johnson distanced himself from King over Vietnam.
Historians now regard him as the most important leader of the movement, and the King holiday was signed into law in 1983 and first observed in January 1986.

Historians increasingly add that he was one leader among many, stressing the role of local activists, women and SNCC organisers such as Ella Baker and Fannie Lou Hamer, so the debate is whether leaders or the wider movement drove change.
By 1965 many black Americans, especially in northern cities, felt that slow change and the limits of the new laws had not touched their lives. Some turned to more radical politics.

Frustration grew for several reasons. Change was slow, the northern ghettos had poor housing and unemployment, police were hostile, and the 1964 and 1965 laws did little for northern cities, where segregation was not written into law.

Malcolm X (born Malcolm Little, 1925) joined the Nation of Islam, led by Elijah Muhammad. He criticised integration and non-violence in the early 1960s, so his message was separation and self-defence.
He left the Nation of Islam in March 1964 and made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1964, after which he adopted a more inclusive position.
He was shot dead at the Audubon Ballroom in Harlem on 21 February 1965. The Autobiography of Malcolm X, written with Alex Haley and published in 1965, made him a hero to many young black people.

Stokely Carmichael of SNCC used the slogan Black Power in June 1966 in Mississippi. It expressed a demand for black self-determination and community control, and it split SNCC and CORE from King's approach of integration and non-violence.

The Black Panther Party for Self-Defense was founded in Oakland, California, in October 1966 by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale. It combined armed self-defence with community programmes such as a free breakfast programme for children.
The Panthers clashed with police and were infiltrated by the FBI, so they faced hostility from the authorities.
In the mid-1960s the northern ghettos exploded in violence. The riots showed that the laws passed in the South had not touched the problems of poor black neighbourhoods in the cities.
The Watts riot in Los Angeles began on 11 August 1965 after a police traffic stop. The National Guard was called in, large areas burned and about 34 people died.
Newark in July 1967 had 26 deaths. Detroit in July 1967 had 43 deaths and needed federal paratroops, sent in by Johnson.
The causes were northern ghettos, police behaviour, unemployment, and laws that did not reach the North.
The riots also produced a white backlash, as many white Americans reacted to the violence by turning against further reform, which fed the politics of law and order.

The Kerner Commission, chaired by Governor Otto Kerner of Illinois, was appointed in July 1967 and published its report on 29 February 1968. It warned that "our nation is moving toward two societies, one black, one white, separate and unequal".
It blamed white racism, poverty and police behaviour for the riots, and recommended large spending on jobs, housing and schools.
Johnson did not adopt its recommendations, so the report changed little.
Poverty in the inner cities became a national concern in the 1960s, and Johnson's War on Poverty was the federal response. Its limits help to explain why the ghettos stayed poor.
Michael Harrington's The Other America (1962) estimated that tens of millions of Americans lived in poverty and were largely invisible to the affluent majority.

Johnson announced "an unconditional war on poverty" in his State of the Union address in January 1964, and the Economic Opportunity Act of August 1964 created the Office of Economic Opportunity, the Job Corps and Community Action Programs.

The Community Action Programs required the maximum feasible participation of the poor. They brought conflict with city governments, because mayors objected to community action bodies that challenged city hall. Head Start began in 1965.
The programmes were underfunded relative to the war in Vietnam, because spending was squeezed by it, and many were cut back as the 1960s ended.
Daniel Patrick Moynihan's report The Negro Family: The Case for National Action (1965) argued that family breakdown held back black progress. Critics said it blamed the victims.
The official poverty rate fell from about 22 per cent in 1959 to about 12 per cent in 1969, helped by economic growth and by Medicare, Medicaid, food stamps and Social Security.
The black poverty rate stayed about two to three times the white rate, which shows that the fall in poverty did not close the racial gap.
Black poverty did not disappear when segregation laws ended, because its causes were economic and geographical as well as legal.
Unemployment was high in the inner cities, and poor schooling left young people without the skills to find work.
Housing segregation kept black families in the ghettos, because discrimination in sales and rentals barred them from the white suburbs where many jobs were moving.
Many industrial jobs in the cities were lost after 1968, and this weakened inner-city economies further.
Poverty rates among black Americans therefore remained far higher than among whites through the 1960s and 1970s.
Crime and drugs became political issues in the 1960s, and presidents began to answer them with new federal powers. The effects fell most heavily on poor black communities.
Heroin addiction was concentrated in inner cities such as Harlem in the 1960s. In 1971 public concern about heroin use by American soldiers in Vietnam added to the alarm.
Crime and urban disorder were used by Nixon in 1968 and by later Republican candidates as a political issue under the slogan of law and order, which appealed to white voters alarmed by the riots.
The Controlled Substances Act was passed in 1970 and the Drug Enforcement Administration was created in 1973.
On 17 June 1971 Nixon called drug abuse "public enemy number one" and launched a war on drugs. His programme included treatment as well as enforcement, so it was not only a policing campaign.
Organised crime was also a concern. Senator Estes Kefauver's televised hearings in 1950 to 1951 exposed the Mafia to a national audience.
The Organized Crime Control Act of 1970 included the RICO provisions, which let prosecutors target criminal organisations.
In the 1980s the war on drugs was escalated and became enforcement-led. Its heaviest effects were on black communities.
Crack cocaine, a cheap smokable form of cocaine, spread in poor urban areas from about 1985. Violence was linked to the trade, which fell on poor black neighbourhoods.

Reagan announced a renewed war on drugs in 1982. Nancy Reagan's Just Say No campaign, also from 1982, promoted drug prevention. Ronald Reagan's own measures were enforcement and the Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986.

The Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986 set mandatory minimum sentences (fixed minimum prison terms that judges could not reduce), with crack sentenced as severely as one hundred times the weight of powder cocaine.
This disparity fell heavily on black defendants, because crack was concentrated in poor black neighbourhoods and powder cocaine was used more by wealthier users.
The prison population rose steeply through the 1980s, and black men were imprisoned at several times the rate of white men.

After 1968 the great laws were in place, but arguments shifted to schools and affirmative action, which means giving preference in admissions or jobs to groups that have suffered discrimination. Black political power grew even as other problems remained.
In Boston in 1974 court-ordered busing, which carried children between neighbourhoods to integrate schools, met violent white protest, showing that northern whites resisted school integration.

In Regents of the University of California v. Bakke in 1978 the Supreme Court struck down fixed racial quotas in university admissions but allowed race as one factor, so affirmative action was limited but not ended.

Black political power rose. Carl Stokes became mayor of Cleveland in 1967 (the first black mayor of a major US city), Thurgood Marshall joined the Supreme Court in 1967, and Harold Washington became mayor of Chicago in 1983.
Jesse Jackson ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1984 and 1988. Black elected officials rose from about 1,500 in 1970 to about 7,000 by 1989.
Housing and school segregation persisted, and white flight, the move of white families from cities to the suburbs, kept neighbourhoods and schools divided.

Examiners reward a judgement, stated early and sustained, that weighs the legal achievements of the movement against the persistence of inequality. The main distinction is between legal and economic equality, and between the periods before and after 1968.

Achievements: the Civil Rights Act, the Voting Rights Act and the Fair Housing Act ended legal segregation and gave black Americans the vote on equal terms in practice. Black officeholders and a black middle class appeared.
Limits: economic inequality, poverty, residential and school segregation, policing, imprisonment and drugs meant that legal equality did not bring equal opportunity.
Different periods: 1945 to 1968 was transformed in law, while 1968 to 1989 saw slow, contested change.

Contemporary white opinion was divided, with many northern whites supporting civil rights laws but resisting busing and open housing in their own neighbourhoods. Black militants judged progress too slow.
Later historians differ: some see the period as a great success that was later undermined, while others argue that its gains were narrower and less lasting than they appeared.

By 1955 black Americans in the South lived under a legal system of racial separation. Montgomery's buses were one everyday place where that system was enforced, and it is the setting for the whole case study.

Discrimination means treating people unequally because of their race. In the South it was not just prejudice but the law: Jim Crow laws (state and local laws enforcing racial segregation) kept black and white people apart in public places, which is why a bus seat could become a legal issue.
The legal basis was the Supreme Court's Plessy v. Ferguson ruling of 1896, which upheld 'separate but equal' facilities. In practice this meant that segregation worked as discrimination.
Black Americans in the South were largely excluded from voting, so they had little power to change the laws through elections. This is why they turned to the courts and to protest.

The NAACP (the national organisation that fought segregation through the courts, with local branches in cities such as Montgomery) was the main legal weapon. Its branch leaders, Rosa Parks and E. D. Nixon among them, later shaped the boycott.
The black church was the main institution free of white control, since ministers did not depend on white employers for a living. This made the churches the natural base for organising protest.

The Supreme Court's Brown v. Board of Education decision of May 1954 ruled school segregation unconstitutional. It raised black hopes, and it also hardened white resistance: the White Citizens' Councils, which began in Mississippi in 1954, spread across the South and were committed to resisting any change.

Montgomery, the state capital of Alabama and the first capital of the Confederacy, enforced bus segregation by city ordinance and by Alabama state law. Because black people were the large majority of riders, the rules were a daily grievance for most of the city's black population.

Buses reserved the front rows for white passengers and the rear for black passengers. The driver could move the dividing line backwards to make room for white riders, so black passengers were made to stand or give up their seats.
Black passengers had to pay at the front and then get off and re-enter by the rear door. Drivers often insulted black riders or drove off before they re-boarded.
Drivers had police powers under the city code, which meant a black passenger who argued with a driver could be arrested. This is why refusing to move a seat was a legal offence, not just rudeness.
Black riders made up the large majority of passengers, so the rules affected most of the city's black working population. Many were maids and labourers who rode to work in white homes and businesses.
This also explains why a boycott could work: if black riders stayed off the buses, the bus company would lose most of its income.
The December 1955 boycott did not appear from nowhere. Black activists in Montgomery had already warned of a boycott and had already been trying to find the right person to challenge the law.

The Women's Political Council (WPC), a group of black women founded in Montgomery in 1946 and led from 1950 by Jo Ann Robinson, wrote to Mayor W. A. Gayle in May 1954 warning of a boycott. So the WPC was ready to act.
In March 1955 Claudette Colvin, a fifteen-year-old schoolgirl, was arrested for refusing to give up her seat. In October 1955 Mary Louise Smith, aged eighteen, was arrested on the same charge.

Local leaders including E. D. Nixon decided not to make Colvin the test case (the case used to challenge the law in court). She was young and became pregnant, and they judged that a respectable adult would command more support.

Bus boycotts had been tried elsewhere before, including in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, in 1953, which Montgomery's organisers knew of. Colvin and Smith later became plaintiffs in Browder v. Gayle, the federal case that ended bus segregation.
The arrest of Rosa Parks on 1 December 1955 gave the organisers the adult test case they wanted. A one-day protest then became a boycott lasting 381 days.
Parks was arrested on Thursday 1 December 1955 on a Cleveland Avenue bus, because she refused to give her seat to a white passenger when the driver, James F. Blake, demanded it.
Parks was no tired, accidental protester. She was a seamstress at the Montgomery Fair department store and secretary of the Montgomery NAACP branch.
Parks had also investigated cases of sexual violence against black women for the NAACP, and in summer 1955 she attended a workshop at the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee.

E. D. Nixon, president of the Montgomery NAACP branch and a Pullman porters' union leader, bailed her out with the help of the white couple Clifford and Virginia Durr. He backed using her case to challenge the law, and Fred Gray was her lawyer.
Parks was tried on 5 December 1955, found guilty of breaking the segregation law and given a small fine. Her case went on in the Alabama courts.

On the night of her arrest Robinson and the WPC, helped by students at Alabama State College, ran off tens of thousands of leaflets calling for a one-day boycott on Monday 5 December. Ministers announced it from their pulpits on Sunday 4 December, and the leaflets were handed out through churches and schools.
The one-day boycott was almost completely observed. That evening about 5,000 people at a mass meeting in the Holt Street Baptist Church voted to continue it.

The three demands were courteous treatment by drivers, seating first-come first-served (white from the front, black from the back), and black drivers on mainly black routes. They did not at first call for an end to segregation.
The city and bus company refused even these modest terms. This is why the demand grew into a demand for desegregation as the boycott went on.
A boycott of this size needed a leadership. The Montgomery Improvement Association (MIA) was formed to run it, and it chose a young minister as its president.
The MIA was formed on 5 December 1955, and the Reverend Martin Luther King Jr. was elected its president. He was 26, pastor of the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, and had arrived in Montgomery in 1954.
King was chosen partly because he was new in the city and had no record of conflict with the white authorities, so he had no enemies among the black leaders and was harder to attack.
At the Holt Street meeting King's address combined a demand for justice with a commitment to non-violence and Christian love. It launched him as the movement's voice.
Other leaders were Ralph Abernathy, E. D. Nixon and Jo Ann Robinson. The movement drew on the black churches, whose ministers were free from white employers' control.

Bayard Rustin, a pacifist and experienced organiser, and Glenn Smiley came to Montgomery in February 1956 to advise King on non-violence. The movement was told to stay disciplined in the face of attacks.
King later said that in January 1956, after threatening phone calls, he had prayed at his kitchen table and felt a sense of divine reassurance, which strengthened his resolve.
About 40,000 black bus riders stayed off the buses for more than a year. They could do this only because the churches and the car pool gave them another way to get to work.

The car pool was run by volunteers with several hundred cars and by black taxi drivers who charged the bus fare of ten cents. It took passengers to work and school, so people could keep their jobs while boycotting.
The MIA organised dispatch points at churches and a pick-up system, which is why the car pool ran like a transport service rather than an informal favour.
Churches raised money to buy station wagons for the car pool. Funds and support also came from northern supporters, unions and churches across the country.
Thousands of people walked, and many black domestic workers kept walking long distances to their jobs in white households. This showed the protest's determination.
The boycott hit the bus company's income hard, and city centre shops lost custom from black shoppers. The economic pressure on white Montgomery was therefore real.
Montgomery's white authorities tried to break the boycott by dividing its supporters, by harassment and arrests, and by violence.

The mayor and city commissioners announced falsely that the boycott had been settled, hoping to divide the boycotters. The police also arrested car pool drivers for minor offences and told taxi drivers to charge a higher minimum fare.
The White Citizens' Councils and the Ku Klux Klan threatened leaders. Employers dismissed black workers who took part, and the police harassed car pool drivers.
King was arrested on 26 January 1956 for driving 30 miles an hour in a 25 mile zone, a minor charge that showed the police were watching the leaders.

On 30 January 1956 a bomb was thrown on the porch of King's house while his wife Coretta and baby daughter were inside. Nobody was hurt, and King urged the angry crowd that gathered to go home and not retaliate.

In February 1956 a grand jury indicted 89 leaders of the boycott, including many ministers, under a 1921 Alabama law against boycotts. King was tried in March 1956 and convicted, fined 500 dollars, and the sentence was suspended pending appeal.
The indictments brought national press attention, and the images of ministers lining up to be booked turned the arrests into a symbol of dignity.
While the boycott kept up economic pressure, a federal court case attacked segregation itself. This case, not Rosa Parks's, was what finally settled the matter.

On 1 February 1956 the lawyer Fred Gray filed Browder v. Gayle in the federal court for four black women: Aurelia Browder, Susie McDonald, Claudette Colvin and Mary Louise Smith. It challenged the constitutionality of bus segregation.
Rosa Parks was not a plaintiff (a person bringing a case), because her case was still in the Alabama courts and could have taken years. Her case did not go to the Supreme Court.
On 5 June 1956 a three-judge federal court ruled by two votes to one that bus segregation violated the Fourteenth Amendment, and the city and state appealed to the Supreme Court.
On 13 November 1956 the Supreme Court affirmed the decision, in a brief unsigned order relying on Brown v. Board of Education and later decisions. It denied a rehearing on 17 December.

On 13 November the city's lawyers also won a state court injunction (a court order) against the car pools as a public nuisance operating without a licence. King was in court for that hearing when reporters brought news of the Supreme Court ruling.
The formal Supreme Court order was served on Montgomery on 20 December 1956, and the MIA voted to end the boycott that day.
The boycott ended bus segregation in Montgomery after 381 days, from 5 December 1955 to 20 December 1956. Violence afterwards, and segregation elsewhere, limited what it changed.
The buses were desegregated on 21 December 1956, with King and Ralph Abernathy among the first to ride, in front of the press.
The MIA issued rules telling its members to be courteous, not to retaliate, and to sit anywhere without boasting.

Violence followed the victory. Snipers fired at buses in late December 1956, and the city suspended night bus service. On 10 January 1957 bombs damaged four black churches and the homes of Robert Graetz and Ralph Abernathy.
In January 1957 King and other ministers met in Atlanta to form a regional organisation, which was named the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC) in August 1957, with King as president.
Segregation remained in Montgomery's schools, housing, restaurants and parks, and black voters were still largely excluded. The ruling covered buses only.
Parks lost her job and received threats, and she moved to Detroit in 1957.
The boycott provoked resistance across Alabama and the South. This shows how far white authorities would go to protect segregation.
The home of Robert Graetz, a white Lutheran minister serving a black congregation who supported the boycott, was bombed in August 1956.
Autherine Lucy was admitted to the University of Alabama in February 1956 but was suspended after white rioting and then expelled. This shows that the state's resistance went beyond the buses.
The state authorities banned the NAACP in Alabama in June 1956, which was designed to cut off the boycott's legal support. The Supreme Court overturned the ban in 1958.
The Southern Manifesto of March 1956 showed that most Southern members of Congress backed resistance to desegregation.
The violence did not break the boycott. National press coverage of the bombings and arrests brought sympathy from northern opinion and brought the matter to the federal courts.
King led the boycott rather than started it, and Montgomery made him a national figure. Here we cover only his part in 1955 and 1956.

King was born in 1929, the son of a prominent Atlanta pastor, and gained a Boston University doctorate in 1955. He had been pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church only since 1954 when the boycott began.

As a direct participant he was elected MIA president on 5 December 1955, gave the Holt Street speech, led the car pool and its non-violent discipline, and was arrested, tried, and the target of a bomb. He was among the first to ride the desegregated bus, with Ralph Abernathy.
He was chosen partly because he was new and had no enemies, and Montgomery made him famous. He was a leader made by the boycott rather than its originator.

He shaped the boycott's tone by insisting on non-violence and on love for the opponent, based on Christian teaching and on Gandhi's methods, which he had studied and which Rustin and Smiley helped him apply during the boycott.
His memoir Stride Toward Freedom (1958) described the boycott and his thinking about non-violence.
Contemporaries in Montgomery's white leadership called him an outside agitator and tried to portray the boycott as run by communists. Black supporters saw him as an inspiring speaker and leader.
Historians such as Taylor Branch (Parting the Waters, 1988) emphasise King's growth into a national leader through Montgomery.
Aldon Morris (The Origins of the Civil Rights Movement, 1984) and others argue that local networks such as the churches existed before him. So King was a product as well as a maker of the movement.
Historians regard Montgomery as a model for the mass civil rights movement of the 1960s, though they disagree about how far it started that movement.
Non-violence became the movement's method. The boycott joined Christian ideas of love and forgiveness to Gandhi's methods of mass non-violent resistance.
It showed that black communities could organise sustained economic pressure on segregation, a method later used in sit-in campaigns.
It made the church the base of protest, and the MIA became a model for the SCLC. It also produced a national leader in King.
The role of women, including Rosa Parks, Jo Ann Robinson and the WPC, was crucial, though men such as King and Nixon were more often given public recognition.
Jeanne Theoharis, in The Rebellious Life of Mrs Rosa Parks (2013), argues that the popular image of a tired seamstress acting on impulse hides Parks's long career as an activist.

Some historians argue that the courts, through Browder v. Gayle, which rested on Brown, rather than the boycott ended bus segregation. Others argue the boycott kept the case alive and made the ruling effective.
The boycott also gave the movement national and international publicity, which mattered in the Cold War, when the Soviet Union used American racism as propaganda.
Montgomery was a clear victory, but a limited one. Examiners reward answers that weigh achievements against limits and that compare how contemporaries and later historians judged it.
Achievement: Montgomery ended bus segregation in the city and defeated white resistance after 381 days, showing that organised, disciplined protest could defeat segregation.
Achievement: it produced a national leader, King, a lasting organisation, the SCLC, and a method of non-violent mass action later used in Birmingham and Selma.
Limit: the legal victory applied only to buses, so it did not change schools, housing, jobs or the voting restrictions in Alabama.

Limit: violence followed the victory, and white resistance across the South hardened after Brown and Montgomery, so real change came slowly until the Civil Rights Act 1964 and the Voting Rights Act 1965.
Contemporary white opinion in Montgomery condemned the boycott and used intimidation, while black residents who had endured segregation for decades saw the victory as a long overdue success.

Later historians stress the organisation the boycott created, the leaders it produced and the example it set. They debate whether it was the start of the civil rights movement or one phase of a longer struggle that began in the 1930s and 1940s.

Historians often describe 1950s America as a society that broadly agreed on its core values, and then ask when and why that agreement broke down. Three ideas run through this subsection: consensus, liberalism and mass media.

Consensus means the shared values said to characterise the 1950s: prosperity, suburban family life and anti-communism in the Cold War (the rivalry with the Soviet Union). Historians argue about how real this agreement was, which is why the term matters in essays.

Liberalism, as used here, means support for civil liberties (freedoms such as speech and a fair hearing) and tolerance of difference. The 1950s tested it, for example in the red scare, and the 1960s movements tried to extend it to more groups.

Mass media means film, television, radio and print that reach a national audience. They helped create a common national culture in the 1950s, so a singer shown on national television could become famous across the country at once.
The same media later carried youth culture and protest to a national audience, which is why local scenes such as San Francisco's hippie district could become national symbols.

Fear of communism at home was already strong: Truman's loyalty programme (checks on the political loyalty of government employees) and McCarthyism (Senator McCarthy's accusations of communist infiltration) formed the wider mood in which Hollywood was investigated.
The backdrop of the 1960s protests was formed by the civil rights movement (the campaign for equal rights for black Americans), the Vietnam War and Nixon's election as president in 1968.

A counter-culture is a youth culture that deliberately rejects the dominant values of the society around it, while multiculturalism is the idea that a society contains many cultures, each with a claim to be recognised, rather than one American culture.

In the postwar years a handful of studios dominated American film, and many of their films celebrated family, prosperity and patriotic values. Their power then weakened as the law and television changed the business.

The studio system meant that major companies such as MGM, Warner Brothers and Paramount controlled film production, distribution and cinemas. The Paramount decree (the Supreme Court's decision of 1948) ordered them to separate production from cinema ownership, and the sale of the chains followed over the next decade.

Frank Capra's It's a Wonderful Life (1946) set small-town community and decency against greed. It was disappointing at the box office on release but was widely shown on television from the 1970s, becoming a Christmas favourite, and it became a lasting image of the American Dream.

The Best Years of Our Lives (1946) dealt with returning veterans and won seven Academy Awards. Social-problem films (films about a social issue) also tackled anti-Semitism in Gentleman's Agreement (1947) and race in Pinky (1949).

Hollywood films of the 1950s increasingly addressed family life, race and juvenile delinquency (crime and misbehaviour by the young), showing that the studios were responding to the anxieties of the decade as well as to its optimism.
Television drew audiences away from cinemas from the early 1950s, so the studios began to sell films to television and to produce television series themselves.

Weekly cinema attendance peaked at about 90 million in 1946 and roughly halved by 1960. The studios fought back with spectacle that television could not match: wide-screen CinemaScope (1953), colour and epics such as The Ten Commandments (1956) and Ben-Hur (1959).

Musicals such as Singin' in the Rain (1952) and family comedies promoted cheerful abundance. The American Dream of home, family and consumption was the staple of studio films and of the new television comedies.

Westerns and science fiction carried Cold War messages. High Noon (1952) is often read as an allegory (a story with a hidden political meaning) of the blacklist, and Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1956) as a fable of conformity or of communist infiltration; both readings are interpretations.
Hollywood policed itself with a moral code that decided what could appear on screen. Its decline in the 1950s and 1960s shows changing attitudes in American culture.
The Production Code (Hollywood's own rulebook of what films could show) was enforced by the Hays Office from 1934, and it continued in the 1950s to restrict the treatment of sex and crime.
The Moon Is Blue (1953) was released without Code approval, which weakened the Code's authority because a film could succeed without it.
A ratings system, which labels films according to the audience they suit instead of cutting them to fit a code, replaced the Production Code in November 1968.

From 1947 the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), a committee of the House of Representatives, investigated communist influence in the film industry. The result was a blacklist, a secret list of people whom employers refused to hire, which ended many careers.

HUAC opened hearings on communist influence in Hollywood in October 1947. The Hollywood Ten, screenwriters and directors who refused to answer questions, were convicted of contempt of Congress and sentenced in 1948; appeals delayed matters, and they served their prison terms from 1950.
The studios' Waldorf Statement of November 1947, in which studio heads pledged not to employ known communists, was their response to the hearings, and a blacklist operated for years afterwards.
Writers who could not work under their own names, such as Dalton Trumbo, kept writing by using pseudonyms or fronts (friends who put their own names on the scripts).
Kirk Douglas credited Trumbo on Spartacus and Otto Preminger did so on Exodus, both in 1960. Openly naming a blacklisted writer broke the blacklist and showed that the industry's rules were changing.

Friendly witnesses (those who cooperated with HUAC) included Ronald Reagan, then president of the Screen Actors Guild, and Walt Disney. In 1952 the director Elia Kazan named former communist colleagues, and he defended that decision in On the Waterfront (1954).
The human cost was large: hundreds of writers, actors and directors were blacklisted, and Charlie Chaplin left the United States in 1952 when his re-entry permit was withdrawn.
The studios also made anti-communist films, such as I Was a Communist for the FBI (1951), to prove their loyalty to a suspicious public.
Marilyn Monroe was one of the biggest film stars of the 1950s. Her career shows how the studio system and the mass media created, sold and then used up a public image.
She was born Norma Jeane Mortenson in Los Angeles in 1926. Her screen career began with small roles in the late 1940s, and The Asphalt Jungle and All About Eve (both 1950) brought wider fame.
She became a star in 1953 with Gentlemen Prefer Blondes and How to Marry a Millionaire. With The Seven Year Itch (1955) she was one of the most popular box office stars of the decade.
She studied at the Actors Studio in New York in the mid-1950s, and her marriage to the playwright Arthur Miller in 1956 linked her to serious drama.
