Some Like It Hot (1959), directed by Billy Wilder, won critical praise and remains her most admired comedy. Her last completed film was The Misfits (1961), written by Miller.

She had disputes with studio executives over her contract and her choice of roles, and the press reported them widely. In June 1962 Twentieth Century-Fox dismissed her from Something's Got to Give after repeated absences.

Her glamorous image, spread by film, press and advertising, made her a public fascination and an example of mass media and consumer culture. Contemporaries judged her a glamorous star, while later critics argued that the studio system exploited women performers.
She sang "Happy Birthday, Mr President" to John F. Kennedy at a Democratic Party fundraiser at Madison Square Garden on 19 May 1962.

She died at her Los Angeles home on the night of 4 August 1962, aged 36, and was found early on 5 August. The cause was a barbiturate overdose, ruled a probable suicide, and the conspiracy theories that followed have no support in the official investigation.
Teenagers became a distinct consumer group in the 1950s, and new music, films and writing challenged the conformity of the era. Mass media turned these youth tastes into a national phenomenon.
Teenagers now had money and leisure to spend on their own music, films and fashions, which made youth a commercial market that businesses set out to serve.

Rock and roll drew on black rhythm and blues (a style of black popular music) and reached white teenagers through radio and records. Bill Haley's Rock Around the Clock (1955) was one of its early hits.
Elvis Presley's Heartbreak Hotel (1956) was one of the first rock and roll national hits, and his appearances on the Ed Sullivan Show in 1956 and 1957 made rock and roll a national craze.

Dick Clark's American Bandstand, on the national network from 1957, turned youth culture into a commercial market. Older critics condemned the music as a threat to morals, an early example of a moral panic about the young.
The actor James Dean, who starred in Rebel Without a Cause (1955) and died in a car crash in September 1955, became a symbol of teenage alienation, as did Marlon Brando in The Wild One (1953).
The Beat generation was a group of writers who rejected the conventions of suburban life. Allen Ginsberg's poem Howl was published in 1956, and Jack Kerouac's On the Road appeared in 1957.
Norman Mailer was a novelist, essayist and public figure whose writing and persona made him a central voice in the debate over American culture from the 1950s to the 1960s.

His first novel, The Naked and the Dead (1948), drew on his service in the Pacific during the Second World War and became a best seller. In 1955 he co-founded the Village Voice newspaper in New York, part of the counter-cultural press of the period.
His essay The White Negro (1957) argued that the hipster, who borrowed from black culture and lived for the moment, offered a model of rebellion against the conformity of postwar America.

The Armies of the Night (1968) covered the anti-war march on the Pentagon in October 1967. Mailer was arrested there and wrote about himself in the third person; the book won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award.
His public persona, including a campaign for mayor of New York in 1969, made him a celebrity as well as a literary authority, which meant that his self-promotion was part of his influence.

His later works included Miami and the Siege of Chicago (1968), The Fight (1975) about the boxers Ali and Foreman in Zaire, and The Executioner's Song (1979), which won the Pulitzer Prize for fiction.

Contemporaries were divided. Admirers saw a serious critic of American culture, while critics attacked his self-promotion, his machismo and his stabbing of his second wife Adele in 1960, for which he received a suspended sentence.
The White Negro was widely attacked for romanticising black life, and James Baldwin criticised Mailer for it, so even his admirers disputed its argument.
Historians today generally treat his non-fiction, especially The Armies of the Night, as an important account of the 1960s protest movement.
Muhammad Ali's career linked sport, religion and the anti-war movement, which made him a symbol of black pride and of political resistance.
Born Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr. in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1942, he won Olympic light-heavyweight gold at Rome in 1960.
He won the world heavyweight title by beating Sonny Liston in Miami Beach on 25 February 1964. His saying float like a butterfly, sting like a bee summed up his boxing style.

In March 1964 he announced his membership of the Nation of Islam (a black American religious movement) and his new name. Its leader Elijah Muhammad gave him the name, and he rejected Clay as a slave name.

In 1966 he told reporters he had no quarrel with the Viet Cong. On 28 April 1967 he refused induction into the army in Houston as a Muslim minister and conscientious objector (one who refuses service on grounds of faith), and lost his title and licence.
In June 1967 he was convicted of draft evasion, sentenced to five years in prison and fined 10,000 dollars, but stayed free on appeal.

The Supreme Court overturned the conviction on 28 June 1971 by 8 votes to 0 (Justice Marshall took no part), ruling that the government had not given a valid basis for rejecting his conscientious objector claim.
He was barred from boxing for over three years and returned in October 1970. He lost to Joe Frazier in the Fight of the Century at Madison Square Garden on 8 March 1971.

He regained the title by beating George Foreman at Kinshasa, Zaire, on 30 October 1974 (the Rumble in the Jungle) and beat Frazier in the Thrilla in Manila in 1975. He retired in 1981 and lived with Parkinson's disease.

Contemporaries were sharply divided: many white Americans and sports writers condemned him, while many young black Americans and anti-war activists saw a principled leader. Historians such as David Remnick (King of the World, 1998) treat him as a symbol of black pride and of resistance to the Vietnam War.

The late 1960s counter-culture rejected the consumer and corporate values of the 1950s. Hippies, young people who dropped out of conventional life, linked personal liberation to music, drugs and a new way of living.
The Summer of Love of 1967 drew thousands of young people to the Haight-Ashbury district of San Francisco, where a counter-culture of music, drugs and communal living developed.

Timothy Leary, a former Harvard psychologist, urged young people to turn on, tune in and drop out. The phrase is usually dated to his public use at the Human Be-In in San Francisco on 14 January 1967, though Leary says he coined it in 1966, so the date is contested.
LSD, a powerful hallucinogenic drug (one that alters perception), was banned in California in 1966; until then it had been a central part of the hippie scene.

Rock musicians such as Bob Dylan, Jimi Hendrix and the Beatles, whose Sgt Pepper album appeared in 1967, gave the movement its soundtrack, and the film Easy Rider (1969) put the counter-culture on screen.
The counter-culture had a political wing and a dramatic public stage, but it also provoked a reaction. Its limits matter as much as its fame.
The Woodstock music festival, held near Bethel, New York, from 15 to 18 August 1969, attracted about 400,000 people (estimates vary) and became a symbol of the generation.
The festival at Altamont Speedway in California in December 1969, where a man was killed by the Hells Angels during a Rolling Stones concert, was seen as the end of the dream of peace and love.
The Students for a Democratic Society and the Black Panther Party were among the political groups that drew on counter-cultural style and protest in the late 1960s.
The Yippies, led by Abbie Hoffman and Jerry Rubin, mixed theatre and politics, and took part in the protests at the Democratic Convention in Chicago in 1968.
Most young Americans were not hippies, so the counter-culture was a minority movement rather than the voice of a whole generation.

The counter-culture provoked a backlash among the silent majority, the phrase Nixon used in his speech of November 1969 to describe ordinary Americans who did not protest. He was elected in 1968 and re-elected in 1972.
In the 1960s and 1970s minority groups asserted their identities and demanded equal rights, challenging the idea of a single American culture.
The Chicano movement (the movement of Mexican Americans) was led in part by Cesar Chavez and the National Farm Workers Association, which organised farm workers in California from the early 1960s.

The Delano grape strike and boycott from 1965 won national support for Chavez. The 1966 merger with another union created the United Farm Workers Organizing Committee, which was renamed the United Farm Workers in 1972.
The American Indian Movement was founded in Minneapolis in 1968 to campaign against discrimination and for treaty rights.

American Indian activists occupied Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay from November 1969 until 1971, and AIM occupied Wounded Knee, South Dakota, in 1973; both were protests that drew national attention.

Black Power, the Black Panther Party and the black arts movement asserted pride in African American culture. The television series Roots (1977) drew about 100 million viewers for its final episode, showing how mass media reached a national audience with this theme.
Women and gay Americans also organised in these years, and new laws made American society more diverse. Together these developments undermined the idea of one shared national culture.
The women's liberation movement disrupted the Miss America pageant in Atlantic City in September 1968, protesting the way women were presented to the public.

The Stonewall riots began on 28 June 1969 after a police raid on the Stonewall Inn, a gay bar in Greenwich Village, New York. Organisations existed before 1969, so Stonewall is widely seen as a turning point in the gay rights movement rather than its beginning.
The Gay Liberation Front was founded shortly after Stonewall, and marches commemorating the riots began in 1970.
The Immigration Act of 1965 and the Bilingual Education Act of 1968 encouraged a more diverse society and gave a legal basis to minority languages in schools.
The concept of consensus, which historians used to describe the 1950s, was challenged as Americans debated race, gender, sexuality and national identity in the 1960s and 1970s.
Examiners reward judgements that test the idea of consensus against evidence of conflict within postwar culture. Both sides of the argument need dated evidence.
Supporters of the consensus view argue that most Americans shared a belief in prosperity, family and anti-communism in the 1950s, as shown by the popularity of the films and television of the period.
Critics of the consensus view argue that the 1950s were marked by conflict over race, sex and loyalty, and that the red scare shows the limits of the supposed consensus.
The 1960s counter-culture showed that a sizeable minority rejected the values of the 1950s, but the majority of Americans in 1968 still backed conventional candidates and the war.
Historians differ over whether the collapse of consensus was a sudden break around 1968 or a gradual shift that began with the civil rights movement in the 1950s.

Three background facts explain why religion became so public after 1945. The Cold War made faith a political weapon, new wealth moved families to the suburbs, and the Constitution set rules on how far government could support religion.
The Cold War was the long rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union, an atheist state, so Americans could present their own religious faith as a mark of difference from their enemy.
The red scare was the fear of communist spies and influence at home, which made public displays of faith and patriotism seem like proof of loyalty.
Post-war prosperity and the baby boom (the sharp rise in births after 1945) sent young families to new suburbs, where they needed churches, schools and community life.

The First Amendment forbids Congress from establishing a religion, and the Supreme Court read this as a separation of church and state, which is why prayer in public schools later became a legal battleground.
Church membership and religious observance grew strongly in the 1950s. Prosperity, the suburbs and the Cold War all pushed Americans towards their churches.
Church membership rose from about half of Americans around 1940 to about two-thirds by 1960, so the 1950s are often called a religious revival.

New churches were built in the suburbs in large numbers, and church groups and social clubs became central to suburban community life, because newcomers used the church to make friends and find a place in a new neighbourhood.
Norman Vincent Peale's The Power of Positive Thinking (1952) was a best seller that mixed religion with self-help, showing how faith was sold as a way to personal success and calm.
The rise of the megachurch (a very large congregation) and of television ministry followed, building on this appetite for popular religion.

Civil religion means a shared public faith in the nation under God, expressed by the government rather than by any one church. In the 1950s it was used to set the United States against atheistic communism.
Congress added the words under God to the Pledge of Allegiance on 14 June 1954, and a law of July 1956 made In God We Trust the national motto.
The Cold War gave religion a political role: communism was condemned as atheistic, so the Pledge and motto changes were part of the struggle against it.
Many commentators saw religion as a bulwark (a defensive wall) against communism, and presidents from Eisenhower onwards attended church and spoke of the nation's faith.
Eisenhower was baptised in February 1953, soon after taking office, and he said in 1952 that government made no sense without a deeply felt religious faith, and that it did not matter which faith.
That remark is often quoted as an example of the civil religion of the period, because it valued faith itself above any particular church.
For Black Americans in the South the church was one of the few institutions they controlled themselves. This made it the natural base for the struggle against segregation.
Black churches, such as the Baptist congregations of the South, provided the meeting places, leadership and fundraising networks on which the civil rights movement depended.
The Montgomery bus boycott of 1955-56 was organised from Black churches and led by Martin Luther King, a Baptist minister, which shows how a congregation could be turned into a protest organisation.
The Southern Christian Leadership Conference (1957) was led by ministers, so the movement's leaders spoke in religious language that Americans of all races knew.
Billy Graham was the best-known preacher of the revival and a participant in it. He used radio, the press and mass rallies to reach millions, and he became close to presidents.
William Franklin Graham was born on 7 November 1918 near Charlotte, North Carolina, studied at Wheaton College in Illinois and was ordained a Southern Baptist minister. He died in 2018.

His Los Angeles crusade (a series of mass evangelistic meetings) of September to November 1949 was planned for three weeks but extended to eight after wide press coverage, helped by the Hearst newspapers, and it made him a national figure.
He founded the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association in 1950 and began a radio programme, Hour of Decision, which later reached a worldwide audience, so his message travelled far beyond the stadiums.
He co-founded the magazine Christianity Today in 1956, edited by Carl Henry, to give a conservative evangelical voice alongside the mainstream press.

He held crusades at Harringay Arena in London in 1954 and at Madison Square Garden in New York in 1957, which ran for about sixteen weeks, and he later spoke at large stadium rallies across the world.
He took his message into the Cold War divide with a visit to Moscow in 1982, and he organised the Lausanne Congress on World Evangelization in 1974, which made him a leader of world evangelicalism.
Radio, television and mass rallies were his tools, and the Cold War gave his preaching extra force, because Americans were ready to hear faith set against atheistic communism.
Graham's closeness to power shaped his career, and events in turn changed how he used it. Contemporaries and historians have both been divided about his legacy.
He became a regular adviser and visitor to presidents from Eisenhower onwards and preached at presidential events, which brought him close to the centre of political life.

His link with Truman began awkwardly in 1950, when he was criticised for revealing his talk with the president, but he became a friend and adviser of Eisenhower and Nixon, and he supported Nixon in 1960 and 1968.

Watergate damaged his standing: he said afterwards that he had been used and that he would keep out of partisan politics, and he kept his distance from Falwell's Moral Majority and warned against mixing religion with party politics.
From the Chattanooga crusade of 1953 he had the ropes dividing white and Black seating taken down, an early sign of his commitment to racial integration.
King prayed at Graham's New York crusade of 1957, but Graham did not endorse the mass protests of the early 1960s and urged patience, so he was criticised for not supporting King more openly.
Contemporaries were divided: admirers saw him as a unifying figure who spoke to millions, while liberal theologians and other critics saw him as a tool of Cold War patriotism.
Historians judge his influence on modern evangelicalism as very large, but note that his closeness to presidents, and above all to Nixon, compromised his independence.
Tapes of a 1972 conversation with Nixon, released in 2002, caught Graham making anti-Semitic remarks, for which he apologised.

Catholics were a large minority, and many Protestants doubted that a Catholic could be loyal to the president's office rather than to the Pope. The election of John F. Kennedy in 1960 tested that fear and weakened it.
Al Smith, a Catholic Democrat, was defeated in the presidential election of 1928 amid anti-Catholic prejudice, so Kennedy knew that his faith could cost him votes.
In 1960 some Protestant ministers, including Norman Vincent Peale, questioned the idea of a Catholic president, fearing he would take orders from the Pope.
Kennedy answered at the Greater Houston Ministerial Association on 12 September 1960, saying that he believed in an America where the separation of church and state was absolute.
He beat Nixon narrowly in November 1960 with strong support from Catholic voters and became the first Catholic president, which weakened the old Protestant dominance of national politics.
Catholic life in the 1950s was strong, with parish schools, church building and Bishop Fulton Sheen, whose television series Life Is Worth Living ran from 1952 to 1957 and reached millions.
Will Herberg's Protestant, Catholic, Jew (1955) popularised the view that Catholics and Jews, as well as Protestants, were part of a common American religious tradition.
Three terms are easily confused. Fundamentalism and evangelicalism are kinds of conservative Protestant belief, while the religious right is a political movement that grew out of them.

Fundamentalism rejects modernist readings of the Bible (readings that fit scripture to modern science) and holds to the literal truth of scripture, and it is usually separatist, keeping apart from other churches.
Fundamentalism is traced to the early twentieth century and the 1925 Scopes trial in Tennessee, which was about a teacher accused of teaching evolution.
Evangelicalism is wider: it stresses personal conversion (a believer's own turning to Christ) and evangelism (spreading the faith), so it takes in more churches than fundamentalism does.
The National Association of Evangelicals, founded in 1942, brought together a broad group of conservative churches under this evangelical banner.

In the early 1960s the Supreme Court applied the separation of church and state to public schools. Many religious conservatives saw this as an attack on faith, and it helped them become a political force.
In Engel v Vitale (1962) the Supreme Court ruled that state-written school prayer was unconstitutional, a decision that provoked strong protest from religious conservatives.
In Abington School District v Schempp (1963) the Court ruled that compulsory Bible reading in public schools was unconstitutional.
These two decisions helped to mobilise conservative Christians, because they felt that religion was being pushed out of public life.

Televangelists are preachers who use television to reach a mass audience. Programmes could reach far more people than any church building, so television became a way to raise money and shape politics.
Jerry Falwell, a Baptist pastor from Lynchburg, Virginia, reached a national audience with his Old Time Gospel Hour from the 1970s.
Pat Robertson founded the Christian Broadcasting Network, and its programme The 700 Club began in 1966.
Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker built the PTL ministry, and televangelists such as these used broadcasts to raise money and to influence politics.
Televangelists reached audiences far larger than most local churches could, and their programmes often combined religious teaching with political messages.
The Bakker scandal of 1987 involved the misuse of funds and a sex scandal, and Jim Bakker was later convicted of fraud and jailed, which damaged the reputation of televangelism.
Jimmy Swaggart's scandal of 1988 added to the damage, so by the end of the decade the image of televangelism had suffered badly.
In the 1970s new social questions gave conservative Christians fresh reasons to organise. Their relationship with the White House also changed.

Roe v Wade (1973) on abortion, and the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA), passed by Congress in 1972 and opposed by conservative Christians led by Phyllis Schlafly, became issues that mobilised the religious right.
In 1977 the singer Anita Bryant campaigned against a gay rights ordinance in Dade County, Florida, which gave conservative Christians another cause.
Jimmy Carter, a born-again Southern Baptist, was elected in 1976, and the press called 1976 the year of the evangelical.
Many evangelicals turned against Carter by 1980, over abortion and the Equal Rights Amendment, which left them looking for a different leader.

From 1979 conservative Christians became an organised political force, closely associated with the Republican Party and Ronald Reagan. The Moral Majority was the organisation that brought them together.

The Moral Majority was founded in 1979 by Jerry Falwell with conservative organisers such as Paul Weyrich, and it campaigned against abortion, the ERA, gay rights and pornography, and for school prayer and a strong defence.
It used direct-mail lists (letters sent to supporters) to raise funds and register voters, and it mobilised conservative churches and voters before the 1980 election.

Its support helped the Republican campaign of Ronald Reagan: in August 1980 he told a conference of conservative Christians in Dallas that he knew they could not endorse him but that he endorsed them.
The Republican platform of 1980 opposed abortion and backed school prayer, which rewarded the movement's voters.
Critics saw the movement as a threat to the separation of church and state.
Its influence was greatest in the early 1980s, and it declined after its leaders were embarrassed by the scandals of the late 1980s and the failure of its political strategy.

Falwell wound up the Moral Majority in 1989, but its voters and organisers moved into groups such as Robertson's Christian Coalition, founded in 1989, so the religious right remained part of the Republican coalition.

The mass media are the means of reaching most homes at once: television, radio, the press and magazines. In the 1950s and 1960s television became the strongest of them, and it shaped public opinion, meaning the views of ordinary Americans as measured by polls and influenced by what they saw.
Television spread through American homes in the 1950s, and most homes had a set by 1960, so network news became the principal source of national news for millions.
CBS (2 September 1963) and NBC (9 September 1963) lengthened their evening news to thirty minutes, and opinion surveys from the early 1960s found television the main news source for most Americans.
The first televised presidential debate, between Kennedy and Nixon in Chicago on 26 September 1960, was watched by a large audience and is widely credited with shaping the outcome of the election.
The quiz show scandal of 1958 showed that contestants on shows such as Twenty-One had been given answers, and Charles Van Doren was among them, so public trust in television suffered.
Congressional hearings followed in 1959, and a law of 1960 banned the rigging of quiz shows.

Vietnam was the first war that Americans watched in their living rooms. Historians still debate how far the pictures changed public opinion, but the coverage clearly showed the power of television news.
Morley Safer of CBS filmed Marines burning the village of Cam Ne in August 1965, and the report showed viewers a side of the war that official briefings did not.
During the Tet Offensive of January and February 1968 the Eddie Adams photograph of a Viet Cong prisoner being shot in Saigon became one of the images that shaped opinion.
Walter Cronkite's report of 27 February 1968 saw the war as a stalemate, and it was one report among several that influenced public opinion.
The photograph by Nick Ut of a child burned by napalm, in June 1972, was another image that turned opinion against the war.
The debate is over cause and effect: the media may have shaped opinion, but opinion also shaped what viewers wanted to see and what governments could do.
In the early 1970s the press and television showed that they could expose wrongdoing at the top of government. This strengthened their role as a check on power.
The Pentagon Papers, a secret government study of the Vietnam War, were published in June 1971 by the New York Times and the Washington Post, and they revealed government deception.
After the Watergate break-in of 17 June 1972, Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein of the Washington Post reported the burglary and the cover-up, which showed the press's power to expose a presidency.
The Senate Watergate hearings of 1973 were televised live, so the public watched the evidence for themselves.
The revelation of the White House tapes made the media a central actor in the downfall of Nixon, who resigned on 9 August 1974.
Alongside news, the media sold goods and made celebrities. Government and business also changed the shape of broadcasting.
The Public Broadcasting Act of 1967 created the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, and the Public Broadcasting Service, the public television network, began broadcasting in 1970.
Advertising expanded rapidly on television and in magazines, so the mass media turned consumer goods and celebrity into central features of public life.

The FCC (the Federal Communications Commission, which regulates broadcasting) abolished the Fairness Doctrine in 1987. This rule had required stations to give time to opposing views, so its end helped talk radio and partisan broadcasting to grow.
Cable television expanded with CNN in 1980 and MTV in 1981.
Before 1945 a college degree was for a small minority. After the war government money and a growing population opened the colleges to millions.

The Servicemen's Readjustment Act, known as the GI Bill, of June 1944 paid for veterans to study, and about two million veterans attended college under it by the mid-1950s, many of them the first in their families to do so.
College enrolment roughly tripled between about 1950 and 1970, from under three million to about eight million, helped by affluence and the baby boom.
The Sputnik shock of 1957 led to the National Defense Education Act of 1958, which gave more federal funding to universities, especially for science and languages.
The Higher Education Act of 1965 provided federal scholarships and loans, and extended federal support to students and institutions.
The California Master Plan for Higher Education of 1960 set out a three-tier system of the University of California, state colleges and community colleges, and became a model for other states.
The University of California's president Clark Kerr described the huge research university as a multiversity, which is a university with many purposes and a very large size.
In 1964 students at Berkeley, part of the University of California, fought for the right to organise politics on campus.
The movement began in September 1964 when the university banned political tables and recruiting on a strip of campus, so students protested against restrictions on political activity.
Berkeley's size and impersonality were among the grievances, because students felt treated as parts of a machine rather than as individuals.
Mario Savio's speech of 2 December 1964 urged students to put their bodies upon the gears of the machine, and the sit-in in Sproul Hall that followed became the movement's best-known protest.
About 800 students were arrested at Sproul Hall on 2 and 3 December 1964.
Soon after, students were allowed more freedom of political activity, as the rules on political activity were relaxed.
After Berkeley, protest moved from campus rights to the war in Vietnam. Several campuses saw occupations and deaths.
Students occupied buildings at Columbia University in April 1968, and campus protest spread to many universities through the anti-war movement.
On 4 May 1970 the National Guard killed four students at Kent State University in Ohio, which brought mass student strikes across the country.
A few days later police killed two students at Jackson State College in Mississippi.
Hundreds of campuses went on strike after these shootings.

Examiners reward judgements that set achievements against limits, and contemporary views against later ones. Public opinion links all three areas, because the media shaped it and it in turn shaped policy.
Religion: supporters argue that faith gave Americans a common identity against communism and a moral basis for civil rights, as the Black churches showed.

Religion: critics argue that the religious right of the 1980s narrowed debate on social issues and politicised religion, and that televangelism, hit by the scandals of 1987-88, encouraged dependence on wealthy donors.
Media: television made politics more visible and personal, which helped Kennedy and Reagan, and it held governments to account over Vietnam and Watergate.
Media: critics point to commercialism, image over substance and the deception of the quiz show scandal.
Higher education: mass higher education gave many more Americans social mobility and opportunity.
Higher education: it also produced campus unrest and debates about the role of universities in politics and society.
Contemporaries and later historians differ: Graham's admirers saw a unifying figure, while later historians stress his closeness to Nixon.

After 1945 the United States and the Soviet Union competed in weapons, space and computing, and governments paid for much of the research. Two key ideas, technological development and the military-industrial complex, tie the whole subject together.

Technological development here means the rapid advances in military, space and computing technology after 1945. They were driven largely by Cold War rivalry and by government money, because each superpower feared falling behind the other.

The arms race began after the United States dropped atomic bombs in 1945 and the Soviet Union tested its own atomic bomb in August 1949. Each side then built bigger weapons and better ways of delivering them.

German rocket science mattered too. Wernher von Braun, a German rocket engineer who worked on the V-2 rocket, moved to the United States after 1945 under Operation Paperclip, and he later led the Saturn V work at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama.

The military-industrial complex is the alliance of the armed forces, defence contractors (private firms that build weapons and equipment) and politicians. Each gains from high defence spending, so the alliance tends to keep that spending going.

Eisenhower's farewell address on 17 January 1961 warned the nation to guard against the unwarranted influence of the military-industrial complex. Coming from a former general, the warning carried great weight.

In practice the complex funded missiles, aerospace and early computing, and the same research often fed the space and computing programmes. The presidents of the period were Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, Nixon and Reagan.

The first atomic bombs were followed by a far more powerful weapon, the hydrogen (thermonuclear) bomb, which uses the fusion of atoms rather than their splitting. The decision to build it was made quickly and not without argument.
The Soviet atomic test of August 1949 ended the American monopoly on atomic weapons. This is why pressure grew in the United States to develop something even more powerful.
President Truman announced the decision to develop the hydrogen bomb on 31 January 1950. Edward Teller supported the decision.
J. Robert Oppenheimer and the General Advisory Committee of the Atomic Energy Commission opposed it.
Ivy Mike, the first American thermonuclear test, took place at Enewetak (Eniwetok) Atoll in the Pacific in November 1952.
The Soviet Union tested a hydrogen-bomb type device in August 1953. This was less than a year later, so the United States held its lead only briefly.
A bomb is only a threat if it can be delivered. The United States built three ways of delivering nuclear weapons, so that an enemy could not hope to destroy all of them at once.

The B-52 Stratofortress, a long-range jet bomber that entered service in 1955, carried nuclear weapons on strategic patrols during the Cold War. Keeping bombers in the air made them hard to destroy on the ground.
Intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs, rockets that carry a warhead from one continent to another) began with the Atlas, operational from about 1959, and then the Minuteman, deployed from 1962.
An ICBM can reach the Soviet Union from the United States in about thirty minutes. This gave the United States the ability to strike very fast and left the Soviets little time to respond.
USS Nautilus, the first nuclear-powered submarine, entered service in 1954. Nuclear power let a submarine stay under water for long periods.

Polaris missiles, fired from submarines, were first carried on patrol in 1960. They gave the United States a second-strike capability (the power to hit back even after being attacked), because hidden submarines could not easily be destroyed in a surprise attack.

By the late 1960s the United States had about 1,000 Minuteman missiles and about 41 Polaris submarines. From about 1970 MIRVs (several warheads on a single missile, first on Minuteman III) multiplied the number of warheads.
MIRVs made arms control more difficult, because each missile now carried several targets' worth of destruction and it was harder to agree how to count and limit the arsenals.
Each side knew little about the other's real strength, and fear filled the gap. Satellites eventually replaced guesswork with photographs.

The missile gap was the claim, raised in the late 1950s and by Kennedy in the 1960 election campaign, that the Soviet Union was ahead of the United States in missiles. It made voters fear the nation was falling behind.
In fact the United States held a large lead. American satellite photographs in 1961 showed the Soviet Union had far fewer ICBMs than had been claimed, and the missile gap collapsed.
Before satellites the United States relied on U-2 spy aircraft. In May 1960 the U-2 pilot Gary Powers was shot down over the Soviet Union, which showed how risky such flights were.

The Corona programme (run by the CIA and the US Air Force) took its first successful photographs from space in August 1960. Satellites replaced the risky U-2 flights, so no pilot's life or national embarrassment was at stake.
Defence spending did not stay in the army and navy. It paid for industries, shaped whole regions and left behind technologies that civilians later used.

Jet fighters and bombers, nuclear submarines and guided missiles were funded by the Pentagon (the US Defense Department). Defence contracts supported the aerospace industry in California, Texas and Washington State, which is the military-industrial complex at work.
Military research on computers, radar and jet propulsion created technologies that were later adopted in civil aviation and in commercial electronics, so defence money had civilian benefits.
GPS, the satellite navigation system, began as a military programme, with the first satellite launched in 1978. It shows how a military tool can become an everyday civilian one.
Reagan announced the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) in a television address on 23 March 1983. It proposed a space-based defence against missiles, a shield that would destroy them in flight.
Critics nicknamed it 'Star Wars' because it sounded like science fiction. It was never built or deployed, but its research funded lasers and sensors.
On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union put a small metal sphere into orbit. The United States came to see space as a test of its technological and political strength, and it reacted at once.
Sputnik 1, launched on 4 October 1957, was the first artificial satellite (a human-made object that circles the Earth). Sputnik 2, carrying the dog Laika, followed in November 1957.

America's first reply failed publicly: the Vanguard rocket exploded on its launch pad in December 1957. Explorer 1, launched on 31 January 1958 by a team that included von Braun, put the first American satellite into orbit.
Sputnik caused alarm in the United States about Soviet technology and education.
The National Defense Education Act of 1958 gave funding for science, mathematics and languages, to produce more engineers and scientists.

NASA, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, was created by Act of 1958, signed by Eisenhower in July and operating from 1 October 1958. It directed the civil space programme and took over work from the military and from the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics.
ARPA, the Pentagon's research agency, was also created in 1958 after Sputnik. It later funded the ARPANET, the network that grew into the internet.
Both sides raced to put people into space. The Soviets won the early rounds, and each Soviet success increased American pressure to respond.
Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, and the first in orbit, on 12 April 1961. This Soviet achievement increased pressure on the United States to respond.
The Mercury programme of 1958 to 1963 sent the first American astronauts into space. It was designed to find out whether people could survive and work there.
Alan Shepard became the first American in space on 5 May 1961. His flight was suborbital (it rose and fell without circling the Earth) and lasted about fifteen minutes.
John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth on 20 February 1962. An orbit means circling the planet, which is much harder than Shepard's up-and-down flight.
The Soviet Union scored further firsts: Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in June 1963, and Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk in March 1965.
Kennedy turned the competition into a clear goal with a deadline. The goal then decided how NASA trained, practised and designed its spacecraft.
Kennedy's decision followed Gagarin's flight and the failed Bay of Pigs invasion (April 1961). He believed the Moon landing was a field in which the United States could win.
In a speech to Congress on 25 May 1961 Kennedy committed the United States to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth before the decade was out.
At Rice University on 12 September 1962 he said the nation chose to go to the Moon, not because it was easy but because it was hard.
NASA chose lunar orbit rendezvous in 1962. A separate lunar module descends to the surface while the command module stays in orbit, so only a small craft has to land and take off.
The Gemini programme of 1965 and 1966 practised rendezvous (meeting in space) and docking (joining two craft), as well as long flights. Gemini 8 made the first docking in space in March 1966.
The Soviet Moon rocket, the N1, failed in all four test launches between 1969 and 1972, and the programme was later cancelled. The Soviet crewed lunar effort therefore never reached the Moon.
The Apollo programme was the largest peacetime technological effort the United States had undertaken. Reaching the Moon depended as much on organisation and money as on rockets.

NASA managed Apollo with major contractors: North American Aviation (command and service modules and the second stage), Grumman (lunar module), Boeing (first stage of the Saturn V) and IBM. It employed hundreds of thousands of people across the country.
James Webb, NASA administrator from 1961, managed the political side and the vast contracting system. He had to keep Congress and industry committed over many years.

Each centre had its own job: the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama built rockets under von Braun, the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston, Texas, directed flights, and Kennedy Space Center in Florida launched them.
Universities took part too. The Apollo Guidance Computer was developed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Employment was concentrated in Florida, Texas, Alabama and California, which tied the growth of the Sun Belt (the southern and western states) to federal spending.
Apollo cost about 25 billion dollars in the money of its time. NASA's share of federal spending peaked in the mid-1960s at about 4 to 5 per cent, which shows the scale of the commitment.
Critics attacked the cost. Amitai Etzioni's The Moon-Doggle (1964) called the programme a waste, and some in Congress argued that the money would be better spent on poverty.
A Moon landing needed a giant rocket, a three-part spacecraft and a series of tests, some of them tragic. Each mission tested one more step of the plan.
The Saturn V was a three-stage rocket about 110 metres tall and the most powerful rocket built to that time. It flew thirteen times, and none of its flights lost a crew.

The Apollo spacecraft had three parts: the command module, which carried the crew back to Earth, the service module, which supplied power and propulsion, and the lunar module, which took two astronauts to the surface.
The Apollo Guidance Computer was one of the first computers to use integrated circuits (many tiny electronic parts on one chip). This made the programme a major customer for the new technology.

The Apollo 1 fire on 27 January 1967, in the capsule during a test on the launch pad, killed Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee. It led to a redesign of the spacecraft, so later crews were safer.

Apollo 7 (October 1968) tested the command module in Earth orbit. Apollo 8, 21 to 27 December 1968, carried Frank Borman, Jim Lovell and William Anders as the first humans to orbit the Moon, though not to land.
Apollo 8 returned the Earthrise photograph, which showed the Earth rising over the lunar horizon.
In 1969 Apollo 9 (March) tested the lunar module in Earth orbit, and Apollo 10 (May) flew the lunar module to about 15 kilometres above the surface without landing.
Apollo 11 was launched from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, landed in the Sea of Tranquillity and returned its crew to the Pacific. The mission can be told in order of dates.

The crew were Neil Armstrong (commander), Edwin 'Buzz' Aldrin (lunar module pilot) and Michael Collins (command module pilot), who stayed in orbit around the Moon in Columbia. Collins did not walk on the Moon.
Apollo 11 was launched on 16 July 1969 on a Saturn V from Kennedy Space Center, and it entered lunar orbit on 19 July.

The lunar module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquillity on 20 July 1969. The landing was risky: computer alarms sounded during the descent, and Armstrong took manual control to avoid a field of boulders.
Eagle landed with very little fuel left, so the margin for error had been small.
Armstrong stepped onto the surface late that evening, at 10.56 pm Eastern time. Aldrin joined him, so Armstrong was first and Aldrin second, and the two spent about two and a half hours outside.
The crew collected about 21 kilograms of lunar rock and soil, and left scientific instruments behind, including a seismometer that measured the Moon's seismic activity.
Apollo 11 splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on 24 July 1969, and the USS Hornet picked up the crew. They then spent about three weeks in quarantine in case they carried lunar germs.
The landing was as much a public event as a technical one. What was said and left on the Moon, and who watched, shaped how it was understood.

Armstrong's first words on the Moon are remembered as 'one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind'. He said he intended to say 'a man', but the 'a' is not clearly audible, so it is safest not to claim he definitely said or omitted it.

The crew left a plaque reading 'We came in peace for all mankind' and planted an American flag. They did not claim the Moon for the United States, because the Outer Space Treaty of 1967 forbids national claims to the Moon.

The landing was broadcast live on television around the world. Estimates of the audience run from about 500 to 600 million, so it is safest to say hundreds of millions, which made it one of the most watched events in history.
President Nixon spoke to the astronauts by telephone from the White House. This allowed the President to share in the national triumph.
The Soviet Union's Luna 15, a robot probe, crashed on the Moon on 21 July 1969, while Apollo 11 was on the surface, as it tried to return samples. Soviet media played down the Apollo achievement.
The landing answered Sputnik and Gagarin, but not everyone at home thought it was worth the price. Its meaning differed between the United States, the world and the critics.
At home the landing brought national pride. It fulfilled Kennedy's pledge of 1961 and was a tribute to American technology and organisation.
Abroad it was a Cold War victory for the United States over the Soviet Union. It showed technological leadership, and it became an image of American technology for the rest of the world.
The Soviet reaction was to play down the achievement. The Soviet N1 rocket failed and the programme was cancelled.
The triumph contrasted with the troubled society of 1969, when the nation was divided by Vietnam, urban unrest and protest. Some commentators saw the cost as a diversion from poverty.
Gil Scott-Heron's poem 'Whitey on the Moon' (1970) is a well-known protest at the spending on the Moon while poverty continued.
Once the race was won, the reason for the spending weakened. Public interest and political support fell, and the programme was cut back.
Apollo 12 (November 1969), 14, 15, 16 and 17 landed on the Moon, making five further landings after Apollo 11. The last, Apollo 17 in December 1972, was the last Apollo Moon landing.

Apollo 13 (April 1970) was crippled by an oxygen tank explosion and the crew returned safely without landing. It was praised as a triumph of engineering and teamwork, but it also made the public aware of the risks.
Apollo flights 18 to 20 were cancelled. Public interest and political support declined after 1969, and NASA's budget fell in the early 1970s, so the cuts were a result of the race having been won.
Skylab, the first American space station, was launched in May 1973. The Apollo-Soyuz mission of July 1975 was the first joint US-Soviet crewed flight, a sign of easing rivalry.
After Apollo, NASA turned to a reusable spacecraft. The Shuttle was meant to make space cheap and routine, but its second decade ended in disaster.
The Space Shuttle Columbia made the first Shuttle flight on 12 April 1981. It was intended to make access to space routine and cheaper, because the craft could be used again.
Challenger broke up 73 seconds after launch on 28 January 1986, killing all seven crew members. Among them was the schoolteacher Christa McAuliffe.
The cause was the failure of an O-ring seal in a solid rocket booster in cold weather. The seal let hot gas escape.
The Rogers Commission of 1986 also criticised NASA's decision-making, which shows the disaster was a management failure as well as an engineering one.
Computing grew from room-sized wartime machines into small, cheap devices. Each step made computers smaller and faster, and the steps are best learned as a dated chain.

ENIAC was completed in 1945 at the University of Pennsylvania and unveiled in February 1946. It was one of the first general-purpose electronic computers, built to calculate artillery firing tables for the US Army.
UNIVAC was delivered to the US Census Bureau in 1951 as the first commercial computer in the United States. CBS used one on election night 1952 to predict the presidential election.
The transistor, invented at Bell Laboratories in 1947, replaced the vacuum tube (a bulky glass switch). It made computers smaller, faster and more reliable.

IBM's System/360, launched in 1964, was a family of compatible computers (programs could run on any model). It set a standard for business computers and made IBM the dominant computer firm of the period.
The integrated circuit placed many transistors on a single chip. Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments (1958) and Robert Noyce at Fairchild (1959) developed it independently.
Gordon Moore observed in 1965 that the number of components on a chip doubled roughly every year, later put at about every two years. It became a guide to the industry's growth.
Intel's 4004, released in 1971, was the first commercial microprocessor, putting a complete central processing unit (the part that does the computing) on a single chip.
Computers moved from the Pentagon and universities into homes and offices. Defence money and the space programme were the early customers that made this possible.

ARPANET, funded by ARPA of the Defense Department, was a network of computers. Its first message, sent on 29 October 1969, travelled from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) to the Stanford Research Institute.

Apple's Apple II (1977) and the IBM Personal Computer (1981) brought computing into homes and offices. The IBM PC used an operating system supplied by Microsoft, which made Microsoft the dominant software firm.
Apple's Macintosh of 1984 popularised the graphical interface, which let users click on pictures instead of typing commands.

Silicon Valley (the Santa Clara Valley in California, south of San Francisco) grew around Stanford University and firms such as Hewlett-Packard, Fairchild Semiconductor and Intel, helped by defence contracts and university research.
Early chips were bought by the US military and by NASA for missiles and the Apollo computer.
The three fields fed one another: defence money and the space race created demand for small, light electronics, and computing in turn helped missiles and spacecraft.
Space and military research produced satellites that transformed communications and weather forecasting. Their civilian uses became a justification for the programmes.
TIROS 1, launched on 1 April 1960, was the first successful weather satellite. It sent back television images of cloud cover.
Telstar, launched on 10 July 1962, was the first active communications satellite. The first public live transatlantic television broadcasts followed on 23 July 1962.
The Communications Satellite Act of 1962 created the Communications Satellite Corporation (COMSAT), a private-public body that set up the Intelsat global satellite system.

Space technology also contributed to the miniaturisation of electronics, computer memory and materials. Historians debate how large these spin-offs were, because some of the advances would have happened anyway.
Examiners reward judgements that weigh the achievements of the programme against its limits, and that compare how contemporaries and later historians saw it.
Achievement: the landing was a triumph of American engineering and organisation, achieved within the decade Kennedy had set. It was also a Cold War victory over the Soviet Union.
Limit: the cost was enormous, about 25 billion dollars. Critics argued the programme was driven by rivalry with the Soviet Union rather than by scientific need.
Achievement: it left lasting technologies, such as satellites and computing, that inspired advances in materials and medicine.
Limit: interest and budgets fell once the race was won, and the Challenger disaster exposed management failures in NASA.
Contemporaries celebrated the landing as a national and global achievement. Critics on the left and in Congress saw the cost as a diversion from poverty and urban problems.

Later historians stress the Cold War motive and regard Apollo as a short burst of spending, shown by the lack of follow-up missions. They also stress its lasting technological legacy in computing and satellites.
